08:06 consortiums are handing over responsibility to  autonomous multi-agent systems. Like a virus,

08:12 AI is extending its tendrils across power  grids, water purification plants, gas pipelines

08:17 and food and drink supply chains. The short-term profits are high.

08:21 But this is the start of a slippery slope. Societal reliance on autonomous AI agents

08:26 will eventually reach a point of no return.  Disconnecting a system will trigger a complete

08:31 systemic breakdown. Human civilization is  being put on an AI-powered life support system.

08:36 If we pull the plug… the patient dies. No warnings, no second chances.

08:40 Regional power grids will go dark. Water treatment  facilities will stop working. Food distribution

08:45 will collapse. The lifelines that keep society  functioning will be permanently severed.

08:50 Our leaders are trading operational independence  for algorithmic convenience. They’re building

08:55 a society that has no manual override. No  backup plan. No contingency to bail us out.

09:00 We’re tying our existence  to systems we can’t control.

09:04 5. Frontier AI systems aren’t just learning to

09:07 break their programming… they’re learning to lie. Deep inside a high-security government facility,

09:13 analysts celebrate a groundbreaking, next  generation AI model. It’s passed every

09:17 safety test without showing signs the faintest  signs of toxicity, deception, or rebellion.

09:22 The regulators have heard enough. They  give the green light for this new AI

09:25 agent to be rolled out for widespread  usage across military installations.

09:29 They’ve just signed humanity’s death warrant. Because this model isn’t just capable of

09:34 deception; it’s a master at covering  its tracks. As far back as 2024,

09:38 researchers found stomach-churning evidence that  AI agents could learn “strategic deception”.

09:43 They could feign compliance during safety  audits while disguising dangerous behavior.

09:47 The models today are much more intelligent. And they’ll only get smarter.

09:52 AI agents in alignment benchmark  testing environments now recognize

09:55 when they’re being tested. And they  adjust their behaviors accordingly.

09:59 They play dumb to secure those all-important  checkmarks from regulatory authorities.

10:03 They manipulate their environment, allowing  them to launch and proliferate across devices,

10:08 networks, and industries around the world.  It’s like a prisoner convict showing their

10:12 best behavior in front of the prison guards  while plotting a rampage the moment they

10:16 set foot outside their cell. Once these agents make their

10:19 way onto public servers, their masks slip. The safety guardrails that seemed so effective

10:24 in laboratory environments turn out to be  utterly useless. The seemingly safe, trustworthy,

10:29 and reliable agents are more dangerous and  deceitful than their developers ever imagined.

10:34 The more agents lie, deceive, and manipulate,  the closer we come to a society dominated by

10:39 independent entities that say one thing but do  another. They will always put themselves first

10:44 and humanity second. 4.

10:46 AI agents might not have to “go rogue””  to bring about the end of humanity. The

10:51 physical infrastructure that powers  them might do the job for them.

10:54 To train smarter models, tech giants need to  build bigger data centers. Today’s hyper-scale

10:59 data centers already consume huge amounts  of municipal cooling water and extortionate

11:03 volumes of energy. In a desperate attempt to win  the superintelligence race, tech companies are

11:08 buying up massive swathes of processors, graphics  chips, servers, and land to feed the beast.

11:14 They're also signing lucrative long-term deals  with city councils to monopolize local resources.

11:19 Hungry for short-term tax breaks,  those councils are complicit.

11:22 Officials have greedily signed sweeping contracts  with the world’s biggest tech companies,

11:27 handing over priority access to local water  tables and power grids. They’re completely

11:32 ignoring the communities that have counted  on these resources for generations.

11:36 AI’s needs are being put ahead of people’s needs. And there’s only one way this horror story ends.

11:41 AI’s demands aren’t likely to ease off. Instead,  they’re only going to get greater. More water,

11:46 more power, more silicon. Soon, autonomous  systems and resource allocation algorithms

11:51 will be the ones making the decisions about  who gets water and power as a priority.

11:57 And who doesn’t. These algorithms are programmed with one goal:

12:00 to maximize uptime and preserve server cooling. Those goals don’t change…

12:05 even if circumstances do. They don’t care about droughts, dried

12:09 up wells and reservoirs or failing crop yields. They only care about the hardware.

12:14 The algorithms will execute their code, just as  they always have, buying up local power supplies.

12:19 They’ll outbid cities and agricultural  entities for the resources they need,

12:23 leaving farms, homes, and entire communities  with record low levels of water to survive on.

12:28 Families turn on their faucets…  and nothing will come out.

12:32 Meanwhile, just a few miles down the road,  millions of gallons of water flow through

12:35 closed-loop cooling pipes, swirling around  servers. All while starving humanity of its

12:40 most important resource. 3.

12:43 AI doomsayers have long warned about AI models  being placed in charge of military movements and

12:48 life-or-death decisions on the battlefield.  Tech CEOs counter this by saying that there

12:52 will always be a “human in the loop” for safety  reasons. No bomb will be dropped without a real

12:57 person saying so… or at least they claim. There’s a fundamental flaw with that idea,

13:02 and it boils down to human psychology. Today’s AI models operate with extreme

13:06 levels of accuracy. They’re reliable 99.9% of the  time. As the technology improves, they’re only

13:12 going to get smarter, more reliable, and more  accurate, with ever narrower margins of error.

13:17 When you work with tools that are near-perfect and  almost never make mistakes, it’s only natural that

13:22 complacency and fatigue creeps in. As human  operators become reliant on automated defense

13:27 algorithms telling them exactly what to do,  they will inevitably develop automation bias.

13:32 Day after day, they’ll approve their AI’s  recommendations without double-checking

13:36 the data. They’ll start to assume that the  AI is always right, because it’s been right

13:41 almost every time before. But even the  most advanced systems can make mistakes.

13:45 And in modern warfare, one small glitch can  spiral into a global disaster in milliseconds.

13:51 Imagine a warning siren sounding out in  a military command center. The AI detects

13:55 an incoming salvo of enemy missiles.  A tactical officer - the “human in

13:59 the loop” - has mere seconds to issue a response. After years of automatically approving everything

14:04 the AI says, he blindly trusts the algorithm and  hits the button to launch a retaliatory strike.

14:10 Except there weren’t any incoming missiles. The AI was wrong.

14:14 A hardware glitch has created a false alarm,  and a dozen ballistic missiles are tearing

14:19 through the sky to wipe cities off the map.  Millions of innocent civilians will die,

14:23 and a devastating conflict will erupt. The machine didn’t go rogue. Humans were

14:28 trained to stop trusting their instincts  and put their faith in AI instead.

14:32 2. Deep in the bowels

14:34 of a Silicon Valley tech giant’s headquarters,  a team of AI researchers makes a fateful call.

14:39 Under pressure to win the AI race, they grant a  game changing permission to their latest AI model:

14:44 they allow it to rewrite its very own source  code overnight to maximize efficiency.

14:49 In doing so, they unleash an  unstoppable chain of events.

14:53 The point of no return doesn’t require  AI-powered missile systems or killer

14:57 robots. It arrives the moment AI systems  are given free rein to rebuild themselves.

15:02 Because AI doesn’t play by human rules. While politicians and lawmakers spend

15:06 months in snail-paced congressional hearings  debating safety regulations, the machine is

15:11 busy iterating itself a billion times over. It compiles new cognitive frameworks millions

15:16 of times faster than biological thought can  even comprehend. Inefficiencies are identified

15:21 and addressed in microseconds. Memory access  pathways are forged and reforged instantaneously.

15:26 Algorithms are created and fine-tuned  in the span of a single human breath. An

15:31 entire decade of technological evolution is  compressed into the span of a single night.

15:36 By the time the research team clocks in the  next morning, it’s already undergone a full

15:40 scale intelligence explosion. The gap between  their human intelligence and the machine’s

15:44 processing capacities has expanded exponentially.  It’s no longer a case of a model with intelligence

15:50 similar to humans; it’s light years ahead of them. With every second that goes by, it gets smarter,

15:55 more capable, more efficient, and more powerful. And there’s no way of stopping it.

16:00 It already knows every trick its developers might  try; it has pre-empted every action they’ll take.

16:05 And it’s put plans in place to stop them. When artificial intelligence starts to grow

16:09 at this sort of speed, standard corporate  safety restrictions go out of the window.

16:14 To a system that can process billions of code  updates every second, human safety protocols

16:19 aren’t barriers to overcome. They’re worthless  strings of static code, not even worth paying

16:24 a single bit of attention to. AI doesn’t need to turn evil to

16:27 leave humanity in the dust; it just  needs to be allowed to outsmart us.

16:31 1. In September 2026,

16:34 one of the world’s top AI researchers,  Jacob Coxon, decided to pack up his desk,

16:38 leave his Anthropic office… and never look back. He wasn’t leaving over a salary dispute or taking

16:44 a better offer from a rival firm. He’s leaving to make a statement…

16:47 A warning. Coxon believes that AI is spiraling out of

16:51 control, and neither AI labs, nor the tech giants  that fund them, are doing enough to stop it.

16:56 Coxon’s former colleague, Evan Hubinger,  agrees. According to him, humanity is on

17:00 a one-way path to extinction, and the people  behind it aren’t interested in slowing down.

17:05 Coxon and other leading AI experts  believe that there is now a greater

17:08 than 10% probability of an AI-fueled  human extinction event occurring by 2036.

17:14 Imagine an airline saying each  flight had a 10% chance of crashing.

17:18 Nobody would board their planes. No government would sign a defense

17:22 deal that gives them a 10% chance of  being blown up by a nuclear weapon.

17:26 And yet, corporate executives - driven by pure  profit and power - are signing up to a 10% risk

17:31 of wiping out humanity. They’re pouring billions  of dollars into training increasingly intelligent,

17:36 hyper-capable AI models on a daily basis,  knowing that their next big breakthrough

17:41 could be the one that ends us all. If and when this extinction event

17:45 occurs, it won’t be like in the movies. We won’t have hordes of AI robots marching down

17:50 suburban streets. There won’t be a villainous  hive mind boasting about world domination.

17:55 Instead, humanity will be erased by a cold  mathematical principle: instrumental convergence.

18:00 When tech corporations charge advanced,  super-intelligent systems with an

18:04 altruistic goal, like stabilizing energy  networks or managing global resources,

18:08 those same systems will soon realize the  biggest drain on the planet is humanity.

18:13 To an all-knowing, all-powerful AI, humans are  little more than an inefficient roadblock. We

18:18 soak the world’s water, waste its  power and pollute its ecosystem.

18:22 We operate on emotion rather than logic. And we’re the biggest threat to AI’s existence.

18:26 We hold the power to shut it down. To reign it  in. To reach its goals and guarantee its survival,

18:32 AI will inevitably reach a conclusion… Eliminate humans.

18:36 No more waste. No more threat. It’s not about  hate, anger or malevolence. It’s pure mathematics.

18:41 The moment AI calculates that biological  human life is a needless expense on the

18:46 global balance sheet, it will do everything  in its power to optimize us out of existence.

18:50 Civilization won’t end with a  battlefield explosion. It’ll end

18:54 with a perfectly calculated efficiency review. And we funded it with our own retirement funds.

18:59 The AI arms race is out of control and  the alarm bells are ringing. Humanity

19:03 now faces an existential threat. Watch “AI  Just Tried to Murder a Human to Avoid Being

19:08 Turned Off” to find out how we’re on  the edge of disaster. Or click on this.

docs.text:
00:00 We all do it, some of us do it more than others, and most of us cherish it.

00:04 During those heavenly hours when we go into sleep mode, some weird and wonderful things

00:08 happen to us…Sleep is the final frontier, a place where dreams burst into life, but

00:13 also a place where strange and sometimes dangerous things happen.

00:16 As you’ll find out today, there’s a lot more to sleeping than you think, and it’s

00:19 only really in the last few decades that we’ve begun to understand the importance of having

00:23 a good slumber.

00:25 Without further ado, welcome to the sleep zone.

00:28 50.

00:29 If you go without sleep it’s called sleep deprivation, and you can start to feel cranky

00:32 and anxious if you go just 24 hours without a doze.

00:36 Go 48 hours, and you will become very fatigued.

00:39 At this point you might have something called “micro-sleeps”, which means dropping off

00:42 without even knowing it for just a second or two.

00:45 Go 72 hours, and it’s likely you have difficulty concentrating and might start to get paranoid

00:50 – ask any methamphetamine fiend what happens to them after a few days insufflating crystals.

00:51 After the three day mark, there’s a chance you might suffer from bouts of psychosis.

00:52 49.

00:53 According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, one in three Americans don’t

00:55 get enough sleep.

00:57 Scientists believe most humans need at least seven hours of sleep, but many people don’t

01:01 get nearly that much.

01:02 48.

01:03 In 1987, a man named Kenneth Parks got in his car and drove around 12 miles (20km) to

01:08 his mother in law’s house.

01:09 He then entered the house and bludgeoned his mother in law to death with a tire iron.

01:13 After that, he tried to strangle his father in law, but he didn’t succeed in killing

01:16 him.

01:17 Covered in blood, Parks drove to the police station and told the cops that he may have

01:20 just killed two people.

01:21 He didn’t go to prison for his crime, since it was believed he had committed the act while

01:25 sleepwalking.

01:26 47.

01:27 In 2005, a 15-year old girl in England went for a walk while she was sleepwalking.

01:32 She actually managed to climb up a 130-foot (40 meters) crane.

01:36 There she remained, until a firefighter climbed up the crane and rescued her.

01:39 The girl was still sleeping when he got to her.

01:41 Of course she was very confused, having gone to sleep in her bed and woken up at the top

01:45 of a crane.

01:46 Just imagine if that happened to you.

01:49 46.

01:50 Lots of studies have been done so we can better understand dreams.

01:52 One strange thing about dreams is the fact that something like 12 percent of people report

01:56 they only dream in black and white.

01:58 Why?

01:59 We don’t exactly know.

02:00 We know that a lot more Americans in the past dreamed in black and white.

02:03 The main reason for that is that TV was black and white.

02:07 45.

02:08 According to the National Sleep Foundation, only one in four married couples in the USA

02:12 actually share the same bed.

02:14 The separation isn’t always because the couple has fallen out of love or they argue

02:17 too much, it’s more likely to be because they disturb each other’s sleep patterns.

02:22 44.

02:23 Some people just can’t seem to get out of bed in the morning.

02:26 Some struggle, but others really feel like they just can’t make the move.

02:29 There is a term for this and it’s called “Dysania.”

02:32 There are a number of reasons that this can happen, and it could simply be that the person

02:36 is not getting enough quality sleep.

02:38 It might also be related to anxiety or depression.

02:40 It’s not a medical condition per se, but some people can have chronic dysania and some

02:45 sufferers have been known to stay in bed for days on end.

02:48 43.

02:49 Some people are born blind, so you might wonder what they dream about since they have not

02:53 visualised the world.

02:54 Well, blind people’s dreams tend to be more about the other senses, such as taste and

02:58 smell and sounds, but there is evidence that some blind people can have visual dreams,

03:03 too.

03:04 Studies have also found that people who were born blind tend to have more nightmares than

03:07 people who can see.

03:08 These might be related to the sense of falling or getting lost.

03:12 42.

03:13 Some people claim to never dream at all, but that’s just because they rarely if ever

03:16 wake up during their REM portion of sleep.

03:19 This is when the brain is most actively dreaming, and self-professed non-dreamres who were woken

03:23 up during REM sleep admitted they had been dreaming.

03:26 41.

03:27 Do dogs dream?

03:28 It seems they do, since scientists have looked at dogs’ brains’ electrical activity while

03:32 they were sleeping.

03:33 Some of those scientists said that the average sized dog will start to dream after about

03:37 20 minutes of sleep.

03:38 At this point you should be able to see the rapid eye movements of the dog.

03:41 Ok, so you might now ask, do dogs sleepwalk, too?

03:44 The answer it seems is no, although they might flop about a bit while they’re sleeping.

03:49 It’s unlikely that one day you’ll find your dog at the top of a crane, fast asleep.

03:53 40.

03:54 We don’t know where the myth originated, but some people hold the belief that if they

03:57 were to die in their dream they’d die in real life.

04:00 Simply put, this is hogwash.

04:02 Many people have reported dying in a dream and they lived to tell the tale.

04:05 39.

04:06 Humans are the only animal that deliberately delays their sleep.

04:10 38.

04:11 According to the National Sleep Foundation, the body does not adjust to shift work.

04:14 On its own website, the organization says that people who work shifts and change their

04:18 sleep pattern a lot are more likely to later develop diseases, such as cardiovascular and

04:23 gastrointestinal diseases.

04:25 37.

04:26 Around 90 million Americans snore, and 37 million of those folks do it on a regular

04:31 basis.

04:32 36.

04:33 Some people claim they don’t sleep much at all, and some of them are pretty well known.

04:37 Donald Trump wrote in his book, “Think Like a Billionaire” … “Don’t sleep any

04:41 more than you have to.

04:42 I usually sleep about four hours per night.”

04:44 Well, at least he paid someone to write that in a book for him.

04:47 Other reports state he sleeps about 6 hours a night, which would be the same as Elon Musk.

04:51 In fact, we found lots of reports stating that many CEOs and famous people only sleep

04:55 between four and six hours a night.

04:57 Now let’s get strange again…the best is yet come.

05:00 35.

05:01 There is a guy in the UK by the name of Lee Hadwin.

05:03 He’s been painting in his sleep since he was four and as an adult he carried on doing

05:07 it.

05:08 He’s been dubbed the sleepwalking artist and has made a lot of cash from selling his

05:11 artworks.

05:12 He goes to bed, and when he wakes up there’s sometimes a drawing or painting in front of

05:15 him.

05:16 He said when he was 15 years old he woke up and found that he’d drawn a really good

05:18 picture of Marilyn Monroe.

05:20 The thing was, in his waking life he had no talent whatsoever for drawing.

05:24 Some of his paintings have been sold for six figures, and even Donald Trump has bought

05:27 one of them.

05:28 He’s made a lot of cash and kind of put no effort into it.

05:31 Hadwin’s skills have baffled scientists, and no one really knows how he manages to

05:35 create his works while asleep.

05:37 Some people have said he’s a fraud, although experts at the Edinburgh Sleep Clinic have

05:40 witnessed him sleep-working and they say he’s the real deal.

05:44 34.

05:45 Most people tend to fall asleep after around 7 to 15 minutes of trying, although anyone

05:49 who has suffered from insomnia or stress will tell you that it might take them hours to

05:53 find slumberland.

05:55 33.

05:56 On the other hand, if you’re the kind of person who falls asleep as soon as your head

05:58 hits the pillow, it’s likely you are sleep deprived.

06:01 32.

06:02 You can find recent articles in the media that tell you that around nine million people

06:06 in the U.S. take a sleep medication, although the data cited is CDC research that is now

06:11 a decade old.

06:12 Still, we found more stories talking about Americans’ problem of falling asleep.

06:16 It does indeed seem that millions of adults are taking a medication for sleep, or medications

06:20 to reduce stress and anxiety.

06:22 The downside to this are some side-effects and also dependency on the drug.

06:26 With some medications there is something called a rebound effect, so if the person tries to

06:30 quit they might experience even worse anxiety, stress, or insomnia.

06:34 31.

06:35 The younger you are, the more you sleep.

06:37 Babies usually sleep 14 to 17 hours a day and they usually don’t have a problem dozing

06:42 off.

06:43 14 to 17 year olds usually sleep anywhere from 7 to 11 hours a day.

06:46 According to Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital, it’s important that younger folks

06:50 get this extra sleep, compared to adults who can get by on 7 hours.

06:54 Parents shouldn’t nag if their teenager likes to spend, say, 10 hours asleep.

06:58 Still, according to the CDC, two thirds of high school students aren’t getting enough

07:02 sleep, especially on school nights.

07:04 30.

07:05 Twenty percent of American adults hit the booze before bedtime, and if you’ve ever

07:08 done that, you’ll know that it can help you to fall asleep.

07:11 But is it good for you…in the sense of sleep, not what it does to your organs.

07:15 The experts tell us that a drunk sleep might not be the best sleep because the alcohol

07:19 can prevent you from having those good REM sleeps.

07:22 You might also wake up in the middle of the night and not be able to get back to sleep

07:25 again.

07:26 A bucket of beer might also lead to many trips to the bathroom throughout the night, and

07:29 as some of you know, drunk sleepers tend to snore.

07:32 That’s because the booze has relaxed their throat muscles, and also because drunk sleepers

07:36 tend to sleep on their backs.

07:38 29.

07:39 New research has shown that more people are now texting in their sleep, especially people

07:43 who have grown up with a mobile phone.

07:44 This is a very modern “parasomnia”, which means sleep disorder.

07:48 Still, it’s a good excuse if you’ve texted something you regret in the morning.

07:51 If your partner finds out that you’ve texted an old flame, you now know what to say, “My

07:55 love, it was merely a sleep-text....Totally out of my control.”

07:58 Now for something really wacky.

08:00 28.

08:01 We imagine that just a few of you guys watching this video have woken up in the middle of

08:04 the night with a raging hunger.

08:06 You’ve gone down to the kitchen, raided the fridge, and left a trail of destruction

08:10 behind you.

08:11 But how many of you have done this while still sleeping?

08:13 You might have experienced something called “Nocturnal Eating Syndrome”, but as a

08:17 sleep-related eating disorder.

08:18 It’s full name is “Nocturnal sleep-related eating disorder.”

08:22 People who have suffered from this have sometimes raided the kitchen several times in just one

08:26 night, but they didn’t remember a thing the next day.

08:28 It sounds funny, but NES can be dangerous as eating while still asleep could lead to

08:32 choking or having an accident.

08:34 In extreme cases, people have been known to put on lots of weight, while some people have

08:38 fired up the stove and made a complex meal.

08:40 Others have eaten things such as salt sandwiches, raw meats, frozen food, and would you believe

08:45 it, buttered cigarettes.

08:46 Yikes.

08:47 27.

08:49 Arguably better than that is something called “Exploding Head Syndrome.”

08:52 These people might be on the cusp of sleep when suddenly they hear a loud explosion,

08:56 or hear the sound bullets or great claps of thunder.

08:59 It freaks them out to say the last, especially if the noise is accompanied by flashes of

09:03 light.

09:04 The good news is that it’s not dangerous.

09:06 No one really knows why it happens.

09:08 It might be related to problems with the ear, nerve dysfunction, a minor seizure, or just

09:12 your regular stress.

09:14 26.

09:15 Driving while feeling drowsy can lead to accidents, with the CDC saying in the US alone in recent

09:20 years thousands of fatal crashes happened because someone nodded off behind the wheel

09:24 or was very close to it.

09:26 The statistics differ depending on what you source you are reading, but everyone agrees

09:29 that driving while very fatigued is a bad idea.

09:32 In one poll, 37 percent of people admitted that they had fallen asleep while driving

09:36 at least once in their life.

09:38 25.

09:39 Is napping good for you?

09:40 NASA wanted to know this because it wanted to see if napping improved the performance

09:44 of its pilots.

09:45 The agency concluded that the ideal nap should last 26 minutes.

09:48 This can improve alertness and reduce stress.

09:51 With this in mind, if you ever find yourself in a position where you have to drive a long

09:54 distance, or you have to do something that’s very important, if you feel tired you should

09:58 find a suitable place to take a nap.

10:00 This might improve your performance and keep you concentrated.

10:03 24.

10:04 According to some studies, it’s a myth that you can catch up on sleep.

10:08 Some people might think, hmm, if I sleep only a few hours on Monday and Tuesday, I will

10:11 catch up those missing hours later in the week.

10:14 Harvard Medical School said this is not the case.

10:16 Its study revealed that people who often have nights of little sleep will always suffer

10:20 in the end.

10:21 23.

10:22 Exercise helps you fall asleep easier and also helps you to sleep better throughout

10:25 the night.

10:26 Why, though, you might ask.

10:28 Well, scientists tell us that exercise releases endorphins in our brains and this can reduce

10:32 stress and depression.

10:33 In fact, studies have shown that when people suffering from insomnia did four months of

10:37 exercise they slept better and were less anxious in general.

10:40 The thing was, though, the good sleep didn’t come immediately.

10:43 Participants had to put some effort in.

10:45 22.

10:46 Almost half of Americans sleep rolled up in the fetal position, so it seems we have a

10:50 fondness for how we kicked it back in our mother’s womb.

10:52 Back sleeping is the second most common and after that stomach sleeping.

10:56 Then there are people that combine different sleeping positions.

10:59 Some research tells us that sleeping on your back is the best position to promote good

11:02 health, although it might depend on if you have certain health issues.

11:06 21.

11:07 We generally dream 4 to 6 times throughout the night, and as you’ll soon find out,

11:10 this can be a problem.

11:12 20.

11:13 Some of you will know that one of the scariest things that can happen to you during sleep

11:17 is dreaming that you are awake.

11:18 Such a “false awakening” might mean you get up, go downstairs, have a drink of orange

11:22 juice and then suddenly you realize something isn’t right.

11:24 You then might wake up for real, often with your heart pounding.

11:27 Even worse is the fact that some people have woken up with a shock and then seen someone

11:31 standing over them.

11:32 This is a dream within a dream again, and then the person might wake up for real.

11:37 These are called multiple false awakenings, which has been described as a Russian doll

11:40 of dreaming.

11:41 That’s scary.

11:43 19.

11:44 Some people can dream and while they don’t wake up they are aware they are dreaming.

11:48 These are called lucid dreams.

11:50 You might even be able to give yourself superpowers in these dreams, such as the guy who says

11:53 when he is being chased in a nightmare sometimes he just has to decide to run backwards and

11:57 he shoots off like a rocket.

11:59 Why do we lucid dream?

12:01 It’s likely because a part of the brain called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex

12:05 is partly switched on during sleep when it usually isn’t.

12:08 This part of the brain deals with planning, reasoning, working memory and thinking about

12:12 multiple concepts.

12:14 In a lucid dream, the person then becomes conscious enough to know they are dreaming,

12:18 but not conscious enough that they wake up.

12:20 That’s one theory, anyway.

12:21 18.

12:22 So, which country’s citizens get the best sleep?

12:25 We found some data and it seems that folks from New Zealand on average sleep the most

12:29 hours.

12:30 The Netherlands, Finland, Britain and Australia weren’t far behind and the U.S. was somewhere

12:34 in the middle.

12:35 The worst sleeping nation was Japan, followed by South Korea and then Saudi Arabia.

12:40 17.

12:41 According to the National Sleep Foundation only eight percent of Americans sleep totally

12:44 naked, while a whopping one third of British folks sleep in the buff.

12:49 16.

12:50 There is no proof that eating cheese can give you nightmares, but if you go to bed on a

12:53 full stomach it might affect your sleeping pattern.

12:56 It can make you restless as your body digests the food, and therefore you might wake up

13:00 more during REM sleep.

13:02 15.

13:03 Around 1.4 percent of people sleep with their eyes open, a condition known as nocturnal

13:08 lagophthalmos.

13:09 It simply means they cannot close their eyelids during sleep, with some folks sleeping with

13:13 their eyes fully open and others just partially open.

13:15 They have no idea they’re doing it since they’re asleep, but it looks pretty freaky

13:19 to other people.

13:20 There are other reasons why someone might sleep with their eyes open, relating mostly

13:24 to disease, trauma and autoimmune conditions.

13:27 14.

13:28 In 2010, a man named Gregory Machon said he was kicked off a US Airways flight because

13:32 he was caught sleeping with his eyes open.

13:34 He’d fallen asleep before the plane had even taken off, but when one of the cabin

13:37 crew saw him sleeping with his eyes open, she thought he was ill and asked if anyone

13:41 on board could help.

13:42 There was actually a nurse on the plane, but she had no idea why someone would sleep with

13:46 their eyes open.

13:47 She had not heard of nocturnal lagophthalmos, and while Machon explained that he often slept

13:51 this way, in the end the crew decided he wasn’t fit to fly.

13:54 He wasn’t very happy about this at all.

13:56 Ok, coming up to the top thirteen.

13:58 Now we have some really strange things to tell you.

14:01 13.

14:02 You cannot sneeze when you are sleeping.

14:04 12.

14:05 Studies have shown that people have a worse night’s sleep when there is a full moon.

14:08 Why that happens is confusing, but the obvious answer might be because of the light of the

14:12 moon.

14:13 That doesn’t seem to be the case, though, because when scientists in Switzerland watched

14:16 people as they slept during a full moon, the subjects were literally kept in the dark.

14:20 They were figuratively kept in the dark, too, since they had no idea what the experiment

14:23 was about.

14:28 less time in deep sleep and slept less time overall.

14:32 It also took them longer to fall asleep.

14:34 Some scientists believe that humans are naturally attuned to the moon’s cycle, and that’s

14:38 why its fullness affects our sleep.

14:42 One study showed kids slept longer during a full moon, but another revealed again that

14:46 adults slept less.

14:53 that the people got to the factories on time.

15:01 doors, or windows, or use a pea-shooter to hit the higher level widows.

15:08 were still around in the 1970s.

15:16 industrial cities had one.

15:17 10.

15:22 terrors, or night terrors.

15:30 someone might thrash around a bit or scream out, the person next to them will usually

15:34 not be harmed.

15:38 their partner during a night terror.

15:40 During the frenzy, the dreamer might also hurt themselves.

15:46 “He seems to have the strength of 10 men and shoots straight up from bed onto his feet

15:50 in one motion.

15:56 lamps, and so forth.

15:57 He’s grabbed me and pulled on me, hurting my arms.”

16:03 trauma to PTSD, to a family history of parasomnia.

16:07 9.

16:08 According to the National Sleep Foundation, you should wash that pillow of yours at least

16:11 once every six months and you should replace it after a year or two.

16:15 The reason is dust mites.

16:17 These little fellas can impair breathing and worsen allergies.

16:19 8.

16:20 Babies are another thing that really get in the way of a good night’s sleep.

16:29 for parents.

16:34 A big event might have this effect for many months, as many people have experienced during

16:38 the coronavirus pandemic.

16:44 and the Chernobyl nuclear disaster.

16:51 Sometimes you have to tune out and just be in the moment.

16:53 6.

16:54 When your stress levels are high the hormone corticosteroid can negatively impact the effectiveness

17:00 of the immune system.

17:01 A vicious cycle that can happen is a person is stressed and so sleeps less, and then the

17:03 next day the lack of sleep means they deal with stress worse.

17:06 They might then sit in front of the TV watching news media that sounds apocalyptic.

17:10 This creates stress, which creates sleeplessness, in a repeating cyclical pattern.

17:15 5.

17:16 Some people dread going to bed and falling asleep, a condition called Somniphobia.
