docs.title: YouTube Transcript: The Pentagon Just Declassified 50 UFO Encounters
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: The Pentagon Just Declassified 50 UFO Encounters
  • Video ID: 0UvrxfAgu48
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 The Pentagon didn’t just release UFO files…  it released proof of things that shouldn’t

00:05 be possible. These aren’t rumors or  leaks. tThey’re documented encounters

00:09 the Pentagon still can’t explain. And the most unsettling part?

00:13 These are the things they want you to see. 50.

00:18 In September, 2023, the FBI was trying to  understand what a drone operator at a U.S

00:23 site had just seen. In a declassified video the  man explains that he and his colleagues had all

00:28 witnessed a “bright light over the horizon.” Surrounded by a dazzling glow the object was,

00:34 quote, “metallic gray”, “linear” about “one  to two Blackhawk helicopters in length and

00:40 definitely bigger than a drone”. It looked  like a vehicle of some kind but had no exhaust

00:44 or wings. It hovered at about 5,000 feet  (15,24 meters), moved from east to west,

00:49 and then, within 5 to 10 seconds, it was gone. It freaked the man out, but that night a storm

00:54 battered the town. He was still on edge as  he sat in his hotel room, when suddenly his

00:59 TV went black. He told the FBI for the next 2  nights he could barely sleep and when he did,

01:04 his mind was tormented with strange dreams. Had he made contact?

01:09 To better understand, let’s go back to when all  this talk of UFOs in the USA first got off the

01:15 ground. 49.

01:17 At the end of World War II, US and British  intelligence were trying to figure out if Nazi

01:21 scientists had built superweapons. They actually  had: the V1 and V2 rockets, but declassified

01:27 documents show us something was spotted in the  skies above Europe… and it wasn’t a rocket.

01:33 On November 4th, 1948, a Top-Secret USAFE  (United States Air Force Europe) document stated:

01:38 “For some time, we have been concerned by  the recurring reports on flying saucers.”

01:42 One of these machines was observed, quote,  “hovering over Neubiberg Air Base for

01:47 about 30 minutes.” US authorities were stumped,  writing that whatever these vehicles were might,

01:53 quote, be “beyond the scope of our  present intelligence thinking.”

01:57 48. In a secret report,

01:58 one of these machines was described as having: “Extreme maneuverability and apparent ability to

02:04 almost hover; a plan approximating that an oval or  disc with done shape on the surface; the ability

02:10 to quickly disappear by high, the speed or by  complete disintegration; the ability to group

02:15 together or very quickly in a tight formation.” Nothing built by man could do that, so what had

02:21 they seen? 47.

02:23 One of the men tasked with understanding these  alien-like machines was the FBI director J. Edgar

02:28 Hoover. Declassified files show he wasn’t  a believer, but more or less every week,

02:34 another UFO document landed on his desk. One of them shows that on October 9th,

02:39 1967, a woman appeared at the FBI office in  Dallas. She claimed in July of that year,

02:44 she’d been kidnapped by aliens. A, quote, “being  from another planet who had assumed earthly form,”

02:50 took her into the sky aboard a spaceship  and gave her some important information.

02:55 She claimed the aliens had told her that on  May 22nd, 1962, American forces had fired a

03:01 missile at a UFO over Africa, but the craft  had protected itself using a “force field.”

03:06 She also alleged that U.S. forces had tracked  another UFO over Antarctica on August 20th, 1967.

03:13 The woman insisted that if investigators could  verify those incidents, it would prove her story

03:18 was genuine. But she refused to give her name. Why?

03:21 Because, she warned, UFO whistleblowers had a  habit of disappearing or meeting unfortunate ends.

03:27 As bizarre as that sounds, similar  claims kept pouring into FBI offices.

03:32 On May 14th, 1969, a man named Larry  Stephens wrote to the Bureau asking

03:37 agents to investigate rumors of mysterious  men, dressed in black and driving black cars,

03:43 who allegedly intimidated UFO witnesses  while sometimes impersonating FBI agents.

03:48 It is easy to dismiss everyone in  these files as either crazy or just

03:52 looking for attention. But many of the  reports came from very credible sources.

03:57 46.

03:58 Three servicemen from the 147th Airways and Air  Communications Squadron stationed in Guam reported

04:04 that at 10:40 a.m. on August 14th 1946 they saw  two crescent-shaped objects streaking overhead.

04:12 They estimated it was travelling at twice the  speed of America’s fastest fighter aircraft.

04:16 Flying at roughly 1,200 feet (365 meters),  the objects suddenly broke into a sharp

04:20 zig-zag maneuver before disappearing from sight. It sounds strange, coming from military personnel,

04:25 but reports like this carried  on well into the 21st century.

04:30 45. In just 2 days

04:31 in May in 2023, 7 different people who worked  for the federal government reported seeing the

04:36 unexplainable in the sky in the western US. Event One: Three separate teams of federal

04:42 law enforcement special agents reported  seeing 2 or 3 glowing red orbs hanging in

04:47 the night sky. According to their accounts, the  larger objects appeared to release smaller orbs,

04:52 almost like a mother craft deploying smaller  vehicles. The smaller lights swooped downward

04:57 before all of them suddenly vanished. Event Two: Several agents described

05:01 witnessing a single red orb suspended above  a rocky peak, seemingly connected to it by

05:06 what looked like a glowing spindle of light. The  object hovered in complete silence. One witness

05:11 compared it to the “Eye of Sauron” from The  Lord of the Rings. After remaining motionless

05:15 for roughly a minute, it disappeared. Event Three: Two agents reported spotting

05:20 what first appeared to be a car moving through a  restricted area at night. But something was wrong.

05:25 The vehicle, displaying one  red light and one white light,

05:28 seemed to hover around 3 feet (0.9 meters) above  the ground. When the agents moved toward it,

05:32 the object slid sideways across the desert with  what one witness described as “zero resistance.”

05:38 To this day, neither the witnesses nor  U.S. authorities have offered a definitive

05:42 explanation for what they saw. Let’s keep this next one simple.

05:46 Simple but insane. 44.

05:49 A now-declassified composite sketch reveals what  witnesses told the FBI they saw in the sky. Except

05:55 this didn’t happen during the UFO hysteria  of the 1940s or ’50s. This happened in 2023.

06:01 Witnesses described a “bronze metallic  ellipsoid” bursting from a blinding light

06:06 before vanishing without a trace. And this is just the start.

06:10 43. On April 24th, 1964, police officer

06:14 Lonnie Zamora was giving chase to a speeding car  in Socorro, New Mexico, when in the distance he

06:20 saw a flame and heard a strange roaring sound. He  thought it might be a building explosion, but the

06:26 closer he got to it, he noticed it was flying. There was no smoke. The roar changed frequency.

06:31 He drove closer and noticed what  appeared to be a shiny object with

06:35 two legs fixed to the ground. Meanwhile,  two people in white overalls lurked nearby

06:40 Was it some kind of crash? He drove closer so he could help out,

06:43 but there was another roar and suddenly the  object was moving vertically upwards with

06:48 fire bursting beneath it. The sighting became

06:51 known as the Lonnie Zamora incident. It’s never been established what he saw that

06:55 day, but it sounded a lot like what a senior US  intelligence official witnessed sometime in 2025.

07:02 42. This declassified file is heavily

07:05 redacted. Not even a location is given, but  around 5 pm at a high-security test site in the

07:11 US an official saw an orb in the sky and heard a  thud as if it had hit the ground. He subsequently

07:17 took out a helicopter to go in search. The man claimed he and another official spotted

07:22 a “super-hot” object hovering in the sky near  to where the first object had landed. It headed

07:27 east and then south and seemed to break off into  two separate pieces, both moving at high speed.

07:32 Then it became clear. Two large orbs hovering

07:35 at the side of each other that seemed to  flare. They were oval, orange with a white

07:40 or yellow center with light emitting from them. Suddenly, another appeare…, and then another,

07:46 until there were 5 in total, all  hovering for a while and vanishing.

07:50 The men saw them again later near a  mountain moving in a horizontal line.

07:54 They disappeared, but 3 of them then came  out of nowhere in a triangle formation.

07:59 It’s not certain what they’d seen. So, are we being watched?

08:03 41. If we are, that might explain what

08:06 NASA astronauts saw in December 1972 during the  Apollo 17 mission. The agency took a photograph

08:12 of what appeared to be three dots in space seen  from the moon, each one forming a triangle.

08:18 To this day, there’s no  consensus on what they were.

08:21 40. In 2025, FBI officially

08:24 submitted a photo to the Pentagon’s All-domain  Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) in 2025 as an

08:29 unidentified anomalous phenomenon. At first glance, this photo looks

08:33 completely empty, just another blurry sky shot.  But look closer, and there is a small black dot.

08:39 It doesn’t look like anything special,  but neither can it be explained,

08:43 just as the figure that appeared in another  image. This one had the shape of a helicopter,

08:48 but there certainly wasn’t a helicopter in  the sky when the image was seen and recorded.

08:52 And sometimes those objects  get too close for comfort.

08:56 39. Wladyslaw Krasuski was a Polish POW in 1944

09:01 when he was driving a tractor close to the German  camp where he was a laborer. As he approached

09:05 some swamp land, the engine suddenly cut out and  he heard a high-pitched whine in the distance.

09:10 An SS guard soon appeared on the scene and helped  start the tractor. The laborers didn’t think too

09:15 much about it until about 3 hours later, the work  crew looked up and saw some kind of vehicle rise

09:20 vertically into the sky. It hovered slowly to  the side, then disappeared behind some trees.

09:26 It was circular and 225 to 300 (69 -  91 m) in diameter, dark grey in color

09:32 with two main sections. One of the parts  spun around at high-speed creating what

09:36 the documents called a “continuous blur.” Krasuski told this story when he landed

09:40 in the US after the war. He swore that he  and about 18 other crew – Polish, French,

09:45 and Russians - had all seen the same thing. The information was kept secret for many

09:50 years. As US authorities were telling  people there was no such thing as UFOs,

09:55 they were actively investigating stories  such as the one told by Krasuski.

09:59 But sometimes, the saucers were just hoaxes. 38.

10:04 The declassified documents contain  letters sent between various departments.

10:08 They describe everything from unexplainable  phenomena to kids playing tricks in what

10:12 was fast-becoming a nation obsessed with UFOs. One of those letters is dated July 11th, 1947,

10:18 and reveals a Mrs. Easterbrook appeared  to find a flying saucer in her backyard

10:23 of her house in Twin Falls, Idaho. She heard  a crash and went outside to investigate. She

10:28 found two discs with a plastic dome attached. US media reported “flying saucers have invaded”

10:34 Twin Falls. FBI Special Agent in Charge, Guy  Banister, got on the case. Despite the press

10:39 saying the US government was involved in a  cover-up, the FBI claimed the flying saucer

10:44 was actually a contraption made by local kids. Maybe it was, but that doesn’t mean the agency

10:50 wasn’t taking other sightings seriously. 37.

10:54 By the year 2024, UAP sightings were no longer  landing on the desk of the FBI and very rarely,

11:00 if ever, did they make it into the newspapers. Like the sighting in October when an unnamed

11:05 soldier in Syria reported observing  a “misshapen and uneven ball of white

11:09 light” He described seeing multiple “glares  or light” emanating from an “unknown origin.”

11:14 That was just another report that went into the  basket of things that couldn’t be explained.

11:19 36. On September 23rd 1947, General Nathan Twining — a

11:24 highly respected officer who would later become  Chief of Staff of the United States Air Force —

11:29 wrote a classified memo titled “Flying Discs.” Twining was not joking when he wrote:

11:34 “The phenomenon reported is something  real and not visionary or fictitious.”

11:39 He described the reported objects as  displaying “extreme rates of climb,

11:43 maneuverability (particularly in roll), and  action which must be considered evasive.”

11:48 He admitted it was unclear whether the craft  were manually piloted, remotely controlled,

11:53 or operated automatically. But of one thing he was  certain: whatever people were seeing, it was real.

11:59 And the witnesses were not attention  seekers or flying-saucer obsessives. Many

12:03 were trained military personnel, pilots, and  observers accustomed to identifying aircraft.

12:09 That didn’t mean Twining believed the objects  came from outer space. His main concern was

12:14 just as frightening: that a foreign power  might have developed a revolutionary form of

12:18 propulsion “outside of our domestic knowledge.” Then someone died while trying to chase one.

12:24 35. On January 7th, 1948, Thomas

12:28 Mantell, a 25-year-old pilot with Kentucky’s  National Guard, died while pursuing what he’d

12:33 been told was a potentially dangerous UFO. Earlier that day, ordinary citizens around

12:38 Maysville, Kentucky, roughly 80 miles  (129 km) from Goodman Air Force Base,

12:42 began calling local police to report something  strange moving across the sky. Then more calls

12:47 came in. People were describing an object  unlike anything they’d ever seen before.

12:52 This wasn’t a prank. The situation escalated when

12:55 Air Force personnel, including a base commander  and a colonel, also reported seeing the object.

13:00 The colonel described it as “very white,” saying  it “looked like an umbrella,” with what appeared

13:06 to be red bands around its underside. Multiple  witnesses observed it for at least an hour.

13:11 At the time, four F-51 Mustangs were already  in the air, including Mantell’s aircraft. One

13:16 plane landed for fuel while the others  were ordered to intercept the object.

13:20 Mantell soon radioed back: “It is on sight  above and ahead of me, and it appears to

13:24 be moving about half my speed or approximately  180 miles an hour.” (290 kph) He described the

13:29 object as “metallic” and of “tremendous size.” Two pilots continued the pursuit at first,

13:34 but one eventually turned back. Mantell kept climbing.

13:38 Then radio contact was lost. Moments later,  his aircraft crashed into a fiery heap.

13:43 The next day, newspapers carried  headlines like: “F-51 and Capt.

13:47 Mantell Destroyed Chasing Flying Saucer.” U.S. authorities later claimed Mantell

13:52 had actually been pursuing a  classified Skyhook balloon,

13:55 a top-secret high-altitude research device that  could not be publicly discussed at the time.

14:00 To this day, there’s still some  doubt about what he actually saw.

14:04 Just like in the next case, the U.S. military  still can’t always explain what its personnel

14:09 see in the sky. 34.

14:12 In January, 2024, somewhere over the Mediterranean  Sea close to Greece, an operator reported spotting

14:17 something diamond-shaped traveling at  about 434 knots (499 mph). He described

14:21 it as having a “non-maneuvering probe at  the bottom” and only visible when viewed

14:26 via an onboard Short-Wave Infrared sensor. It was there and 2 minutes later, it was gone.

14:32 US military personnel often report  seeing these objects moving in a

14:35 way that is scientifically impossible. Like what an operator saw above the Arabia

14:40 Sea in October, 2020. 33.

14:43 The declassified file states that the man noticed  a “round, cold object” via infrared sensor,

14:49 traveling at 319 degrees (northwest)  at approximately 20 mph (32 kph).

14:54 The part that was impossible was that it was  able to make, quote, “abrupt directional changes”

14:59 that aircraft just aren’t capable of doing. Like the next cases, these were kept secret

15:04 from the public. 32.

15:06 For years, U.S. authorities publicly downplayed  UFOs, insisting they posed no major threat,

15:12 while quietly investigating them through a  series of secretive programs: Project Sign,

15:17 Project Grudge, and later Project Blue Book. One case that ended up in those files involved

15:22 an American Airlines DC-6 departing Washington  National Airport in 1950. Shortly after takeoff,

15:28 the crew encountered what the pilot  described as a brilliant glowing object

15:32 heading directly toward the aircraft. “As I looked to my left,” the pilot

15:36 later reported, “the object appeared to come  to a stop.” He described it as “perfectly

15:40 streamlined” and “without wings or tail section.” The object then maneuvered around the aircraft,

15:46 moved off to the right side of the plane,  and paced it briefly before suddenly

15:50 accelerating away into the distance. “We watched it for several seconds

15:54 more until it disappeared in the east out  of sight,” the captain said. “I have never

15:58 seen anything like it before or since.” Even more concerning were the reports of

16:02 similar objects sometimes surfacing near some  of America’s most sensitive nuclear facilities.

16:08 31. In 1952, the FBI received a classified message.

16:12 Several staff at the U.S. Atomic Energy  Commission’s Savannah River Plant facility

16:16 in South Carolina had seen 4 disc-shaped  flying objects approach the plant and

16:22 then vanish. They appeared again and vanished  again. Described as a goldish color and moving

16:27 at high speed, they were completely silent. That became just another report that gathered

16:33 dust. 30.

16:34 Like the one made by Mr. John P. Legge  in Codroy, Newfoundland in July 1947.

16:40 Legge told authorities he was standing outside  his store when something lit up the sky. Not a

16:45 shooting star. Not a plane. He’d never seen  anything like it. For about 15 seconds,

16:49 he saw this thing fly through the  night sky, a disc-shaped object

16:53 followed by a cone-shaped afterglow. That was it. The report was filed as

16:58 confidential and hidden for many decades. Just like this next declassified report,

17:03 which is even more mind-bending. 29.

17:06 When M. Lenore Corey wrote to the Director  of Military Intelligence in August 1947,

17:12 she made a point of saying she didn’t  want to be dismissed as a “victim of mass

17:16 psychology” or some kind of “crackpot.” She was educated. She wasn’t interested

17:21 in silly flying saucer stories. But what she claimed to have seen

17:24 from a bus window in Los Angeles couldn’t  be easily explained: a saucer-shaped object

17:29 flying across the sky with several more  following behind it in a trail. Beautiful

17:34 rays of light seemed to beam from the objects. Corey reasoned that the U.S. Army wouldn’t

17:39 be firing mysterious rays over the people  of LA, so what exactly had she witnessed?

17:44 28. In 1952, CIA reports stated

17:47 that flying saucers had been seen zig-zagging over  mining regions in the Belgian Congo. According to

17:53 the files, a Belgian military pilot pursued one  of the objects in a jet and managed to get within

17:59 roughly 395 feet (120 meters) of it. He described  the craft as silver, with a rotating underside,

18:04 capable of speeds beyond Mach 1. When it  accelerated, he said, flames appeared behind it.

18:09 The CIA paid close attention. At the  time, the agency had significant strategic

18:14 interests in the Congo and its natural resources. For a while, parts of the UK became a UFO hotspot.

18:22 27. The FBI’s

18:24 news clippings found in the files include a  British news media report from December 3,

18:28 1950 “Football crowds see flying saucer.” The report said a soccer match had to be

18:34 stopped as hundreds of fans looked up and  saw a “strange white phenomenon dart across

18:38 the sky.” Nearby, a rugby game also came  to a halt when the players looked up and

18:43 saw what looked like an alien spaceship. The US authorities were obviously keeping

18:47 tabs on what was happening across the pond. But  unfortunately, most of the news clippings in the

18:52 files don’t come with an explanation of what US  agencies thought about the strange goings-on.

18:58 26. In October 2001,

19:01 the Russians sent a message to the US State  Department denying it had flown mysterious

19:05 planes over Georgian Airspace and started bombing. The Georgian Foreign Ministry complained and the

19:11 Russians countered that what had been seen can’t  have been Russian, so it must have been a UFO.

19:16 The confidential cables addressed  this by saying the Russians are

19:20 prone to making the odd “bold lie.” It seems UFOs at times can function as

19:24 excuses, but maybe the Russians were right. Now for a real-life space horror movie.

19:30 25. Some very strange

19:32 things happened on the Apollo 17 mission. Command Module Pilot, Ronald Evans,

19:37 said in a report that he’d witnessed “very  bright particles or fragments” drifting and

19:42 “tumbling” near the spacecraft as it maneuvered. Lunar Module Pilot, Harrison “Jack” Schmitt,

19:47 backed him up, describing what he saw  as looking “like the Fourth of July.”

19:51 Another astronaut, Mission Commander Eugene  A. Cernan, had a different experience.

19:55 He’d not been able to sleep, saying that  after experiencing seeing bright streaks

20:00 he saw an “imposing” intense light  flashing in with the intensity of a

20:04 train’s headlights. He believed he saw these  things, they weren’t just optical phenomena.

20:10 And down on Earth things  were also getting strange.

20:13 24. The recent

20:14 files release shows how dedicated the FBI was  at collecting UFO-related newspaper articles.

20:20 One of them, dated October 14th,  1957, featured Captain W.J. Hull,

20:25 a Western Airlines pilot who’d once gone  on record and called UFOs a load of “bunk.”

20:31 But he changed his mind when he saw  one for himself in Mobile, Alabama.

20:35 He was flying a small plane when he saw what  he described as a “brilliant” meteor flying

20:40 through the sky. Except this meteor  just stopped and did an about-turn.

20:45 Something that’s physically impossible. It then performed a series of violent turns,

20:49 mesmerizing and scaring him, and suffice  it to say, this once stalwart skeptic of

20:54 UFOs was a changed man. He wasn’t the only one.

20:58 23. That same year, retired Navy Admiral Delmer S.

21:01 Fahrney - the man once overseeing America’s guided  missile program - made a chilling admission.

21:06 He said he’d seen evidence of objects in  the sky moving too fast, too intelligently,

21:11 and too impossibly to belong to  the U.S., Russia… or anyone else.

21:15 He never claimed to see a flying saucer  himself. But he made one thing clear…

21:20 something unexplainable was out there. These were serious people. Not crackpots.

21:25 And then saucers turned into cigars. 22.

21:28 In 1954, witnesses swore they’d seen a  cigar-shaped object flying over Sétif,

21:34 Algeria - an object that CIA files said  left a glowing blue trail behind it.

21:39 That same year, dock workers in  Kuala Lumpur reported seeing another

21:42 cigar-shaped craft streaking overhead,  also leaving a trail in its wake. Then,

21:47 over the following 5 days, declassified  documents recorded three more separate

21:51 sightings in Kuala Lumpur of what witnesses  described as a cylindrical flying machine.

21:57 What exactly was this cigar-shaped object  people across continents kept reporting?

22:02 A group of hikers near Saint-Mexant,  France, all described seeing the same thing:

22:07 a giant flying cigar moving silently around  2,000 feet (610 meters) above their heads.

22:12 Were flying cigars real? 21.

22:15 Over the years, the US took these reports  seriously. Experts often said many of the

22:20 events could be explained by natural phenomena. But about 20% were too strange to be rational.

22:26 As for the rational explanation, one man that  often appears in declassified files said he knew

22:31 exactly what these machines were. 20.

22:34 George Klein had been a top scientist in the  war for the Nazi War Production Ministry.

22:39 He was also one of the men who  said Nazi flying saucers were real.

22:43 So when the FBI was collecting newspaper  clippings, there was one with Klein stating

22:47 that all these UFOs were actually just the US  and Russia making super weapons after stealing

22:53 Nazi scientists at the end of the war. The problem with his theory was that

22:58 no such Nazi wonder weapon was ever uncovered. Still, Klein insisted he’d personally worked on

23:03 a Nazi flying saucer prototype, one he claimed  could climb to 40,000 feet (12,192 meters) in

23:08 just 3 minutes. At the time, no publicly known  aircraft on Earth could do anything close to that.

23:13 Maybe Klein was lying. Maybe he was exaggerating. Or maybe the superpowers of the world really

23:19 were developing technologies far beyond  anything the public had been told existed.

23:24 19. In 1954, Major James Zicherelli

23:28 reported seeing a UFO at Brookley Air Force Base  in Alabama. He described it as a plane he’d never

23:34 seen before with short stubby wings. He and others  at the base saw it on radar, saying it moved

23:40 gracefully and silent and then just vanished. And there were more sightings of something

23:45 similar in Europe. 18.

23:47 In Sweden, Bengt Nordenskiöld, the  commander-in-chief of the Swedish Air Force,

23:51 said his personnel had witnessed something  impossible over the Baltic coast. Witnesses

23:56 described a metallic, disc-shaped object moving  in ways no conventional aircraft should have

24:01 been able to. According to the reports, it  flew faster than the speed of sound at an

24:05 altitude of roughly 5,000 feet (1,524 meters). What made the sighting even more unsettling

24:09 was where it occurred: close to a  former Nazi research facility that

24:14 had since fallen under Soviet control. But one man had a different explanation.

24:19 17. Major Donald Keyhoe, a former Marine

24:22 Corp naval aviator, had a very different theory  from Klein. In statements that later appeared in

24:27 classified files, Keyhoe argued that the flying  saucers weren’t secret superweapons at all.

24:32 They were interplanetary craft  operated by an alien civilization.

24:37 Keyhoe — a man who should’ve understood the  inner workings of the Air Force better than

24:41 most civilians — claimed the U.S. government  already knew this. It was deliberately

24:46 hiding the truth to avoid public panic. The Air Force pushed back hard. Officials insisted

24:51 they would continue investigating UFO reports, but  they refused to publicly acknowledge that flying

24:57 saucers were real or extraterrestrial in origin. So what did the experts behind closed doors

25:02 actually believe? 16.

25:05 On May 5, 1955, the U.S. Air Force released  Special Report No. 14, titled “Analysis

25:11 of Reports of Unidentified Aerial Objects.” The study examined roughly 4,000 UFO sightings

25:17 reported mainly by ordinary citizens, but also  by military personnel, police officers, pilots,

25:22 and other officials. The report concluded  that many of the “apparently unexplained

25:27 events” lacked reliable measurements or enough  physical evidence to reach firm conclusions.

25:32 It was one of the largest official UFO studies  ever conducted. Its overall conclusion was

25:37 that it was “highly improbable” the unidentified  aerial objects were extraterrestrial in origin.

25:42 But the report also admitted a number of  sightings still could not be explained.

25:47 And not everyone involved  agreed with the conclusions.

25:50 15. The Blue Book director Edward James Ruppelt,

25:54 the man usually credited with replacing the term  flying saucer with UFO, called the military's

25:58 press release about the report “worthless.” He went to the effort to write a book about

26:03 it saying that we’re stuck with UFOs. He didn’t  think they could all be explained, but so far,

26:07 the investigations had all been weak. This was an important piece of writing,

26:12 changing the flying saucer to UFO was  more in line with scientific reasoning.

26:17 But humans were back to  square one. We knew nothing.

26:20 Well, maybe. 14.

26:22 In 1960, Roscoe H. Hillenkoetter, former  CIA director and later on the board of

26:27 the National Investigations Committee On  Aerial Phenomena, dropped a bombshell in an

26:32 article published in the New York Times. This man was a major figure in American

26:36 intelligence and now he was saying that  the US Air Force was silencing its own

26:41 personnel about UFOs to hide the truth. In  his own words, he said, “Behind the scenes,

26:47 high-ranking Air Force officers are soberly  concerned about UFOs. But through official

26:52 secrecy and ridicule, many citizens are led to  believe the unknown flying objects are nonsense.”

26:57 He was wrong about things. Not all personnel were silenced.

27:02 13. B-29 test mechanic Robert B. Gardener said

27:05 he’d spotted 2 silver-green objects flying over  San Francisco airport at “terrific speeds.” He

27:11 explained they looked like a cone clipped at both  ends, flying at about 12,000 feet (3,657 kph) at

27:16 a staggering 1,800 miles an hour (2,897 kph).  The date was 1953 and at that point in time,

27:22 the fastest flying machine was the Bell X-1A,  which could reach about 1,600 mph (2,575 kph).

27:28 Did any of these incidents  produce believable photographs?

27:32 12. One of the events that

27:33 has perplexed experts is the photograph a couple  at a farm in McMinnville, Oregon, took in 1950.

27:39 Paul and Evelyn Trent claimed they’d seen  a saucer-shaped object roughly 300 feet (91

27:44 meters) wide hovering above their property,  with what they described as a flat underside.

27:49 The CIA quietly examined the photographs, while  Life later published them for the world to see.

27:55 Over the years, both the original prints and  their negatives underwent professional analysis.

28:00 In 1967, astronomer William Hartmann of the  University of Colorado — a scientist specifically

28:05 tasked with critically examining and debunking  UFO claims — reached a shocking conclusion:

28:11 “This is one of the few UFO reports in which all  factors investigated, geometric, psychological,

28:17 and physical, appear to be consistent with the  assertion that an extraordinary flying object,

28:22 silvery, metallic, disk-shaped, tens of  meters in diameter, and evidently artificial,

28:27 flew within sight of two witnesses.” The Trents never changed their story.

28:32 Decades later, when interviewed as an elderly  couple in 1997, they still insisted the

28:37 photographs showed exactly what they’d seen that  day. They said they’d originally hesitated to make

28:42 the images public because they feared the object  might’ve been part of a secret military project.

28:47 And there was another image  that would become legendary.

28:51 11. One of the FBI documents dated June 8th,

28:54 1967, shows us that a man named Paul Peyerl  provided the agency information that possibly

29:00 proved the Nazis had built a UFO. Peyerl claimed  he saw it hover above the Black Forest in 1944.

29:07 The now declassified document states: “During this period, he observed the

29:11 aircraft described above. It was disc-shaped…  remotely controlled, and equipped with several

29:16 jet engines on the outer part of the structure.” The machine had an outer section that spun

29:21 around a central dome, while the  rest of it remained stationary.

29:24 It’s interesting that the UFOs people often  see looked exactly like the ones in sci-fi

29:29 movies. But Peyerl took a picture.  All that remains of it is a Xerox

29:33 copy of this negative, so it’s not very clear. The hardest events to explain are those in which

29:39 several people saw the same thing. 10.

29:42 On February 10th, 1951, just before 1 a.m., a  U.S. Navy Douglas R5D transport plane carrying

29:50 31 people crossed the skies above Keflavík  when the crew spotted something impossible.

29:55 Roughly 1,500 feet (457 meters) above the  ocean, a strange glowing object appeared

30:00 beneath them. It was silent, bright, and  moving in ways they couldn’t explain.

30:04 Everyone onboard reportedly saw it. A disc-shaped object with an orange-red glow

30:09 around its perimeter. As the object drew closer,  the pilots said their instruments began to fail.

30:15 The heading indicator malfunctioned, along with  the magnetic compass and two direction finders.

30:20 Then, as the aircraft moved away from the object,  the instruments suddenly returned to normal.

30:25 The incident remained classified for years, but  surviving documents suggest Navy intelligence

30:30 took the encounter seriously. Roughly 9 months  later, investigators reportedly visited the pilot

30:35 and showed him what amounted to a police lineup  of UFO photographs, asking whether any matched

30:41 what he’d seen that night over the Atlantic. This wasn’t some publicity-seeker or eccentric

30:46 chasing fame. He was a trusted military pilot  whose account was treated as credible by the

30:51 people investigating it. Just like this next man.

30:54 9. Again in 1951,

30:57 L. Gordon Cooper was flying his F-86 Thunderjet  in Germany when he saw a group of objects moving

31:03 in ways not possible with human engineering. He would later work for NASA in Project Mercury,

31:08 the US’s first space program. He  was smart and trustworthy. So when

31:13 he told his superiors he’d seen a metallic  silver saucer in the sky, people listened.

31:17 After retiring from NASA with the rank of  colonel and 222 hours in space under his belt,

31:23 he wrote a book claiming the government was  actively suppressing information about UFOS.

31:28 He detailed a separate incident in 1957 where his  crew had captured footage of a landed saucer at

31:34 a California Air Force base. When he handed  the film over to Washington, everything went

31:38 quiet. He was locked out of his own story. Until his dying breath, he was certain the

31:44 government was involved in a UFO cover-up. Some stories were just too crazy to rationally

31:49 explain. 8.

31:51 Over the years, there have been claims that  the CIA used UFOs as a form of misdirection.

31:56 There may be some truth to that idea, but the  declassified documents show us a more complicated

32:01 picture. Some people within the CIA were, on  paper, deeply concerned about what it saw as

32:06 the public’s growing gullibility and how hostile  powers might exploit it. Some files even discussed

32:12 the danger of Soviet-engineered mass hysteria  or psychological warfare built around UFO panic.

32:18 One document stated the agency needed to “reduce  the current gullibility of the public and

32:23 consequently their susceptibility to propaganda.” That concern helped lead to the creation of the

32:28 Robertson Panel in 1953,backed by the CIA and  chaired by Howard P. Robertson, one of the most

32:34 respected physicists in the world. Its mission  was straightforward: investigate the flying saucer

32:39 phenomenon and debunk it once and for all. And when the panel finally got to work,

32:44 this is what happened. 7.

32:46 The same year the panel was convened, a major  stationed at George Air Force Base in California

32:51 reported seeing 5 enormous disc-shaped  objects flying in formation above the base.

32:57 And he was far from the only witness. Over the next 12 weeks, 9 more

33:00 sightings of similar objects were  reported at the same installation.

33:04 Then, on the very same day the major witnessed  the discs, military personnel at Davis-Monthan

33:10 Air Force Base in Arizona reported something  equally weird. 12 unidentified objects flying in

33:16 formation at estimated speeds of between 1,500  and 2,000 miles per hour (2,414 - 3,218 kph).

33:21 It was the kind of performance that was beyond  anything publicly known to exist in the 1950s.

33:27 The legendary Lockheed SR-71  Blackbird wouldn’t emerge from

33:31 the secret world of Area 51 until the mid-1960s. And these super-fast vehicle sightings weren’t

33:37 only confined to the US. 6.

33:39 In September 1953, NATO warships participating  in Operation Mainbrace were crossing the North

33:44 Atlantic. During the mission, a Danish  naval commander and his crew reported

33:49 a glowing triangular object tearing across the  sky at roughly 900 miles per hour (1,448 kph).

33:54 It was also glowing with an eerie blue light. Over the following weeks, more sightings

33:59 emerged from personnel involved in the  exercise. None of them were explained.

34:03 Then right after came an incident in Yorkshire,  northern England. RAF personnel reported that

34:08 an unidentified object appeared to shadow one of  their Meteor jet fighters in flight. One airman

34:14 later described the object as a silver disc. “It stopped its descent and hung in the air,

34:19 rotating as if on its own axis,” he said. “Then it  accelerated at an incredible speed to the West.”

34:25 But what happened when investigators believed  they’d found not just a sighting, but actual

34:30 physical evidence? 5.

34:32 Arthur Stansel, a technician connected to the  Nevada Test Site, would later become part of

34:37 UFO legend. In a sworn statement, he claimed  that on May 21st 1953, he’d helped recover part

34:43 of a crashed UFO near Kingman, Arizona. According to his account, the object was

34:49 “constructed of an unfamiliar metal which  resembled brushed aluminum.” He said he and

34:54 several other men dug it out of the sand where  it had partially embedded itself after impact.

34:58 The craft, he claimed, was oval-shaped, roughly 30  feet (9 meters) in diameter, with two swivel seats

35:04 and a cabin filled with strange instruments. He later described it as something so many

35:08 people had seen all over the world – “a  teardrop-shaped cigar... a streamlined cigar.”

35:14 Then came the detail that would one day  make Americans feel like they weren’t alone.

35:18 “A tent pitched near the object sheltered the  dead remains of the only occupant,” he stated.

35:24 Occupant, as in… alien. So what exactly had Stansel claimed to have seen?

35:29 In his own words, the being was  “about 4 feet (1.21 meters) tall,

35:32 with a dark brown complexion, and had two eyes,  two nostrils, two ears, and a small mouth.” He

35:38 said it wore “a silvery metallic suit” along  with a skullcap made from the same material.

35:43 And according to Stansel, he wasn’t  alone. Other technicians present that

35:47 day supposedly saw the same thing. And now comes the strangest part.

35:51 4. In classified government documents,

35:54 intelligence officials reportedly referred to  Arthur Stansel using the name Fritz Werner.

35:59 Those files describe how Stansel and other  technicians were allegedly transported to the

36:04 crash site aboard a bus with blacked-out windows. Then, in 2024, another document surfaced online

36:10 relating to Werner. It appeared to  contain messages exchanged between a

36:14 U.S. government official and Christopher  Mellon, the former Senate Intelligence

36:19 Committee staffer who later became involved  in the Pentagon’s investigation into UAPs.

36:24 In the exchange, the official suggested that the  truth about the Kingman crash would leave people

36:29 “slack-jawed.” He spoke about the incident  as though it remained an active matter

36:33 even into the 2020s, reportedly saying: “We’re  vacuuming up info”. That’s the kind of language

36:39 that could be interpreted as an admission  that authorities were still suppressing or

36:44 collecting information connected to the case. If genuine, the messages appeared to suggest

36:49 that a supposedly high-ranking official  believed there was at least some truth

36:54 behind Stansel’s extraordinary claims. Unfortunately, the latest tranche of

36:58 released documents doesn’t appear to add  much concrete evidence to the Kingman story.

37:02 But the allegations remind us of  something that went down in the UK.

37:06 3. After years of

37:08 sightings – and growing distrust in CIA-linked  UFO investigations – the Condon Committee was

37:13 formed. It was a project funded by the U.S.  Air Force and the University of Colorado to

37:18 scientifically study unidentified flying objects. One of the cases that got the committee’s

37:23 attention took place in 1956 at  RAF Bentwaters in Suffolk, England.

37:27 Radar operators tracked an object moving  at several thousand miles per hour. Then,

37:32 suddenly, the radar began showing dozens  of them. According to the reports,

37:36 the equipment was checked and found to be  functioning properly. Witnesses said smaller

37:40 objects appeared to dart around a much larger  one, and multiple servicemen observed the event.

37:46 Something very similar happened nearby at  RAF Lakenheath. There, the object wasn’t

37:50 only picked up on radar, it was reportedly  seen visually as well. Witnesses described

37:55 it stopping dead in the sky, accelerating  instantly, and moving at extraordinary speeds.

38:00 Lakenheath personnel contacted RAF Neatishead,  also in Suffolk, which scrambled a de Havilland

38:06 Venom night fighter to intercept the target. The Venom’s two-man crew later reported that they

38:10 had the object both on radar and in direct  visual sight. Then, without warning,

38:14 the target appeared behind them before they could  react. Eventually, the jet ran low on fuel and was

38:20 forced to break off the pursuit and land. The Condon Report would later describe the

38:23 encounter as the “most puzzling and  unusual case” it had ever examined.

38:28 So what exactly were these objects  that seemed capable of outrunning and

38:32 outmaneuvering military aircraft? Were they connected to the same

38:35 phenomena reported by American test pilots  and radar crews across the Cold War world?

38:41 2. X-15 pilot

38:43 Joseph Walker was flying at Mach 4 when he said  into the radio: “Two UFOs just passed overhead.”

38:48 They flew right past him, and were doing 3,400 mph  (5,471 kph), as fast as any plane in existence.

38:54 He said he got within about 200 feet (61 meters)  of them and saw they were disc-shaped. Walker

38:59 never got to speak about UFOs later in his life,  he died in a group formation accident in 1966.

39:06 But his words resonated with Major Robert  White, another X-15 pilot. He was traveling

39:11 at 314,000 feet (95,707 meters) when  he saw several objects flying nearby.

39:16 He told Time magazine, “There are  things out there. There absolutely are!”

39:20 This last one is important. 1.

39:23 In 2014, The Guardian posed a question: “Rather  than covering up the existence of aliens,

39:28 could it be that the real conspiracy has  been persuading us to believe in them?”

39:33 The article referred to what appeared to be  a CIA-linked psychological operation in which

39:37 fake classified UFO documents were deliberately  circulated to the public. The documents became

39:43 known as Majestic 12 papers – secret files  ostensibly proving top U.S. officials had

39:48 concealed evidence of alien contact for decades. Except the documents were exposed as forgeries.

39:54 Disinformation designed to inflame  UFO hysteria rather than calm it down.

39:59 The fallout destroyed UFO researcher, Paul  Bennewitz. After receiving supposedly leaked

40:04 information from Air Force intelligence sources,  he became convinced extraterrestrials were

40:09 operating on Earth. He later suffered  a severe psychological breakdown.

40:13 So for years, the files show us that  intelligence agencies had warned that the

40:17 American public was vulnerable to mass hysteria  surrounding UFOs. Yet there were allegations

40:23 that elements inside the national security  world had actively fueled those same fears.

40:28 Why? No one knows.

40:29 But some researchers point toward  the Psychological Strategy Board,

40:33 a Cold War-era body created to coordinate American  psychological operations and propaganda efforts.

40:39 Few ideas can capture the public imagination  more effectively than UFOs and little green men.

40:45 All the documents you’ve heard about  today are real. But as history shows,

40:49 facts and fiction have a habit of becoming  tangled, especially when governments, fear,

40:54 propaganda, and the unknown collide. The truth is out there, somewhere,

40:59 and it might be very human. Or, maybe, it’s not.

41:02 But if you’re looking for proof, it’s not  just buried in Pentagon files anymore.

41:06 It’s in close encounters, witnessed  up close by trained personnel who knew

41:11 exactly what should and shouldn’t  be in their skies. Find out what

41:14 they saw in “Actual Video Of US Military  Intercepting UFO’s”. Or watch this instead.

00:13 It’s an understatement to say that housing is incredibly important to everybody, and

00:17 for even more reasons that being a basic human need.

00:20 The financial success of families, communities and countries are intertwined with real estate,

00:25 which is why it seems silly that people can just take these homes and legally claim them

00:29 as their own.

00:31 Squatters rights on the surface sound ridiculous.

00:33 Reports exist of families going on holidays for as little as three weeks before coming

00:38 back to their home with changed locks and a new family living in it.

00:41 People in these situations can’t rely on law enforcement because they too are powerless

00:45 to remove these people from a home that they claim is their own.

00:48 A Soldier from Florida had to go through months of civil court to rid his home of squatters

00:53 who had moved onto the property while the soldier was deployed in Afghanistan.

00:57 Even after successfully appealing the squatters claim to the property, the serviceman was

01:01 left with thousands of dollars in damages that he had no way of recuperating off the

01:04 evicted squatters.

01:06 This horrible situation is also unique to housing, after all you can’t steal a car,

01:10 hide it in your garage for a year and then claim it’s yours.

01:14 So if that kind of legal protection extends to automobiles, why not our most important

01:18 assets?

01:19 Well it’s mostly because without the rules that make nightmare scenarios like this possible,

01:24 our housing system simply wouldn’t work at all.

01:31 Daily Upside.

01:32 The Daily Upside is a totally free high quality email newsletter with a strong focus on business

01:37 and finance.

01:38 Their short articles are written daily by industry insiders and financial analysts who

01:43 are able to make sense of world events in a way that is both informative and simple

01:47 to understand, even simple enough for me while I am working through my first coffee of the

01:51 morning.

01:52 Do you want to know the real reason why Elon Musk is now the biggest shareholder in Twiiter,

01:55 or why Walmart Truck Drivers are earning the same as Goldman Sachs Analysts?

01:59 Well you would if you were subscribed to the daily upside.

02:03 Sign up using the link below to make sure you keep up to date with everything in the

02:06 world of business and finance with the daily upside.

02:09 …

02:10 Squatters rights (like a lot of things wrong with America) originated in England.

02:13 This place is seriously old and it’s filled with land claims that date back hundreds of

02:17 years.

02:19 Squatters rights were originally established because it was almost impossible to keep track

02:22 of who owned what at a time when all records were kept on paper stashed in damp towers

02:27 and watched over by a barely literate population.

02:30 The laws were set up to avoid two things, wasted space, and wars.

02:35 Land owners in the middle ages were nobility and they owned thousands of acres.

02:40 Most of this land was used for farming or hunting.

02:43 Unused land was wasted land that would be better off in the hands of another lord who

02:47 could use it to feed the kingdom.

02:49 Use of land being the decider of ownership forced the lords to use it or lose it so to

02:54 speak.

02:55 It also avoided a situation where two lords would try to claim ownership over the same

02:58 piece of unused land.

03:00 Internal wars were bad for kingdoms so higher lords would usually settle these squabbles

03:04 by awarding the land to whoever they determined to be to person using it.

03:08 As the world got less feudal it made sense to keep these laws in place because all of

03:12 a sudden regular peasants were starting to own land of their own, oh and these people

03:17 could vote on why made their laws now, so the lawmakers wanted to keep them happy.

03:21 Land use rights prevented the great great great great grandchild of a lord, finding

03:25 a land deed in a dungeon somewhere and using it to claim ownership over a new housing development.

03:30 I think most of you can agree that kind of situation is worth avoiding, but where is

03:34 the line drawn?

03:36 What timeframe is too long, or too short?

03:39 Records have only been migrated onto computer databases in the last three decades at most.

03:44 If you live in a country that’s been around for more than a hundred years, it’s almost

03:47 a certainty that there is a document out there that says your land belongs to someone else.

03:52 The difficulty in keeping records indefinitely is why most legal systems have a statue of

03:56 limitations.

03:57 In plain English a time limit on events you can challenge legally.

04:01 Records get lost, stolen, destroyed, forged and even hacked.

04:05 The last thing a law abiding home owner would want is for someone to come along and claim

04:09 that their home actually didn’t actually belong to them.

04:11 Land use laws are designed to protect people from these situations.

04:15 This is also why squatters rights style laws don’t apply to cars or other goods.

04:20 Land is unique in the sense that it is the only commodity not created with human labour,

04:23 and that can last indefinitely.

04:25 A block of land was created 4.5 billion years ago, a car is at most 100 years old so they

04:31 are not liable to have the same problems with multiple ownership claims.

04:35 One exception to this is that there are variations of squatters rights rules do exists for things

04:40 like ancient artifacts.

04:41 Any given ancient Greek statue will have a different legal owner today than the first

04:45 person who laid claim to it hundreds of years ago.

04:48 …

04:49 Ok so maybe these laws make sense in a places like England, but what about America?

04:53 It’s been ruled by one single system of government since it’s independence so why

04:57 do we need these laws?

04:58 Well for much the same reasons.

05:00 Early American settlers basically just claimed land out west and records were even worse

05:05 than what existed in Europe at the time.

05:07 So sorry my fellow Americans, we aren’t any better that the Europeans.

05:12 Not to mention the fact that none of us really want to be beating our chest too loudly about

05:15 eternal land ownership rights now do we?

05:18 …

05:19 At this point I should probably explain what squatters’ rights are, because, what we

05:22 are hearing about when we read stories like this, are not in fact squatters rights, they

05:26 are instead, civil disputes over oral contracts.

05:29 In America oral contract are just as binding as written and signed contracts, they are

05:34 just much harder to dispute because it just becomes a case of he said she said.

05:38 If a family moves into an empty home law enforcement is in most instances powerless to remove them,

05:44 but this has nothing to do with squatters rights.

05:47 People just assume squatters rights are at play here because the people taking the home

05:50 are called squatters.

05:52 The reason that police cannot bust them out of the home is because the squatting occupants

05:55 can claim that they home is theirs, or that they are renting it, or that they have a private

05:59 agreement in place with the owners to live there.

06:01 Police officers are not judges and they cannot and should not have the authority to make

06:05 discretionary decisions about peoples housing arrangements, that’s the job of the courts.

06:10 Needing to take squatters to court to prove that no oral contract was established is unbelievably

06:15 frustrating, but it’s better than the alternative.

06:17 If you have a private agreement with room mates to pay a share of rent every month you

06:21 don’t want to get thrown out on your ass by the police because your room mates are

06:24 sick of you cooking fish in the communal microwave (although honestly that should be consider

06:28 a war crime).

06:29 It’s also not right that landlords could get police to kick families out of a rented

06:33 home if they weren’t able to provide suitable evidence of rights to residency right there

06:37 and then on the spot.

06:39 Think to yourself, if a police team busted into your home today and tried to kick you

06:43 out, how would you definitively prove that you owned the place and weren’t just living

06:46 in there as a squatter?

06:48 It’s not that easy, and that’s why we have courts, and while you are going through

06:52 that court process you would probably appreciate being able to stay in your home while you

06:56 prove that you definitively do or do not have a right to live there.

06:59 Actual squatters rights cases are EXTREMELY rare, all of these stories are just legal

07:04 challenges that needed their day in court.

07:06 OKAY, But what if you wanted to get a free house by exploiting these laws?

07:10 How would one go about doing that?

07:12 As a renter in the bay area I will admit that the thought has crossed my mind.

07:16 Well in America it is almost impossible to get squatters rights, with almost being the

07:20 imperative word here.

07:22 To claim squatters rights you need to move onto a property that you reasonably believed

07:25 to be your own.

07:27 This is basically impossible in suburbs or cities because land holdings in these areas

07:30 are well defined by fences and buildings.

07:33 A patch of land directly adjacent to a poorly demarcated field is probably your best bet.

07:38 Sometimes it’s hard to know where your field ends and your neighbours begins, mistakes

07:42 happen.

07:43 The second important step is that you need to prove that you didn’t have permission

07:46 from the actual land owners to dwell on the property.

07:49 This might sound counterintuitive, but if a landowner says it’s cool that you stay

07:52 in their house, then they have acknowledged your lodging and you have acknowledged their

07:56 ownership.

07:57 Think of it this way.

07:58 If your friend came over to your house and they told you they would let you to sleep

08:01 in your bed, you would immediately challenge that statement by saying “you’re god damn

08:05 right I’m allowed to sleep in my bed, it’s my damn bed!”.

08:08 If someone with no rightful claim to a landholding gave permission to the rightful land owner

08:12 to use the land, the legal assumption is that the true land owner would challenge the assumption

08:16 that the land is not theirs in court.

08:18 So if you want a free house, you can’t have permission to live in it and you have got

08:22 to be able to prove it was reasonable for you to think you owned it.

08:25 You then need to maintain this status quo for the duration of the statue of limitations

08:29 period in your civil jurisdiction for California that is ten years, for other places it’s

08:34 as little as 1 year or as much as 100 years.

08:36 Your milage will vary.

08:38 Once you have done that the property is yours for all intents and purposes, if the previous

08:42 owner challenges your claim, they won’t be able to provide proof of ownership that

08:45 falls within the statue of limitations timeframe.

08:48 The same rules that stop a seventeenth-generation lord claiming medieval land holdings are the

08:52 same rules that will stop a family unlucky enough to leave an unmarked piece of land

08:56 unattended for just slightly too long.

08:58 On a positive note as digital records and satellite mapping become standard practice

09:02 these kinds of disputes are going to become far less common than they already are.

09:06 So, sorry if you thought this was your only chance at owning a home you are probably going

09:11 to need a better plan.

09:12 Maybe a side hustle to accelerate your savings plan?

09:15 But then again, maybe not.

09:17 Go and watch my video outlining all of the lies you have been told about side hustles

09:21 and multiple streams of income to find out why.

09:23 Thanks again to the daily upside for making it possible for everybody to keep on learning

09:27 How Money Works.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Americans Have Turned Against AI
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: Americans Have Turned Against AI
  • Video ID: 14Uc2WCSPiw
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Millions of Americans will open  ChatGPT in the next 10 minutes…

00:03 And most of them believe it's making  the world worse. Half the country uses

00:07 AI now. Yet only 16% of Americans  think it will be good for society.

00:12 It’s the lowest level of optimism any  major technology has launched with.

00:16 The people building AI call it humanity's greatest

00:18 breakthrough. The people using it describe  something closer to a hostage situation.

00:23 So how did the fastest-adopted technology of  our lifetime also become one of the most hated?

00:28 You might expect that it’s the older  generations that are pushing back on

00:31 the AI revolution. After all, every new  technology has faced resistance from

00:36 people who didn't grow up with it. But that's not what's happening.

00:39 The biggest users of AI are Americans  under 30. They use it for schoolwork,

00:44 job applications, coding, brainstorming,  and as a substitute for Google. By every

00:49 indicator, they should be AI's biggest fans. Instead, they're some of its biggest critics.

00:54 A Gallup study found the share of Gen Z who  say AI makes them feel angry climbed from

00:58 22% to 31% by early 2026. And according to Pew  Research, 40% of young Americans said it would

01:05 make the country worse than better. But this isn't just a Gen Z story.

01:09 Trust in AI is collapsing all  across the U.S. Two thirds of

01:13 people think it's being developed too  quickly. 59% don't trust the companies

01:17 building it. And most don't believe the  government can keep it under control.

01:20 Yet people keep using it. ChatGPT alone is  used by 44% of American adults, more than

01:27 double its share in 2023. That's the AI paradox.

01:31 So why does adoption keep accelerating  if confidence keeps falling?

01:34 For most people, it wasn’t really adopted.  Workplaces began implementing it in their

01:39 workflow. Schools added it to assignments. Apps  and search engines displayed it as a main feature.

01:44 People had no other choice. It was forced  upon them. AI didn’t earn their trust.

01:49 They have no other option.

01:51 The shift happened so gradually  that most people barely noticed it.

01:54 Until suddenly, it was everywhere.

01:56 The moment you open Google and search  for something, you’re hit with a block

02:00 of AI-written text answering the question  before you even reach the search results.

02:04 The company that’s supposed to help you find  information is now deciding what you see first.

02:09 And it works.

02:10 60% of Americans say they read the summaries  regularly, because there’s no way to avoid

02:15 them. The moment Google started answering  the question itself, the experience changed.

02:20 And the more the internet degraded, the less  people trusted it. In 2021, 37% of Americans said

02:26 the spread of AI worried them more than it excited  them. By 2025, that number had climbed to 50%,

02:32 even though most people hadn't been personally  affected by AI in a professional capacity.

02:37 That would soon change.

02:39 In April 2025, Tobi Lütke,  Shopify’s chief executive,

02:43 posted a memo to his staff. Before any team could  ask him for a bigger budget or another employee,

02:47 they had to prove that a machine  couldn’t do the work first. Lütke

02:51 insisted that “reflexive AI use  was the new baseline expectation”.

02:55 Shopify wasn’t the only  company going all in on AI.

02:59 Language learning platform Duolingo was next. CEO,  Luis von Ahn, told his staff the company was going

03:04 “AI-first.” It would rely on AI before hiring,  reduce the number of contractors, and weigh AI

03:10 use in performance reviews. Within a week, 148 new  courses were shipped, it was work that would take

03:17 staff years to develop. The same AI implementation  turned up at Box, at Fiverr, and other firms.

03:23 The wording barely changed. Run the software  before you ask for new hires or extra money.

03:28 Then the pushback happened.

03:29 Longtime Duolingo users filmed themselves deleting  the app in protest. Staff started asking if they

03:34 had to use AI well or just use it. Almost a year  later Luis von Ahn walked his decision back.

03:40 He acknowledged that the AI-written code was  hard to debug and the lessons weren’t reliable.

03:45 But the damage had been done.

03:47 And it was just the beginning.

03:48 The fear of AI taking jobs is real, so in the  summer of 2025, a Stanford economist named Erik

03:54 Brynjolfsson decided to look into it. His team at  the Digital Economy Lab pulled the records from

03:59 ADP, the firm that processes the payroll for  millions of American workers, and studied who

04:04 still had a job, month after month. The AI impact was real.

04:09 Just now where people expected it.

04:11 The results showed that workers aged 22 to 25  in software and customer support had dropped

04:16 about 13% since late 2022. Workers over  30 in the same roles remained stable or

04:22 actually grew. It was the people just walking  in the door that were at risk of an AI cull.

04:27 Some don’t get in the door at all.

04:29 Revelio Labs, which tracks hiring across the  economy, counts roughly 35% fewer entry-level

04:35 postings since the start of 2023. Once  employers saw what the best models could do,

04:40 many stopped graduate hiring. That freeze only  surfaced in the payroll data a year or 2 later.

04:46 Brynjolfsson’s team found that when a company  used AI to take over a task completely,

04:51 employment among younger workers fell.  When AI was used to make a person faster,

04:55 employment remained stable, and sometimes grew.

04:58 Same technology, opposite result.

05:00 Everything comes down to one decision:

05:02 does a company use AI to replace  a worker, or to back one up?

05:05 Near the bottom of the pay  scale, replacement is winning.

05:08 Salesforce froze much of its junior  hiring for a stretch and credited its

05:12 own AI for work graduates used  to do. Goldman Sachs economists

05:16 found the results. The big names  weren’t even pretending anymore.

05:19 But not every bet paid off.

05:21 Klarna, the buy-now-pay-later company, spent a  year bragging that its chatbot did the work of

05:26 hundreds of agents and that it had stopped hiring  people. They later admitted the bot gave “lower

05:32 quality” service and started hiring humans back.  But some companies didn’t see that as a reason

05:36 to slow down. They saw it as a reason to aim  lower… and the contractor was in the cross hairs.

05:42 An MIT report on AI in business found that AI  is wiping out outsourced and contract roles,

05:47 not full-time staff. In mid-2025, the  data-labeling firm Scale AI laid off 200

05:53 staff and cut ties with 500 contractors.  That same report put the share of jobs

05:57 AI can already do at roughly 3% today,  and saw it climbing over the longer run.

06:02 Graduates weren’t losing out  to people with a better resume.

06:05 They were losing out period. There was not job.

06:09 By early 2026, nearly half of employed Gen Z said  AI's risks at work now outweigh its benefits,

06:14 a jump of 11 percentage points in just one year.  And when they're handed the same piece of work,

06:20 69% overwhelmingly trust the human version over  the AI one. An entire generation now spends its

06:26 days training the technology that's replacing  the jobs they're trying to build careers in.

06:31 The lost jobs are easy enough to measure. But the resentment isn't just about money.

06:35 In July 2024, all it took was a power surge  across northern Virginia for nearly 60 data

06:40 centers to drop off the grid. Roughly 1,500  megawatts of demand vanished instantly.

06:45 Operators scrambled to get the surge under  control before it took down anything else.

06:49 For a few seconds, the densest data-center  hub in the country just wasn’t there.

06:54 Virginia holds more of these  buildings than anywhere else,

06:57 and by 2023 they were already drawing about  26% of the state’s electricity. That’s why

07:02 one voltage swing could shock the whole grid. Each of those buildings runs hot. One question

07:08 to a chatbot burns about 2.9 watt-hours,  that’s roughly 10 times a normal web search.

07:13 On its own, it’s nothing. But nobody asks just one question.

07:17 Multiply it by billions of questions a day, every  day, in warehouses that never switch off, and it

07:22 becomes 183 terawatt-hours a year. That’s about  4% of all the power the country burns. That's

07:28 already 540 kilowatt-hours running in your name  every year, whether you've ever touched a chatbot

07:34 or not. And the forecasts are only going up, as  high as 17% of the nation's electricity by 2030.

07:41 More than 40% of the power fuelling the data  centres comes from natural gas. Before the decade

07:46 is out, these buildings are set to burn more  electricity than the entire country uses to make

07:50 its steel, cement, aluminum, and chemicals… Combined.

07:54 A high-voltage line takes up to 8 years to build,  meaning a fifth of these data center projects are

07:59 about to run straight into a power shortage.  To cover the expense of these extra lines,

08:04 utilities are going to regulators to demand  more money from regular consumers. This means

08:09 your monthly expenses are going up by 2030 just to  keep the lights on at a server farm down the road.

08:15 You didn't leave your lights on or  crank up your AC, but your money

08:18 is bleeding out anyway to power the  massive cooling fans of a tech giant.

08:22 Researchers at Carnegie Mellon estimate  it could push the average American

08:26 power bill up about 8% by 2030, and in the  worst-hit parts of Virginia, north of 25%.

08:33 There simply isn’t enough  energy or money to fund it.

08:36 So, some companies got tired of waiting.

08:38 Instead of waiting years for the power  grid to catch up, they built their own

08:42 power plants beside the data centers. And  one company took that idea to the extreme.

08:47 To power Colossus, the supercomputer  training Elon Musk's Grok chatbot,

08:51 xAI deployed a fleet of gas turbines in  South Memphis.The entire site was up and

08:56 running in under 122 days, a project that  would normally take years. By the time the

09:01 Southern Environmental Law Center flew thermal  drones overhead, it counted around 35 turbines,

09:06 most of them without air permits. Just downwind sits Boxtown,

09:10 a neighborhood that has spent decades  surrounded by refineries and chemical plants.

09:14 Residents began showing up at public hearings  describing a rotten-egg smell in the air and

09:19 children wheezing through the night. Memphis  already earns an "F" for ozone pollution from

09:24 the American Lung Association, and Boxtown's  cancer risk is about 4 times the national average.

09:29 Then researchers at the University of Tennessee  analyzed satellite data for TIME and found peak

09:34 nitrogen dioxide levels near the site had jumped  roughly 79% compared with before xAI arrived.

09:41 The turbines were labelled as temporary,

09:43 a workaround that allowed them to keep running  and bypass the regulations. Lawsuits followed,

09:48 but by the time the case moved forward, the  servers had already been running for a year.

09:52 Power isn't the only resource  these data centers consume.

09:55 In Newton County, Georgia, about  an hour and a half east of Atlanta,

09:59 Beverly and Jeff Morris live 1,000 feet (305  meters) from a Meta data center. Their house

10:04 runs on a private well, which means their  drinking water comes straight out of the

10:07 ground. It worked fine for years, right up  until Meta broke ground next door in 2018.

10:13 A few months after construction began,  the water pressure slowed to a trickle,

10:17 then stopped altogether. When it eventually  came back, it was brown and murky. Beverly

10:22 Morris told the New York Times she was afraid  to drink the water coming from her own tap.

10:26 The neighboring data center uses roughly  500,000 gallons every day, nearly a tenth

10:31 of all the water Newton County pumps. County  projections show demand outpacing supply by 2030,

10:37 while residents face water bills  expected to jump 33% in just 2 years,

10:41 compared with the usual 2% increase. A Meta  funded study said the company’s operations

10:46 probably aren't to blame and has invested more  than $4.5 million in local schools and nonprofits.

10:52 Private wells like the Morrises' fall  outside the federal Safe Drinking Water Act,

10:57 so Meta didn’t break any laws. The Environmental  Protection Agency is powerless, so Meta keeps

11:02 pulling water to cool the chips. And these hubs are insatiable.

11:07 A 2023 study by UC Riverside and the University  of Texas found that training one model, GPT-3, ran

11:13 through about 5.4 million liters of fresh water…  before the public ever typed a word. The same

11:20 researchers found that a short back-and-forth,  around 100 words, consumes close to a full bottle.

11:25 One Google data center in Papillion, Nebraska,  went through about 1.5 billion liters in 2024,

11:31 more than 600 Olympic pools, and it’s one site  among thousands. That daily draw dwarfs the

11:37 one-time cost of training. Nationally, data  centers used over 60 billion liters in 2023,

11:42 and the World Resources Institute expects AI  to pass a trillion gallons a year by 2030.

11:47 In August 2025, Tucson’s city council  voted 7 to 0 to reject Project Blue,

11:53 an Amazon-linked data-center campus  that would have drained millions of

11:56 gallons of city water in the middle of a  desert. Residents had packed the chamber

12:01 for weeks under a banner that read  No Desert Data Center. For one night,

12:05 it looked like a regular city could tell a  tech giant no, and actually make it stick.

12:10 It didn’t end there.

12:11 The developer already owned land just outside  the city limits and kept building anyway. Then,

12:16 in the spring of 2026, the contractor was  caught drawing enough Tucson water to supply

12:21 5 households for a year. The city shut it  off. Mayor, Regina Romero, has been writing

12:26 ordinances to guard against the next data  center, because there’s always a next one.

12:31 Tucson wasn’t alone.

12:32 In The Dalles, Oregon, a Google plant ended up  using close to a quarter of the entire town’s

12:37 water. The company fought to keep those numbers  hidden from the public through court orders.

12:41 Newer facilities can cool with air or  closed-loop systems that use almost no

12:46 local water. Microsoft has already converted  2 Arizona sites to do exactly that. But the

12:51 biggest water users aren't the new builds,  they're the older data centers. The ones

12:55 still sucking up millions of gallons  instead of returning it to the river.

12:58 So while families shorten their showers  and wait until dark to water the lawn,

13:02 the data center down the road keeps pulling  water at full capacity, every hour, every night.

13:07 Jobs. Electricity. Water. Three separate  battles happening in different parts of

13:11 the country. But they all lead back  to the exact same business model.

13:14 In 2024 alone, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta  spent more than $200 billion building the data

13:20 centers behind AI, up over 60% in a single year.  Management consultancy firm McKinsey expects $5.2

13:27 trillion to be funnelled into them by 2030. That  money buys the land, the power, and the water.

13:33 But there’s one more thing it buys. Something  nobody signs off on: the writing, art,

13:38 and code scraped off the open internet  to train the models in the first place.

13:42 To the companies, that’s an investment  in the platform of the century. To the

13:46 creatives whose work fed it, it  looks different. Their work was

13:50 harvested for free, then rented  back to everyone by the month.

13:54 Not one of them was asked.  Not one of them got paid.

13:57 Publishers and authors have sued in waves arguing  their work was stolen and used to train AI without

14:02 permission. The courts still haven't decided  where the legal line is, and so far none of

14:06 it has been ruled illegal. But AI is built on  other people's writing, powered by other people's

14:12 electricity, cooled with other people's water… Then sold back to those same people as progress.

14:17 Now, Americans are starting to notice. The  companies insist the costs are temporary.

14:21 Google and Microsoft both promise they'll return  more water than they use by 2030 and keep shifting

14:27 to cleaner energy. But if you've already lost  your job, your power bill just went up, or your

14:32 town's water is running low, a promise four years  from now doesn't feel like much of an answer.

14:36 Between May 2024 and March 2025, that anger  blocked or delayed about $64 billion in

14:43 data-center projects nationwide, according  to Data Center Watch. In Virginia alone,

14:48 42 separate groups were working  to slow or stop new ones.

14:51 What nobody agrees on is what to do about it.

14:54 No one is demanding an outright  ban. No one is cheering it on.

14:58 There’s just a country caught between  needing the tool and resenting it.

15:02 Most of these fights end the same  way. A council denies the water,

15:05 the way Tucson did. The county next door sells  the land. A state commission signs off on the

15:11 power. The building goes up anyway, trading its  thirst for water for a heavier pull on the grid.

15:16 Residents keep learning the same lesson: the  project can almost always route around them.

15:20 This was never about whether AI would  arrive.That was inevitable. It was about

15:24 whether anyone still had the power to stop it. By the time we started asking that question,

15:29 the answer was already no. It’s not just ordinary Americans

15:32 who are losing faith in AI. The people building  it are too. Watch Why AI Researchers Are Quitting

15:38 and Panicking on the Way Out to find out why the  industry is collapsing. Or click on this video.
