docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 A man is sitting in front of his computer mindlessly scrolling down his Facebook news

00:04 feed.

00:05 He’s been feeling a bit insecure since losing his job and getting dumped by his girlfriend,

00:09 so it’s his good fortune on this particular dark day that he comes across one of those

00:13 bunkum posts that say, “If you can correctly answer these questions you have a genius-level

00:19 IQ.”

00:20 Lo and behold, like his friends before him, he scores 10 out of 10 and is rewarded with

00:24 the knowledge that he’s a genius with an IQ of over 160.

00:28 He seems blissfully unaware that most 10-year olds could get those questions right.

00:32 Nonetheless, he’s not too bright and so he shares his results, which is exactly what

00:36 the creators of the post wanted him to do.

00:39 Poor guy, if he had a higher IQ, he might be savvier to the manipulative guff that does

00:43 the rounds on social media.

00:44 Ok, so this guy knew the capital city of France and he understood that the chemical formula

00:49 for water is H2O.

00:51 He even knew that Earth was the third rock from the sun.

00:55 We hate to burst his bubble here, but that doesn’t mean he has a high IQ, far from

00:58 it.

00:59 You can’t base IQ on the ability to answer a handful of easy general knowledge questions.

01:03 There are even games of “spot of the difference” surfacing on Facebook these days, stating

01:07 that if you can spot the 10 differences you have an IQ of 180 or over.

01:13 Before we tell you how you can easily improve your own IQ, you need to know a few things

01:17 about what IQ actually means.

01:20 Its full name is intelligence quotient.

01:22 Such standardized tests have been around since the late 19th century, with their purpose

01:26 being to help judge a person’s intelligence.

01:29 Sometimes the tests were given to see if a person’s background, often a child, affects

01:33 their intelligence.

01:34 For example, does poverty affect IQ, or does bloodline make a difference?

01:38 During the First World War, the American Army gave new recruits such intelligence tests

01:42 so it could try and judge what a person could or couldn’t do.

01:45 It still does that now.

01:47 Later, industry and education started using such tests.

01:50 There are lots of different IQ tests, but if you’ve ever taken one that has a vast

01:54 number of questions and gives you a headache, you’ll know that to get a lot of questions

01:58 right you’ll need to be good at a few things.

02:01 Those are usually arithmetic, abstract reasoning, logic, vocabulary, and spatial reasoning.

02:06 Other tests focus more on memory.

02:08 The average IQ is around 100.

02:10 If you score over 145, you are in the top 0.1 percentile.

02:15 If you get below 70 you are in the bottom 2.1 percentile.

02:17 We shouldn’t have to say it, but if you can spot a missing cat paw on a sketch it

02:22 has no bearing whatsoever on your IQ.

02:24 In fact, if you fell for that test it would likely mean that your reasoning faculties

02:28 are not top-notch.

02:29 It’s not easy scoring well past 100.

02:32 Singapore citizens have the highest average IQ in the world at 108.

02:36 China is 105.

02:37 Switzerland is the highest European nation at an average of 102.

02:41 Canada is the highest in the Americas at an average of 99.

02:44 The U.S. average is 98.

02:46 The UK average is 100.

02:48 Brazil is just 87.

02:49 India, 81.

02:50 South Africa, 77.

02:52 Don’t fear if you did a test and were below average, because between 85 and 115 is considered

02:58 in the normal range.

02:59 There are different kinds of intelligence, too.

03:01 No doubt a gifted computer programmer would score high in a general IQ test, but someone

03:06 who’d grown up farming in a hill tribe in South East Asia would likely score low.

03:10 Ask that programmer to survive up in those hills and for all his intelligence, he’d

03:14 likely fail.

03:15 All the same, if that farmer had an IQ higher than his peers he might be faster than them

03:20 deducing tricky problems on the farm.

03:22 You might have an average IQ and still write a novel or a historical piece of nonfiction

03:26 that will be read for centuries to come because your insights were outstanding.

03:30 There are also plenty of people with genius-level IQs who struggle to get a job.

03:34 Still, a high IQ overall is an indicator of success.

03:38 Although social class is way more important when it comes to making it in life.

03:42 Success also often depends on the environment you grew up in.

03:45 You might only have an average intelligence but were schooled at Eton, where British political

03:49 leaders and other ruthless capitalists often cut their teeth.

03:52 You could have a high intelligence in Britain but were schooled at a place nicknamed the

03:56 “Zoo” and grew up with selfish parents that at best acknowledged your existence when

04:00 feeding you your meager daily ration of baked beans on toast.

04:03 But if you had parents that instilled in you self-confidence, perseverance, self-awareness,

04:08 open-mindedness, creative thinking, critical thinking- well, that could work out well,

04:12 even if you are poor.

04:13 There are so many factors when it comes to success, including having lady luck on your

04:17 side, but in general, a high IQ is better than a low IQ when it comes to getting by

04:22 in the world of work.

04:23 But again, we must point out the environment you grew up in.

04:26 Poverty and trauma is a serious issue that should never be overlooked when considering

04:31 intelligence.

04:32 For centuries the wealthy folks in the world have looked down on the poor for their alleged

04:35 low intelligence, calling them names like white trash.

04:38 It’s not as if those rich folks were born with big brains.

04:41 Their success was simply down to where they were born, in some cases at least.

04:45 Before we get to the teaching part of the video, let’s look at some examples of high

04:48 IQs in the real world.

04:51 You have an American man named Richard Rosner.

04:53 His IQ is off the charts.

04:55 He’s scored 190 on some tests.

04:57 He’s had some strange jobs, too, at one time working as a nude model and another time

05:01 working as a bouncer.

05:02 Then there’s the Greek man, Evangelos Katsioulis.

05:05 With an IQ of around 198, he’s said to have one of the highest IQs in the entire world.

05:10 He currently works as a psychiatrist in Greece and is also the founder of the World Intelligence

05:15 Network.

05:16 The South Korean/Japanese man named Sho Yano started college at the young age of nine and

05:20 had a Ph.D. by the time he was 21.

05:22 His IQ is an astounding 200.

05:24 This former child genius now works in child neurology.

05:28 The Guinness Book of Records once had an American woman named Marilyn vos Savant as having the

05:33 highest IQ.

05:34 She once scored 228 on an IQ test, although some people have questioned the formula used

05:39 on that test.

05:40 Still, she’s a genius, there’s no doubt about that.

05:42 These people seemed to do well in life, giving strength to the theory that high IQ leads

05:47 to success.

05:48 But what about the American guy named Nathan Leopold?

05:51 He had an IQ of around 200, but he ended up in prison for committing murder.

05:55 He thought he was so darn clever that he could commit the crime of the century and get away

05:59 with it, but he was wrong.

06:00 At a young age, he was obsessed with German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche’s theory

06:04 of the “Superman”.

06:05 It seems a lot of people who take this route end up in dark places, including Mr. Hitler.

06:10 Perhaps humility is a sign of intelligence, too.

06:12 By the way, Nietzsche hated nationalism and he certainly was not an anti-Semite, but some

06:17 people don’t have the intelligence to see that.

06:20 Ok, so some of you might already know you have a high IQ because you’ve taken the

06:24 tests or you were dubbed a child genius after getting your physics degree at age 12.

06:28 But, we are guessing that most of you watching this are average when it comes to IQ.

06:33 The question is, would it help you to have a higher IQ?

06:35 The answer to that depends on what you want in life and what you think a high IQ will

06:39 get you.

06:40 We had a look at a study that was undertaken to try and compare certain IQs with various

06:44 jobs.

06:45 That doesn’t mean that all workers of one job will have an IQ close to other workers

06:48 in that job, but some occupations on average seem to be filled with higher or lower IQs.

06:53 Janitors, for instance, were at the lower end of the scale with an average IQ spanning

06:57 from about 75 to 110.

06:59 Auto mechanics ranged from 75 to 118.

07:02 High school teachers from 92 to 126, and at the top of the scale were college professors.

07:07 They scored on average from the high 90s to over 130.

07:11 Physicians scored ever higher, from 106 to over 130.

07:14 What this means of course is you can be an auto mechanic or a janitor with the same IQ

07:18 as a college professor, but in general, if you work as a professor or a doctor, your

07:22 IQ will likely be higher than that of a janitor.

07:24 From what we can see, a lot of the high-paying jobs employ people with higher IQs.

07:28 If you want a higher paying job, then, maybe improving your IQ couldn’t hurt.

07:32 You’d think that just by taking lots and lots of tests, you’d be able to improve

07:35 your IQ score.

07:36 That’s actually debatable.

07:37 It might work, it might not.

07:39 There’s a saying that goes, “The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and

07:43 over again, but expecting different results.”

07:45 This maxim is often attributed to Albert Einstein, but he never said it.

07:49 The saying is kind of true, though.

07:51 If you want to improve at something it’s better to explore different avenues as to

07:54 the problem you want to solve, in this case, your IQ score.

07:58 One thing that has seen positive results in doing just that is working on your memory.

08:02 According to studies we found, a better memory can help you to attain a higher standard of

08:06 something called, “fluid intelligence.”

08:08 You need good fluid intelligence to attain a high IQ score because it relates to solving

08:12 problems on your feet, meaning you don’t have the key to the problem but you can figure

08:16 it out.

08:17 That’s what a real IQ test will have in wait for you; lots of tricky problems you

08:21 haven’t seen before.

08:22 During one study, participants all had to take tests relating to their fluid intelligence.

08:26 But, some people took the tests without any memory training and others had some memory

08:30 training.

08:31 By memory, we mean, working memory, which refers to the memory you use for temporary

08:35 tasks.

08:36 If we say the words, sheep, ghost, Steve Jobs, Ukraine, blue, incredible, and we tell you

08:41 to repeat that to us in 10 seconds, you’re using your working memory.

08:45 In the tests in the study, each time someone was asked to remember something, there was

08:49 never any pattern.

08:50 Each test was different, making the person think on their feet.

08:53 There was no key to the puzzle.

08:54 Each time they had to adapt to a different test.

08:56 This in fact was training their brains, and as you know, being able to think on your feet

09:00 is good for IQ tests.

09:02 Once those people were good at solving the memory questions, they were asked to take

09:05 the fluid memory test, as were the people in the study that hadn’t done the memory

09:09 tests.

09:10 What was the outcome?

09:11 The researchers said that those who’d taken the memory tests showed a striking difference

09:15 in how they fared with the fluid intelligence test.

09:18 Their conclusion was: “Our findings are of general significance

09:20 because they provide evidence for enhancement of fluid intelligence by cognitive training

09:25 different from training the test itself.”

09:27 By different, they mean you don’t have to train at an IQ test to necessarily become

09:32 better at it.

09:33 You can just improve your working memory.

09:34 To do this yourself, just go online and find working memory tests.

09:38 There are tons of them.

09:39 The researchers said their work was remarkable because it has always been thought that fluid

09:44 intelligence wasn’t something that could be improved.

09:46 It was previously thought to be innate, unchangeable, but it isn’t.

09:50 We suggest you take an IQ test before you do this and see what score you get.

09:54 Then do the memory tests and do them until you see some improvement.

09:57 After that, take the IQ test again, or one that is similar, and then see what score you

10:01 get.

10:02 If the researchers are right, you might just see an improvement.

10:05 The brain’s elastic, or what people often say, a muscle, so don’t go thinking you

10:09 can’t improve.

10:10 You can.

10:11 So, even though you might think you need to be going online and doing lots of IQ tests,

10:15 it’s working memory improvement that will get you ahead.

10:18 If you’ve done IQ tests, you’ll also know a lot of questions relate to spatial awareness.

10:23 That can be putting shapes in the right place.

10:25 Believe it or not, just by doing jigsaw puzzles you can improve upon this.

10:29 You can also play games where objects are put in a certain place, then removed, and

10:33 subsequently, the person has to tell someone to put the object back in the right place

10:37 with words.

10:38 Like the star of the Netflix series, “The Queen’s Gambit”, you could also imagine

10:41 playing chess in your head.

10:43 This will train what’s called, “Spatial Cognition.”

10:45 There are other games you can play that might help you to solve problems on an IQ test,

10:49 as long as they are problem-solving games.

10:52 Take Scrabble for instance, in that game you not only have to create the highest-scoring

10:56 words but you have to place a word in a sometimes-complex grid of letters.

11:00 You use something called your executive functions when you play games like Scrabble or similar

11:05 games.

11:06 These functions are what you need to solve challenges that are sometimes not anticipated.

11:09 Again, you have to think on your feet, and if you play such games, you can improve your

11:13 fluid intelligence.

11:15 Many games that ask you to think outside the box to attain a good score could help you

11:19 improve your IQ score.

11:20 When doing these tests, you can’t rely on old habits, and you can’t just be impulsive,

11:25 you need this ability to look at things from all angles.

11:28 We found another study relating to the improvement of fluid intelligence, called, “Multi-modal

11:32 fitness and cognitive training to enhance fluid intelligence.”

11:36 That’s a bit of a mouthful.

11:37 In layman's terms, it means doing different stuff to train your brain to solve problems

11:41 you might not have seen before.

11:43 They took 424 healthy adults and split them up.

11:47 Some did just fitness training.

11:48 Others did fitness along with cognitive training.

11:51 Others did those two but with some added meditation.

11:54 The last group did nothing.

11:55 The long and short of this was the people that did the training were better at visuospatial

11:59 reasoning, which means moving objects around and knowing where things should go.

12:03 Those people then performed better on fluid intelligence tests.

12:07 So, like those study participants, you could do the same.

12:10 Try and keep fit; play some cognitive games online, and maybe even practice some mindfulness.

12:14 There’s no solid proof that things like learning a second language or reading books

12:18 will help you improve your IQ score, but learning a new language does make you think about how

12:23 language is constructed.

12:25 This might help you with the verbal reasoning part of the test.

12:27 As for reading books, well, you should try it.

12:29 It’s massively underrated, and the more you read, the less likely you’ll end up

12:33 playing spot the difference so you can bask in the warmth of having a completely unsubstantiated

12:38 high IQ score.

12:39 We’ll finish with a real quote from Einstein, something very relevant to you getting a better

12:43 brain, “One should not pursue goals that are easily achieved.

12:47 One must develop an instinct for what one can just barely achieve through one's greatest

12:51 efforts.”

12:52 Now you need to watch, “How To ACTUALLY Learn Anything (The Feynman Technique)”.

12:56 Or, have a look at, “Scientifically Proven Best Ways to Study.”

00:00 PROFESSOR: Independent events are events that have nothing

00:02 to do with each other.

00:04 And needless to say, it's a lot easier to work with them

00:07 because you don't have to figure out

00:09 some weird interaction between two events that

00:11 do have something to do with each other.

00:13 Typical case where independent events come up

00:16 is, for example, you toss a coin five times,

00:19 and then you're about to toss a coin the sixth time.

00:21 Is there any reason to think that

00:23 what the coins did the first five times is going

00:25 to have any influence on the flip

00:27 of the coin for the sixth time?

00:30 Well, it's reasonable to assume not,

00:33 which is to say that the outcome of the sixth toss

00:36 is arguably independent of the outcome of all

00:40 the previous tosses.

00:42 OK.

00:43 Let's look at a formal definition

00:46 now in this short video of just what

00:48 is the technical definition of independent events.

00:51 So what we said is that they are independent if they have

00:54 nothing to do with each other.

00:55 What that means is that if I tell you that B happened,

00:59 it doesn't have any effect on the probability of A. That is,

01:03 the probability of A, given that B happened,

01:06 doesn't change the probability of A at all.

01:09 That's it.

01:10 Now this is one definition.

01:11 Maybe this is the more intuitive definition.

01:13 But another definition that's equivalent and is standard

01:16 is that two events are equivalent if the product

01:19 of their probabilities is equal to the probability

01:22 that they both happen, that is, the probability

01:24 of their intersection.

01:25 Now definition one and definition two

01:27 are trivial equivalent, just using the definition

01:30 of conditional probability.

01:32 And if you don't see that, this would be a moment

01:34 to stop, get a pencil and paper, and write down

01:38 the three-line proof of the equivalence of these two

01:43 equalities.

01:44 In fact, the three-line proof has this as the first line

01:46 and that as the second line.

01:47 So you could argue it's really just the middle line

01:49 that you're adding.

01:51 OK.

01:53 Definition two has the slight advantage that it always works,

01:56 whereas definition one implicitly

01:58 requires that the divisor-- remember probability of A given

02:03 B is defined as the probability of the intersection divided

02:06 by the probability B. It's only defined if the probability of B

02:09 is positive.

02:10 Whereas the second definition always works,

02:12 so we don't have to put a proviso

02:15 in about the probability of B being non-zero.

02:17 So that's the definition of independence.

02:19

02:22 Looking at this definition, what you can see immediately

02:24 is that it's completely symmetric in A and B.

02:27 Since multiplication is commutative

02:28 and intersection is commutative, which is A

02:31 and which is B doesn't matter.

02:33 And what that implies then is that A is independent of B

02:36 if and only if B is independent of A.

02:41 Now another fact that holds is that if the probability of B

02:45 happens to be zero, then vacuously B

02:49 is independent of everything-- even itself.

02:52 Which isn't important, but is a small technicality that's worth

02:56 remembering by that definition.

03:00 Now again, the intuitive idea that A and B have nothing

03:03 to do with each other is that A is independent of B means

03:07 that A is independent of whether or not B occurs.

03:11 That is to say, if A is independent of B,

03:13 it ought to be independent of the complement of B.

03:16 And that's a lemma that's also easily proved.

03:18 A is independent of B if and only

03:20 if A is independent of the complement of B.

03:23 It's a simple proof using the difference rule.

03:26 And again, I encourage you to stop

03:28 with a piece of paper and a pencil

03:31 and convince yourself that that follows with a one-line proof.

03:35

docs.text:
00:00 Right now, millions of people have nicotine

00:02 bleeding into their system. And  they don’t even need to be awake.

00:05 When Big Tobacco was staring down the barrel of  vaping taxes and bans, they didn’t panic. They

00:10 already had the answer… a nicotine pouch that  slips under your lip and drip-feeds you a fix.

00:16 They found a loophole to bypass  restrictions and make your addiction

00:19 completely invisible. They killed the  cloud and pivoted to a ghost habit.

00:23 And you can’t escape it.

00:25 For decades, tobacco firms had society in a  vice like grip. Cigarette smoke was a part

00:29 of everyday life, and no one thought  twice about it. The toxic haze was a

00:33 permanent fixture in restaurants, theaters,  bars and even airplanes. Children were seen

00:38 as the next generation of customers while  corporations pocketed billions in profits.

00:42 Then it all came crashing down.

00:44 The truth about cancer and lung disease risks  came out. Cigarettes weren’t just unhealthy,

00:49 they were a major risk factor in millions of  deaths. Suddenly, anti-smoking PSAs flooded

00:54 the airwaves. Governments banned smoking in public  places and raised the legal smoking age. Companies

00:59 like Philip Morris were forced to pay massive  settlements to the government, slap graphic

01:03 warning labels on their packs, and fund the  anti-smoking message that was out to destroy them.

01:08 The golden age of smoking was over.

01:11 But millions were still addicted.

01:12 Quitting nicotine is like a form of  psychological warfare. It triggers

01:16 a deep-seated urge to pick up a  cigarette. It robs you of sleep,

01:20 destroys your concentration and takes you  on a rollercoaster of frustration, sadness,

01:24 or anxiety. There’s also an insatiable urge to  replace the craving with another destructive

01:29 habit, like excessive eating. The odds of  successfully quitting are less than 10%.

01:34 There was a market of desperate people.

01:36 And Big Tobacco was ready to swoop in.

01:38 There’s nothing a company loves more than to  be able to capitalize on consumer weakness.

01:43 And that includes the people trying  to escape. The first products aimed

01:46 at creating ex-smokers had a simple  pitch: painless weaning. They were

01:51 marketed as tools to take the edge off the  process and slowly draw down the dependence.

01:56 After all, it's not the nicotine  that’s the problem… not really.

02:00 Nicotine is the active, addictive hook,  but the real killer in cigarettes is the

02:04 toxic cocktail produced by burning tobacco. Tar  especially has devastating long-term effects on

02:10 the lungs and increases cancer risks. By  isolating the nicotine and delivering it

02:15 via an alternative method meant the cigarette  companies could have their cake and eat it.

02:20 First came nicotine gum in delivering a low oral  dose of nicotine directly into the system. Then

02:25 came nicotine patches that pumped a slow,  steady dose of nicotine through the skin.

02:30 They were helpful.

02:31 But they weren’t satisfying.

02:33 They made it easier to quit, but they weren’t  scratching the itch. Smoking isn’t just a chemical

02:37 hit, it's a psychological ritual. People find  the oral sensation an important part of calming

02:42 down. Sure, nicotine gum gives something to chew  on, but for millions of users, it wasn’t enough.

02:48 They needed something more.

02:50 And the tobacco companies  were always ready to innovate.

02:53 When vaping pens hit the market around  2003, they gave the same hit as smoking,

02:57 but without any of the toxins. Or so it seemed.  It was quick, easy and incredibly appealing.

03:03 Too appealing for some.

03:04 A combination of anti-smoking PSAs, heavy  taxes on cigarettes, and strict enforcement

03:08 of age limits heavily reduced the number  of teens who smoked. And vaping undid all

03:13 of that. No one wanted to smoke cigarettes, but  puffing cotton candy vapor out of an electronic

03:18 device? Gen Z was suddenly intrigued. Soon,  there was a massive surge in teen vaping,

03:24 even though the devices were still  supposed to be for 18 and over.

03:27 The inevitable crackdown soon followed.

03:29 As vaping use by young people skyrocketed,  the health risks became hard to ignore.

03:34 Reports of severe lung issues saw states  started cracking down on the practice.

03:38 Suddenly getting a vape pen became as hard as  getting a cigarette. Flavored cartridges were

03:42 banned. States started levying heavy taxes on  vapes, turning a cheap habit into a luxury.

03:48 So… it was time to build a better mousetrap.

03:50 One of the biggest challenges of creating an  alternative to smoking is the social element.

03:55 Designated smoking areas are rare and vapes  are mostly banned indoors. and those typically

04:00 include electronic cigarettes by now. The only  real alternatives left are gum and patches,

04:05 but those are designed to dull the need  for a fix but not to give a full hit.

04:09 Big Tobacco needed a way to  deliver the hit in secret.

04:13 And Scandinavia had the blueprint.

04:15 In Sweden, one of the most popular ways to  get a nicotine hit is with snus. It’s a small

04:20 pouch packed with finely ground tobacco  leaves that sits under the upper lip.

04:24 Nicotine slowly soaks into their gum  over the course of the day. However,

04:28 it does have many of the negatives of  smoking, including all the oral effects

04:32 of chewing tobacco, including damage  to the gums and yellowing of the teeth.

04:36 But what if you remove the tobacco entirely?

04:39 Enter the nicotine pouch, a seemingly clean  alternative to chewing tobacco and other oral

04:43 nicotine options. Instead of using tobacco,  it’s composed of plant fibers infused with

04:48 pharmaceutical-grade nicotine powder. It’s tucked  under the lip and absorbed through the gums.

04:53 Far more potent than nicotine gum, it’s  an unobtrusive way for former smokers or

04:57 vapers to get their nicotine through the day  without smoking or wearing nicotine patches.

05:02 It’s all a little too easy.

05:04 And that might just be the point.

05:05 The official instructions for using nicotine  pouches say they should be used for 30 to 60

05:10 minutes at a time and then discarded.  But that’s not how it winds up being

05:14 used. Slipping the pouch under the lip becomes  second nature after a while. The result is that

05:19 people forget about it and enjoy having  it there, keeping the pouches there for

05:23 hours at a time. Even when they fall asleep.  While a heavy vaper might use their device

05:28 for an hour or 2 a day, pouch users might  have it in their mouth for 16 hours a day.

05:33 It was perfect… in more ways than one.

05:36 Right now, nicotine pouches are the cheapest  way to feed the addiction. And the tendrils

05:40 of Big Tobacco are all over them. They are  manufactured by the same brands that sell vapes,

05:45 gums, and patches. And most of them are owned  by the giant tobacco firms. For decades,

05:49 they’ve seen their profits collapse due to  smoking bans and heavy taxation. Each time

05:53 a new regulation targets smokers, they pivot.  They just find a loophole to bypass the laws.

05:58 And for now, they may have succeeded.

06:01 Currently, all 50 states have excise taxes  on cigarettes, while an additional 34 states

06:06 and the District of Columbia have extra  taxes on vaping products. By contrast,

06:10 only 21 states have taxes on all nicotine  products. That means that in 29 states,

06:15 nicotine pouches slip under the radar. Users  can get tins of these addictive, nicotine-packed

06:20 tabs without having to pay any extra money.  Combined with how long each one lasts and the

06:25 affordable price of a tin, many former smokers  and vapers have turned to them as an alternative.

06:30 But what is it doing under the surface?

06:32 If there’s one thing tobacco companies are  known for, it’s claiming that their products

06:35 are safe. At least until they’re forced to  admit otherwise. First, there were decades

06:40 of campaigns that portrayed smoking not just as  fine, but fashionable and good for your health.

06:44 Then came vaping, which was portrayed as a  harmless alternative… until all the evidence

06:49 of lung disorders leaked in the press. Now,  nicotine pouches are being painted as the version

06:53 of this habit that removes all the risk factors.  There’s no tobacco after all. No stained teeth,

06:58 no black tar flooding into your lungs,  and no mysterious electronically treated

07:02 vapors being breathed in. Just you, and a  simple white pouch containing pure nicotine.

07:07 It seems too good to be true.

07:09 And it probably is.

07:10 The pull of nicotine is strong, but  the social habit is just as hard to

07:14 crack. It was never about eliminating  the habit, but finding the version of

07:18 it with the fewest side effects. If you  listen to the corporate PR, both are safe

07:22 alternatives to cigarettes. But behind the  scenes, a very different story is emerging.

07:27 And one has been racking up a body count.

07:29 A vape looks like a simple, sleek device.  It bypasses the poisonous tar-filled smoke

07:34 of traditional tobacco by vaporizing a  liquid blend of chemicals and flavorings.

07:38 It should cause the same damage as a cigarette.

07:41 But it does its damage in a different way.

07:44 The biggest risk with vapes is that people weren’t  supposed to inhale this stuff. The superheated

07:48 vapor has a subtle effect on the body as it gets  absorbed into the body. The most obvious effect

07:53 is in our skin. Much of the water that leaves  the body is through transepidermal water loss,

07:58 where moisture passes through our skin and  evaporates into the air. Vaping disrupts that,

08:03 accelerating moisture loss, causing  dehydration and reducing blood flow.

08:07 The rest of the damage is even harder to detect… Until it hits home.

08:11 For those with pre-existing lung issues  like asthma, heavy use of vaping has been

08:14 shown to increase the risk of flare-ups.  It’s an even bigger risk during pregnancy,

08:18 with direct links to heavy use and children  born with lung issues. But in some cases,

08:23 the flare-up can be life-threatening.  That’s what happened to Ryan, who started

08:26 vaping during college. He was soon addicted,  loving the ability to vape whenever he wanted.

08:31 But soon, it would catch up to him.

08:33 It started with what felt like an upper  respiratory infection that regular medication

08:37 couldn’t shift. Just days later, Ryan suffered  a sudden respiratory collapse and was hooked

08:41 up to a ventilator. He was ultimately  diagnosed with a rare form of pneumonia,

08:46 caused by vaping while sick. Bacteria had  aggressively spread through his lungs, riddling

08:51 his entire system with blood clots. Things were  so serious, Ryan was touch and go for weeks.

08:56 That’s the scariest thing about vaping…  we don’t fully know all the dangers yet.

09:00 And it’s the same with nicotine pouches.

09:02 Oral nicotine fixes are nothing new, but the  older forms died out for a reason. Chewing

09:07 tobacco was consigned to history because  of oral cancer, teeth discoloration and

09:11 bad breath. Snus was more popular abroad,  but never caught on over here. However,

09:16 nicotine pouches were designed  to be unobtrusive, smell-free,

09:19 and easy to use without any ill effects… assuming  that they were used as they were described.

09:24 But with addiction, that’s never a safe bet.

09:27 Nicotine patches were designed for a similar  purpose as the pouches, but they’re also designed

09:31 to be taken off regularly. Wearing a nicotine  patch that never comes off, even during sleep,

09:36 will create a whole new kind of dependence.  And that’s what someone who keeps the pouch

09:40 in their mouth at all times does to themselves.  Many people are essentially using one per day,

09:45 only replacing it when they wake  up and it’s run out of nicotine.

09:48 But the long-term effects are still unknown.

09:51 For decades, the tobacco industry has been  hunting for the holy grail. A way to sell

09:54 their products without running afoul  of regulations or killing their users.

09:59 And pouches are the closest they’ve come.

10:01 Because they contain no actual tobacco or harmful  chemicals, they’re classified as non-carcinogenic.

10:06 They don’t require smoke, they don’t produce  a cloud and they leave the lungs untouched. On

10:10 paper, it looks perfect. But there’s a catch.

10:13 They might bypass the lungs, but they  go straight for the heart. Nicotine is

10:17 a highly potent stimulant. When you  feed your body a 16 hour daily fix,

10:21 your entire cardiovascular  system is put under stress.

10:24 And these pouches pack a punch.

10:26 Studies show that nicotine pouches are the most  potent option for nicotine delivery so far. 30-MG

10:32 pouches deliver twice as much nicotine into  the bloodstream as cigarettes. They also reach

10:36 the clinical maximum of release in around 30 to  60 minutes, as opposed to only 5 to 10 minutes

10:42 for vapes, meaning they’re meant to be used for  longer. Anti-tobacco agencies might acknowledge

10:47 that pouches are the lesser of two evils  due to the lack of additional toxic content,

10:52 but the long-term effects on the body’s critical  systems are unknown. Especially if people continue

10:56 to regularly overuse them, leaching every  last drop of nicotine out of the pouch.

11:01 But the biggest threat may be to the entry point.

11:04 Anytime something goes in the mouth, there’s  the risk of accidental ingestion. Especially

11:08 among children. Poison control data  indicates that between 2020 and 2023,

11:13 there was a 763% increase in accidental  ingestion by kids who found their parents pouches

11:19 But even when used as intended,  they might not be completely safe.

11:23 Early studies have shown that frequent use  of nicotine pouches can have some of the same

11:27 effects as snus and chewing tobacco, including  irritation, gum recession, and painful white spots

11:32 on the gums. It’s not clear if this is related  to oral cancer yet, because the pouches haven’t

11:37 been around long enough for long-term studies.  Despite these early warning signs, most doctors

11:41 acknowledge that the pouches are likely the  safest current alternative to smoking or vaping.

11:46 And for Big Tobacco, that’s a lifeline.

11:49 The companies have always been adaptable.  Every time they take a loss in the court of

11:53 public opinion, they shift to a new alternative.  And the shift to smokeless alternatives has been

11:57 a gold mine. Phillip Morris International was  hit the heaviest of the surviving companies by

12:02 Big Tobacco lawsuits. But by 2024, a full 39.3%  of their revenue was smoke-free alternatives.

12:08 They built a billion dollar safety net just as  the younger generation abandoned cigarettes.

12:14 Then came the gold rush.

12:15 Companies like Zyn completely  revolutionized the industry by

12:18 importing the pouches to the U.S..  The Swedish brand watched their

12:22 sales explode by over 60%. For a long  time, they dominated the pouch market.

12:27 And it’s not the only area where they’re winning.

12:29 For years, Juul was king of the e-cigarette  world, being the dominant force in flavored

12:33 vapes that took off among the young. But as  the reports of complications increased and

12:37 the public mood shifted against them,  they were forced to drop many of their

12:40 eye-catching flavors and cater primarily  to ex-smokers. Their presence dropped off,

12:45 and Zyn’s increased, to the point where now,  Zyn has more mentions than Juul on social media.

12:50 And it all plays into a victory  that’s been a long time coming.

12:54 For decades, the death of big tobacco has been  looming. They were devastated by lawsuits and

12:58 regulations that turned their product from a  cultural icon into a literal death sentence.

13:03 But now, they’ve created a better mousetrap,  one that hits the brain’s pleasure centers

13:07 to create a slow, chemical drip. They claim  to have solved the health crisis associated

13:11 with their products. They claim to have  found a way to feed addictions without

13:14 any additional damage. They claim this  is the future of the tobacco industry.

13:19 But… they said the same about  cigarettes and vapes too.

13:22 Everyone is going to have an opinion  about which method is safe. But what

13:25 happens the second you take a hit?  Watch ‘What Nicotine REALLY Does

13:29 to Your Body’ to find out what’s  really going on. Or click this.

00:36 same thing about their very first hit. It’s like a  super-orgasm, like your brain is on a rocket ship

00:42 on a mission to planet Euphoria, or as one user  said, you feel “like Superman for ten minutes.”

00:47 And there’s the problem: ten minutes. It might  even be less, more like five minutes. Another

00:53 crack user said his first time featured “orgasmic  feelings running up and down my spine, exploding

00:58 into infinity.” And at the end of that very  positive review, he said, “Best 5 minutes EVER.”

01:04 After the intense blast-off, your spaceship  comes hurtling back down to Earth and lands

01:08 with a resounding thud. That’s when the novice  user might utter the infamous words, “Have you

01:13 got any more?” Crack is very moreish. Over 6  million people over the age of 12 in the U.S.

01:19 will know this, because statistically, they’ve  tried crack at least once in their lifetime.

01:24 When you snort the powder version of cocaine, the  drug enters your bloodstream via blood vessels

01:28 in your nose, which is a longer route to get all  those happy chemicals - mainly dopamine - flooding

01:34 into what experts call your brain’s “hedonic  hotspots.” When you take a hit of a crack pipe,

01:38 the smoke hits your lungs and disperses into  your bloodstream fast, making the high immediate.

01:43 So, you take that first hit of the pipe-  your heart rate suddenly increases,

01:47 your pupils dilate, and your blood pressure  and temperature rise. If you do too much,

01:52 you might feel restless and a  bit anxious. As you’ll see later,

01:55 some people can get very aggressive.  They can become paranoid and delusional.

01:59 With all these quick and intense changes going  on in the body there’s the risk of overdose,

02:04 even on your first time. Maybe you didn’t get the  memo about not overloading your pipe. At best,

02:09 you might just feel nauseous, but at worst,  you could be on your way to an early death.

02:13 If you live in North America, you have the added  danger of your crack possibly being mixed with

02:18 fentanyl, the US’s public enemy number one.  In a 2023 study, 12–15% of cocaine samples

02:24 that went to a lab contained this very strong  synthetic opiate. Experts are calling this era of

02:30 contamination the “fourth wave” of the opioid  crisis, meaning a new wave of deaths. A guy

02:35 in the US was recently sentenced to 16 years in  prison because the crack he sold was mixed with

02:40 fentanyl and four people died in a single day. The National Institutes of Drug Abuse, or NIDA,

02:46 said there were just over 27,000 overdose  deaths from cocaine mixed with opioids,

02:51 mostly fentanyl, in 2022. For most of  the 2000s, it was less than 5,000 a year.

02:57 NIDA said there have been many deaths  involving all kinds of stimulants,

03:00 stating that drug overdose deaths involving  stimulants rose from around 12,000 in

03:05 2015 to over 57,000 in 2022. Nearly 70% of  stimulant-involved overdose deaths in 2022 also

03:13 involved fentanyl. From 2000 to 2014, the death  rates were anywhere from about 3,000 to 10,000.

03:20 But you don’t need fentanyl to die on crack. Your blood vessels constrict, your heart starts

03:26 to beat like a drum and bass song, and your blood  pressure goes through the roof. This might be more

03:30 intense because you’ve been drinking alcohol.  When you mix the two, a psychoactive metabolite

03:35 called cocaethylene can be produced, which makes  the whole crack experience even more intense.

03:40 It can lead to cocaethylene toxicity, which  is associated with seizures, liver damage,

03:45 and compromised functioning of the immune  system. It’s said that cocaethylene can

03:49 make the risk of an immediate death  on crack 18 to 25 times more likely.

03:54 In a study of 124 dead crack users in the 1990s,  10% of the deaths were from an overdose. The

04:01 rest died from diseases and murder. So, even on that first time, you can

04:05 draw the short straw by doing the wrong pipe. Maybe you keep hitting that pipe all night,

04:09 and then suddenly you have chest pain. This might  be acute cocaine toxicity, which can have lethal

04:15 effects on the cardiovascular system. You can  die from stroke or a heart attack. Many of the

04:19 cocaine-related ER visits in the US are people  complaining of chest pain. Since coke inflames

04:24 the heart muscle, and makes it harder for the  heart to contract, the pain could be an aortic

04:29 rupture. We guess another term for that is an  exploding heart, but don’t quote us on that.

04:34 You can even overheat like an old car you’ve  decided to floor all the way to Las Vegas, leaving

04:38 you slumped on the ground dying from hypothermia. And then there is the risk of seizures. This

04:42 can also happen on your first-ever crack  odyssey, especially if you hit that pipe hard.

04:47 In 1986, the American basketball star Len  Bias, took some cocaine, not crack cocaine,

04:52 had a seizure and died. The medical examiner  said the normal electrical control of his

04:57 heartbeat was interrupted, resulting in the  sudden onset of seizures and cardiac arrest.

05:02 We don’t know how much coke he’d done in  his life, but he was 22 and supremely fit,

05:07 and we doubt his career allowed him to be stoned  every day of the week. You obviously don’t have to

05:12 be a chronic abuser to go down with a seizure. But let’s say you survived your first night on

05:17 crack and like so many people on this planet,  you gave it another shot. While crack isn’t as

05:21 physically addictive as a drug like heroin, it’s  very, very psychologically addictive. In 2022,

05:28 about 920,000 people aged 12 or older in the  US bought crack, but it’s not certain how many

05:33 kept buying it. It’s thought about 10-20%  of users in general will become addicted.

05:38 You being you – you never do things by halves  – you started smoking enough rocks to power a

05:43 train. One of the problems with this was extreme  agitation. You became paranoid during your daily

05:48 binges, just like 68 to 84% of users who do  crack long-term. One day you looked out of the

05:54 window one day and swore you saw FBI agents hiding  in the garden. This was cocaine-induced psychosis,

05:59 a fear and loathing which can  happen to 55% of habitual users.

06:04 All that dopamine rushing around your brain  has a downside, which is anger, aggressiveness,

06:09 hallucinations, delusions, and other psychotic  symptoms. The extra norepinephrine, a hormone,

06:14 that crack gives you also doesn’t help. It  puts you in a super alert state all the time,

06:19 so you’re constantly in fight or flight mode,  which is bad for your heart and blood pressure,

06:23 but also messes with your mind. As we said at the start,

06:26 the worst thing that can happen when you lose  your mind on crack is delirium, not just a

06:30 paranoid hallucination, but all-out delirium. This can actually kill you. Medical papers call

06:35 it “excited delirium” although we particularly  like the term “acute exhaustive mania.” In 2005,

06:42 a man in the US had a fight with cops outside a  fast food restaurant. The man was restrained then

06:47 collapsed and died. Excited delirium was blamed. Being held down seems to make it worse. In

06:53 a study, coked-up rats also  didn’t like being restrained,

06:56 dying more often than coked-up rats allowed  to run around and do drug-fuelled rat things.

07:01 So, now you’ve been on crack for a while, you’ve  experienced paranoia. Your heart is being damaged

07:06 from the constant work it has to do. But you’ve  also noticed it’s becoming a bit harder to

07:10 breathe. The reason for that is a thermal injury  to your throat. After all, you’ve been taking in

07:16 really hot smoke all day for months on end. The other day you passed out and had to be

07:20 taken to the hospital. Doctors told you  that you had “crack lung.” The symptoms

07:24 were a bit like pneumonia. An acute case can  happen up to 48 hours after your last smoke.

07:30 Another symptom of smoking crack day in, day  out is bronchitis. You could also get chronic

07:34 obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD. So, after that initial rocket ride,

07:40 things aren’t looking too good these  days, but it’s going to get worse.

07:43 Your teeth have started falling out. For  one thing, since you started doing crack,

07:47 you don’t care much about dental hygiene. All  that really matters to you is getting your next

07:51 rock. On top of that, you spend much of your  life clenching your teeth when you’re high,

07:56 which has weakened them. And then the crack  constantly entering your mouth means less saliva

08:01 production, and this is also bad for your teeth. Then came the constant stomach aches, which are

08:06 a result of what is sometimes called crack belly.  Reduced blood flow to all your organs isn’t good,

08:12 and that includes your gastrointestinal system. Your rocket ship is broken. The FBI is still in

08:17 your garden, now with armed Mossad agents, Osama  Bin Laden, and Mr. Snuffleupagus from Sesame

08:23 Street, and the fact is, at some point you’ll  probably run into fentanyl-laced rocks you might

08:27 not wake up from. If you get out now, you might  be able to reverse some of the damage you’ve done.

08:32 Once the money runs out, you might end up like the  46% of users in a study in the US who committed a

08:38 violent crime to get more crack. Crack messes  with your brain’s prefrontal lobe, the part

08:44 that regulates impulse control, so doing something  stupid to get your next hit becomes more possible.

08:49 Sure, if you stop now, you’ll experience intense  anxiety and cravings during the initial “crash”,

08:55 and there’ll be a period of intense depression,  anxiety, and even some hostility and paranoia,

09:01 but the sun will come out again, once your brain  regains its normal non-crack-addicted circuitry.

09:06 Just don’t go back on it again. If you do,  you might experience the “kindling” effect,

09:11 which means a lot of the psychiatric symptoms,  the paranoia, the seizures, the psychosis and

09:17 suspiciousness, seem to happen with lower doses. Now you need to watch “Real Reason Fentanyl

09:22 Is So Deadly.” Or, have a look at  “The Only Drug You Can't Survive.”

38:43 And you have to call your parents and say, I didn't get

38:45 tenure, and your parents go, come on, if you just slept

38:47 better, you would've gotten tenure.

38:48 [LAUGHTER]

38:50 PROFESSOR: Remember the piano lessons you didn't take.

38:54 So it's a bit of a nuisance, right?

38:56 On top of that--

38:57 because weirdly, in academics, we tend to be super

38:59 specialized-- you have to move out of town.

39:01 You don't have to, but typically, a person who

39:04 doesn't get tenure will get a job somewhere else.

39:06 There's plenty of stories of people who don't get tenure at

39:08 awesome places who were geniuses in history.

39:11 The tenure decisions are often wrong.

39:13 But still, you'd rather get it than not.

39:15 You'd rather get into the medical school than not.

39:17 You'd rather make a sports team you want

39:18 to be on than not.

39:21 So here's what they found out.

39:22 If they asked them what happens if you don't get

39:24 tenure, everybody says, oh, it's gonna be awful.

39:26 It's gonna be miserable.

39:27 I'm gonna be such an unhappy person.

39:29 Two years later, the average happiness of people who didn't

39:33 get tenure was equal to the average happiness of people

39:36 who did get tenure.

39:38 So you can say, well, tenure-- only

39:39 professors care about tenure.

39:41 Well, how about winning the lottery?

39:43 What if I won hundreds of thousands of dollars?

39:45 There' been a lot of psychology on this, actually.

39:48 In about a year to two, the average happiness of a lottery

39:52 winner who won a substantial amount of money is rated the

39:54 same by him or her as it was the population as a whole.

39:58 Yeah?

39:59 AUDIENCE: How did they go about

40:00 measuring average happiness?

40:01 PROFESSOR: Yeah, so we'll come back to this,

40:03 but I'll tell you.

40:04 You can like this or not like this.

40:06 In some parts of psychology, we measure things like

40:08 reaction time to the millisecond.

40:10 That's good data, right?

40:12 Our brain activation, that's good data.

40:14 When you ask a person how happy they are, the only thing

40:17 we can do is have you basically fill a scale from

40:19 one to seven.

40:20 How happy are you?

40:22 And you could go, well I'm a little worried about that,

40:24 because sometimes people say, I hope that it makes you happy

40:26 or something.

40:27 So you could say, how much can we trust

40:30 subjective reports of happiness?

40:31 And that's a very good question.

40:33 On the other hand, it's hard to know what would

40:35 be better than that.

40:37 If we measure your pulse, is that a

40:39 better measure of happiness?

40:41 Your pulse could be racing because you're sad or happy,

40:43 scared or enthusiastic.

40:45 So we don't have a better one that we can think of.

40:48 But psychologists do worry that sometimes people will

40:50 just say what they're supposed to say.

40:51 Or they'll pretend they're happy or things like that.

40:54 We have to worry about those things.

40:56 So you could worry deep down, but a year or two later,

40:59 people who win huge amounts of money don't report themselves

41:02 as any happier than people around them.

41:05 And kind of amazingly--

41:07 but I think it's deep about life--

41:10 accidents leading to quadriplegia or paraplegia,

41:12 accidents that, before you had such an accident you would

41:16 imagine that it would be something extremely difficult.

41:20 And it can be in many ways.

41:21 But by self report, ratings of happiness return to typical

41:26 average populations of the same age

41:28 in about three months.

41:29 So what's a huge lesson here in happiness research--

41:32 a huge surprise.

41:33 It's two things.

41:34 We're kind of bad at predicting what will make us

41:37 happy or sad, which is kind of weird, right?

41:40 We're kind of bad at predicting it.

41:42 Here's all these things where we think they would make us

41:44 happy or make us not so happy.

41:45 It turns out we're wrong when this is studied at all

41:49 scientifically.

41:52 So we'll come back to that later on, because it's a very

41:54 deep thing about being a human--

41:56 what makes you happy and your wrong guesses

41:59 sometimes about what does.

42:01 So let me end with a last experiment.

42:03 So we've really haven't done experiments until right now.

42:06 And this is now a sensitive and difficult issue, which is

42:10 problems we have in dealing with racism.

42:13 And here's a study that did the following.

42:15 It said, well, in North America, certainly, Canada,

42:18 the US-- a study was done in Canada--

42:20 racism is widely condemned, as I think most of us

42:24 believe it should be.

42:26 But examples of blatant racism still occurred.

42:29 One recent poll said that about a third of white

42:32 individuals reported hearing anti-black slurs in the

42:34 workplace in the last couple years--

42:36 to pick one thing.

42:38 So how does this happen in a society that speaks so much

42:41 about not being racist, about treating everybody equally and

42:45 fairly and kindly?

42:46 How does it happen that we still struggle.

42:47 And it's such a very deep, difficult question about human

42:50 nature and the world we live in.

42:52 But here's something again that's a hint about why it's

42:55 hard to get society to change some of its behaviors.

43:00 So here's the experiment--

43:01 so it's an actual experiment.

43:03 So they took two groups of college undergraduates and

43:07 randomly assigned one to be in the forecaster group.

43:09 That's a group that tells you how they think they would feel

43:12 and how they think they would act under certain

43:15 circumstances.

43:17 And then an experiencer group--

43:19 that's a group who actually undergoes an experience, and

43:21 I'll tell you what that is now.

43:24 So in the experiencer group, pretend you were their

43:26 research participant.

43:27 You walk into a room, and you see in that room a black male

43:31 and a white male.

43:31 Now those two are what psychologists, for some

43:34 reason, have called confederates.

43:36 Those are role players.

43:37 They know what they're doing.

43:40 They have a plan of what they're going to do.

43:41 They're going to put on a little show for you.

43:43 But you don't know that.

43:46 And the black male stands up and leaves the room to get his

43:48 cell phone, and he gently bumps the white male's knee.

43:51 This is all set up.

43:52 You're just sitting there and you see that little bump.

43:55 And now, there's three different groups.

43:58 One group, that's it.

43:59 Nothing else happens--

44:00 A small bump, and the person leaves.

44:02 A second group--

44:04 as you sit there, the black individual leaves the room and

44:07 the white individual says, quote, "Typical, I hate it

44:10 when black people do that." It's meant to be obviously

44:12 provocative and racist.

44:14 And then what they consider an extreme slur--

44:17 the white person in the room playing this role uses the

44:20 derogatory word that's meant to be an extreme slur.

44:25 So there's one more thing you need to know.

44:28 Now, you're sitting there, and you're either in the control

44:30 group where there's been the slight bump, or there's been a

44:33 moderate slur, or an extreme slur in their words.

44:37 The black male returns.

44:38 Don't forget, he's in on it, and so is that white male.

44:40 But you're not in on it.

44:41 You just think there was a bump, and something else may

44:43 have happened, depending on which condition you're in.

44:46 And the experimenter then gives you a survey about how

44:48 you feel right now.

44:50 Sort of like the happiness, but it's not that.

44:52 It's like, how do you feel right now?

44:53 And then asks you to pick between those two people a

44:56 partner for an anagram experiment that

44:59 you're about to do.

45:01 So they're going to ask you--

45:02 this is sort of this question you have.

45:04 What's the difference or similarity between what you

45:07 say you're feeling is and what you really do?

45:10 Both things are important, but do they line up, do

45:12 they not line up?

45:13 So here's the results.

45:15 Here's a graph.

45:16 And here's how this works.

45:17 Negative emotional distress the higher the bar, the more

45:20 you say, I feel really bad about what's just happened.

45:23 I just heard this comment or no comment.

45:26 So let's take a look, the higher the bar.

45:28 If you heard no comment, here's how you begin.

45:31 So let's start with the forecasters.

45:33 All of you are forecasters, because you're pretending

45:35 you're in the situation but you're not in it.

45:38 So here is there was no comments.

45:40 That's sort of average or something.

45:41 And then you said if you heard a racial slur

45:44 you would feel terrible.

45:46 You would feel terrible.

45:49 But look at the other students who are randomly picked.

45:52 So we don't think it's a difference among students.

45:54 Look at these grey bars.

45:55 They're pretty flat.

45:57 The person on the spot is somehow not processing this.

46:02 And they're filling out, I feel average.

46:06 You see the split--

46:08 the split between the values that the person thinks they

46:11 would have, and the values that are responded to on the

46:14 spot in the moment.

46:16 And what we'll talk about later on in social psychology

46:18 is there's a tough gap, often, between the values we espouse

46:23 and how we act when there's especially unexpected,

46:26 difficult things.

46:27 And very often--

46:29 if you've had any experience like this-- afterwards, you

46:31 go, oh, what I should have done is this.

46:32 Or I wish I would've said that.

46:34 But that moment is not happening at that moment,

46:37 probably because you're kind of weirded out

46:38 by the whole thing.

46:38 What's going on?

46:39 Why would the person say this?

46:41 Something doesn't seem right.

46:42 I can't sort it out.

46:44 And so people tend to shrink in terms of making a strong

46:47 conclusion of what's going on if something seems unusually

46:50 provocative.

46:51 And you could say, well, OK, that's their attitudes.

46:53 But how about their action?

46:53 Who do they pick to be their partner?

46:55 And again, the people forecasting said, if I was in

46:58 this situation, I would never pick that racist white person

47:04 to be my partner, because that person stinks--

47:08 if I was in that situation.

47:10 But if the people are in the situation--

47:12 look at the grey bars--

47:14 pretty flat.

47:15 It's a if on the spot, in the moment, they can't quite

47:19 process the values they feel and the action

47:22 they're going to take.

47:24 And we'll talk about that.

47:25 And it's very hard, often, in part, to be brave

47:28 and stand up to things.

47:29 It turns out there's a lot of evidence for this.

47:31 It's a human nature thing.

47:33 It's very hard to be brave and stand up to things when things

47:36 are kind of weird, because almost everybody at first

47:38 thinks, I don't want to make a fool of myself.

47:40 I don't want make trouble.

47:41 Maybe I'm not getting the whole picture on this.

47:43 And we shrink back from acting in a way that aligns with the

47:47 values that are clearly shown here.

47:51 So this, again, is something about human

47:53 nature that's very weird.

47:54 And it's powerful to come into social psychology.

47:56 And that's why it's very hard to stand up to things like

47:59 oppression and bias.

48:00 It's very hard to do, because we tend to not act on our

48:04 values when we're in complicated

48:05 situations on the spot.

48:08 And there's a tremendous amount of evidence for that.

48:10 So again, how we interpret the situation--

48:12 very different in our mind when we imagine we're there,

48:16 and when we actually sit there.

48:17 And so what these researchers say is this is partly why it's

48:20 been hard to eradicate some vestiges of stereotypes and

48:25 racism, because people have a hard time clamping down on it

48:29 in the moment.

48:33 So that's a tough topic, but we know we want to deal both

48:35 with things that are less controversial but also things

48:38 that touch people's lives in the real world

48:40 that we live in.

48:41 So we talked about a scientific study

48:43 of the human nature--

48:44 mind and behavior--

48:45 how what we see and hear is determined so much but how our

48:50 mind interprets the world around us; how we remember

48:53 things like word lists or stories, that's hugely

48:55 influenced by what we expect to see, like in the picture;

48:58 how we think we know things like where Reno is compared to

49:01 San Francisco; how we think about things like the

49:04 probability that somebody else will have the same birthday,

49:06 that somebody else will in a group; and the relationship

49:10 between how we feel and how we act.

49:12 The very feelings we have are often disconnected for actions

49:15 in the moment.

49:16 And sometimes that has a sort of a difficult consequence.

49:19 And so we'll explore all these things through the semester,

49:22 all the different facets that we could possibly get through

49:24 in one semester of what it is to be human, and where science

49:26 has showed us something about human nature, the

49:28 mind, and the brain.
