docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Hour 0 April 25, 1986.

00:03 Chernobyl power plant, located about 2 miles (3km)  from Pripyat, a small town in northern Ukraine.

00:09 At just before midnight the engineer-mechanic  Alexander Yuvchenko clocks on for his nightshift,

00:14 a shift that will go down on record as one of  the most controversial few hours in history,

00:18 creating a panic that will take over the planet.

00:21 The mood among the workers is joyful.  It’s a beautiful night after a sunny day

00:24 and the May Day holiday is just around the corner. At home sleeping in his small apartment is his

00:29 wife Natasha, and his two-year-old son, Kirill.  The family is well taken of, and although Natasha

00:35 has some misgivings about the safety of nuclear  power, only recently those fears were diminished

00:39 when she heard a Soviet official on TV saying  nuclear meltdowns just don’t happen, or, if they

00:44 do, he said there might be one every 10,000 years. In just over 24 hours from now, people who Natasha

00:50 knows will be out in the street looking into the  sky at a dazzling laser beam shooting up to the

00:54 stars. At exactly the same time, her husband  will be in a party of four men who are exposed

00:59 to deadly amounts of radiation after being sent  to assess damage at Chernobyl’s reactor number 4.

01:05 Three of them will die in excruciating pain,  their bodies destroyed from within. Alexander

01:10 will survive because he doesn’t enter the reactor  hall but only holds a door for his friends.

01:15 The arm and leg and shoulder that he uses  will later turn black. He’ll tell Natasha

01:19 with what he thinks could be his dying  words that he’s been turned into a mutant.

01:23 Alexander will see things the communist government  will want to keep secret. Death by radiation is

01:28 a monstrous thing to behold and the Chernobyl  power plant disaster will be one of the most

01:32 monstrous events in world history. At the heart  of the matter is a design flaw that the Soviets

01:36 will not want to admit. What the capitalists can  do, they can do just as well, or so they think.

01:42 One thing you don’t want at a nuclear  power station is a total shutdown.

01:46 If that happens, things can heat up,  and if an explosion follows, what you

01:49 have is a massive leakage of deadly radiation. So, every reactor at Chernobyl has three backup

01:55 diesel generators that will kick in if power is  suddenly lost. The problem is that it takes 60 to

02:00 75 seconds for them to fully power the coolant  pumps. The theory, and it is only a theory,

02:05 is that the slowing turbines after being  turned off will create enough electrical power

02:09 to keep the pumps running during that gap before  the generators are running at full capacity.

02:14 To know if this works, they need to do some  tests. The first came in 1982 and it wasn’t

02:19 successful. They tried again in 1984 and again  the results weren’t good. Then they tried in 1985,

02:25 and yet again, a message was sent back to Moscow  saying things hadn’t gone as planned. This was not

02:30 what the bigwigs wanted to hear, and they made  that known. The pressure was on…excuse the pun.

02:36 The realtor has already been slowed down to run at  about 25 percent of its normal power. Importantly,

02:40 the reactor’s emergency core cooling system  has been disabled so it doesn’t get in the way

02:45 of seeing if the turbines can power the  generators. More importantly, some of the

02:49 nightshift workers that have arrived haven’t been  properly briefed about the test. The reason is the

02:54 test should have happened on the day shift, but  there was a power outage earlier in the day at

02:58 a coal plant, so Chernobyl had to keep running  at full power to give people their electricity.

03:03 To fully appreciate this story, you need to know  how we get electricity from a nuclear power plant,

03:08 so here we’ll give you the very basics in laymans  terms. Inside the reactor, neutrons split uranium

03:13 atoms, and that makes more neutrons. They  split more atoms, and we have more neutrons,

03:18 and on and on and on. This is called a chain  reaction, and it produces a crapload of heat.

03:23 You harness that heat and make it turn water  into steam, and the steam runs those turbines

03:27 we’ve already talked about. As they move  all this energy becomes electricity that

03:32 ensures people like Natasha can cook, clean,  eat, see, watch TV, and stay warm in winter.

03:37 All that heat and energy, of course, can be  a bit unstable so you have to have control

03:41 mechanisms to make sure there isn’t an overload.  If not, the chain reactions would just keep going,

03:46 becoming highly dangerous. Control rods are the  things used to slow down the chain reactions.

03:51 These are a bunch of rods that can be inserted  into the reactor in different numbers or different

03:56 lengths allowing the nuclear technicians to  control the rate of the nuclear chain reaction.

04:00 They’re made out of special materials that can  absorb neutrons, so if all does suddenly go to

04:04 hell, you will hope those rods can come and save  the day. No one at Chernobyl doubts their safety,

04:11 or at least the less experienced operators don’t. Hour 1

04:15 Now you know the night shift isn’t properly  prepared for the test and it might be their

04:19 fault that the power out of the plant falls too  much at 28 minutes past midnight on April 26.

04:25 They try to increase power, but something  is wrong. They’ve never seen this before.

04:29 This is partly because there’s been  a build-up of Xenon during the test.

04:32 You don’t need to know what Xenon is, and to be  frank, it’s too complicated to fully explain,

04:36 but when there is a build-up of the stuff it can  cause Xenon poisoning. Xenon would usually burn

04:41 away when the reactor is at full power, but the  slow down has caused the build-up and the build-up

04:46 has caused a further slowdown. This is not good. It’s because of this overabundance of Xenon

04:51 that even when the guys take most of  the control rods out, 200 from 206,

04:55 they still can’t get enough power. As you know,  by taking out the rods, they should get more power

05:00 since the nuclear reaction isn’t hampered. Doing  this, though, can be pretty dangerous. In fact,

05:05 they shouldn’t be doing this in the first place. A young operator gets on the phone and asks,

05:10 “‘What shall I do? In the program, there are  instructions of what to do, and then a lot

05:14 of things are crossed out.” The guy on the other  end pauses and then says, “Follow the crossed-out

05:18 instructions.” Hour 2

05:20 At around 1.05 am, they have the power  stabilized, although the reactor is running

05:24 well below what the shift supervisor, Anatoly  Dyatlov, thinks is ideal. One day he’ll lie

05:29 and say he wasn’t in the room when mistakes  were made, but he was. Don’t forget his name.

05:34 The reactor is certainly running at  less power than is safe for a test,

05:37 but they carry on anyway on the orders of  Dyatlov. He doesn’t want a black mark against

05:41 his name in the form of another failed test. At 1.24 and four seconds, the test really starts,

05:47 meaning they are going to simulate a  power outage and as we have explained,

05:51 see if the slowing turbines can power the  coolant pumps before the generators can turn on.

05:56 This is when all hell breaks loose. What happens  is a sudden and massive increase in power.

06:00 It’s dangerously high, and this  is now very serious. So serious,

06:04 that someone hits the SCRAM button. At  Chernobyl, this was the AZ-5 button.

06:09 It’s an emergency off-switch, which makes all of  the control rods drop down to stop the nuclear

06:14 reactions. This is a big mistake, and one which  exposes one of a few design flaws at Chernobyl.

06:20 The rods have a graphite tip, which in  short actually increases the reaction rate,

06:24 not the opposite, as is wanted. The boron in the rods reduces reactivity, but

06:28 not those tips. As so many rods hit the reactor at  the same time there is a huge surge in reactivity.

06:34 The operators don’t know what they have done. The  graphite tips are fixed in position and the heat

06:39 creates a massive amount of hot steam,  in effect, a bomb. The operators are not

06:44 aware of this or they wouldn’t have dropped the  rods into a reactor already surging with power.

06:48 The man in the reactor hall watches this  as it happens and is shocked to see those

06:52 200 rods and their caps, each weighing  772 pounds (350 kg), jumping up and down

06:57 within the reactor lid. It’s as if they  are being pushed by the power of a God.

07:01 The output of the reactor is now at  ten times the power it should be. And

07:05 that’s it. BANG. The bomb goes off. The world  will never be the same again after this moment.

07:10 The explosion causes the reactor’s  steel lid, weighing about 10,000

07:14 tons (2,000 medium-sized male African elephants)  to fly off and go straight through the roof.

07:21 Shortly after, there’s another big explosion,  likely down to a build-up of hydrogen from

07:25 zirconium-steam reactions. Bits of radioactive  materials and fuel are sent everywhere.

07:30 Fires rage and the core is exposed to the  world. Right now, it’s not obvious to most

07:34 of the men in the plant what is happening.  They all think the reactor is still intact,

07:38 only because reactors normally don’t just blow up. The roof is destroyed. The floor is in pieces.

07:44 Radioactive materials are lying about everywhere.  The air is filled with clouds of dust,

07:48 pieces of radioactive graphite  are flung great distances,

07:52 and radiation is now spilling into the atmosphere. To say this is bad would be putting it lightly.

07:57 Soon a few men will know this, but the one that  knows it best will be too dead to tell the story.

08:02 Right now, Alexander is in a state of shock.  Just a moment ago, he was in his office with

08:06 some colleagues reading some documents but  now everything around them now is shuddering,

08:10 on the brink of what feels like imminent  collapse. His first thought is this is

08:13 war. The USA has attacked us! He’s not alone in  thinking this. What else could have happened?

08:18 The phone rings. It’s the guys from building  number three. “Bring some stretchers,” they

08:22 shout over the noise. Alexander takes off  down some dark corridors in search of the men

08:26 he knows are the closest to the explosion site. As he gets closer to a deafening hissing sound,

08:31 he finds his buddy. His face is horribly  disfigured, so much so that he only knows who

08:35 it is when he hears the sound of his voice. More  people are injured, the guy tells Alexander.

08:40 He then meets with Yuri Tregub, who’s come  from control room number 4. He tells Alexander

08:45 that Deatlov has asked for the emergency  high-pressure coolant water to flood the area.

08:50 Deatlov still doesn’t know that the reactor has  blown and he won’t even believe it when he’s told.

08:54 Now waste deep in water, Alexander and a few other  men try to get to the coolant taps, but through

08:59 a door, they see that the giant water containers  have been blown apart. All the men are terrified.

09:04 This is worse than they thought. Alexander  looks around at what’s left of the room and

09:08 sees his colleague Khodemchuk on the floor, dead. He then looks up at the roof, or where the roof

09:14 was, and he sees something magical. A great  beam of light is reaching to the heavens.

09:18 It’s magnificent and beautiful, and as things now  stand, Alexander is not aware of how deadly it is.

09:24 For a few seconds, he just stares at what  he doesn’t know are gamma rays and neutrons.

09:28 A more experienced colleague who knows what  it is grabs him by the shoulder and pulls

09:32 him away. He likely saves his life doing so. Alexander sets off to control room number four

09:37 and there he meets three other guys who’ve  been ordered by Deatlov to go to the reactor

09:41 hall and lower the control rods by hand. This  is madness, sheer madness. Alexander screams,

09:47 “There is no reactor hall. The reactor has  blown up. There are no control rods. They’ve

09:52 blown up, too. There’s nothing left but space.” The guys think he’s crazy. Reactors don’t explode.

09:57 Alexander has to admit that what he’s  seen, he’s seen only from the bottom floor.

10:02 The men tell him they need to assess the damage  from above to really know what’s happened.

10:05 The four of them head to the reactor hall upper  floor. Little do they know that this is a journey

10:10 to the end of the night, for three of them  anyway. As you know, Alexander only survives

10:14 because he’s the one that holds the door, being  the strongest of the four. When the guys come out,

10:19 they say nothing can be done. They look at  Alexander and tell him he’s right. They say

10:22 the reactor hall now looks like a volcano crater. They understand that radiation levels are high,

10:28 of course, they do, it’s their job, but they don’t  know just how high. They look at the radiation

10:32 level reader device they have, the dosimeter,  and the needle is off the scales, but they

10:37 still don’t know how bad things are because  what is happening is just so unprecedented.

10:42 It’s still only just after 1.55 but the  firefighters are already outside on the

10:46 scene. They too don’t have much of an idea of the  gravity of the situation, and when they start to

10:50 try and put out the fires that have started  in various places, they are not even wearing

10:55 protective clothing. Some of them will die in  agony very soon. Others will pass away in a month,

11:00 their immune systems destroyed by the radiation. Back in Piryrat, most people are in bed asleep,

11:05 although a few people are now standing  outside, mesmerized by the ethereal beam

11:09 in the sky that they don't know is caused by  irradiated air. They just think it looks cool.

11:13 In years to come, stories told in the West will  say there was a large group of them on a bridge,

11:18 watching radioactive blue dust fall like  snowflakes. This will be called “The Bridge

11:22 of Death.” The stories will say they all died,  but none of that is true. There was no Bridge

11:27 of Death. Most people were asleep at the time. In the end, most people who actually were close

11:31 to the accident, recovered, with just 20 percent  of those who suffered acute radiation poisoning

11:36 biting the dust. As you’ll see again in this  show, it sometimes pays not to believe everything

11:40 you see on TV or in the newspapers. If you don’t know, the way radiation

11:44 poisoning works on the body is it takes out  electrons from atoms in a person’s molecules,

11:48 destroying the chemical bonds and thus  damaging tissue. We don’t need to tell

11:52 you that this isn’t good for a person. In short, after an hour or two,

11:55 diarrhea and vomiting can occur as tissue in the  GI tract breaks down and bacteria is let loose

12:01 on the body. Bone marrow stops producing white  blood cells, and infections can’t be fought,

12:05 since the person’s immune system is  incredibly weak. Without an immune system,

12:09 your countless bacteria eat you from within. This might take some time, so even though the

12:14 person is covered in blisters and ulcers, they  could start to feel ok after a couple of days,

12:18 but then a blood infection  might lead to deadly sepsis.

12:21 For some at Chernobyl, even a blood transfusion  and bone marrow transplant won’t help them.

12:26 One of the town’s people is Lyudmila Ignatenko.  She’s already awake and has seen the glow. Her

12:31 husband, Vasily, is currently fighting the fires.  The two are due to have a child in two months.

12:36 Fast-forward a week, and his skin is covered  in boils, and when he turns on his pillow

12:40 he leaves skin and hair behind. The lesions spread  and some of his skin now looks like white film.

12:45 At one point he asks Lyudmila for a mirror but  when he sees his own disfigured face he cries

12:50 out in horror. Vasily will be buried in a zinc  casket under cement, his body still radioactive.

12:56 Lyudmila is lucky she even got to see him.  A nurse told her it was too dangerous.

13:00 She looked at Lyudmila and warned, “If you  start crying, I'll kick you out right away.

13:04 No hugging or kissing. Don't even  get near him. You have half an hour.”

13:08 Lyudmila will have much to say about this in  time to come, and she’ll also lose the child.

13:12 It will be born with congenital heart defects  and liver cirrhosis and die after a few hours.

13:17 Many people will criticize her for this,  asking why did she visit her dying husband.

13:21 The radiation from him contaminated her and  the fetus, they’ll say, but you can’t just

13:26 catch radiation from a cleaned person and  there’s no proof this is how the baby died.

13:30 A falsity that will be talked about for years  is that the baby somehow took the radiation

13:34 and that saved her. This is not scientific at all,  but it makes good newspaper copy and great TV.

13:40 The consequences of this misinformation will mean  the lives and lights of hundreds of thousands

13:44 of babies are put out before they get going. We should say, though, that while seeing her dying

13:49 husband wasn’t the reason for the baby dying, it  was very likely radiation exposure from somewhere

13:54 else that led to the death. Back in 1986, the  nurse that told Lyudmila not to touch her husband

13:59 couldn’t have known radiation doesn’t spread to  people after they’ve been cleaned and are out of

14:03 their contaminated clothes. It’s not contagious.  We should also tell you that a person’s hand

14:08 can’t suddenly burn when they touch the hand of  a contaminated person. That’s TV, not reality.

14:14 One of the firefighters turns to his friend and  jokes, saying, “There must be an incredible amount

14:18 of radiation here. We’ll be lucky if we’re all  still alive in the morning.” As the survivors will

14:22 later testify, they were never told the reactor  was on fire, only that there were regular fires

14:27 to put out. Some of them kicked the radioactive  blocks, even picking them with their hands after

14:32 they’d doused them. They would never have done  any of these things had they known the truth.

14:36 One of the firefighters who survived  explained how little they knew,

14:40 saying some of his colleagues went up to the roof  to work from there. Soberingly, he said, “Then

14:44 those boys who died went up to the roof—Vashchik,  Kolya and others, and Volodya Pravik. They went up

14:50 the ladder ... and I never saw them again.” Hour 3

14:54 Local officials have already arrived on the scene  to discuss what’s happening. When they’re told,

14:58 they’re not told the entire truth. That’s  because only a handful of people right now

15:02 truly understand that the reactor has blown  up, and some of them are now burned, vomiting,

15:06 so not in a meeting explaining what they’ve seen. Dyatlov still thinks what he always has, that a

15:11 water tank has blown up and the radiation  currently making some people very sick

15:15 is from the contaminated water. He just can’t  believe the core would blow, even though some

15:20 people are starting to realise that a water tank  blowing up wouldn’t lead to so much destruction.

15:25 Hour 4 More firemen arrive to help with the fires.

15:28 The last thing anyone wants is reactor three to  set on fire, which is looking like a possibility.

15:33 It’s soon safely shut down, but reactors  1 and 2 keep going until the next day.

15:37 Inside reactor 4 is now a molten reactor core; a  large graphite and concrete slag that is burning

15:43 at around 1200 degrees Celsius. Hour 5

15:46 Another meeting is held, now with experts.  Some ask about the high levels of radiation,

15:51 proffering a theory that the core might  have blown. Nonsense, says Dyatlov,

15:55 even though he’s not far from keeling over  himself. A second later, he throws up.

15:59 A decision is made that no one will leave the  town, not yet. Perhaps they can be evacuated in

16:04 three days. All the phone lines are blocked  in case anyone starts spreading rumors,

16:08 which one official calls “misinformation”  that can negatively affect the Soviet Union.

16:12 Police soon start blocking the roads, just as  soldiers pass them on their way in to help with

16:17 the clean-up job. Hour 7

16:19 At 6.35 am, most of the fires are out, but  by no means does this mean the problems

16:24 are over. They’re only just beginning. Real  horror is taking place inside that reactor.

16:28 A man who understands this horror is Valery  Legasov, the deputy director of the Kurchatov

16:34 Institute of Atomic Energy and the man that will  lead the commission to deal with the accident.

16:38 He’ll also be the one that testifies during  the tribunal, and as you’ll see, he’s the guy

16:42 that exposes the Soviet Union’s shortcomings  when it comes to producing nuclear energy.

16:47 Hour 8 He’s called

16:48 on the phone soon he’s at the airport with the  man who’ll manage the crisis, Boris Shcherbina.

16:54 In time, both these men will suffer from radiation  poisoning, but for now, they still don’t know

16:58 exactly what’s happened. Hour 13

17:01 It’s around midday when they attend a meeting  to discuss matters. Legasov already knows about

17:06 the people in the hospital, suffering from  severe radiation burns, so he and others agree

17:10 the town needs to be evacuated. Hour 30

17:13 Legasov is driven in an armored personnel carrier  to assess the damage for himself. It’s bad,

17:18 very bad, and he says they have to  get that main fire under control or

17:22 radiation will be taken by the wind for  many, many miles. Many parts of Europe,

17:26 not just Ukraine, are at risk. This is  a disaster of unbelievable proportions.

17:30 It’s agreed that dropping sand and boron on  the reactor fire from helicopters might be the

17:34 best way to go, even though Legasov knows it  might not work. They have no choice, he says,

17:39 something needs to be done right now. The military will need to help with the cleanup,

17:43 and many men will be expected to risk their  lives. These people will become known as the

17:47 liquidators and many of them will suffer  long-term health effects from their work.

17:51 Hour 33 Shcherbina

17:53 gets on the phone with Moscow and reports,  “We’ve measured the radiation. Prypiat has

17:57 to be evacuated. Immediately. The station  is close by, and it’s emitting radioactive

18:02 contagion. And people in the city are living  it up full blast; weddings are going on.”

18:06 Levels of radioactivity in the town are rising at  an alarming rate. Earlier in the day, the level

18:12 was between 14-140 milliroentgens per hour, but  that has gone up to 180 and 300 milliroentgens,

18:18 and in areas closer to the plant,  600. 50 milliroentgens or more

18:22 per year can be dangerous with 400  milliroentgens per year can kill you.

18:26 The people in that town now have a  much higher risk of developing cancer,

18:30 and they have no idea about this. Still,  in parts of the plant, the level reached

18:34 an astounding 20,000 milliroentgens per hour, and  that’s why some men died so soon after exposure.

18:39 How 36 Sometime in the morning,

18:42 the first helicopters start dropping the sand and  boron on the fire. It’s a perilous job. Getting

18:47 too close to the hole where the reactor  was can lead to acute radiation sickness.

18:51 It’s dangerous enough anyway, as can  be seen when one helicopter collides

18:55 with a chain and crashes, killing the men onboard.

18:58 Hour 38 The evacuation begins

19:01 From speakers all over the town comes a woman’s  voice, saying the same thing over and over again.

19:06 “Attention! Attention! In connection with the  accident at the Chernobyl atomic power station,

19:11 unfavorable radiation conditions are  developing in the city of Prypiat.

19:14 In order to ensure complete safety for  residents, children first and foremost,

19:18 it has become necessary to carry  out a temporary evacuation.”

19:21 They are told to take everything with them that is  important, including all their personal documents.

19:26 They don’t know it, but they are never going  back to their homes. Just one hour before

19:30 this announcement, families were enjoying the  weekend. In the cafeteria in the shopping mall,

19:34 kids and their mothers were hanging out and  eating ice cream. For them, it was just a normal

19:38 day. There were kids playing on the bumper cars,  then suddenly they were told the ride is over.

19:43 Now they are taken aback when  they hear the speakers say,

19:45 “Comrades, on leaving your dwellings, please  do not forget to close windows, switch off

19:49 electrical and gas appliances and turn off water  taps. Please remain calm, organized, and orderly.”

19:54 What’s startling is these people have not  been told the full story and certainly

19:58 aren’t given any protective clothing, in  spite of the fact that Soviet officials

20:02 know about the dangerous levels of radiation.  So far, they don’t want to cause too much panic,

20:06 or for the word to get out about the disaster. Hour 42

20:11 Shcherbina calls Premier  Nikolai Ryzhkovand and explains,

20:14 “There are no people left in Pripyat.  There are only dogs running around.”

20:18 What happens to the mutts, in the end,  is awful, but that’s a few days away yet.

20:22 Shcherbina’s not exactly correct  about all the people leaving.

20:25 Some young folks have hidden so they can stay  together in their parents’ apartments and get

20:30 it on for once with some privacy. They don’t care  about some little radiation leak. Old folks, too,

20:35 have stayed behind, or some of them have. They’re  well past the age of moving away and they’re too

20:40 tough to worry about radiation. Some have lived  through wars, famine and Stalin’s reign of terror.

20:45 Hour 46 116,000 people have

20:48 left, but about 1,200 have stayed behind, mostly  the aged, and many of them women – babushkas as

20:53 they say in Russian. They have refused to budge,  and it’s hard to argue with a stubborn babushka.

20:59 One woman, Hanna Zavorotnya is given a stern order  to leave after she’s been found by a soldier.

21:04 She looks him square in the face and  says, “Shoot us and dig the grave,

21:07 otherwise we’re staying.” After listening to  the soldier explain the danger, she replies,

21:11 “Radiation doesn’t scare me. Starvation does.” The world still doesn’t know the extent of what’s

21:15 happened, and you can be sure the Soviet leaders  are determined to try and keep matters within a

21:19 fairly small circle. The KGB is told to stop  the “spread of panicky rumors and unreliable

21:24 information” getting out, although nothing  they can do can prevent what happens next.

21:29 Hour 52

21:30 The Soviets get word that Sweden has detected  radiation and it has been identified as coming

21:35 from Chernobyl. On top of this, soon the USA  will have satellite photos of the disaster.

21:40 The news carries as fast as the radiation,  with presenters all over the world telling

21:43 people that this major accident, something  that’s never happened before on this scale,

21:48 could mean dangerous radiation being carried  from Ukraine to other European countries.

21:52 As the children of Chernobyl settle into their new  surroundings, school kids in Germany are kept home

21:57 in fear of radiation poisoning. Panic reverberates  from North America back to Europe and into Asia.

22:02 Hour 55 It’s not until the evening

22:05 that the official news is shown on Russian TV.  A report states, “There has been an accident at

22:09 the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant. One of the  nuclear reactors was damaged. The effects of

22:14 the accident are being remedied. Assistance  has been provided for any affected people.

22:18 An investigative commission has been set up.” More Russian news follows, and this time with

22:22 in-depth discussions. Not surprisingly, experts  talk about the Three Mile Island nuclear accident

22:27 of the USA and some other American nuclear  mishaps. What the news doesn’t talk about is

22:31 what could happen at Chernobyl right now, a  new kind of disaster could be in the works.

22:36 Hour 58 It was thought that the water tanks were empty,

22:39 which isn’t actually the case. To make things  worse, fire hoses have been filling the place

22:43 with more water. Soviet scientists are now saying  that if that smoldering graphite, remember heated

22:48 to about 1,200 °C (2,190 °F), hits the water,  there could be another massive explosion,

22:53 even bigger than the last one, and that could  mean Europe being hit with even more radiation.

22:58 They don’t know it yet, but it’s highly unlikely  this explosion will happen. They think it could,

23:02 and so tell three men who know the area  inside out that they will have to drain

23:06 the 20,000 tons of water through a sluice gate. These men know that there’s a good chance they

23:11 might not make it out, and even if they do, they  may not live very long after. Hence the name,

23:15 the Chernobyl Suicide Squad: Alexei  Ananenko, Valeri Bezpalov and Boris Baranov.

23:21 Hour 60 Finding the valves in the dark is

23:24 like finding a needle in a haystack, but they do  it in the end. For them, it is just another day at

23:29 work. They knew they’d be fired if they didn’t do  as asked, and unlike what will be said in years to

23:34 come, they didn’t get any reward for their work. As we’ve explained, there will be a lot of western

23:39 misinformation flying about in regard  to the Chernobyl disaster. One falsity

23:43 told time and again is that these men all died  shortly after they succeeded in their mission,

23:47 but they didn’t. They lived long, healthy lives  after their time in the darkness of Chernobyl.

23:52 Hour 66 The Soviet government

23:54 is now worried that the molten core will burn  through the cement and get to the groundwater,

23:58 thereby contaminating it and spreading radiation  into the rest of Ukraine and into Europe,

24:03 possibly making some places uninhabitable. A mining team is brought in to dig a huge

24:07 tunnel below the reactor to act as a cooling  system. They are given respirators for the work,

24:12 but it’s hard to breathe with  them on. It’s also very hot,

24:15 but they don’t work naked, as  will be told on TV in the future.

24:18 Again, it’s a big job and risky job for  the 400 or so miners. The Soviets don’t

24:23 have to be too concerned because the  core won’t melt through the concrete.

24:26 Obviously, they don’t know that yet  and have to take all precautions.

24:30 Hour 100 The debris removal starts. At first,

24:33 the 100 tons of radioactive material is said to  be so dangerous that men shouldn’t go near it.

24:38 They opt to use robots, but most of the robots  break as soon as deployed due to the radiation.

24:43 The liquidators are chosen to do the job,  men who are now camping close to the plant.

24:47 Thousands of them are there, and in time, 600,000  or so of them will help with this clean-up.

24:52 They’re given protective clothing, but still told  they shouldn’t stay on the roof for longer than

24:56 40–90 seconds since the graphite and other  materials up there are about as radiative

25:01 as you can get. Of the 5,000 men who do the  job, some will go up as many as six times,

25:05 but it’s hard to say how many will  have health problems because of it.

25:08 Alexander, as you know, survives.

25:10 He’s flown to Moscow. His hair falls  out and he finds it hard to breathe.

25:14 His eyes, nose, and most of his face  hurts, but then after a couple of days,

25:18 he and the other men all start to  feel pretty good. As you already know,

25:21 this doesn’t mean they are good. One day he’s in pain again and he

25:25 pulls back his bedsheets to see massive ulcers  and necrotic skin on his shoulder, hip, and calf,

25:30 all the bits exposed when he held that door open.  He is turning black and feels like he’s a monster,

25:35 telling himself he looks like  some kind of radioactive mutant.

25:38 Luckily for him, his body accepts the skin grafts,  and blood transfusions and bone marrow transplants

25:43 do the rest. His arm is in really bad shape and  will stay in bandages for years. In the hospital,

25:48 ever so often someone walks in the room and  tells him another of his colleagues is dead.

25:53 One of them first goes blind, and then the  infection in his blood finishes him off. For

25:57 two months, Alexander lies in bed close to death  thinking about when it will be his turn to die.

26:03 He will later be awarded medals for  his bravery, but once he’s better,

26:06 he’ll keep his Chernobyl experience mostly to  himself. For many years to come, people in this

26:10 part of the world will cross the street if they  see a Chernobyl survivor walking toward them.

26:15 These people, not educated about  radiation, wrongly assume the

26:18 survivors are still contaminated. This  fear has devesting consequences.

26:27 Chernobyl, in fact, will make much of the world  wrongly over-estimate the dangers of producing

26:31 nuclear power. This will go on for decades and  is still a factor in some people’s minds today

26:36 when they think about nuclear energy. What or who is to blame for the disaster

26:40 is the question that the Soviets and  many other countries will be asking

26:43 for some time to come. The investigations at the  start will mostly blame human error rather than

26:49 technical error and pick out a few names to  shame and send to prison, such as Mr. Dyatlo.

26:54 Sure, he messed up a bit, as did others at  the plant, but the fault lies in many people,

26:59 going right up to the top brass  in the Communist government.

27:02 1 year later It's now 1987 and Legasov is very

27:07 ill from radiation poisoning and is in and out of  hospital all the time. He knows he’s going to die,

27:12 so he records himself on tape telling the whole  truth about how and why this disaster happened.

27:17 Part of the tape goes: “The Chernobyl disaster is an apotheosis,

27:21 the pinnacle of all the mismanagement that has  been carried out for decades in our country…

27:25 When one looks at the chain of events, why  someone acted in this way and another in that way,

27:29 and so on, it is impossible to point to  a single culprit, an initiator of all

27:33 the unpleasant events that led to the crime.  Because it is a chain that links to itself.”

27:38 He finishes off by warning that as he speaks,  the Soviet Union does not have safe nuclear power

27:43 plants, not because the production of energy is  dangerous in itself, but because too many mistakes

27:48 have been made and too many corners have been cut.  He says when you can’t hold the state accountable

27:53 then the state is broken. 2 years later

27:56 In 1988, the day after the second anniversary of  the accident, he is found dead in his apartment.

28:01 Shcherbina, who had become a close friend,  said, “Valery was too great, I loved him

28:05 more than all the people I knew, he gave all of  himself to work, to Chernobyl. He burnt out.”

28:10 Of the 237 people that suffered acute radiation  sickness, 31 died within a couple of months. The

28:16 amount of people that died from cancer due  to radiation poisoning reached around 4,000,

28:21 and many more survived cancer. Still,  the health effects of the disaster

28:24 have been argued about for many years. As for reactor 4, it was covered with a

28:28 giant steel and concrete building called  the sarcophagus containment structure.

28:33 An Exclusion Zone was formed, covering an  area of around 1,000 sq. miles (2,600 km2) of

28:37 Ukraine. Over the years, the town of  Pripyat became home to life again,

28:41 but of the wild animal kind, not the human kind.

28:44 20 years later As for all those pet

28:46 dogs and cats, they were killed by special  teams not long after the disaster became

28:50 worldwide knowledge. Some may have survived,  though, because in the years to come, dogs in

28:55 the town will be seen alongside wolves, brown  bears, dear, badgers, lynx, bison, and moose.

29:01 In 20,000 years, the town of Pripyat might be  safe again for humans to go and live there.

29:06 You can visit now, but experts recommend you  don’t eat the wild mushrooms or other plants

29:10 you can find there, and wear something you’re  prepared to throw away later. Radiation sucks,

29:14 but we can’t live without it. Now you need to watch,

29:17 “What If There Was A Nuclear War Between  the US and Russia?” Or, have a look at,

29:21 “Man Receives Highest Dose of Nuclear  Radiation - This Is What Happened To Him.”

00:04

00:04 In the previous video, we generated

00:06 a CART tree with three splits, but why

00:10 not two, or four, or even five?

00:13 There are different ways to control

00:15 how many splits are generated.

00:18 One way is by setting a lower bound for the number of data

00:21 points in each subset.

00:23 In R, this is called the minbucket parameter,

00:27 for the minimum number of observations

00:29 in each bucket or subset.

00:32 The smaller minbucket is, the more splits will be generated.

00:36 But if it's too small, overfitting will occur.

00:40 This means that CART will fit the training set

00:43 almost perfectly.

00:45 But this is bad because then the model will probably not

00:48 perform well on test set data or new data.

00:52 On the other hand, if the minbucket parameter

00:54 is too large, the model will be too simple

00:57 and the accuracy will be poor.

01:00 Later in the lecture, we will learn about a nice method

01:03 for selecting the stopping parameter.

01:08 In each subset of a CART tree, we

01:10 have a bucket of observations, which

01:12 may contain both possible outcomes.

01:15 In the small example we showed in the previous video,

01:19 we have classified each subset as either red or gray

01:22 depending on the majority in that subset.

01:25 In the Supreme Court case, we'll be classifying observations

01:29 as either affirm or reverse.

01:32 Instead of just taking the majority outcome

01:34 to be the prediction, we can compute the percentage

01:38 of data in a subset of each type of outcome.

01:42 As an example, if we have a subset

01:44 with 10 affirms and two reverses, then 87% of the data

01:50 is affirm.

01:52 Then, just like in logistic regression,

01:55 we can use a threshold value to obtain our prediction.

01:59 For this example, we would predict affirm

02:02 with a threshold of 0.5 since the majority is affirm.

02:07 But if we increase that threshold to 0.9,

02:10 we would predict reverse for this example.

02:15 Then by varying the threshold value,

02:18 we can compute an ROC curve and compute

02:21 an AUC value to evaluate our model.

02:25 In the next video, we'll build a CART tree in R

02:28 to predict the decisions of Justice Stevens

02:31 and evaluate our model using a ROC curve.

00:00 ALBERT MEYER: The pigeonhole principle

00:01 is accounting principle.

00:02 It's so obvious that you may not have

00:05 noticed that you're using it.

00:06 In simple form, it says that if there

00:10 are more pigeons than pigeonholes, then

00:15 you have to have at least two pigeons in the same hole.

00:20 OK.

00:22 We'll get some mileage out of that shortly.

00:25 But let's remember that this is actually

00:27 just an informal way of saying something that we've formally

00:30 seen already.

00:32 One of the mapping rules is that if you

00:33 have a total injection from a set A to a set B,

00:37 that implies that the size of A is

00:39 less than or equal to the size of B.

00:41 And taking the contrapositive of that,

00:44 it means that if the size of A is greater than the size of B,

00:47 then no total injection from A to B is possible.

00:51 No total injection means that there's

00:53 no relation that has an arrow out of everything in A

00:59 and at most one arrow into B. If everything out of A

01:02 has an arrow out of it, there have

01:04 to be at least two arrows, two pigeons, coming

01:08 to the same pigeonhole in B.

01:11 So we know this rule already.

01:13 And the only thing that's surprising about it

01:15 is how you make use of it.

01:17 We're not going to make elaborate uses of it

01:19 in this little video.

01:20 You can read in the text about some amusing applications

01:24 about proving that there have to be 3 people in the Boston area

01:27 with more than 10,000 hairs in their heads.

01:30 But the exact same number, or that

01:32 there have to be two different subsets of 90 numbers,

01:38 of 25 digits, that have the same sum.

01:43 But we will take a much more modest application

01:46 of the pigeonholing principle.

01:47 Namely, if I have a set of five cards

01:50 that I have to have at least two cards with the same suit, why?

01:55 Well, there are four suits-- spades hearts, diamonds,

01:58 clubs-- indicated here.

01:59 And if you have five cards, there's

02:01 more pigeons cards than suits holes.

02:04 So if you're going to assign a pigeon to a hole,

02:08 again, the pigeons are going to have to crowd up.

02:10 There are going to have to be at least two pigeons

02:13 in the same hole, at least two cards of the same suit,

02:15 maybe more.

02:18 OK.

02:19 Slight generalizations.

02:20 Suppose I have 10 cards.

02:21 How many cards must I have of the same suit?

02:25 What number of cards of the same suit

02:27 am I guaranteed to have no matter what the 10 cards are?

02:30 Well, now, if I have the four slots

02:33 and I'm trying to distribute 10 cards,

02:36 is it possible that I had less than three cards in every hole?

02:39 No, because if I have only two cards in every hole,

02:43 then I have at most 8 elements and I got 10

02:46 to distribute in the four slots.

02:48 I have to bunch them up and have at least three cards

02:51 of the same suit.

02:52 You could check that I needn't have any more of course.

02:56 So the reasoning here is that the number

02:58 of cards with the same suit is going

03:00 to be what you get by dividing up the 10 cards that you

03:05 have by the four slots.

03:08 And argue that at least one of the slots

03:10 has to have an average number of cards, namely, 10 over 4.

03:14 They can't all be below average.

03:16 And of course since there are an integer number of cards,

03:19 you could round up this-- remember,

03:21 these corner braces mean round up to the nearest integer.

03:25 So 10 divided by 4 rounded up is 3,

03:29 and that's a lower bound on the number of cards

03:34 that you have to bunch up in one slot.

03:37

03:40 More generally, if I have n pigeons,

03:43 and I'm going to be assigning pigeons to unique holes,

03:46 and if I have H holes, then some hole

03:50 has to have n divided by H rounded up.

03:53 Again, n divided by H can be understood

03:56 as the average number of pigeons per hole.

03:59 And the pigeonhole principle can be

04:01 formulated as saying at least one whole has

04:04 to have greater than or equal to the average number.

04:07 And that is the generalized pigeonhole principle.

04:11

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: WTF is Happening with South Korean Economy
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: WTF is Happening with South Korean Economy
  • Video ID: 4EPW0Ht7XCc
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Wall Street is panicking. And the problem started 6,000 miles away.

00:04 In the summer of 2026, more than 320,000 South  Korean investors saw their accounts liquidated

00:10 in a matter of hours. Why?

00:13 Because the world's most profitable company  just did something it hasn't done in 20 years.

00:17 Alphabet, Google’s parent company, burned  $5.9 billion in a single quarter. All on AI.

00:24 Big Tech's AI obsession isn't an unlimitless cash  machine… it's a value-destroying black hole. When

00:31 Seoul stops trading, New York is next. And you’ll be in the fallout.

00:35 For the last 5 years, the US Nasdaq 100 and  the South Korean stock market, the Kospi,

00:41 barely paid attention to each other.  The 60 day rolling correlation average,

00:45 how they move over time, stood at 0.16. It  was pretty much background noise. By mid-2026,

00:52 it exploded, climbing to between 0.46 and 0.50. In  other words, the two markets are moving together.

01:00 And it all comes down to one thing. AI.

01:03 South Korea builds the hardware that  keeps the US tech bubble intact.

01:07 Every night, while Wall Street sleeps, companies  like Samsung and SK Hynix open for trading. Their

01:12 earnings, their guidance, their panic, all of it  lands on trading screens of American investors

01:18 when they finish their coffee. When U.S. traders  see major dips in Asia’s hardware supplies,

01:23 it dictates their own behavior. If those  companies are in trouble, it sets off a

01:27 chain reaction that impacts companies like  Alphabet, who are trying - and failing - to

01:32 reap the benefits of AI infrastructure projects. Korea’s stock exchange is a monitor for the

01:36 health of the entire AI sector. And that monitor just flatlined.

01:41 Behind it all, is Google’s $5.9 billion cash burn. It exposes a circular illusion. A closed loop

01:48 where tech giants manufacture their own  demand. Nvidia makes the physical chips

01:52 that power nearly every major AI system on  the planet. In 2025, Nvidia invested $100

01:58 billion into OpenAI. OpenAI used a large  chunk of that money to buy Nvidia’s chips.

02:04 The cash goes out, and the  cash comes right back in.

02:07 Nvidia’s revenue looks strong. OpenAI looks  well-capitalized. Valuations go up. But the

02:13 closed loop means they don't even need paying  customers to make the balance sheet look good.

02:18 That’s the important part for  investors and shareholders.

02:21 They see cash inflow and outflow, and they see  confidence in AI systems, making them more likely

02:26 to invest their own money into similar companies.  That same problem isn’t solely in investment, but

02:32 in the timing of the returns. Unlike “traditional”  investments where people would expect to see

02:37 returns in a year or 2, many AI investors believe  that the real payoff is 3 or even 5 years away.

02:44 That “hype” leads to the second part  of why AI investment is so rampant.

02:48 FOMO. Investors want to get their foot in

02:51 the door early. If they don’t, someone else ends  up reaping the rewards. And that can be millions.

02:56 Nvidia isn’t alone in running this playbook.  Microsoft poured billions into OpenAI,

03:01 and that money flowed straight back to Microsoft  in the form of cloud computing contracts. It’s

03:06 the same loop under different branding. But Google’s cash burn is what happens when

03:10 a company tries to compete in that environment  without relying on circular deals. They try to

03:15 absorb the cost of either building infrastructure  or getting the necessary server load. Alphabet

03:20 managed to spend $44.9 billion in just three  months. The entire premise was that it was

03:26 banking on its own sustained growth to cover it. It was a record quarter for Alphabet. Revenue

03:31 hit $119.8 billion, up 24%. Operating income  climbed 30%. So Google took those profits and

03:39 chose to burn billions in cash. The alternative is  losing the AI race to Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon,

03:45 who are all on their own AI spending spree. It’s not just one company making a gamble on AI.

03:51 Every major player in the AI race is  using some kind of cover-up to spend

03:55 more but report that it’s spending less. If  it pays off, then it’s hailed as a perfect

04:00 strategy. A calculated gamble that came in. But  while all that cash was disappearing into data

04:05 centers, a second story was unfolding. And it made things in Korea much worse.

04:10 A report surfaced that a homegrown  Chinese company, based in Shanghai,

04:14 was building its own deep ultraviolet  lithography machines. The very equipment

04:18 used to manufacture advanced semiconductors. According to the report, the company is planning

04:23 to build 5 of these machines in 2026 and 20  more the following year. Most of the components

04:28 are sourced domestically, with only a handful of  parts still coming from Japan. 2 weeks later, the

04:33 company was named: Shanghai Aishengna Electronic  Technology Group, also known as Aishengna. And

04:39 it turned out to be majority state-owned. The news sent shockwaves through the markets.

04:44 The existing manufacturing was almost monopolized  by ASML, based in the Netherlands. It’s the

04:49 dominant supplier of both deep ultraviolet,  or DUV, and extreme ultraviolet, or EUV,

04:55 lithography machines. These are tools that  actually etch circuits onto chips at a scale

05:00 measured in nanometers. Out of the two, DUV  is considered less technologically impressive,

05:05 but it still delivers results. But ASML has been barred from

05:09 selling its most advanced EUV systems to  China. Even if Aishengna makes the less

05:13 advanced version domestically, it means China  is suddenly free from the imposed export ban

05:18 that kept its huge industrial potential in check. When the report of the Aishengna's existence went

05:23 out, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix share prices  went down by more than 10% in a single session.

05:29 Tokyo Electron and TSMC dropped alongside them. The fear wasn’t abstract.

05:34 For years, the assumption was that IP  restrictions and export controls kept

05:38 China years behind on the equipment needed to  make advanced chips. Analysts estimated that

05:43 gap at 7 to 10 years. But the market immediately  reacted to the possibility that China might close

05:48 that gap much faster than expected. But there’s another side to this.

05:52 One that has executives worrying. For years, Chinese firms have offered

05:56 lucrative signing bonuses to entice engineers  away from Samsung and other Korean chipmakers.

06:01 They have been importing decades of institutional  knowledge one hire at a time. Lee Byung-chul,

06:06 a Sejong Institute research fellow, has stated  that Samsung and SK Hynix DRAM technology has

06:12 already been leaked to China. He also believes  that a separate attempt to leak HBM packaging

06:17 technology was caught before it got out. That’s only half of the problem

06:21 A civil war is erupting in  South Korea’s tech industry.

06:24 Samsung is watching its chip engineers - the  brains behind the hardware - walk out the front

06:29 door to join SK Hynix. The insane AI profits  have been weaponized with eye-watering bonus

06:34 packages of up to $500,000 being offered to  poach employees. The company that’s supposed

06:40 to be defending Korea’s semiconductor edge  against China is completely helpless as its

06:45 own talent signs up with a domestic rival. It’s not illegal and it isn’t new.

06:50 Corporate espionage, a talent war, and a Chinese  domestic lithography program are now threatening

06:55 South Korea’s AI industry. And the global AI  market relies on a country with no backup plan.

07:01 If cheap Chinese alternatives start chipping away  at this monopoly, the entire financial foundation

07:05 built by American AI giants collapses. But China isn’t stopping there.

07:10 It has another option. It can flood the  global market with cheap chips to crush

07:15 South Korea. Or, it can ban chip exports  entirely, fund their own AI industry,

07:20 and steal a market of over a billion people. For an industry running on pure speculation,

07:25 that’s a massive problem. Because AI isn’t a finished product.

07:29 Back in 2023, Alphabet’s chairman John Hennessy  told Reuters that a single exchange with a

07:34 large language model costs 10 times more than a  traditional search. When the numbers were run,

07:39 the added cost of AI searches could run to $6  billion a year. Google says those per-query costs

07:45 have fallen sharply since, as much as 33 times  less, as hardware and models get more efficient.

07:51 But this just leads to another problem. Reduced costs mean that the product

07:55 gets used more often. That means burning through

07:58 more resources. It’s an example of Jevons  paradox: as technology becomes more efficient,

08:03 we don't save resources, we just use them more. In 2025, Google’s own environmental report

08:09 admitted its emissions had surged by 50%  compared to 2019, before the AI trend started.

08:15 Tech giants are burning the world to  build a product that has no clear purpose.

08:20 According to a S&P Global Market Intelligence  survey, 42% of companies abandoned most of their

08:25 AI initiatives in 2025. That’s more than double  the 17% recorded the year before. On average,

08:31 organizations scrapped nearly half of their AI  proof-of-concept projects before the projects ever

08:36 reached production. Budgets got approved. Pilots  got built. Demos got applause in the boardroom.

08:42 Then… nothing shipped. This pattern has a precedent: IBM.

08:47 IBM spent years and billions of dollars  building Watson Health into what was supposed

08:52 to be a revolution in AI-powered medicine. It was  supposed to read scans faster than radiologists,

08:57 and cross-reference treatment options. Instead,  the project was sold off in pieces in 2022 before

09:03 mainstream AI LLMs grabbed the public’s attention. Watson Health failed because, despite having solid

09:09 results in testing, no company could see how it  would make them money. IBM also mandated that

09:14 any prospective buyer abandon its existing  tech stack and adopt Watson’s, essentially

09:19 pigeonholing themselves for one solution. The trillion dollar valuations are all resting

09:24 on a lie. The uncontrollable growth is based  on investments leading to more investments.

09:28 It’s a corporate carousel. So who actually eats the

09:32 loss when the leverage begins to unravel? Remember those Korean retail investors and

09:36 those 360,000 liquidated accounts? Well, 62% of  them belonged to people under 35. These were young

09:43 people who borrowed money because the market had  been rising in a way that felt less like investing

09:48 and more like a game everyone was winning. When  the leverage snapped back, it snapped back on

09:53 people with the least capacity to absorb it. Some  of them are now left owing brokers more money than

09:58 the positions were ever worth. This affects America too.

10:01 A large share of ordinary retirement savings,  the kind sitting in index funds and 401(k)s,

10:06 is concentrated in the same AI-heavy companies  burning cash at record rates. When you contribute

10:12 to a retirement account without picking  individual stocks, a portion of that money

10:16 is flowing into the AI ambitions of a small  group of companies, whether you like it or not.

10:20 Passive investing was supposed to be the safe,  boring choice after the dot-com crash. The 2008

10:26 housing crash taught a generation not to gamble  on individual names. Instead, the index itself

10:32 became the concentrated bet. Then there are pension funds.

10:35 Public-sector retirement systems – the  accounts backing teachers, municipal workers,

10:39 and union pensioners – have been increasing their  exposure to the same AI-concentrated indices.

10:44 These are some of the most consequential and least  visible fault lines sitting inside this entire

10:50 trade. The upside from AI spending, if it ever  fully materializes, gets captured by the companies

10:56 making the bets and the executives holding the  stock options. If the bet goes wrong instead,

11:01 the losses land on people who never had a say in  the decision and can least afford to take the hit.

11:07 That’s the part that gets ignored  every time this story gets told in

11:10 terms of stock tickers and index points. A crash isn’t just numbers on a screen.

11:15 It’s a transfer of risk. One  passed from the people who chose

11:18 to take it, to the people who didn’t. The worst part? It’s not the first time.

11:23 In August 2024, Japan’s Nikkei and Topix indexes  plunged more than 12% in a single session,

11:30 the steepest one-day drop since 1987. The  trigger was a surprise rate hike from the

11:35 Bank of Japan that sent the yen surging. It forced  a violent unwind of the so-called “carry trade,”

11:41 where investors had been borrowing cheap  yen to fund bets on assets like American

11:45 tech stocks. When the yen strengthened, those  investors had to sell to cover their positions,

11:50 which pushed the yen higher still, triggering  more forced selling. On the same day,

11:54 Korea’s Kospi dropped more than  8% and briefly halted trading.

11:58 Go back further, 25 years to the dot-com  bubble, the parallel gets sharper.

12:03 At the peak of that boom, the top 20 companies  in the S&P 500 made up 38% of the index’s total

12:09 value. In the 5 years before the crash, the Nasdaq  had climbed 572%, pulling in investors who’d never

12:16 bought a stock before. When the crash came,  the Nasdaq fell 78% over the space of 2 years,

12:22 wiping out more than $5 trillion in market value.  It didn’t reclaim its old high for 15 years.

12:28 Today, the top 20 companies in the S&P 500 account  for more than half the index’s total value,

12:34 with roughly 10 of them tied directly to AI  and semiconductors. The reasoning investors

12:39 give for holding on sounds almost identical  to 2000. There are no meaningful earnings yet,

12:44 but there’s untapped potential in AI. And the  companies investing in them are big on FOMO.

12:50 There is one big difference this time. During the dot-com crash, the infrastructure

12:54 that got built, the fiber-optic cable  laid by companies that went bankrupt,

12:59 didn’t disappear. Cheap, abandoned fiber ended  up carrying the internet traffic of the next 2

13:04 decades. Someone paid pennies on the dollar for  that fiber and built real businesses on top of it.

13:09 But AI infrastructure doesn’t  leave that kind of gift behind.

13:12 The chips inside these data centers physically  degrade within 1 to 3 years, even losing most

13:17 of their economic value the moment the next  generation of hardware ships. After 3 years,

13:22 a data center is full of outdated chips and has  ruined the local environment by soaking up water,

13:27 emitting noise and pollution, and devastating the  local real-estate market. If the AI bet doesn’t

13:32 pay off, that data center is as good as scrap. The AI-era doesn’t leave a legacy. It ends with

13:38 sky high debt, and a pile of useless  tech that no one will want in 5 years.

13:43 Put these two stories side by  side, and it gets uncomfortable.

13:46 In 2024, we saw how quickly a currency move on  the other side of the world can force a same-day,

13:51 double-digit selloff in Seoul. The year 2000  showed what happens when an entire market

13:56 convinces itself that potential is the same thing  as profit, right up until the moment it isn’t.

14:01 2026’s crash carries pieces of the leverage and  the speed of 2024 while having the concentration

14:07 and the mispriced potential of 2000. And this  time it’s unfolding when the two markets most

14:12 linked to it, Korea’s chipmakers and America’s  AI giants, are more tightly bound together

14:17 than at any point in the last 5 years. The question that actually matters isn’t

14:22 whether this ends. Bubbles always end.

14:25 The question is who’s still standing when the  leverage finally runs out of places to hide,

14:29 and who gets handed the bill  they never agreed to pay.

14:32 And China might be ready to pick up the pieces.  To learn more, watch “What China Understands About

14:38 AI That the US Doesn’t” to see how it’s ready to  shake up the tech sector. Or click on this video.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: The Why and How of the Megalodon Extinction (What Killed the Giant Shark)
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: The Why and How of the Megalodon Extinction (What Killed the Giant Shark)
  • Video ID: 4HF4Phgafdw
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Imagine swimming in the ocean. You’re  splashing around, minding your own business,

00:04 when all of a sudden a shark fin the size  of a boat pops out of the water and heads

00:09 straight towards you. That would probably be  the last time you stepped foot in the ocean,

00:12 if you made it out alive that is. The only  shark that could have a dorsal fin of that

00:16 size would belong to a megalodon. Luckily  for you—and all of us—the megalodon went

00:20 extinct around 3.6 million years ago. But what  caused this massive apex predator to die off?

00:26 And is there a chance that it is still  lurking in the depths of the oceans?

00:30 The megalodon or Carcharocles megalodon first  inhabited the oceans of planet Earth around

00:35 23 million years ago. They were the largest  shark to ever live. Megalodons varied in size,

00:40 but studies suggest that on average a female  meg could be between 45 and 59 feet long. This

00:45 range varies so widely because scientists need  to extrapolate the size based on teeth and jaw

00:51 fragments found in the fossil record. At this  point in time a full megalodon skeleton has not

00:55 been found. However, from the remains we do have,  it is clear that these creatures were enormous.

01:00 Adult megalodons had no predators because  of their massive body size. The shark’s

01:04 main prey was small whales. That’s right,  they ate whales, that's how big they were.

01:08 Megalodons roamed every ocean of  the world, although they stayed away

01:11 from the polar regions where the water would  be too cold. What we know about the megalodon

01:15 species comes from fossil remains, and scientific  observations of their much smaller relatives that

01:20 live today. The largest predatory shark  species alive today is the great white.

01:24 The largest great white ever recorded  was around 36 feet long. This makes it

01:28 20 feet shorter than the megalodon.  Megs were truly massive sharks.

01:33 Megalodons were incredibly successful at what  they did. They outcompeted other predators for

01:37 about 20 million years, and stayed at the top of  the food chain for that entire time. Their size,

01:42 razor sharp teeth, and speed allowed them to  hunt and kill prey with deadly efficiency. So,

01:47 what caused the Megalodon to go extinct? Why isn’t

01:50 this incredibly successful killing  machine ruling over the oceans today?

01:54 There were probably several factors, but evidence  points to a few clear changes that had a big

01:58 impact on the megalodon survival rate. Between  3 and 5 million years ago the climate began to

02:03 change on planet Earth. The world began to cool  as it entered the epoch known as the Plioscene.

02:08 As global temperatures dropped the oceans were  affected. One major change that occurred as

02:12 temperatures cooled was that the sea levels  began to drop. This happens during ice ages,

02:16 and periods of cooling, because the water of  the oceans gets trapped in ice and glaciers.

02:20 As water gets converted into its solid form,

02:22 it is removed from the oceans. This  causes the overall sea level to drop.

02:26 The dropping of the global sea level wouldn’t  have been a problem for megalodon if that was

02:30 the only change that occured, but when the  sea level dropped, new land started to form

02:34 that had previously been underwater. During  the Pliocene the Isthmus of Panama began to

02:38 take shape. The collision of tectonic plates in  the area caused volcanic activity that resulted

02:43 in the formation of the mountains that  now stretch from North to South America.

02:46 The emergence of this new land that connected the  Americas had a huge impact on the animals of the

02:51 oceans. The land that would become Central America  had been under water for millions of years,

02:56 meaning that there was nothing blocking marine  species from crossing between what would become

03:00 the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans near the equator.

03:03 Once the access between the Americas was blocked  off by land, many species were now stuck either

03:08 on one side of the continents or the other. This  meant that access to some of megalodon’s prey may

03:13 have been separated from them. Ocean currents and  movement of nutrients in the oceans began to shift

03:18 once the equatorial connection between the oceans  was impeded. This would have caused species to

03:22 migrate to new areas, or if they could not adjust  to the new environment they would go extinct.

03:26 The currents and nutrients that once flowed  between the Americas would have been abruptly

03:30 brought to a halt. Without these nutrients,  biodiversity would drop. This change would

03:34 have a domino effect on all species living  throughout the oceans. Nutrients would no

03:38 longer be where they once were, and entire  ecosystems would have vanished. This alone

03:42 would have caused mass extinctions of aquatic  organisms, leaving room for new species to evolve.

03:47 Even if this lowering of ocean levels,  and the blockage between the oceans,

03:50 did not directly cause megalodon to go extinct,  it most likely had an impact on their prey.

03:55 Since megalodon was large and slow to  reproduce, it filled one specific niche,

04:00 that of apex predator. If the environment  suddenly changed, it was unlikely that

04:04 megalodon had the genetic diversity to  adapt to a new environment with less prey.

04:08 Another impact of the lowering of ocean levels  is that the oceans become saltier. As more

04:12 and more water is trapped in ice and glaciers  the salt to water ratio in the ocean changes.

04:17 The salt does not get trapped with the water, so  salt levels remain constant, while water levels

04:22 decrease. This causes an increase in salinity  throughout parts of the oceans. The difference in

04:26 saltiness would have shifted the ocean currents,  and nutrient cycles, ever more. In fact,

04:30 this change in salinity is one of the main  reasons we have the ocean conveyor belt of today.

04:35 All of these changes to the  oceans would have meant the

04:37 environment that the megalodon had been  so successful in for millions of years,

04:42 was now different. It is very difficult for large  specialist predators to adapt to changes in their

04:46 environment. Think about what is happening in  the arctic right now to polar bears. They are

04:50 highly specialized for the environment they  evolved in, but if the ice continues to melt,

04:54 and global temperature continues to rise, they  will go extinct. The polar bear species just

04:58 does not have enough genetic diversity to allow  them to be successful in a warmer environment.

05:03 As the environment changed during the Pliocene,  marine diversity diminished for a while before

05:07 natural selection caused new species to evolve  and thrive. Unfortunately, this would have taken

05:12 thousands and thousands of years; time that the  megalodon did not have. With less biodiversity,

05:18 and animals to eat, all predators in the  ocean would need to compete for similar

05:21 food sources. The prey that megalodon  once thrived on would have diminished,

05:25 which meant that either they had to compete for  a different food source, or starve to death.

05:29 Before the change in the environment of the  Pliocene, the oceans were filled with large marine

05:33 animals. Many of these animals ate krill or small  fish like the baleen whales of today. This meant

05:38 that there was an abundance of prey for megalodon  to hunt. However, after the climate shift

05:42 organisms such as toothless walruses, aquatic  sloths, and dwarf baleen whales did not survive

05:48 into the new environment. Slowly, but surely,  the megalodons variety of food was diminished.

05:53 This is where the real problem for megalodon came  in. Changing of climate most likely contributed

05:58 to the extinction of the species, but scientists  now believe there was one main culprit that drove

06:02 the nail into the coffin of the megalodon. At  around the same time as megalodon went extinct,

06:06 a new apex predator had just started to  make its appearance, the great white shark.

06:10 Carcharodon carcharias, or the great white  shark, appeared around the same time as the

06:15 megalodon species began to decline. It would seem  this new species of shark could out compete the

06:19 megalodon. The smaller size of great whites  allowed them to catch and eat smaller prey,

06:23 which was more abundant after the climate shift.  The ability to eat many different species,

06:27 other than just small whales, gave  the great whites an advantage.

06:30 Not only did the great white have a wider  variety of food it could choose from,

06:34 but the smaller body size actually worked in its  favor. Since the megalodon had such a massive

06:39 body it needed to stay in relatively warm waters,  so that it could maintain its body temperature.

06:43 Sharks are ectotherms meaning that they don’t  regulate their internal body temperature,

06:47 but instead, rely on factors such as sunlight  and muscle movement to increase the temperature

06:51 of their bodies. The smaller bodies of the  great white sharks meant they could venture

06:55 into cooler waters, since they had less body  mass to keep warm. Their muscles did not need

06:59 to work quite as hard as megalodon to keep  their body temperature up, and therefore,

07:03 they didn’t need as much energy from  food as their larger cousins either.

07:06 It was also likely that great whites hunted  some of the same prey as megalodon. Perhaps

07:10 the great whites targeted the young of  the species that megalodon was hunting,

07:14 thus reducing the amount of adult prey available  for the megalodon to eat. The great white sharks

07:18 were by no means trying to outcompete and cause  the megalodon to go extinct, but they were,

07:23 and still are, very efficient predators, who  in the new ocean environment thrived. The great

07:27 white shark’s success most likely played a role  in the extinction of the once great megalodon.

07:32 Scientists also think that the evolution of other  smaller species of shark could have put pressure

07:36 on the megalodons. For example, tiger sharks  which lived during the same time as megalodon,

07:41 and in very similar environments, may have  contributed to the larger shark's demise.

07:45 It has been suggested that great whites and  tiger sharks may have fed on megalodon young

07:50 that had not grown to their full size  yet, causing even fewer numbers of the

07:53 species to reach maturity. As we gather more  evidence, we may find that megalodon was not

07:58 just outcompeted by smaller species of shark, but  their babies may have been hunted by them as well.

08:03 One theory of what caused the megalodon  to go extinct is really out there,

08:06 literally. Some astronomers suggest that  a supernova may have contributed to the

08:10 extinction of the largest sharks that ever lived.  The claim is that a nearby star went supernova,

08:15 enveloping the Earth in harmful muon radiation.  This radiation would have been harmful to many

08:20 species. But ones that reproduce slowly like the  megalodon, would have been affected much more

08:25 drastically because of the build up of mutations  and lack of genetic diversity in the species.

08:30 All of these factors may have played  a role in the extinction of megalodon,

08:33 but are we so sure that the species is really  extinct? Could there be a gigantic 60 foot shark

08:40 lurking in the blackness of the oceans? Well,  let's look at the evidence. Humans have been

08:43 exploring the oceans, and recording their  observations, for hundreds of years. In all

08:47 that time there have been no reliable accounts,  or documentation, of megalodons being sighted.

08:52 If megalodons were still alive, we would at  least expect to find whales or other prey

08:56 with 10 foot bite marks on them from the jaws of a  megalodon. But such evidence has never been found.

09:02 We would also expect to find at least some  megalodon fossils in layers of the Earth

09:06 younger than 3.5 million years old, but to  this day no such fossils have been found.

09:10 Scientists also believe that megalodons  established nurseries for their young in

09:14 shallow seas, which means that we should see  baby megalodons near the surface of the ocean.

09:18 Even a baby megalodon would be a massive shark,  and would most definitely make the news. Yet,

09:23 this has never occurred. It is important to  remember that for any species to continue on

09:27 it needs to reproduce, and megalodons, like  all sharks and animals, don’t live forever.

09:31 The fact that there has never been a reliable  sighting of a full grown, or baby megalodon,

09:36 is a good indication the  species went extinct long ago.
