00:39 money on these products thinking that they’ll for  at least a few years before you need to find a

00:44 replacement. It’s not an unreasonable expectation.  One that consumers across the world have been able

00:49 to enjoy for generations. Then AI came along.

00:53 And everything changed. As AI’s tendrils extend across industries

00:57 and infiltrate almost every facet of modern life,  the lifespans of standard computers are dropping

01:02 quickly. In homes and offices around the world  there are hundreds of millions of laptops and

01:06 desktop devices that are less than 2 years old. They look good. Their keyboards aren’t fading.

01:11 The displays are crisp. They boot up in a  matter of seconds. Yet beneath their sleek

01:15 exteriors, a death sentence has been issued. The countdown clocking is about to hit zero.

01:20 The numbers highlight the problem. There are  around 2 billion machines in use today. They’re

01:25 used by people from all walks of life, for all  manner of tasks, both personal and professional.

01:30 Without them, lives would fall apart. Yet the majority of those devices - more

01:34 than 1.3 billion - are missing  the Neural Processing Units (NPUs)

01:39 or the base amount of system memory required  to complete local, next-generation AI tasks.

01:44 Those are the same tasks that tech companies  are forcing on us. The tasks that are about to

01:49 become essential, not optional, for anyone  who wants to browse the internet and use

01:53 the software they’ve relied on for decades. The entire baseline of functional computing

01:57 has shifted. Forever.

01:59 It’s like waking up and finding that 3 lanes  of a 4 lane highway have been permanently

02:03 barricaded and are now exclusively reserved for  a convoy of corporate VIPs. The rest of us are

02:09 forced to battle it out over a single, crumbling  lane, trapped in a bottleneck that never ends.

02:14 That’s what’s happening in the  consumer computer market in 2026.

02:17 And there’s nothing you can do about it. You didn’t make a mistake. You didn’t buy

02:21 broken hardware or download a system-destroying  virus, yet your device has been shut off from the

02:26 future of the internet. There was no warning, no  compensation, and no mercy. It all boils down to

02:32 something relatively simple… Memory.

02:34 That all-important component that has rapidly  become one of the most valuable technological

02:39 resources on the planet. As AI has become  more prominent, the world’s largest tech

02:44 companies have started spending huge amounts of  money on powerful AI infrastructure to run it.

02:49 Memory is a vital piece of that infrastructure.  Brands like OpenAI, Microsoft, Google,

02:54 and Amazon are buying it in droves. The impact of this record-setting RAM

02:58 investment can be seen and felt in the pockets  of millions of consumers the world over.

03:02 Take the smartphone market. For years, this  sector has followed a familiar pattern. Each year,

03:07 the big brands release their latest devices.  Each time, they promise incremental improvements:

03:12 a faster processor, a better display, or a  stronger camera. This is how they have justified

03:17 their price hikes and encouraged users to abandon  their old models in favor of the latest releases.

03:22 But smartphones - just like laptops and computers  - require RAM to function. The AI boom has sent

03:28 the cost of memory soaring to never-before-seen  highs. This has impacted the “Bill of Materials”,

03:34 or BOM, for a smartphone released in 2026. A BOM is a list of all the materials and

03:39 components that go into a device, along with  the raw costs of those materials. In 2022,

03:45 memory made up a small part of the overall cost.  Since then, however, it has dramatically risen,

03:51 to the point where memory now accounts for almost  60% of the BOM in phones worth $400 or less.

03:57 Even in mid-range devices, the BOM cost  of memory has risen to around 40% as RAM

04:03 effectively becomes a luxury good. This leave smartphone manufacturers

04:07 in a difficult position. They need to give people a

04:09 reason to buy their latest devices, but are  having to spend far more to make them. They

04:14 can’t pass all of those costs onto the consumer  by raising the price of the devices themselves.

04:19 People have budgets. Not many are willing to hand  over an extra few hundred dollars for a phone that

04:24 is more or less the same as last year’s model. So, they opt for a different tactic.

04:29 A tactic that revolves around minimizing  manufacturing costs by cutting corners

04:34 as subtly as possible. They swap out camera  sensors for smaller and simpler alternatives.

04:38 They make the phone’s frame from  a cheaper, less durable material.

04:42 They trade the battery for one with a shorter  lifespan, but is more affordable to source.

04:47 They actively make their devices worse,  using cheaper parts and materials to make

04:51 changes that most people won’t notice right  away. On their own, any one of these changes

04:55 would be almost invisible to the consumer. Together, they become a kind of hidden tax.

05:00 The spiraling costs of money have to be accounted  for, somehow. So, even as the product gets worse,

05:05 the price tag stays the same. The customer absorbs  the added cost of RAM and ends up with an inferior

05:11 phone. They might not realize that until a year  or two down the line when it starts freezing or

05:16 failing and they’re forced to buy another. It’s not just affecting smartphones.

05:20 It’s happening all across the tech sector.  Tablets, laptops, gaming PCs, and everything in

05:25 between. The brands that make these products are  no longer just competing with each other for RAM.

05:30 They’re competing with something bigger. Enormous, insatiable beasts that eat up

05:35 energy and computing power far faster, and in  far greater quantities, than anything the world

05:40 has ever seen before. AI data centers.

05:43 These windowless, concrete building are lined  with hyper-efficient cooling towers that pump

05:47 vast plumes of steam into the atmosphere. And  inside each one are rows upon rows of servers.

05:53 Each server is filled with thousands of AI  accelerators, or GPUs, running round-the-clock,

05:58 carrying out the complex mathematical computations  required to train and run machine learning models.

06:04 All of those accelerators rely on RAM to function. With every passing month, more of these data

06:09 centers are springing up around the  world. And they’re getting bigger.

06:12 It’s the physical embodiment of the AI arms race. It doesn’t stop. It continues to hurtle forward

06:17 at breakneck speed. There is a constant,  unrelenting push towards the next big thing:

06:22 the next model, the next leap in intelligence,  the next stage of digital evolution. The only

06:26 way to achieve any of those objectives is growth. Bigger data centers. More servers. More power.

06:32 More memory. Companies like Microsoft, Meta, and

06:35 Alphabet want to dominate the market, and release  the AI tools that millions or even billions of

06:39 people want to pay for. To do that, they have to  stay one step ahead of their rivals. Because in a

06:45 race as ruthless as this, even a tiniest setback  can spiral into a multi-billion dollar loss.

06:50 They have no choice but to purchase all the memory  they can afford as quickly as humanly possible.

06:55 And that’s exactly what they’re doing. The numbers speak for themselves.

06:58 Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet,  are set to allocate $725 billion

07:03 in combined capital expenditure towards their  AI ambitions in 2026 alone. It’s a huge amount

07:09 of money and it’s only going to increase. Experts estimate the combined CapEx for

07:14 the biggest AI brands will reach a whopping $1.2  trillion in 2027, rising to $1.4 trillion in 2028.

07:21 Compare that sort of spending with people  just trying to buy a new device. Like a

07:25 family looking for a new computer or a student  on a tight budget, searching for a laptop they

07:30 can carry around campus. Around the world, there  are millions of people in the market for a new

07:34 computer. But the prices they pay are no longer  influenced by conventional supply and demand.

07:39 Instead, they’re being controlled  by a handful of mega-corporations.

07:43 The technological elite are leveraging  their almost infinite cash reserves

07:47 to outbid the consumer market for silicon chips.  They’re buying up global factory capacity,

07:52 leaving retail brands - and their  customers - to fight over the scraps.

07:56 This is the brutal truth of the AI arms race. It’s not just about companies competing with

08:00 one another to get ahead of the game  and release the next big AI asset.

08:04 It’s about those same companies carrying out a  violent assault on the consumer computer market.

08:09 And the worst part of all is  that there’s no end in sight.

08:13 This isn’t a temporary shortage. It’s not a blip.

08:16 Things aren’t going to simply sort  themselves out and get back on track.

08:19 AI only moves in one direction: models are  only going to get smarter and more demanding.

08:24 They are going to hoover up resources year after  year. As long as that continues, these companies

08:29 will keep on consuming memory in record-setting  amounts, leaving everyone else in the dust.

08:33 The scale of their greed is only getting worse. Because these companies don’t accept the classic

08:38 kind of RAM you’d find in an everyday  laptop or an entry-level smartphone.

08:43 They want the best of the best:  High Bandwidth Memory, or HBM.

08:47 HBM produces incredible speeds by stacking  multiple memory chips together, creating a level

08:52 of performance far beyond traditional RAM. The  gap between advanced AI enterprise systems, like

08:57 NVIDIA H100s clusters, and the 8GB of DDR5 memory  found in a typical consumer laptop is massive.

09:05 The best HBM products score at least 50  times higher on performance benchmarks

09:09 compared to regular RAM. It’s like having  a supersonic fifth-generation fighter jet

09:14 racing against a toddler on a plastic tricycle. This has created a new technological hierarchy.

09:20 The largest companies can process trillions  of data points in fractions of a second,

09:25 while everyday users are left with  machines that struggle with basic AI tasks.

09:29 That’s why HBM has become the backbone of  modern AI processors and supercomputers.

09:34 But in technology, every  breakthrough comes with a cost.

09:37 For HBM, that cost is measured in silicon. Producing a single gigabyte of HBM for AI systems

09:43 requires around 3 times more silicon capacity  than making standard DDR5 memory. So when a

09:49 factory shifts its focus toward HBM to chase the  AI boom, regular RAM production gets squeezed.

09:56 These two markets can’t grow side by side. Every piece of silicon dedicated to high-end

10:01 AI memory is silicon that can’t be used to make  RAM for millions of everyday devices like laptops,

10:07 phones, and tablets. The result is a brutal  trade-off: the AI industry is consuming the

10:12 resources that powered the consumer market. And when you look at the profits involved,

10:16 it’s easy to understand why memory manufacturers  are choosing to chase the HBM orders.

10:22 In today’s market conditions, manufacturers can  easily have operating margins in excess of 50%.

10:28 Some are even being forecast to see  their margins rise close to 80%.

10:33 That’s a massive difference compared to the  much slimmer margins these same companies

10:36 had to cope with when making regular  RAM before the AI boom really began.

10:41 The problem is, this isn’t a market with  dozens of companies making different choices.

10:46 The global memory industry is controlled by 3  giants: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. Together,

10:53 they produce around 93% of all memory chips. That gives them enormous control over where

10:58 the industry goes. And they’re choosing  the path that makes them the most money.

11:03 They can cater to a small, elite market,  rather than worrying about pleasing the masses.

11:07 Even when their CEOs acknowledge the shortfalls  in the DDR markets, they’ve continued to pour

11:12 resources into expanding HBM production. Their loyalties lie with Big Tech.

11:17 Of course, they won’t admit  that they’re “abandoning” the

11:20 general public or leaving millions of  consumers to fight for scraps. Instead,

11:24 they talk about “diversifying” their product  lineup or “expanding” into emerging markets.

11:29 It’s boring business speak to cover up  the consequences of their decisions.

11:33 But no matter how much they dress it up, the end  result is the same: the HBM market gets bigger

11:39 and richer, all at the expense of the DDR market. The likes of Meta and Microsoft get the massive

11:44 stacks of chips they need to build bigger  data centers and train their AI models.

11:49 Families, students, and struggling  professionals have to make do with less.

11:52 This isn’t a supply chain hiccup or “Act of God.” It’s not some evil masterplan, either.

11:58 It’s a cold, calculated, and entirely legal  corporate strategy, driven by the oldest and

12:03 purest bedrock of the business world: The pursuit of profit.

12:06 During the final quarter of 2025, SK Hynix saw  a 66% increase in revenue compared to the same

12:12 period a year earlier. Operating profits also  surged by 137% over the same span of time.

12:19 It was a similar story at  the other big memory firms.

12:22 They didn’t go all-in on HBM and starve  the DDR market entirely, but they made a

12:27 big enough investment to send their profits - and  shareholder satisfaction rates - to record levels.

12:32 The ugly by-product of this strategy, however,  is a ruthless reallocation of global resources

12:38 away from the working and middle classes. While the market evolves to optimize yields

12:42 for every single square millimeter of silicon  in existence, a memory famine has swept across

12:47 large parts of the world. And, in the wake  of that famine, a frightening new world is

12:51 beginning to emerge. A divided reality.

12:54 A digital caste system. A world in which two

12:57 contrasting extremes exist in a state of chaos. On the one hand, there are hyper advanced AI

13:03 systems, training on never-ending sets  of data, chewing through resources.

13:07 As these systems grow smarter and stronger,  their capabilities increase exponentially,

13:11 to the point where almost no task is impossible. At the other end of the spectrum sits the

13:16 consumers. You.

13:18 The everyday people who are looking for  devices that let them do the things they

13:21 need but are increasingly being made to pay  higher prices for lower quality machines.

13:26 To make matters worse, most of these  machines aren’t just falling slightly behind,

13:31 they’re heading toward obsolescence. AI is being  pushed into everyday devices and workplaces.

13:36 That leaves millions of people with basic  laptops and mid-range PCs that can’t keep

13:41 up with the wave of AI-powered apps and operating  systems. So, they’ll be left with only one option.

13:46 The cloud. The same cloud owned and operated by

13:49 those very same mega-corps. The same cloud they  power with all the silicon and other computing

13:54 components they steal from the rest of the world. People will either buy an expensive

13:59 AI-ready machine, or pay tech giants  monthly just to use basic features.

14:03 That’s the future we’re moving toward. It’s not just about big tech using billion dollar

14:07 budgets to dominate the market. It’s about turning  one-time purchases into endless subscriptions.

14:12 It’s a slow shift toward “digital serfdom,”  where people no longer truly own their computers.

14:17 Instead, they become portals for accessing  services and renting digital lives from the

14:21 same companies that built the system. These are the harrowing consequences

14:25 of the AI boom. The tech giants are  only going to become more powerful,

14:29 while the people gradually lose whatever  control, choice, and freedom they once had.

14:34 They told you AI would transform the  world and unlock opportunities for all.

14:38 They just forgot to mention the price  you’d have to pay for that transformation.

14:42 Now people are starting to see the real  cost… and it’s already too late to stop it.

14:46 The AI bubble is growing and affecting us daily.  But is it sustainable? Watch $115 Billion Burn

14:53 Rate. The AI Bubble Just POPPED to find out  where it all ends. Or click on this video.

00:00 It was called the war to end all wars.

00:03 Unfortunately, World War I didn’t deliver on that promise.

00:06 It was however the first time in the history of planet Earth that nations from around the

00:10 world fought in a single war.

00:12 It started with an assassination and a series of questionable decisions.

00:16 We can point fingers and play the blame game, but really there is no single person or country

00:21 that holds all of the responsibility.

00:23 Could the war that killed millions have been prevented?

00:26 Most definitely.

00:27 Let’s take a look at what caused the Great War, explore how it could have been prevented,

00:32 and learn how to not repeat the mistakes of the past.

00:35 World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918 and included countries in Europe, Russia, the United States,

00:42 and countries in the Middle East.

00:44 The two main sides of the war were the Central Powers which consisted of Germany, Austria-Hungary,

00:48 Italy, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria, who fought against the Allied Powers of France,

00:54 Britain, Russia, Portugal and Japan.

00:57 Later in the war the United States would also join the side of the Allies.

01:00 But what happened?

01:01 Why did all of these nations get involved in one of the most disastrous wars in history?

01:06 Let’s explore the mechanisms and missteps that led to the first World War.

01:10 Although there were many players in World War 1, the conflict started with Serbia and

01:15 Austria-Hungary.

01:16 The Serbian government was eager to claim more territory for the nation.

01:20 Serbia was already in a state of aggression due to the Balkan Wars that ended just a year

01:24 before the start of World War I.

01:26 After the Balkan War, Serbian nationalists wanted to liberate the South Slavs of Austria-Hungary,

01:32 thus unifying the Slavic peoples under one nation.

01:35 This extreme nationalism led to the assissnation of the Archduke Franz Ferdinand who was heir

01:40 to the Astro-Hungarian Empire.

01:42 At 11:15 AM on June 28, 1914 Franz Ferdinand and his wife, Sophie, duchess of Hohenberg,

01:49 were shot to death in Sarajevo, Bosnia by Gavrilo Princip.

01:53 Princip was a Serbian extremist who had connections to a secret society called the Black Hand.

01:57 The assaisnation was the match that ignited the first world war, however, there were many

02:02 other factors that led to the powderkeg that would explode.

02:06 Should the assassination of Franz Ferdinand have led to an all out War?

02:09 Probably not.

02:10 There is more to the story here.

02:12 In the shadows lurked Kaiser Wilhelm II, who may be as much to blame as Gavrilo Princip

02:17 in starting World War I. Wilhelm II was the leader of Germany and he was diabolical.

02:23 Kaiser Wilhelm II wanted a strong Germany that dominated Europe both economically and

02:28 militarily in strength.

02:29 He did not want Russia or Great Britain to have more influence and power than he did.

02:34 Therefore, Wilhelm II allied himself, and Germany, with Austria-Hungary.

02:38 He knew that if Austria-Hungary went to war with Serbia, then Russia would come to Serbia’s

02:43 aid.

02:44 This would drag Russia's ally France into the conflict.

02:46 We will examine later why Wilhelm wanted this war to happen so badly.

02:50 Kaiser Wilhelm II secretly funded Austria-Hungary in their endeavor to suppress Serbia.

02:55 He allowed Germany to give Austria-Hungary a carte blanche, or “blank check.”

03:00 Basically Germany would fund the war effort using their wealthy economy to ensure Austria-Hungary

03:05 came out on top.

03:06 With the assassination of their heir, and the backing of Germany, Austria-Hungary felt

03:10 empowered to start their war with Serbia.

03:13 They sent Serbia an ultimatum with such harsh terms that it was impossible to accept.

03:18 There was only one alternative.

03:20 War.

03:21 But there was more to the story.

03:22 The decisions of Austria-Hungary and Germany were clearly geared towards war.

03:26 It is undeniable that World War I started because of these aggressive decisions.

03:30 But could the whole conflict have been avoided if other countries had made better decisions?

03:35 Were there strings being pulled behind the scenes by the countries on both sides of the

03:39 war?

03:40 Let’s find out.

03:41 First let’s take a look at the Triple Entente nations, which consisted of a secret pact

03:45 between Great Britain, France, and Russia.

03:47 Could any of these nations have secretly wanted a world war to heighten their power?

03:51 Could there have been a secret plot by the Allies to set up a war they would eventually

03:55 win?

03:56 Russia is, and always has been, a large, powerful nation.

04:00 What could Russia gain from a war against the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary,

04:04 and Italy?

04:05 At first glance Russia’s role in World War I seems to be based around supporting their

04:10 ally of Serbia.

04:11 But as we look closer it seems that Russia’s alliance only played a superficial role in

04:16 their decisions to go to war.

04:18 In fact Russia barely even tried to find a diplomatic solution to prevent this conflict.

04:22 Instead, they immediately started to deploy troops and ramp up military production once

04:27 Austria-Hungary showed aggression towards Serbia.

04:29 It would seem Russia had no intentions on working out the conflict diplomatically.

04:34 History shows it was Russia, not Germany, that mobilized its military first.

04:39 Russia may have wanted war to claim more territory and power for the nation.

04:43 But there was another player on the Triple Entente side who may have played a behind

04:47 the scenes role of starting World War I. France did not make any outwardly aggressive moves

04:52 in the months that led to the outbreak of war, but they were making secret strategic

04:57 moves.

04:58 France may be the only reason that Russia prepared for war in the first place.

05:02 During talks of what was to be done about the Central Powers, France offered Russia

05:06 its own blank cheque.

05:07 The stipulation was that Russia would help Europeanise the Austrian-Hungry Empire.

05:12 France had an idea of what this part of the world should look like, and rather than entering

05:16 directly into conflict, they funded the Russian military to start a war that they could benefit

05:21 from.

05:22 France encouraged Russia’s aggression towards Austria-Hungary and Germany.

05:25 French leaders seemed not to like the idea of having the powerful nation of Germany right

05:29 next door.

05:30 If Germany was focused on fighting Russia on the Eastern front, it would provide France

05:35 with the opportunity to either protect itself, or launch an uncontested invasion into Germany

05:41 from the western front.

05:42 It would seem that things did not play out exactly as France predicted because of Germany’s

05:46 deployment of troops to fight on both the Russian and French fronts simultaneously.

05:51 If the shady actions of France leading up to the start of World War I surprised you

05:55 then what Great Britain did may shock you even more.

05:58 Britain was a dominant force in colonization and had control of the seas with their powerful

06:02 Navy.

06:03 Would they benefit from an all out war in Europe?

06:06 Germany was becoming powerful, both economically and militarily.

06:09 Britain knew that this was a threat to their empire.

06:12 In the eyes of Great Britain’s leaders the world wasn’t big enough for both a German

06:16 empire and British empire.

06:18 If Germany continued on the path it was headed, Britain’s global dominance of the seas and

06:22 financial system would be threatened, and perhaps lost.

06:25 This was unacceptable to the leaders of Great Britain.

06:29 These notions of loss of dominance may have driven Great Britain to stay out of diplomatic

06:33 talks, and instead encourage Russian aggression.

06:36 It would seem that at the time Great Britain had an inferiority complex when it came to

06:40 Germany.

06:41 They had failed to meditate during the Balkan Wars and they refused to meditate during the

06:45 lead up to World War I.

06:46 The thought process may have been that the more conflicts Germany was a part of, the

06:50 more likely they were to be weakened.

06:52 Great Britain had clearly won the naval arm race by 1910, it just seemed that it wasn’t

06:57 enough.

06:58 They were still living in fear of Germany’s threats.

07:01 And it would appear rightfully so as history showed over the next several decades.

07:04 It needs to be said that if Great Britain wanted to prevent war, they should have contributed

07:09 to the mediation discussions.

07:11 The fact that they actively avoided the mediations shows Britain may have had other motives.

07:15 Especially if war meant a weakened Germany.

07:18 History is written by the victors.

07:20 Therefore, history textbooks tend to attribute most of, if not all of, the blame for World

07:24 War I to Austria-Hungary and Germany.

07:27 You have to wonder who would be blamed if the outcome of the war was reversed.

07:31 We discussed how the nations of the Triple Entente were by no means free of blame for

07:35 the start of this conflict.

07:36 But let’s take a closer look at the motives and actions of the Triple Alliance, which

07:40 was the secret pact between Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy.

07:44 Let’s find out if they really are to blame like so many textbooks say.

07:48 Other than retaliation, what was Austria-Hungary after?

07:51 In a word, territory.

07:53 Austria-Hungary wanted to add more land and people to its already large empire.

07:57 More land equals more resources, and more men for their military.

08:01 Austria-Hungary had its sights set on Serbia for a while.

08:04 The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand allowed them the perfect opportunity to make

08:09 their dreams of taking over Serbian lands a reality.

08:12 Austria-Hungary’s desires were made clear when they offered an obscene ultimatum to

08:16 Serbia.

08:17 The ultimatum itself was delivered on July 23, 1914.

08:21 It required Serbia to accept an Austro-Hungarian inquiry into the assassination of Archduke

08:26 Ferdinand.

08:27 The inquiry would be conducted solely by Austria-Hungarian investigators.

08:31 Serbia also needed to suppress all anti-Austrian propaganda and eliminate any terrorist or

08:36 extremist organizations within its borders.

08:39 The leaders of Austria-Hungary demanded that an answer to the ultimatum be sent within

08:43 48 hours.

08:44 However, the ambassador to Serbia delivered the ultimatum and immediately left the country

08:48 to return back to Austria-Hungary.

08:50 He already knew what was going to happen next.

08:52 There was no way that Serbia would accept the ultimatum.

08:55 This meant war.

08:56 The ultimatum served one purpose.

08:58 Austria-Hungary knew Serbia would never accept their terms, but they also knew if they attacked

09:02 without warning it would make Serbia look like the victim.

09:06 By sending the ultimatum it pushed the burden of avoiding war onto the Serbian government.

09:10 This way Austria-Hungary created the illusion of giving Serbia a chance to stop the war.

09:16 When they didn’t, Serbia would look like the bad guy.

09:19 But the ridiculous ultimatum did not stand up to the test of history, and Austria-Hungary

09:23 is still seen as the aggressors.

09:26 Really what it came down to was that Austria-Hungary wanted to control more territory in the Balkan

09:30 region.

09:31 They needed a reason to go to war with Serbia to secure that land and they found it in the

09:36 assassination of their Archduke.

09:38 Was the assassination a reason to conduct an all out war?

09:41 Probably not, but it was sufficient enough reason for the Austria-Hungary government

09:45 at the time.

09:49 I am sure you can guess what is coming next.

10:24 would both get pulled in.

10:25 It was almost as if Germany needed to find a way to declare war on their competitors

10:29 in the region without doing it themselves.

10:32 Germany could never just outright declare war on the other nations or they would risk

10:35 unifying the entire continent of Europe against them.

10:39 But by strategically destabilizing the Balkans they could gode Russia, and therefore France,

10:44 into a war with their ally, thus allowing Germany to start a war to suit their needs.

10:49 The other reason that Germany wanted war was because it had peaked as a nation.

10:53 If Germany allowed the rest of Europe to catch up they would lose power and prestige.

10:57 This upset no one more than Kaiser Wilhelm II, who was an angry militaristic autocrat.

11:02 He believed that he was predestined by God to lead his country to greatness.

11:06 He hated diplomats and maintained that the only way to ensure Germany's spot of power

11:11 was through war.

11:12 He knew it was now or never if Germany was going to become the predominant world power.

11:17 When a power hungry autocrat is in charge of one of the world’s most wealthy and armed

11:21 nations there is only one outcome.

11:23 War.

11:24 In the end World War I was caused by many different factors and countries.

11:27 There is not just one person or nation to blame.

11:30 However, some are more responsible than others.

11:33 If the leaders of Europe were less hungry for power, and more willing to sit down and

11:37 negotiate, the war could have been avoided.

11:39 Make no mistake, World War I was not unavoidable.

11:42 But the leaders in charge saw war as a desirable outcome, or were forced into it by allies.

11:47 A situation that would repeat itself again 21 years later.

11:51 If you are interested in more World War I information check out 50 Insane World War

11:56 1 Facts That Will Shock You!

11:58 Or if you want to know how World War I and World War II stack up watch World War 1 VS

12:03 World War 2 - How Do They Compare?

00:12 Today we're asking: jail vs prison- what's the difference?

00:15 First we'll start with jail, since if you were forced to choose this is definitely the

00:19 one you want to get sent to.

00:21 Typically this is what's known as the clink, with prison being known as the big house.

00:25 Jails are normally much smaller facilities that hold a smaller number of inmates than

00:29 prisons, which can have populations of several thousand.

00:32 They're typically run by local governments- think city versus the state- and supervised

00:36 by a county Sheriff's department.

00:38 Their population is mostly made up of people who have recently been arrested for minor

00:42 offenses or a misdemeanor, and their sentences are far shorter than in a prison- typically

00:46 less than a year.

00:48 Yet jails are themselves different from temporary lockups which are typically located inside

00:52 police departments and hold individuals who can't post bail, those arrested for public

00:57 drunkenness, or individuals waiting to be processed into a jail.

01:01 Jails can also serve to hold prisoners awaiting trial or to hold a prisoner during a very

01:05 long and extended trial.

01:07 While they typically only hold individuals guilty of misdemeanors, if the sentences for

01:11 several misdemeanors are not served concurrently then an individual could be held for far longer

01:16 than the typical period of less than a year.

01:18 However jails often offer work release programs, boot camps, educational programs, substance

01:23 abuse support groups, and vocational training programs.

01:26 Prisons however are a vastly different world than jails, and this is where the most hardened

01:31 criminals are sent to.

01:33 You'll find no misdemeanors here, and instead prisons hold men who have been convicted of

01:38 felonies.

01:39 If you're wondering the difference between felonies and misdemeanors, misdemeanors include

01:42 such offenses as petty theft, prostitution, simple assault, trespassing, vandalism, and

01:47 reckless driving.

01:49 Felonies on the other hand include crimes such as assault with a deadly weapon, grand

01:53 theft, rape, and murder.

01:54 If you had to pick which of the two populations to spend a year or more with, we're pretty

01:59 sure you'd want to go with the misdemeanor crowd.

02:01 While jails are run by local governments, prisons are run by the state or even the federal

02:05 government, who has its own prison system apart from that of state government-run prisons.

02:09 The difference between the two types of prisons is pretty obvious- state prisons hold individuals

02:13 who break state laws, and federal prisons hold individuals guilty of breaking federal

02:18 laws.

02:19 The difference between the two offenses can be a bit murky though, and federal prisoners

02:22 can range from individuals who rob banks- because banks are insured by the federal government-

02:27 to people accused of political crimes, and many white-collar criminals.

02:31 For these reasons state prisons are often much more dangerous than federal prisons,

02:35 as they hold many more violent offenders.

02:37 If you plan on breaking the law then make sure it's a federal law and not a state law

02:42 for a much safer prison experience.

02:44 Both federal and state prisons range from minimum security to maximum security though,

02:48 and the degree of the offense determines where you'll end up.

02:51 Many white collar crimes such as tax evasion can net you a stay in a federal minimum security

02:56 prison.

02:57 Here you'll enjoy many amenities including team sports and a dining facility, with few

03:01 guards and typically just a single fence.

03:04 Minimum security prisons tend to resemble adult camps more than actual prisons, and

03:08 some even have internet access for their prisoners.

03:11 Visits with family are common, and violence is exceptionally rare.

03:14 You'll also be able to enjoy a dorm instead of a cell, and over all your stay will resemble

03:19 something more like a college dorm than an actual prison.

03:22 Offenders here typically have non-violent convictions and clean prior criminal records,

03:27 though some can be prisoners who have been transferred form higher security prisons thanks

03:31 to exemplary behavior.

03:33 Medium security prisons are what you probably think of when you think of prison, and though

03:37 the inmates do enjoy some degree of independence their movements are all very tightly controlled.

03:42 You can forget things such as team sports and internet access- though some prisons may

03:46 offer use of library computers as incentives to well-behaved individuals.

03:50 Medium security prisons also often don't have cells, and instead have spanning dormitories

03:55 that house dozens of inmates together.

03:57 Orange Is The New Black is a good example of a medium security prison facility.

04:02 Maximum security prison, or SuperMaxes, is where the worst of the worst go-yet this is

04:07 where the least of all prisoners in the US serve their time.

04:10 These places are inhabited by inmates with very violent offenses or those who have caused

04:14 trouble in lower security prisons, earning them a trip to a much more restrictive life.

04:19 Inmates who have tried to escape, or successfully escaped and then been caught, are also automatically

04:24 sent to a maximum security prison so their movements can be very closely monitored.

04:28 Unsurprisingly an inmate's daily life is extremely restricted in a supermax, and head counts

04:33 are common.

04:34 Prisoners typically share a small cell with another prisoner and may get some freedom

04:38 to move about cells during the day time, but must always be ready for headcounts by lights

04:43 out.

04:44 Prisoners also enjoy cafeteria meals and time spent on recreation out on the yard where

04:48 they can do things like play basketball or lift weights.

04:51 While gang activity permeates the entire prison system, and even jails, it's in maximum security

04:56 prison where it is at its peak, and along with the restrictions imposed by the prison

05:00 system, inmates live under a code of conduct further restricted by the gangs they join.

05:05 Not joining a gang is possible, but typically hazardous to your health.

05:09 Inside a maximum security prison you can also find solitary lockup, which is where the worst

05:14 of the worst end up doing much of their time.

05:16 Here offenders who trespass while serving time in prison will get sent as a punishment,

05:20 and though most stays last only a few weeks, they can end up serving as much as years in

05:25 solitary.

05:26 Offenses such as assaulting a guard will not only get you more prison time, but earn you

05:30 several months or more in solitary, where you'll spend your entire day cramped up in

05:35 a tiny cell with one hour of outside recreation a day.

05:39 During that hour you'll be allowed to sit in a small fenced-in outdoor area that's typically

05:43 a few paces long by a few paces wide, though often you may not be allowed outside as short

05:48 staffed prisons simply can't spare the manpower to get you your hour of rec.

05:53 Other times guards may simply deny you your hour as a punishment measure.

05:57 Between the two you definitely want to serve your time in jail if you can, or at least

06:01 in a minimum security prison where you'll enjoy many of the perks of what basically

06:04 amounts to an adult camp.

06:06 End up in a medium or maximum security prison though and not only are you going to be there

06:10 a long time, but your stay is going to be much more difficult and much more uncomfortable.

06:16 Which would you rather serve your time in?

06:18 Let us know in the comments!

06:19 And as always if you enjoyed this video don't forget to Like, Share, and Subscribe for more

06:23 great content!

docs.text:
00:00 You’ve been working seven days a week all year round, taking only a few holidays, and

00:04 being told constantly that your work needs to be changed.

00:07 Two guys on your developing team have had to quit due to almost having mental breakdowns.

00:11 You’re working on what could be the greatest game the world has ever known, perhaps the

00:16 most complex game ever created…well, partly created, because every time you get close

00:21 to finishing just one part of the game you’re told it’s just not right.

00:24 In fact, you’re starting to feel like you're looking for a pot of gold at the end of a

00:28 rainbow, chasing your own shadow, being asked to believe in something that doesn’t actually

00:32 exist.

00:33 This is the story of the most expensive game never created.

00:37 First of all, modern video games are very expensive to make and they take a long time

00:41 to complete.

00:42 Here at the Infographics Show we actually know a guy who spent years working on some

00:45 very big video game titles.

00:47 He had two nervous breakdowns in those years and said developing video games was the most

00:51 stressful environment he’d ever worked in.

00:53 We guess making games sounds like a really fun job, but trust us, playing them is not

00:58 like making them.

01:00 So you have these big teams of developers working really long shifts and going out of

01:03 their minds.

01:04 They need to be paid a fair bit of money for this, and then after that you’ve got marketing

01:08 and packaging and office space to pay for.

01:11 You might have a team of say, 150 core people, to make a complex game such as “Grand Theft

01:16 Auto”, and they might be working on it for three of four whole years before any cash

01:20 comes back.

01:21 “Grand Theft Auto V” is estimated to have cost anything from $139 million to $270 million

01:27 to make.

01:28 The good news is, it also made tons of money for its publisher, Rockstar Games.

01:32 That was about $6 billion in total revenue.

01:36 The game “Destiny” cost about $500 million to make and market, which is more than any

01:41 movie that’s ever been made.

01:43 Ok, so it can be costly to make a game, and of course it’s a big risk.

01:47 It certainly paid off for Rockstar with their Grand Theft Auto franchise, and we reckon

01:52 Nintendo with its Super Mario franchise has a bank full of billions of gold coins.

01:56 But imagine this for a second…you’re spending years and years on a game, you, and lots of

02:01 over-worked, stressed-out, Adderall-eating developers, and you just can’t finish the

02:05 thing.

02:06 It’s like the search for the Holy Grail, but not quite as exciting.

02:09 Maybe a better comparison would be quarantine with a computer.

02:12 The game we are talking about is called “Star Citizen”, and its story is mind-blowing,

02:16 if not confusing.

02:17 You see, back in 2011 when this game got off the ground it did so only with the help of

02:21 the public.

02:22 It had raised two million in crowdfunding by 2013, and the bosses said, ok, now we can

02:27 start- developers, start writing code.

02:29 That was seven years ago, and you know, those guys, the ones that lasted, are still at their

02:34 stations, no doubt now on an Adderall drip.

02:36 The team of guys in charge of making this game belong to a company called Cloud Imperium.

02:40 They’ve been busy getting more funding, and believe it or not, they’re now at around

02:43 $328 million.

02:45 This makes it the most expensive game ever, in terms of development.

02:49 The game Destiny might have cost around $500 million, but that was the full shebang…there

02:53 was tons of money on marketing and packaging.

02:56 Destiny’s creators actually said the production alone was not even close to $500 million,

03:00 and Destiny is actually finished, which is quite important indeed.

03:04 So, we have Star Citizen, right now the most expensive game, not ever made, but never made.

03:09 We’re not going to go into details about the game itself, but will tell you that it’s

03:13 in the “space trading and combat simulator” genre of games, meaning you’ll be flying

03:16 around space, shooting things and buying things.

03:19 Did we ever tell you this amazing fact; space is a big place…like, really big...there’s

03:24 a lot to work with if you’re trying to make a space game seem realistic.

03:27 Let’s say there are around 2 trillion galaxies in the universe, and each of them holds millions

03:32 and millions of stars.

03:33 Then you've got a star system, like our solar system.

03:36 That in itself is pretty big, but we hear that Star Citizen wants to create 100 star

03:41 systems.

03:42 Maybe that is just too ambitious.

03:43 We think you’ll soon find out that it is.

03:45 That’s kind of the whole problem these guys are having making this damn game.

03:49 Just how BIG do you make space when you’re trying to make the best space game ever?

03:53 How perfect do you make it all?

03:54 There have been investors sinking millions into this game, but the majority of the cash,

03:58 over $250 million of the money, has been crowdfunded.

04:02 That’s Joe Public putting his hard-earned money into a game that can’t seem to be

04:07 finished.

04:08 People are starting to say, well, if Rockstar could blow your mind and do a GTA title in

04:11 three years, then surely Star Citizen is not just literally going to be out of this world,

04:16 but figuratively, too.

04:17 Almost a decade on a game.

04:19 Surely they’ve got something really special already...or maybe not.

04:23 There are people out there that think Star Citizen won’t be that mind-blowing at all,

04:27 and the money has all been virtually vaporized.

04:29 Those critics, and we are reading one right now, say there is no Holy Grail.

04:34 They say Star Citizen is a chimera, the game-version of Keyser Soze.

04:38 Other’s just say it’s a scam, or has just been very badly managed.

04:42 We have no idea.

04:43 Don’t shoot the messenger...we're just telling you what we’ve read.

04:46 This is how one reporter put it: “Star Citizen has become a lightning-rod

04:49 for controversy, with several entire forums’ worth of people dedicated to forensically

04:54 dissecting every tiny detail, rumor or allegation surrounding the project.”

04:59 The thing is, that report was made almost four years ago, and the game STILL hasn’t

05:03 been completed and the guys are still asking for more money.

05:07 One thing might just be that the person at the head of the production team is a perfectionist,

05:11 but you know, one of those perfectionists that can be quite hard to work with.

05:14 Creating the perfect universe might not be so easy.

05:17 More recent reports we found say the game has been mishandled, mismanaged, and working

05:21 on Star Citizen has been “chaotic.”

05:23 That’s 537 employees at five different offices, all being micromanaged by a perfectionist

05:29 and likely so over-worked they haven’t even been told it’s 2020.

05:33 They get paid well though, with $30 million being paid out in total in salaries in 2019.

05:39 That’s quite a lot of cash for a game that hasn’t been made and may never be made.

05:44 Imagine you paid some construction company 300+plus million to build you an amazing house,

05:49 and after ten years they told you they still hadn’t quite finished the bathroom toilet.

05:53 We actually found out where some of the cash went.

05:55 We found one graphics engineer who spent months on visual effects, but for a really small

06:00 element of the game.

06:01 A developer said he quit after spending 17 months on making characters, and then was

06:05 told to change them.

06:06 He said this was going on all the time, meanwhile the company was spending lots of money on

06:10 making demos so it could impress people and get more funding.

06:13 The enterprise was a money-making machine, but for the workers it was like being trapped

06:17 in a Franz Kafka novel…like going down a rabbit hole and getting lost in a network

06:21 of confusing tunnels, or being told to travel to a Castle it’s just impossible to get

06:25 to.

06:26 This is what one investor said after he saw where his money had gone and how far the game

06:30 had got in terms of development: “The game they promised us can't even barely

06:34 run.

06:35 The performance is terrible and it's still in an 'Alpha' state.

06:37 I want out.

06:38 They lied to us.”

06:39 He wanted his money back.

06:40 This guy said that back in mid-2019.

06:43 He was promised that the game would have 100 star systems, but guess what, when he looked

06:47 at the Alpha mode, it didn’t even have one fully-completed star system.

06:51 Hmm, not one star system in one entire decade.

06:55 Let’s do some math…10 years...1….100…Maybe the game will be completed around 2120.

07:01 All its fans will be dead by then, or at least have grown out of computer games.

07:05 Now check out, “Why Do Games Cost $60?

07:08 Why Hasn't The Price of Video Games Changed?” or, “Are You Playing The Losing Game: Fortnite

07:13 vs Apex vs PUBG”

00:00 So, you’ve committed a crime.

00:02 Save the reasons for your next appeal, because you’ve already been tried, convicted, and

00:06 sentenced to a term in prison.

00:07 The question now is which prison you’ll be sentenced to – state or federal prison.

00:12 Aren’t all prisons created equal, you wonder?

00:14 Well, there I’m afraid, you’d be terribly wrong.

00:20 What they are, what gets you admitted, what the general experience is like inside, and

00:25 which one you’d prefer to serve your sentence in.

00:27 First, let’s take a look at state prisons.

00:29 These are, as the name suggests, government prisons run by the state in which they’re

00:33 located.

00:34 Referred to as “State Penitentiaries” in Pennsylvania and most Southern states,

00:38 these jails are intended for criminals who committed minor to major crimes within a single

00:43 state.

00:44 They’re tried by state judges, in state courts.

00:46 And the care of state prisoners and the maintenance of the prisons themselves are funded by taxpayers

00:51 within the given state.

00:52 State prisons also make up the grand majority of prison facilities in the United States,

00:56 as state crimes are significantly more common than federal.

01:00 To give you some perspective, there are 122 federal prisons operated by the Bureau of

01:05 Prisons in the United States.

01:06 For comparison, there are 1,719 state prisons.

01:11 Between them, they manage 1,518,559 inmates.

01:15 1,328,599 of these are state prison inmates.

01:21 State prisons also more commonly offer the possibility of parole, and – on average

01:25 – have lower sentences than their federal counterparts.

01:28 The exact workings of a state prison can sometimes vary from state to state, and these prisons

01:33 are significantly more likely to admit violent criminals – such as murderers, sex criminals,

01:38 and people found guilty of most gun-related offenses.

01:41 In spite of this, state prisons generally have a lower standard of security than federal

01:45 prisons.

01:46 Some state prisons are even run by private companies contracted by the state authorities,

01:50 because the problem of overcrowding in state prisons has required the intervention of outside

01:55 help.

01:56 There are three different types of state prison facility: Minor, Medium, and Maximum-security

02:00 prisons.

02:01 Some of these prisons even have the facilities to execute prisoners, in states that still

02:05 practice Capital Punishment like Texas and North Carolina.

02:08 Due to their overpopulation problems, these prisons are often underfunded, understaffed,

02:12 and pretty dangerous.

02:14 Getting hundreds or even thousands of violent offenders together in poor living conditions

02:18 is a recipe for disaster.

02:20 Prison mortality rates and suicides have been on the uptick since 2010, and prison riots

02:24 are also a constant risk.

02:26 Recently, tensions boiled over at the Mississippi State Penitentiary in Parchman, Mississippi.

02:31 Brutal gang violence broke out, killing five inmates and allowing a further two to escape.

02:37 Conditions in these state jails are often shoddy – with filthy cells and low-quality

02:40 cafeteria meals.

02:42 The ACLU has even presented lawsuits against state prisons on the grounds of inhumane treatment,

02:47 physical and sexual violence, and racial discrimination.

02:51 Because 20% of all US prison inmates are convicted for drug offences – and the grand majority

02:56 of these inmates end up in state prisons – state prison populations are often disproportionately

03:00 made up of minorities.

03:01 This, in turn, is because mass drug incarceration disproportionately targets minorities to begin

03:07 with.

03:08 Non-violent drug offenders end up shoulder to shoulder with violent criminals, creating

03:11 huge risks to their safety.

03:13 This is only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the horrific conditions faced in a lot

03:18 of state prisons, particularly in the South.

03:20 The civil rights division of the Justice Department investigated a number of state prisons in

03:24 Alabama and their findings were deeply disturbing: Prisoners left face-down, dead in their cells,

03:30 for so long that their faces rotted and flattened.

03:33 There was other evidence that prisoners had been tied up and tortured for days on end.

03:37 Attacks included a prisoner being doused with shaving cream so dangerously hot that it left

03:42 the prisoner with second-degree chemical burns.

03:44 And a prisoner having industrial bleach poured onto their skin, before being beaten senseless

03:49 with a broom handle.

03:50 According to Justice Department reports, some Alabama state prisons have murder rates at

03:55 eight times the national average.

03:57 The lack of funding also means that security standards have slipped, with prisoners sneaking

04:01 in contraband like drugs and improvised weapons.

04:04 These same Justice Department reports have reported rudimentary improvised knives, guns,

04:08 hammers, and even small swords.

04:11 Sexual violence also runs rife in many state prisons, with guards underqualified or simply

04:16 unwilling to intervene and help.

04:18 In order to make up for being understaffed, state prisons often force guards to work gruelling

04:22 hours for very little pay.

04:24 Fusing exhausted, understaffed prison guards with frustrated, overcrowded and often violent

04:28 prisoners creates a dangerous powder keg.

04:31 Federal investigators described the violations of prisoners Eighth Amendment Rights as “severe,

04:36 systemic, and exacerbated.”

04:38 Even the most well-staffed prisons often only operate with seventy-five percent of the staff

04:43 necessary to properly run the facilities and attend to the prisoners.

04:47 Many state prisons are basically an accident waiting to happen, and the staff of these

04:51 prisons are rarely able to contain the results of these accidents.

04:54 Even worse, with very little state government oversight, corrupt and poorly-trained prison

04:59 guards are often responsible for the violence and abuse.

05:02 State prisons are often criticised for their collaboration with private prison companies,

05:06 such as the Corrections Corporation of America and the GEO Group, Inc.

05:09 The stated objective of State Prisons is to rehabilitate inmates and reintroduce them

05:14 into society.

05:15 However, through prison violence and gang activity, prisoners admitted for non-violent

05:19 offences often end up being transformed into hardcore crooks.

05:23 While this could easily seem like an accidental result of the previously mentioned understaffing

05:27 and mismanagement issues, there have been accusations of a profit motivation.

05:31 Because these private prison companies receive government subsidies based on the number of

05:35 inmates housed, these companies benefit from large inmate populations and high recidivism

05:41 rates.

05:42 So, if you’re unlucky enough to get sent to a state prison, you better hope it’s

05:45 a short term and that you’ve got an excellent attorney.

05:49 Because you’re at risk of experiencing dehumanising and unsanitary conditions, violence from both

05:53 other prisoners and the guards, and the damaging effects of gang activity.

05:58 Government oversight bodies like the Department of Justice and activist groups like the Equal

06:02 Justice Initiatives have campaigned for state prison reform, in order to end mass incarceration

06:07 and improve the treatment of prisoners.

06:09 But until these groups win their hard-fought battles for justice, state prisons are probably

06:14 going to remain horrible places to be.

06:16 This brings us to the other subject of today’s video: Federal prisons.

06:20 What exactly is a federal prison?

06:22 Well, the clue is in the name.

06:24 Established under the Hoover administration in the 1930s, Federal prisons are reserved

06:28 for criminals who’ve broken federal laws – such as one or more of the following examples.

06:33 Crimes taking place on federal land or crimes committed against federal officers.

06:37 A crime involving the crossing of state lines.

06:39 Immigrations and customs violations.

06:41 And a grand majority of financial crimes, like fraud, embezzlement, and identity theft.

06:47 Violations of federal law tend to be less violent than state crimes, and this difference

06:51 is also often reflected in the facilities themselves.

06:54 Federal prisons are run by the Federal Bureau of Prisons (or BOP), a government body under

06:58 the Department of Justice.

07:00 The BOP is typically allocated a yearly budget of around $6.5 billion.

07:05 Divided between the Bureau’s fewer than 200 facilities, this results in far better

07:09 funding for each facility than their state-run counterparts.

07:12 This often results in better-quality buildings, living conditions, training programs, and

07:17 food.

07:18 Despite having fewer inmates to process than state prisons, there are five main types of

07:21 federal prison facility rather than three, mostly divided by the level of security.

07:26 There are minimum security federal prisons, referred to by the BOP as Federal Prison Camps.

07:31 These are for prisoners judged to pose no risk of escape or danger to public safety.

07:36 These are the facilities often referred to as “Club Fed” – as prison goes, these

07:40 are about as easy-going as you get.

07:42 Larry Levine, director of the Wall Street Prison Consultants – an organisation that

07:46 helps future inmates from the financial industry adjust to their impending imprisonment – compared

07:51 the experience to junior college.

07:54 Prisoners are hosted in dormitories rather than cells, and the ratio of guards to inmates

07:58 is low.

07:59 While it isn’t exactly a day spa, it’s far from the terrifying environment of an

08:02 Alabama State Prison.

08:04 For Federal Prison Camp inmates, the biggest threat is the soul-crushing boredom of the

08:08 daily routine.

08:10 Low security federal prisons are similar, but with slightly stronger security precautions

08:14 – such as double-fenced perimeters.

08:16 Prisoners are still housed in dormitories and cubicles rather than cells.

08:20 Medium security federal prisons, on the other hand, do have largely cell-based living facilities.

08:25 They also have higher security and a greater number of guards.

08:27 High security federal prison institutions – also referred to as United States Penitentiaries

08:32 – are the closest to state prisons in terms of control over their inmates.

08:36 These prisons are reserved for the most violent criminals, and criminals with the highest

08:40 probability of escape attempts.

08:42 Examples include violent political criminals, murderers, and high-level members of organised

08:47 crime.

08:48 There are also some Federal Corrections Complexes, wherein two different federal prison facilities

08:52 work closely together, despite having different security levels.

08:56 These facilities pool resources in order to better achieve their respective missions.

08:59 It’s a level of cooperation and coordination not found in state prisons.

09:04 Lower-end security facilities also have smaller facilities nearby, referred to as Satellite

09:08 Prison Camps, that use inmate labour and work programs to support the main institution.

09:13 Despite state prison’s stated intention to rehabilitate inmates and re-introduce them

09:18 into society, Federal prison seems a lot better equipped for successfully rehabilitating its

09:23 inmates.

09:24 But the differences between these two institutions don’t stop there.

09:27 On average, sentences served in federal prison tend to be longer than their state counterparts.

09:31 This is both because federal prisoners tend to have a narrower spectrum of crimes – most

09:35 of which are typically more severe – and because these crimes tend to have higher mandatory

09:39 minimums.

09:40 People convicted for federal crimes are also a lot less likely to be offered probation.

09:45 Compared to the disproportionate number of minorities imprisoned in state prisons, the

09:49 populations of federal prisons are disproportionately white.

09:51 Out of a total of around 190,000 inmates, 59% of the federal prison population is white

09:57 and only 38% is African-American.

09:59 Whereas, in state prisons, these stats are a lot more even.

10:04 Almost 50% of the inmates in federal prisons have been convicted of drug-related offenses,

10:08 such as production and trafficking.

10:10 The rest is largely white-collar crime.

10:12 Unlike criminals sentenced to state prisons, federal criminals aren’t always admitted

10:15 to a prison in the state where they’re convicted.

10:18 People convicted of federal crimes can be housed in any federal prison facility in the

10:22 country.

10:23 Federal criminals convicted of white-collar crimes – if not judged to be a flight risk

10:27 – can even self-report to their prison facility on the first day of their sentence.

10:31 People in state prisons are likely to spend the duration of their trial in a local jail.

10:35 While federal prisons do have violent inmates, violence within the prisons themselves is

10:39 a less frequent issue because these prisons aren’t as overcrowded.

10:43 Unlike most state prisons, federal inmates are often moved from facility to facility

10:46 as needed.

10:47 Federal facilities work closely with the US Marshall service, who handle tracking and

10:51 transporting federal inmates across the country.

10:54 Federal inmates that become violent or repeatedly break prison rules may be transferred to a

10:58 higher security federal prison.

11:00 Though the facility is more likely to put a troublesome inmate in solitary confinement

11:04 before resorting to these costlier methods.

11:07 Compared to the overcrowded, brutal conditions of state prisons, medium, lower, and minimum

11:11 security federal prisons also regularly offer a wide range of recreational activities.

11:16 In the prison yard, inmates may have access to sports like tennis, bocce ball, and volleyball

11:21 to maintain physical fitness.

11:23 Inside the building, there are often gymnasiums with basketball, exercise, and wellness facilities.

11:28 Many federal prisons also offer arts and crafts classes, allowing inmates to develop skills

11:32 like painting, crochet, and leather-craft.

11:35 If you’re lucky, you may also have access to televisions and computers with closed-network

11:39 internet connection.

11:41 Federal prisons also offer rec rooms where inmates can interact and let off steam.

11:45 While these facilities have been known to help reduce prison violence – and keep inmates

11:49 in a more relaxed, cooperative mindset – this must feel almost like a cruel joke to non-violent

11:54 drug offenders left for dead in overcrowded, underfunded state prisons.

11:58 But hey, nobody ever said prison was fair.

12:00 So, if you plan on committing a major crime sometime soon, you should probably do yourself

12:04 a favour and keep it federal.

12:06 Especially if you live in Alabama.

12:08 Thanks for watching this video.

12:09 We don’t think you should commit any crimes, because when you’re in jail, you can’t

12:14 watch videos like “What Actually Happens If You Get Beat Up In Prison?” and “How

12:17 To Survive In Prison?”

12:19 We’ve got your watch history on maximum-security lockdown.

Video Information

  • Video ID: D4nPxik59oE

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Today we’re going to talk about the darker aspects of war.

00:03 Yes, war is dark enough in itself, but as you’ll know from some of our other shows

00:07 many despicable things happen in war behind what we might call closed doors.

00:12 We only need to look at the Nazi doctor, Josef Mengele, who conducted experiments on people

00:18 that make your stomach churn.

00:20 We might also look at the Nazi ‘Death Marches”, the massacres, the genocides, the torture

00:24 of prisoners and prisoners literally being worked to death.

00:28 These things all happened during the Second World War, as did biological warfare and the

00:33 testing of deadly agents on those captured by certain militaries.

00:36 But today we’ll focus on just one matter of total depravity during that war, in this

00:41 episode of the Infographics Show, The Horror of Unit 731.

00:45 Unit 731 was the brainchild of the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.

00:50 It was a biological and chemical warfare research unit that conducted experiments on prisoners

00:55 with the aim of developing deadly weapons.

00:57 It’s written that at its base in China – remember the Japanese were at war with China – around

01:02 3,000 men, women, and children were tested on.

01:05 Most of these we are told were Chinese, but some of them were from the Allied Nations,

01:10 the Soviet Union, Korea and Mongolia.

01:12 The unit lasted until the end of the war in 1945 and it’s written that it had ample

01:17 funding from the Japanese government.

01:19 Ok, so this unit was developing dastardly weapons and it needed to test those weapons

01:23 on people first.

01:25 But other tests were also done, related to trying to understand what the human body could

01:29 endure.

01:30 That way the Japanese military might better understand what its own soldiers could go

01:34 through.

01:35 The Cold One of the things many soldiers had to put

01:37 up with during the war was cold, and cold did kill a lot of people.

01:42 At Unit 731 they wanted to understand just how cold someone could get and still survive.

01:47 The website Unit731.org tells us, “Some human test subjects were taken outside during

01:53 the harsh winter until their limbs froze off for the doctors to experiment how best to

01:57 treat frostbite.”

01:59 The New York Times, which had testimonies from people who had seen the horrors of this

02:02 unit, wrote that these people would be taken outside and guards would throw water on them

02:07 until they saw the victim had frostbite.

02:09 Sometimes, wrote the newspaper, the guard would hit the arm of the prisoner with a stick

02:13 and if he heard something like a wood-against-wood sound he knew the arm was totally frozen.

02:18 What happened next is the doctors would use various methods to try and unfreeze the arm

02:22 or other body part.

02:24 Sometimes the prisoner would be left alone to unfreeze, sometimes warm water would be

02:28 thrown on him or her and sometimes much warmer water.

02:32 The Japanese doctors, according to The Times, concluded that water over 100 degrees fahrenheit

02:36 but never more than 122 degrees fahrenheit worked the best.

02:41 Vivisection The Japanese military also wanted to know

02:43 how best to treat disease and injuries, but we are told that to do this they would often

02:48 use live prisoners to operate on.

02:50 It’s said that some of these prisoners would be deliberately given a disease, and then

02:54 the doctors would open up the body of the patient without any kind of anesthesia.

02:57 They wanted to look at the effects of the disease before the body began decomposing,

03:01 and that’s why they kept the subjects alive.

03:05 These people were called marutas, or logs.

03:07 The New York Times, with testimony from a former surgeon, said they just wanted to know

03:11 what had happened inside.

03:13 That man told the Times, “I cut him open from the chest to the stomach, and he screamed

03:18 terribly, and his face was all twisted in agony.

03:20 He made this unimaginable sound, he was screaming so horribly.

03:24 But then finally he stopped.

03:26 This was all in a day's work for the surgeons, but it really left an impression on me because

03:30 it was my first time.”

03:32 Testing Pathogens One of the major experiments at Unit 731 was

03:36 to test how certain pathogens, including cholera or anthrax, would affect a number of people

03:42 if they were exposed to the pathogens.

03:43 They didn’t just do this inside the camp, but also did what they called field testing.

03:48 This was done by dropping the pathogens on small communities in China.

03:52 They wanted to see if they could cause an outbreak of disease.

03:55 We are told some of these experiments were successful, so the Japanese then had the idea

03:59 to carry these pathogens to the United States in what were called balloon bombs.

04:03 It’s written that the Japanese did send about 200 balloons to the U.S. but these failed

04:08 for the most part, only leading to the death of seven people.

04:11 They also had a plan to drop plague-infected fleas on San Diego by using Kamikaze pilots.

04:18 Testing Weapons The Japanese also wanted to test weapons that

04:21 they could use on the battlefield, and this included regular weapons but also toxic gases.

04:26 To do this prisoners would be taken out to a field and tied to a spot with a stake.

04:30 The soldiers would then start testing, which sometimes just meant shooting guns at the

04:34 target, and other times throwing grenades at certain distances to see how effective

04:38 they were.

04:39 The bodies of the victims would then be analyzed so the Japanese knew exactly what damage their

04:44 weapons could do.

04:45 We are told that in one experiment gas was fired at the tied-up prisoners, but the wind

04:49 changed direction and it sent the Japanese soldiers running.

04:53 It’s also said that the soldiers would occasionally test their flamethrowers on the prisoners.

04:57 The pressure chamber and spinning While Japanese people who had worked in the

05:01 camp later recalled how many parts of prisoners could be seen in jars all over the camp, it’s

05:06 not always known how those people died.

05:08 Perhaps one of the worst deaths was the pressure chamber.

05:10 We are told that prisoners would be placed inside a pressure chamber, sometimes alongside

05:14 another prisoner, and the pressure would be turned up until basically the prisoners’

05:19 eyes popped and they eventually died.

05:21 If that wasn’t horrific enough, other prisoners would be literally spun to death so that the

05:26 military could test centrifugal forces.

05:28 Operations The Japanese also wanted to have better surgeons,

05:32 and those surgeons needed subjects to work on.

05:34 One report found tells us how one subject was given an appendectomy.

05:38 After that, his arm was removed and after that he received a tracheotomy.

05:42 This all took about 90 minutes and when the doctors were done, they just killed that patient.

05:47 The man who did these surgeries was at the time a student doctor.

05:50 He told the media that he’d had no idea what to expect when he was told he was going

05:54 to China to practice surgeries.

05:57 Spreading syphilis This is the testimony from a worker at Unit

06:00 731: “Infection of venereal disease by injection was abandoned, and the researchers started

06:06 forcing the prisoners into sexual acts with each other.”

06:09 It’s said that if the pair refused, they would be shot.

06:11 At other times children were infected with the disease.

06:14 The reason this happened was so those infected prisoners could be vivisected at various stages

06:18 of the disease and the doctors at the camp could better understand how it affected a

06:23 person’s organs during that stage of infection.

06:26 Forced pregnancy It’s said that female prisoners would be

06:29 made pregnant by force so that the doctors could understand if disease was passed to

06:33 the child.

06:34 They also wanted to know what damage a disease may have caused to the woman’s reproductive

06:38 organs during pregnancy.

06:39 It’s said the guards would just take women and do this, even to those already injured

06:44 from other experiments.

06:45 While many children were thought to have been born on the camp, it’s said that none survived.

06:50 One former soldier said this sometime later, “Of course there were experiments on children.

06:54 But probably their fathers were spies.”

06:57 For a long time this unit was not talked about, but The Guardian reported in 2018 that Japan

07:02 released lots of information from its national archives relating to Unit 731.

07:07 Prior to this, much of what we knew was only based on testimonies.

07:10 No one has denied what we have talked about today did not happen, but there are more reports

07:15 that tell us smaller experiments also happened.

07:18 These included people being exposed to dangerous levels of radiation, being injected with the

07:22 blood from animals, being injected with sea water and also being burned alive.

07:27 It’s said during the war the Americans knew about the camp and after they granted immunity

07:32 to the physicians of Unit 731 if they shared all their findings with the U.S. military

07:36 as some of those findings might be useful and the U.S. didn’t want the Soviets getting

07:40 hold of the research.

07:42 We will leave you with a comment made by a former Unit 731 worker when he was contacted

07:47 some years later.

07:48 “I don't want to think about Unit 731.

07:50 Fifty years have passed since the war.

07:52 Please let me remain silent.”

07:54 Do you think anything like this could happen again?

07:57 How do you think people could do to this other human beings?

08:00 Tell us in the comments.

08:01 Also, be sure to check out our other video Could You Survive the Stanford Prison Experiment.

08:05 Thanks for watching, and as always, don’t forget to like, share and subscribe.

08:09 See you next time.

docs.text:
00:14 According to the Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, smoking causes nearly 6 million

00:18 deaths around the world each year, and current trends show that tobacco use will be responsible

00:23 for more than 8 million deaths annually by 2030.

00:26 It is the leading cause of preventable death in America, and as many as 16 million people

00:31 are living with a disease caused by smoking, including cancer, heart disease, stroke, lung

00:36 disease, and diabetes.

00:38 So what if you quit the habit?

00:39 How reversible are these risks?

00:41 That’s what we’ll be exploring today, in this episode of The Infographics Show:

00:45 What Happens To Your Body When You Stop Smoking?

00:47 Apart from that fact it’s bad for your health, there are many other reasons to quit smoking.

00:51 It's expensive, it makes your hair and clothes stink, and in many places in the world, it’s

00:56 considered unsociable with bans in bars and restaurants meaning you’ll need to leave

00:59 the crowd and head outside for a puff.

01:02 There are plenty of plusses to kicking the habit, but what will the health results be?

01:06 Let’s take a look at how your body will change as time passes once you’ve quit smoking…

01:10 20 Minutes – In less time than it takes to commute to work, your body will already

01:15 be fixing itself.

01:16 20 minutes after the last cigarette is stubbed out, your pulse and blood pressure start to

01:20 drop back to normal, circulation will start to improve, and your hands and feet will warm

01:24 to their usual temperature.

01:26 12 Hours - Cigarettes contain a lot of known toxins including a harmful gas, carbon monoxide.

01:31 This gas can be fatal in high doses, as it prevents oxygen from entering the lungs and

01:36 blood.

01:37 At 12 hours, halfway through your first day, your carbon monoxide level is back to normal,

01:41 which is great for your heart, as it doesn’t have to pump as hard to get enough oxygen

01:45 to your body.

01:46 Unfortunately though, it’s at this point you’ll be feeling the withdrawal and cravings.

01:49 A couple of ways to fight these feelings are by chewing gum or sipping water.

01:54 24 Hours – Well done, you’ve hit the one day mark!

01:57 And the good news is that after just 24 hours, a person's blood pressure begins to drop,

02:02 decreasing the risk of heart disease, and blood clots that can lead to stroke.

02:05 If you smoke a pack a day, you’re twice as likely to have a heart attack as a nonsmoker,

02:10 and that risk has already been reduced considerably after just 24 hours.

02:14 And with oxygen levels on the rise, physical activity and exercise will already feel easier.

02:20 48 Hours – 2 days in is a good time for a tasty snack.

02:24 Smoking damages the nerve endings which decreases your ability to smell and taste properly,

02:28 and after only 48 hours, your senses will get sharper as nerve endings begin to heal.

02:33 Your body will also enter a detoxification phase, with your lungs kicking out mucus left

02:38 from cigarettes.

02:39 The downside is that this is when the toughest withdrawal symptoms show up.

02:42 If you were a heavy smoker, you might feel dizzy, anxious, or tired.

02:46 And you may also crave more food than usual.

02:48 3 Days – After 3 days, the nicotine levels in a person's body are depleted.

02:53 Ridding the body of nicotine leaves a person much healthier, but initially this also adds

02:58 to the effects of withdrawal.

02:59 At the 3 day mark, many people will become moody and irritable, experiencing severe headaches

03:04 and cravings, as the body readjusts.

03:06 On the positive side, energy levels will increase and you will breathe more easily.

03:11 During the first 3 Months – This is when the major improvements start.

03:14 After a couple of weeks, the cravings will subside and the chance of going back to the

03:18 habit, is far less likely.

03:20 Your lungs become stronger and clearer, and your blood flow has greatly improved.

03:24 You can exercise without huffing and puffing so much, and the risk of a heart attack goes

03:28 down even more.

03:29 9 Months – 9 months after quitting, there will be major physical changes and improvements

03:34 in the body.

03:35 The lungs have significantly healed themselves.

03:37 The delicate, hair-like structures inside the lungs known as cilia, which help to fight

03:42 infections, will have recovered from the toll of cigarette smoke.

03:45 Around this time, many former smokers notice a decrease in the frequency of lung infections

03:50 because the healed cilia can do their job more easily.

03:53 You’ll also be able to take deeper breaths, and energy levels will be a lot higher and

03:57 back to normal.

03:58 1 Year – A big milestone with the habit in the distant past.

04:02 Time to celebrate the achievement.

04:03 The risk of heart disease has decreased by half and will continue to drop beyond this

04:07 1-year mark.

04:08 5 Years – After 5 years without smoking, the body has healed itself so that the arteries

04:13 and blood vessels begin to widen again.

04:15 This means blood is less likely to clot which lowers the risk of stroke, to the same level

04:19 as a nonsmoker.

04:21 And compared to when you first quit, you’re half as likely to get cancer of the mouth,

04:25 throat, esophagus, or bladder.

04:26 10 Years - Lung cancer is one of the greatest risks a smoker faces and after 10 years, a

04:32 person's chances of developing lung cancer and dying from it are about half compared

04:36 to a smoker.

04:37 15 Years – And finally, after 15 years of not smoking, the chances that you’ll get

04:42 heart disease are the same as if you never smoked at all.

04:44 Your body has done a huge amount of recovery and healing, rejuvenating the tissue and cells.
