00:00 [music]

00:03 >> Hey, I'm Dave. Welcome to my shop. Now,

00:05 I've got a great UDP joke, but I'm

00:07 afraid you wouldn't get it, which is

00:09 basically the entire point of UDP.

00:12 If I send 10 packets across a network

00:14 and number them 1 through 10, most

00:16 people assume that the network's job is

00:17 simple, deliver all 10 in order without

00:20 losing any of them.

00:21 And most of the time, that's exactly

00:23 what happens. But sometimes packet five

00:25 just vanishes. Packet six arrives fine,

00:28 and the smartest thing the network can

00:30 do is absolutely nothing about it. No

00:32 retry, no recovery, no heroic attempts

00:35 to make things whole again. Just let

00:37 number five die.

00:39 And today I want to show you why that

00:40 can be exactly the right answer. I've

00:42 set up a simple experiment between two

00:44 computers where I can deliberately

00:45 murder one piece of network traffic in

00:47 transit. We're going to send the same

00:49 number of data twice, first with UDP and

00:52 then with TCP, and watch what happens in

00:54 Wireshark when number five disappears.

00:57 The difference is dramatic enough that

00:58 once you see it, you'll understand far

01:00 more about these two protocols than you

01:02 would from memorizing their header

01:03 fields.

01:04 Let's start with UDP.

01:06 The first four datagrams arrive exactly

01:08 as expected. Somehow number five gets

01:11 thrown into the electronic wood chipper

01:12 in the middle of the network. Then

01:14 number six arrives normally, followed by

01:15 seven through 10. So, the receiving

01:17 program ends up with 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7,

01:21 8, 9, and 10. There is no UDP error

01:24 message. UDP does not stop the network,

01:26 interrogate the routers, or send a

01:28 search party.

01:29 That datagram simply never arrives, but

01:31 life continues. Now, do the same

01:33 experiment over TCP. Again, the first

01:36 four pieces of data make it across. And

01:38 again, the next chunk, number five,

01:40 disappears in transit. Later traffic

01:42 still physically reaches the receiving

01:44 computer. But this time something

01:46 strange happens. The application appears

01:48 to stop after number four. Later TCP

01:51 segments can already be inside the

01:52 machine, safely received by the network

01:54 card, and sitting in kernel memory, and

01:56 TCP will still refuse to hand that data

01:59 to the program. That is called

02:01 head-of-line blocking, and it is one of

02:03 the most counterintuitive things in

02:04 networking.

02:05 TCP promises the application an ordered

02:08 stream of bytes. If byte number 50,000

02:11 is missing, TCP cannot simply hand over

02:13 a byte 51,000 and hope that nobody

02:15 notices. Doing so would violate the

02:17 abstraction that it has promised, so it

02:19 waits. Even when all the data beyond the

02:21 hole has already arrived, the

02:23 application is not allowed to see any of

02:25 it until that gap is repaired. And this

02:27 is the moment where the two protocols

02:29 stop being abstract and start having

02:31 real consequences.

02:33 Imagine the missing data is 20

02:34 milliseconds of somebody speaking in a

02:36 live voice call. The packet is detected

02:38 as lost, retransmitted, and finally

02:40 arrives, but by then another 100 or 200

02:43 milliseconds have passed. The data is

02:45 now technically correct and also

02:47 temporally useless.

02:48 We have perfectly reconstructed a tiny

02:50 slice of the past. Human speech can

02:52 tolerate a small missing fragment.

02:54 Codecs in our brains are surprisingly

02:56 good at filling little gaps, but what is

02:58 much harder to hide is latency. Once the

03:00 conversation starts feeling delayed,

03:02 people talk over top of each other, and

03:04 the whole interaction begins to fall

03:05 apart.

03:07 Games make the same principle even more

03:08 obvious. Suppose a multiplayer game is

03:11 sending frequent updates about another

03:12 player's position, 100, then 103, and

03:15 then 107.

03:16 If the update for 103 disappears, but

03:18 107 arrives correctly, there's almost no

03:21 reason to freeze the remote player at

03:23 100 while we dig through the network for

03:25 his former because we already know

03:27 something newer.

03:28 So, in both cases, stale data can be

03:30 worse than missing data.

03:32 And that is why the behavior we just

03:33 watched matters so much. TCP's refusal

03:36 to deliver later data is not a bug. It

03:39 is the direct result of the contract it

03:41 offers the application, every byte in

03:43 order. For some applications, that

03:45 contract is perfect. For others, it is

03:48 the wrong tool.

03:49 And now that you've seen the effect,

03:51 let's take a look at the machinery that

03:52 produces it.

03:54 UDP is almost comically small. Its

03:56 header is only 8 bytes: source port,

03:58 destination port, length, and a

04:00 checksum.

04:01 More importantly, each UDP datagram is

04:04 an independent message. If I send 10 of

04:06 them, the receiver can still tell them

04:08 apart. Message boundaries stay intact.

04:11 What UDP does not contain is just as

04:13 important. No sequence numbers to

04:15 guarantee their order, no

04:16 acknowledgements, no retransmission, no

04:18 reordering, and no built-in flow

04:20 control.

04:22 IP underneath it is a best effort

04:23 network, and UDP largely accepts that

04:25 bargain.

04:27 TCP takes the opposite approach. It is

04:29 not really thinking packets at all. It

04:30 thinks in bytes. Packets are just the

04:32 envelopes that carry portions of a

04:34 continuous byte stream across the

04:35 network.

04:37 When two TCP endpoints connect, they

04:39 exchange initial sequence information in

04:41 the SYN, the SYN-ACK, ACK handshake. And

04:44 from that point forward, every byte in

04:46 the connection lives in a numbered

04:47 space. If a segment begins with a

04:49 sequence number 50,000 and carries 1,000

04:52 bytes, the next segment should begin at

04:53 51,000.

04:55 Sequence number is not packet 17. It

04:58 tells the receiver exactly where these

05:00 bytes belong in the larger stream.

05:02 And acknowledgements work in the same

05:04 way. An ACK of 51,000 means I have

05:07 everything through byte 50,999.

05:10 The next byte I want is 51,000.

05:13 But back to our murder scene. The

05:15 receiver has everything up through byte

05:17 49,999,

05:18 so it's waiting for 50,000. Then a later

05:21 segment beginning at 51,000 arrives

05:23 successfully, as does maybe one at

05:25 52,000 and 53,000, but the receiver

05:27 cannot advance its cumulative

05:29 acknowledgement because there is still a

05:30 hole. It therefore keeps acknowledging

05:33 50,000. Another later segment arrives,

05:35 and again, it says 50,000. In Wireshark,

05:38 you can watch the acknowledgement number

05:40 freeze while later data continues to

05:42 reach the machine. That stuck

05:43 acknowledgement is the visible signature

05:45 of head-of-line blocking. Classic TCP

05:49 used repeated duplicate acknowledgements

05:51 as a strong signal. Three duplicate acts

05:53 for the same position was traditionally

05:55 enough for the sender to conclude that

05:57 the segment was lost rather than merely

05:59 delayed and to retransmit before the

06:01 normal timer expired. And that's called

06:03 fast retransmit. Modern stacks have more

06:06 sophisticated loss detection, but the

06:08 core idea remains. Acknowledgements

06:10 reveal not only what arrived, but where

06:12 progress stopped.

06:14 Selective acknowledgement or sack makes

06:16 the conversation even richer. Without

06:18 sack, the receiver can only keep saying,

06:20 "I'm still waiting for byte 50,000." But

06:22 with sack, it can also say, "And by the

06:24 way, I already have these later blocks,

06:27 so please don't send those again."

06:29 The sender can then repair only the

06:30 hole.

06:31 And if and when the missing segment

06:33 finally arrives, the most satisfying

06:35 moment in the demonstration happens.

06:37 That gap gets filled and the receive

06:38 window becomes contiguous again, and

06:40 everything that was waiting beyond the

06:42 hole is suddenly released to the

06:43 application all at once.

06:45 Data that appeared to have stopped comes

06:47 pouring through.

06:48 And that is head of line blocking made

06:50 physical. The later packets were not

06:52 necessarily late. Some of them had

06:54 already arrived. The delay was by the

06:56 TCP's contract, every byte in order.

07:00 For a zip file or an executable or a

07:01 database transaction or an SSH session,

07:04 that contract is exactly right. I do not

07:07 want 9.9999 gigabytes very quickly and

07:10 then a note saying that one critical

07:11 byte could not be located. Correctness

07:13 outranks punctuality.

07:15 But the moment the data is live audio,

07:18 rapidly changing game state or

07:19 telemetry, the value of waiting changes.

07:22 And that's the deeper point here. UDP

07:24 does not eliminate reliability. It

07:26 simply refuses to impose one universal

07:29 reliability policy on every application.

07:31 It lets the application decide which

07:33 information must arrive correctly and

07:35 which information is allowed to expire.

07:38 There's another practical difference

07:39 that becomes obvious the first time you

07:40 write real network code. UDP preserves

07:43 datagram boundaries. TCP does not

07:46 preserve application message boundaries

07:47 at all. Two UDP sends of hello and world

07:50 arrive as two separate messages, if they

07:52 arrive at all,

07:54 but two TCP sends of the same data may

07:56 arrive as hello world or he and then low

07:58 world and you know, all broken up. TCP

08:01 only promises that the bytes will

08:03 eventually arrive in the correct order.

08:05 Your application has to supply any

08:07 framing.

08:08 TCP also solves two problems that are

08:10 often a mashed together, flow control

08:12 and congestion control.

08:14 Flow control protects the receiver by

08:16 advertising its available buffer space.

08:18 Congestion control protects the network

08:20 by reacting to loss and delay signals

08:23 and by becoming less aggressive. A lost

08:25 segment on a high bandwidth high latency

08:27 path can therefore cost far more than

08:29 simply re-transmitting one segment. It

08:31 can stall ordered delivery, shrink the

08:34 congestion window and force the sender

08:35 to rebuild its rate cautiously

08:37 afterwards.

08:38 And that is why when looking at a slow

08:40 TCP capture, I care far more about

08:43 re-transmissions, duplicate acts, sack

08:45 blocks and periods where the

08:47 acknowledgement number stops advancing

08:49 than I do about every little header

08:50 field.

08:51 And all of this brings us to a modern

08:53 example of engineers deliberately

08:55 choosing the smaller contract, QUIC.

08:58 QUIC is the transport underneath HTTP/3

09:02 and it runs over UDP.

09:04 And at first that sounds almost a little

09:05 perverse because we spent decades making

09:07 TCP mature and reliable and then the

09:10 newest generation of web shows up riding

09:12 on the protocol whose reaction to our

09:14 missing package is to basically shrug.

09:16 And our experiment explains why. HTTP/2

09:20 can carry many logical streams over a

09:21 single TCP connection. That's better

09:24 than opening dozens of separate

09:25 connections, but underneath all those

09:27 streams, there are still one TCP byte

09:29 stream. If a single TCP segment

09:31 disappears, TCP's ordering promise

09:34 applies to the entire connection.

09:36 Later data belonging to completely

09:38 unrelated streams can be trapped behind

09:40 that hole. So, QUIC still provides

09:43 reliability, acknowledgements,

09:44 retransmission, congestion control, and

09:46 encryption.

09:48 But, because it implements its own

09:49 streams above UDP, loss on one stream

09:52 does not automatically freeze data

09:54 belonging to other independent streams.

09:56 QUIC does not make packet loss

09:58 disappear, it changes what must wait for

10:01 what. Same network, same missing data,

10:03 but three different contracts.

10:05 TCP says every byte in order. UDP says

10:08 every datagram that happens to arrive.

10:11 And QUIC says, "I want reliability, but

10:13 I also want to vote on which missing

10:14 data is allowed to stop everything

10:16 else." Once you've watched the missing

10:18 packet experiment, TCP and UDP stop

10:21 looking like two nearly identical

10:22 entries on a certification exam. They

10:24 become answers to a much more

10:26 interesting engineering question. When

10:28 the network loses something, what is the

10:30 value of waiting for it? For a file,

10:32 waiting is cheap and corruption is

10:34 expensive. For live audio, waiting may

10:36 be expensive and a tiny loss may be

10:38 almost free. For games and telemetry,

10:41 the answer can change from one message

10:42 to the next. Reliability is not an

10:45 absolute virtue anymore than speed or

10:47 consistency are absolute virtues.

10:49 Engineering begins when you ask what the

10:51 system is actually trying to preserve.

10:53 If the most important thing is every

10:55 byte, then TCP gives you an

10:56 extraordinarily capable machine for

10:58 turning an unreliable packet network

11:00 into something that looks like a

11:01 reliable stream. If the most important

11:03 thing is right now, sometimes the

11:05 smartest thing the network can do when

11:07 packet five disappears is exactly what

11:08 UDP did at beginning. Let it die. If you

11:11 found today's episode interesting or

11:13 useful, I'd be honored if you'd consider

11:14 leaving a like and a subscribe. In the

11:17 meantime and in between time, I hope to

11:18 see you next time, right here in Dave's

11:20 garage.

11:21 >> Do it, Glen. Do it. Do it.

00:13 GUOLONG: That is Friday in one of the classrooms of Building

00:18 26, 11:00 AM.

00:19 MARZIEH: So I was quite nervous.

00:21 SHAWN: The first day is a little bit nervous for me.

00:24 CARLA: I was nervous.

00:25 I'm not going to deny it.

00:27 NARRATOR: Facing your students for the first time

00:29 can be a little scary, but it's also

00:31 an opportunity to establish that your class will

00:34 be user-friendly.

00:35 BILLY: I think the first day of class

00:37 really sets the tone for the rest of the semester.

00:42 NARRATOR: How can you set the right tone?

00:44 As they make their way to your classroom on the first day,

00:47 what qualities are your students hoping for?

00:49 BILLY: Being knowledgeable and understanding the concept.

00:52 ADRIAN: And you need to feel that you can approach them.

00:56 CHANDLER: Have just an air of confidence.

00:57 ADRIAN: Being easy to understand.

00:59 BILLY: And being enthusiastic.

01:01 CHANDLER: Being there, having a presence,

01:03 having a lesson plan ready.

01:04 CAROL: They're well-organized.

01:06 NARRATOR: That may sound like a lot.

01:08 Let's start with approachability.

01:10 ADRIAN: That is important that you feel accepted and welcomed

01:14 in the environment.

01:16 NARRATOR: Being approachable can be

01:18 as simple as facing the class and smiling-- even if you feel

01:21 like hiding behind your papers.

01:24 And making eye contact.

01:26 BILLY: Making eye contact just is a personal connection

01:29 to the person you are talking to-- the audience in general.

01:33 So students feel like the explanation you are making

01:36 is for them.

01:37 CAROL: It is an important form of communication

01:39 for them to do that.

01:40 It definitely holds the students' attention.

01:42 BILLY: In terms of international TAs, in general,

01:44 there may be some misunderstanding

01:46 here and there, but I think it's important to make

01:50 the students comfortable asking for the TA

01:54 to repeat any word or any sentence.

01:56 CAROL: I think at the beginning of the semester,

01:59 they should maybe say that it's OK for the students

02:06 to ask for clarifications if something isn't clear.

02:09 I think that's generally a good thing for all TAs

02:13 to welcome any questions.

02:15 ADRIAN: Show that you are open and you

02:19 care about the success of the students

02:22 that you are trying to teach.

02:26 NARRATOR: Enthusiasm is another way

02:27 to show your students your class will be friendly.

02:31 BILLY: Being enthusiastic and showing that you're actually

02:33 passionate about the material you

02:34 are teaching-- that also gives a little more comfortable

02:39 atmosphere during recitation.

02:41 CAROL: I think TAs who are excited about what they're

02:44 teaching-- or if what they're teaching

02:46 is very specific to their research--

02:49 you can tell that they want to teach it

02:51 and they want you to learn it because they're

02:53 very excited about it.

02:54 Then the student is probably going to be more engaged.

02:59 NARRATOR: And before any other quality,

03:00 students say they want knowledge,

03:03 but they're also confident you'll have it.

03:05 CAROL: I think I personally trust

03:07 that MIT has selected fine TAs to teach us the material.

03:12 NARRATOR: So on the first day, rather

03:14 than trying to impress the students,

03:16 stick with the simple explanation of why you are

03:18 a good fit to teach the class.

03:21 GUOLONG: I'm a third year grad student in the department of

03:26 [INAUDIBLE].

03:27 I'm working with Professor Oppenheim, who is also

03:30 the lecturer of this class.

03:33 NARRATOR: Students also want TAs to show self confidence.

03:36 CAROL: When I think of confidence in a TA,

03:37 I think of someone who is very-- they come off as, OK, I

03:40 know this material better than you,

03:42 and I'm going to teach it to you.

03:44 So often, I think TAs who speak not super fast and just pretty

03:50 articulate and slower, so that their point gets across,

03:53 usually I feel more sure that they're pretty

03:57 good at explaining things.

03:58 BILLY: The speed you have when you talk in a conversation,

04:00 just divide that by two.

04:02 And just because you're nervous in front of people,

04:04 the speed will increase either way.

04:06 So, speaking a little bit more slowly

04:09 helps a lot because you can also have the time

04:13 to think about what you're saying,

04:14 and the audience and the students you're speaking to

04:17 will have a better time understanding, especially

04:19 if pronunciation or if you have a certain accent.

04:22 NARRATOR: So, speed makes a difference

04:24 in how students see you.

04:26 What about volume?

04:28 SHAWN: In a big classroom, I definitely

04:31 have to remind myself that I have to raise

04:33 my voice a little bit louder.

04:35 NARRATOR: Speaking too quietly can also

04:37 give the impression of nervousness.

04:39 GUOLONG: This week's lecture focuses

04:41 on sampling rate conversion.

04:45 NARRATOR: A stronger voice projects confidence

04:47 and commands attention.

04:50 GUOLONG: This week's lecture focuses

04:51 on sampling rate conversion.

04:55 NARRATOR: Getting to the classroom early

04:56 can also help you to feel more confident, because you

04:59 can get to know the students before you start teaching.

05:03 And planning ahead not only makes

05:05 you feel more confident, it also makes

05:07 students confident in you.

05:10 CAROL: So, I think one TA that I had--

05:13 when I think of a user friendly class, I think of his class,

05:17 because every day he had his recitation planned

05:22 to the minute-- which is pretty ridiculous--

05:24 but it actually was very logical in a way that

05:28 helped the students learn.

05:29 So he would pretty much write the agenda on the blackboard.

05:34 Like from minute zero to minute five,

05:36 we're going to take a quiz.

05:37 And from minute five to minute 10,

05:39 we're going to talk about the quiz.

05:40 If they seem like they're well organized--

05:43 they have their papers in a nice, little folder--

05:47 I definitely look at that.

05:48 CHANDLER: Having a real lesson plan

05:49 and showing that there's going to productivity

05:51 in the recitations is important.

05:53 Having someone prepared shows that they

05:54 were thinking about us when we weren't in class.

05:58 NARRATOR: Finally, international teaching assistants

06:01 also stress preparation and planning

06:03 in their advice for a successful first day.

06:06 SHAWN: As an international teaching assistant,

06:10 we have some disadvantages probably

06:12 compared to native speakers.

06:14 But if we are prepared, if we show our enthusiasm

06:19 towards the subject, I think the students

06:21 will feel them as well.

06:23 CARLA: Just be prepared.

06:24 That's what speaks scores about you-- if you're very prepared.

06:27 MARZIEH: I went through all the notes, all the books that

06:31 are related to the course.

06:33 And I tried to prepare some good examples.

06:37 GUOLONG: I think for that class, I did over preparation

06:42 that if I discussed everything on my notebook,

06:47 it would take two hours instead of one hour.

06:50 So I think never running out of materials

06:53 seems another source of my confidence.

06:58 CARLA: I should be confident enough just

07:01 by the sake of being the TA.

07:03 You shouldn't be nervous because you do know more

07:05 about the topic than they do.

07:08 MARZIEH: It was challenging, but in a good way.

07:11 SHAWN: Get everything prepared.

07:13 Do your best.

00:04

00:04 You should have already downloaded and installed

00:06 R on your computer.

00:09 If you have not downloaded and installed R yet,

00:12 please follow the instructions on the course website

00:15 before continuing with this lecture.

00:18 Once you've installed R, go ahead and start it.

00:22 You should see the R console like we see here.

00:26 This is where we'll type commands and perform

00:28 data analysis.

00:31 In this course, we'll mostly be working in the R console,

00:35 but sometimes you'll also want to use

00:37 what are known as "script files."

00:40 We'll see an example of how to use a script

00:43 file at the end of this lecture.

00:46 In your R console, you'll always type commands after the arrow,

00:51 or "greater than" sign.

00:53 Let's start with some basic calculations.

00:56 So with your cursor at the arrow,

00:59 let's type 8, and then the star symbol for "times,"

01:04 the number 6, and hit Enter.

01:06 You should see the result 48, or 8 times 6.

01:11 In this way, R can be used as a basic calculator.

01:16 We can perform many other basic calculations, like 2,

01:20 "raised to the power," by typing the carrot symbol, and then

01:24 the number 16, and hitting Enter.

01:27 You should see the result 65,536-- or 2 the power 16.

01:35 Note that each of the results here are labeled with a 1

01:38 in brackets.

01:40 This is just R's way of labeling the output

01:43 and we can safely ignore it.

01:46 If you type something in your R console

01:48 but don't finish it properly-- for example,

01:52 try typing 2 and the carrot symbol,

01:55 and hitting Enter-- R will show you a plus sign

01:59 and will wait for you to finish the command.

02:02 You can either finish the command-- in this case,

02:05 by typing a number-- or you can hit Escape,

02:09 and R will take you back to the arrow sign.

02:13 So if you ever see a plus sign while working in R,

02:16 it means that R is waiting for you to finish the line.

02:20 If you're not sure how to finish it,

02:22 you can always just hit Escape.

02:25 A nice feature of the R console is

02:27 that you can scroll through your previous commands

02:31 by using the up and down arrows on your keyboard.

02:35 If you hit the up arrow three times,

02:38 you should go back to the 8 times 6 command.

02:43 If you hit Enter, you can run this command again.

02:47 You could also adjust previous commands.

02:50 Hit the up arrow again to go back to the 8 times 6 command.

02:54 This time, delete the 6, type a 10, and hit Enter.

03:00 We'll use this approach to re-run

03:03 or adjust commands many times in this class.

03:08 Generally, R works in terms of functions and variables.

03:14 A function can take in several arguments, or inputs,

03:18 and returns an output value.

03:21 An example is the square root, or sqrt, function.

03:27 In your R console, type sqrt, and then

03:31 in parentheses, the number 2, and hit Enter.

03:36 The function is sqrt, the input, or argument, is the number 2,

03:43 and the output is 1.414214.

03:49 There are thousands of functions in R. Some of them

03:52 are built into R-- like this one--

03:55 and some can be added in by installing packages, which

03:59 we'll do several times in this class.

04:03 Another example of a function is the abs, or absolute value

04:07 function, which returns the absolute value of a number.

04:11 So if we type abs and then in parentheses negative 65

04:18 and hit Enter, we should get the result 65 as our output.

04:24 You can get help on any function in R

04:27 by typing a question mark and then the function name.

04:31 So if we type ?sqrt and hit Enter,

04:36 you should see the R Help Page for the sqrt function.

04:42 The help pages are often very useful,

04:45 and if you want to learn more about a function,

04:47 you should refer to the help page in R.

04:51 Now, get rid of the Help Page, and go back to your R console.

04:56 Suppose we now want to save the output of a function.

05:00 We can do this by saving it to a variable.

05:04 In your R console, type SquareRoot2 and then an

05:11 equals sign, and then sqrt, and in parentheses the number 2.

05:17 And hit Enter.

05:19 Now you don't see the output of sqrt(2)

05:23 because we saved it to the variable named "SquareRoot2."

05:27 You can see the value of a variable by typing its name

05:31 and hitting Enter.

05:32 So type SquareRoot2 exactly how you typed it before, and hit

05:38 Enter.

05:39 You should see that it takes the value 1.414214.

05:45 SquareRoot2 is a name that we created,

05:48 and we could have named it many other things.

05:51 Generally, you have a lot of freedom

05:53 in naming your variables, but there are a couple basic rules.

05:57 One is that you should not use spaces in variable names.

06:02 If you want to easily separate words in a variable name,

06:06 popular strategies are using a mix of capital and lowercase

06:09 letters-- as we did here-- or to separate

06:12 the words using periods.

06:15 Another basic rule is that you should not

06:17 start variable names with a number.

06:20 Keep in mind that variable names in R are case-sensitive.

06:24 Capital and lowercase letters are seen differently by R.

06:29 When we created our variable SquareRoot2,

06:32 we used the equals sign for assignment,

06:35 or to assign the value of sqrt(2)

06:39 to the variable named SquareRoot2.

06:42 You could instead use a "less than" sign with a dash.

06:46 For example, let's create a new variable called HoursYear,

06:52 and then type the less than sign and a dash,

06:56 followed by 365 times 24.

07:01 If you hit Enter and then type HoursYear to look at its value,

07:06 you should see 8,760-- or the number of hours in a year.

07:12 By doing this, the less than sign and the dash

07:15 did the exact same thing as it would

07:17 have done if we used the equals sign.

07:20 In this course, we'll typically use the equals sign.

07:23 But if you see this less than sign and a dash used,

07:28 keep in mind that it means the same thing as an equals sign.

07:32 Lastly, if you type ls and then empty parentheses in your R

07:36 console and hit Enter, you should

07:39 see a list of all of the variables

07:41 that you've created in your current R session.

07:45 Here, we've created two variables--

07:47 HoursYear and SquareRoot2.

07:50 This can be useful if you forget exactly how you

07:53 typed a variable name.

07:56 These are our basic building blocks in R-- functions,

08:00 like square root and absolute value, and variables,

08:04 like HoursYear and SquareRoot2.

docs.text:
00:00 In 2016, the world spent 2.5 billion dollars  (€2.1 billion) to build a massive steel tomb

00:04 over Chernobyl Reactor 4. It was supposed  to suffocate the radiation for 100 years.

00:10 The nightmare was over. Or so people thought.

00:12 By sealing the reactor tight, they  didn't kill the problem. They’d built a

00:16 mausoleum… now, something inside is waking up. Something they might not be able to contain.

00:22 The problem lies within the ruins of Chernobyl. In  Room 305/02. It’s a sealed vault of toxic waste,

00:29 so radioactive, it can kill anything that enters  the room. For years, scientists have monitored

00:33 the plant, and Room 305 in particular. The chamber  was believed to be locked in time. But recently,

00:39 there have been spikes in neutron levels. Now we’re hurtling toward a slow motion crisis.

00:45 And it’s been a catastrophe decades in the making. In 1986, the original sarcophagus, then called the

00:51 Shelter Object, was built over reactor  4 at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant.

00:55 It was thought the danger was over. To some extent, it was.

00:59 But as always, the truth was more complicated. The sarcophagus was constructed under extreme

01:04 circumstances. It was cobbled together in a  radioactive hell under a blanket of Soviet

01:09 secrecy. Badly paid workers were attempting  to contain the ruins of a nuclear reactor,

01:14 working in places where hanging around for  too long could become a death sentence.

01:17 It was immense pressure. When the roof over this pit

01:20 of radioactive carnage was secured, the  media failed to mention that the “most

01:24 dangerous waste in the world” still posed a  threat to anything that lived and breathed.

01:29 Still, what those workers had done  was nothing short of a miracle.

01:32 They’d moved over 14 million cubic feet  (400,000 cubic meters) of concrete and

01:35 7,300 tons of metal framework that made up the  original sarcophagus. It was impressive but it

01:41 was never meant to last forever. The world was  too busy clapping to see the holes in the story.

01:46 And there were literal holes. Within a decade, the shelter was

01:50 crumbling. The giant beams holding it up had  started moving as the structure was corroded

01:54 by rain. The whole thing was in danger  of collapsing. It would be an engineering

01:58 disaster that would have spewed a second  catastrophic cloud of radiation across the world.

02:03 No one knew just how radioactive the waste was. It was too dangerous to even measure.

02:08 In other words, humanity was staring at a  ticking bomb. Something had to be done before

02:12 this radioactive nightmare became a reality. The world forgot its political differences.

02:17 45 countries together came up with  billions of dollars in funding to

02:21 build the giant tomb that exists today. The  parts, from locations all around the world,

02:26 were shipped from Italy and exported in 18 ships  and 2,500 trucks to Ukraine. When it was finished,

02:33 the giant arch stretched 843 feet (257 meters)  across, and 354 feet (108 meters) into the sky.

02:38 You could put the Statue of Liberty underneath it  and there’d still be plenty of free space above.

02:44 Impressive sure, but there were issues. The tomb couldn’t be built directly over

02:49 the reactor. The radiation levels were just  too high. It’s always been the problem with

02:53 Chernobyl. It’s still a problem right now. In November 2016, they slid the entire

02:58 36,000-ton coffin over the top of the old  crumbling sarcophagus. Trapped underneath the

03:04 coffin lurks around 180 tons of volatile nuclear  fuel and mountains of lethal radioactive dust.

03:11 And the fuel buried down there  isn’t like anything else on earth.

03:15 There are shattered fragments of the original  core, all covered in microscopic particles. Then

03:20 there’s the radioactive lava created during the  meltdown While there are several of these hostile

03:24 mounds but the most infamous is the “Elephant's  Foot” – a hideous, twisted black mass of molten

03:30 reactor fuel, concrete, sand that seeped into  the rooms beneath Reactor 4 before cooling down.

03:36 Back in 1986, it was reported that if you  stood next to it for just a few minutes,

03:40 you’d be going home in a body bag. Even today, you  wouldn’t want to hang around. If you did, you’d

03:46 more or less melt from the inside as radiation  ripped through the cells in your body, damaging

03:50 DNA and destroying tissues. But the real problem is the dust.

03:55 It can become airborne. It gets into  people’s lungs and settles on their

03:58 skin. It falls onto the ground where animals  graze or is carried down into the water table.

04:04 The new tomb seems to be airtight, but a single  structural collapse could launch radioactive

04:09 particles back into the atmosphere. The  surrounding area and any workers would

04:13 instantly be at risk of poisoning. That’s why the tomb was built.

04:17 Named the New Safe Confinement, or NSC, it  should, in theory, prevent any of these things

04:22 from happening. And this time, the elements  aren’t going to degrade it. It’s been built to

04:26 survive extreme weather events. It can withstand  major tornados and earth-moving seismic tremors

04:32 and it has no problem with temperatures  as low as -45 Fahrenheit (43°C) and as

04:36 high as 113 Fahrenheit (+45°C). It will last for 100 years.

04:41 That was the narrative. The unbreakable promise. But with Chernobyl,

04:45 it’s never wise to make predictions… A few years after the NSC was finished,

04:50 strange things began happening.  Suddenly, the 100 year guarantee

04:53 started looking like it might have to be revised. In 2021, scientists at Ukraine's Institute for

04:59 Safety Problems of Nuclear Power Plants reported  a troubling development deep inside the ruins:

05:04 in one inaccessible area, the number  of neutrons being detected was rising.

05:09 Neutrons are the particles that drive nuclear  fission. When enough radioactive material reaches

05:14 the right conditions, one splitting uranium atom  creates a domino effect. Neighboring atoms begin

05:19 to split. Under the right circumstances, a  self-sustaining chain reaction can begin.

05:24 It’s an unwanted phenomenon  when humans can’t control it.

05:28 No one could just walk into the tomb to see  what was happening. It was still too dangerous.

05:32 Scientists did their best and said they  were “carefully studying and monitoring the

05:36 damaged unit.” Another nuclear scientist  summed up the problem and was far from

05:40 reassuring when he told the media: “There are many uncertainties.”

05:43 When Reactor Number 4 melted in 1986, the heat  was so extreme that it liquified everything:

05:49 uranium fuel, zirconium cladding, steel,  concrete and other materials including the sand

05:55 dumped all over the burning reactor. This radioactive molten lava surged

05:59 through openings, pipes and passages into  rooms beneath the reactor. As it cooled

06:05 and solidified, it formed strange and alluring  deposits, known as fuel-containing materials,

06:10 or FCMs, including The Elephant’s Foot. But other mounds are scattered across the site.

06:15 And they all have unique characteristics. They’re no longer burning but that doesn’t

06:19 matter. What matters is that the 180  or so tons of irradiated uranium in

06:24 the ruins. It might not look as dangerous as  super-hot lava but it’s still very active.

06:30 Even decades later, neutrons are still  being produced inside those ruins. Usually,

06:35 they amount to little more than a radioactive  burp. But scientists still have to constantly

06:39 watch them. If the conditions inside one  of those masses changed even slightly,

06:43 we could have a problem on our hands. That’s exactly what happened.

06:47 The neutron numbers started increasing at a  rate of concern. But the strangest part is

06:52 this has happened before. Scientists thought it  had been fixed when the tomb was put in place.

06:57 After the original sarcophagus was hastily  erected, rainwater leaked in through gaps in the

07:02 shell. And it did more than damage the structure. Water can slow down neutrons, which sounds good.

07:08 Not in this case, it isn’t. Slower neutrons  can be more effective at striking and

07:12 splitting uranium nuclei. This can increase  the possibility of a nuclear chain reaction.

07:17 Because of that, in 1990, scientists ventured into  the ruins and sprayed neutron-absorbing gadolinium

07:23 nitrate solution onto areas of fuel-containing  material. It was a dangerous mission. So,

07:29 sprinklers were later installed that could  deliver the same neutron poison if readings

07:34 began climbing dangerously high again. But then came the NSC and for a moment,

07:38 everyone believed the problem was over. Rain  couldn’t get in. There was no need for neutron

07:43 killing sprinklers and scientists were quite  sure that the days of worrying reactions were

07:47 a thing of the past. No rain. No problem.

07:49 As the ruins dried, sensors recorded neutron  counts that were stable or even declining.

07:54 But the good days didn’t last long. At several points inside the Shelter,

07:59 scientists then started detecting rising neutron  levels again. Not having rain was now suddenly

08:04 an issue. It didn’t seem to make any sense  based on what scientists already understood

08:08 about the nuclear physics inside the ruins. An area of particular concern was Room 305/2.

08:15 Buried beneath tons of concrete and debris,  this room contains large quantities of

08:20 fuel-containing material. And there, over  several years, neutron counts didn’t just rise,

08:25 they more or less doubled. No one knew why.

08:29 This obviously wasn’t the rain problem. If  anything, it looked like dryness was the issue.

08:34 As Science reported in 2021, “The drying  of the fuel is somehow making neutrons

08:38 ricocheting through it more, rather than  less, effective at splitting uranium nuclei.”

08:43 Somehow… they still don’t  know why this is happening.

08:46 And that matters… The giant new dome was fine.

08:49 It was doing exactly what it had been designed  to do: keeping the weather out. But now the new

08:54 conditions seemed to be affecting the nuclear  material in ways nobody had fully anticipated.

08:58 A slightly rising neutron count wasn’t  a major cause for panic and still isn’t.

09:04 But what if it keeps rising?  What will happen then?

09:07 The mildly good news is the potential  nightmare won’t be a repeat of 1986.

09:12 Reactor 4 won’t suddenly explode again in  anything like the way it did that night.

09:16 But the bad news is that, in an extreme scenario,  a runaway fission reaction inside one of these

09:22 masses could generate colossal amounts of heat.  The FCM could begin to melt or break apart,

09:27 potentially releasing radioactive dust  into the interior of the Shelter. If

09:31 containment were compromised, some of that  material could escape into the atmosphere.

09:35 It wouldn't irradiate half of Europe or create  another Chernobyl-sized exclusion zone. But no

09:40 one wants some of the most radioactive  wreckage on Earth behaving in ways we

09:44 don't completely understand. Another problem is Room 305/2

09:48 is essentially inaccessible. So what happens in 305 stays

09:52 in 305 and that’s not a good thing. Scientists can’t take samples and find

09:56 out what is happening. Layers of concrete  and highly dangerous debris stand between

10:00 them and the material causing concern. One  proposal so far has involved developing

10:05 robots capable of surviving the radiation.  They could drill into the FCM and insert

10:10 neutron-absorbing materials directly into it. Essentially, engineers would have to reach

10:14 inside Chernobyl's frozen nuclear  lava and switch the reaction off.

10:19 One particular country has  been watching developments

10:21 like these with eyes wide open: Japan. Japan has its own nuclear meltdown problem.

10:26 While it’s different from the scene at  Chernobyl, there are some similarities.

10:30 After the earthquake and tsunami of 2011, the  world witnessed the worst nuclear disaster

10:35 since Chernobyl. 3 reactors at the Fukushima  Daiichi Nuclear Power Station suffered meltdowns.

10:41 Like Chernobyl, some of the most radioactive  spots at Fukushima are too dangerous for

10:45 humans to enter. As a result, Japan has spent  years keeping the damaged reactors stable and

10:50 contained. Robots, remotely operated cameras and  other machines venture into places people cannot.

10:55 But that has created another problem. It turns out that massive doses of radiation

11:00 doesn't just melt human organs. It kills machines, too.

11:04 In 2017, Japanese engineers were investigating  deep inside the containment vessel at Unit 2

11:09 when they encountered what almost seemed like  unbelievable radiation levels. An earlier

11:14 reading elsewhere at Fukushima had reached 73  sieverts per hour. That was high, but nothing

11:18 like what they’d just seen: an estimated  dose rate of up to 530 sieverts per hour.

11:24 A subsequent robot encountered an estimated level  as high as 650 sieverts per hour. These were

11:30 localized measurements and so came with some  uncertainty. TEPCO, the Tokyo Electric Power

11:35 Company, put the margin of error at around 30%. A whole-body dose of around 1 solitary sievert

11:41 received quickly is enough to make a  human sick. Several sieverts can be

11:45 life-threatening. Somewhere around 10 delivered  to the entire body in a short period of time

11:50 would almost certainly kill you even if  you received intensive medical treatment.

11:54 650 is a lot. It’s too much to ever consider sending a human

11:59 anywhere near the most radioactive areas. And  it’s already proven to be deadly to machines, too.

12:04 One of those machines sent into Unit 2 in February  2017 was specifically designed for an environment

12:10 where humans could never survive. Its cameras  and electronics were supposed to withstand the

12:14 massive doses of radiation. When faced with these  incredibly high levels, everything went black way

12:20 before anyone expected. Within a couple of hours,  the robot’s internal electronics were fried.

12:25 TEPCO eventually retrieved the machine, and  another robot – nicknamed Scorpion – was then

12:30 given the unenviable task of pushing even deeper  into the containment area. This machine was being

12:35 sent into a place so radioactive that engineers  had to calculate not just mission performance

12:40 but the possibility of a retreat. You can record radiation remotely,

12:44 but the machines cost a fortune to build.  You don’t want dead robots blocking the

12:49 path for other machines that head off  into the darkness on future missions.

12:53 But it didn’t matter how well the robots  were built. The radiation gradually damages

12:57 semiconductor electronics, corrupting signals and  degrading cameras, processors and other components

13:02 until the machine can no longer function. So robots can help at Fukushima,

13:06 just as they might help at Chernobyl with  its neutron problem. But until we can

13:10 figure out how to build almost-invincible  machines, they’re not a magic solution.

13:14 That means whatever is going on at both those  containment sites cannot be fully understood.

13:19 This brings us back to another possible  disaster situation at Chernobyl.

13:23 Something we should be able to avoid but  seem hellbent on ignoring or making worse.

13:28 Reports have stated that workers can only  legally spend 20 hours a year working at

13:33 the NSC before they reach their yearly  radiation exposure limit. Therefore,

13:37 if a major repair needed to be done due to damage,  it would take large teams of workers rotating,

13:43 each working for no more than a few hours at a  time, maybe even minutes. Considering the skills

13:49 required to work there, there could be a severe  staff problem if things take a turn for the worse.

13:54 This could mean even a small amount of damage  could result in a very precarious situation.

13:59 More severe damage could be disastrous. When a Russian drone strike hit the NSC on

14:04 Valentine’s Day in 2025, it was a major cause for  concern. The drone, a Geran-2, broke through the

14:11 inner and outer wall, creating a 161 square foot  (15 square-meter) hole. A rubber sealing membrane

14:16 caught fire and took 3 weeks to extinguish.  Even worse, the Ukraine government said it was

14:22 intentional, although that can’t be confirmed. Russia didn’t just deny it. It called

14:27 the event a “staged” “provocation.” The Ukrainian authorities reported the main

14:31 confinement function keeping the radioactive  waste inside was “compromised”. The humidity

14:36 control system that keeps the massive steel  structure from corroding was also compromised.

14:41 This increased the risk of future collapse. Now, there’s something else

14:44 causing concern at Chernobyl. And it’s something we might one day

14:48 need to get a handle on. Fungi.

14:50 OIt goes without saying that not much  thrives in an environment capable of

14:54 turning human organs to liquid and frying  a robot's electronics in a matter of hours.

14:59 But fungi are special. When scientists began

15:02 exploring the ruined Chernobyl reactor in  the 1990s, they discovered them growing

15:06 across its highly radioactive interior. Not merely surviving, but thriving.

15:11 Many were ugly, jet-black things but that  ominous color turned out to be important.

15:16 One of the 37 species that scientists  studied was Cladosporium sphaerospermum,

15:22 a fungus rich in the pigment melanin. And there might be magic in the melanin.

15:26 Experiments suggested that ionizing radiation  could actually enhance – not kill –the fungi.

15:32 To scientists, the melanin looked capable  of interacting with radiation and changing

15:36 its chemical properties in a way that could  potentially help the organism's metabolism.

15:40 In loose laymen’s terms, the radiation  was kind of acting like sunlight does

15:45 with plants in the process of photosynthesis. It’s still a highly controversial theory. But

15:49 if it’s true then these containment mushrooms  were living off the very stuff that kills just

15:54 about everything else, a process the  scientists called “radiosynthesis”.

15:58 Exactly how much energy the fungi obtain this way  and how important it is to their survival is still

16:03 a mystery. But scientists found something else  fascinating hanging out on the Chernobyl walls:

16:08 some fungi exhibited what’s called “radiotropism.” The fungi grew toward the radiation.

16:14 They seemingly couldn’t get enough of it. That opened up a whole new world of possibilities.

16:19 Especially for space. Astronauts are bombarded with radiation once

16:22 they pass through Earth’s two natural protective  shields: the atmosphere and the magnetosphere.

16:27 Researchers have already experimented  with Cladosporium sphaerospermum aboard

16:32 the International Space Station. They are  investigating if a living layer of fungus

16:36 might provide some protection against  that possibly deadly cosmic blasts.

16:40 And it did. Not by much, but

16:43 enough to show that fungi could indeed be the next  path forward in protecting humans adrift in space.

16:49 So, it’s very possible organisms  originally studied in the ruins of

16:52 Chernobyl could help keep astronauts alive. Chernobyl, a veritable radioactive heart of

16:58 darkness, might have inadvertently helped us  discover virtually limitless energy resources

17:03 or space materials. And the best part is the  fungi are self-replicating. Just give them their

17:08 daily blast of radiation and it should keep them  growing around us, layer upon protective layer.

17:13 But there’s also bad news. Like everything else on planet Earth,

17:16 the fungi want to survive and  in doing so can be destructive.

17:20 Some fungi and other microorganisms  have been shown to attack concrete.

17:24 Research shows they can penetrate microscopic  pores and cracks and produce acids and other

17:29 compounds capable of altering the cement matrix.  The leech minerals from it and, over long periods,

17:35 contribute to its deterioration. And there is a lot of concrete

17:38 surrounding the radioactive remains  beneath Chernobyl's giant steel arch.

17:42 Currently, there’s no evidence  that Chernobyl's radiotrophic

17:45 fungi are eating their way through the NSC  or threatening to bring the structure down.

17:50 But these three things are facts: Fungi thrive inside parts of the

17:54 Chernobyl environment. Some fungi can exploit  radioactive environments and propagate.

17:59 And microorganisms can degrade concrete. For a structure intended to contain one of the

18:04 most dangerous piles of radioactive material on  Earth for generations, that's something engineers

18:09 should probably look into. It might not be a  problem yet, but a lot can happen in the 100

18:14 years the NSC is supposed to keep us safe. When we buried Chernobyl in 1986, we knew

18:19 we were covering up a problem that wasn’t going  to go away. But what happened under that shield

18:23 took on a life of its own, doing things we  didn’t predict, that we still can’t fathom.

18:28 The legacy of Chernobyl still looms large today.  To find out what really happened that night

18:33 watch Chernobyl Nuclear Explosion Disaster  Explained (Hour by Hour). Or click on this.

docs.text:
00:00 AI is so smart that it’s replaced developers.  It’s faster, cheaper and more productive.

00:05 Except… that’s a lie. “AI efficiency” is just a

00:08 convenient cover story for something much darker.  A massive, multi-billion dollar corporate panic.

00:14 Big Tech took on a mountain of debt to fund  their AI buildouts. But the returns haven’t

00:18 materialized. Now, with investors breathing  down their neck and soaring interest rates,

00:23 these companies are desperate to cut  costs just to keep the lights on.

00:26 And software engineers are in the firing line. But they aren’t just axing jobs. They’re

00:31 destroying the code itself. Software development  is being shattered in ways that can’t be repaired.

00:37 And it’s about to crash the U.S. economy… Taking the rest of the world down with it.

00:41 The early promise of AI software  development was so impressive,

00:45 you can’t really blame the Big Tech companies  for embracing it at scale. By most estimates,

00:50 AI allows code to be churned out at anywhere  from 4 to 10 times the rate of non-AI coding.

00:55 In theory, faster output should translate  into more products delivered more rapidly.

01:00 That means more profits and higher share prices. But faster code doesn’t equate to better code.

01:06 That’s precisely where the problem  with “AI coding efficiency” lies.

01:10 You just need to look at the code churn rates.  That’s the frequency that code is written,

01:15 modified or tossed into the trash. According to  GitClear’s analysis of 211 million lines of code,

01:21 the churn rate has more than doubled  since the adoption of AI coding began.

01:25 In 2021, it was roughly 3.3%. In other words,  for every 1,000 lines of code written originally,

01:31 33 would need to be rewritten or binned  somewhere down the line. The more time

01:37 developers spend fixing broken code, the  less time they have to ship new products.

01:41 Ideally the churn rate is as  close to zero as possible.

01:44 AI was supposed to be the ultimate cheat code. It  would increase output without a spike in costly

01:49 down-the-line maintenance. But the opposite happened.

01:52 By 2025, code churn had increased to 6.87%. More  code is being rewritten or revised, potentially

01:59 increasing maintenance and review costs. And that brings vulnerabilities.

02:03 Veracode’s analysis of between 100 and 150 large  language models, or LLMs, consistently finds that

02:10 45% of AI code-generation tasks introduce at  least one known security risk. In other words,

02:16 just over half of AI-generated code  passes even basic security tests.

02:20 Depending on the programming language and testing  method, that number varies. Java is the weakest

02:26 performer with failure rates exceeding  70%. Python performs slightly better but

02:30 still has a vulnerability rate of around 38%. That might be acceptable if the result is a

02:36 market-ready product being shipped quicker.  But again, the opposite is happening.

02:40 A 2026 study by research firm DX analyzed over  400 companies. Between November 2024 and February

02:47 2026, they increased their use of AI tools by 65%,  expecting a notable increase in shipped software.

02:54 The results said otherwise. The median PR throughput - the

02:58 number of pull requests completed by  each developer - rose by just 7.76%.

03:04 The more pull requests there are, the greater the  output. The return from AI was pretty pathetic.

03:10 AI might let individual developers generate  code faster, but it’s not translated into

03:14 shipped value. Not even close.

03:16 The total cost of ownership of AI-assisted  software is significantly higher than what

03:21 it was supposed to be. A technology  touted as a cost-cutter has turned

03:25 out to be a cost multiplier. A 2026 industry analyses found

03:29 that the Total Cost of Ownership, or TCO, for  AI-assisted software will be 30 to 40% higher

03:35 by 2027 compared to traditional development.  Fixing twice as many bugs is time-consuming

03:42 and expensive. GitClear’s data indicates that  by year 2 of using AI to code, if unmanaged,

03:48 it will drive maintenance costs up to  4 times that of traditional levels.

03:52 That’s a huge amount of extra work for the  human developers who need to fix the mess.

03:57 The costs don’t outweigh the benefits. It’s much harder and takes longer to

04:01 fix code once it’s been uploaded into the full  codebase. If a bug slips into actual production,

04:06 the problems become even worse. In  addition to the extra engineering costs,

04:10 there’s also the possibility of security  incidents, compliance fines, legal issues.

04:15 In the pre-AI era, the main bottleneck  in delivering shippable code usually

04:19 took place at the code generation phase.  AI writing code was supposed to fix that.

04:23 Instead it just moved the  bottleneck further down the line.

04:26 Because there’s so much more buggy code being  generated, review queues are clogged. Reviewers

04:32 are forced to spend more time per pull request to  ensure the code actually does what it’s supposed

04:36 to. And while generated code is sitting in  review queues, companies are bleeding money.

04:42 Whatever savings were made from faster  code generation are burned by the massive,

04:46 growing overhead of reviewing, securing,  and constantly rewriting that very code.

04:51 In the end, somewhat ironically, AI  hasn’t replaced developers. It’s created

04:55 new demand for them. To clean up its mess.

04:58 From 2022 to 2025, the tech industry laid  off tens of thousands of developers. And that

05:04 might have broken the entire software development  process permanently. The developer layoffs haven’t

05:09 happened uniformly across all tiers of developers. It’s the junior developers, the ones who did the

05:14 grunt work, that have been culled. Companies were  left with a dilemma: Pay an $80,000 annual salary

05:21 or a $100 per month subscription to Claude Max. The companies chose AI over juniors.

05:27 Data from SignalFire and ZipRecruiter shows that  entry-level tech postings fell by roughly 25 to

05:33 35% between 2023 and 2024. Big Tech cut new grad  hiring by around 50% compared to pre-pandemic

05:41 levels. The trend continued into 2025 and 2026,  with entry-level job postings down around 29%.

05:47 So much for “learn to code.” But that’s only half the story.

05:51 At the same time as the tech companies have been  hollowing out their junior development teams,

05:55 demand for senior engineers has exploded. In 2024, applications for roles requiring

06:00 10 or more years of experience rose by 27%, and  roles requiring 5 to 10 years of experience rose

06:07 by 40%. By early 2026, senior job postings  were taking up over 41% of the total IT mix,

06:15 vastly outperforming the overall market. But this sudden job boom is misleading.

06:20 The rise in tech postings might  suggest a hiring recovery,

06:23 or at least that the talent bleed has stopped.  But in reality, this is a phantom recovery.

06:28 There’s a “senior boom” masking a “junior bust.” The entire structure of the software development

06:34 industry has been flipped upside down. Before AI,  most teams were structured like a pyramid. At the

06:40 bottom, junior developers were hired and trained,  with some moving up to become mid-level devs and

06:45 senior positions at the top. Now, it’s more like  a diamond. There are very few junior devs being

06:50 hired, with mid-level and particularly senior  developers becoming an increasingly hot commodity.

06:56 The very definition of “entry level” has changed. The term used to refer to recent graduates or

07:02 those with little to no experience. Today,  “entry-level” job offers often require 2 to 5

07:08 years of experience. For real entry-level  candidates,it’s a tough job market. One

07:13 that’s roughly 35% smaller than in 2022. So, why has the market shape inverted?

07:18 It’s a direct response to the buggy  and vulnerable, AI generated code.

07:23 The companies that replaced their junior  devs don’t need them to clean up AI’s

07:26 mess. They’re desperate for senior developers,  specifically the ones who can find and fix the

07:31 bugs lurking in the code. That’s what the  senior engineer hiring spree is all about.

07:36 It’s an attempt to fix the mess caused by AI. The junior developers handled the ordinary,

07:41 boilerplate coding. They were responsible for  testing and improving the code before even

07:45 submitting it for review by senior teammates.  That made the senior reviewers’ job easier.

07:50 It took less of their time and allowed  them to focus on more high-level tasks.

07:54 Today, with 45% of AI code containing  security flaws and twice as much of it

07:59 needing additional work as before, the  role of senior developers has changed.

08:04 They’ve become full-time janitors. Very well-paid and highly skilled

08:08 janitors… but janitors at the same. And it’s taking its toll.

08:13 Burnouts are on the rise. Entire  organizations are grinding to halt,

08:16 wiping out any theoretical speed gains from  replacing juniors with AI in the first place.

08:21 But there’s another, more alarming, consequence  for the software development industry:

08:25 The “junior death spiral.” By cutting entry-level roles,

08:28 companies are effectively destroying their future  talent pipeline. There was a defined career path.

08:34 Junior developers worked their way up over  a process of years. The only way to get the

08:38 experience is by putting in the years. Now the chain is broken.

08:42 In as little as 2 to 3 years, the industry  might be staring at a severe shortage of

08:46 mid-level engineers because they never had the  “apprenticeship” phase of fixing AI mistakes.

08:52 That creates a worrying paradox. If there aren’t any juniors gaining

08:56 the experience to become seniors… where exactly  are all the new seniors supposed to come from?

09:02 It’s unlikely that the role of junior developer  will disappear completely. Companies that chose to

09:06 augment juniors with AI rather than replacing them  already seem to be reaping the benefits. For some,

09:12 AI can be a force multiplier. But those  companies that have been hollowed out by AI,

09:17 it’s the opposite. It’s a force divider.

09:20 And now, costs are spiraling,  while profits are flatlining.

09:23 Tech companies thought it was worth the  gamble. It still might pay off. But the

09:27 truth is that the tech companies haven’t  laid off all those developers because of

09:31 greatly improved “AI efficiency”... At least that’s not the main reason.

09:36 The real reason runs much deeper. The AI spending boom started during

09:41 the pre-pandemic “cheap money” period. With  interest rates at or near zero percent, the big

09:46 tech companies piled on cheap debt. They wanted  to grow their businesses and fund enormous stock

09:51 buybacks which pushed their share prices into the  stratosphere. During the pandemic, companies like

09:56 Microsoft and Amazon saw how lockdowns had changed  consumer behavior to their benefit. They believed

10:02 that the future would be more of the same. So, they went on a developer hiring spree

10:07 to start their AI build outs.The amount required  was well beyond their fast-growing revenues. So,

10:13 they funded the growth with even more debt. Then the pandemic ended.

10:17 And the bubble well and truly burst. Governments across the world flooded the global

10:22 economy to compensate for the lack of spending  lockdowns. Then, it came home to roost in the form

10:27 of rampant inflation. The Fed had to do something,  so it raised interest rates to slow it down.

10:32 Again. And again.

10:35 Before the economy had time to react,  interest rates had shot up from 0.25% to

10:40 around 5%. For the tech companies, all that  cheap debt suddenly wasn’t cheap anymore.

10:46 And that’s a huge problem for the “Big  Five” who are sitting on $1.65 trillion

10:51 in off-balance-sheet debt. And it’s growing.

10:54 You might think that with the cost of servicing  the debt much higher, Big Tech might have scaled

10:58 back on new investments. They haven’t.

11:00 In the rush to build out AI infrastructure, the  biggest companies have doubled down. The size of

11:05 the off-balance-sheet liabilities  has grown eightfold since 2022,

11:09 despite the extra cost of servicing them. Meta holds the largest hidden burden at

11:13 around $420 billion, nearly 3 times its reported  debt. Oracle’s off-balance-sheet commitments have

11:19 exploded by 30 times to around $273 billion.  Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon hold the rest.

11:26 It’s a massive amount of debt. And it’s misleading for investors.

11:31 By keeping these obligations off their primary  balance sheets, companies are masking their true

11:35 leverage. Investors and credit rating agencies  might underestimate the financial risk as a

11:40 result, leading to inflated asset prices. It’s flirting with disaster.

11:45 It’s the kind of “creative accounting”  that was at the heart of the notorious

11:48 Enron collapse a few decades back. The majority of these liabilities are long-term

11:53 leases for data centers, purchase commitments for  hardware, and similar obligations. Unlike equity,

11:58 they are mostly fixed mandatory payments. That presents another layer of risk.

12:04 If the anticipated revenue from the “AI boom”  doesn’t materialize quickly enough to cover

12:08 the interest, these firms will be on the edge  of a financial cliff. Despite their current

12:13 cash richness, their debt is so large that  it dwarfs the GDP of all but a few nations.

12:18 And they're locked into these long term deals. If they can’t break free, the financial

12:23 weight will tip them over the edge. Taking the entire global economy with them.

12:28 But arguably, an even bigger issue has emerged. During the AI hype years, investors – including

12:33 many of the biggest and richest – bought into  Big Tech in a big way. They piled billions into

12:39 these companies, confident that the ends  would justify the means. The mega-returns

12:43 would roll in sooner rather than later. Their investments pushed the share prices

12:47 of the tech companies even higher. Today, around  a third of the value of the stock exchange is

12:51 held in just the so-called Magnificent Seven  companies. But that concentration is dangerous,

12:57 and the smart money isn’t falling  for the “AI efficiency” hype anymore.

13:01 Instead, they’re demanding that  Big Tech shows them the money.

13:04 And that leaves Big Tech in a difficult position. They’re all-in on AI to the tune of several

13:10 trillion dollars, and plan to spend even more.  At the same time, they’re slashing budgets to

13:15 peel back their pandemic overspending and fund  their AI buildout. Those are hard enough books

13:20 to balance under normal conditions. Add in  higher interest rates and the pain gets worse.

13:26 Now investors are turning up the heat. They want to see revenue growth. Or at

13:29 least a more sustainable balance between  expenditure and returns until it does.

13:34 That means mass layoffs and  other forms of cost-cutting.

13:37 Anytime a company shows  honesty, the markets react.

13:41 When Salesforce cut 8,000 jobs in 2023 citing  “over-hiring” and macroeconomic weakness,

13:47 the stock fell by roughly 32% in the  following months. When Nike cut around

13:52 800 jobs to “enhance automation,” the market  saw this as a reaction to slumping sales and

13:57 inventory issues. The share price  dropped by nearly 35% as a result.

14:02 But if companies frame the austerity and layoffs  as “driven by AI efficiency”, regardless of the

14:08 truth, the market’s response is chalk and cheese. When Meta announced massive layoffs explicitly

14:14 tied to a “Year of Efficiency” and AI  reallocation in 2023, its stock surged

14:19 over 190% in the following year. Investors  viewed the cuts as a decisive move to fund AI

14:26 infrastructure, not as a sign of trouble. Likewise, when Alphabet cut 12,000 jobs

14:30 in early 2023 while simultaneously  highlighting AI integration, the stock

14:35 jumped around 5% in a single day. A clear dynamic has emerged.

14:39 A 2026 study of S&P 500 companies found that  56% of firms announcing AI-linked layoffs saw

14:46 their stock prices fall by an average of 25% If  a company says “We are cutting 10% of staff to

14:53 redirect capital to high-margin AI agents,” the  stock rises. The market hears as future profits.

14:59 It all comes down to PR spin. This creates a powerful incentive

15:03 for CEOs to frame any cost-cutting  measure as an “AI transformation.”

15:08 So, that’s what they do. The practice has become so

15:10 widespread that analysts have begun  referring to it as “AI washing.”

15:14 And it’s growing. Outplacement firm Challenger,

15:17 Gray & Christmas reported that in May 2026,  AI was the most-cited reason for job cuts.

15:23 It’s a category that barely existed in  layoff reports 2 years earlier. A Deutsche

15:28 Bank analysis from July found that mentions of “AI  disruption” in earnings calls jumped 310% in the

15:34 first half of 2026 alone compared to late 2025. Whenever you hear CEOs citing “AI efficiency”,

15:41 you can be pretty sure layoffs will follow. In early 2026, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said

15:47 that the company would need “fewer people  doing some of the jobs that are being done

15:51 today” due to AI efficiency gains. The statement  coincided with a 16,000-person cut. Meta laid

15:58 off 8,000 workers while moving another 7,000  to AI roles, framing the move as a necessary

16:03 reallocation for an AI-first future. It’s a growing, unmistakable trend.

16:08 It might help to keep share prices at what  many are starting to believe are vastly

16:12 inflated levels. But it does nothing to solve  the underlying issues with the hidden debt,

16:17 problematic AI code, and a potentially  terminal hollowing out of the developer force.

16:22 Based on current 2026 data from Goldman Sachs,  MIT, and the Bank for International Settlements,

16:27 in the best-case scenario, the current  productivity dip is a temporary blip.

16:32 The “installation phase” of a  new technological revolution.

16:35 Some predict that by late-2027, AI models will  achieve reliable agentic reasoning, moving beyond

16:41 code generation to full-system architecture and  self-healing. When that happens, all the issues

16:46 with dodgy code will disappear. Development  productivity will increase exponentially.

16:51 The result will be a massive explosion in global  GDP, which turns the mountain of hidden debt into

16:56 a shrewd investment. And all those displaced  workers will transition to high-value “AI

17:01 orchestration” roles. There’s maybe a 15%

17:04 chance it all works out this way. On the other end of the spectrum,

17:07 it all could blow up like the 2000  Dot-com crash… only at a greater scale.

17:12 Just a few high-profile bankruptcies due to the  $1.65 trillion in off-balance-sheet liabilities

17:18 could trigger a credit crunch that bursts the  AI bubble. Trillions in global wealth would

17:23 be wiped out. Data centers would be abandoned,  with energy contracts reduced to toxic assets.

17:28 As a result, the “Junior Death  Spiral” would become permanent.

17:32 With no entry-level roles and seniors burned  out by maintaining broken AI code, the tech

17:37 sector might contract by as much as a third.  A severe global recession would ensue, and who

17:42 knows what the future of software might look like. Unfortunately, there’s a greater probability of

17:47 this outcome at this point, although it’s  still relatively unlikely at around 25%.

17:52 The most likely outcome is a messy  middle ground: a slow deflation of

17:56 hype rather than a catastrophic crash,  leading to a permanently divided market.

18:01 Sooner or later the “AI washing” narrative will  die. The market will stop rewarding mentions of

18:05 AI and start punishing companies that can’t prove  their real earnings. 5 to 12% of companies that

18:11 augmented rather than replaced humans will  start generating serious returns. The $1.65

18:16 trillion liability will continue being serviced  but increasingly act as a drag on growth.

18:22 Big Tech will have years of austerity  to pay down the hidden debt.

18:26 The software development industry will shift  to a more or less permanent “diamond” structure

18:30 based around small teams of elites using AI.  They’d be supported by a shrinking pool of

18:35 mid-level engineers, with almost no juniors. The industry will be left with higher costs,

18:40 a broken talent pipeline, and a debt hangover  that will take a decade or more to clear.

18:45 That’s the best case scenario. “AI efficiency” isn’t a corporate

18:48 buzzword. It’s a warning sign of a massive  economic shift. And if you’re a junior developer

18:53 whose CEO starts talking about AI’s benefits,  it’s probably a good idea to start job-hunting.

18:58 It’s not just developers who are feeling the  pressure from AI build outs. The architects

19:02 are starting to crack too. key Watch “Why AI  Researchers Are Quitting and Panicking on the

19:07 Way Out” to see the crisis unfolding  behind closed doors. Or click on this.
