04:12 takes a long time and puts most students into a  massive amount of debt. According to the AAMC,

04:18 the median medical student was graduating  $25,000 in debt. And that's accounting for

04:23 some people who were able to get a scholarship or  had parents to fund their education. For students

04:28 going the private college route, that number can  be as high as $400,000. To compensate for these

04:33 immense upfront costs and several years  of loss earnings compared to their peers,

04:36 it's always been the expectation that American  doctors are paid extremely well. And on average,

04:42 they are. Physicians in America are  paid on average almost double that

04:45 of other OECD countries and even extremely  high-income outliers like Switzerland. Oh,

04:51 and as something of foreshadowing, you might have  noticed that Canada is right up there with us. But

04:55 more on that later. In a lot of other countries,  being a doctor is still a prestigious and highly

05:00 respected job. But it doesn't come with nearly the  same expectation of earnings. And in America, this

05:06 wasn't by mistake either. The American Medical  Association, which represents physicians, has

05:11 lobbyed Congress relentlessly to limit residency  positions for students graduating from medical

05:15 school. The Medicare graduate medical education  funding has remained more or less intact since

05:20 1997. But during that same time, we have added  70 million people to our population. This has all

05:25 limited the supply of doctors to the point where  the AAMC estimates that we will have 139,000 fewer

05:31 physicians than we need by 2033 as our population  continues to age. But on the demand side,

05:36 there has been just as much meddling. One of the  other big pushes by the AMA is to make sure that

05:42 there are lots of things that can only legally be  done by a doctor, even when they could be done by

05:46 a nurse practitioner, a physician assistant, or  a non-fysician specialist, like an occupational

05:51 therapist for a lot of this work. Now, of course,  something like brain surgery should probably

05:56 require a specialist to be present, but a lot of  the tasks that legally only doctors can perform

06:01 really aren't that important or that sensitive.  One of the most egregious examples of this scope

06:05 creep is the amount of time that doctors spend  justifying routine prescriptions and procedures

06:09 to health insurance providers. Now, despite being  some more foreshadowing about how bureaucracy

06:14 creates bureaucracy, even if this was all totally  necessary, most of this work is simple data entry,

06:19 which could easily be done by a trained  receptionist. But because only doctors are deemed

06:24 worthy of these specific tasks, they have to spend  their valuable time filling out online forms,

06:28 a cost which is ultimately passed along to their  patients. America has by far the highest medical

06:33 administration cost per capita anywhere in the  world. We spend more than triple the runner up

06:38 which is Germany and bureaucratic administration  is basically their cultural identity. Mandated

06:43 inefficiency is just one of the causes. A simple  combination of bottlenecking the number of doctors

06:48 entering the field and then wasting their time  once they are there means that their hours become

06:52 extremely valuable. Medical schools have realized  this which means they can charge more. And even

06:58 the doctors themselves who largely do just want  to help people aren't going to turn down a far

07:02 higher than average income because they need it  to pay off their far higher than average debt.

07:07 The same goes for things like indemnity insurance,  licensing, and training. All of these things can

07:11 be expensive because doctors are paid well. But  doctors need to be paid well because everything

07:15 they do to maintain their professional  standings is expensive. But all right,

07:20 so far all of this is still only counting the  groups that do still largely want to help people.

07:25 And of course, these little inefficiencies  have snowballed into something much larger.

07:29 There are fewer than a million direct patient  care physicians in America, but over 20 million

07:34 people employed by the healthcare industry  in total, with an alarming share doing very

07:38 little in the way of actually caring for anybody's  health. So, it's time to learn how money works to

07:43 find out how it got this bad and why it's become  almost impossible to undo. If you've ever looked

07:48 at a system like healthcare and wondered why it  never seems to change, then this free report from

07:53 HubSpot called Industries Right for Disruption is  exactly what you should read next. It breaks down

07:57 the industries that are most overdue for major  change and explains what's holding them back.

08:01 This report covers everything from healthcare and  education to real estate and insurance. Basically,

08:06 the sectors where outdated business models and  regulation have created massive inefficiencies.

08:10 If you've ever looked at an industry and thought,  "How has nobody fixed this yet?" This report digs

08:15 into exactly that. My favorite section is the  breakdown of what makes an industry disruptible

08:19 in the first place. Things like high customer  frustration, fragmented incumbents, and regulatory

08:24 modes that are starting to crack. It's the kind of  framework that actually changes how you evaluate

08:28 opportunities. Whether you're looking to build  something in one of these spaces, or just want

08:33 to understand where the biggest shifts are coming,  this is worth bookmarking. This resource was made

08:37 by HubSpot, who's sponsoring this video. Download  it for free at the link in my description and see

08:42 what sectors are next. Okay, so another group that  is often overlooked in this whole equation are

08:47 the hospitals themselves. Like a lot of things in  the economy, hospitals and practices have become

08:52 another entrenched strain on the system simply  because of how consolidated they have become.

08:57 Medical groups have become so dominant in certain  areas that patients effectively have no other

09:01 options if they want a certain procedure outside  of traveling several hours. At the same time,

09:06 the number of doctors that run their own private  practice has been consistently shrinking as

09:10 the industry pressure has pushed doctors into  these collective health systems. Oh, and well,

09:15 you know, I had to bring it up eventually. But the  Government Accountability Office has also pointed

09:20 out the role of private equity in strategically  buying up regional medical practices to create

09:25 local monopolies on care. Now, anti-competitive  practices are nothing new in any industry anymore.

09:30 The FTC has been infamously flaccid with their  enforcement for the last 45 years. But the medical

09:36 industry in particular gets away with a lot more  than it should for two specific reasons. The first

09:41 is that healthcare is complicated. The average  regulator hasn't been to medical school to argue

09:45 against industry groups claiming that a merger  is necessary for patient outcomes. The second

09:50 is that the actual costs that come out of these  mergers are extraordinarily opaque. Of course,

09:55 public enemy number one in this whole game are  the private insurance companies. And don't worry,

09:59 we will get to them soon enough. But a lot of  these combined groups have become so large that

10:03 not even insurance providers can push back against  their market power. If a hospital system has a

10:09 monopoly over a critical medical service in an  area, people will change their insurance if their

10:13 current insurance provider doesn't cover that  network. Large insurers do have more negotiating

10:18 power than individual payers. But if a hospital  is the only game in town, there really isn't much

10:23 they can do. This consolidation has also pushed  insurers into all or nothing contracts where large

10:28 health systems will require insurers to include  all their facilities in their coverage, including

10:33 the expensive ones, or else they won't provide  access to any of them. Now, obviously, health

10:38 insurers aren't the victim here. But in certain  areas, this does prevent them from making a

10:42 narrower network of providers just offering basic  services for a potentially more cost-effective

10:47 plan. All or nothing contracts also incentivize  hospitals to provide services that may not have

10:52 been demanded. even by the massively distorted  market since they are being strongarmed into

10:57 covering it anyway. Even for services provided to  patients on Medicare, there are logical incentives

11:03 that push up prices. One of the key groups that  decide how much a medical service should cost

11:07 Medicare is the Specialty Society Relative Value  Scale Update Committee. A bit of a mouthful,

11:13 so it's normally called Ruck. This is a group of  31 physicians who volunteer to provide guidance on

11:18 how to value a physician's work for computing  healthcare prices. Now, naturally, a group of

11:22 physicians would like to say that physicians  are worth quite a lot. But this group is also

11:27 overwhelmingly made up of specialists, creating  a bias that overvalues specialist procedures over

11:32 simple primary care. Now, the reason why this  is important is because the prices this group

11:37 lays out are almost always adopted by Medicare.  And the prices adopted by Medicare act as a price

11:42 floor template for the rest of the industry as  a whole with various built-in markups. Honestly,

11:47 it's not too dissimilar to how government  treasuries determine the rates that people

11:51 pay on their home loans and credit cards. All  of these conflicting groups obviously create

11:55 a lot of friction in an already very complex  industry, which also allows for other groups

12:00 to cash in in ways that are harder to notice with  everything else going on. Pharmaceutical companies

12:05 make roughly 40% of their global revenue here in  America, even though we have 4% of the world's

12:10 population. It's no secret that we massively  overpay for medicine. But within this whole mess,

12:16 who's going to notice? The US market has become  so lucrative that we have effectively subsidized

12:21 R&D for the rest of the world because selling a  new drug to Americans is so profitable that every

12:26 other country can basically just break even.  And then of course, boxing this whole thing in

12:31 are health insurance companies, which may get some  push back from some of the big health care groups,

12:35 but can still ultimately pass everything along  to regular consumers in costs that are usually

12:40 obfiscated by employer healthare plans. These guys  keep everything out of sight and out of mind for

12:45 most people until they actually need to deal with  it. And then of course they have an incentive to

12:50 delay, deny, and defend. Even if it did function  without this log jam of conflicting interests,

12:55 healthcare is never going to be a normal market.  The information asymmetry is huge. The groups

13:00 paying the bills are rarely the ones receiving  the support. Prices are borderline impossible

13:05 to find. And even if you could get access to  this information and actually understand it,

13:09 you can't shop around while you're dying. Now,  it certainly doesn't help that the regulators who

13:15 should be in there trying to direct this traffic  jam towards something slightly more functional

13:19 are being paid off by these various parties to let  them get a little bit further ahead in traffic at

13:24 the expense of making it impossible to fix the  system as a whole. According to Open Secrets,

13:29 the healthc care sector is the number one lobbying  spender in the country, spending almost 3/4 of a

13:34 billion dollars in 2024 alone, just at the  federal level. But now, the thing is, this

13:40 has been going on for so long that even if it was  completely fixed and ironed out tomorrow, there is

13:44 too much built up in it. Every one of these groups  employs tens of thousands of people to negotiate,

13:49 coordinate, lobby, market to, or just plain old  sue all of the other groups. Each and every one

13:55 of these groups is just trying to serve their  own self-interest, but none of those interests

13:59 are aligned. And the group that is consistently  made to compromise is the patient right in the

14:04 middle of everything with the least understanding  and negotiating power. Another slightly darker

14:09 visual metaphor is that often rats will get their  tails caught together. And as they run to try and

14:14 free themselves, they only end up pulling the knot  tighter. Collectively, this administrative bloat

14:19 built to service the administrative bloat is one  of the largest employers in the country and at

14:24 least up until recently has been one of the only  industries safe from layoffs. If we could snap our

14:29 fingers tomorrow and replace our healthcare system  with something like what exists in Australia,

14:33 we would lose 7 12% of our economic uh  productivity and shed millions of these

14:39 jobs. It's also worth noting that Australia's  system is not exactly an unfair comparison.

14:45 They also have very well-compensated doctors  on average. They have extremely good health

14:49 outcomes and rely on a blended system of private  health insurance and public Medicare. Either way,

14:54 this would be a larger hit to both of these  numbers than the global financial crisis. However,

15:00 that doesn't mean it's not worth trying because  over time, this problem is only getting worse. The

15:06 size of the healthcare industry has consistently  been growing faster than the size of the overall

15:10 economy. By 2033, the Centers for Medicare and  Medicaid Services predicts that more than 1/5if of

15:16 our entire economy will be dedicated to healthcare  and the apparatus that is built up around it.

15:20 But just like healthcare has slowly grown on the  economy, it can also slowly be disassembled over

15:26 time as well. Simple things like antitrust  enforcement, proper lobbying, regulation,

15:30 and more transparency will at the very least deal  with the elements that are intentionally trying to

15:35 pile more logs into the log jam. We may lose some  jobs like internal auditors for the legal firms,

15:40 servicing the investment banks, managing the deals  between market information providers, giving leads

15:45 to pharmaceutical sales businesses that sell  third-party generic substitutes to regional

15:49 healthcare groups. But that's just measuring  the uh downsides. One of the biggest hurdles

15:54 to skilled professionals starting businesses of  their own is losing the healthcare security that

15:59 comes along with being a skilled professional.  Removing one of the biggest obstacles to genuine

16:03 business development in the long term would be  far healthier for the economy than piling another

16:08 layer of administration on top of our health  care system. Finally, it might also solve what

16:12 some consider to be one of the most existential  problems in the world. We aren't having enough

16:17 babies. But when a visit to the hospital can be  bankrupting, maybe this shouldn't be too shocking,

16:22 especially to the same group of people who want  to replace us all with AI anyway. But go and watch

16:27 this video next to find out why they still really  want you to have a child anyway. because it gets

16:32 really weird. There was a lot more to talk about  in this video which I will be writing a newsletter

16:36 on in my totally free newsletter compounded daily.  So, make sure to sign up for that if you want to

16:41 learn about it more. And don't forget to like and  subscribe to keep on learning how money works.

00:00 On July 28th, 2026, the impossible happened. Halo: Campaign Evolved launched on the Playstation

00:06 5. For the first time, Master Chief  was sitting in the PlayStation Store

00:10 next to the games he was built to destroy. Most people shrugged it off as a cash grab.

00:15 On the surface, it makes sense. Games cost a  fortune to develop and putting your product on

00:20 more shelves is textbook business. Except the cash didn’t flow.

00:25 The game bombed. It opened at a pathetic 29 on Sony’s

00:30 active player list. But behind closed doors, the  failure exposed a more brutal reality. A company

00:35 that had once spent over $1 billion to save its  gamers suddenly decided those gamers don’t matter.

00:41 Xbox had officially lost the console wars. This was their unconditional surrender.

00:47 The crisis began in November 2005. The Xbox  360 launched fast… and it launched broken.

00:53 Gamers reported three red lights around the power  button, signalling general hardware failure.

00:58 Overnight, millions of consoles  became expensive bricks.

01:01 For 18 months, Microsoft downplayed the issue.  They extended warranties in small increments,

01:06 tried to reassure everyone and hoped  the gaming community would just move on.

01:11 They didn’t. By July 2007,

01:13 Microsoft stopped hiding behind PR releases and  decided to throw money at the problem. Every Xbox

01:18 360 sold since launch was covered for 3 more years  against the red ring failure. Anyone who had paid

01:24 out of pocket got a voucher for a new device. Then came the financial cost.

01:28 Microsoft revealed they would take a pre-tax  hit of $1.15 billion for that quarter.

01:33 With 12 million consoles sold, the billion dollar  price tag meant Microsoft was budgeting to fix

01:38 almost every console it had ever sold. The company  was planning for a 100% failure rate. Legally,

01:44 they didn’t have to do that. The original 90-day  warranty had already expired for most of the

01:49 machines it was agreeing to repair. But they did it anyway.

01:53 The previous quarter, Microsoft’s entire  Entertainment and Devices division, which

01:56 included Xbox, Zune, and Windows Mobile,  had made only $929 million in revenue.

02:03 The apology cost more than the  division earned in 3 months.

02:06 At the time, Microsoft dubbed it “an investment  in the customer base.” If gamers could get their

02:11 devices fixed quickly, they might just stick with  the Xbox rather the “other” console at the time.

02:17 And it paid off… Initially.

02:19 Console sales follow a predictable pattern.Volumes  peak around year 3 or 4. By then most of the bugs

02:25 are fixed, and developers have figured out  how to squeeze every bit of power from the

02:28 hardware. But that peak is short lived. After  that, sales plummet as the hardware ages,

02:34 and another console looms on the horizon. The 360 broke the model entirely.

02:39 Microsoft’s own marketing later pointed  out that sales increased year after year.

02:43 It seemed like the console was unstoppable. By early 2013, more than 76 million Xbox

02:49 360 consoles had been sold worldwide.  Microsoft had earned a loyal audience,

02:54 which would hopefully translate into  selling the next console when it came out.

02:57 All it took was a bit over $1 billion. But that loyalty was gone in just an hour.

03:03 On February 11, 2013, in Dana Point, California,  two Microsoft executives sat down at a media

03:08 conference called “D: Dive Into Media.” One was Nancy Tellem, a former CBS television

03:14 executive that Microsoft had recently hired to  build a production studio in Los Angeles. The

03:19 other was Yusuf Mehdi, senior vice president of  Microsoft’s Interactive Entertainment Business.

03:24 Mehdi came with numbers, and the numbers were  extraordinary. He described the Xbox 360 as

03:29 being in the middle of a transition. It would  move from a gaming console to an entertainment

03:34 console. American users spent roughly 87 hours  a month on the machine. The console supported

03:39 more than a hundred voice-controlled television  and entertainment apps on Xbox Live. Xbox users

03:45 were spending large amounts of time watching  videos and using the apps, rather than gaming.

03:50 But there’s a huge problem with using  that argument for selling consoles.

03:54 A gaming console sits in the living room,  usually plugged into the best television in

03:58 the house. People turn it on to play something,  finish playing, and then leave it running. Thanks

04:03 to those entertainment apps, the Xbox 360 could  for Netflix, watching movies, and even playing

04:09 music. It would get turned on and run for as  long as the TV itself did, day in, day out.

04:15 Microsoft looked at that and decided to hijack the  tv as well. It wanted the Xbox to become the hum

04:21 everything else in the room plugs into. It was a huge strategic error.

04:25 Microsoft had survived the red ring. It had  fought the PlayStation 3 to a draw. It had

04:29 the best-selling console in the United States  for years running. And it had done it all as

04:34 the outsider in a business Sony and Nintendo had  owned for two decades. When you have been right

04:39 about a hard thing, it becomes very difficult  to hear you’re about to fail at an easy one.

04:45 There was another problem lurking. Smartphones and tablets were pulling

04:48 attention out of the living room and even from  the PC itself, where Microsoft had an undeniable

04:53 lead. Apple was circling television. Netflix was  becoming the default verb for watching something.

04:59 So, Microsoft decided to  double down on the TV strategy.

05:03 On May 21st, 2013, the company held another  grand unveiling in front of the gaming

05:08 world. The hype was huge. Every gaming  outlet on Earth was carrying the stream.

05:13 The console was the Xbox One. What followed was an hour of television.

05:17 The bulk of the event went to the future of TV  entertainment and to voice commands. Television

05:23 was mentioned over 45 times in a single hour.  TIME’s correspondent wrote that gamers watching

05:27 the stream only caught glimpses of in-game  footage… and not until the presentation’s finale.

05:33 The centerpiece was a feature called HDMI-in. It meant your cable box wouldn’t plug into

05:39 the television. Instead, it plugged into the Xbox  One. The console would become the middle-man. Say

05:44 a channel name out loud, and it changes. Microsoft  had gone and built a television that could also do

05:50 games. And it announced that to an audience that  had been looking for a console to rival Sony’s.

05:55 Things got much worse. The Xbox One would authenticate

05:58 its games against Microsoft’s servers, checking in  every 24 hours to ensure the game was legitimate

06:03 and the user was properly logged in. Games  were licensed to an account rather than

06:08 existing on a disc. Second-hand copies would  be subject to fees and publisher permissions.

06:13 In other words, you couldn’t hand  a game to your friend. You would

06:16 own nothing and be happy with it. The 24-hour check-in meant if the

06:21 servers were down, or the broadband was out,  single-player games stopped working. Regardless

06:26 of whether it had online-based features  or if it could fully operate offline,

06:30 it just stopped. Players would get a  notification that it needed to be authenticated.

06:34 The games market itself was impacted. Stock in GameStop, a retailer whose entire

06:39 physical footprint exists because used games  change hands, dropped 5%. Pre-owned products

06:45 had represented $2.4 billion in sales, or  27.4% of the company’s revenue. It made

06:51 up nearly half of its gross profit in the  previous fiscal year. Microsoft had just

06:56 announced a console that put nearly half of a  major retail chain’s profit engine in question.

07:01 And it had done it without warning. It didn’t take long for the presentation

07:05 to be edited by the internet into a supercut  of executives saying the word “television.”

07:10 One of the gaming industry’s biggest moments  of 2013 was meme’d in less than 24 hours.

07:15 And there was one more thing in the box. The new Kinect camera was mandatory. Kinect

07:21 was originally released back in 2010 and, at  the time, was hailed as one of the biggest

07:25 inventions in gaming. It sold 8 million  units in 2 months. It allowed Xbox games

07:30 to utilize a camera instead of a controller.  It spawned a new genre of family-oriented

07:35 games like virtual sports for the console. But with the Xbox 360, the Kinect came as

07:40 a separate attachment. You could turn it off  and unplug it. But as soon as the Xbox One was

07:45 switched on, the camera started. The microphone  listened for the actions to turn the console on,

07:50 but it also listened to everything else.  Microsoft launched a literal tracking device

07:55 at the exact time headlines were exposing  how Big Tech was spying on the public.

07:59 It took a week to rebrand the new  console as a “monitoring device.”

08:03 Two weeks after the announcement,  outlets leaked the PRISM documents,

08:07 a then-secret program that allowed the NSA to  monitor users for possible links to terrorism.

08:12 Techniques included wiretapping video chats,  call logs, and connection logs. Among the 9

08:18 companies listed, was Microsoft. They became a  part of PRISM in 2007, 3 years before Kinect.

08:24 So Kinect quickly became a marketing disaster. And it wasn’t even free.

08:29 A teardown by the analysis firm IHS found  that Kinect added $75 to the Xbox One’s

08:35 bill of materials and manufacturing cost.  It took 3 months after the initial unveiling

08:39 for Microsoft to disable the requirement of  keeping Kinect plugged in for the console to

08:44 work. Despite that, multiple manufacturers  began selling “Kinect covers” costing $20.

08:49 On June 10th, 2013, Sony and Microsoft  took the stage at E3 in Los Angeles.

08:54 Microsoft went first and reiterated  the claims of needing Kinect. Then Sony

08:59 walked out and changed the game in 90 seconds. Jack Tretton, who ran Sony’s American operation,

09:04 told the room that PlayStation 4 owners could  trade in their disc games, lend them to friends,

09:10 sell them, or keep them. He also said the console  would not require an internet connection to play a

09:14 single-player game. Then, Sony announced the  price of $399, $100 less than the Xbox One.

09:21 And in the same week, Sony published a video. It lasted 22 seconds, and it was titled,

09:27 “The Official PlayStation Used Game Instructional  Video.” Out of those 22 seconds, roughly 12 were

09:32 taken by the intro and outro. In the video, Shuhei  Yoshida, president of Sony’s worldwide studios,

09:38 held up a copy of Killzone Shadow Fall and  explained how to share games on PlayStation

09:43 4. In “Step One” Yoshida handed the  disc to his colleague Adam Boyes.

09:47 The video ended. There was no “Step two.”

09:50 Years later, Yoshida said that the intent wasn’t  designed to make fun of Xbox. Microsoft had

09:55 announced its policy first and the press  were asking Sony what it planned to do.

09:59 The company answered in the shortest  form available. Whatever the intent,

10:03 it was the cheapest attack advertisement  in the history of consumer electronics.

10:07 And it worked. The pre-order data performed a 180 within a week.

10:11 Before the press conferences, Amazon’s UK numbers  had the Xbox One narrowly ahead. Days after Sony’s

10:16 conference, the PlayStation 4 sat at the top of  Amazon UK’s chart while the Xbox One had fallen to

10:22 third, behind a two-month-old PlayStation 3 game. In the United States, the tracking firm VGChartz

10:27 estimated roughly 75,000 PlayStation 4 pre-orders  against about 45,000 for the Xbox One for the week

10:34 ending June 15th. While neither platform holder  published pre-order numbers, every independent

10:40 count pointed in the same direction. It wasn’t close.

10:43 On June 19th, 8 days after E3, Microsoft  reversed their policy. No 24-hour check-in.

10:49 Used games worked normally. Discs could be lent. The reversal is often filed as a last-ditch effort

10:55 to take back the audience share that Microsoft  lost through its own blunders. But if you look a

10:59 bit deeper, it was basically a confession that the  company built a strategy that was indefensible. It

11:05 countered the very idea of using game consoles  in the first place. The underlying design of

11:10 the device didn’t change. It was still a $499  television box with a camera shipped alongside it.

11:16 Kinect was unbundled the following year, and  the price dropped to $399. The Kinect system

11:21 itself would end up becoming obsolete in late  2017. Microsoft wouldn’t even manufacture the

11:26 adapter for it starting in 2018. It was a glimpse into

11:29 the slow decline of Xbox One. The head of Microsoft’s Xbox division,

11:33 Don Mattrick, didn’t stay to watch that  decline. On July 1st, 2013, Zynga announced

11:38 that he would become its chief executive,  effective the following week. Microsoft’s

11:43 CEO Steve Ballmer confirmed it to Microsoft  employees in an internal email the same day.

11:48 He noted that Xbox Live membership had grown from  6 million to 48 million during Mattrick’s tenure,

11:53 and that Microsoft’s efforts would be focused  on shipping Xbox One in the coming holiday.

11:58 4 months before the console reached shops,  the man who had shaped it jumped ship to

12:03 the company that made FarmVille. When the consoles were launched,

12:06 Sony shipped 117.2 million PlayStation 4 units  and then stopped reporting in 2022. The console’s

12:13 life was over and it was time for the next one.  Microsoft, which had happily published the count

12:18 for Xbox 360 at 76 million consoles, went quiet  and has stayed quiet. The most commonly cited

12:25 statistic is that Xbox One sold between 50  and 60 million units, roughly half of Sony’s.

12:30 The next console generation added  a lock on the door that no previous

12:35 generation had: the digital library. The Xbox One era was the first in

12:39 which most people stopped buying discs.  Purchases became entries on an account,

12:44 and an account doesn’t move between manufacturers. In May 2023, Phil Spencer, the man Xbox for a

12:50 decade, said, “We lost the worst generation to  lose in the Xbox One generation,” because that

12:55 was the generation in which everybody built  their digital libraries. He went further,

13:00 suggesting that around 90% of people walking  into a shop in the 2020s to buy a console already

13:05 belong to one of the three ecosystems. And no game reverses that.

13:10 Including Halo. If you can’t move players to your hardware,

13:14 you move your software to their hardware and take  the margin. The logic is flawless. But it’s also

13:20 the mindset of a software publisher, not a console  platform. Microsoft entered this business with the

13:25 Xbox explicitly to be a platform. The current leadership knows that.

13:29 In June 2026, at the Xbox Games Showcase,  Sharma confirmed that Gears of War:

13:34 E-Day and Clockwork Revolution would stay  on Xbox and PC and that these were not timed

13:40 exclusives. It was a line drawn in the sand on  the brand’s 25th anniversary, after 2 years of

13:45 sending nearly everything to Sony’s console. The Xbox One was not a bad machine. Its

13:51 architecture was close enough to the PlayStation  4’s that the same chip supplier built the heart

13:55 of both. Microsoft’s studios didn’t forget how  to make games overnight. The company had more

14:00 money than its competitor, more engineers,  and a decade of goodwill in the bank.

14:05 But none of that mattered. It took only an  hour of poor stagecraft in which a company

14:10 told its most committed customers that  it had found a more interesting audience.

14:14 That was the exact moment the console wars ended. All that was left… was to count the bodies.

14:19 The gaming world is changing forever. And some  classics have been left behind… or worse. Watch

14:25 Real Reason Why Video Games Are Banned to see some  how dark the industry can get. Or click on this.

00:00 A planet-killing asteroid could  already be hurtling toward Earth…

00:03 and we might not see it until it’s too late. Despite the idea of 24/7 sky monitoring,

00:09 there are still blind spots. And that’s  exactly where something catastrophic

00:12 could come from. Objects can slip past our  detection networks depending on their angle

00:16 of approach,especially steep “above the plane”  trajectories no one is continuously watching.

00:22 It’s happened before… and it will happen again. We got lucky once.

00:26 Next time, we might not. Humans have built systems

00:28 designed to watch the sky for anything coming our  way. Constant surveillance. Precision tracking.

00:33 The ability to map the paths of objects moving  millions of miles through space. And if something

00:38 looks dangerous, in theory, we can respond. For decades, that idea has given billions

00:43 of people a quiet sense of security. That idea is fundamentally flawed.

00:48 On September 9th 2017 an interstellar  object slingshotted past the Sun.

00:52 The cigar-shaped structure, estimated at around  a quarter of a mile (400 meters) in length,

00:56 travelled at almost 196,000 miles per hour  (315,431 kph). Just over a month later,

01:01 it made its closest approach to Earth. And nobody saw it.

01:05 It wasn’t until October 19 that  the object was detected. By then,

01:09 it had already spent years in our vast solar  system and was already on its way towards the

01:13 exit. Weeks had passed with this large, anomalous  object speeding through our solar system unseen.

01:18 This object was later named ‘Oumuamua.  It passed through the solar system and

01:22 left again without impact. Now imagine the same kind of

01:26 arrival… but with something actually locked  onto Earth. A massive hunk of rock and metal,

01:31 moving straight through space toward us and  nothing in our satellite networks, telescopes,

01:36 or monitoring systems picks it up in time. Not until it’s already too late.

01:40 If it happened once, it can happen again. How did we miss it?

01:44 Simp;e. We weren’t looking in the right places. Not because we didn’t want to, but because we

01:49 weren’t able to. It turns out that even  the most advanced observatories on Earth,

01:54 like Pan-STARRS and the Vera C.  Rubin Observatory, have blind spots.

01:59 In other words, the planetary defence systems  we count on… aren’t as reliable as they seem.

02:04 They’re designed to map objects  moving across the full 3D dome of

02:07 the night sky. But there are regions  they struggle to watch clearly,

02:11 especially the bright, sun-facing areas  where detection becomes far harder.

02:15 It was from that same abyss that ‘Oumuamua  emerged, ‘dropping into’ our system from

02:20 above. By the time we understood what  we had seen, it was already gone.

02:24 It proved we’re vulnerable. So, if we’re blind to this

02:27 part of our solar system, why haven’t we  simply sent probes to take a look for us?

02:31 To understand how humanity became so worryingly  blind to this enormous existential vulnerability,

02:37 we have to go back to the  birth of our solar system.

02:39 4.5 billion years ago, it was little more  than a flattened disk of gas and dust,

02:45 spinning wildly in the deep darkness of  space. It was collapsing, reshaping itself

02:49 under gravity. As it contracted, it didn’t just  fall inward, it spun faster. Collisions built

02:55 structure. Small grains became larger bodies. At the center of it all, the future Sun.

03:01 The result was a single shared orbital plane: a  cosmic “disc” everything would eventually follow.

03:07 Every planet and asteroid were into the same  general lane of motion. And that structure shaped

03:12 how we see everything around our solar system. For thousands of years, mankind watched the night

03:17 sky and tracked the movements of the stars.  And because our planet moves along a flat,

03:22 ecliptic plane, all the other planets appear to  move in narrow, predictable paths across the sky.

03:27 In short, we grew up in a world where everything  happened along the same horizontal axis, which

03:31 embedded a kind of ‘two dimensional bias’ into our  collective consciousness. And that bias persisted

03:37 right up to the time when we finally invented the  type of technology we needed to build high-power

03:43 telescopes and send rockets into space. We still operated outside the

03:47 intense glare of the Sun. We sent our most advanced

03:50 probes outside that glare, where they  could function safely and consistently.

03:55 We built our detection and planetary defense  systems with a heavy bias toward the ecliptic

03:59 plane, because that’s where most comets,  asteroids, and debris were expected to

04:04 emerge from. We built, in effect, a 2D  surveillance system in a 3D universe.

04:09 It all traces back to those ancient laws of  physics that shaped the architecture of our

04:13 solar system. It defined the orbits of planets  and the limits of where we looked. But the void

04:18 above and below was outside that limit. But this isn’t a mere psychological bias

04:23 that we can easily overcome; it’s a physical  barrier that demands an immense amount of

04:27 energy for rockets to break through. In the field of space exploration,

04:31 distance and speed aren’t necessarily  the most important metrics. Instead,

04:35 numerous theories and projections are built  around a measurement known as Delta-V.

04:40 It’s arguably the only metric that  matters. It measures the total change

04:44 in velocity a spacecraft is capable of producing. It’s sometimes referred to as the ‘fuel budget’

04:49 or ‘range’ of a rocket. Every maneuver in space,  whether it be launching from Earth, landing on

04:54 the moon, or adjusting from one orbital trajectory  to another, demands a certain amount of Delta-V.

05:00 We’ve built rockets and probes with enough delta-v  to explore the solar system, and even leave it. So

05:05 why is it so difficult to send them in a different  direction and map the space above and below us?

05:11 It all comes down to one thing. ‘Gravity Prison.’

05:15 When a rocket takes off from the Earth’s surface,  it inherits the Earth’s orbital velocity,

05:19 traveling around the Sun at a rate approaching  19 miles per second (30 kilometers a second).

05:23 That powerful forward momentum is helpful when  you want to travel to another location along the

05:28 same plane, somewhere like Mars, for example.  If we want to send a rocket to the outer edges

05:33 of the solar system, past Pluto, it would  only need an additional Delta-V of around 10

05:38 miles per second (16 kilometers per second). It’s because the rocket or probe is

05:41 benefiting from the Earth’s orbit. It’s already moving the right way,

05:45 but just needs a relatively small  push to move further across the plane.

05:49 If we want to turn a corner, however, and  move out of that ecliptic plane, then that

05:53 means a much greater amount of energy. To pull off a maneuver like that,

05:57 you can’t rely on Earth’s orbit. You  have to fight against it, canceling out

06:00 that horizontal momentum while accelerating the  spacecraft in a completely different direction.

06:05 Because of this, the estimated amount of  Delta-V required to achieve a 90-degree

06:10 solar polar orbit is approximately 20 miles  per second (32 kilometers per second).

06:14 Double the amount of energy needed to  get past Pluto and exit the solar system.

06:18 It’s like launching a rocket from Earth,  pushing it to maximum speed, and then

06:22 trying to stop it instantly by slamming into  a wall at 67,000 miles per hour. (107,826 kph)

06:27 That kind of maneuver is beyond what our  current propulsion systems are built to handle.

06:32 This is the Gravity Prison. The laws of orbital mechanics and the pull of our

06:36 planet effectively lock us into a flat, horizontal  corridor that’s almost impossible to escape.

06:42 Almost. Because, despite

06:43 this massive barrier, NASA actually managed  to send one probe out of the plane in 1990.

06:49 What it found broke our understanding of the Sun. NASA called its 1990 probe Ulysses and

06:54 it represented something unprecedented. A blind and daring leap into the unknown.

06:59 Because engineers couldn’t rely on conventional  chemical propulsion alone to conquer the Delta-V

07:04 barrier, they had to get creative. Ulysses was  launched towards Jupiter. The gas giant’s huge

07:09 gravitational field slingshotted the probe out  of the ecliptic plane and into a high-inclination

07:15 polar orbit around the Sun. Somehow, it worked.

07:18 The data started pouring in. And it defied every expectation.

07:22 Before the Ulysses mission, the scientific  community operated according to a rigid belief

07:26 in something called the Parker spiral model. It  dictates that the Sun’s magnetic field twists

07:32 into a neat spiral-like structure as it extends  across the solar system. According to this model,

07:37 the solar poles were relatively quiet and orderly  regions where magnetic lines returned to the star.

07:43 Ulysses revealed that our polar  magnetic fields are unwound and chaotic.

07:48 Far from following a precise, predictable  pattern, the lines are wildly disorganized

07:53 and entirely unpredictable. This suggests that  all of our established mathematical models of

07:57 solar physics weren’t just a little ‘off’. They were missing 50% of the picture.

08:03 In an instant, entire theories and formulas fell  apart. Everything we thought we knew about the

08:08 most important star of all had to be rewritten. The drama didn’t end there.

08:12 The environment that Ulysses encountered above the  Sun was almost unimaginably violent. Solar winds

08:18 reached speeds of around 466 to 497 miles per  second (750 to 800 kilometers a second). That’s

08:23 almost double the winds  found at the solar equator.

08:25 It was the equivalent of passing from  a breezy day at the beach to a Category

08:30 5 hurricane simply by changing latitude. The space above us was not some peaceful,

08:35 empty, uninteresting void. It was a torrent of  energetic chaos, a whirlwind of magnetic violence,

08:41 far beyond our wildest expectations. The swift solar winds of the poles

08:45 were only the beginning. As scientists scrambled to

08:48 analyze the new data, they realized that this was  just one part of a much larger systemic crisis:

08:54 the space above us isn’t just unstable. It’s crushing our entire solar system.

08:59 For generations, space agencies presented a clear  visual model of our solar system and its position

09:04 in the wider galaxy. We were told that our  world and the planets that share the surrounding

09:09 space travel through the universe inside a  stable, symmetrical, bubble-shaped shield.

09:14 The heliosphere. It was a reassuring concept.

09:17 We didn’t have to worry about world-ending  catastrophes and interstellar radiation,

09:22 because there was always this vast invisible  force-field to keep us safe. That model isn’t

09:27 exactly wrong. But it misses something vital:  our so-called shield is under immense pressure.

09:32 And the cracks are already starting to show. In recent years, data gathered by deep space

09:37 probes and interstellar satellites has revealed  that the cosmic architecture we depend on is being

09:42 forcefully altered. Professor Merav Opher, one  of the world’s leading astrophysicists, famously

09:47 concluded that while ‘sphere’ may be a part of its  name, the heliosphere is anything but spherical.

09:52 It’s more like a flat croissant. A flat croissant that is constantly being

09:57 crushed and warped by intense magnetic pressure,  leaving dangerously thin spots at the poles.

10:02 In other words, Earth’s protective  magnetic field bends, stretches,

10:06 and shifts over time. It’s not a secure bunker  or impenetrable barrier. It’s more like a

10:11 plastic tent with a sagging roof, struggling to  withstand the weight raining down from above.

10:16 The fragility of our situation was highlighted  in 2009. NASA’s Interstellar Boundary Explorer

10:21 satellite, or IBEX, turned towards the  edges of our system and saw something

10:26 humanity had never seen before. The so-called IBEX Ribbon.

10:30 A massive, mysterious structure made up of  enhanced energetic atom emissions, spanning across

10:35 the sky. Containing particle densities that are 2  to 3 times higher than surrounding space, the IBEX

10:41 Ribbon acts like a kind of ‘magnetic mirror’  which reflects escaped solar wind particles

10:46 right back into the core of the solar system. It’s like a glowing neon fence surrounding our

10:51 entire solar system. We had no idea it was even  there until 2009. But that same energetic ribbon

10:57 extends right through the high-latitude  polar regions of our dynamic shield.

11:01 That same barrier, meant to protect us from the  lethal radiation of outer space, isn’t fixed. It

11:06 shifts and flexes at its edges over time. Because  we’ve been so busy looking out across our own flat

11:12 2D plane, we’ve had no way of knowing about it,  and no way of tracking its changes over time.

11:18 In fact, the only way to monitor the highly active  poles required an extreme gravitational maneuver.

11:24 All of the problems outlined so far  boil down to one underlying cause:

11:28 the conservation of angular momentum. It’s that very same physical law that

11:33 formed our solar system and gave our  planet life that blinds us today.

11:37 It’s a true case of cosmic irony. Billions of years ago, it was the conservation of

11:41 angular momentum that helped the early condensing  chaos of the solar system flatten and extend

11:47 outwards into a life-sustaining disk. A miracle of  physics that paved the way for life as we know it.

11:53 Without that flattening, the Earth wouldn’t  have formed. It wouldn’t have begun to follow

11:57 that perfectly precise and stable circular  orbit it has to follow to sustain life..

12:02 The flat ecliptic plane - the end  result of angular momentum - is the

12:06 only reason we exist at all. Yet that same law of physics

12:10 now traps us in a gravity wall prison. If humanity truly wants to set up an early

12:14 warning or defense system above the solar system  to scan for signs of the next ‘Oumuamua, it can’t

12:20 fight the rules of physics. It has to use them to  its advantage. In real terms, that means the only

12:25 option is to slingshot us where we want to go. If we can survive it, that is.

12:30 One way we’re ever getting out into the abyss  relies on a high-stakes orbital strategy called

12:34 the Oberth Maneuver, otherwise known as  a Powered Flyby. It’s an extremely risky

12:39 orbital technique in which a spacecraft allows  itself to fall inside a gravity well. It waits

12:44 until the very last moment - at the lowest  point of that well - to fire its engines.

12:49 This, in turn, takes advantage  of the so-called Oberth effect,

12:53 which states firing a rocket’s engines at high  velocity produces far more kinetic energy than

12:58 doing so at lower speeds. If we can’t achieve  enough Delta-V through conventional propulsion,

13:03 this becomes our only remaining option. We have to literally make a

13:07 spacecraft fall into the sun. As it falls deeper and deeper,

13:11 it will accelerate to an extreme speed, activating  its on-board propulsion systems at the very nadir

13:16 of its orbit. This would give it a boost that  might just be big enough to send it slingshotting

13:21 out of the ecliptic plane. It’s an extreme maneuver.

13:24 At that distance from the Sun, no  conventional spacecraft would survive.

13:28 Even our strongest current heat shields would melt  in an instant. The spacecraft would be subjected

13:33 to a thermal bombardment it would have no hope of  withstanding. And with no shields to guard them,

13:38 all of the sensors, cameras, communications  systems, and other components required to collect

13:43 and send data back to Earth would be vaporized. In short, this desperate ‘jailbreak’ gamble

13:49 requires technology we don’t have yet. Until then, we’re sitting ducks.

13:53 A potentially world-ending threat could be  somewhere in space right now, speeding towards us.

13:58 The world’s leading space agencies  spend vast amounts of time and

14:01 resources on planetary defense initiatives. They scan the stars for signs of Potentially

14:06 Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs) with an estimated  diameter larger than 460 feet (140 meters) and

14:12 an orbit that brings them within 4.64 million  miles (7.48 million km) of the Earth’s path.

14:17 There are thousands of known  PHAs in existence today.

14:20 There could be countless  others we don’t yet know about.

14:23 Less than 1% of known PHAs have an  inclination greater than 45 degrees.

14:29 The interstellar void - the vast regions above  and below our solar system - doesn’t follow the

14:34 same flat plane we live in. ‘Oumuamua wasn’t a one-off.

14:37 It was a warning shot. It was the wider universe sending a message that

14:41 we aren’t as safe as we’ve been led to believe.  The space that surrounds us is much greater - and

14:46 more dangerous - than we ever could have imagined. Since ‘Oumuamua’s arrival, much has changed

14:51 in the way we observe the universe. We retuned software algorithms for the

14:55 upcoming Vera Rubin Observatory, approving an  ESA Comet Interceptor mission and scanning the

15:01 skies to specifically chase the next object. A potential planet killer might already be on

15:06 its way, set to descend through the thin,  flaking layers of our crushed croissant

15:10 shield. It might past the blind spots of  the Pan-STARRS and other observatories,

15:14 ready to catch us all entirely off guard. It won’t announce itself.

15:18 And it won’t follow the rules we want it to. Our survival depends on mapping the full 3D

15:23 sphere of our origin, breaking past the Delta-V  barrier, using gravity assists, and looking

15:29 above and below, not just across the plane. Until then, we’re relying on telescopes,

15:34 surveys, and deflection physics to keep us  safe from the one impact we never see coming.

15:39 And that only works… until it doesn’t. There’s little we can do if a planet

15:44 killer is already on its way. Watch “The  Last 60 Minutes Before Asteroid Impacts with

15:48 Earth” to see what those final moments would  actually look like. Or click on this video.
