00:00 People think the Holocaust was the greatest  tragedy in human history, all driven by ego

00:04 and the personal madness of a failed artist. The  reality is far more terrifying. In January 1942,

00:12 15 senior Nazi officials met at a lakeside villa,  not to debate whether it should happen, but how

00:17 to make it work. Over Cognac, they synchronized a  continental operation, treating mass murder as a

00:23 logistical problem. In just 90 minutes, they  decided the fate of millions across Europe.

00:28 This wasn't a breakdown of civilization. It was  a product of it. On January 20th, 1942, Reinhardt

00:35 Hydrrich summoned 14 other top Nazis to a villa  in the Berlin [music] suburb of Vonyi. Hydrish,

00:41 who Hitler once called the man with the iron  heart, wouldn't make his mark in popular history

00:46 like Hitler's inner circle. But he was without a  doubt one of the most important and most sinister

00:51 figures in the entire apparatus of the Third  Reich. He [music] was a talented violinist,

00:56 fighter pilot, and fencer who oozed charisma. That  saw him rise through the ranks to become the head

01:01 of the Reich security main office, overseeing  the Gestapo, the criminal police, and the SD,

01:07 the intelligence arm of the SS. Hydrrich wasn't  so much the epitome of the benality of evil. He

01:13 was too ruthless to be called Benal. But he was a  cold, brutal administrator. He was also one of the

01:19 principal architects of the Nazi policy toward  what the regime called the Jewish question. The

01:25 Jewish question, what to do with millions of Jews  across Europe. The Nazis called them the unbench,

01:31 subhuman, a parasitic race at the bottom of  the Nazi racial hierarchy. Naturally, they

01:36 saw themselves as the Aryans, the master race.  The meeting comprised representatives from the

01:41 ministries of the interior and justice, the Reich  Chancellory, the Foreign Office, and the Office

01:46 of the 4-year Plan, and the Ministry for the  Occupied Eastern Territories. Also present were

01:51 representatives from the SS, including the Race  and Settlement Main Office, and the Office of the

01:56 Reich Commissioner for the Consolidation of German  Nationhood. These weren't fringe [music] fanatics.

02:01 They were lawyers, administrators, civil servants,  and senior government officials. The educated

02:06 bureaucratic elite of Nazi Germany. Most would be  dead within 10 years. But in 42, they felt on top

02:13 of the world. One of the most infamous was Adolf  Ikeman, a logistics man and an expert in Jewish

02:18 affairs. After the war, he would go on the run and  be captured and hanged in 1962. The big question

02:24 of the meeting was how to achieve the regime's  ambition of nullifying Europe's Jews. The Nazis

02:30 were masters of euphemism. Rarely in official  documents did they openly discuss mass murder,

02:35 genocide, or extermination. Instead, they  talked about evacuation, special treatment,

02:41 labor deployment, and resettlement, cleansing,  and pacification. The Nazi Minister of Propaganda,

02:47 Joseph Goubles, was more to the point in  his private diary. On December 13th, 1941,

02:53 just over a month before Vonyy, he recorded his  thoughts following a discussion with Adolf Hitler.

02:58 Here we can see the stark reality behind the veils  of Nazi persecution language. Quote, "As regards

03:04 the Jewish question, the Furer has decided [music]  to sweep the floor clean." That was more Nazi

03:09 metaphor, but he was clearer when he wrote that  Hitler had told him, quote, "The extermination

03:13 of the Jews is the necessary consequence, that it  should be regarded without any sentimentality." It

03:19 was the sheer lack of sentimentality or even  anger that would surprise many concentration

03:23 camp inmates. One of the most chilling passages in  Holocaust survivor Primo Levy's book, If This Is a

03:29 Man, [music] is when he watched a German guard  beat a prisoner without emotion. He was amazed

03:34 and he asked [music] himself, "How can one hit  a man without anger?" Levy's question stands as

03:39 a testament to the bureaucratic, [music] detached  nature of Nazi cruelty. But the practical question

03:44 before any of that happened was how to dispose of  so many people. [music] On December 16th, 1941,

03:50 at a government meeting in Kkow, Hans Frank, the  government general of occupied Poland, discussed

03:55 the same topic when he remarked, "We cannot shoot  or poison these 3,500,000 [music] Jews in Poland,

04:01 but we take the measures which will lead to their  annihilation." As for where this would happen and

04:07 by what means, Frank said that would be determined  in due course, and it was. A month later,

04:12 those men met in Vansi, an affluent suburb of  Berlin associated with bankers, industrialists,

04:17 scientists, and artists. Inside the lakeside  villa, refreshments were served and cigarettes

04:22 smoked as officials gathered around the conference  table. Notes were taken and later distilled into

04:27 a document that would become known as the Vansi  protocol. Hydrish had the answer to the question

04:32 everyone had been asking. The Fior had approved a  solution. The Jews would be evacuated to the east.

04:38 But it was what Hydrish said next that would  attract the attention of future historians.

04:42 These actions are nevertheless to be seen only  as temporary relief, but they are providing the

04:48 practical experience that is of great significance  for the coming final solution of the Jewish

04:53 question. In his presentation, he discussed the  approximately 11 million Jews living throughout

04:58 Europe. [music] 4.3 million were already under  Nazi control by early 1942. The number of Jews

05:04 in each country was listed on a prepared document.  The Jews would be put to work as forced laborers.

05:09 Hydrish was clear that many would die in the  process. [music] Doubtless the large majority

05:13 will be eliminated by natural causes, he said.  But he added something just as chilling. Any

05:19 final remnant that survives will have to be  dealt with appropriately because otherwise by

05:24 natural selection they would form the germ cell of  a new Jewish revival. Many historians regard this

05:30 passage as one of the clearest indications for the  Nazis. No permanent place existed for Jews within

05:36 their vision of Europe. The slaughter had already  started. The Einat Groupen Nazi death squads had

05:41 already executed hundreds of thousands of Jews or  more in Soviet territory that included women and

05:47 children. They also murdered Soviet political  officials, prisoners of war, and others deemed

05:52 enemies of the Reich. This was how they intended  to go on. But as was being discussed in the

05:56 meeting before the slaughter, the Nazis envisioned  Jews as being deported eastward. Germany and the

06:02 protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia were among  the first areas to be addressed. From there the

06:07 process would be extended across Europe. Men,  women, and children would be concentrated in

06:11 ghettos, deported by rail, and subjected to forced  labor and ultimately for most death. The meeting

06:17 participants discussed what to do about mixed  race Jews and Jews married to non-Jews. Various

06:23 exemptions, classifications, and special cases  were considered. Sterilization was proposed as a

06:28 solution to prevent any more Jews from being born.  Otto Hoffman of the SS Race and Settlement Main

06:33 Office, who would outlive almost every other  participant in the meeting and die in 1982,

06:39 argued that extensive use should be made of  sterilization. Those classified as half Jews,

06:45 he believed, would often prefer sterilization  to deportation. From the regime's perspective,

06:50 it offered a way to eliminate what it considered  a racial problem while avoiding many of the legal

06:54 and administrative complications surrounding  mixed ancestry and mixed marriages. Considering

06:59 the topic and the pain it would cause, this was  brutally cold language. But for them, it was an

07:05 administrative solution for an [music] existential  problem. For Jews already in mixed marriages,

07:10 they agreed that the matters would be handled on  a case-by case basis. Much depended on who the

07:15 Jewish spouse was married to and whether special  exemptions might apply. The men agreed that if a

07:20 Jew was married to a prominent Aryan, deportation  could prove politically awkward. Similar concerns

07:25 arose for Jews working in industries considered  vital to the war effort. After all, they might

07:30 actually need these people. Erish Noman of the  4-year plan organization argued that Jews employed

07:36 in essential sectors should remain in their  positions until suitable replacements could be

07:40 found. The meeting came to an end after about 90  minutes. In the years that followed, historians,

07:45 lawyers, and judges would debate precisely how  explicit the participants had been about their

07:50 intentions. The methods of mass murder were not  detailed in the surviving minutes. Many post-war

07:55 investigators would say that the language  of the meeting pointed toward a policy whose

07:59 ultimate objective was the total annihilation of  Europe's Jews. If sterilization was presented as

08:05 a preferable alternative for some categories of  Jews, what fate awaited those who were deported?

08:10 When Adolf Ikeman was captured in 1960, he  answered that question. He testified that he

08:16 remembered discussions about shootings and the  quote business with the engine, but he claimed

08:21 poison gas hadn't been mentioned in the meeting.  By engine, he was referring to the mobile gas

08:25 vans already being used to murder Jews in occupied  territories. Ikeman had witnessed prisoners being

08:31 shot in 1941, an experience he later claimed  had deeply disturbed him. In another case,

08:37 he saw victims of the gas vans thrown into a pit,  but only after the gold teeth had been extracted.

08:42 He also recalled the conversation with Hydrrich.  He told me the Furer had ordered the physical

08:47 extermination of the Jews. He didn't witness the  gas chambers in use, but he had said he had once

08:52 seen the terrible airtight rooms being prepared  at Trebinka extermination camp. What the minutes

08:57 of the meeting leave out is this. In September  1941 at the Awitz Burkanau concentration camp,

09:04 the Nazis had already started testing a method  of wholesale murder. They were unleashing the

09:09 deadly gas cyclon be on Soviet prisoners. But  after the von conference, Awitz would become

09:14 the largest killing center in the Holocaust.  The implementation for what the Nazis called

09:19 the expulsion of the Jews was ready. But where  did the blueprint for this intense enmity begin?

09:25 Between 9 and 11 million military personnel and  about 6 to 13 million civilians died in World War

09:31 I. Germany lost over two million soldiers  and somewhere between 400,000 and 763,000

09:37 civilians. It was a disaster. Germany was said  to be the primary [music] aggressor it had to

09:43 pay. Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany  was ordered to pay reparations totaling 132

09:48 billion gold marks around 500 to600 billion  today. It lost around 13% of its European

09:55 territory and all of its overseas colonies. It  was a national humiliation. That sentiment was

10:01 never deeper than after the Wall Street crash of  1929 and the Great Depression that followed. The

10:06 German economy collapsed. Unemployment soared and  faith in the political establishment crumbled.

10:11 Men of working age queued for free soup at the  homeless shelters and soup kitchens. Meanwhile,

10:16 women told their children that they'd have  to go hungry. For millions of Germans,

10:20 the promise of stability and prosperity that their  government talked about after the First World War

10:25 was a lie. The country was broken. It was in this  atmosphere of gloom and disenchantment that Adolf

10:31 Hitler transformed from a minor political agitator  into a major political force. He promised that

10:36 Germany would rise from the ashes and reclaim its  lost greatness. But to do so, he needed a legend,

10:43 a conspiracy theory, one that said Germany had not  been defeated on the battlefield in World War I,

10:49 but had been stabbed in the back by disloyal  elements at home. He found it. According to his

10:54 narrative, liberal democrats, socialists, and  especially Jews had undermined the war effort.

11:00 They were the people who betrayed the nation at  the moment of need. He had taken this partly from

11:05 a 1919 parliamentary inquiry into Germany's  defeat. Field Marshal Paul von Hindenberg had

11:10 stated that the German army had been betrayed from  within. Hindenburg's exact words translated were,

11:16 "The German army was stabbed in the back. No  guilt applies to the good core of the army."

11:21 Supporters of the conspiracy theory pointed to  labor strikes, political unrest, and anti-war

11:26 sentiment on the home front at the end of World  War I. They blamed the Jews in part for what

11:31 they said were the strikes in the arms industry  that had left soldiers without war materials.

11:36 Hindenburg had claimed that he hadn't been  supported by the new German government. He

11:40 also claimed that the respected British military  writer, General Sir Frederick Maurice, had agreed

11:46 that Germany was stabbed in the back by certain  influential bad actors. On December 18th, 1918,

11:52 the reactionary newspaper Deutsche Tagon printed  a story that talked up those claims, which further

11:58 fired up German nationalists. Maurice later denied  he'd ever said that. While civilians letting

12:03 Germany down, had been discussed in some circles  in Britain, Maurice confirmed in his 1919 book,

12:08 The Last Four Months, that quote, "There is no  question that the German armies were completely

12:13 and decisively beaten in the field. It didn't  matter. The conspiracy theorists had already made

12:18 up their minds. The German National People's  Party, DNVP, and Hitler's National Socialist

12:24 German Workers Party, or NSDAP, ran with it. For  them, Maurice's original words were evidence of

12:30 Jewish sabotage." The myth was further emboldened  in Germany by the words of Douglas Hayek,

12:36 commander of the British and Commonwealth forces  on the Western Front. Prior to Germany surrender,

12:41 he had said, "Germany has not broken in the  military since her forces have withdrawn fighting

12:46 very bravely and in excellent order." But the  conspiracy theory didn't include another of Hig's

12:51 assertions when in October 1918, he had written  in his diary, "I think we have their army beaten

12:57 now." The truth was that Germany lost the war on  the battlefield worn down by years of attrition

13:03 and Allied superiority. There was plenty of  evidence to support [music] this including

13:07 the words of General Eric Ludenorf in 1918. He  concluded that Germany could no longer win the war

13:13 and so he urged that peace negotiations begin. Yet  after the war he became one of the most prominent

13:19 supporters of the stabbed in the back myth. He  had backed the claim that the social democrats,

13:24 the Catholic center party, socialists, trade  unions, and the Jews had betrayed Germany. The

13:29 conspiracy theory was transformed into a powerful  political weapon that poisoned German politics and

13:34 helped undermine the VHimar Republic. For some, it  would advance their political careers. For others,

13:39 it offered a convenient explanation for defeat  that shifted the blame away from the military

13:44 leadership and onto political enemies. For many  ordinary Germans struggling through the turmoil

13:49 of the 1920s, the myth and betrayal provided  a simple explanation for a complex defeat. It

13:55 helped them to preserve both personal pride  and national honor. The narrative provided

14:00 a scapegoat not just for losing the war, but for  many of Germany's problems, Jews. Around 100,000

14:06 Jews had served for Germany in the First World  War, and roughly 12,000 had died fighting. Some

14:12 were decorated for bravery. The data came from  a report after Jews had been accused of being

14:17 sherkers who had served away from the danger of  the front line. The report [music] published by

14:22 the war ministry census on Jewish participation in  the war discovered that this wasn't true. But the

14:28 report was suppressed. The myth of sherking lived  on. The German Nationalist Protection and Defiance

14:33 Federation, the largest anti-semitic organization  in Germany, claimed that Jews were proiteeers,

14:39 spies, and defeists undermining the war effort.  Nazi propagandists repeated the same story,

14:44 portraying Jews as disloyal outsiders responsible  for Germany's suffering during and after the

14:49 war. But a giant lie needs a messenger. Enter a  traumatized veteran searching for an explanation

14:55 for his country's humiliation. Historians  often disagree as to when exactly Hitler's

15:00 views hardened into the racial ideology he  would later embrace. The first sour notes

15:04 of his antise-semitism seemed to emerge when he  was trying and failing to become a professional

15:09 artist in Vienna. There the once positive young  man became disillusioned as he lived in near

15:14 poverty among the unemployed and dispossessed.  This likely contributed to the bitterness that

15:19 later shaped his worldview. [music] But those  experiences alone don't explain the genocidal

15:24 policies he would eventually pursue. In fact, one  of the Jews Hitler knew during his younger years

15:30 he greatly trusted and respected. Dr. Edward Blah,  the Jewish physician who cared for Hitler's mother

15:35 as she suffered from breast cancer. This was the  same man who had once treated young Adolf for

15:41 colds and tonsillitis. After his mother's death,  Hitler wrote to Block, "I shall be grateful to

15:46 you forever." He wrote to Block often. Some of  the postcards, embarrassing for the Nazi party,

15:51 were later confiscated from Block by the  Gestapo. On another occasion, Hitler wrote,

15:55 "The Hitler family sends you the best wishes for  a happy new year in everlasting thankfulness,

16:00 Adolf Hitler." This was the same man who would  later state that all Jewish people were polluting

16:06 Western civilization. It was a startling  contradiction. But Hitler's anti-semitism

16:11 wasn't rooted in primarily personal experiences  with particular Jewish individuals. Rather,

16:16 he transformed the Jew into an abstract racial  and political enemy. It wasn't personal hatred, he

16:22 told himself. He believed he was applying reason,  history, and science. His opinions of Jews,

16:27 he claimed, was a kind of scientific rationalism.  The evidence was in letters he sent before he came

16:32 to power. In September 1919, he wrote to a soldier  named Adolf Gamlich on the topic of the Jewish

16:39 question. The Nazis didn't invent the quote  Jewish question. The term emerged in the 18th

16:45 and 19th centuries as Jews across Europe began  gaining civil rights after centuries of exclusion.

16:50 The question facing many European states was how  Jewish emancipation would affect society. What to

16:56 do with their citizenship and political rights?  What about cultural assimilation, immigration,

17:01 and national identity? And not all of the  proposed solutions were rooted in anti-semitism.

17:06 Many had argued for Jewish equal rights and full  integration into European society. But that wasn't

17:12 what the Nazis wanted. Hitler made that abundantly  clear when he talked to Glish about it. The letter

17:17 stands as evidence that Hitler had rationalized  his hatred toward Jews, not any particular Jew,

17:23 but the entire Jewish race for what he conceived  was its pernitious effect on German society.

17:29 Anti-semitism as a political movement, he  wrote, may not and cannot be determined by

17:34 emotional factors, but only by the recognition of  facts. He said the fact was the dangers posed by

17:40 jewelry find expression in the undeniable  aversion of wide sections of our people.

17:45 Hitler already knew he could rouse the rabble  if needed. Not just the openly anti-semitic,

17:49 but the [music] majority, people he believed were  rightly racist. Nonetheless, he wasn't advocating

17:55 mass murder at that point in his life. He wrote,  "An anti-semitism based on purely emotional

18:00 grounds will find its ultimate expression in the  form of the pilgrim." But bloody pilgrims weren't

18:05 the solution for young Hitler. Bureaucracy was. He  wrote that a healthy anti-semitism should be based

18:11 on reason and this would quote lead to systematic  legal combating and elimination of the privileges

18:17 of the Jews. The legislation would lead to the  ultimate objective, the irrevocable removal of

18:22 the Jews in general. It wasn't personal. It  was much worse than that. Jews, he believed,

18:27 were a [music] parasite sucking on the lifeblood  of the German people. He contended that they

18:32 stuck together and would eventually have so much  power they would destroy Western civilization. At

18:37 the time, German Jews were disproportionately  represented in some fields, including finance,

18:41 law, science, publishing, medicine, and the arts.  But what Hitler ignored was that most Jews were

18:47 shopkeepers, clerks, [music] tailor, teachers,  factory workers, and war veterans. Many were

18:52 poor and almost completely powerless. Like other  Germans, they held a wide range of political views

18:57 and social positions. The vast majority had  no influence over government policy, banking,

19:03 the media, or the course of world events.  It didn't matter. With the right propaganda,

19:07 Hitler knew that many hard-working  Germans, some filled with resentment,

19:11 would express the enmity [music] against Jews  he so dearly wanted. He had seen with his own

19:16 eyes how an anti-Jewish policy can win votes. The  mayor of Vienna, Carl Luger, had repeatedly won

19:22 elections using violently anti-semitic language  that had stirred the masses. [music] He claimed

19:28 that Jews had control over too many businesses.  He said that the poor craftsman had to beg the

19:32 Jewish furniture dealer. banking high finance  he said was in the hands of the Jews Jews who

19:38 operated a kind of terrorism on society voting  for him was to liberate Christian people from

19:43 the hegemony of jewelry [music] his radical  anti-semitism depicted Jews as only specialists

19:48 in vile profits [music] in what he said amounted  to an expropriation of the indigenous population

19:54 this taring of millions of European Jews with  the same [music] brush was partly why Hitler

20:00 would call him the greatest German mayor  of all times of course Luger Anti-semitism

20:05 was mostly driven by selfish motives. It  was all backed by highly discriminative,

20:09 dehumanizing language. Luger would describe Jews  as quote beasts of prey in human form. For Hitler,

20:16 they were vermin pests and parasites. [music]  Importantly, such feelings weren't limited

20:20 to Germany and Austria. Anti-semitism was  rampant all over Europe, especially in Poland,

20:26 the Russian Empire, Romania, Hungary, and France.  Even in Britain, where the Jews had better legal

20:31 protections, they faced prejudice and were subject  to enduring conspiracy theories. Luger and men

20:37 like him across Europe argued that capitalism's  inequalities were deliberate [music] and that

20:42 Jews were the architects of the system.  As Europe searched for answers to poverty,

20:46 instability, and social upheaval, many found them  in anti-semitism. Hitler knew he could exploit

20:52 this. He just needed an audience. But when people  finally started listening, a secret would emerge

20:57 that contradicted his entire worldview. When World  War I ended and the Democratic VHimar Republic was

21:03 established, many German Jews supported the new  government. Meanwhile, in Russia, the Bolsheviks

21:08 had overthrown the old regime during the Russian  Revolution. Several prominent Bolshevik leaders

21:12 were of Jewish origin. Jews supporting the German  government, Jews participating in communist

21:18 movements. Hitler would claim that this was  evidence that the Jews were overrunning Europe.

21:22 They were orchestrating both capitalism and  communism from behind the scenes. At first glance,

21:26 that seemed like a contradiction. How could  Jews be both Marxist revolutionaries? And the

21:31 supposed puppet masters of international  finance? Anti-semites had an answer. They

21:36 supposedly controlled capitalism through banks  and finance, profited from war, and kept ordinary

21:41 people poor. At that same time, they were accused  of using communism to destroy nations from within.

21:46 The theory didn't need to make sense. Hitler's  ideology worked on the basis of turning an entire

21:51 race of people into villains and caricatures.  He would make complex stories a straightforward

21:56 good versus evil narrative. But his actions and  beliefs didn't square with his life. One of his

22:01 senior officers during the First World War was  Ernst Hess, a highly decorated officer of Jewish

22:07 ancestry whom Hitler respected. Another superior  officer was Hugo Gutman, who recommended Hitler

22:13 for the Iron Cross First Class, one of the most  important awards he would ever receive. There were

22:18 other examples and not just his family doctor.  Hitler's former associate, Reinhold Hanish, who

22:24 knew him during his years in Vienna, later claimed  that many of Hitler's acquaintances at the time

22:28 were Jews. Among them was Ysef Noman, who helped  Hitler sell his paintings, and Simon Robinson,

22:34 a one-eyed locksmith whom Hitler said to have  befriended. Like many from the stories of Hitler's

22:39 Vienna years, some details remain disputed. What  is clear though is that before politics consumed

22:44 his life, Hitler lived and worked alongside Jews  on a daily basis. How could Jews be portrayed as

22:50 inherently disloyal when many had fought bravely  for Germany? How could they be depicted as

22:55 parasites when some had helped Hitler personally?  These people were clearly not a monolithic group

23:00 sharing identical beliefs, loyalties, or character  traits. Yet, Hitler would depict them as a single

23:06 hostile force working against Germany. Rather than  abandoning the theory when confronted with seeming

23:11 contradictions, he treated those exceptions  as anomalies. [music] The existence of Jewish

23:16 soldiers, Jewish patriots, and Jews he personally  admired did not alter a world view. But in those

23:22 early years, few were listening. [music] It might  have stayed that way had something cataclysmic not

23:26 happened, something that cleared the path for the  rise of a tyrant. The hyperinflation of the early

23:31 1920s had made money almost useless in Germany.  Still, the country recovered and enjoyed what

23:37 became a golden 20s. Life remained depressingly  difficult for many working-class families,

23:42 but larger sections of the middle class saw their  fortunes improve. Berlin became one of the most

23:47 cosmopolitan cities in the world, a center of  artistic brilliance, technological innovation,

23:52 and cultural experimentation. And then came the  crash. The American financial system imploded,

23:58 and Germany was hit hard because it was heavily  dependent on American loans and investment.

24:02 The country was suddenly ravaged by severe  unemployment and business failures. Families

24:07 lost their [music] savings. Young men out of work  scoured the streets for discarded food. Crime

24:12 and rates of self harm increased while political  extremists battled in the streets. Germans weren't

24:18 in this together. Far from it. Some wealthy  Germans lost substantial fortunes, but others

24:23 survived the crisis intact. In certain cases, they  even profited by purchasing distressed assets and

24:29 taking advantage of collapsing prices. To many  ordinary Germans, it appeared that those at

24:33 the top remained protected [music] while everyone  else suffered. Adolf Hitler was watching closely.

24:39 The cynicism Germans now felt at their elites, the  anger they felt toward capitalism and its winners,

24:45 was never more intense. Hitler's furious speeches,  once viewed by many as the words of a madman,

24:50 gained momentum. His ideas and his book Minecom,  had remained largely on the sidelines since he'd

24:56 written it. But within a period of about three  years, as German banks collapsed and factories

25:01 closed, many people felt that they had been  betrayed by a government that could not provide

25:05 stability. Betrayal was Hitler's favorite  explanation. The VHimar politicians were

25:10 weak and corrupt. He said the Versail treaty  was humiliating. He had reminded the people

25:15 who had not been listening years ago that their  country had been stabbed in the back. Suddenly,

25:20 this resonated, as [music] did his theory that  the Jews were at the center of all the carnage.

25:25 Germany needed national unity. He said it needed  strong leadership, a man who gets things done and

25:30 won't bow to selfish elites. With 6 million people  unemployed, compared to about 1.3 million before

25:36 the crash, many people were desperate. Hitler  suddenly seemed relevant. To many, he became a

25:41 savior, the man who would put Germany back on the  map. His hyper nationalist and racist ravings now

25:47 sounded not like rants, but workable solutions.  He had been chairman of the NSDAP since 1921,

25:54 but in those days it was a small movement of  hardline political outsiders. When Hitler was

25:59 imprisoned for attempting a violent coup, people  saw it as proof that he was an extremist. It was a

26:04 view reflected in the 1928 election when the Nazis  won just 2.6% of the votes. Yet by July 1932,

26:12 when Germany had floundered in a sea of economic  gloom, the Nazis had become the largest party in

26:17 the country, winning 37.3% of the vote. Those  were not merely votes of extremist thinkers,

26:23 but farmers, shopkeepers, clerks, laborers, paid  soccer players, doctors, and factory workers. In

26:29 just four years, a man once viewed as a malcontent  had persuaded nearly half of the country that he

26:34 could save the country. Under him, other nations  [music] would quiver. The economy would prosper.

26:39 The working people would be happy and proud. The  humiliation was over. But not for everyone. For

26:45 success to happen, someone would have to suffer.  The people Hitler blamed for the crash were shrewd

26:50 and unholy players on Wall Street. Invisible hands  he claimed controlled international finance. Jews,

26:57 German, American, rich, and poor. They were  all the same according to Hitler's reasoning.

27:01 And [music] once in power, the rhetoric that  demonized these people had to be codified into

27:05 law. In the 1930s, Germany was a very homogeneous  society. Out of a population of between 65 to 67

27:12 million, only between 500,000 to 525,000 people  were Jewish. Black and Asian communities were

27:19 tiny, maybe amounting to a few thousand people,  although census data isn't available. Jews were

27:24 the largest minority, but they were diverse. They  differed in wealth, region, politics, and culture.

27:30 Some of them married non-Jews, thereby seen to be  assimilating into a non-Jewish culture. According

27:34 to an academic paper, about 35,000 Jews, or 6%  of the total Jewish population, were married

27:41 to non-Jews throughout the 1930s. [music] It was  a small number, but intermarriage in those days,

27:46 regardless of ethnicity, was often frowned  upon. If the Nazis had their way, these numbers

27:51 wouldn't even exist. They did everything to unmix  society. The Nazis had a specific term for people

27:56 with mixed or part Jewish blood, Mitchinga. They  created elaborate racial categories to classify

28:02 them. A Micheling of the first degree was someone  with two Jewish grandparents. A Micheling of the

28:08 second degree had one Jewish grandparent. [music]  According to the 1939 census, Nazi officials

28:13 recorded roughly 72,000 first-degree Michelinga  and about 39,000 [music] secondderee Michelinga.

28:19 When they introduced the Nuremberg laws in 1935,  [music] the horror expanded. The Nazis wanted to

28:24 know exactly who belonged to [music] what they  considered the higher and lower races. They began

28:29 cataloging people according to ancestry and  bloodline. Under the Reich citizenship law,

28:34 people classified as Jews lost their citizenship  and basic rights. Roma, who were also regarded

28:39 as racial outsiders, would later face similar  treatment with Slavs. The Nazis racial thinking

28:44 was sometimes less straightforward. They were  viewed as possessing related blood, but millions

28:49 still died in German captivity and citizens  were annihilated in their villages. [music] The

28:54 brutality and rigidity of the system was further  outlined in the law for protection of German blood

28:59 and German honor. The law declared that the  Jews who married and had children with Germans

29:04 were polluting the nation's blood. Intermarriage  between Jews and Germans was outlawed. For many

29:09 already married and listed as privileged, [music]  they were sent to live in harsh conditions in

29:14 one of the Nazis Jew houses. The men were often  sent to work in factories where they were often

29:19 mistreated and humiliated. Extrammarital sexual  relations were also banned. The Nazis even banned

29:25 wealthy Jews from hiring German women under 45  as domestic servants. It was partly to prevent

29:30 the men of the household from [music] having sex  with them. Of course, love is a strong motivator,

29:35 and there were Jews and non-Jews who maintained  their romantic or sexual relationships. Some even

29:41 started relationships, but they risked  being exposed by neighbors, co-workers,

29:45 or disgruntled family members. The Nazis seemed  particularly outraged at relationships between

29:50 Jewish men [music] and non-Jewish women, but not  so much the other way around. Nazi propaganda

29:56 frequently portrayed Jewish men as predators,  [music] corrupting German womanhood. But when

30:00 the woman was Jewish and her husband Aryan, the  Nazis deemed this an Aryan household. The women

30:06 mostly avoided deportation and didn't always have  to wear the yellow star marking them as ripe for

30:11 persecution. Under Himmler's 1943 plan for the  elimination of Jews from the Reich territory, many

30:17 thousands of Jews were rounded up just [music]  in Berlin. Many of the non-Jewish wives refused

30:22 to abandon their Jewish husbands. In February and  March 1943, hundreds of them took to the streets

30:27 and protested against Nazi racial policy. The  women [music] stood their ground despite threats

30:32 from the authorities, and it worked. To the  embarrassment of the regime, and many of the men

30:37 were eventually released, the protest exposed an  uncomfortable truth for the Nazis. They could not

30:43 always separate people as easily as their racial  theories demanded. Their propaganda had failed

30:48 on those women. love had won out not because of  Nazi compassion but because they were trying to

30:53 nazify everything and everyone. They didn't want  to alienate Aryan people by taking away their

30:58 family members. It was strategic. They chose  pragmatism over ideological purity purely for

31:04 optics. Same-sex relations were also outlawed, but  they were already illegal in Germany before the

31:10 Nazis came to power. The law hadn't been strictly  enforced, though. Big cities like Berlin had an

31:15 open gay scene. The Nazis cracked down once in  power, raiding clubs and suspected gay people's

31:21 houses. About 100,000 were arrested and about half  of those were sentenced. It's believed that about

31:27 5,000 and 15,000 were sent to concentration  camps. Close to 60% of them didn't make it

31:32 out. This was the Nazis attempt to eliminate all  traces of homosexuality from Germany. They often

31:38 called samesex attraction a Jewish conspiracy  that was undermining German society. To be gay

31:44 and Jewish was almost unthinkable for the typical  Nazi ideologue, but such people existed. There's a

31:51 famous case of a lesbian couple, Lily Vers and  Feliz Strajenheim. Feliz, a Jewish resistance

31:57 member living under a false identity, worked  for a Nazi newspaper. Lily was the wife of a

32:02 Vermach soldier. When Lily learned that Feliz was  Jewish, she didn't turn her in. She stood by her.

32:08 Their relationship endured despite a regime built  on racial hatred. For them, love proved stronger

32:14 than ideology. Did they have a happy ending?  No. As the Nazis widened the net in Berlin,

32:19 Feliz was arrested and sent to Awitz and later  Gross Rozen. It's believed that she was one of

32:24 the many Jews who died on a death march during  an evacuation. If there is a happy ending, it's

32:30 that Lily helped other Jews avoid the same fate.  One of the sticking points for Hinrich Himmler,

32:35 one of the main architects of the Holocaust, was  all of the half Jews and quarter Jews serving in

32:41 the German military. There were maybe 160,000 in  total. Some were tolerated and even decorated for

32:47 bravery, a glaring contradiction at the heart of  Nazi racial ideology. But as the war progressed

32:53 and the regime became more and more radicalized,  most Michelin soldiers and officers were pushed

32:58 out. Many faced discrimination, forced labor,  or imprisonment. conditions for them were often

33:03 harsh, but not comparable to the extermination and  starvation policies inflicted on those sent to the

33:08 concentration in death camps. Historians have  said that maybe 90% of Jews in mixed marriages,

33:14 including soldiers, survived the war, but they  were all counted. They were all condemned almost.

33:22 Edward BL and other Jews he had known were treated  with soft hands. Even Hitler's former right-hand

33:28 man, confidant, and bodyguard, and the SS's  second ever member, Emil Maurice, was discovered

33:34 to have Jewish ancestry. He was 1/8 Jewish by  Nazi racial calculations. Rather than discard

33:40 a loyal follower, Hitler overrode his own rules.  Like a handful of others whose existence exposed

33:45 the contradictions in Nazi ideology, Maurice was  declared an honorary Aryan. The public didn't see

33:51 this as openly contradictory because the Nazis  controlled all the narratives. When it came to

33:56 information and truth, they were uncompromising  and ruthless. Ysef Gubbles, a highly educated man

34:02 with a PhD in literature and a strong knowledge  of philosophy and history, understood the power

34:07 of myth. He knew how repeating lies constantly  can brainwash the public. He helped construct

34:13 one of the greatest lies many Germans had ever  been told, that their country's problems could

34:17 be traced to a single enemy. The timing was just  right. The sense of hopelessness and anxiety that

34:23 came with the economic crash paved the way for  totalitarianism. The Nazis hypnotized the people,

34:28 making once unthinkable ideas seem reasonable.  It's something modern academics have said is more

34:34 possible after a major crisis or what the writer  Naomi Klein called shock therapy. It is a fact.

34:40 When people are desperate and anxious, they can  more easily be molded to believe extreme ideas.

34:45 Mythmaking and villain creation became the task  of the Ministry of Propaganda. In films, Jews

34:51 were always the bad guys. Toxic, untrustworthy,  manipulative, and parasitical. People saw it or

34:57 heard it in daily radio broadcasts, in  cinemas, in the theater, in classrooms,

35:01 and in heavily censored newspapers. The language  used for these Jews was always dehumanizing. Rats,

35:08 foxes, lice, cockroaches, and vultures. By denying  a Jewish person their humanity to feel and think,

35:14 the Nazis justified the abuse and violence they  perpetrated. If citizens wanted to find criticism

35:19 of those stereotypes, there were few places they  could look. Some books were promoted, others were

35:24 banned and burned. Intellectual stimulation was  viewed as dangerous in what academics have said

35:30 became a cultural genocide. People had to tow  the line. A misplaced joke at work could get a

35:36 person arrested, maybe even executed, especially  if they'd already been labeled as politically

35:40 unreliable, an artistic degenerate, or worse,  a friend of the Jews. The Nazis, like many

35:46 totalitarian regimes, relied heavily on labels.  Citizens were encouraged to report suspicious

35:51 behavior, and denunciations became a routine part  of daily life. Neighbors informed on neighbors,

35:57 co-workers on co-workers, and in some documented  cases, even children reported their own parents.

36:02 Like the communists in the Soviet Union and later  in China, the Nazis sought to dominate the flow

36:08 of information. They aimed to shape how people  thought about almost every aspect of daily life.

36:13 From cooking food to falling in love to smoking  cigarettes or how they felt about gardening and

36:18 sport, they molded it all. Propaganda was not  viewed as a dirty word. To goubles, it was an

36:25 essential tool of government, a means of creating  unity and binding society. And it was very

36:30 expensive. The Nazis spent about 14 million Reichs  marks on its Ministry of Propaganda in 1933.

36:36 By 1941, it had risen to nearly 187 million, an  increase of over 1,200%. Gobles claimed it would

36:44 intellectually mobilize Germany. The ministry  started off with just five departments and about

36:49 350 staff. It eventually grew to 17 departments  and 2,000 staff. In what was a 10-year campaign

36:56 of lies and exaggerations, a minority of Germans  actively criticized the Nazis. sometimes for what

37:01 they perceived to be spreading misinformation.  They were usually arrested for it. Historians

37:06 estimate that between 15,000 and 77,000 German  critics and resistance were executed. But the

37:12 majority of Germans, their thoughts overwhelmed by  propaganda, either supported the Nazi policies or

37:18 quietly ignored what was happening. They believed  their leaders were restoring order. A kind of

37:23 collective double think took hold. Peace could  only be won through war. Unity would be achieved

37:29 through exclusion. Compassion became weakness and  brutality became strength. Truth became a rewrite

37:35 of history. Every morning the radio played and  the Reich Broadcasting Corporation talked about

37:40 the Jewish problem and how it was being dealt  with. To think anything else was a crime. Many

37:45 Germans who kept quiet likely didn't agree with  the more extreme measures, but they turned a blind

37:50 eye because life was indeed improving for them.  If it hadn't, the Nazis wouldn't have become so

37:55 powerful. Some of that working class gained access  to cultural events and leisure activities that had

38:00 once seemed out of reach. Many farmers, the people  the Nazis said were the bedrock of the Aryan race,

38:06 rejoiced at their higher incomes. Some  middle-class families saved for radios,

38:10 vacations in Europe, maybe even a car. After years  of depression and instability, millions felt that

38:16 Germany was finally getting back on its feet.  So, they said nothing as brutality took place

38:21 all around them. But over time, these propaganda  and laws eventually hit a logistical wall, forcing

38:27 the regime into its darkest corner. History shows  us that totalitarianism is not sustainable. The

38:33 power devour itself from within as each of  its organs v for a higher kind of ideological

38:38 purity. [music] Tyrants, bureaucrats, and  ideological citizens look to signal their higher

38:43 virtue and turn on each other. in the Nazi party  proper internal paranoia led to assassinations

38:49 and bitter power struggles as Hitler's faith in  his generals faded. The distrust came to a head

38:54 on July 20th, 1944 when a coupet failed and Hitler  barely escaped assassination by bomb. The Gestapo

39:02 cracked down immediately with pure vengeance. Some  of the conspirators were executed by firing squad

39:07 that same night [music] and another 7,000 people  were arrested. The Nazis eventually executed

39:13 nearly 5,000 [music] of them. Many were just  loosely connected to the plot or swept up in the

39:18 wider purge along with roughly 200 people directly  involved in the conspiracy. [music] People were

39:24 tortured as the Gustapo attempted to find  out who was for and was against them. Again,

39:29 Hitler and his inner circle claimed that they  had been stabbed in the back by traitors. They'd

39:34 even punished the accused men's families. The  exact reasons for the coup have been debated.

39:39 The plotters were mostly aristocratic Germans who  saw the war as a lost cause and [music] planned to

39:44 make peace with the allies. For Hitler, they were  cowards. But some of them, like General Friedrich

39:50 Olri, were critical of the extreme nature of the  Nazis anti-Jewish policy. Barbaric, he'd said

39:55 about Cristalln, the 1938 pilgrim, when German  Jews were hunted, beaten, and murdered. Businesses

40:01 were destroyed and plundered while synagogues  were burned to the ground. Not all high-ranking

40:06 Nazis and military officers agreed with the  final solution. Some viewed the mass murder

40:10 of Jewish and Soviet civilians as a moral stain on  Germany and a betrayal of the values they claimed

40:16 to defend. Still, the reasons for the coup attempt  were much more complicated. Some of the plotters

40:21 were conservatives, some liberals, [music] some  monarchists, and some were motivated primarily by

40:26 religious conviction. But for many, after watching  their countrymen die on mass in the Soviet Union,

40:31 they concluded that the war was unwinable and  that Hitler had to go. The Germans had been

40:36 beaten in Britain. Hitler's ambition to take  the Soviet Union in 6 to 10 weeks and operation

40:40 Barbar Roa had turned into a bloodbath. Troops  froze to death in that first winter and later

40:46 the battle of Stalingrad was a major loss. Those  men had been ordered on a mission of annihilation.

40:52 They thought that they were fighting to save  Western civilization from being overrun by the

40:56 lower races. Again, Jews were at the forefront of  the contempt. Each German soldier had heard the

41:02 order. This struggle demands ruthless, drastic  action against Bolevik agitators, savurs, Jews,

41:08 and complete elimination of any active or passive  resistance. [music] As Hinrich Hitler once said,

41:13 "The destruction of Asia and Jewry was necessary  for evolution of the species. So when things

41:19 started to go wrong, the Nazis became even  more ruthless toward the Jews at home and in

41:24 their camps. They escalated their extermination  policies. Historians have always debated exactly

41:29 how the Holocaust evolved. Some of them emphasize  Hitler's central role. Others focus on the actions

41:34 of subordinates who anticipated Hitler's wishes  and competed to fulfill them. They also disagree

41:40 about why the killing accelerated so fast. Was  mass extermination the plan from the start or did

41:46 it radicalize as the war turned against Germany?  One of the most influential explanations comes

41:51 from the British historian Ian Kershaw. He favored  the view of what the German historian Hans Momson

41:57 formerly coined as a cumulative radicalization.  In this theory, rather than following a single

42:03 detailed blueprint, the Nazi state became trapped  in a cycle of escalation. Bureaucrats competed

42:08 with other bureaucrats. Party officials competed  with the military. each vi to demonstrate loyalty,

42:13 ideological commitment, and their usefulness  to the regime as military defeats mounted and

42:18 paranoia spread throughout the leadership.  Extreme measures expanded. The result was a

42:23 system that continually radicalized  itself, driving the persecution and

42:27 murder of Europe's Jews to greater extremes.  There is no one-sizefits-all explanation,

42:32 but at the heart of it all lay the total  eradication of Jews from Europe that Hitler and

42:36 the Nazis had discussed at Vonyi. Human beings are  often tempted by explanations that reduce complex

42:42 conditions to the actions [music] of a single  villainous group. Jews, minorities, immigrants,

42:47 the defective. It will likely happen time and  time again in the future. And each time the group

42:52 casting the blame will tell themselves they are  the good guys. This kind of thinking [music] is

42:57 one of humanity's most destructive impulses. And  nowhere was it more evident than in Nazi Germany.

43:03 Unrest was exploited by a group of men who were  able to convince ordinary people that a minority

43:08 was responsible for their suffering. The Holocaust  is not just history. It's a warning. It shows what

43:13 happens when societies abandon nuance for simple  hateful answers. [music] And once that happens,

43:19 the outcome is never uncertain. Nazi Germany  was built on hatred. But what happens when the

43:24 regime collapses? Find out in how did Germany  get rid of the Nazis so fast or watch this

00:53 You have to take all these things into consideration

00:56 to help the art director decide whether or not the image is

01:00 good enough for a cover.

01:06 logo.

04:02 from the rest of the image.

00:00 Today, we're going to talk about one of

00:01 the internet's favorite questions, can

00:03 men and women actually be friends? Now,

00:06 I'm of the mind that the answer is

00:08 absolutely yes. People can be friends,

00:11 but it requires a skill set that not all

00:14 of us were taught. And on the other

00:15 side, there's people who believe that

00:17 men and women can't be friends, and

00:18 there's always going to be some kind of

00:20 attraction that carries a risk. Because

00:23 you guys may have heard of this

00:24 scenario, right? You're dating someone

00:26 who is your romantic partner, and they

00:28 have a friend, and you're kind of

00:30 worried about their friend. You can sort

00:32 of tell that their friend is into them,

00:33 but they're like, "Oh, no, they're

00:35 friends. We've been friends for years.

00:36 There's nothing going on." And then

00:38 after y'all break up, 3 months later, 6

00:41 months later, lo and behold, they're

00:42 actually in a relationship. And the

00:44 scary thing is there's a lot of truth to

00:46 that as well. So, in order to navigate

00:48 this question of can men and women be

00:50 friends or not, we're actually going to

00:52 explore both of those paths. What is a

00:54 friendship? What does a platonic

00:55 friendship look like? And what's the

00:57 deal with all these people in the friend

00:59 zone who end up dating later on. Let's

01:02 start with the side of men and women can

01:04 be friends. But this requires a skill

01:07 set that is different that not everyone

01:09 has. Now, some people grew up with

01:11 parents who had a good template for

01:14 cross-sex relationships. We're assuming

01:16 a heteronormative perspective here,

01:18 okay? So, if you grew up with your mom

01:21 having male friends that she was close

01:23 to, or your dad having female friends

01:26 that he was close to, there's a good

01:28 chance that you internalized

01:30 a lot of the skills that they utilized.

01:33 And this may be subtle things, right?

01:35 So, you notice that your mom, while she

01:38 may have had female friends and male

01:39 friends, she was way more touchy with

01:42 her female friends than she may have

01:43 been with her male friends. There are

01:45 all kinds of subtle boundaries that are

01:47 a part of this template of a cross-sex

01:50 relationship, which explains why it's so

01:52 easy for some people and so difficult

01:55 for others. Because a lot of this stuff

01:57 gets baked in when we're growing up. So,

01:59 what kinds of skills do these entail?

02:02 The first thing that I think is really

02:03 important is actually emotional

02:05 regulation. I'm a psychiatrist and on

02:07 this mental health channel, we always

02:08 talk about emotional regulation. But,

02:10 let's understand what we mean by this,

02:11 okay? So, why can't men and women be

02:13 friends? Well, because at some point,

02:15 someone's going to catch feelings,

02:16 right? That's the main argument. At some

02:18 point, you're going to start getting

02:19 attracted to this person, you'll start

02:21 maybe falling in love with them. And

02:23 this is a key thing to understand. If

02:25 you fall in love with someone, what are

02:27 your options? So, this is what I mean by

02:29 emotional regulation. Love is an

02:31 emotion, right? At its core, for the

02:34 most part, there's at least an emotional

02:36 component to it. And so, if you can

02:38 manage your anger and not give in to

02:41 your anger. So, I'm pissed at someone,

02:43 but I'm going to go ahead and hold my

02:45 head up high and not sink to their

02:46 level. If I'm feeling sad or depressed

02:48 and I don't feel like getting out of

02:49 bed, but I'm able to regulate that

02:51 emotion and be able to get out of bed

02:54 anyway, then those emotions do not

02:56 dictate my life. And this is [snorts]

02:58 where love is no different, right? So,

03:01 if we kind of think about it, everyone's

03:03 all for emotional regulation of sadness.

03:06 If I feel ashamed, Dr. K, how do I hold

03:08 my head up high? If I feel like I've got

03:10 low self-confidence, how do I build that

03:13 self-esteem? What are the techniques of

03:14 emotional regulation to deal with these

03:16 emotions? But, when it comes to love, we

03:18 don't think about this as something that

03:20 needs to be emotionally regulated. And

03:22 in the same way that I can regulate my

03:23 anger, it no longer controls me, I can

03:25 also regulate my love and it no longer

03:28 controls me. So, a huge deciding factor

03:30 is when you catch feelings, what is the

03:33 way that you deal with those feelings,

03:36 right? Some people will pull away, which

03:38 can be a healthy thing to do cuz we

03:40 don't want to foster those feelings.

03:42 Another important skill that you can

03:43 have is having a conversation about it,

03:46 right? So, can you go to this friend of

03:47 yours and have a mature conversation as

03:50 friends and say, "Hey, I noticed that

03:52 like I'm starting to have some romantic

03:55 feelings towards you." And this is

03:56 important to understand. If you're truly

03:59 friends, this does not have to be like a

04:02 confession, right? Which is what a lot

04:03 of people default to. I think it's a

04:04 terrible move. Just going to your friend

04:06 and saying like, "Hey, I'm catching some

04:07 weird feelings. Wondering if you're

04:08 experiencing anything similar. We as

04:11 friends, how are we going to navigate

04:13 this, right?" And you're not trying to

04:15 tell them, "Hey, I want a relationship

04:16 with you." Which by the way is another

04:18 really basic skill. If you catch

04:20 feelings, do you need to follow them? If

04:22 you feel lust, is that something that

04:23 you're defaulting to gratifying? And

04:26 what I find in a lot of people who

04:27 struggle to have cross-sex relationships

04:31 is that they're not able to have

04:32 conversations. They're not able to

04:34 regulate their emotions. And if they

04:36 catch feelings, that means they need to

04:38 act on them. But then we have another

04:40 problem, which is that we sort of think

04:42 that, "Okay, once I'm in love, then I

04:44 will stay in love, right?" Like this

04:46 feeling will grow and grow and grow and

04:48 this will be torture, so I need to pull

04:49 out of this relationship. Totally fine

04:51 to do that. But this is where we also

04:52 have to understand something else about

04:54 emotions, which is that they tend to

04:56 equilibriate over time. One of the

04:57 biggest problems with relationships is

05:00 that we fall in love and then we fall

05:02 out of love. The spark from the

05:04 relationship disappears. And in fact,

05:06 that is more common than the spark

05:09 staying, right? So the average person

05:11 will date several people that they feel

05:13 some degree of chemistry, some degree of

05:15 attraction, but then over time that

05:17 attraction will kind of potter out, will

05:19 wane. I work with a lot of married

05:21 couples who've been together for 10

05:22 years, 15 years, 20 years, and they've

05:24 started the process of falling out of

05:26 love. About 50% 40 to 45% of

05:30 relationships end in marriages end in

05:32 divorce, and a big part of that is that

05:35 people fall out of love. So just because

05:37 you are catching feelings doesn't mean

05:39 that those feelings will continue to

05:41 grow. You can talk about it, you can

05:43 manage those feelings, you can do some

05:45 meditation, you can spend some

05:47 meaningful time with your significant

05:49 other over here. There are a lot of

05:50 things that you can actually do to

05:52 manage those feelings. Second thing to

05:53 keep in mind is that over time,

05:55 generally speaking, if you catch

05:57 feelings for someone, the research on

05:58 love shows that it usually requires

06:01 investment on your part to maintain that

06:05 feeling of love. The first stage of love

06:07 is governed a lot by dopamine, right?

06:09 So, their presence is, "Oh my god, the

06:11 [snorts] thought of them, I'm so like

06:12 you just get this dopamine trickle in

06:14 your brain when you're in their

06:16 presence. Just being in their presence

06:17 feels amazing. Oh my god, I can't the

06:20 the touch to just brush against them is

06:22 electricity in my skin. Oh my god." That

06:24 feeling is dopamine. But, when people

06:26 are in a relationship for 20 or 30

06:28 years, that feeling usually does not

06:30 persist. What we know about long-term

06:32 relationships is that you need to add

06:35 other kinds of love, oxytocin love,

06:37 which is a sense of bonding, a sense of

06:39 connectedness. There's also types of

06:41 love that involve sacrifice, planning

06:44 together, living together, having

06:46 nurturing things that kind of tie you

06:48 together, like having kids or starting a

06:50 business or whatever. So, we know from

06:52 the science of love, which you guys can

06:53 see more about in Dr. K's Guide to Love,

06:55 Sex, and Relationships, is that there

06:57 are several different kinds of love,

06:58 several different phases of attraction.

07:00 And actually, the most common thing is

07:02 for us to catch feelings for someone,

07:04 and then over time, those feelings will

07:06 wane just like any other emotion will.

07:08 So, if you're able to regulate your

07:09 emotions, if you're able to have

07:12 conversations with your friend, if

07:13 you're able to observe boundaries. So,

07:16 this is also something that I'm kind of

07:17 careful about, which is that if I'm

07:19 attracted to a friend of mine, I'm very

07:22 careful about the kind of time I spend

07:25 with them. And I'm not going to engage

07:26 in behaviors that foster the growth of

07:29 that attraction. So, if I have a friend

07:31 that I'm attracted to, I'll go to lunch

07:33 instead of dinner. If we go to dinner,

07:35 we'll have maybe one or two drinks, but

07:37 generally speaking, I try not to drink

07:39 around people that I'm attracted to. And

07:41 the other really important part is that

07:43 when I have friends that I could be

07:44 attracted to or we feel some kind of

07:46 connection, I've noticed they do this

07:47 too, we'll also include our partners in

07:50 our relationship. So, we'll do like a

07:52 double date or something. We'll hang out

07:54 with our kids or whatever. So, we sort

07:56 of encourage sort of a more platonic

07:59 energy by bringing other factors into

08:01 it. And so, it may not be surprising

08:03 that actually if you poll people who

08:06 have friends of the opposite sex, both

08:08 men and women, people actually consider

08:10 physical attractiveness between friends

08:12 to be a cost or burden of the

08:14 relationship, not an advantage. So, if

08:17 you ask, is this a benefit or a cost to

08:19 be attracted to your platonic friends,

08:21 would you consider that a benefit? 6% of

08:23 people say, yes, it's a benefit to have

08:26 an attractive friend. 32% of people,

08:28 five times as many people will say that

08:30 being attracted to your friends is a

08:32 cost or burden on the relationship. So,

08:35 it does get complicated if you're into

08:37 them, but generally speaking, a lot of

08:39 people are capable of having platonic

08:41 relationships without any romantic

08:43 involvement. But, what's the flip side

08:45 of the argument, right? Because there

08:46 are all are a lot of people who say men

08:48 and women can't be friends and there's

08:49 the one that your boyfriend or

08:51 girlfriend told you not to worry about,

08:53 which you know you should worry about.

08:56 So, this is what's really fascinating.

08:57 If you look at the way that most

08:59 relationships form, this is kind of not

09:01 counting online dating because that's a

09:03 different kind of environment, but if

09:05 you look at the organic way that

09:06 relationships form, in one study of

09:08 1,857

09:10 people, 70.3%

09:13 of these people said that they were

09:15 friends first before they engaged in a

09:18 romantic relationship. So, over

09:20 two-thirds of people, over two-thirds of

09:22 relationships start as friendships,

09:25 okay? Other interesting thing is that

09:27 the average duration of friendship is

09:29 21.9

09:31 months. So, these people are usually

09:33 friends for about two years before they

09:36 start dating. So, it kind of tracks with

09:39 your experience of your dating your

09:40 let's say your girlfriend and then you

09:42 guys date for a year, there's a friend

09:44 that you're worried about, they break up

09:46 or y'all break up and then 8 months

09:48 later they are dating the friend that

09:49 you were worried about. The data behind

09:52 this stuff actually absolutely tracks

09:54 with that. But, if we want to

09:56 understand, you know, how does this

09:57 happen? What's the deal with the friend

09:59 zone? The moment that we say that there

10:01 is a pathway and by the way, in the

10:02 literature this is called the

10:04 friends-to-lovers pathway, which is the

10:06 most common way to enter into a romantic

10:09 relationship. Now, we've triggered all

10:10 the friend zone people, right? So, like

10:12 not in a bad way, but like there are a

10:13 lot of us who have romantic feelings for

10:16 a friend or maybe they have romantic

10:18 feelings for us and we've been told, "Oh
