00:00 In 2017, 24-year-old Koo Jeong-hwa accomplished  something many of the 26 million people in North

00:06 Korea have dreamed of. She sneaked across the  border into China, taking her son with her.

00:11 Her happiness was short-lived. Soon she  was in handcuffs, weeping, envisioning

00:15 barbaric torture and her untimely death. The question is, what would make a mother so

00:20 desperate to compel her to risk obscene punishment  and execution, of her and her son - who,

00:26 by the way, was suffering from severe frostbite? This, we will now explain, and tell you what

00:31 happened to Koo Jeong-hwa and her son later. To an outsider looking in, you could sometimes

00:36 be forgiven for thinking that life  in North Korea isn’t all that bad.

00:39 Children go to school; folks  go ice-skating on the weekend;

00:42 they cheer at soccer matches and make snowmen  in winter, but when you peel back some layers of

00:47 this mysterious rotten onion of a country, your  eyes will tear with incomprehension and grief.

00:53 North Korea is a country with many faces.  For the outside visitors that experience it,

00:57 they see a carefully orchestrated version of the  country, not the grim reality. They hear nothing

01:03 about how people working in Pyongyang’s  cushy government jobs barely get by on

01:07 their $4-a-month wage or factory workers get  a solitary dollar a month. Some get 50 cents.

01:14 They certainly don’t see the  hungry masses out in the provinces,

01:17 who are at risk of starvation and freezing  to death during North Korea’s incredibly

01:21 bleak winters. People who work on  the land of which only 20% is arable.

01:25 These people are told daily they live in the  best country in the world. First and foremost,

01:30 in the daily life of a North Korean is a large  dose of propaganda. The enemy is always a threat,

01:36 they are told, intent on wrecking that great life  they have. Japan, the United States of America,

01:41 and the Republic of Korea, want them dead.  This is a constant message in all media.

01:46 The so-called “eternal leaders of Korea”  are everywhere people look. Every day is

01:50 a reminder that they should be grateful to  have such a literally supreme guy in charge,

01:54 a man from a family almost touched by Gods.

01:57 The people of North Korea start being fed  propaganda from a very young age. All children

02:02 should go to kindergarten and then to a primary  school, called the “People’s School,” where

02:07 they stay from six years of age to nine. They  study in a secondary school until they’re 16,

02:11 and then possibly go on to a university.  Some do, but most join the military.

02:16 All education is state-funded. If you can say  something positive about North Korean education

02:21 standards, it’s that according to UNESCO, the  country has a 98-100 percent literacy rate.

02:27 You kind of need that, though, when propaganda  is being shoved down your throat all your life.

02:31 Some lucky students might go on to study  at the prestigious Kim Il-Sung University,

02:35 but only if they have excelled  during their previous studies.

02:39 Others go to one of the thousands of vocation  schools, and many of those who excel in science

02:43 or mathematics often end up at the University of  National Defense, where one day they might find

02:48 themselves becoming a leader in hypersonic missile  technology. In 2021, a new part of the university

02:54 was opened, a special department of hypersonic  missiles. This is what many students aspire to do.

02:59 You might be wondering how all this is  possible when North Korea conscripts its

03:03 young into military service. That is true, at  17, men must begin ten years’ military service.

03:09 Women may also serve but only until they’re 23.  In both cases, there is a selection process,

03:14 and the most academically gifted kids can  ignore the military entirely, as can the kids

03:19 of the elites who are born into high status. Something very important in North Korea is

03:24 “songbun”. This is a status system in  which certain acts gain people social

03:28 credit. Good songbun means more choices  are available to people. On the other hand,

03:33 if someone is related to a defector, their  score will likely be low and their options dire.

03:38 North Korea states that students must “acquire  the concept of revolution and endless loyalty

03:43 toward the party and the supreme leader.” All  education is based on the “revolutionary ideal.”

03:48 Every day that a kid goes to elementary school,

03:50 he’s learning the idolization of the supreme  leader. When he gets home, the TV shows him how

03:55 he can be a good revolutionary. Regularly, the  TV explains how to accrue better social credit.

03:59 Not too long ago, a woman was roundly chastised  by the Korean media for saving her kid in a house

04:05 fire and not saving the pictures of the leaders  on her kitchen wall. North Korean media applauded

04:10 the neighbor, who ran into the house to save the  pictures. That’s how you get some good songbun!

04:16 The State Security Department uses various  surveillance systems to keep an eye on people.

04:19 The secret police is everywhere. People never know  if their neighbors will snitch on them. This not

04:25 knowing who to trust creates an atmosphere of  intense fear, which, as you’ll see today, has

04:30 wide-ranging negative effects on mental health. It was recently reported that over 200

04:35 executions happened throughout the country, with  teenagers expected to watch in many instances.

04:40 Some teens were executed just for  having USB sticks containing K-Pop

04:44 and South Korean soap operas. In one case,  the kid was wheeled out into a stadium and

04:49 shot nine times as his school buddies watched  from the seats. They were expected to clap,

04:55 even though some kids were close to tears. Another report says someone had “a slip

04:59 of the tongue” and criticized the government.  Such cases do not reach Amnesty International.

05:04 They happen behind closed doors. Like  in medieval Europe, often, the bodies

05:08 are left to rot where they fall, a reminder  to the public of what could happen to them.

05:12 A defector named Oh Se-hyek explained,  “They hanged people in crowded places

05:16 like markets and left the bodies there for  hours to instill fear among the people.”

05:20 Another defector in the same report was just 7  years old. In a painting class in South Korea,

05:25 he surprised his teachers when he sketched  a scene of a firing squad in the countryside

05:29 killing locals in a field. This was his reality. So, when we’re talking about learning math

05:35 in school in North Korea, it can sound  normal, but we should not underestimate

05:39 the distressing climate of fear these kids have  to live through, although to many this is what

05:43 their normal day to day life is like. Things  are made worse because being a good snitch

05:47 might mean the difference between starving  to death in the next famine or being sent to

05:51 the capital to work in relative comfort. In 2019, a cadre on state-sponsored TV

05:56 announced that new rewards were available  for snitching on people for engaging in

06:00 illegal activities. They were told, “People  who want to get the rewards can file reports,

06:05 and the government can then eliminate people  filled with discontent.” The reward was $6.

06:10 In North Korea, selling things on the black  market, such as foreign entertainment or goods,

06:15 is one of the only ways to make money.  According to a North Korean source, most

06:18 people didn’t want the reward money. That would  upset the black economy. The source explained:

06:23 “It did not work out well. The state can’t even  guarantee basic living conditions for the people,

06:27 and the people can’t make their own living  without breaking the law, so why would

06:31 anyone want to report on anyone else?” He said these crackdowns happen ever so

06:35 often when the government feels like it's losing  its grip on the populace. In 2015, there was a

06:40 similar snitch scheme. A source said the Security  Services “is cracking down hard on asylum seekers

06:45 and smugglers, and it has promised incredible  rewards to anyone who points to defectors or

06:51 smugglers.” Poor farmers, he said, were tempted. In 2021, someone snitched. It was reported that

06:56 a villager and a soldier were shot in  a field for the crime of “disturbing

07:00 entertainment,” what leader Kim Jong-un had  recently called a “vicious cancer” trying to

07:05 destroy the North Korean way of life. In one case, a large crowd congregates

07:08 at the town square, and a young man is  dragged out, accused of being found with,

07:13 wait for it… “a movie and 75 songs from South  Korea.” This is daily life in North Korea.

07:20 A North Korean girl who escaped said she and her  classmates were there when a kid was executed,

07:30 again, for nothing but distributing  entertainment. Like many North Koreans,

07:34 she suffered from mental problems  after seeing such savagery. She said:

07:37 “The prisoner could hardly walk and had  to be dragged out. I was so terrified

07:41 that I could not dare look at a soldier  in uniform for six months afterward.”

07:45 It’s not that North Koreans don’t know  anything about the West. They’ve been

07:49 buying bootleg DVDs for years now. North Korean  TV has innocently featured the Rocky theme tune,

07:55 and ​Mickey and Minnie Mouse have appeared now and  again. In 2018, prior to peace talks with the US

08:00 breaking down, even South Korean K-pop stars  were invited to Pyongyang. Kim clapped after

08:05 some of the songs and asked questions about the  lyrics, which was surprising, to say the least.

08:09 But that was just him playing the part of a  benevolent leader, the good guy who now and

08:15 again can relax. This comes straight out  of a dictator’s playbook. Every so often,

08:19 they are supposed to show they have mercy. Kim  often pardons people from their death sentences,

08:23 usually to great applause, just as happened  in those bloody Roman arenas when the emperor

08:28 spared a life because he thought it  would get the populace on his side.

08:31 When kids get older, they might go to university,  but if they choose a humanities subject,

08:36 it’s still based on the ideology of the  party. The word for this ever-present

08:40 ideology is Juche. For instance, some philosophy  courses are “Philosophy of the Juche ideology” or

08:47 “Juche Political Economy.” It’s brainwashing; you  can be sure they aren’t learning about anarchy,

08:52 skepticism, and the wonders of liberal democracy.  Capitalism is evil, say the men teaching them as

08:58 they drive home in their imported luxury cars. Ironically, the North Korean Constitution under

09:02 articles 64 and 65 guarantees democratic  rights and freedoms for all citizens in

09:08 all spheres of state and social life. That’s  what they call Orwellian double-speak. North

09:13 Korea is totalitarian. Its mission is “to  carry out the military-first revolutionary

09:18 line in order to protect the nerve center of  the revolution.” Students can’t question this.

09:23 Academic courses are full of lies. Students can  read that their supreme leader Kim Jong-Il fired

09:28 off a round of golf and, after 11 holes in one,  got a 38 under par. This was on a professional

09:34 course by a man who’d never swung a golf  club. The students know it’s impossible,

09:38 but they can’t question it. Some know it’s  not true that one of their leaders invented

09:42 the hamburger, but can’t disagree nonetheless.  Students who study medicine might question if

09:47 it’s true that North Korean scientists cured  HIV/AIDS and Ebola. They just can’t say that.

09:53 North Koreans learn Korean nationalism, which has  little or nothing to do with Marxist communism

09:58 and ideas about widespread well-being.  They hear how their people are racially

10:03 pure. That mankind itself started in North  Korea, where the first humans arose. They’re

10:08 told that their purity is always in a battle  with imperialist-capitalist foreign powers.

10:13 The divine, they are told, can only be found  in the Kims. Like Europeans Kings and Queens

10:18 in times past, North Koreans are told the  Kims rule by divine right. In 1992, American

10:24 evangelist Billy Graham visited North Korea and  spent time with the then-leader, Kim il-Sung.

10:28 North Koreans learned how this Christian man  was highly impressed by Kim. These days they can

10:33 read in books and in newspapers that Graham said: “Having observed the Supreme Leader Kim Il-sung’s

10:38 unique political leadership, I can only think that  he is God.” The texts then say Graham looked at

10:43 Kim and announced, “Kim is this world’s God. Why  would a country like this need the Holy Bible?”

10:48 North Koreans aren’t religious, but the Kims  are portrayed as a kind of holy incarnation

10:54 born to rule. If Billy Graham said so, it must  be true…Imagine if the people knew their present

10:59 leader likes to play World of Tanks online  and occasionally watch western pornography!

11:03 Some of North Korea’s best students become  scientists, so you might wonder how they do

11:08 their job knowing many things they’ve been told  are a lie. After all, science shouldn’t lie. To

11:13 get better at it, to improve something,  you have to work with scientific facts.

11:17 This is why the best scientists work behind great  big, guarded walls. One of them, Kim Hyeongsoo,

11:23 said before he defected, he worked in a  lab trying to better under diseases such

11:27 as the hardening of the arteries. Everything  he did was in secret. What he discovered was

11:32 only heard by the party bosses. Hyeongsoo once told the press

11:35 that he had a colleague with a Ph.D. in  medicine who told his close buddies what

11:39 he did. He was subsequently arrested as  a political prisoner, as was his entire

11:43 family. Knowledge is dangerous in North Korea. Talking about the general state of research,

11:48 he said, “Scientists don’t believe  what the propaganda feeds them,

11:52 but they cannot discredit it either. You have  to think what the party tells you to think.”

11:56 Most people, though, don’t work in science.  The average Joe works six days a week in a

12:01 factory or on a farm. Article 22 of the Labor  Law says they should work eight hours a day.

12:05 They should also get national holidays,  off-days, and have enough rest time.

12:09 Like you, they might eat three times a day.  Breakfast might consist of rice and soup,

12:13 possibly with some side dishes. The  richer you are, the more you get.

12:17 People often take a lunchbox to work with them,  which again will feature rice and side dishes.

12:22 Dinner is more rice, soup, and, again, those side  dishes. People near the coast might get seafood.

12:27 The more money you have, the more meat you can  buy. Farmers tend to eat vegetables and herbs

12:32 they’ve collected themselves. A former North  Korean soldier explained his rations, saying:

12:36 “I still cannot forget North Korean army food.  The standard meal was a bowl of 30% white rice

12:41 and 70% cornmeal, one bowl of lettuce, and soybean  paste soup. This was served with salted radish,

12:48 soybean fried radish, and cabbage  kimchi.” Soldiers had this every day,

12:53 but special food was given for their  birthdays and national holidays.

12:56 All defectors say the same thing. You need to make  money on the black market to feed yourself well.

13:01 The government's rice rations are not enough. One really cheap thing is smoking. North Korean

13:07 cigarettes can be as cheap as eight cents a pack.  The standard price is 17 to 32 cents a pack.

13:12 Almost half of the males in North Korea smoke,

13:14 but very few females do; maybe  only about three percent.

13:17 It’s also a heavy-drinking country,  with people preferring hard liquor,

13:21 often bought at the market under the table.  The reason for all the boozing, of course,

13:25 is stress. As a German doctor and activist once  said, “There is a lot of alcoholism. It’s the

13:30 only pleasure they have...Fear creates sickness.  I saw many victims of alcoholism in the hospital.”

13:35 It’s common for people to buy their booze  straight from the factory. If they can afford it,

13:40 they get the Chinese stuff. One of the most  popular drinks is Kaoliang Liquor from China,

13:44 which can be 38 between 63 percent  alcohol by volume: very strong.

13:49 Many North Koreans can’t afford that, so  people brew their own stuff, even though

13:54 it’s illegal. The government doesn’t see this  as the same kind of risk as listening to K-pop,

13:58 so most officials turn a blind eye to people  making their own hooch. One guy explained:

14:03 “In my town, one out of every 10 households  made alcohol at home. The most widely used

14:07 ingredients were potatoes and corn.” He said beer was seen as such a soft

14:11 drink that kids would regularly drink it.  There was an age limit of 18 for booze,

14:15 but he said no one gave a damn about it. Again,  this shows how lax North Korean rules can be for

14:20 some things. You can destroy your liver or smoke  until you speak out of a hole in your throat,

14:24 but for God’s sake, whatever you do,  don’t dare listen to the latest BTS song.

14:29 Folks like to drink with their buddies  after they’ve just had to watch mind-numbing

14:33 state-controlled television programs on TV. They  might have to sing revolutionary songs in public

14:37 and look like they mean it, but that doesn’t  mean they won’t be laughing about that later

14:42 over a glass of hooch. People do see through  all the lies there, some people. It’s just very

14:47 dangerous to speak about it. A defector once said this:

14:50 “While the North Korean government wanted people  to see their lovers as ‘fellow revolutionary

14:54 comrades’, the truth was that this feeling never  truly existed for many of us. We pretended to

14:59 have that quality only because we were forced to.” He learned about the supreme leader in high school

15:04 but said he and his friends sometimes ignored  all that and had fun. He and his buddies used

15:09 to drink together. They used to date girls,  but since dating was not allowed in school,

15:13 the couples would sneak off to one of their  parents’ apartments they knew was empty.

15:16 Much of the entertainment made in North Korea  is just more propaganda. There used to be a

15:21 long-running comedy show called “It’s So  Funny,” which sounds like the least funny

15:25 thing you’ve seen in your life. This is some actual dialogue from

15:29 one of the episodes. The man and woman  are talking about how great beans are.

15:34 Man: “If we soldiers see beans, we become  happy.” He starts laughing out loud.

15:38 Woman: “If we farm in the way the  General tells us, we will become happy.”

15:42 They both laugh together, slapping each  other on the back. That’s the joke.

15:46 Presumably, the viewers at home were also in  hysterics. That, or they were busy trying to

15:51 choke themselves with their own fists while  frantically looking for the booze. When a

15:55 defector was asked about this show, he said: “The show is delivering the same material

15:58 over and over again. They are still talking  about beans. The country hasn’t changed at

16:02 all since I defected about 20 years ago.” One thing you definitely don’t get are

16:07 documentaries detailing how many North Koreans  in the far-off provinces are living on the brink

16:11 of starvation or being worked to death in labor  camps. This brings us to the matter of crime.

16:16 If you can be executed for watching a South Korean  soap opera, it can be expected that other kinds

16:21 of crimes also lead to severe punishments.  North Korea has all the same criminals as

16:26 everywhere else on the planet. However, the highly  corrupt government tries to portray the country as

16:30 crime-free, unlike America, where it says society  has become decadent, depraved, and divided.

16:36 North Koreans steal. They kill each other  in arguments. They work so damn hard in

16:40 the countryside that they take methamphetamines  when they can get their hands on them. Ordinary

16:44 crimes like these are called “kyohwaso.” If it’s perceived that a person has engaged in

16:48 anti-socialist activities, they might be exiled.  If they have property, it will be confiscated,

16:53 as will their worldly goods. Exiles have their  ration cards taken away and lose all their

16:58 citizen rights. They will usually end up working  on a farm or doing something like building roads.

17:02 The people who have it worse are the 150,000 to  200,000 serving five to twenty years in a labor

17:08 camp. The UN says about 40% of the prisoners  in labor camps die from malnutrition. They are

17:13 fed very little and often have to do grueling  work, such as mining. Some of these prisoners

17:18 are not being re-educated. The government  has classified them as “unredeemable.”

17:22 After a hard day’s work on a farm or in a  mine, starting at 5 am and finishing at night,

17:27 they’re often given a small portion of cabbage or  corn. Many prisoners look for insects or vermin,

17:32 a good source of protein. Some former prisoners  have said people have eaten grass mixed with

17:37 cow poop. There are even reports of  cannibalism happening in the camps.

17:41 A defector who now lives in the US  after defecting said he was born and

17:44 brought up in a labor camp.  His name is Shin Dong-hyuk.

17:47 In the camp, he knew nothing, not the existence  of the USA or other countries and certainly not

17:52 that the world was a sphere. All he knew was  pain and hunger. When asked if he loved his

17:57 parents in the camp, he said he had no concept  of love. He explained that once, a girl stole

18:01 some corn and was beaten to death for it in  front of him. He said he felt nothing. He was

18:06 a child of the camp. This was normal life for him. He went on to say, “If you escape, you would be

18:11 shot. If you try to escape or plan to escape, you  would be shot. Even if you did not report someone

18:15 who is trying to escape, you would be shot.” One time they dragged him and his family to the

18:19 front when it was announced another execution was  imminent. Since he was at the front, he thought

18:24 it might be him. It wasn’t. It was his mother and  brother. Was he sad? No, he didn’t know what love

18:30 was. He said at the time; he thought they got  what they deserved for breaking prison rules.

18:34 The rules were clear to everyone. They  were stapled to the walls. Try to escape:

18:38 death. Steal: death. Talk in a group of more  than three people: death. Rebel against a guard:

18:44 death. Don’t report suspicious activity:  death. Don’t admit you’re wrong: death.

18:49 As for a minor transgression, Shin Dong-hyuk  explained that he once annoyed a guard when

18:54 he was still young, and the guard decided to  cut off his finger. He added, “I was taken to

18:59 the clinic and given medical attention,  but without any anesthesia whatsoever.”

19:02 The guards wanted the men and women to have  relationships. The more kids in the camp,

19:06 the more labor available. But the guards often  didn’t let the people wait to meet someone they

19:11 liked. Matchmaking would often go like this: Guard: “You two, you’ve been matched. From today

19:16 on, you’re married. Work hard, and don’t waste  your time. If you slack, I’ll split you up!”

19:19 Shin Dong-hyuk said for most people,  “Resistance is simply unthinkable.”

19:23 He took the risk of his life and escaped,  and now he’s trying to make sense of that

19:27 deep heart of darkness where he once lived. In less severe cases, let’s say some shirked

19:32 at work, or maybe they were found to keep a messy  kitchen; they might face public ostracism. That

19:36 will consist of being ignored by colleagues.  Your neighbors tutting when you walk past them.

19:40 All this causes severe stress. People feel the  weight of their oppression at all times. Not only

19:46 do many people smoke and drink a lot, but these  days they’re on drugs. In 2019, news reports said

19:51 that during the Lunar New Year, one of the main  gifts people exchanged was methamphetamine. It had

19:56 seeped out of the countryside and into the cities. As with everything in North Korea, dealers were

20:01 able to bribe officials, and so the stuff was  being exchanged openly and very liberally. Drug

20:06 dealing is also a great way to make money in a  country where making a buck isn’t easy at all.

20:10 Psychiatrists that have helped defectors once they  got to South Korea said they found many people

20:15 suffered from a whole host of mental problems. In  a research paper, it said many of them were still

20:19 totally focused “on survival amid continuity of  intense suffering” even though they were now free.

20:25 In short, they were traumatized.  A separate study found that the

20:29 cause of their trauma was “witnessing  government executions, enduring starvation,

20:33 starvation-related deaths of family and  friends, witnessing extreme physical assaults.”

20:38 There’s a Catch-22 in North Korea.  People feel crazy with all that stress,

20:42 but if they admit they’re feeling depressed,  that can be classed as anti-socialist behavior.

20:46 If they say they’re happy even though they  aren’t, they are being good citizens. That’s

20:51 the reason a report stated, “Anxiety disorders  and depression seem to receive no specialized

20:55 psychiatric treatment in North Korea.” If patients are worse, perhaps psychotic,

20:59 or just manically screaming how bad things  are, they are packed off to special “Number

21:04 49 Hospitals.” They receive zero counseling and  psychotherapy and instead are given intravenous

21:09 insulin that renders them comatose. Life gets much worse when there are

21:13 droughts or floods, or any number of natural  disasters. The World Food Program has said

21:18 that the North Korean government used  to give 400g of food daily per person,

21:21 but in 2019 because of crop shortages, that went  down to 300g per person per day. The UN says

21:28 survival rations should be 600g daily per person. A nurse who defected in 2013 talked about the

21:34 lack of sustenance, saying, “Since there  isn’t anything to eat in North Korea,

21:37 we eat everything we can get. We eat roots  and anything that is chewable.” She added,

21:42 “There was a mother who entrusted the nursery with  her three kids. But all three starved to death.”

21:46 Out in the countryside, it’s doubtful there will  be power to heat huts and ramshackle houses when

21:51 the temperatures sometimes go down to -13°C  (8.5F). They use wood or coal, but that’s

21:56 not always available. Meanwhile, the elites are  warm and cozy with their state-sponsored harems,

22:01 women who’ve been taught to make a man happy in  various ways. These are sometimes referred to as

22:06 “pleasure squads” or, in Korean, “Kippumjo.” But they are only for the two thousand or so

22:11 top officials who also enjoy luxury goods from  the West, such as cigars, perfume, or the Rolls

22:17 Royce and Mercedes-Benzes that they often drive  around in. These top dogs own mansions and palaces

22:22 and have bank accounts in countries all over  the world. Kim Jung-il himself is said to be

22:26 worth $5 billion. He’s reported to have over 100  luxury cars, a private jet, and a luxury yacht.

22:32 Now you can understand why he has people executed  for contacting the outside world. His propaganda

22:37 is not a noble lie. It’s plain old greed,  and those at the top use the fear of the

22:42 so-called imperialists so they can maintain their  exquisite status. This is the absolute opposite

22:48 of social happiness, but all totalitarian  governments work under the principle that

22:51 they are doing everything for the common good. The retirement age in North Korea is 60 for men

22:56 and 55 for women, upon which they are supposed  to receive 30 percent of their last salary plus

23:01 300 grams of food. Many will sell things  at the market, despite it being illegal,

23:06 so they can try to get enough money for snacks or  possibly drinking at friends’ houses. The women,

23:10 according to one defector, prefer  to spend their time practicing

23:13 such things as embroidery or handicrafts. Still, North Korea’s social security system

23:17 is not stable, so most old folks work. Teachers  do private classes. Some people mend shoes or

23:23 umbrellas. Others will walk around the  streets charging close to nothing to refill

23:27 people’s overworked cigarette lighters. As always, the people with any power,

23:31 the cadres, can always make extra cash from  being paid bribes. A retired policeman might

23:36 tell a young cop to turn a blind eye to  that guy selling DVDs. In North Korea,

23:40 most of the money that changes hands is black  market money. Very few poor people in the capital

23:44 will ever head to glittering places such as the  Pothonggang Department Store to buy their goods.

23:49 Western journalists often say barely  anyone in North Korea can go there for

23:53 things like the Heinz Ketchup and foreign clothes.

23:56 They say the place was only created to show  western tourists and journalists how North

24:00 Korea is no longer a place of abject poverty. Je Son Lee, who defected a long time ago, said she

24:05 was never fooled. Sure, she hated the Japanese due  to historical reasons but didn’t hate Americans

24:11 as she was told to. She remembers when she was  young; she was told that during the Korean War,

24:15 American soldiers tore off the limbs of innocent  Korean civilians. Her young mind heard how these

24:20 soldiers gouged out people’s eyes, sliced off  their lips, and then hung them from trees as

24:25 they would decorate a Christmas tree at home. But then she decided to ask the older people in

24:29 her village about this. She said they  told “us a different story. They said

24:33 American soldiers adored Korean children  and showered them with chocolate and gum.”

24:37 Like everyone in North Korea, by law, she had  to stay in her province. She had to listen as

24:42 the local government pumped out propaganda about  the glorious leader, and TV every day had its two

24:47 minutes of hate aimed at the evil imperialists. But now she’s a woman of the world, and it’s no

24:53 longer a crime to wear the wrong facial expression  in public or to think the wrong thoughts. She’s

24:58 learned that there’s good and bad everywhere,  that not all Americans gave candy to kids.

25:02 Some committed war crimes in Korea, that’s true,  but now she can talk about that freely just as

25:07 she can say what she wants about North Korea. As for poor Koo Jeong-hwa who we talked about

25:12 in the intro, she was not so lucky. Amnesty  says after she was caught, her son recovered

25:17 from his frostbite and was sent to live with his  grandmother. Her husband, who was in South Korea,

25:21 said the one good thing is for some reason  Koo Jeong-hwa didn’t end up in a labor camp.

25:26 The reason, we expect, is the fact Amnesty  published the case. She might not be imprisoned,

25:31 but her bad Songbun probably hasn’t done her  any favors. The other eight escapees that were

25:36 arrested and sent back were not published by name,  and their whereabouts are unknown. There’s a good

25:41 chance crowds gathered for their execution. The  children covered their eyes. The guns sounded, and

25:46 the blood leaked from their bodies. Then everyone  got back to work as if nothing had happened.

25:50 Now you need to watch “Did North Korea Really  Hack Sony Pictures Because Of a Movie?” Or,

25:55 have a look at “So I went looking for  NORTH KOREAN websites and found THIS…”

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: The 7 Trillion AI Gamble Is Failing. Big Tech is TRAPPED Right NOW.

docs.text:
• Title: The 7 Trillion AI Gamble Is Failing. Big Tech is TRAPPED Right NOW.
  • Video ID: OunJtLnyPT4
  • Published: Unknown

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 AI was supposed to kick off a

00:01 white-collar purge, but the reality is

00:04 different. In Fortune 500 boardrooms

00:05 across the country, thousands of AI

00:07 agents are being shut down. Not because

00:10 they didn't work, [music] but because

00:11 they're a legal timebomb. The narrative

00:14 is that tech giants are spending

00:16 everything to win an AI arms race, but

00:18 the reality is much messier. They're

00:20 stripping the liability out of their

00:22 systems while pouring billions into the

00:24 buildout. And when the dust settles,

00:27 someone [music] still has to pay for it.

00:29 The US Interstate Highway system is

00:31 48,000 mi long. It took 35 years to

00:34 build and cost $630 billion in today's

00:37 money. It is, by any measure, one of the

00:39 most consequential infrastructure

00:40 investments in human history. Meanwhile,

00:42 Big Tech is spending $725 [music]

00:45 billion in 2026 on AI infrastructure

00:48 alone. That number has more than doubled

00:50 in just 2 years and is projected to keep

00:53 climbing into the trillions by 2030. In

00:55 fact, Goldman Sachs [music] now

00:56 estimates that the total AI

00:58 infrastructure bill between now and 2031

01:00 will exceed $7.61 trillion. For that

01:04 kind of money, you'd expect a

01:05 revolution. What these companies are

01:07 getting right now is cents on the

01:08 dollar. The entire global AI services

01:10 market in 2025 generated around $25

01:13 billion against hundreds of billions of

01:15 infrastructure spending. When a Chinese

01:17 startup called DeepSeek revealed in

01:19 January 2025 that it had built a

01:21 competitive AI model using Nvidia's

01:23 [music] lower-end chips for under $6

01:25 million, it seemed almost impossible,

01:27 but it still shook the market, wiping

01:30 out around $590 billion from Nvidia's

01:32 market cap in a single day.

01:34 >> [music]

01:34 >> It was the largest single-day loss in US

01:37 stock market history. DeepSeek, far from

01:39 breaking AI, merely raised the question

01:41 every investor had asked himself,

01:42 [music]

01:43 "What exactly are we paying for?" The

01:45 companies spending this money don't just

01:47 have it lying around. They are borrowing

01:48 it. While Alphabet quadrupled its

01:50 long-term debt in 2025 to $46.5 billion,

01:54 the five biggest tech companies issued

01:56 $108 billion in new bonds last year

01:59 alone. Bank of America now estimates

02:01 that AI CapEx now consumes 95% of

02:04 operating cash flows after dividends.

02:06 >> [music]

02:06 >> Amazon is projecting a 95% decline in

02:09 free cash flow thanks to its AI

02:10 build-out costs. They are in essence

02:13 mortgaging their present against a

02:14 future that hasn't shown up yet. The

02:17 gamble is genuinely alarming. If it were

02:19 startups chasing hype, that would be one

02:21 thing. These are the most sophisticated

02:23 capital allocators on the earth. When

02:25 they spend like this, they either know

02:27 something the rest of us don't or

02:28 they're caught up in something they

02:29 [music] can't stop without admitting

02:31 they were wrong. Either way, something

02:33 has broken. To understand what, you have

02:35 to go [music] back to the moment a

02:37 grieving man in Vancouver asked an

02:39 airline chatbot a simple question and

02:41 changed [music] corporate legal history

02:43 forever. On the day his grandmother

02:45 died, Jake Moffatt opened his laptop and

02:47 went to Air Canada's [music] website to

02:49 book a flight from Vancouver to Toronto.

02:51 He had one question, did the airline

02:53 offer bereavement fares? And could

02:55 [music] he apply for one after the fact?

02:57 He asked the chatbot and it said yes. It

02:59 told him to submit his request within 90

03:01 days of purchase and the discount would

03:03 be retroactively applied. So, Moffatt

03:05 booked the ticket, flew to Toronto, came

03:07 home, and then filed the request like

03:09 he'd been [music] told, and Air Canada

03:11 denied it. Their actual policy, as it

03:13 turns out, required bereavement fare

03:15 requests to be made before [music]

03:17 travel. The AI chatbot had simply made

03:19 up a policy that didn't exist, stated it

03:21 with complete confidence, and sent a

03:23 grieving man to buy a full-price ticket

03:25 based on a lie. So, Moffatt sued. And

03:28 what happened next is the reason every

03:30 corporate lawyer in America now has an

03:32 opinion about chatbots. Air Canada's

03:34 legal defense was [music] interesting.

03:36 They argued it could not be held liable

03:38 for information provided by its chatbot

03:40 because the chatbot was, quote, "a

03:42 separate legal entity responsible for

03:44 its own actions." They had deployed a

03:46 piece of software to represent their

03:47 company, and when that software caused

03:49 harm, their position was essentially,

03:52 "Don't look at us. Tribunal member

03:54 Christopher Rivers was not impressed.

03:56 While a chatbot has an interactive

03:57 component, he wrote, it is still just a

03:59 part of Air Canada's website. It should

04:01 be obvious to Air Canada that it is

04:04 responsible for all the information on

04:05 its website. [music] It makes no

04:07 difference whether the information comes

04:08 from a static page or a chatbot. Air

04:11 Canada was ordered to pay 812 Canadian

04:13 dollars, and in perspective, that amount

04:15 is trivial. The precedent was not.

04:18 [music] That ruling landed in February

04:20 2024. What followed was a corporate

04:22 panic that never made headlines,

04:24 >> [music]

04:24 >> but could be seen in the risk sections

04:26 of SEC filings. In 2020, 4% of public

04:29 companies mentioned AI as a material

04:32 risk in their annual filings.

04:33 >> [music]

04:33 >> By 2024, that number was 43%. Among the

04:37 Fortune 500 specifically, 56% now list

04:40 AI as a formal risk factor. Among media

04:42 and entertainment companies, it's 92%.

04:45 The SEC itself has been sending

04:47 enforcement letters demanding more

04:48 specific disclosures, backed by 8.2

04:51 billion dollars in financial remedies in

04:53 the [music] year 2024 alone. Climate

04:55 change took decades to achieve similar

04:57 disclosure penetration across corporate

04:59 America. AI did it in three years. What

05:02 the Air Canada ruling established is

05:04 that whatever your AI says to a

05:06 customer, you said it. You can't

05:08 outsource the liability to the software

05:10 you employ. You can't just point at the

05:12 machine and then look innocent. You are

05:14 the machine. For a technology that can't

05:16 guarantee it won't make things up,

05:18 [music] that ruling created an absolute

05:20 certainty. Deploy AI at scale and

05:22 eventually liability follows. The bigger

05:25 question is will there be anyone left to

05:27 cover the bill? In July 2024, research

05:29 and advisory firm Gartner predicted that

05:31 at least 30% of enterprise gen AI

05:34 projects [music]

05:34 would be abandoned after proof of

05:36 concept by the end of 2025. By April

05:39 2026, they had to revise their original

05:41 estimate. [music] It turns out that it

05:42 was actually more like 40% of enterprise

05:45 AI projects launched in the previous

05:47 [music] two years that would be scrapped

05:49 before they ever shipped. Separately,

05:50 Gartner now predicts that over 40% of

05:53 agentic AI projects, the next generation

05:55 of AI tools companies are currently

05:57 betting on, will be canceled by the end

05:59 of 2027. [music]

06:00 The graveyard keeps growing. S&P Global

06:02 Market Intelligence put some finer

06:04 numbers on it. The average organization

06:06 scrapped [music] 46% of AI proof of

06:08 concepts before reaching production. Of

06:10 the projects initiated, only 48% make it

06:13 to production with an average of 8

06:15 months between prototype and launch.

06:17 That is 8 months of engineering hours,

06:19 infrastructure [music] costs, and

06:20 executive attention on a coin flip

06:22 chance of shipping anything at the end

06:24 of it. McKinsey, another consulting

06:26 firm, [music] surveyed organizations

06:27 globally in late 2025 and they found

06:30 that 88% use AI in at least one business

06:33 function. If that sounds like [music] a

06:35 success story, it's not. Only 39%

06:38 reported any measurable impact on

06:40 earnings. At most, 61% reported no

06:42 meaningful financial impact on their

06:44 business whatsoever. Roughly six in 10

06:47 companies [music] have plugged AI into

06:48 their operations and can't point to a

06:50 measurable return it's made [music]

06:52 them. The reasons are familiar enough

06:53 that Gartner has named them outright.

06:55 Poor data quality, weak risk [music]

06:57 controls, rising costs, and unclear

06:59 business value. Each project costs

07:01 between 5 and 20 million dollars to

07:03 build and deploy. Multiply that across

07:06 thousands of Fortune 500 initiatives and

07:08 you're looking at tens of billions of

07:10 dollars buried in the corporate

07:11 graveyard. It gets even [music] worse

07:13 for Big Tech. A 2024 Deloitte survey

07:15 found that 47% of enterprise AI users

07:18 admitted [music] to making at least one

07:20 major business decision based on the

07:22 content AI had simply invented. In other

07:24 words, nearly half had already trusted a

07:27 hallucination with real-world [music]

07:28 consequences.
