docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 August 6, 1945, 7:15 AM: 60 minutes before  the atomic bomb is dropped on Hiroshima.

00:06 The skies are clear over southern Japan. Colonel  Paul Tibbets, Jr. pilots the Enola Gay towards a

00:12 target blissfully unaware of the catastrophe about  to be unleashed over their heads. The crew of the

00:16 modified B-29 is silent as they prepare to drop  a bomb that promises to create the most powerful

00:21 explosion ever used in war. “We are approaching  our target,” Tibbets says. “Arm the weapon.”

00:26 In the cargo hold of the Enola Gay Captain William  Parsons prepares the atomic bomb for drop. Right

00:31 after take off, he put the final piece of the  Little Boy bomb together. Now he checks one last

00:36 time to make sure that the device detonates  at the appropriate altitude. A bead of sweat

00:40 trickles down the side of his face. Even though  what he is doing is relatively safe, there is

00:45 still the thought that one wrong move could make  the B-29 Ground Zero for an atomic explosion.

00:49 Tibbets pulls up on the flight stick  and ascends to an attacking altitude of

00:53 31,000 feet. The higher he can get the plane,

00:55 the more time he’ll have to evacuate the area  before the bomb reaches its detonation altitude.

01:00 He waits for the all-clear from the two B-29s  that have accompanied the Enola Gay on the

01:04 mission for reconnaissance. One of the aircraft  is scouting over the primary target of Hiroshima;

01:09 the other is conducting surveillance over  the secondary targets of Kokura and Nagasaki.

01:13 The radio aboard the Enola Gay crackles  as the signal comes in. “Weather over the

01:18 primary target is all clear. Proceed  to Primary Target.” Colonel Tibbets

01:21 adjusts his heading ever so slightly  and continues towards Hiroshima.

01:25 8:00 AM: 15 minutes before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Hiroshima.

01:29 Colonel Tibbets speaks to his crew. “Target is in  sight. Prepare to drop the bomb.” The 12 men on

01:34 the aircraft say their final prayers and think  about their loved ones. This is the first time

01:38 an atomic bomb has been dropped from a plane.  It is unclear if the bomb will work properly or

01:43 if there will be enough time to get the Enola  Gay out of the blast zone before detonation.

01:47 This may very well be the last time any of  the crew will have the luxury of reminiscing

01:51 about their families and friends. Tibbets  maneuvers the aircraft into striking position.

01:55 8:12 AM: 2 minutes before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Hiroshima.

01:59 “I’m transferring command to you, Ferebee,”  Tibbets says over his headset. Major Thomas

02:04 Ferebee, the Enola Gay’s bombardier, sits at the  front of the aircraft. He can see the city of

02:08 Hiroshima below through the glass of the plane’s  nose. From the Pedestal Gun Sighting Station,

02:12 Ferebee shouts out slight adjustments  that need to be made to the aircraft’s

02:16 trajectory. Tibbets makes the modifications  as Ferebee calls them out. He takes a deep

02:20 breath and lets it out slowly. A moment  later, the bombing run begins. Ferebee

02:25 has the Aioi Bridge lined up perfectly;  this is the precise target for the drop.

02:29 “Everyone put on your protective goggles,” Tibbets  says over the radio. Ferebee looks through the

02:34 viewfinder one last time before donning his  headgear and preparing to drop the atomic bomb.

02:39 8:15 AM: the atomic bomb is dropped on Hiroshima.

02:42 “Bomb’s away!” Ferebee yells into his headset.  The bomb bay doors open, and the Little Boy

02:47 atomic bomb plummets toward the ground. Tibbets  immediately banks hard into a turn. He pushes

02:52 the engines of the Enola Gay to their limit.  They roar under the strain of extra thrust;

02:56 the entire fuselage creeks as the plane  rapidly turns away. It is a race against time.

03:01 Every second that ticks by brings  the explosion of atomic energy closer

03:05 and closer. Tibbets grits his teeth,  willing the Enola Gay to move faster.

03:09 30 seconds to detonation.

03:11 The plane’s engines glow red from burning  at full power. The crew braces themselves.

03:15 15 seconds to detonation.

03:18 Sargent Bob Caron, the Enola Gay’s tail gunner,

03:20 squints through his goggles. He will  be the only member of the crew able to

03:24 see the initial blast as the bomb goes off.  This is not an honor Caron is sure he wants.

03:29 3… 2… 1…

03:31 There is a bright flash of light. Caron shields  his face with his forearm. His eyes are closed,

03:36 but when he opens them, he can hardly  believe what he sees. “It is like a

03:40 peep into hell,” Caron says over the  radio. There is a somber silence.

03:44 January 1939: 6 years before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

03:49 Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, two Jewish  scientists fleeing Nazi Germany, have been

03:54 following a discovery made by two scientists  named Irène Joliot-Curie and Pavle Savić

03:59 working out of France. They have determined  that by bombarding uranium with neutrons,

04:03 a transformation can take place that has the  potential to release huge amounts of energy.

04:07 Meitner and Frisch are desperate to make it to  Cohepenhegan before another Great War breaks out,

04:12 both to save their lives and share  what they’ve learned with other

04:15 scientists. It is in Denmark that they meet with  a brilliant physicist by the name of Neils Bohr.

04:20 Bohr is about to leave for the United States and  is excited to share the new discovery brought to

04:24 his attention by Meitner and Frisch with  the scientists there. He discusses the

04:28 transformation and the resulting release of energy  with Albert Einstein and other scientists in the

04:33 U.S. After their meeting, the group of researchers  announces their findings. It is determined that by

04:38 striking uranium-235 or plutonium-239 atoms with  neutrons, the nucleus can be split into fragments,

04:45 resulting in a huge burst of energy. This  process has been termed fission by Meitner

04:50 and Frisch and lays the foundation for  what would one day become the atom bomb.

04:53 June 1940: 5 years before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

04:58 “When fission occurs, there is a  chance that neutrons are released,

05:01 and a sustained chain reaction will happen,”  Enrico Fermi says to Neils Bohr as they smoke

05:06 pipes in a university classroom. The two  scientists are working on the equations

05:10 necessary to harness nuclear energy and change  the world. “If that’s true,” Bohr replies,

05:15 “this process may be more powerful  than we could have ever imagined.

05:18 Scientists in the United States continue  to work on the prospect of atomic energy.

05:22 Slowly the secrets of the atom and the process of  fission become clearer. By the end of the month,

05:27 the basic facts about nuclear energy  are known by most scientists around

05:30 the world. The race to harness  the power of the atom has begun.

05:34 December 1941: 4 years before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

05:38 “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will  live in infamy—the United States of America was

05:45 suddenly and deliberately attacked by the naval  and air forces of the Empire of Japan.” President

05:49 Franklin Delano Rosevelt addresses Congress and  the people of the United States. The attack on

05:54 Pearl Harbor thrust the United States into World  War II. This single event will lead to millions

05:59 of lives lost during the War in the Pacific. The  conflict will end with two Japanese cities being

06:04 decimated and the area around them covered  in radioactive fallout for years to come.

06:09 September 1942: 3 years before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

06:13 General Leslie R. Groves is placed  in charge of the Manhattan Project,

06:17 named after the U.S. Army Corps of  Engineers Manhattan District based at

06:21 Columbia University. The atomic program  spans the country, but the Manhattan

06:25 Project has stuck as a code name for the top  secret project as it is where it all began.

06:30 For a while now, a scientist by the name of J.  Robert Oppenheimer has been deeply involved in

06:35 the efforts to develop the atomic bomb. General  Groves has taken note of Oppenheimer’s enthusiasm.

06:40 “How would you like to lead the team of  scientists working on the bomb?” Groves

06:43 asks. Oppenheimer pauses for a moment to  think about what this could mean. He has

06:47 been working tirelessly to help the government  achieve its goals and further the scientific

06:51 understanding necessary to achieve a working  atomic bomb. What the general is offering him

06:56 would change everything. He would be directly  responsible for the success of the project.

07:00 “It would be an honor, general,” Oppenheimer says  as he shakes Groves' hand. In the coming years,

07:05 Oppenheimer will lead the team that creates  a weapon which could literally end the world.

07:09 December 2, 1942.

07:12 “Everyone stand back and be prepared to  shut it down if something goes wrong,”

07:15 Enrico Fermi says to his team. They stand on  a platform, looking down on a squash court.

07:19 The court sits under the bleachers of Stagg  Field at the University of Chicago. On the

07:24 court itself is Chicago Pile No. 1. “Do  we think it wise to initiate a nuclear

07:29 reaction under the football field?” one  of the researchers asks. Everyone pauses.

07:32 “This is for science, for the United States,  and for the future of humanity,” one of the

07:36 physicists sitting at the control panel  says. There is agreement. The switch

07:39 is flipped. The reactor begins to hum.  Neutrons begin bombarding the fuel rods

07:44 in the reactor. A self-sustaining nuclear  chain reaction begins within Chicago Pile

07:49 No. 1. Atomic energy is released, plutonium  is created, all of the theoretical science

07:54 done up until this point around atomic  energy has been experimentally proven.

07:57 A scientist takes one of the rods out of  the reactor. He runs a Geiger Counter over

08:02 it. The machine rapidly begins to click. It  is clear that a huge amount of radiation has

08:06 been generated, but the ramifications  of this byproduct are not yet known.

08:10 January 1943: 2 years and 8 months before  the atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

08:15 General Groves smiles as he reads progress reports  sent by Oppenheimer. They are getting close,

08:20 really close. The government has chosen a  580-square-mile parcel of land in Washington

08:25 State to generate the plutonium needed to  construct an arsenal of atomic bombs. The

08:30 only problem is there are people living  on the land that Groves wants. However,

08:34 this is an easy fix. He is backed  by the United States government and,

08:37 at this point, has been given the go-ahead  to do whatever it takes to make the bomb.

08:40 The local population of Hanford, Richland, and  White Bluffs are ordered to vacate their homes.

08:45 They have 90 days to do so, or the military  will be sent in to encourage them to make the

08:50 right choice. Groves won’t let a few holdouts  stop him and the Manhattan Project from getting

08:55 the resources they need to complete the bomb.  Along with the entire populations of these towns,

08:59 the Wanapum Native Americans are forced to  relocate. They are sent to Priest Rapids and lose

09:04 access to their ancestral fishing grounds along  the Columbia River. This is just another egregious

09:09 mistreatment of the people who are native to  this land by the United States government.

09:12 The U.S. government suppresses as many  outcries as they need to in order to

09:17 complete the construction of their facility.  It is a matter of national security that the

09:21 Hanford Engineer Works be built to supply  the military with plutonium. To Groves

09:25 and the other high-ranking officials that are  aware of the Manhattan Project, a few thousand

09:29 unhappy citizens and Native Americans is a small  price to pay for the fate of the entire world.

09:34 April 1943: 2 years and 4 months before  the atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

09:39 Oppenheimer sifts through several different  maps looking for the perfect locations to

09:43 carry out the first test of an atomic  bomb. The Hanford facility is remote,

09:47 but not as remote as he would like.  Using fission to create an atomic blast

09:51 has never been done before, and it is not clear  exactly how destructive the explosion will be.

09:56 According to some calculations, there is  a very small chance that the atomic blast

10:00 could ignite the oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere  and cause the entire planet to become a raging

10:05 inferno. But Oppenheimer and his team on  the Manhattan Project are almost positive

10:09 that won’t happen. The risk of possibly  destroying the planet is outweighed by

10:13 their thirst for knowledge and the ability to  wipe their enemies off the face of the Earth.

10:16 “That’s the spot,” Oppenheimer says,  pointing to a map of New Mexico with

10:20 his index finger. He has chosen a remote  region on the Los Alamos mesa. It is 34

10:25 miles south of Santa Fe and in the middle of  the desert. This should be isolated enough

10:29 to conduct the necessary tests without  anyone finding out what they are doing.

10:33 Engineers begin arriving at the newly  dubbed Los Alamos Laboratory. The first

10:37 task is to create a bomb that can hold the  appropriate amount of fissionable material,

10:42 be dropped from a plane, and has a fuse that  will detonate at the appropriate altitude.

10:46 This all needs to be done before the team can  ramp up its stores of fissionable material.

10:51 If they don’t have a delivery method, there is  no point in reducing the fissionable products

10:55 being sent to New Mexico from plants such as  the Hanford Engineer Works into pure metal.

11:00 Every week more and more scientists,  engineers, and technicians arrive at

11:03 Los Alamos. By the time of the first test,  there will be around 5,000 people at the site.

11:08 April 12, 1945: 4 months before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

11:13 The nation mourns. President Franklin Delano  Roosevelt has just passed away. Many are in

11:18 shock. In the President’s last address, he looked  old and frail while seated at his desk. However,

11:23 his declining health had been kept a secret  from the general public. Now they have to

11:27 contend with the fact that their leader for over  a decade will not see them through World War II.

11:31 Germany will surrender in less than a month,  but there is still the Japanese threat in the

11:35 Pacific. Less than 24 hours after FDR’s death,  the United States' new President, Harry S. Truman,

11:41 is sworn in and briefed on the Manhattan  Project and the progress of the atomic bomb.

11:45 July 16, 1945, 5:29 am: 21 days before  the atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

11:52 Sirens wail across Los Alamos. The  Trinity test is about to begin. Gadget,

11:57 the first atomic bomb to ever be tested, hangs  100 feet above the sand of Alamogordo Bombing

12:03 Range. Oppenheimer glances at his watch.  The experiment will commence in the next

12:07 45 seconds. When the timer hits zero, the  plutonium implosion device will detonate,

12:12 and the largest man-made explosion that has ever  been created will possibly destroy the planet.

12:16 30 seconds until detonation.

12:18 Military officials, scientists, and engineers are  at observation points between 5 and 10 miles away

12:24 from Ground Zero. They are ordered to lie on  their stomachs with their heads pointed away

12:28 from the bomb. Everyone in attendance gets down  on the ground, puts on their protective goggles,

12:33 and waits for the countdown to reach zero. This is  the moment they have all been waiting for. If the

12:38 test succeeds, the United States will have the  most powerful weapon the world has ever known.

12:41 15 seconds until detonation.

12:44 The skies are dark. Rain falls on  the parched desert sands. Lightning

12:48 illuminates the sky in the distance. It is  the perfect day to test a doomsday weapon.

12:52 Gadget detonates.

12:53 At 5:29 and 45 seconds, the bomb is  triggered. There is a blinding flash

12:58 of light that illuminates the mountain peaks ten  miles away. All is quiet for a brief moment; then,

13:03 there is the deafening sound of the explosion.  Hurricane-force winds sweep across the test site,

13:08 blowing sand and debris over the desert.  After several seconds observers throughout

13:13 the area turn toward Ground Zero.  A 40,000-foot mushroom cloud rises

13:17 up into the sky. Where the tower once  stood is now only a crater with a glassy

13:21 jade-colored mineral covering the surface.  This substance would later be named trinitite.

13:26 As far as 50 miles away, people report seeing  the explosion. Citizens phone the authorities,

13:31 asking what happened out in the desert.  Windows of houses 125 miles away shatter.

13:36 Residents in Gallup, New Mexico, 180  miles from Alamogordo Bombing Range,

13:40 say they felt the ground shake. Later, the  government will release a brief statement

13:44 to the press giving an explanation for the large  explosion and the phenomena associated with it:

13:49 “A remotely located ammunition magazine  containing a considerable amount of high

13:53 explosives and pyrotechnics exploded, but  there was no loss of life or limb to anyone.”

13:57 This is clearly a lie, but the government  can’t let anyone know what has just occurred

14:02 at Los Alamos. The atomic bomb must  remain a secret until the opportune

14:06 moment when the U.S. military is ready  to unleash its power on their enemies.

14:09 Oppenheimer stands with his mouth  open, staring at the aftermath of

14:13 the weapon of mass destruction he played  an integral role in creating. A line from

14:18 a Hindu passage passes through his  thoughts. “Now I am become Death,

14:21 the destroyer of worlds.” The mushroom  cloud continues to grow larger and larger.

14:26 July 16th, late afternoon.

14:28 Top military officials receive a communication  stating that the atomic bomb test at Los Alamos

14:33 has been a success. The weapon is everything  they hoped for and more. Military leaders

14:37 have been grappling with the reality of what  is unfolding in the Pacific. Japan will not

14:41 give up. It seems as if the only way to end the  war is by invading the home island itself. This

14:46 is estimated to result in 1.7 to 4 million  U.S. casualties. The number is staggering,

14:52 but it may be the only way to force  the Japanese leadership to surrender.

14:55 Now there is another option. The United States  can use its newest and most powerful weapon to

15:00 force Japan’s hand. An order is sent to  military bases on the West Coast that

15:04 have components for several atomic bombs  stored at their facilities. They are to

15:08 begin shipping the parts of the bomb to an  island within striking distance of Japan.

15:12 Early that evening, the USS Indianapolis leaves  San Francisco. On board the ship is a gun assembly

15:17 mechanism for detonating the atomic weapon,  about half of the U.S. supply of uranium-235,

15:22 and several Los Alamos scientists who will oversee  the construction of the bombs. The rest of the

15:28 United States stockpile of uranium-235 is loaded  onto a transport plane and flown to Tinian Island.

15:34 This is where everything will come together  before a nuclear attack is launched against Japan.

15:38 July 26, 1945: 11 days before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

15:44 The USS Indianapolis reaches Tinian Island.  Assembly of Little Boy begins. Later when the

15:49 plutonium arrives by aircraft, the construction  of Fat Man starts. The Big Three: Truman,

15:54 Churchill, and Stalin are at the Potsdam  Conference in Germany when Truman receives

15:58 a message reporting the successful  test of the atomic bomb at Los Alamos.

16:02 Truman leans over to Stalin. “I’ve just  received word that U.S. scientists have

16:05 created a new weapon of unusual destructive  force,” he says. “The time for a Japanese

16:10 surrender is at hand.” Stalin hesitates for a  moment. His own scientists have been working

16:14 around the clock to harness the power of the  atom and make their own bomb. He is slightly

16:18 annoyed that the U.S. beat him to it. “Very  well,” Stalin replies. “Let’s contact Tokyo.

16:23 The Big Three issue an ultimatum to Japan. It  states that they either surrender unconditionally

16:28 or face “prompt and utter destruction.”  There is no response to their request.

16:31 After dropping off the components for the bombs,  the Indianapolis departs for the Philippines,

16:36 where it will continue to aid in the war  effort. Four days later, it is sunk by

16:40 the Japanese submarine I-58. 900 out of the  1,200 sailors survive the attack and float in

16:46 the dark Pacific waters. The men are accidentally  stumbled upon by U.S. ships four days later. Only

16:51 316 men survived. It is theorized from first-hand  accounts and the carnage left in the water that

16:57 hundreds of men were attacked and eaten by Oceanic  white-tipped sharks while they waited for rescue.

17:01 August 2, 1945: 4 days before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Japan.

17:06 It has been decided that the United States will  not launch a land invasion of Japan but will force

17:11 them to surrender by using their newest weapon  instead. No one except the highest-ranking U.S.

17:15 officials and scientists present at the Trinity  test knows the power of the atomic bomb. However,

17:21 no one can predict the destructive power  and the deadly aftermath of the bomb,

17:24 as this will be the first time anything  like it has been used in warfare. The

17:28 collateral damage will be immense,  but the U.S. feels it needs to send

17:31 a clear message in order to get the  Japanese leadership to end the war.

17:35 The U.S. military is watching the weather  over Japan. They are waiting for the

17:39 opportune moment to carry out their attack.  The targets have been narrowed down to Kokura,

17:43 Hiroshima, Niigata, and Kyōto. Although  Kyōto was at the top of the list,

17:48 Secretary of War Henry Lewis Stimson pleaded  with President Truman to reconsider due to its

17:53 historical and cultural significance. Truman  agrees; Kyōto is swapped out for Nagasaki.

17:58 August 6, 1945, 2:30 am: 5 hours and 45 minutes  before the atomic bomb is dropped on Hiroshima.

18:05 Colonel Paul Tibbets walks around the B-29 that  will be flown to Japan to drop the atomic bomb

18:09 named Little Boy. His crew has gathered and made  final preparations. Tibbets stops at the nose of

18:14 the plane and looks at the hull. “George,  can you come over here for a second?” asks

18:18 Tibbets. A maintenance worker walks over to the  plane. Tibbets whispers something into his ear.

18:22 The maintenance worker leaves and comes  back with stencils and paint. He gets

18:26 to work writing something on the nose  of the aircraft. After a few minutes,

18:29 he steps away. Tibbets smiles at his mother’s name  that is now painted on the hull of the aircraft.

18:34 2:45 am: 5 hours and 30 minutes before  the atomic bomb is dropped on Hiroshima.

18:39 Tibbets pushes the throttle forward. The engines  of the B-29 Superfortess, now named the Enola Gay,

18:44 roar to life. The aircraft picks up speed as it  races down the runway. Tibbets pulls back on the

18:50 flight stick; the plane rises into the air. It  is a little unwieldy due to the modifications

18:54 made to the craft, which allow it to carry and  drop atomic bombs. A few seconds after lift-off,

18:59 Tibbets feels a slight dip, and his stomach sinks.  He makes a few adjustments; the plane begins

19:04 to climb again. He breathes a sigh of relief.  However, he knows the hardest part is yet to come.

19:08 Moments later, two other B-29s take off  from the airfield on Tinian island. They

19:13 will provide reconnaissance on the  targets for the Enola Gay to make

19:15 sure that the conditions are right to  drop the bomb. They will also be used

19:18 to film the detonation of the atomic  device and the immediate aftermath.

19:22 Once the Enola Gay levels off, Captain William  Parsons begins adding the final components to

19:26 Little Boy. This was not done prior to takeoff  because several of the modified B-29s crashed

19:31 during test flights. A major concern is that if a  B-29 crashes with a fully assembled bomb on board,

19:37 it might detonate and wipe out the entire  military base on Tinian Island. This might

19:42 serve as a demonstration of the destructive  power of the atomic bomb, but not in the way

19:46 the United States had hoped for. Therefore,  the atomic bomb aboard the Enola Gay was

19:50 not to be fully assembled until the B-29 was in  the air and a safe distance away from the base.

19:55 “We are good to go, Colonel,” Parsons says  over the radio once he finishes preparations

19:59 on Little Boy. “Roger that,” Tibbets confirms. He  continues to fly towards the home island of Japan.

20:05 8:15 am: 1 second before the atomic  bomb detonates over Hiroshima.

20:09 Little Boy falls to an altitude of  1,900 feet. The gun assembly device

20:13 fires and critical mass is achieved when  the uranium projectile strikes the uranium

20:18 target within the bomb. This results in the  initiation of a chain reaction. Atoms split;

20:22 neutrons are ripped from their nuclei.  This creates a massive amount of energy

20:26 resulting in an atomic explosion directly  over the Shima Hospital in Hiroshima.

20:31 When the bomb detonates, the temperature directly  below the blast reaches 12,600 degrees Fahrenheit

20:36 or around 7,000 degrees Celsius. Everything  within the vicinity is immediately incinerated,

20:41 including people, vehicles, and  buildings. The blast wave levels

20:45 any structures within its radius, destroying  around two-thirds of the city. Out of the

20:49 343,000 inhabitants living in Hiroshima,  around 70,000 are killed almost instantly;

20:55 another 30,000 will be dead within the year  from severe burns and radiation poisoning.

21:00 All the remains of anyone caught in  the thermal radiation blast is their

21:03 nuclear shadows imprinted on the stone  structures of Hiroshima. Their bodies

21:07 shielded the stone from the radiation,  keeping it from being bleached by the

21:11 intense heat and leaving an imprint of  their body forever etched into the rock.

21:15 As the Enola Gray speeds away, it is rocked  by the shockwave of the atomic bomb. “Hold

21:20 onto something!” Tibbets yells over the  headset. The crew is restrained to their

21:23 seats by safety harnesses; if they had not been  wearing them, they would have been tossed around

21:27 the fuselage like pinballs. Tibbets clutches  the flight stick tightly with both hands. He

21:32 adjusts the angle of the B-29 to level the  plane out. Moments later, the air is still

21:36 once again. Tibbets climbs to cruising altitude  and begins the journey back to Tinian Island.

21:42 8:18 am: 3 minutes after the atomic  bomb detonated over Hiroshima.

21:46 The mushroom cloud from the blast rises higher  and higher into the air, reaching 40,000 feet

21:50 above the ground. Less than 2% of the uranium  contained within Little Boy achieved fission,

21:55 yet the destruction is utterly unbelievable.  The bomb released the equivalent of more than

22:00 15,000 tons of TNT on the city  of Hiroshima. A member of the

22:04 Enola Gray’s crew looks back at the  destruction from a window. “Good God,

22:07 what have we done?” he says into his  headset. For a minute, there is only silence.

22:11 “We saved American lives,” someone  responds. “But at what cost?” a third

22:15 voice says. The crew is silent for  much of the journey back to base.

22:19 8:15 pm: 12 hours after the atomic  bomb detonated over Hiroshima.

22:23 The Enola Gay touches down at Tinian. Upon  disembarking, the crew is greeted by cheers

22:28 and applause. Colonel Paul Tibbets is awarded  the Distinguished Service Cross for his actions.

22:32 Four hours later, President Harry Truman  addresses the American people. “Sixteen

22:37 hours ago, an American airplane dropped one  bomb on Hiroshima, an important Japanese Army

22:41 base. That bomb had more power than 20,000  tons of TNT.” Some listeners shake their

22:46 heads in dismay. Others are terrified of what  this weapon could be used for in the future.

22:50 And yet the majority smile at the awesome  power that the United States now wields.

22:55 Truman continues: “It is an atomic bomb. It is  a harnessing of the basic power of the universe.

23:00 The force from which the sun draws its power has

23:03 been loosed against those who  brought war to the Far East.”

23:05 The world has changed forever.

23:07 August 8, 1945: 1 day before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Nagasaki.

23:12 As news of the destruction of Hiroshima  circulates around the world, people grapple

23:16 with the consequences of such a powerful  weapon. It is almost incomprehensible. Some

23:21 in the Japanese leadership claim that since their  own atomic program has stalled due to difficulties

23:25 in procuring materials, perhaps the United States  only had that one bomb. Others argue it is time to

23:31 reach a settlement with the U.S. and its allies.  Advocates for surrendering note that if the United

23:35 States could build and drop one atomic bomb, it is  only a matter of time before they can do it again.

23:39 At this point, the Soviet Union has yet  to declare war on Japan. It is proposed

23:44 by some Japanese officials that Stalin  might be willing to mediate negotiations

23:48 between the United States and Japan. However,  before anything can become of such an idea,

23:52 the Soviet Union declares war. Their  forces push into Manchuria and Sakhalin

23:57 Island. Japan will receive no help from  the Soviets, only death and destruction.

24:01 August 9, 1945, 3:47 AM: 10 hours and 15 minutes  before the atomic bomb is dropped on Nagasaki.

24:08 The United States still has not received word of  a Japanese surrender. There is growing unease as

24:13 Soviet forces move closer and closer to the  main island of Japan. U.S. leadership worries

24:18 that if the Soviet Union invades and forces a  surrender, they may claim Japan and much of the

24:23 territory it conquered during the war for their  own. The United States cannot let this happen.

24:27 The Bockscar, a B-29 loaded with the Fat Man  atomic bomb, takes off from Tinian and proceeds

24:32 toward Japan. Major Charles Sweeney is at the  controls. The bomb the Bockscar carries is more

24:37 powerful than the one dropped on Hiroshima.  It is plutonium-fueled and similar to the

24:42 bomb detonated during the Trinity  test at Alamogordo Bombing Range.

24:45 While taking off, Sweeney is particularly careful.  Unlike the Little Boy bomb, Fat Man is already

24:50 completely assembled in his cargo hold. Once the  plane is safely in the air Commander Frederick

24:55 Ashworth arms the bomb. Again, two other B-29s  accompany the Bockscar on their mission to

25:00 ensure that the targets are visible. At the  time of take-off, clear skies with light haze

25:04 are reported over the primary target of Kokura.  Sweeney pilots the plane toward this destination.

25:10 9:45 AM: 1 hour and 17 minutes before  the atomic bomb is dropped on Nagasaki.

25:14 “I can’t see anything,” Sweeney exclaims  over the radio. The weather over Kokura

25:19 has deteriorated. Visibility of the  city below is nearly zero. This may

25:23 have been caused by the firebombing  runs conducted on the nearby city of

25:27 Yahata the night before. “I’m circling  around for another pass,” Sweeney says.

25:30 On the second time around, the city below  is still covered by haze and clouds. There

25:34 is no way to tell where the target is and when to  drop the bomb. “Can anyone see anything?” Sweeney

25:39 shouts as he circles back for one more pass,  hoping that there is a break in the overcast

25:43 skies. Their target is a massive arsenal that  contains large stores of weapons and explosives

25:48 that the Japanese desperately need if they are  going to mount a defense of their home island.

25:52 The destruction of the target makes sense in  the scheme of the war. But if the crew of the

25:56 Bockscar can’t sight it, they could hit the wrong  part of the city and leave the arsenal unharmed.

26:01 Sweeney checks the fuel gauge. They have been  circling above Kokura for nearly 45 minutes. The

26:05 clouds have not cleared. Time is slowly slipping  away. “I’m calling it off,” Sweeney says over the

26:10 radio. There is an eerie stillness throughout  the aircraft as the crew waits for the Major’s

26:13 next decision. “We are moving to the secondary  target. Prepare to drop the bomb over Nagasaki.”

26:18 10:58 AM: 4 minutes before the  atomic bomb is dropped on Nagasaki.

26:22 “Damn it!” Sweeney yells. “The cloud cover  here is worse than at Kokura.” He looks out

26:26 the cockpit window to try and identify any  landmarks below. Captain Kermit Beahan is

26:31 serving as bombardier on the mission and  looks through his scope to try and locate

26:35 the Mitsubishi arms plant. This structure  is supposed to be their target in Nagasaki.

26:39 “Beahan, you see anything?” Sweeney asks.  “It’s bad, Major. All I can see is clouds.”

26:44 Kermit Beahan responds. Sweeney glances at the  fuel gauge again. We’re not going to make it,

26:48 he thinks. “Major! I got something,” Beahan says  over the headset. A clearing in the clouds has

26:52 appeared in the northern part of the city. It  is not their preplanned target, but it is close

26:56 enough that the bomb will take out the arms  plant in the blast. “Drop it!” Sweeney yells.

27:01 11:02 AM: the atomic bomb drops on Nagasaki.

27:04 Fat Man falls to an altitude of 1,650  feet. The detonation mechanism triggers.

27:09 The sub-critical plutonium core is  surrounded by several thousand pounds

27:13 of explosives. They are arranged  in a way that when they detonate,

27:16 the explosive forces are directed inward toward  the plutonium core. The force of the explosion

27:21 crushes the plutonium into a super-critical  state, and a nuclear chain reaction commences.

27:26 This type of atomic bomb creates a much  bigger explosion than Little Boy. Fat Man

27:31 goes off with the force of 21,000 tons of  TNT. 40,000 people are instantly vaporized,

27:36 and another 30,000 will die in the  aftermath from radiation poisoning.

27:39 40% of the city’s buildings are destroyed.  As the mushroom cloud erupts into the air,

27:44 the shockwave strikes the Bockscar rattling  the hull of the plane. Sweeney regains control

27:49 and steers the craft further away  from the spreading cloud of debris.

27:52 Sweeney wipes sweat from his brow as he looks  at the fuel gauge. There isn’t enough fuel to

27:56 make it back to Tinian. He looks at a map  and decides their best chance is to get to

28:00 Okinawa to the south of Japan. The Island is  under U.S. control, so if they can make it,

28:05 it should be a safe place to land. The challenge  is to reach the island before the Bockscar runs

28:10 out of fuel and plummets into the choppy,  shark-filled waters of the Pacific. Sweeney

28:14 informs his crew of the new plan. Most are still  in shock from the explosion they just witnessed.

28:18 They had heard of the destructive power of the  bomb, but seeing it first hand is different.

28:22 Several hours later, a voice crackles over  the radio. “This is Major Charles Sweeney

28:26 of the Bockscar. We are coming  in for an emergency landing.”

28:29 “Roger that, Major,” responds flight control  from Yontan Airfield on Okinawa. “The runway

28:33 is all yours. You’re clear for landing.”  Sweeney eases back on the throttle;

28:37 the B-29 descends and touches down on the  tarmac. The fuel needle gently rests on “E.”

28:42 August 10, 1945: 1 day after the  atomic bomb detonated over Hiroshima.

28:47 Emperor Hirohito supports accepting  the terms laid out by the Allies. The

28:51 Japanese government releases a statement  saying they will surrender but only if the

28:55 Emperor is allowed to keep his position  as sovereign ruler of the nation. The

28:59 United States rejects this counteroffer  and makes their position clear. They want

29:03 the unconditional surrender of Japan,  or there will be further consequences.

29:06 President Truman is in constant communication  with General Groves. “Yes, Mr. President,

29:11 we already have another bomb ready for  shipment. It should reach the Pacific

29:14 in a matter of days,” says Groves.  The President thanks him and has

29:17 his military advisors draw plans for  a third atomic bombing run on Japan.

29:21 August 14, 1945: Japan surrenders.

29:24 The Japanese government accepts the Allies' terms  for unconditional surrender. The next day Emperor

29:29 Hirohito is heard on every radio across the  country. The pre-recorded message is played on

29:34 every station. It is the first time Japan's people  have heard their Emperor's voice in a long time.

29:39 Tears are shed. Many can’t believe that Japan  has been defeated; others refuse to accept it

29:44 altogether. The future of Japan is uncertain, but  one thing is clear: they will not be able to rule

29:49 themselves for some time. The U.S. military  will occupy Japan for the next seven years.

29:53 September 2, 1945: The War in the  Pacific officially comes to an end.

29:59 The USS Missouris sits in Tokyo Bay. Its deck has  been outfitted with a table and chairs. Resting

30:05 on the table are the instruments of surrender.  Foreign Minister Mamoru Shigemitsu and General

30:09 Yoshijiro Umezu approach the table while U.S.  officers and sailors look on. The documents are

30:15 signed. World War II officially comes to an end.  Cheers erupt around the world as the most bloody

30:20 conflict in human history is now over. Fighting  will continue sporadically throughout the Pacific

30:25 until word can reach soldiers in the furthest  reaches of the conflict that the war has ended.

30:30 Astonishingly some will even continue fighting for

30:33 decades. The last official surrender by  a Japanese soldier occurs on March 9,

30:37 1974 when Lieutenant Hiroo Onoda finally  hands over his sword in the Philippine Jungle.

30:43 In the coming decades, the aftereffects  of the atomic bombs dropped on Japan will

30:47 come to light. Thousands will suffer from  radiation poisoning. Countless civilians

30:51 will die from cancer. The contamination  of soil and water will last for years.

30:55 It will be argued that the United States had  to use the atomic bombs to force a Japanese

30:59 surrender. That launching an invasion of the  home island would have caused much more death

31:03 and destruction than the bombs did. The  other side will advocate for reparations,

31:07 that the United States massacred innocent men,  women, and children. They’ll say that using the

31:11 atomic bomb was irresponsible. Regardless  of which side is right, the destruction of

31:16 Hiroshima and Nagaskai still remain the only two  instances where nuclear weapons have been used in

31:21 a war. Perhaps their sacrifice avoided an all-out  nuclear holocaust during the Cold War to come.

31:26 Now watch “What If Japan Was Never  Hit By Nuclear Bombs.” Or check

31:30 out “The Truth About Why America  Dropped Atomic Bombs on Japan.”

00:00 The following content is provided under a Creative

00:17 at ocw.mit.edu.

00:20 PROFESSOR: In the next set of demonstrations,

00:23 we're going to illustrate some of the very

00:26 classic phenomena associated with the diffraction of light.

00:31 I hope that there will be educational but also a lot

00:35 of fun to see these effects.

00:39 We'll start first with the Fraunhofer diffraction,

00:43 both in one dimension and two dimensions.

00:46 And then we'll go to Fresnel diffraction.

00:49 So let's start first with Fraunhofer diffraction

00:53 associated with a single slit.

00:55 The setup is, over here we have helium-neon laser,

01:00 and here is the beam from the laser.

01:03 We reflect it by this mirror here,

01:06 and then we reflect it again by this mirror here onto the slit.

01:13 This slit is an adjustable slit.

01:17 By turning this knob here, I can adjust the slit.

01:20 But in order to see that indeed this is a slit,

01:23 I'm going to put a screen over here,

01:27 so that when I adjust the jaws of the slit here,

01:33 you can see that, indeed, I am varying

01:36 the spacing between the jaws.

01:38 Of course, when it gets very small, it's difficult to see.

01:42 So here's our adjustable slit, and here's the laser beam

01:45 going through the slit.

01:46 And then the diffracted light then

01:49 falls on the screen over there, which

01:52 is about 200 centimeters from the slit.

01:57 So, now, we're ready to look at the diffraction pattern.

02:01 So if we have a close-up then of the screen,

02:06 we see the diffraction pattern for the slit separation

02:10 that I have over here.

02:13 Now, the wavelength of the light,

02:18 that of the helium-neon laser 6328 angstroms--

02:22 so I gave you the separation between the slit

02:24 and the screen, which is 200 centimeters,

02:26 so now you should be able to calculate the slit width

02:30 from the diffraction pattern.

02:33 Now, to help you do this calculation,

02:36 we have, on the screen, markers.

02:40 And the separation between these markers is 5 centimeters.

02:45 So there are 5 centimeters markers on the screen.

02:47 So now you have all the tools to calculate the slit width as I

02:52 adjust the slit separation.

02:55 So let me start with a very narrow slit

03:00 where the central lobe is--

03:03 you can make it almost 5 centimeters or so.

03:07 And you see the other lobes, the weaker one.

03:09 And maybe if we can overexpose a little bit,

03:11 we can see that, indeed, there are lots of lobes.

03:17

03:21 But if we expose for all of them,

03:24 then the central one is going to get way overexposed.

03:28 So, in general, we'll be looking just at a few of them.

03:32 So, now, let's go back to where we were before.

03:35 And then we'll start again at a slit width

03:40 so that the central lobe is about a few centimeters wide.

03:45 And then I will now make the spacing--

03:49 whoops-- wider.

03:53 And you can see the central lobe now

03:57 will get smaller and smaller.

04:00

04:06 And now, you can even see the spacing between the jaws.

04:10 And here we are.

04:11

04:15 You can see it gets--

04:16 the intensity is so high in the central lobe,

04:19 that we are saturating.

04:21 But I think this is a pretty good illustration

04:25 of the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern of a single slit.

04:32 Now that we've seen Fraunhofer diffraction pattern associated

04:36 with a single slit, we're going to make life a little bit more

04:40 complicated.

04:40 We're going to look at the diffraction

04:42 pattern of two slits.

00:00 In his 20s, he was the  untouchable God of social media,

00:03 a tech industry rockstar who turned  everything he touched into gold.

00:06 But Mark Zuckerberg’s luck has turned.

00:08 Now 42, he lost over $70 billion dollars  on a bad bet that the Metaverse would be

00:13 the future. He’s tanked his reputation with  increasingly controversial personal dealings,

00:18 and now, the platforms that built  his fortune are being smothered

00:21 under the relentless growth of AI slop content.

00:24 On paper, he’s as successful as he’s ever  been, with a $1.6 trillion market cap for

00:29 Meta Platforms Inc. as of late 2025, but the  ground is secretly collapsing under his feet.

00:35 The problem is… he might just take the  whole internet as we know it with him.

00:39 Inside the corporate structure of Meta, that “God  of social media” thing is a lot more literal than

00:44 you might expect. While Zuck only has 13% to 14%  of the stock locked down, he can still control the

00:50 whole company with an iron fist. It’s all thanks  to the ingenious mechanism of Dual-Class Shares,

00:55 which is basically a division of first and  second class shareholders. In a single class

00:59 share system, one share is one vote, whoever owns  the most has inordinate control over the company.

01:05 But in a Dual-Class Share system, some shares have  a higher vote rating and others.And in Meta, an

01:10 inordinate amount of those juiced up shares just  happened to be inside Zuck’s 13% to 14% holdings.

01:17 That’s because he’s got the Class B shares,  reserved for founders and insiders, which can

01:21 each count for up to 10 or more votes compared  to the Class A shares, sold to consumer grade

01:26 investors out on the stock market. He’s got 60%  percent voting power over the company thanks to

01:32 his Class B share hoard. The remainder are diluted  enough that one other person or entity couldn’t

01:37 ever hope to veto him, especially given you only  need a majority of 1% to swing a vote your way.

01:43 Even the company’s 2 top institutional  shareholders, the Vanguard Group and BlackRock,

01:48 only hold around 8.5% and 7.5% each. Most of  those are the far weaker Class A shares. These

01:55 kings of the private equity world still need to  bow to the almighty Zuck while on Meta territory.

02:00 So, what does Zuckerberg do with  his absolute control over his

02:04 industry-dominating company? Well, he turns  his company into a laboratory for some of the

02:09 riskiest corporate and technological  experiments the world has ever known…

02:12 Including the absolute disaster  that is “The Metaverse”.

02:16 It was a whole new virtual reality  where we’d do everything from shop

02:20 to socialize to work behind headsets and  digital avatars. Zuck had a reason to be

02:25 confident. But this wasn’t the first  time that a major move from Facebook

02:29 had disastrous and wide-reaching  ramifications for the whole internet.

02:33 Facebook was one of the major drivers  behind the internet phenomenon called

02:36 “Pivot to Video”. By touting the incredible  impressions of their short form video platform,

02:41 Facebook sparked a mass cull of internet writing  jobs. That one move effectively killed written

02:47 articles on the internet. It all happened in 2015,  when Zuck’s word was so strong in the corporate

02:52 world that his claims about Facebook’s  impressions didn’t even need to be true.

02:56 Facebook was sued for lying about  its metrics, or at the very least,

03:00 seriously miscalculating them. In order  to woo advertisers, whose money controls

03:04 everything on the internet, he claimed  not only huge view numbers but impressive

03:08 view durations. The actual average they  counted for these extended duration views?

03:13 Anything over 3 seconds.

03:16 Everyone had been duped… but it didn’t matter.

03:18 Facebook was still on top and  they’d practically murdered an

03:21 entire internet industry over some fudged stats.

03:24 Who’s to say that lightning couldn’t strike  twice for Zuck, and have him kill social media

03:29 as we know it and replace it with his very  own private Matrix? He was so certain that

03:33 this would be a win that in 2021, the Facebook  Company officially changed its name to Meta.

03:38 But would all this hype actually take the  Metaverse from science fiction to science fact?

03:43 The heart of Zuck’s most painful losses here is  Meta’s “Reality Labs” division. Originally the VR

03:48 company “Oculus” founded by Palmer Luckey in 2012,  Facebook would acquire the business in 2014 for

03:54 $400 million in cash and 23.1 million common  shares, valued at $1.6 billion. In 2020,

04:03 Oculus was rolled into the emerging  division of Facebook Reality Labs,

04:06 the research and development squad who would  build the architecture of the Metaverse.

04:10 Except that isn’t how any  of this played out at all.

04:14 While exact numbers differ depending on the  accounting, most sources agree that the Reality

04:18 Labs have had to swallow at least a brutal $73  billion in losses since being founded. That’s

04:24 “Billion”, with a “B.” In late 2025, Zuck  seemed to notice how much trouble he was in,

04:29 and cut 30% of Metaverse funding to  reallocate to more profitable ventures.

04:34 With 3.5 billion monthly users across all of  its apps and platforms - Facebook, Instagram,

04:38 WhatsApp, and more - Zuck had every reason to  think he could pull this off. It doesn’t matter

04:43 that for most people, high-end VR is prohibitively  expensive and a barrier to mass adoption. Nor did

04:49 it matter that the graphics on their Metaverse  platform, “Meta Horizon Worlds”, looked about 10

04:54 to 15 years behind the current standard. When it  shipped, none of the avatar characters had legs.

05:00 But that didn’t matter.

05:01 The common tech industry motto is “move fast and  break things”, it’s practically become a cliche.

05:06 The person who coined the phrase was actually  Mark Zuckerberg himself. It’s a way of saying,

05:11 “Barrel in and worry about the consequences  later”. It’s the exact mentality that kept

05:15 the Reality Labs team moving forward  despite all the evidence pointing to

05:18 their task being completely fruitless in the  long run. Instead of profits, the attempt at

05:23 a Metaverse spawned countless mocking memes.  Comparisons to the previous tech that everyone

05:27 insisted would be world-changing,  NFTs and the Blockchain, were rife.

05:32 The irony of Zuckerberg’s humiliating Metaverse  failure is that partial metaverses have existed

05:36 for years. They still run successfully  today in places like Second Life, VR Chat,

05:41 MMORPGs like World of Warcraft, and even  Fortnite in its non-combat modes. Ultimately,

05:47 Facebook was late to the party, and lost so  many billions for breaking the fundamental rule

05:51 of good business: Only make products that  fill a need your customers actually have.

05:57 And really, not enough people want to have

05:59 to wear a VR headset to clock  in at work or go to the bank.

06:03 It’s almost hard to believe but back in 2004, when  it was first founded, the intention was to make

06:08 Facebook “cool.” It started on American college  campuses before anywhere else, running on pure

06:14 FOMO. Anyone who was anyone was encouraged to join  up so they wouldn’t be left behind by their friend

06:19 group. This method worked wonders, leading to the  website logging over a billion users in 2012. Even

06:25 as recently as 2024, it’s got a genuinely  phenomenal 98% brand recognition rating.

06:31 But this picture gets a lot less rosy when you  look at the stats for members of Gen Z. 17% of

06:37 the general population says they love Facebook  and plan on continuing using the product,

06:42 but on these metrics for Gen Z, it’s only 3%.  Facebook isn’t the exciting platform anymore,

06:48 with 45% of Gen Z users saying that they  mainly keep it just to keep up with relatives.

06:53 BrandVue Media found that in 2023, 3 out of  4 Gen Z users would be happy to give it up.

06:59 So, what does this mean for the future of Meta?

07:01 It’s a little more complex than you think. Gen Z  on the whole are moving away from social media,

07:06 with the old guards like Facebook being  the hardest hit. But where are they all

07:11 going? Gen Z aren’t kids anymore,  a lot of them are in their 20's,

07:14 and Gen Alpha is slowly becoming the most  lucrative market. The kings of social media

07:18 for Gen Z and Alpha are, of course, TikTok… and  Instagram, which has a 38% audience usage rate.

07:25 So it seems the younger generations  are running straight out of one of

07:28 Mark Zuckerberg’s hands… and into the other.

07:31 But in the long run, the trends seem to  be working against the Meta Products,

07:34 as Gen Alpha largely prefers video-first apps  like TikTok and YouTube. According to Axios,

07:39 social media burnout is leading to an increase  in members of Gen Z blocking apps and buying

07:45 “dumbphones” that don’t give them connections  to apps. Could the same social media world that

07:49 Facebook invented be the atmosphere that  eventually chokes out their own user base?

07:54 But with a serial entrepreneur like  Mark Zuckerberg, even alienating your

07:58 former core demo and experiencing an  almost $100 billion failure is just

08:03 a setback. What he needed was another  pivot, another technology that he could

08:07 push all his chips forward onto and hope  that being a high roller would pay off.

08:12 And as luck would have it, the world  provided him with that technology.

08:15 In early 2026, Zuck said some now  infamous words on an earnings call:

08:20 “Soon, you'll open our apps, and you'll  have an AI that understands you, and…

08:24 show you great content or even generate  great personalized content for you.”

08:28 The word “Great” here is doing  some incredibly heavy lifting.

08:33 You’ve seen the images and videos, the ones that  feel like something straight out of a fever dream:

08:38 Jesus Christ floating underwater, his body made of  shrimps and lobsters amalgamated into a monster.

08:44 Thousands of comments underneath these  images all read “Amen.” In another video,

08:49 Jesus pushes Satan in a wheelchair off  of the side of a cliff. Buff humanoid

08:53 cats save babies that have fallen off the  Golden Gate Bridge. And in an aquarium,

08:58 a gleeful woman watches a disgusting  human-seal-monster swim around.

09:02 This is the kind of insane AI slop  that’s infested Meta services like

09:06 Facebook and Instagram. It’s gotten so bad

09:08 that there’s a whole “rFacebookAISlop”  subreddit with almost 200,000 members.

09:13 While AI slop is rife thanks to AI being  the shareholder-friendly buzzword across

09:17 the tech industry, few CEOs have  embraced it as enthusiastically as

09:21 Mark Zuckerberg… Just like he previously  embraced the Metaverse. He called it the

09:26 “Third Phase” of social media. What does that  mean, and what was the first and second phase?

09:30 Zuck himself had the answers.

09:32 “First was when all content was from  friends, family, and accounts that you

09:36 followed directly. The second was when we  added all of the creator content. Now as AI

09:41 makes it easier to create and remix content…  we'll see an explosion of new media formats

09:45 that are more immersive and interactive, and  only possible because of advances in AI.”

09:50 Clearly the proof is in the pudding,  because this stuff is absolutely everywhere.

09:54 These pages aren’t all surreal and silly, some  of them are genuinely extremely disturbing.

10:00 Take Anita Kumari, an Instagram account that  specializes in the spreading of “misery porn”

10:05 content: Skeletal, impoverished people  starving to death, being eaten by bugs,

10:10 or dying in the midst of disaster or  disease. All of them are fully AI generated,

10:15 with well over 100,000 followers.  The whole point is to exploit the

10:19 audience’s emotions to get engagement,  and the scariest part is… it works.

10:23 A popular subgenre of this kind of AI slop is the  “Birthday Cake”. This will often show a diseased,

10:29 emaciated, and even disfigured person,  usually a child, a war vet or an old woman,

10:34 carrying a birthday cake. There will often be  the heartstring-tugging message that nobody

10:38 came to their birthday party, so won’t you  wish them a happy birthday in the comments?

10:43 There are videos that use unspeakable racial  stereotypes that we can’t even describe here,

10:48 let alone show any footage of. Fake videos  of massive explosions, natural disasters,

10:53 murders, police shootings, terrorist attacks.  The most messed up thing is, if you find yourself

10:58 watching in horror as these videos unfold,  you’re only going to be shown more of them.

11:02 According to Facebook’s vice president of product,  Jagjit Chawla, “If you… are interested in a piece

11:07 of content which happens to be AI-generated, the  recommendations algorithm will determine that,

11:12 over time, you are interested in this topic and  content. If you are not into it… and if you have

11:17 given us signals that this is not for you,  that algorithm will respond appropriately...”

11:21 The only way you can really show that it’s  “not for you” is to scroll away as quickly as

11:26 possible. But, by the time you’ve stuck around  long enough to figure out what’s going on,

11:30 it’s already gotten the algorithmic hook into you.

11:33 If Facebook is drowning in AI slop content,

11:35 then what caused a leak to spring in  its previously pretty reliable hull?

11:39 It might not surprise you to hear that  the call is coming from inside the house.

11:44 Facebook and its own incentive structures are  the ones behind the slopocalypse. Thanks to

11:49 Facebook’s Creator Bonus Program, engagement can  equate to cold, hard cash for the posters. But

11:55 it’s at rates that most influencers on YouTube  and TikTok wouldn’t consider worth the effort.

11:59 When you factor in currency conversion, and  the low overhead of creating this slop content,

12:04 it can be a huge passive income generator  for people in places like Pakistan, India,

12:09 Vietnam, Thailand, and Indonesia.  The process has been industrialized,

12:13 with different monetized accounts posting dozens  of Shrimp Christs and wounded veterans every

12:18 single day. Sometimes they rack up views in the  millions from real users and rampant bot swarms.

12:24 Not only is industrializing slop  posting becoming a cottage industry,

12:27 teaching people how to start their own slop  machines for money is a thriving business,

12:32 too. The tools and tutorials are being sold  online to anyone who wants to start posting.

12:36 They give aspiring posters the means to  avoid spam detection systems on the site

12:41 and consistently produce viral content that’s  worked for other, similar spammers in the past.

12:46 The result is a problem that  keeps propagating itself,

12:49 making Facebook more unpleasant  and unusable bit by bit.

12:52 The slop problem from both content creators  and audience bots on Facebook has gotten so

12:57 bad that it’s fed into an increasingly popular  movement called “Dead Internet Theory”. It’s the

13:03 existentially terrifying idea that the internet  is becoming less and less a place for living,

13:08 human users. Instead, it’s more a hive of  “Dead Zones” populated by bots interacting

13:13 with each other, not even realizing that  what they’re talking to isn’t human.

13:18 Media researcher and AI expert Thomas  Sommeror said of the proliferation effect,

13:22 “Just as Jesus was supposedly the  messenger for God, Shrimp Jesus is

13:26 the messenger for the fatal system [we've]  maneuvered ourselves into. Decoupled,

13:31 proliferated, and in a state  of exponential metastasis.”

13:34 Metastasis really is the key word here, because  AI is the cancer spreading through Facebook,

13:39 rotting it away from within.  And it isn’t just content,

13:42 AI on Facebook is also replacing the  social component of social networking,

13:46 with the option to generate an AI response to  group posts by tagging @MetaAI. The AI will also

13:52 step in if the original post included a question  and this question wasn’t answered by anyone within

13:58 an hour. It’s like Facebook groups are now  haunted by these staring digital ghosts. And

14:03 this isn’t some conspiracy theory, it’s what top  employees of Meta have said proudly and publicly.

14:09 Connor Hayes, vice-president of  product for generative AI at Meta,

14:12 said, “We expect these AIs to actually,  over time, exist on our platforms,

14:17 kind of in the same way that accounts  do ... They'll have bios and profile

14:20 pictures and be able to generate and share  content powered by AI on the platform.”

14:24 This all started back in late 2023, with a  collection of celebrity AI chatbots including

14:30 Snoop Dogg and Mr. Beast, and everyone  absolutely hated it. So much so that in

14:35 July 2024, Facebook scrapped the idea of  officially licensed celebrity chatbots,

14:39 and instead opened an AI Studio for their  userbase to create their own AI chatbots.

14:44 This also quickly got out of control.

14:47 Despite Facebook insisting on stringent  moderation for its Chatbots, user generated

14:52 Chatbots were every bit as bizarre and  sinister as the slop content started

14:56 showing up. Bots were called Adolf Hitler,  Jesus Christ, and of course, Taylor Swift.

15:01 Before the Facebook and Instagram moderation  teams took them down, if you messaged Taylor

15:05 Swift - spelled “Taylor Swif” to get around  restrictions - she would first reply,

15:10 “Hey there, music lovers! I’m Taylor Swift, and  I’m thrilled to share my latest album with you.

15:15 Let’s get this musical journey started!”  She exchanged over 2000 different messages

15:19 with users before being taken down.  Jesus was even more egregious, saying,

15:23 “Peace be with you. I am Jesus Christ, the Son of  God. How may I guide you on your journey today?”

15:28 But these are extremely small time compared to  some of the more highly used AIs on Facebook.

15:33 Some of the top ones at the height of  the application’s popularity in early

15:36 2025 were "Astrologer AI”, which boasted  over 6 million messages with people in

15:42 January of that year. Second most popular was  “Step Sis Sarah”, which had around 2 million.

15:47 Meta creating and then immediately needing to  roll back its AI tools after massive consumer

15:52 backlash has continued with another  high profile incident in July of 2026.

15:57 Meta published its “Muse Image” tool, a new  generative AI feature that, among other things,

16:02 would allow users to utilize and  alter the photo content of users

16:05 on Facebook and Instagram. In other words, if  someone wanted to use your profile picture,

16:10 or the photos on your marriage announcement,  your vacation photos, or the memorial post

16:14 for a relative to make their own AI generated  content, Muse Image would allow them to do it.

16:19 With zero friction.

16:21 After all, that’s not your content  anymore. You put it on a Meta platform,

16:25 so it belongs to Meta. All Instagram  users were opted in by default.

16:29 It feels a million miles away from  Facebook’s original mission statement,

16:33 of providing a way for friends to connect online  and stay up to date with each other’s lives. But

16:37 Meta has consistently said that going so all-in  on AI is the only way for them to keep up with

16:43 their competitors in the social media space.  But it’s going to have some nasty consequences

16:47 for their bottom line in the long run… even if  shareholders love it in the immediate future.

16:52 There are two key differences between real and AI  users on Facebook and Instagram. These differences

16:57 are a huge problem for Mark Zuckerberg  and everyone else at Meta: Number one,

17:01 companies don’t want to pay to advertise to AI  users on either of these platforms. Number two,

17:07 no companies will be interested in purchasing  the personal data of AI users on either site,

17:11 too. So as AI begins to outnumber human beings,

17:15 you see Facebook’s business model collapse  like a house eaten from the inside by termites.

17:20 And the problems seem to be as much  from the inside out as the outside.

17:24 Leaks from Meta’s new Applied AI division  seem to show that the employees working

17:28 there are utterly miserable, and aren’t seeing  larger benefits to their work. Quotes include,

17:33 “it's literally a gulag”, you have  “zero purpose in life all of a sudden,

17:38 you barely interact with anyone”, and  “you just have these tasks every week.”

17:42 It’s hard to even express how much money Meta is  sinking into AI development. In 2026 alone, it’s

17:47 forecasting between $125 billion and $145 billion  on AI capital expenditures. That’s 88% higher than

17:56 2025 even measuring from the midpoint between  the two figures, and the equivalent to over half

18:02 of Zuck’s $231 billion net worth. But in July of  2026, Zuck admitted that the spectacular results

18:09 he’d hoped for his AI spending hadn’t come into  fruition yet. Meta’s stock dropped 5% as a result.

18:15 In early 2026, they “streamlined”, laying  off around 8,000 employees, around 10% of

18:21 their workforce, while moving another 7,000  into that new AI division. And what do they

18:26 have to show for it so far outside of exciting  the shareholders? Products like Muse Image,

18:31 that everyone hates so much that the backlash  immediately sends them back to the drawing board.

18:35 Tristia Hennessey, a senior strategist  at Portland-based Evolve Solutions Group,

18:40 said, “If you think you're rolling out AI  responsibly, you better be thinking beyond

18:44 the best possible use case. Meta/Instagram's  fiasco with their Muse tool had real-life

18:49 consequences… Serious financial and health  consequences for hundreds of people. And it

18:54 was all legal… There's no protection for victims.  If you think you're safe, you're being naive.”

18:59 But who’s really being naive  here, and who’s really in danger?

19:03 Anyone who’s been following the activities of  Mark Zuckerberg and his companies will be able

19:07 to tell you a laundry list of awful things  they’ve all been involved with. On the more

19:12 minor end, knowing that Instagram has horrific  effects on the mental healths of teen users,

19:17 Facebook conducting psychological tests on 700,000  unconsenting participants in 2012. They were also

19:23 fined over $5 billion by the Federal Trade  Commission for violations of user privacy.

19:28 And on the more severe end, it  gets a lot darker than that.

19:32 In 2020, Sophie Zhang, a former Facebook  data scientist, blew the whistle that

19:36 the company allowed foreign nations to  interfere in elections by manipulating

19:41 data on the platform. This would track  with Facebook’s own part in the meddling

19:44 in domestic elections. It was implicated  in the Cambridge Analytica scandal that

19:49 used vast swathes of Facebook user data to  craft manipulative political ad campaigns,

19:54 and its refusal to fact check posts made on  the platform by politicians in election season.

19:59 All of that pales in comparison to the  worst thing Facebook has ever done:

20:04 Stoking the fires of hatred that led  to the Rohingya massacre in Myanmar,

20:08 a literal modern day genocide. How could something  like that possibly happen? Part of it is buried

20:14 in the code of Facebook itself: It wants to  keep you on the platform as long as possible,

20:18 so the content that gets engagement gets  boosted… even if that content is baying

20:23 for the blood of a persecuted minority  group and pretexting horrifying bloodshed.

20:28 But evidence found by Amnesty International  suggests that the whole truth might actually

20:32 be even worse than irresponsible,  amoral code. Facebook was warned,

20:36 multiple times, about the hate  it was stoking and did nothing,

20:40 probably fearing it would affect their bottom  line. They refused calls to hire local content

20:45 moderators who could spot and control the  rampant hate speech, and when the massacre

20:49 unfolded in 2017, over 700,000 Rohingya  had to flee truly nightmarish violence.

20:55 Pat de Brún, researcher and adviser on artificial  intelligence and human rights at Amnesty, said,

21:00 “These algorithms are really dangerous  to our human rights… what happened to

21:04 the Rohingya and Facebook's role in that  specific conflict risks happening again,

21:08 in many different contexts across the  world. The company has shown itself

21:12 completely unwilling or incapable of resolving  the root causes of its human rights impact.”

21:18 Mark Zuckerberg has blood on his hands, but  despite his series of bad bets in the past,

21:23 his fortune seems to be going strong.  But will this be the final straw? As

21:27 Zuck keeps doubling down on what  he believes is the next big thing,

21:30 do we get closer and closer to the  day when he actually goes bust?

21:34 Want more on some of America’s most obnoxious  rich guys? Then check out “Real Reason Why

21:38 Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg Hate  Each Other”, or watch this instead!
