docs.text:
00:00 The FBI is the United States' premier law enforcement agency, and has responsibilities

00:04 that range from counter-terrorism to drug interdiction and investigating financial crimes.

00:10 With such a broad range of responsibilities, it's only natural that FBI agents are going

00:14 to come across a wide variety of suspects, and this makes FBI interrogators some of the

00:18 most skilled in the world.

00:20 Today we're going to teach you some basic interrogation techniques used by the FBI and

00:24 other agencies that you can use in everyday life to get to the truth of the matter, or

00:28 perhaps figure out when someone is lying to you or not.

00:32 First though, it's important to note that there's a difference between an interrogation

00:35 and an interview.

00:36 An interview is typically a fact-finding mission, while an interrogation is much more focused.

00:41 In an interview, the interrogator is typically not fully aware of most of the elements of

00:46 a crime, and is seeking more general information about the events that took place.

00:50 Interviews are commonly undertaken with witnesses, though sometimes suspects can be interviewed

00:54 as well, and based off information gleaned, an interview can later turn into a full-blown

00:59 interrogation.

01:00 An interrogation on the other hand is a quest for specific information, or an attempt to

01:04 gain a confession.

01:06 In an interrogation, the person conducting the proceeding is typically aware of most

01:10 facts of a case or incident, and is simply seeking specific key pieces that may still

01:14 be missing.

01:15 An interrogation can also serve to force a suspect into admitting that they lied in a

01:20 previous interview, or to encourage them to divulge facts they are reluctant to.

01:24 Finally, an interrogator may be perfectly aware of all the facts of a case, and simply

01:28 use an interrogation to gain a confession.

01:30 Despite what you might think, the FBI does not endorse overly aggressive interrogations,

01:35 and instead it is department policy that establishing a rapport with an individual is far more productive

01:40 to fact gathering than intimidation, misdirection, or threats.

01:44 In the early 2000s when the Abu Ghraib prison scandal broke out and the world learned that

01:49 the CIA and the US military had been beating prisoners to gain information, The United

01:53 States Inspector General announced that the FBI had always conducted itself according

01:57 to department guidelines.

01:58 In fact, many FBI interrogators flat-out refused to take part in interrogations that used,

02:04 as the CIA and the military put it, 'enhanced interrogation techniques', and walked out

02:09 of interrogations, then reported the individuals to their superiors.

02:13 This integrity from the FBI is what helped bring the scandal to light, and put a stop

02:17 to the abuses by military and CIA personnel.

02:20 So how can you better get at the truth in your own life?

02:23 What techniques can you learn and apply to use day to day?

02:27 First, a former FBI agent and interrogator warns that you should always be aware of as

02:31 many of the facts of what you're seeking information on as possible.

02:34 If a suspect believes that the interrogator is grasping at straws or not fully aware of

02:39 events, then the tone of the interrogation dramatically changes.

02:42 This might encourage a suspect to be deceitful, or embolden them to withhold facts.

02:47 So say that you're interrogating your co-worker, Kelly, because your food has gone missing

02:51 from the refrigerator and you suspect it was her.

02:54 First, make sure you're as well informed as you can possibly be before you start your

02:58 interrogation.

03:00 This means gathering intelligence on Kelly- what does she typically eat?

03:03 What does she like to eat?

03:04 When does she typically eat?

03:06 Are there witnesses that can perhaps let you know if she was at her desk or not around

03:10 the time your lunch went missing?

03:11 More mundane details are important as well, such as the general state of the refrigerator

03:16 when the sandwich went missing, how many other people brought food, how many ordered in...

03:20 basically the more facts you're aware of, the better.

03:22 When most people are confronted in a situation where their interrogator is obviously well-informed,

03:27 it can act as an intimidating force, making them feel that deceitfulness will not work

03:32 on you.

03:33 Also, the more obviously well-informed you are, the more the suspect will realize that

03:36 you're willing to sit down for an extensive discussion, and might make them feel like

03:41 it would just be better to give up the goods early.

03:43 You've probably seen cop shows on tv where the investigator will lay out a cunning trap

03:48 for a suspect they're sure committed a crime.

03:50 Typically the detective will lie about evidence they possess, making the suspect fear that

03:54 he's about to be discovered and might as well give himself, or herself up.

03:58 While there are some instances where lying is allowed for police interrogators, it's

04:02 not recommended that you do so.

04:04 Your lie may work, but if it doesn't and the suspect realizes you're lying, it can backfire

04:08 in a major way.

04:10 Once you've lied to a suspect and they've realized it, they'll become convinced that

04:13 they can't trust you, and clam up.

04:15 They could also assume that any plea deals or offers of amnesty are also lies, and you

04:21 effectively take away any leverage you might have over them.

04:24 You know Kelly took that sandwich, you can see the crumbs on the corner of her mouth

04:27 and smell the chicken parmesan on her breath- but if you lie to her and tell her that you

04:32 have security camera footage of the deed, she might realize you're full of it.

04:36 In that case, your interrogation is over, and Kelly is walking away a free woman- or,

04:40 a woman that doesn't owe you a sandwich since we're pretty sure sandwich theft isn't a criminal

04:45 offense.

04:46 Rather than trying to trick or intimidate a suspect, former FBI interrogators state

04:49 that you should build a rapport with the suspect instead.

04:52 If the suspect learns that they can trust you, or at least respect you, they might be

04:56 more prone to sharing information they wouldn't with anyone else.

04:59 Also, in the criminal system a suspect that has good rapport with the interrogator may

05:04 believe that the interrogator will later tell the prosecutor that they were helpful, and

05:08 thus reduce their criminal penalty.

05:10 You want to slam a book down on the table, maybe toss a chair or two.

05:14 It's time for good cop, bad cop, because now Kelly burped and you could practically taste

05:18 the chicken parm yourself.

05:20 Yet she won't admit it, she steadfastly refuses to take the blame for the missing sandwich.

05:24 So rein in your anger and center yourself.

05:26 Be courteous, ask her about her typical lunch, share some of the same interests that you

05:30 have together as far as food is concerned.

05:33 You'll be working to drop Kelly's guard and at the same time she'll be thinking that if

05:36 you're this nice to her now, maybe you'll put in a good word with the boss when it comes

05:40 time to punishing the person responsible for chicken parm theft.

05:44 Now it's time to turn up the heat, it's time for the Reid technique.

05:48 Developed by a professional consultant and polygraph expert named John E. Reid, the Reid

05:52 technique is one of the most widely adopted interrogation techniques across the world.

05:57 The first step is to confront the suspect with the facts, as well as the evidence against

06:01 them.

06:02 Tell Kelly that your sandwich went missing, and that during the fifteen minutes that it

06:05 went missing, she was not at her desk according to fellow co-workers.

06:09 Further, let her know that you're aware of the fact that last friday she ordered chicken

06:13 parmesan from Grubhub.

06:14 Be confident and start letting Kelly know that you know she was involved in the theft.

06:18 Her stress levels will begin to rise, and if she's being deceitful you should be on

06:22 the lookout for fidgeting, licking of lips, or touching of hair- these are all signs that

06:27 Kelly ate your damn chicken parm and is lying to you about it.

06:30 Next step is called theme development, and here is where you'll weave a story about why

06:34 Kelly committed the crime that she did.

06:36 You'll re-tell the criminal act, but with Kelly as the main character.

06:40 You should speak to her in a soft, soothing voice, appearing non-threatening and lulling

06:44 Kelly into a false sense of security.

06:46 Be aware of how she reacts to your theme as you lay it out, and if it becomes clear that

06:50 she isn't responding at all, change the story up and try again.

06:53 This will make up the bulk of your interrogation, and you'll be using the other techniques to

06:57 reinforce this step.

06:58 Kelly forgot her lunch that day, so she figured, well I'll just order something on my phone

07:03 again.

07:04 Then lunch time came though and Kelly realized that she has T-mobile as a cell provider,

07:08 and that means she doesn't have service ever, anywhere.

07:11 Oh no, Kelly thought, what am I going to do for lunch now?!

07:14 That's when she went to the employee refrigerator, opening it and hoping that perhaps there was

07:18 a stray cup of yogurt someone never ate, perhaps something close to expiration date, left alone

07:24 and forgotten.

07:25 Nobody would miss that lonely cup of yogurt.

07:28 But that's when she saw it, your delicious chicken parmesan on sourdough bread.

07:32 Next to the refrigerator, the microwave... and down the hall, an unused storage closet-

07:36 the perfect place to hide and enjoy an ill-gotten chicken parmesan sandwich.

07:41 Kelly could practically taste the melting cheese... it was either this, or eat nothing

07:45 at all, and her stomach was rumbling.

07:47 She's not a bad person, she just had a small breakfast is all...

07:50 See what we did there?

07:51 We created a theme that was sympathetic to Kelly's plight, recreated events from a point

07:56 of view that didn't treat Kelly like the dirty, rotten criminal that she actually is.

08:00 We excused her theft, appealed to her sense of helplessness in the situation, let her

08:04 believe that we understood and were sympathetic to the theft.

08:07 Throughout your building of the theme though, you'll have to stop Kelly's denials on the

08:11 spot.

08:12 Once a suspect is allowed to voice a denial, it increases their confidence.

08:15 Every time Kelly tries to object and voice a denial, simply cut her off and let her know

08:19 it'll be her turn to talk in a minute.

08:21 Don't let her start to voice denials or she'll become emboldened and immune to your tactics.

08:26 Be polite, but very firm.

08:28 Next, you'll have to be ready to overcome objections, which differ from denials.

08:33 Denials are basically just brief, “I didn't do it!”

08:35 statements.

08:36 Objections however offer logic-based reasons for why the suspect simply couldn't have committed

08:40 the crime.

08:41 Kelly might say, “I could never have stolen your sandwich, my father died of starvation

08:44 because someone stole his sandwich!”

08:46 It's your job to use the information she gives you and turn it around on her.

08:50 You can for instance reply with, “I understand that you could never plan to do something

08:54 so awful after what happened to your father, it was just a one-time mistake, you were hungry,

08:58 and out of control.

08:59 I understand.”

09:01 You should turn objections into admissions of guilt.

09:03 At this point, Kelly is frustrated, she's literally marinating in her own guilt.

09:07 It's your job to vent some of that pressure, and earn more of her trust.

09:11 This whole time you should have been either across the table from Kelly, or walking around

09:15 the room, towering over her.

09:17 That makes her feel smaller, and vulnerable, but now you're going to sit down on her side

09:21 of the table, lower yourself to her level and draw close.

09:24 Put a hand on her shoulder and offer physical gestures of concern.

09:27 Now it's time to get your confession, it's time to build alternatives.

09:31 At this stage, you offer two different motives for the crime.

09:34 One should be more reasonable, so as to nudge the suspect along, while the other should

09:38 be more morally repugnant- this will help the suspect agree to the more reasonable motivation

09:42 and lead to confession.

09:44 It doesn't matter if this motivation is real or not, all that matters is the almighty confession.

09:49 Tell Kelly that perhaps she stole the sandwich because she just couldn't resist the temptation,

09:53 heck you couldn't resist the temptation of that snicker's bar you ate last night even

09:57 though you're supposed to be dieting!

09:59 This motive is understandable, and relatable, it's something that a rational, reasonable

10:04 person could excuse.

10:05 It's just a mistake, that's all!

10:07 Then tell Kelly that perhaps she stole the sandwich because it was her that stole her

10:11 father's sandwich which led to his death by starvation.

10:14 Perhaps Kelly loves to starve people to death, one sandwich at a time, and she thought she

10:18 could get away with it again today!

10:20 This motive is outrageous, and morally repugnant, likely causing Kelly to object loudly to it-

10:28 her down the road of the first motive.

10:34 such a nice person.

10:35 You were just hungry, it was a mistake, I understand.

10:38 At this point, Kelly's probably in tears, and more than ready to confess.

10:44 Because you've just used FBI interrogation techniques to get your co-worker to confess

10:48 to stealing your sandwich- and it's good that you have a solid grasp on these techniques

01:01 engine converts gasoline into forward

01:05 that most of us never need to learn the

01:07 ugly details. We plug a cable into a

01:09 switch, the little lights begin

01:10 blinking, and gigabits of data

01:12 obediently race around the building. The

01:14 collisions are gone, the signaling is

01:18 disagreeable physics have been buried

01:21 clever engineering. Just look at this

01:23 early 1980s Ethernet adapter. This is

01:25 two full sixtab interl boards for my

01:28 PDP11 devoted largely to accomplishing

01:30 the physical Ethernet signaling. You

01:33 might think of Ethernet as just a cute

01:34 little chipset these days, but that

01:36 hides a lot of electronics under the

01:37 covers. And so any notions you had about

01:40 wiring up Ethernet on a breadboard with

01:42 a couple of transistors and a 555 timer

01:44 should probably be abandoned about now.

01:46 Ethernet began with some fellows in the

01:48 1970s drilling taps into thick yellow

01:50 coaxial cable, attaching entire

01:52 computers to the same shared wire and

01:54 hoping that everybody followed the same

01:56 rules. It worked, but the path from that

01:58 yellow cable to the tiny twisted pair in

02:00 your wall today is long, technically

02:02 fascinating, and completely unreasonable

02:04 as an introductory explanation. I could

02:06 therefore give you one of two

02:08 explanations of Ethernet electrical

02:09 signaling. I could give you the short

02:11 explanation, which would be useless, or

02:12 I could give you the complete

02:14 explanation, which would be uselessly

02:15 long. So instead, we're going to begin

02:17 with a network that solves many of the

02:19 same fundamental problems using

02:20 dramatically less machinery. It has no

02:23 switches, no routers, no MAC learning

02:25 tables, and no central controller

02:26 deciding who may speak. It's just a

02:28 collection of computers connected to the

02:30 same two wires, all listening to one

02:32 another, all capable of transmitting and

02:34 all somehow able to resolve the problem

02:36 when several of them decide to speak at

02:38 exactly the same time. And that network

02:40 is known as CANBUS. And CANbus is both

02:43 incredibly powerful and almost

02:44 suspiciously simple. It's the kind of

02:46 network that you might invent for a

02:48 custom LAN party using old speaker wires

02:50 where you know there will only ever be a

02:52 couple of dozen machines. None of them

02:53 is ever trying to contact a server in

02:55 Singapore. And the most important design

02:57 goal is that everybody can communicate

02:59 reliably without dragging a Cisco

03:00 certification into the room. That is

03:03 approximately the problem that can was

03:05 designed to solve. Now CAN stands for

03:07 controller area network. Bosch developed

03:10 it for communication among electronic

03:12 controllers in vehicles, publicly

03:14 introduced the protocol in 1986 and it

03:16 was later standardized internationally.

03:18 It subsequently spread well beyond cars

03:20 into factories, forklifts, agricultural

03:23 machinery, elevators, medical systems

03:25 and all manner of industrial equipment.

03:27 You experience CAN almost every time you

03:29 climb into a modern car. The engine

03:31 controller is on the CAN network. The

03:33 transmission controller is on the

03:34 network. So were the brakes, the

03:36 airbags, the steering system, the

03:37 climate control, and often several dozen

03:40 other computers that you didn't know

03:41 that you owned. And sitting directly in

03:43 front of you is the most visible member

03:44 of that network, the dashboard. The

03:46 dashboard is not necessarily the master

03:48 controller because CAN does not require

03:50 one, but it is effectively your view

03:52 into the entire operation, the task

03:55 manager of your car, if you will. Engine

03:57 speed, vehicle speed, cool and

03:59 temperature, oil pressure, transmission

04:00 state, warning lamps, traction control

04:03 activity, and dozens of other values

04:05 arrive there as network messages. And

04:07 just like Task Manager, when your car is

04:09 acting weird, the dashboard is the first

04:11 place you check. What looks like a

04:13 collection of gauges is really a display

04:15 terminal listening to an ongoing

04:16 conversation among many computers

04:18 distributed throughout the car. There's

04:20 an engine controller and sometimes a

04:22 separate transmission controller.

04:23 There's a controller for your radiator

04:25 fans, your HVAC system, your power seat,

04:29 in the car that is driven by an

04:31 electronics module. And for today's

04:33 demo, I have built a simple example of

04:35 that conversation right here on the

04:36 bench. I have two ESP32

04:38 microcontrollers, each connected through

04:40 a CAN transceiver, and sitting between

04:42 them is an engine control module from a

04:43 2015 Corvette. I have the ECM powered up

04:51 of optimism that the rest of the

04:58 control module is missing. The dashboard

05:57 it's the purple and blue wires that I

05:58 happen to grab. The signal is

06:00 differential, which means the receiver

06:02 does not primarily care about the

06:03 absolute voltage on either wire. It

06:06 cares about the voltage difference

06:07 between them. And that distinction

06:09 matters because cars are electrically

06:11 dreadful places. You have ignition

06:12 coils, injectors, electric motors,

06:14 alternators, relays, switching power

06:17 supplies, and several meters of wiring

06:19 distributed through a steel box that

06:20 moves through rain, snow, heat, cold,

06:22 vibration, and the occasional shopping

06:24 cart. Unlike my bench, it is not a

06:26 laboratory experiment. It is like an

06:29 electrical knife fight inside of a

06:30 rolling steel cage with cup holders.

06:32 Remember how I said the signal on our

06:33 two wires was differential? Well, here's

06:35 where it matters. If interference pushes

06:37 both CAN wires upward by half a volt,

06:40 the receiver can largely ignore that

06:42 because the difference between the two

06:43 wires remains the same and noise common

06:46 to both wires is thus rejected as well.

06:48 The information lives in the distance

06:50 between the signals. When high-speed CAN

06:53 transmits what it calls a dominant bit,

06:55 which represents logical zero, the

06:57 transceiver drives CAN high upward and

06:59 CAN low downward. that creates a

07:02 significant differential voltage between

07:04 the two conductors. So a big difference

07:06 means zero. When it receives a recessive

07:08 bit representing logical one, the

07:10 receiver just releases the bus and both

07:12 wires settle towards the same common

07:14 mode voltage, leaving very little

07:15 differential voltage between them.

07:17 Typical high-speed CAN transceivers bias

07:19 both lines near 2.5 volts while

07:21 recessive and then separate them during

07:23 a dominant bit. On the oscilloscope,

07:25 it's wonderfully literal. One trace

07:27 rises while the other one falls like a

07:29 pair of tiny electronic scissors opening

07:30 and closing. And if you turn on the math

07:32 function and set it to be the delta

07:34 between them, you can see the actual

07:35 bits. And that momentary motion is why

07:38 simply describing CAN high as the one

07:40 that goes high and CAN low is the one

07:42 that goes low is not quite enough.

07:44 During a recessive bit, both are sitting

07:46 in the middle. During a dominant bit,

07:48 they separate. Now, the receiver looks

07:50 at that separation, decides whether the

07:52 bus is dominant or recessive. And every

07:54 controller attached to those two same

07:56 wires sees the same thing. And since the

07:58 wire runs are short enough for all

08:00 intents and purposes, they all see the

08:02 same thing at the same time. The engine

08:04 controller can hear the transmission

08:05 controller. The transmission controller

08:11 controller. There's no Ethernet switch

08:13 in the middle forwarding selected

08:14 traffic to selected destinations. Every

08:19 every controller receives it. The

08:21 individual controllers simply decide

08:22 which messages matter to them. That

08:25 gives us a remarkably compact network.

08:27 Two wires, termination at each end, a

08:29 collection of transceivers, and a room

08:31 full of tiny computers sharing the same

08:33 electrical conversation. The termination

08:35 is important because without

08:37 termination, sending a signal down a

08:38 wire is a little bit like shouting down

08:40 a long hallway. It creates a reflection

08:42 when it hits the end of the wire, and

08:43 that reflection messes up the clean

08:45 edges of our signals. So, a typical

08:47 high-speed CANbust uses 120 ohm resistor

08:49 at each physical end of the cable. And

08:52 since those two resistors appear in

08:53 parallel when measured across the

08:54 unpowered bus, a healthy, fully

08:56 terminated network measures off on

08:58 approximately 60 ohms from CAN high to

09:00 CAN low. Now, my wires are completely

09:03 unterminated, just two colored wires

09:05 laying on the bench and everybody

09:06 connected to them, and it works, but the

09:08 run is only about a foot long. So, once

09:10 you get up to several feet or more,

09:11 you're going to need to terminate that

09:13 bus. But now we have arrived at the

09:15 fundamental problem lurking inside of

09:17 every shared communication system. What

09:19 happens when two computers begin talking

09:21 at the same time? Because sooner or

09:22 later they will. Perhaps the engine

09:24 controller wants to announce the current

09:26 RPM at precisely the same instant that

09:28 the climate controller wants to report

09:29 the cabin temperature. There is no

09:31 central coordinator issuing numbered

09:33 tickets. Both controllers see an idle

09:35 bus. Both decide that now is a perfectly

09:37 good time to transmit and both begin

09:39 placing bits onto the same wires. You've

09:42 probably heard of a network collision in

09:43 Ethernet, then it's pretty much what you

09:45 imagine. On the original shared versions

09:47 of Ethernet, if two devices transmitted

09:49 onto the same cable simultaneously, the

09:51 combined signal became unusable garbage.

09:54 Each transmitter or monitor the cable,

09:56 detected that collision, stopped

09:58 transmitting, and tried again later, and

10:00 the waiting period was deliberately

10:01 randomized. That detail matters because

10:04 if both machines simply waited the same

10:05 fixed amount of time, they would wake up

10:07 together, transmit again together,

10:09 collide again, and spend the afternoon

10:10 politely headbutting one another. So by

10:13 choosing a randomized delay, the odds

10:15 were that one machine would resume first

10:16 and claim the cable while the other was

10:18 still waiting. If they happened to

10:20 choose equivalent delays and collide it

10:22 again, the process repeated with a wider

10:24 range of possible waiting times until

10:26 chance finally separated them. And that

10:29 system worked, but it resolves

10:30 contention by destroying both

10:31 transmissions and starting over. It also

10:34 introduces tiny but real weight states.

10:36 CAN does something much simpler and I

10:38 think much more elegant. Every CAN

10:41 message begins with a unique identifier

10:42 from 0 to 247 because in standard CAN

10:45 that identifier is 11 bits wide.

10:48 Extended CAN uses 29 bits. The

10:51 identifier describes the message rather

10:52 than permanently naming the device that

10:54 sent it. So for example, engine speed

10:56 might have one identifier. Coolant

10:58 temperature might have another. Brake

11:00 status might have a third. And those

11:02 first two come from the engine

11:03 controller module and the third from the

11:05 brake controller, but each message has

11:07 its own ID. Several different

11:09 controllers could theoretically transmit

11:11 the same identifier, though a properly

11:13 designed system must ensure they do not

11:14 transmit conflicting data under that

11:16 identifier at the same time. The

11:18 identifier tells you what the message

11:20 means and just as importantly, how

11:22 urgently it gets to access the bus. And

11:24 here's the key part. The lower the

11:26 numerical identifier, the higher the

11:28 priority of the message. An urgent brake

11:30 system frame can therefore outrank a

11:32 routine climate control update without

11:33 asking any permission from any

11:35 centraluler. But how do two controllers

11:37 transmit simultaneously without one

11:39 stomping on the other? And this is the

11:41 part of CAN that made me fall in love

11:42 with it when I first understood how it

11:44 worked. There is only one unusual

11:46 electrical rule to remember. If anybody

11:48 writes a zero, zero wins because it's

11:50 pushing those lines apart, right? zero

11:52 stops all over ones which are basically

11:54 do nothing on the wire which would cause

11:55 it to settle. So as long as somebody's

11:57 running a zero, those lines will

11:59 separate their voltages and everybody

12:00 will see a zero. Can call zero the

12:03 dominant state and one the lines

12:05 together the recessive state. If I

12:08 transmit zero while you transmit one,

12:10 everybody sees zero on the bus. If you

12:13 transmit a zero while I transmit one,

12:15 everybody still sees zero. A recessive

12:17 one appears only when every controller

12:19 currently transmitting allows the bus to

12:21 remain recessive. Each CAN controller

12:23 also listens to the bus while it is

12:25 talking. So when two controllers begin

12:27 transmitting at the same instance, they

12:29 both start by sending the identifier of

12:31 their message, beginning with the most

12:33 significant bit. As long as they send

12:35 two identical bits, neither knows

12:37 there's any competition, and everything

12:38 continues along. They may both send

12:40 zero, observe zero, and continue. Or

12:42 they may both send one, observe one, and

12:44 continue again. But because they have

12:46 different IDs, eventually they reach the

12:47 first bit where their identifiers

12:49 differ. One controller transmits a

12:52 dominant zero. The other transmits its

12:54 recessive one. The bus becomes zero. The

12:57 controller that sent the zero reads back

12:59 zero sees exactly what it expected and

13:01 continues transmitting. But the

13:03 controller that sent a one reads back

13:04 zero and immediately realizes that it

13:06 has lost arbitration. Another message

13:09 has a lower numerical identifier and

13:10 therefore a higher priority. So it's

13:12 time to shut up and be quiet. The losing

13:15 controller stops transmitting, becomes a

13:17 receiver, and waits for its next

13:18 opportunity. And that's all there is to

13:20 it. No frame was corrupted. No collision

13:23 recovery was required. Nobody generated

13:26 a random delay. The winning frame

13:28 continues as though nothing unusual ever

13:29 happened. And importantly, there is no

13:31 retry. The original message makes it out

13:33 unscathed the first time, the first

13:35 attempt. And better yet, they all come

13:37 out in perfect priority order. The CAN

13:40 specification calls this non-destructive

13:42 bitwise arbitration. A controller loses

13:45 when it transmits recessive but observes

13:47 dominance during the arbitration field

13:49 at which point it withdraws without

13:51 corrupting the winning frame. The reason

13:53 this works is wonderfully compact. At

13:55 the first differing bit, the identifier

13:57 containing zero must be numerically

13:59 smaller than the identifier containing

14:00 one because the identifier is being

14:03 transmitted from its most significant

14:04 end. The electrical properties of the

14:06 bus therefore perform a binary

14:08 comparison among all competing

14:09 identifiers in real time. The network

14:12 does not merely discover which message

14:13 is higher priority. The wires actually

14:15 calculated and that is an important

14:17 distinction. The device itself did not

14:20 win. The message with the identifier

14:22 101. On the next transmission, the very

14:24 same device could send a lower priority

14:26 status frame and lose to another

14:28 controller. Priority belongs to the

14:30 message, not permanently to the machine

14:31 or to the device. This gives CAN an

14:34 elegant form of real-time scheduling.

14:36 Important frames naturally move ahead of

14:38 less important ones. And if the bus is

14:40 lightly loaded, everybody speaks out

14:41 almost immediately. As the bus becomes

14:43 busy, lower priority frames experience

14:46 more delay while higher priority frames

14:48 remain responsive. And the cool part is

14:50 that when the bus is busy, the message

14:51 automatically comes through sorted in

14:53 priority order just by virtue of when

14:55 they are allowed to communicate. And

14:57 that is extremely useful in a car where

14:58 not all information is equally urgent.

15:01 The fact that you press the volume up

15:02 button does matter. The fact that a

15:04 wheel has suddenly stopped rotating

15:06 while the other three continue at

15:07 highway speed probably matters more. But

15:09 priority also introduces a danger. A

15:12 defective or hostile controller that

15:14 continuously transmits valid frames with

15:16 a low ID can consume most of the bus

15:18 bandwidth. Other controllers may remain

15:20 electrically functional and perfectly

15:22 willing to communicate yet rarely or

15:23 never get the chance. Canon includes

15:26 robust mechanisms for dealing with

15:27 maleformed frames and electrically

15:29 broken controllers, but a device

15:30 transmitting valid, correctly formatted,

15:33 high priority message is not necessarily

15:35 violating the protocol. From CAN's

15:37 perspective, it might simply have an

15:38 endless supply of extremely important

15:40 news. So Ken assumes a substantially

15:43 more trusted environment than the public

15:45 internet, which is okay because the

15:46 participating devices are generally

15:48 designed as components of one machine

15:50 installed by its manufacturer and

15:52 expected to cooperate, which is a

15:54 perfectly reasonable assumption right up

15:55 until somebody attaches an untrusted

15:57 device to the diagnostic connector under

15:59 the dash. Before we get to security,

16:01 however, we need to look at what happens

16:02 after arbitration. Once a message has

16:05 one control of the bus, it sends its

16:07 control information, data, air checking

16:09 fields, acknowledgement, and end of

16:11 frame markers. Classic CAN carries as

16:14 many as eight, count them, eight

16:15 databytes in one frame. Now, I get that

16:17 eight bytes does not sound like much

16:19 when your desktop computer routinely

16:21 moves gigabytes around, but it's enough

16:22 for the kind of compact measurements and

16:24 commands that CAN was created to carry.

16:27 After all, an engine speed message does

16:28 not need a JPEG attachment. It may need

16:31 two bytes for RPM, another bite

16:32 containing flags, and perhaps a rolling

16:34 counter and enough context established

16:36 by the vehicle's private message

16:38 definition to make sense of it.

16:39 Importantly, CAN does not itself dictate

16:41 what those eight bytes mean. That's up

16:43 to the sender and any interested

16:45 receivers. And it is one of the most

16:47 important conceptual boundaries in the

16:48 whole system. CAN defines how a frame

16:50 gets onto the wire, how it wins

16:52 arbitration, how receivers detect

16:54 errors, and how the network corrects and

16:56 contains faulty nodes. It does not tell

16:58 you identifier 0x1 A0 contains engine

17:01 speed in bytes three and four scale by

17:03 one quarter of an RPM. That meeting

17:05 belongs to a higher layer protocol or in

17:07 many vehicles to a manufacturer's

17:09 private database. And that is why

17:11 attaching a CAN analyzer to a car

17:13 immediately produces a beautiful stream

17:14 of perfectly valid hexodimal messages

17:17 with almost no useful information. You

17:19 can see that the frame 0x1 A0 has

17:22 arrived and you can see it's a datab.

17:24 You can see that one bite changes as you

17:26 press the accelerator perhaps. But CAN

17:28 does not provide a tiny label saying by

17:30 the way this bite represents throttle

17:31 position multiplied by 392 and please

17:34 ignore the upper two bits. You just have

17:36 to know you have to know the language's

17:38 alphabet and grammar but you don't yet

17:40 have its dictionary. The ESP32 has a

17:42 listenon mode that's especially useful

17:44 here. A CAN controller normally

17:46 participates in the protocol including

17:48 acknowledging valid frames. In

17:50 listenonly mode, our ESP32 can observe

17:52 the network without influencing it,

17:54 which is exactly what you want when

17:55 first connecting test equipment to an

17:57 unfamiliar vehicle network. Espresso

17:59 explicitly provides this mode so the

18:01 controller can receive traffic without

18:03 affecting the bus. Acknowledgement is

18:05 another clever little feature. After a

18:07 transmitter sends a valid frame, it

18:09 releases the bus during the

18:10 acknowledgement slot. Any receiver that

18:12 has correctly received the frame may

18:14 drive that slot dominant. The

18:16 transmitter does not learn which

18:17 controller heard it. It simply learns

18:19 that somebody got it. This is not an

18:21 application level reply. The dashboard

18:23 is not saying, "Yes, I have updated the

18:25 tachometer." It's only a data link

18:26 acknowledgement, meaning that at least

18:28 one other CAN bus module out there saw

18:30 your bits, got them, received them,

18:32 decoded them, and they looked right. If

18:33 nobody acknowledges the frame, though,

18:35 the transmitter knows that it may be all

18:37 alone, disconnected, configured for the

18:39 wrong speed, or otherwise barking into

18:41 the dark. CAN also checks its own work

18:43 obsessively. Every frame carries a CRC.

18:46 Transmitters monitor the bus while

18:48 sending and receivers verify the frame

18:50 structure as it arrives. It also uses

18:52 bit stuffing to keep everybody

18:53 synchronized. After five identical bits

18:56 in a row, the transmitter inserts one

18:58 bit of the opposite value. So, it flips

19:00 the bit. Now, receivers know to discard

19:02 that extra bit. But if the expected

19:04 transition never appears, they know the

19:06 frame is corrupt because the line should

19:08 never be held that long. And when any

19:10 controller detects an error,

19:11 deliberately transmits an error flag

19:12 that invalidates the frame for

19:14 everybody. The message is discarded and

19:16 retrieded. That sounds a bit dangerous

19:18 because one broken controller could

19:19 object to everything and hold the

19:20 network hostage. CAN solves that with

19:22 fault confinement. Every controller

19:25 maintains air counters and repeated

19:26 misbehavior progressively demoted from

19:28 air active to air passive and finally

19:30 bus off where it's effectively exiled

19:32 from transmission. It's a tiny

19:34 distributed society with arbitration,

19:36 proofreading, public rejections, and

19:38 eventually banishment all without a

19:39 central authority. The wiring is equally

19:42 approachable. On a dead CAN bus, you can

19:44 begin with a meter and a scope. An

19:46 unpowered, correctly terminated bus, as

19:48 we said, should measure about 60 ohms

19:49 across CAN high and CAN low. On the

19:52 scope, the line should sit together when

19:53 recessive, separate cleanly during

19:55 dominant bits, and show minimal ringing

19:57 or reflection. That does not make every

19:59 fault easy. A loose connector in a

20:01 vibrating, wet, freezing automobile can

20:03 still produce a sort of intermittent

20:04 failure that makes technicians question

20:06 their career choices. But can let you

20:08 reason all the way from the voltage on

20:10 the wire to the message in the software.

20:12 Which brings us back to the Corvette

20:14 computer. The ECM or computer has no IP

20:17 address and opens no connection to the

20:19 dashboard. It simply has a connection to

20:21 those two wires and broadcast messages

20:23 with defined identifiers and payloads.

20:25 Engine speed is published once and the

20:27 dashboard, transmission, traction

20:28 control system, diagnostic tool, and

20:30 data logger may all consume that same

20:33 frame. That loose coupling is one of

20:35 CAN's greatest strengths. It's also one

20:37 of its central security weaknesses.

20:39 Traditional CAN does not authenticate

20:41 the source of a frame. If a hostile

20:43 controller knows the correct identifier

20:45 in a payload format, it may impersonate

20:47 a legitimate module. The other

20:49 controllers see a valid identifier, a

20:51 valid CRC, and a perfectly legal frame.

20:53 Electrically and structurally, nothing

20:55 is wrong. Now, this can also be handy.

20:58 On my old BMW M3, a 2003 that used

21:01 canvas, I added a feature where if you

21:03 unlock the car three times in a row

21:04 within 5 seconds with the key fob, it

21:07 would see that and then it would inject

21:08 the commands that I otherwise had

21:10 recorded and seen to lower the top. So,

21:13 I lowered the top manually a couple

21:14 times, captured that data, figured out

21:16 what I had to send to simulate a push

21:17 the top down button, and I would do that

21:20 when I saw three unlocks. And that's

21:22 because CAN's designers were not

21:23 careless. They were building a trusted

21:25 physically enclosed network with 1980s

21:27 processors and budgets. The danger

21:29 appeared later when those closed

21:31 networks gained diagnostic ports,

21:33 wireless infotainment, cellular modems,

21:35 aftermarket dongles, and millions of

21:37 lines of externally reachable code. CAN

21:40 is simple because it knows where its

21:41 universe ends. Security problems begin

21:43 when we quietly move that boundary. And

21:45 yet, its limitations make it more

21:47 impressive, not less. Because with two

21:48 wires and a handful of rules, CAM

21:50 provides noise rejection, deterministic

21:52 priority, non-destructive arbitration,

21:54 acknowledgements, retransmission, CRC

21:57 checking, clock recovery, and fault

21:58 confinement. Put two traces on a scope

22:00 and you can see a dominant zero form

22:02 right there. Trigger two controllers

22:04 together and watch the lower identifier

22:06 win at exactly the bit where they

22:07 disagree. Remove a terminator and watch

22:09 the reflections appear. Unplug the

22:11 Corvette ECM and watch the entire family

22:13 of identifiers just vanish from the bus.

22:16 Nothing about it is magic. Now, can

22:18 isn't simple because it does very

22:19 little. It's simple because a few

22:21 exceptionally well-chosen rules do a

22:23 great deal. If you have comments or

22:25 questions on today's episode, please

22:27 leave them in the video comments. And

22:28 then check out an episode of Shop Talk

22:30 every Friday on the second channel where

22:32 we answer the week's best questions and

22:33 insights. If you found today's episode

22:36 interesting or entertaining, remember

22:37 I'm mostly in this for the subs and

22:38 likes. So, I would be honored if you

22:40 consider leaving me one of each before

22:41 you go today. If you don't normally do

22:43 that, I would appreciate it maybe on

22:44 this episode because it's got this

22:46 automotive tie in that is usually death

22:47 for my channel, but I really wanted to

22:49 do Canvas. So, if you did like it, give

22:51 it a like. Thanks. And in the meantime,

22:53 in between time, hope to see you next

22:55 time right here in Dave's garage. Oh, I

00:09 MICHAEL CUTHBERT: Hello, OpenCourseWare learners.

00:12 This is Professor Cuthbert talking to you.

00:14 And I just wanted to say a little bit

00:16 about why the next two classes are

00:19 not to be found on this site.

00:23 MIT and the music department was very

00:26 fortunate to be able to hire a new professor

00:29 in computational music that semester.

00:32 And one of the things that we value as a department

00:34 is people's ability to be good teachers.

00:37 So as part of their interview, the candidates

00:41 came and took over one of the classes

00:44 to teach the content of the class

00:47 and a little bit of their specialties, too.

00:55 21m.383.

01:02 and I wish I could share them their videos with you.

01:05 But we have a feeling that it's already stressful enough

01:09 to be doing a job interview and to have your teaching being

01:13 evaluated by people in the room, and then to know

01:17 that whatever things you did in an unfamiliar classroom

01:21 with unfamiliar students would also be put out online.

01:25 It's just a little bit too much.

01:27 So these-- to ask, too much to ask.

01:30 So these videos are not available.

01:32 I want to say a little bit, though,

01:34 what was in each of them.

01:36 The first class was the continuation

01:40 of our series on music, cognition, and computation,

01:45 and how computers can aid the process of understanding

01:50 how the brain processes music, and also,

01:53 how historically, and I think in the future,

01:57 insights from music cognition have improved the things

02:02 that we do on the computer.

02:04 The most important example of this

02:07 is Carol Krumhansl's probe tone experiments

02:15 in understanding musical expectation in scales and keys.

02:22 And these experiments, which help

02:25 to understand how each note plays in our ability

02:30 to understand what key we're in at this point

02:33 underlies quite a number of algorithms being used today

02:38 by computers to automatically detect the keys of compositions.

02:42 And this includes Music 21's default analyze key method.

02:47 And this is why the assignments on understanding key analysis

02:53 went hand in hand with the section on cognition.

03:01 The lecture also covered and gave

03:03 the opportunity to discuss some of the experiments

03:07 reported by David Huron in his book

03:09 Sweet Anticipation, of which the students

03:12 were assigned to do readings.

03:16 I would encourage, as a substitute

03:18 for the content of this lecture, for you

03:21 to look deeply at this book by a prominent music

03:29 cognition and expert, and also one of the breakthrough

03:34 founders of our field of computational music theory

03:39 and musicology, David Huron.

03:42 And doing so, I think, would give a good sense

03:44 of the majority of what was contained

03:48 in the lecture beyond what the candidate spoke

03:53 about her own particular expertise.

03:55

03:59 The second guest lecturer covered the topic

04:02 of the history of algorithmic composition from its beginnings,

04:08 even before the computer, until today.

04:11 And this lecturer covered the main reading for this week,

04:17 which is on the "Illiac Suite," one of the first pieces to be

04:23 composed by computers using algorithms and to generate

04:26 notes, and continuing up till today with advances in AI,

04:32 such as the music transformer by Ana Huang at Google and other

04:39 new developments.

04:41 One of the reasons why it's so important

04:44 to look at algorithmic music composition in a broader

04:50 historical scope is it's too easy

04:53 to get hung up on the particular problem

04:56 that we have today, where we're getting closer

04:59 and closer to having the computer produce musical scores

05:03 that sound like other compositions,

05:07 like by particular composers, and to work on that problem

05:11 without asking.

05:13 well, why?

05:14 Why should we care?

05:16 Why do we want the computer to compose a new piece

05:21 in the style of Johann Sebastian Bach, unless, by chance,

05:26 you've already heard every piece by Bach, and you're just bored

05:29 and you need more, which most of us

05:33 haven't explored what's actually out there?

05:37 Instead, by looking back at the earliest history,

05:41 when having a computer actually write music

05:44 at that level of sophistication was so far from being possible

05:49 and looking at what people wanted to do with the computer,

05:54 it helps to answer questions.

05:56 How can the computer be used to come up with ideas

06:03 or take ideas that I have that will take too

06:05 long for me to generate on my own

06:08 and make that part more efficient?

06:11 How can it be a tool to help me be a better human composer,

06:17 or just better human?

06:20 So the class went through some of the earliest algorithmic

06:25 compositions from Guido of Arezzo,

06:28 a monk living in the 11th century,

06:31 through Mozart's musical dice games,

06:34 up until the "Illiac Suite" and then beyond.

06:39 Some of what's covered in this class

06:41 also appears in the various videos

06:45 that accompany this class that weren't

06:48 shown to students this year, but are available for you.

06:55 And other aspects touched on the guest speakers

07:00 particular expertise, which was very valuable to be brought in.

07:04 Anybody else teaching this class would

07:07 bring in her or his own specialties that would make

07:11 that class different from mine.

07:13 And nobody should teach this class

07:15 exactly the same way I would teach it, or have taught it.

07:20 So that gives a little bit of a nutshell of what's happening.

07:24 The students then went on to write their own algorithms

07:29 to generate compositions algorithmically,

07:32 and they did a very good job of avoiding the problem of trying

07:39 to get the computer to do something that we already

07:43 do better, that we are not interested really

07:46 in the computer's output, and that we just would only

07:53 want to listen to if we knew a human created.

07:57 And instead, they went beyond that

07:59 and created a piece of music that

08:01 were interesting in themselves and that no human would ever

08:05 choose to write.

08:06

08:10 In addition to the two classes that job candidates covered,

08:16 two other classes at around this time needed to be removed

08:22 and the contents pushed into other classes

08:26 because MIT was in the process of proposing to the full faculty

08:33 a new master's program--

08:35 two new master's programs--

08:37 in music, technology and computation.

08:40 And it happened that these proposals

08:44 had to happen at the same time as this class.

08:46 And so a little bit of time was lost on that.

08:50 I'm hoping that if you've been interested in this class

08:53 and want to go forward, you might

08:55 look into these programs, which I

08:57 assume will be live at the time that these videos are released.

09:03 I think that this is all that I'm

09:04 going to be able to provide specially

09:07 for the OpenCourseWare audience in this class,

09:10 except at the very end, where I have a little message for you

09:14 that I recorded at the time.

09:16 Thank you.

00:17 device on the capital of Japan to end the war?

00:19 We will uncover the answer to this question by following an odd series of events that

00:24 resulted in one city being saved while another was reduced to radioactive rubble.

00:29 And although Tokyo was not annihilated by an atomic bomb, it may have actually gone

00:33 through something worse.

00:34 On July 16, 1945, President Harry S. Truman was notified that the Trinity Test was a success

00:41 and that the United States had detonated the world’s first atomic bomb.

00:44 The question was, what should be done with it?

00:47 Truman called the nuclear weapon “the most terrible bomb in the history of the world.”

00:51 Billions of dollars and thousands of man-hours had been spent on the development of the weapon,

00:56 and now Truman needed to decide whether it would be used in the Pacific or locked away.

01:01 Tokyo would have made sense as an initial target for the weapon of mass destruction

01:04 as it was the capital of Japan.

01:07 However, other factors needed to be taken into consideration.

01:10 First of all, the U.S. needed to determine if they were even going to use the atomic

01:14 bomb.

01:15 There were 4 options under consideration for what would come next.

01:18 Option 1.

01:19 Continue the conventional bombing of Japanese cities instead of dropping the atomic bomb.

01:24 Option 2.

01:25 Invade Japan, knowing it would cost the lives of millions of people.

01:29 Option 3.

01:30 Conduct a demonstration of the atomic bomb on an uninhabited island.

01:34 Option 4.

01:35 Drop the atomic bomb on a Japanese city.

01:37 As we know, Harry S. Truman and the United States military chose option 4.

01:42 But what was the thought process behind the decision, and was Tokyo ever considered a

01:46 target during the meetings?

01:47 Let’s look at each of the options a bit more in depth.

01:50 Option 1: conventional bombing.

01:52 The United States had been bombing parts of the Japanese home islands for some time but

01:56 had only begun to really ramp things up around the middle of 1944.

02:00 By the following year, it was estimated that 333,000 Japanese people were killed, with

02:05 another 473,000 injured during U.S. air raids.

02:09 The problem was that even though the United States was causing massive amounts of casualties

02:13 and destruction on Japanese islands, they still refused to surrender.

02:16 The thought of continuing business as usual and expecting a different result didn’t

02:21 seem to make sense at the time.

02:22 Even after the Tokyo firebombing, which had the highest mortality rate of any single air

02:26 attack in the war, the Japanese leadership still refused to surrender.

02:30 This meant that Truman and his advisors needed another option.

02:34 Conventional bombing did not seem to be working, even if it was causing massive amounts of

02:38 damage.

02:39 Instead, a single bomb that could obliterate an entire city might be just what the U.S.

02:43 needed.

02:44 Therefore, the nuclear option was put on the table.

02:46 By August 1945, the only viable option seemed to be either invading the Japanese home island

02:52 or dropping the atomic bomb.

02:54 Option 2: invading Japan.

02:56 An invasion of Japan seemed inevitable unless there was some sort of power shift in the

03:00 war.

03:01 The atomic bomb provided that catalyst.

03:03 However, before the U.S. even knew that the atomic bomb would successfully detonate if

03:08 dropped from a plane, Truman and his advisors had to prepare for the very real option that

03:12 boots would have to be put on the ground of the Japanese home islands.

03:16 Unfortunately, over the course of several months, whenever U.S. troops landed on Japanese-controlled

03:20 islands, the enemy forces almost always refused to surrender.

03:24 Entire units would fight until the very last man rather than give up, which inflicted massive

03:29 casualties on both sides.

03:31 It was suspected that if the United States invaded Japan, not only would the soldiers

03:35 fight to the bitter end, but the general population would also refuse to give up.

03:39 An invasion plan would end with the deaths of millions of troops and civilians, and it

03:43 wasn’t even clear if the U.S. could take the home islands successfully.

03:46 A preview of how brutal the fighting would be if the U.S. invaded was seen on Iwo Jima

03:51 when American soldiers attempted to take the island on February 19, 1945.

03:56 In this battle, 6,200 US soldiers died.

04:00 Another 13,000 soldiers and sailors were killed in the Battle of Okinawa, which began on March

04:04 26th of the same year.

04:06 The casualty rate on Okinawa was 35%, meaning 1 out of every 3 soldiers who engaged in battle

04:12 died or was wounded.

04:14 Truman even voiced his concern about the invasion option by stating invading the main island

04:18 would be like "Okinawa from one end of Japan to the other."

04:22 The astonishing thing was that Harry Truman was almost certainly right.

04:26 Documents discovered in Japan after the war ended suggested that Japan’s plan for resistance

04:31 was to have every soldier, civilian, and child fight against the Allied soldiers.

04:35 The hope was to make the cost of taking the home island so high that the United States

04:39 would give up and call for a cease-fire.

04:42 This would then allow the Japanese to establish terms that would allow them to keep the territory

04:45 they occupied at the time.

04:47 When considering the invasion of Japan, Harry Truman wrote: “My object is to save as many

04:52 American lives as possible, but I also have a human feeling for the women and children

04:56 of Japan.”

04:57 Option 3: an atomic bomb demonstration.

05:01 Scientists and military officials who were a part of the Manhattan Project were able

05:04 to witness the awesome power of an atomic bomb firsthand when Gadget detonated at the

05:09 Trinity Test Site.

05:10 However, the rest of the world, including Emperor Hirohito, had no idea how powerful

05:15 this weapon was.

05:16 Therefore, it would have made sense to demonstrate its capabilities in the hopes that it would

05:20 cause the Japanese leadership to surrender so that the bomb would never have to be used

05:24 in combat.

05:25 When a demonstration was proposed on an uninhabited island where Japanese scientists and military

05:29 leaders could see the explosion, it was shot down for several reasons.

05:34 The first was because it was unclear who would be chosen to view the detonation and if they

05:38 would have the ability to convince the Japanese leadership to surrender.

05:42 Ideally, a panel of Japanese scientists and high-ranking military officers would have

05:46 been chosen, but even then, it was unclear how long it would take for Japan to make a

05:50 final decision about surrendering, and the U.S. couldn’t wait any longer to act.

05:55 Then there was the very real possibility that when the Japanese saw the demonstration, they

05:59 would double down on their war effort and ramp up production.

06:01 They might have even begun to construct countermeasures such as massive bunkers and increase anti-aircraft

06:06 encampments to keep U.S. planes that could be carrying the atomic bomb away from key

06:11 locations.

06:12 However, the biggest concern for the U.S. was what would happen if the demonstration

06:16 turned out to be a failure.

06:17 What if they dropped one of the bombs and it didn’t explode?

06:20 It is important to remember that only one nuclear device had been successfully detonated

06:24 at this point in time.

06:25 It was not entirely clear if the success could be repeated, especially when the bomb was

06:30 dropped from a plane and had to be triggered at a specific altitude.

06:33 If the test itself was a failure, the Japanese might believe the U.S. was desperate, or worse,

06:38 incompetent, and start to fight even harder.

06:41 Then there was the fact that only 2 atomic bombs existed in the entire world.

06:45 These would be the two bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

06:48 If the United States detonated one in a demonstration, it would only have one left over if Japan

06:53 refused to surrender.

06:54 There were more bombs being produced, but at the time the decision to use nuclear weapons

06:58 was being made, Harry Truman and his advisors only had the 2 on their way to Tinian island

07:03 to work with and it would be a while before they more.

07:07 Some of the military advisors who were on the committee to decide what should be done

07:10 warned that a demonstration would not be impressive enough to force a surrender.

07:14 Instead, they stated, “We can propose no technical demonstration likely to bring an

07:18 end to the war.

07:19 We can see no acceptable alternative to direct military use.”

07:22 The Japanese needed to experience the destructive capabilities and mass casualties firsthand.

07:28 All of these factors led the U.S. to go with option 4.

07:32 Option 4: Drop the atomic bomb on Japan.

07:35 It was suggested that perhaps the best way to use the bomb was to drop it in Tokyo Harbor.

07:39 This would allow the Japanese leadership to see and experience the weapon's awesome power.

07:43 However, most military advisors agreed this would not have the desired effect and concluded

07:48 the bombs must be released over densely populated cities that met certain criteria.

07:53 The first criteria was that target cities had to have suffered little or no damage from

07:57 conventional bombing runs in the past so that it was clear the atomic blast was responsible

08:02 for the destruction and casualties sustained after the detonation.

08:05 The second criteria, and one that appeared to be less important, was that there should

08:09 be some type of military production happening in the city.

08:12 However, since workers' homes and entire neighborhoods were built around military factories, it would

08:17 be impossible to find a strictly military target.

08:20 These criteria eventually led to a short list of possible targets.

08:23 The original list consisted of Hiroshima, Kokura, Niigata, and Kyoto.

08:27 However, a substitute was made at the last moment, and Kyoto was replaced with Nagasaki.

08:32 We are going to examine exactly why Hiroshima and Nagasaki were ultimately chosen, but it

08:37 is worth noting that Tokyo was never actually on the list of possible cities to bomb.

08:41 Later on, it will become apparent why this was the case, but suffice it to say Tokyo

08:45 didn’t meet all of the criteria outlined by the advisory board.

08:49 In the final days before the atomic bombs were dropped, a committee made up of scientists

08:53 including J. Robert Oppenheimer, politicians such as Henry Lewis Stimson, who was also

08:57 the Secretary of War, and Generals like Leslie Groves deliberated on how best to use the

09:02 atomic bomb.

09:03 On May 10th, the committee met to discuss several aspects of the bombs and which cities

09:07 to target.

09:08 Joyce C. Stearns, a scientist from the Air Force, told the rest of the committee the

09:12 names of four locations that were on the shortlist of targets.

09:15 At the time, Kyoto, Hiroshima, Yokohama, and Kokura had been chosen.

09:19 Each were “large urban areas of more than three miles in diameter; capable of being

09:24 effectively damaged by the blast, and likely to be unattacked by next August.”

09:28 In the meeting, someone suggested bombing the emperor's palace in Tokyo, which would

09:32 have sent a clear message to the Japanese leadership.

09:35 But this plan was dismissed for several reasons that we will get into later.

09:39 It was decided that using the bomb must have two psychological effects along with destroying

09:43 military facilities and infrastructure.

09:45 The atomic bomb must scare the Japanese into surrendering while simultaneously showing

09:49 the rest of the world how powerful the United States’ new weapon was.

09:53 Really what it came down to was that the bomb must cause a massive amount of damage and

09:57 result in a staggering number of casualties.

10:00 The committee believed this would be the only way that Japanese leadership would surrender

10:04 unconditionally.

10:05 And since the United States had been engaging in firebombing campaigns that wiped entire

10:09 cities off the map, detonating an atomic bomb to level a key target seemed like the next

10:14 logical step.

10:15 Almost everyone on the committee agreed that Hiroshima would be a good first target as

10:19 it was compact, had military factories, and if the bomb were dropped directly in the middle

10:23 of the urban center, it would end up destroying most, if not all, of the city.

10:27 Hiroshima would show the true potential of the bomb and scare the Japanese population

10:31 into submission; at least, that was what everyone hoped.

10:34 Let’s now look at where the two atomic bombs were actually dropped, how these locations

10:38 were ultimately decided upon, and why Tokyo never made it onto the list of candidate cities

10:43 and was therefore spared from a nuclear blast.

10:46 After analyzing weather conditions, timing, and maps of Hiroshima, the orders were given

10:50 to make the city the primary target.

10:52 It was noted in reports that the city was “the largest untouched target,” which

10:56 meant that any destruction done would be the direct result of the atomic blast.

11:00 Hiroshima had a population of approximately 318,000 and was an important depot and port

11:06 of embarkation for Japan.

11:08 The hills that surrounded the city were also thought to provide a focussing effect that

11:11 would increase the blast damage.

11:13 It had been decided earlier in the war that Hiroshima wasn’t a very good target for

11:17 firebombing as the Ota River ran through it and would act as a firebreak.

11:21 However, an atomic blast would have no problem decimating structures on both sides of the

11:25 river.

11:26 On August 6, 1945, at 0915:15, Thomas Ferebee announced “bomb away” over the Enola Gay’s

11:34 radio as Little Boy was released from the belly of the plane and fell towards the Aioi

11:38 Bridge in Hiroshima.

11:40 At 0916:02, the bomb detonated 1,968 feet or 600 meters above the city.

11:47 Estimates vary, but it is likely that between 70,000 and 100,000 people died in the initial

11:52 blast.

11:53 However, some estimates have this number closer to 140,000 deaths.

11:56 For the scientists and military advisors choosing the targets for the atomic bombs, Hiroshima

12:00 was an obvious choice.

12:01 However, the second city that would be hit if the Japanese didn’t surrender after the

12:05 first blast was hotly disputed by some.

12:08 In fact, Nagasaki wasn’t even supposed to be on the list of targets on August 9th.

12:12 Through a series of unforeseen events, the people of Kyoto and Kokura were spared, and

12:17 the population of Nagasaki was decimated by the Fat Boy atomic bomb.

12:21 Kyoto had originally been chosen as the second target in Japan.

12:24 It had a population of approximately 1 million and met almost all of the criteria that the

12:29 committee had laid out.

12:30 The city was a cultural and intellectual center as it once served as the ancient capital of

12:34 the country.

12:35 The downside was that Kyoto had no significant military installations.

12:39 However, since the goal was to show the destructive power of the bomb and put the fear of God

12:44 into the Japanese people, Kyoto remained high on the list of targets.

12:48 Henry L. Stimson had traveled to Kyoto with his wife before the war and felt a personal

12:52 connection to the city.

12:53 He made it his mission to remove the former capital from the list of targets.

12:57 Stimson argued that the atomic bomb should “be used as a weapon of war in the manner

13:01 prescribed by the laws of war” and “dropped on a military target.”

13:05 Kyoto did not meet these requirements.

13:07 However, other than Stimson’s objections, none of the other committee members saw dropping

13:11 the atomic bombs on Japanese cities full of civilians as unethical or immoral as this

13:17 was war.

13:18 Stimson met with General Groves and asked that Kyoto be removed from the list.

13:22 Groves argued that Kyoto “was large enough an area for us to gain complete knowledge

13:26 of the effects of the atomic bomb.”

13:28 But on June 30th, Groves finally gave in and removed the former capital from the list of

13:32 atomic bomb targets.

13:34 On July 24, 1946, the day that the official strike orders were issued, a handwritten note

13:39 was attached to the list of targets that just said “and Nagasaki.”

13:43 This put the city in the fourth-place position, which indicated it was least likely to be

13:48 bombed.

13:49 The reason that Nagasaki was chosen to replace Kyoto was because of its large shipbuilding

13:52 industry and its importance as a trade center.

13:55 There were also two munitions factories in the city: the Mitsubishi Steel and Arms Works

14:00 and the Mitsubishi-Urakami Torpedo Works.

14:02 However, the hilly geography and presence of a POW camp in the city made it less desirable

14:08 than the others on the list.

14:09 When the B-29 named Bockscar took off from Tinian island in the early hours of the morning

14:14 on August 9th, its target was Kokura, which had been chosen because of the Japanese Imperial

14:19 Army’s massive arsenal located there.

14:21 However, when the bomber arrived above the city at 10:00 a.m., clouds and bad weather

14:25 obscured the ground below.

14:26 The aircraft circled Kokura three times, looking for an opening, but the cloud cover never

14:31 dissipated.

14:32 Running low on fuel, Major Charles W. Sweeney decided to proceed to his alternate target

14:36 of Nagasaki.

14:37 The plane reached its destination but found that the weather was just as bad, if not worse.

14:42 Running out of time and fuel, Sweeny was about to order the plane to return to base without

14:46 dropping its payload when an opening appeared in the clouds, and the city could be seen

14:50 below.

14:51 At 11:02, Fat Boy was dropped over Nagasaki and detonated.

14:55 This was a larger bomb than had been dropped on Hiroshima and produced an explosion with

14:59 more than 21 kilotons of power, killing as many as 40,000 to 70,000 people and leveling

15:05 the city.

15:06 Less than a week later, on August 15th, Emperor Hirohito announced to the Japanese people

15:10 that he would be surrendering to the United States, signaling the beginning of the end

15:14 of World War II in the Pacific.

15:16 But what about Tokyo?

15:17 What specific reasons did the committee have for omitting the capital of the Japanese empire

15:22 from their list of targets?

15:23 The first was that Tokyo housed many of Japan’s military and government leaders.

15:28 Since the bombs were to be dropped without warning, the blast could kill key members

15:31 of the Japanese administration, thereby causing a breakdown in command.

15:36 If this were to happen, the surrender might actually have been delayed as power shifted

15:40 within the government.

15:41 The United States was looking for a quick end to the war and still needed a functioning

15:45 Japanese government to negotiate with.

15:47 An atomic bomb dropped on Tokyo may have ended up prolonging the war.

15:51 But the main reason why Tokyo was not considered a target for the atomic bombs was because

15:55 the city was already in ashes from the deadliest bombing runs of the war.

15:59 On the night of March 9th and into March 10th, 1945, 334 B-29 bombers flew from the Mariana

16:06 Islands to Tokyo.

16:08 The code name for this mission was Operation Meetinghouse, and many military leaders hoped

16:12 the attack would force the Japanese to surrender.

16:15 The B-29s had conducted bombing runs in Japan before, and they had even unleashed a fiery

16:19 hell on other cities, but this time things were different.

16:23 General Curtis LeMay had been newly appointed as the head of B-29 operations in the region.

16:28 He noticed that in past missions where the bombers dropped their payloads from high altitudes,

16:32 they were incredibly inaccurate.

16:34 The planes were more protected high up, but they were ineffective at such altitudes.

16:38 In fact, their accuracy was less than 10%.

16:41 Therefore, on the night of Operation Meetinghouse, LeMay ordered the fleet of airships to descend

16:46 from 30,000 feet to 7,000 feet.

16:49 As they approached Tokyo, the B-29s broke formation and fell into a single file line.

16:53 The decision to bomb the city at night resulted in Japanese fighters being unprepared and

16:58 made it more difficult for the bombers to be spotted by anti-aircraft guns.

17:02 To increase speed, maneuverability, and payload size, the bombers had been stripped of all

17:06 nonessential components, including guns and gunners.

17:09 This allowed them to be loaded with more bombs but left the aircraft completely defenseless.

17:14 However, on the night of March 9th, this didn’t matter.

17:17 The 334 bombers met very little resistance as they approached their targets.

17:21 These B-29s were not just loaded with regular ordinances.

17:24 Instead, they carried napalm-filled incendiary bombs that were designed to create a firestorm

17:29 in the city below.

17:30 United States military strategists knew that Japan, and Tokyo in particular, constructed

17:35 most of its buildings using wood and were tightly packed together.

17:39 This meant that once the bombs went off, the city would ignite, and there would be no stopping

17:43 the fire from burning its way across the city.

17:46 U.S. strategists marked 3 key locations in Tokyo that needed to be hit as they were the

17:51 most flammable sectors and would cause the largest fire.

17:54 Army engineers had actually created a mock Japanese village where they tested setting

17:58 fires in order to figure out the best combination of explosives and napalm.

18:02 The model Japanese village was constructed in Dugway Proving Ground in Utah and served

18:07 as an important preparation tool before the bombing run.

18:10 By the time Operation Meetinghouse began, the engineers knew that Tokyo would burn to

18:14 the ground that night.

18:15 Between March 9th and March 10th, 15 square miles or nearly 40 square kilometers were

18:20 consumed by flames.

18:21 At the time, Tokyo was one of the most densely packed cities in the entire world.

18:25 The fire raged for nearly 4 days leaving more than a million people homeless.

18:30 Reports that came out after the Tokyo firebombing were horrific.

18:33 In some places, the flames were so intense that canals began to boil, metal frames melted,

18:38 and men, women, and children caught in the fire burst into flames.

18:42 When the operation was over, 1,667 tons of napalm-filled incendiary bombs had been dropped

18:48 on Tokyo.

18:49 Some historians have argued that the firebombing of Tokyo was the single deadliest airstrike

18:54 of the entire war and that it likely caused more death and destruction than either of

18:58 the atomic bombs.

18:59 More than 100,000 people died in the firebombing, and hundreds of thousands more suffered from

19:03 third-degree burns and disfigurement.

19:06 Just for a comparison, the firebombing of Dresden in Germany resulted in 25,000 deaths,

19:11 which at the time seemed unfathomable.

19:13 So, this brings us back to the question of why didn’t the United States bomb Tokyo.

19:17 The simplest explanation is that there was nothing left to bomb.

19:20 The entire city had been burnt to the ground as a result of Operation Meetinghouse, which

19:24 meant that it didn’t meet the criteria of being relatively untouched by other attacks.

19:29 The population had been decimated, and the city was little more than charred piles of

19:33 wood.

19:34 If an atomic bomb had been dropped on Tokyo, it would have created a massive mushroom cloud

19:38 and blown a ton of debris outwards from its epicenter, but it wouldn’t have shown off

19:42 the weapon's destructive power.

19:44 At that point, the bomb would have only affected the already injured population, and it wouldn’t

19:48 have really disrupted the Japanese military as there were very few factories or military

19:52 buildings still operational in the city.

19:54 So the main reason an atomic bomb wasn’t dropped on Tokyo was because of the firebombing

19:58 of the city 5 months prior.

20:00 It is estimated that the total civilian casualties in Japan as a result of Allied air attacks

20:05 was around 806,000.

20:07 Of these casualties, 330,000 people died.

20:10 Japan also suffered another 780,000 combat casualties due to American bombing runs.

20:16 Not every Japanese target would have been as affected by a firebombing run as Tokyo

20:20 was, just like not every city would have suffered as much death and destruction as Nagasaki

20:24 and Hiroshima did due to the atomic bomb.

20:27 U.S. strategists meticulously decided on targets and attack methods where the most destruction

20:32 could be done and fear could be instilled in the Japanese people.

20:36 Even though these actions are controversial and can be debated, the result was that the

20:40 Japanese surrendered unconditionally to the United States after the atomic bombs were

20:44 dropped.

20:45 Although it is worth mentioning that the Soviet Union declaring war on Japan and the Red Army

20:49 barreling through East Asia also played a role in Japan’s decision to surrender.

20:54 Now watch “Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (Minute by Minute).”

20:58 Or check out “The Truth About Why America Dropped Atomic Bombs on Japan.”
