docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 A spacecraft launched in 1977 is still traveling  through deep space today—nearly 50 years later.

00:06 On August 20th, 1977, NASA launched the  Voyager II space probe, and over the

00:12 decades it has witnessed things no human ever has. These are 50 of the most extraordinary discoveries

00:18 Voyager II has made. 50.

00:20 Well before the Voyager program began, scientists  theorized that the Sun not only gave us light and

00:26 heat, but protected the entire solar system. They believed the Sun constantly blasts out

00:30 streams of particles that create a giant bubble  around us, shielding Earth and the other planets

00:36 from dangerous radiation coming from deep space. For decades, nobody knew for sure

00:41 if that bubble really existed. Then Voyager II found the answer.

00:45 In 2018, it reached the very edge  of the solar system and crossed a

00:48 boundary known as the heliosphere, which  keeps us safe from galactic cosmic rays.

00:53 Voyager I had crossed the  same boundary back in 2012.

00:56 The two probes confirmed that the Sun doesn't  just keep us warm, it also helps defend our

01:01 corner of the galaxy from forces that could be  far more dangerous than most people realize.

01:06 49. When Voyager II arrived at

01:09 heliopause, it discovered a cosmic wall of fire. Temperatures in this region range from 30,000 to

01:15 50,000 Kelvin, or 54,000 and 90,000°F  (29,982 - 49,982 Celsius). Scientists

01:21 believe this intense heat is created when  the Sun's solar wind crashes into the cold

01:25 gas between the stars and suddenly slows down. As the particles pile up and become compressed,

01:31 they heat up dramatically,  creating a scorching layer

01:34 of plasma at the very edge of our solar system. Somehow, Voyager II managed to pass through the

01:40 wall of fire without melting. That’s because  the plasma there is incredibly thin. So thin,

01:45 in fact, that there aren't enough particles to  actually transfer enough heat energy to the probe

01:50 to damage it. 48.

01:52 The moment Voyager II crossed the  heliopause, everything changed.

01:56 Almost immediately, its instruments detected  a sharp surge in galactic cosmic rays:

02:01 high-energy particles arriving from way beyond  our solar system. The probe measured roughly

02:06 3 times as many cosmic protons as it had  encountered before crossing the boundary.

02:11 This is more evidence to support the existence  of the heliosphere. It also shows just how

02:15 fragile Earth would be if it wasn’t for the  huge protective bubble formed by the Sun.

02:20 Streams of dangerous radiation continuously  emerge from distant supernovae and galaxies

02:25 and head straight towards us. The fiery  barrier of the heliosphere is able to deflect

02:30 around 70% of those rays away from our solar  system and help preserve life as we know it.

02:35 47. After crossing into interstellar space, Voyager

02:39 II discovered that instead of emptying out into  some sort of vacuum, space actually became denser.

02:44 The probe’s Plasma Wave Science  instrument detected that the

02:47 density of matter was actually increasing. Scientists had long believed the space

02:51 beyond our solar system as a vast, almost  empty void. Instead, Voyager revealed a

02:56 dense region just beyond the Sun's protective  bubble. The discovery was so unexpected that

03:01 it forced researchers to rethink some of their  models of how our corner of the galaxy works.

03:06 Even today, scientists aren't completely  sure why this region is denser than expected.

03:10 One leading theory suggests that interstellar  material has been piling up against the outer edge

03:14 of the heliosphere for millions of years, almost  like debris collecting against a cosmic barrier.

03:20 46. Voyager II also helped solve a

03:23 mystery that had baffled scientists for years. When Voyager I crossed the edge of the solar

03:27 system in 2012, it detected something unexpected.  The magnetic field beyond the heliosphere seemed

03:33 to be aligned with the Sun's magnetic field.  It was like the 2 were running side by side.

03:38 But there was a problem. With only one spacecraft crossing the boundary,

03:42 scientists couldn't tell whether it was a  genuine feature of space or simply a coincidence.

03:46 Years later, Voyager II provided the answer. Even though it crossed the heliopause at a

03:51 completely different location, it  detected the same alignment. That

03:54 was exactly the confirmation researchers needed. The finding showed that this isn't some random

03:59 quirk of space, but a real feature of the  environment surrounding our solar system.

04:04 45. Originally, scientists

04:06 believed that there would be some sort of messy  or gradual transition zone at the heliosphere.

04:10 But that’s not what Voyager II discovered. It encountered chaos and violent heat at

04:15 the so-called wall of fire. But it also  encountered order and structure in the form

04:20 of a very clearly defined boundary between  one environment and the start of the next.

04:24 As it crossed over into interstellar space,  its instruments didn’t just detect a huge

04:28 spike in cosmic radiation, but also an  instantaneous drop in solar radiation.

04:33 It also observed almost a complete absence  of any solar plasma flow beyond that line.

04:38 The Sun is the literal center of our solar system,  but this discovery proved that past a certain

04:44 point, its influence is non-existent. 44.

04:47 For decades, many researchers imagined the  heliosphere as a cosmic shield separating our

04:52 solar system from the rest of the galaxy. But Voyager's data hinted at a more

04:56 complicated reality. In some regions,

04:58 particles appear to be able to pass through the  boundary, moving between interstellar space and

05:03 the heliosphere. To help explain this, NASA  scientists have compared the heliosphere to

05:08 a ship moving through a cosmic ocean. Just as water can flow around and

05:12 through different parts of a vessel,  the Sun's protective bubble may be

05:15 stronger in some areas than in others. When Voyager I crossed the boundary,

05:19 it detected signs that particles were  leaking through the shield. Years later,

05:23 Voyager II observed similar evidence after  crossing at a completely different location.

05:27 Together, the two spacecraft revealed  that the heliosphere isn't a perfect wall.

05:32 Instead, it appears to be a dynamic and somewhat  porous boundary between our solar system and the

05:37 vast expanse beyond. 43.

05:40 Scientists had debated over the shape of  our solar system, with some insisting it

05:43 was round or comet-shaped and others  arguing it must have a different form.

05:48 Voyager II settled the argument once and for all. It showed that, far from being perfectly round,

05:53 the solar system is almost like  a squashed or dented bubble.

05:57 Scientists figured this out by comparing  data from both Voyager spacecraft.

06:00 Voyager I crossed the edge of the solar system  at a distance of 121 Astronomical Units, or AU,

06:06 from the Sun. Voyager II crossed at just 119. It might sound like a small difference,

06:12 but it was enough to show that the heliosphere  isn't perfectly symmetrical. Researchers believe

06:16 the distortion is caused by magnetic  fields flowing through our galaxy.

06:20 As the solar system moves through the  Milky Way, those fields press against

06:23 the heliosphere from the outside, almost like  a hand pushing into the side of a balloon.

06:28 The result is a solar system that's slightly  warped by the forces of interstellar space.

06:32 42. Before either Voyager spacecraft could reach the

06:35 edge of the solar system, they had to pass through  a series of strange and violent transition zones.

06:40 The first is known as the termination shock. This is where the Sun’s solar wind,

06:44 racing at speeds of up to 1.5 million  miles per hour (2.4 million kph),

06:48 suddenly slams into the thin gas of interstellar  space, causing it to rapidly slow down.

06:53 The result is extreme turbulence, almost like  hitting a cosmic traffic jam at full speed.

06:58 Beyond that lies the heliosheath. Here, the solar wind doesn’t stop completely,

07:02 but it becomes heavily compressed and chaotic,  flowing far more slowly as it gets pushed back

07:07 by interstellar space. After this is the  heliopause itself, the point where the

07:11 Sun’s influence effectively ends. By traveling  through all of these layers, Voyager II didn’t

07:16 just cross the edge of the solar system. It helped map out what that edge actually

07:20 looks like in detail, revealing that it’s not  a clean line, but a complex, shifting series

07:25 of boundaries. 41.

07:27 NASA teams had long believed that  the heliopause wasn’t fixed in place,

07:31 and that it continuously changed shape and  size, contracting and expanding over time.

07:35 Voyager II’s data confirmed this and provided  the missing pieces of the puzzle scientists

07:39 needed to flesh out their theory. Instead, the heliopause appears to

07:43 shift and change over time, almost like  it’s breathing. This happens in rhythm

07:47 with the Sun’s 11-year solar cycle. During periods of high solar activity,

07:51 the Sun releases stronger solar winds, which  push outward and cause the heliosphere to

07:56 expand. But when the Sun becomes quieter, that  pressure weakens, and the boundary moves inward.

08:00 The heliosphere behaves less like a rigid wall,  and more like a living structure that expands and

08:05 contracts with the activity of the sun. 40.

08:08 One of the strangest things Voyager discovered  was a vast region filled with what scientists

08:12 describe as a kind of magnetic foam.  It exists within the heliosheath,

08:16 near the outer edge of the solar system. There, the Sun's magnetic field becomes twisted

08:20 and compressed, breaking apart into countless  magnetic bubbles. Some of them can be more than

08:25 100 million miles (160 million km) across. The bubbles act like huge cosmic traps.

08:30 When high-energy particles drift inside,  they usually can't escape. Instead,

08:34 they bounce back and forth within the magnetic  fields, becoming imprisoned inside the foam.

08:38 Scientists believe these giant magnetic bubbles  play an important role in controlling how

08:42 particles move into and out of our solar system. And thanks to Voyager, we know that the edge of

08:47 the solar system is far stranger, and  more complex, than anyone realized.

08:52 39. Voyager II was the first

08:55 ever spacecraft to visit the planet of Uranus. Before that, everything we knew about the planet

08:59 came from telescopes. Then, in 1986,

09:02 Voyager II gave us the very first close up look. As it swept past the planet, passing within about

09:07 50,000 miles (80,467 km of the planet’s surface,  gathering and transmitting a wealth of data in the

09:12 process. Among its discoveries was the fact that a  day on Uranus lasts just 17 hours and 14 minutes.

09:18 But that was only the beginning. Voyager also uncovered 10 previously

09:22 unknown moons orbiting the planet.  Later analysis revealed an 11th.

09:26 Today, we now know that Uranus is  surrounded by at least 29 moons.

09:30 38. Voyager II

09:32 was able to capture detailed imagery of several  of Uranus’s moons, and one of them stood out.

09:37 Its name is Miranda, but it has earned  the nickname of the “Frankenstein” moon

09:41 due to its unusual appearance. The smallest and innermost of

09:44 the planet’s 5 major moons, Miranda has a  chaotic, scarred surface that looks like

09:48 it was stitched together from a group of random  parts. It includes a mixture of jagged canyons,

09:53 cratered plains, and racetrack-style ridges. Scientists have shared various theories

09:57 about how this abnormal astral body  formed. Some believe that it may have

10:01 been struck by a massive object and split  into pieces, which eventually reassembled.

10:06 An alternate theory is that the intense  gravitational pull of Uranus warped Miranda’s

10:10 surface. 37.

10:12 Data from Voyager II also found that despite  its small size, Miranda is home to one of the

10:16 solar system’s biggest structures, Verona Rupes.  It’s the tallest known cliff in the solar system.

10:23 According to some estimates, it may be  up to 12 miles (20 kilometers) high.

10:26 That’s over twice as high as Mount Everest.  Scientists say that if someone were to jump off

10:30 Verona Rupes, it could take almost 10 minutes  for them to fall due to the moon’s gravity.

10:36 36. In 2024, thanks to

10:38 Voyager II data, researchers made yet another  extraordinary discovery related to Miranda.

10:43 Up to that point, it was believed the moon  was little more than a frozen ball of ice.

10:47 However, modern computer modeling  techniques told a different story.

10:50 Beneath its surface, Miranda might once  have contained a vast underground ocean.

10:54 Even more surprisingly, researchers believe  that some of that ocean could still exist today.

11:00 If that's true, Miranda would join one of the  most exclusive groups in the solar system:

11:04 the so-called ocean worlds. A rare  trait that has captured the attention

11:08 of astrobiologists around the world. Because wherever liquid water exists,

11:12 there's always the possibility  that life could exist as well.

11:15 That means this small and often overlooked moon  may be more important than anyone realized when

11:20 Voyager II first flew past it. 35.

11:24 Back in 1977, while observing Uranus, scientists  at the Kuiper Airborne Observatory and the Perth

11:29 Observatory in Australia realized that, just  like Saturn, it had its own ring system.

11:35 But Voyager II revealed even more information  about those rings than anyone had expected.

11:39 It found that what was originally believed to be  a system of 9 rings was actually a system of 11.

11:45 The 2 extra rings were so faint and narrow,  scientists couldn’t see them from Earth. Voyager

11:50 revealed that they were very dark and thin,  made up of ice, rocks, and dust particles.

11:55 Almost 2 decades later, with the aid of the  Hubble telescope, another two rings were found,

11:59 forming a total of 13. 34.

12:02 The strangest thing Voyager II discovered at  Uranus may have been the planet's magnetic field.

12:07 On Earth, our magnetic field is closely aligned  with the planet's rotation, which is why the

12:11 magnetic poles sit near the North and South Poles. Uranus doesn't follow those rules.

12:16 The probe discovered that the  planet’s field is tilted at

12:19 59 degrees relative to its rotational axis. This would be like if Earth’s magnetic poles

12:24 were closer to the equator, rather  than at the planet’s physical poles.

12:28 Nothing like it had ever been seen before. 33.

12:31 Years after Voyager II discovered Uranus'  unusual magnetic field, scientists revisited

12:36 the data and arrived at a new possibility. A study published in 2024 suggested that the

12:41 spacecraft may have encountered Uranus during an  intense period of solar activity. This could have

12:46 compressed the planet’s magnetosphere and stripped  most of its plasma, resulting in the obscure data.

12:52 That doesn't mean the  original discovery was wrong.

12:55 Even if Voyager II had arrived at a different  time, Uranus would still possess a wildly

12:59 tilted magnetic field. What changed was  scientists' understanding of exactly

13:03 what Voyager was seeing at that moment. It's a reminder that even decades later,

13:08 Voyager II is still teaching us new things. 32.

13:11 Before Voyager II’s fly-by of Uranus, scientists  believed that this planet was just another “gas

13:17 giant.” Despite being significantly further  from the Sun, it was believed to be similar

13:21 in composition to Jupiter, made up  of the likes of hydrogen and helium.

13:25 Voyager II completely proved that wrong. Rather than having a solid surface,

13:29 the planet is thought to contain a  slushy sort of mixture of water, ammonia,

13:33 and methane existing under extreme temperatures  and crushing pressures deep within its interior.

13:39 In other words, Uranus isn't a giant ball  of rock or gas, but something far stranger.

13:44 The discovery fundamentally changed scientists'  understanding of the planet and helped reshape

13:49 theories about how the outer worlds of  our solar system formed and evolved.

13:53 31.

13:54 One of the first things we're taught about the  solar system is that the farther a planet is

13:58 from the Sun, the colder it should be. The Sun is the primary source of heat,

14:02 so it seems obvious that temperatures  would drop the farther away you travel.

14:05 With that logic, scientists long assumed that  Neptune, the most distant planet in the solar

14:10 system, would also be the coldest. Voyager II disproved that.

14:14 While flying by Uranus, it recorded a  record minimum atmospheric temperature

14:18 of 49 Kelvin (-224.2 degrees Celsius). That would make it the coldest planet

14:21 measured in the solar system, even colder than  Neptune, despite being much closer to the Sun.

14:26 Initially, scientists believed that this was  because Uranus didn’t emit any heat of its own.

14:31 30. For decades, the

14:33 theory held that Uranus’ inability to emit heat  was what made it such an incredibly cold location.

14:38 However, new research published in 2025 challenged  that long-held belief. The study found that Uranus

14:44 actually emits between 12.5 and 15% more energy  than it receives from the Sun. That indicates the

14:50 planet does have some kind of internal heat  source, even if it's a relatively weak one.

14:55 It still gives off far less heat than any other  planet in the solar system, including Neptune,

15:00 but it is no longer considered the thermally dead  world that many scientists once thought it was.

15:05 Exactly why Uranus behaves  this way remains unclear,

15:08 and it continues to be one of the most puzzling

15:10 and unusual planets in the entire solar system. It still radiates far less heat than any other

15:14 planet in the solar system, including Neptune,  but is not thermally dead, as once believed.

15:14 Scientists still aren’t sure exactly why this  happens and what it is that makes Uranus such a

15:14 unique member of the solar system. 29.

15:15 We’ve known for centuries that Saturn had rings. In fact, Galileo discovered them way back in the

15:20 17th century, but the Voyager probes  gave us our first detailed looks at

15:24 the ring systems surrounding Saturn. Voyager II managed to get close enough

15:28 that it was able to experience the chaos of  the rings firsthand. Its on-board instruments

15:33 detected hundreds of tiny impacts to  the probe’s body every single second.

15:37 These were caused by tiny dust  grains striking the craft.

15:40 Fortunately, the impacts were so small that they  didn’t cause any real damage to the probe or its

15:44 instruments. 28.

15:46 While Saturn’s rings were well-known,  Jupiter’s weren’t, at least not

15:50 until the Voyager probes confirmed it. As with many other discoveries, it was Voyager

15:55 I that provided the initial evidence, capturing  some faint images during its fly-by in 1979.

16:00 Voyager II then reinforced the data pool,  providing additional images while traveling

16:05 in the planet’s shadow. Those pictures  helped to confirm a three-part ring system,

16:09 with one main central ring, an inner  halo ring, and an outer gossamer ring.

16:14 During this same period, Voyager II even  confirmed the existence of another small moon,

16:18 which was subsequently named Adrastea, orbiting  the planet just outside the rings’ edges.

16:24 27. Adrastea was only one of several moons

16:27 that Voyager II was able to either confirm the  existence of or completely discover on its own.

16:32 It also discovered 10 new moons during its  flyby of Uranus, and another 6 around Neptune.

16:38 They weren't distant, unreachable objects.  They were sitting within our own solar system,

16:42 unnoticed until Voyager II passed through. Even after centuries of observing the night

16:47 sky with increasingly powerful telescopes and  instruments, Voyager showed just how much we were

16:52 still missing in our own cosmic backyard. 26.

16:55 Voyager II also helped to provide  clear evidence of which of the solar

16:59 system’s moons was the largest. Previously, it was a commonly

17:02 held belief that Saturn’s largest  moon, Titan, was the biggest of all.

17:06 One Jovian moon, known as Ganymede, is  actually slightly bigger, boasting a diameter

17:11 of almost 3,300 miles (5,310 kilometers). That makes it around 2% larger than Titan.

17:16 There isn’t a huge difference between  the 2, but it’s still enough to earn

17:19 Ganymede the top spot in the moon size rankings. The reason why Titan had long been assumed to be

17:24 larger was that it has such a dense atmosphere,  which essentially made it look bigger than it was.

17:30 25. Scientists used to believe that the

17:32 various moons throughout the solar system would  look more or less like our own. They expected

17:37 to discover little more than bare balls of rocks  and metal, without much activity on their surface.

17:42 They were quickly proved wrong. When traveling near Jupiter,

17:45 Voyager I found evidence of active  volcanoes on one of Jupiter’s moons, Io.

17:50 Voyager II later confirmed this. Despite passing  by Io much later, it was able to transmit

17:55 photographs of the same surface volcanoes still  erupting. This proved that the volcanic eruptions

18:00 witnessed by Voyager I weren’t some kind of freak  event or anomaly, but part of a continuous trend.

18:06 Voyager II was even able to estimate that some  of the plumes from the moon’s volcanoes shot an

18:11 estimated 62 miles (100 kilometers) into space. 24.

18:14 Voyager II’s volcano-related  discoveries weren’t done yet.

18:18 While it was passing Triton - Neptune’s largest  moon - it captured images of geyser-like plumes,

18:23 made up of erupting nitrogen gas and dust. It turned out that these geysers were

18:27 coming from ice volcanoes, technically called  cryovolcanoes, dotted across the moon’s surface.

18:33 NASA already had measurements of the moon, so  they knew that they couldn’t be normal volcanoes,

18:37 since the density of the moon was too low to  support molten rock. Voyager 2 helped to fill

18:42 in the blanks. The moon’s ice volcanoes  were able to eject plumes of gas almost 5

18:47 miles (8 kilometers) into the air 23.

18:49 The Voyager probes also gave us  a closer look at what weather

18:52 conditions might be like on the other planets. Voyager I found evidence of possible lightning

18:57 storms on Jupiter during its fly-by  of Earth’s largest planetary neighbor.

19:01 It picked up radio waves which scientists believed  were caused by atmospheric lightning. It also

19:06 captured images of brief flashes of light,  caused by lightning strikes below the clouds.

19:10 When Voyager II traveled through the same  area, it provided additional imaging data

19:15 with clear visual evidence of lightning  flashes inside the planet’s atmosphere.

19:19 These findings revealed that Jupiter’s  Jovian lightning was incredibly strong,

19:24 with some flashes being several times  more powerful than any ever seen on Earth.

19:28 22. Jupiter is also famous for the “Great Red Spot” on

19:32 its surface, which is actually a gigantic storm,  visible from space and twice the size of Earth.

19:38 Astronomers first saw the spot centuries ago,  but the first Voyager probe got close enough

19:43 to see that it was still raging. Scientists  estimate that it is the largest and oldest

19:48 continuous storm in the solar system. However, Voyager II provided evidence

19:51 of perhaps an even more intense storm on  a completely different planet: Neptune.

19:56 Nicknamed the “Great Dark Spot” by researchers  and photographed by the Voyager II probe in August

20:01 1989, the storm is believed to have wind speeds  of up to 1,500 miles per hour (2,400 km per hour).

20:07 Scientists believe that these speeds are related  to the planet’s own heat, plus the fact that it

20:12 has no mountains or valleys to slow the wind down. 21.

20:16 Voyager II also gave us some more valuable  information about the Great Red Spot of Jupiter.

20:21 The Voyager probes provided imagery to  show that the Great Red Spot was more

20:24 dynamic than any existing models had expected. It was found to be an anticylonic storm, rotating

20:30 in a counter-clockwise direction. Images showed it  drifting across the planet’s atmosphere, shaped by

20:35 the planet’s’ intense and turbulent winds. It even interacted with smaller nearby

20:40 storm systems, shifting and changing form between  Voyager II’s observations and earlier data.

20:45 20. The Voyager program also found

20:47 that at least two other moons in our solar system  - Europa of Jupiter and Enceladus of Saturn - had

20:53 the potential to host their own oceans. Traveling close to these moons, the probe captured

20:58 detailed images of their icy surfaces. Scientists  later revealed that there are likely to be

21:02 liquid-water oceans beneath the moons’ exteriors. These discoveries actually paved the way for

21:07 subsequent missions specifically to those two  moons, in which NASA hoped to learn more about

21:12 them. 19.

21:14 One of the most extraordinary successes  of the Voyager program was how the probes

21:18 were able to help scientists map out moons  from hundreds of millions of miles away.

21:22 Two of the vast moons of Jupiter, Ganymede  and Callisto, were photographed so many times

21:26 by Voyager I and Voyager II that we now have  clear imagery of at least 80% of their surfaces.

21:32 These images are incredibly detailed, with a  resolution of around 3 miles (5 kilometers. This

21:37 has allowed scientists to zoom in and explore  the various features, like craters, canyons,

21:41 and ridges, despite the distance from Earth. Similar images were acquired by Voyager II of

21:46 numerous other moons, painting clear pictures  of their surfaces and structures and forever.

21:51 18. There have been

21:52 many cases where Voyager II provided data that  wasn’t fully understood until decades later.

21:57 It was only in 2019, that researchers  reviewed data gathered from the fly-by

22:01 of Uranus. It revealed that the Voyager  II probe passed through a kind of gigantic

22:06 magnetic bubble, known as a plasmoid. Made from electrified gas wrapped in closed

22:11 magnetic loops, the plasmoid carries charged  particles from Uranus’ atmosphere out into space.

22:16 This bubble-like structure means the  planet’s atmosphere is slowly leaking away.

22:21 Some scientists estimate it could lead to a total  atmospheric loss of between 15 and 55% over time.

22:27 17. Voyager II wasn’t just the

22:30 first spacecraft to visit Uranus. It continued its  journey toward the outer edge of the solar system,

22:35 eventually making a flyby of Neptune. By that point, it had travelled 4.3

22:39 billion miles (7 billion kilometers).  Along the way it had to perform its

22:41 largest midcourse correction on February 14th,  1986 just to stay on course for the encounter.

22:48 When it finally arrived, Voyager II revealed a  wealth of new moons and data, while also helping

22:53 answer long-standing questions about Neptune  that had puzzled scientists for centuries.

22:58 16. Just like with Uranus, Voyager II’s

23:01 visit to Neptune completely rewrote the rulebook  about what this planet was supposed to be.

23:06 Prior to that point, many astronomers  had expected Neptune to be a relatively

23:10 calm frozen world. A distant ball of  ice, so far from the Sun that it was,

23:15 for all intents and purposes, a “dead” planet. In reality, however, Voyager II found that Neptune

23:20 is much more dynamic and energetic  than anyone had ever anticipated.

23:24 Even though it receives just 3% of the  sunlight that Jupiter receives, it was

23:29 discovered to have some of the wildest weather  conditions of any location in the solar system.

23:34 15. On Earth,

23:35 the fastest wind speed ever recorded is around 253  miles per hour (408 kilometers per hour). But even

23:40 winds of a few dozen miles per hour are more than  enough to make it quite challenging to get around.

23:46 On Neptune, Voyager II measured  winds traveling faster than

23:49 1,100 miles per hour (2,000 kilometers per hour). That’s faster than the speed of sound.

23:54 These wind speeds were detected moving in a  westward direction close to the planet’s equator,

23:59 and they’re propelled by the planet’s own  internal heat, rather than solar energy.

24:04 14.

24:04 The intense winds and other atmospheric activity  recorded on Neptune were found to be connected to

24:09 the planet’s surprising large internal heat source Voyager’s measurements showed that the planet was

24:14 able to radiate more than 2.5 times as  much heat as it receives from the Sun.

24:19 That same heat is responsible for the intense  storms that manifest in the form of Neptune’s

24:24 Great Dark Spot, as well as its Small Dark  Spot, also captured in images by the probe.

24:29 Called Dark Spot 2 or the Wizard’s Eye, it was a  much smaller cyclonic storm that was raging when

24:35 Voyager II passed by. It eventually died down and  has since disappeared from the planet’s surface,

24:40 as proven by Hubble telescope images. 13.

24:43 Before the Voyager mission, we believed we knew  the colors of the planets in our solar system.

24:48 They were clearly laid out in textbooks  and models, and Neptune was consistently

24:52 shown as a deep, dark blue world. However, Voyager II proved that

24:56 wasn’t exactly accurate. Neptune is actually more of

24:59 a teal or greenish-blue color, quite  close to Uranus. That’s despite the

25:03 two having always seemed different before this. Scientists later explained the color comes from

25:07 the high concentration of methane in Neptune’s  atmosphere, which affects how sunlight is absorbed

25:12 and scattered. 12.

25:14 We’ve already mentioned how Voyager II proved  that Jupiter had a previously unknown ring system.

25:19 Upon its arrival at Neptune, the probe  also confirmed that the final planet

25:23 in the solar system had its own rings, too. While there had been some theories about Neptune’s

25:28 rings, Voyager II was able to confirm them  with clear visual evidence. Its photos revealed

25:32 a distinct 5 ring system. Further analysis  showed that the rings were reasonably young,

25:38 while some of them contained distinctive arcs. Each of the rings has since been given names,

25:43 such as Lassell, Galle, and Arago. They’re  believed to be held in place by the gravitational

25:47 influence of one of Neptune’s moons. 11.

25:51 Another fascinating feature found  by Voyager II while visiting

25:54 Neptune is the so-called “Scooter” cloud. Spotted in 1989, this cloud was given its

25:59 nickname due to how quickly it appears to  “scoot” across the planet. It moves in an

26:04 eastward direction at speeds far greater than  the Great Dark Spot or other cloud features.

26:08 It’s believed to be not one cloud but a whole  group of them, similar in appearance to the

26:13 cirrus clouds we see on Earth. It circles  the planet at a rapid speed, forming part

26:18 of the complex and dynamic system of storms. Scooter changed appearance during Voyager II’s

26:22 visit, but remained present and visible for  the entire time the probe was in the area.

26:27 10. When Voyager II passed by Uranus

26:30 and found evidence that the planet’s magnetic  field was at an angle or “tilted,” they thought

26:34 it was a one-off. A random, freak occurrence  that existed nowhere else in the solar system.

26:39 But then Voyager II found evidence of  Neptune doing the exact same thing.

26:43 The probe discovered that Neptune’s magnetic  field is tilted by around 47 degrees relative

26:49 to its rotational axis. It’s also offset by  about 8,400 (13,518 kilometers) from its center.

26:54 Just like with Uranus, this  means Neptune’s magnetic

26:57 poles don’t line up with its physical poles. Scientists have proposed several theories to

27:01 explain this phenomenon, with many suggesting the  planet’s magnetic field is generated by a fluid,

27:06 conductive mantle layer closer to the surface. 9.

27:10 While Voyager II answered many  questions about the solar system,

27:13 it also revealed new mysteries. Especially  around the ice giants, Uranus and Neptune.

27:18 The probe discovered that both ice giants also  had their own distinctive radiation belts.

27:23 Completely unique, far weaker than expected,  and asymmetric in form, these radiation belts

27:28 are very different to the dipole fields seen  around the likes of Earth, Jupiter, and Saturn.

27:32 Scientists are still digging through the data  provided by Voyager II to learn more about how

27:37 and why these belts formed the way they did. NASA is already planning additional missions to

27:41 the ice giants to investigate them further. 8.

27:44 As Voyager II passed by Triton, Neptune’s largest  moon, the probe confirmed a structural anomaly

27:50 that left the astronomical community in shock:  Triton orbits its host planet backward, against

27:55 the direction of Neptune’s actual rotation. This sort of retrograde motion is physically

28:00 impossible for a moon that formed  over time from planetary debris.

28:05 This means that Triton isn’t a regular moon. Voyager II proved that it was, in fact,

28:10 some sort of cosmic gatecrasher. A massive icy  ball that originated from somewhere in the Kuiper

28:16 Belt and eventually came too close to our solar  system, billions of years ago. At that point,

28:20 it was seized by Neptune’s gravity and locked  in a never-ending backwards loop around its

28:25 new neighbor. 7.

28:27 As Voyager II passed close to Triton, it  also made another astonishing discovery:

28:31 the icy moon had an atmosphere. That puts it in a very exclusive group,

28:35 as only a handful of moons in the entire solar  system are known to have atmospheres of any kind.

28:41 However, Triton’s atmosphere was  found to be incredibly faint.

28:44 Dominated by nitrogen, it exerts a surface  pressure of only 14 microbars. That is a

28:49 microscopic fraction of the Earth’s atmospheric  pressure. But it’s still enough to ensure

28:53 that Triton doesn’t quite exist in a vacuum. It has enough atmospheric pressure to support

28:57 its own weather cycles and generate high altitude  winds. That’s made it one of the more interesting

29:02 moons for NASA to observe since its discovery. 6.

29:06 One feature of Triton that generated much  discussion in the scientific community was

29:10 the moon’s so-called “cantaloupe” terrain. Detailed in images provided by Voyager II,

29:15 the moon’s surface is rugged, covered with  a range of ridges, voids, and dimple-like

29:20 depressions… similar to a melon’s skin. Nowhere else in the solar system has a

29:24 surface quite like this… at least that we  know of. Further analysis suggests that this

29:29 is a reasonably young surface, having  formed less than 10 million years ago.

29:33 There are various theories about why Triton looks  this way. The leading belief is it was formed by

29:37 a process called diapirism, or the rising of  icy material from within the moon’s crust.

29:43 However, experts still aren’t entirely  convinced that this theory is correct.

29:47 5. In 1977, the

29:49 world was introduced to George Lucas’ Star Wars. One of the most distinctive images from that

29:54 famous film series is the Death Star: a  massive moon-sized space station with the

29:59 ability to blast entire planets out of existence. A few years after the first movie hit theaters,

30:04 sci-fi fans were left astonished when both  Voyager I and Voyager II sent back images

30:09 of something that looked exactly like the  Death Star in our very own solar system.

30:13 Fortunately, it wasn’t a massive  space station, it was a moon.

30:17 One of Saturn’s moons, named Mimas, to be precise. This moon had been identified centuries prior.

30:23 But, the Voyager probe’s images showed  just what a distinctive appearance it had,

30:27 with a vast crater on one side that looks  almost uncannily like the Death Star laser.

30:32 4. Upon its arrival at the edge of the solar system,

30:35 Voyager II encountered the Wall of Fire and the  rising density of interstellar space beyond.

30:41 It also encountered something else: the  intensely strong interstellar magnetic field,

30:45 which scientists have suggested acts like a  kind of straitjacket around our solar system.

30:50 It may be shaping the heliosphere in ways we are  only beginning to understand. By squeezing this

30:55 region of space, it’s making it flatter and more  compressed rather than the long, comet-like tail

31:00 scientists expected. 3.

31:02 Even though Voyager I and II are both in  interstellar space and traveling further

31:06 and further away from us, they continue  to make breakthroughs and discoveries

31:10 that shape our understanding of the universe. In February 2026, data from both Voyager probes

31:15 was compared to recent sky maps. It revealed  that our entire solar system sits inside a

31:20 “Local Bubble” of hot, low density gases. These gases were formed by a supernova

31:25 millions of years ago, but we’re  still feeling the effects of it today.

31:29 It’s part of the reason why Earth is protected  from dangerous kinds of cosmic radiation. We’re

31:34 not just protected by the Sun’s heliosphere, but  by this enormous, invisible bubble that acts like

31:39 a kind of force field. 2.

31:41 When we think about the solar  system, it’s easy to think we’ve

31:44 always been parked in the same region of space. However, data from Voyager II and other probes

31:48 has revealed that the Sun is more of a “cosmic  drifter.” It roams from point to point, passing

31:54 through relatively safe spaces and more dangerous  ones over the course of millions of years.

31:58 Right now, it’s believed to be inside the  Local Bubble, which is estimated at 1,000

32:03 light-years in width and provides that  much-needed protection humanity needs.

32:08 But it wasn’t always that way. Evidence suggests it has spent much

32:11 of its history moving through far more chaotic  and hazardous regions of interstellar space.

32:16 1. We may be safe for now, but it won’t last.

32:20 Projections made using Voyager II data suggest  that the Sun and its planets will eventually exit

32:24 the Local Bubble. At that point, the protection  it provides will be gone, and the Earth will,

32:29 in many ways, be left to fend for itself. It’s happened before.

32:33 The Sun orbits the center of the Milky Way,  taking over 200 million years to complete its

32:38 own “Galactic Year.” As it makes this  journey, it sometimes passes through

32:42 the galaxy’s dense, star-packed spiral arms. Astrophysicists have found that when this happens,

32:48 mass extinction events also occur on Earth at the  exact same time. In other words, the next time we

32:54 leave the Local Bubble and head towards the deadly  spiral arms, another mass extinction might occur.

33:00 Luckily, that’s still several million years away. Voyager is just one example of how much we still

33:05 don’t understand about space. And honestly,  that’s barely scratching the surface.

33:10 Check out “50 Surprising Facts About Space  You Didn't Know” or click on this video.

docs.text:
00:00 What does a CPU do when there's nothing

00:02 to do and how does it do it? Open Task

00:05 Manager on a quiet Windows machine and

00:06 you may see something that looks

00:07 absolutely backwards. The system idle

00:10 process sitting there using 90 95 even

00:13 99% of your CPU. And if you've never

00:16 seen it before, your natural reaction

00:18 might be, well, there's the problem.

00:19 It's this idle thing hogging the whole

00:21 machine. But the system idle process is

00:24 not stealing your CPU. It's the

00:26 accounting record for the CPU that

00:28 nobody wanted. It's the empty lane on

00:30 the freeway at 3 in the morning. It's

00:32 not traffic. It's the absence of

00:33 traffic. And yet, that simple little

00:35 number opens a door to one of the most

00:37 important parts of any operating system.

00:39 What does a CPU do when there's nothing

00:41 to do? Because a processor can't just

00:44 wander off and get a coffee. At every

00:46 instant, every logical processor in your

00:48 machine has to be in some defined state.

00:51 It's either running a thread that has

00:53 work to do, handling an interrupt,

00:55 executing kernel code, or sitting in

00:57 some kind of idle path waiting for the

00:59 next event. The system idle process is

01:02 Windows giving a name and a counter to

01:03 that last category. I actually did it

01:06 recently in my night driver code, an

01:07 ESP32 project that runs all these LEDs.

01:10 I had two cores, so I created two idle

01:12 tasks, one for each core, both scheduled

01:14 at the absolute lowest priority. Their

01:17 job was simply to run when nothing else

01:19 could. In my case, I just burned time in

01:22 a busy weight, kept track of how much

01:23 time they wasted, and that made the idle

01:25 measurement easy. Anytime those lower

01:28 priority tasks got scheduled, it meant

01:30 that there was no real task time needed.

01:32 And that's a great model for

01:34 understanding the idea. But it's also

01:36 exactly the wrong model for a modern

01:38 Windows PC. Because on a small embedded

01:40 system, especially one running at a

01:42 fixed clock speed, the idle task that

01:44 spins in a loop may be good enough. It's

01:46 wasteful, but the waste is visible and

01:48 predictable. If your idle task ran 80%

01:51 of the time, then roughly 80% of the CPU

01:53 was unused. Older PCs like the one I

01:56 wrote the original task manager on were

01:58 closer to that world. CPUs often ran at

02:00 a constant speed, so CPU usage was

02:03 mostly a time measurement that felt like

02:05 a work measurement. If the machine said

02:07 it was 50% busy, you could imagine that

02:09 half of the available compute budget had

02:11 been consumed. Modern CPUs laugh at that

02:14 simplification. Today, a processor is

02:16 not like a fixed speed crankshaft or

02:18 flywheel. It's a power managed beast. It

02:21 can run one moment at 5 GHz, the next

02:23 one at 1 ghahertz, and then put a core

02:25 into a shallow nap, then a deeper sleep,

02:27 then wake up on an interrupt and turbo

02:29 again before you have a chance at all of

02:32 catching that on a graph. So, if you see

02:34 50% CPU today, that might mean that the

02:36 CPU spent half the time doing work at

02:38 high speed and the other half resting at

02:40 low power. Or it might mean that all

02:42 cores were lightly loaded, or one core

02:44 was pegged while the others were asleep,

02:47 or a hybrid CPU was juggling work

02:49 between performance cores and efficiency

02:50 cores. And so that percentage is not the

02:53 whole truth. It's kind of a cartoon

02:54 version of the truth. Windows does not

02:57 schedule programs. It schedules threads.

02:59 Every processor you think of as an app

03:01 is really a container for one or more

03:03 threads. And those threads are what the

03:05 scheduleuler actually chooses between.

03:07 If a thread is ready to run, it goes

03:09 into a ready queue. Theuler looks at

03:12 priorities, processor affinity, recent

03:14 history, fairness, power policy, and a

03:16 pile of other details, and then chooses

03:18 what should run next on each logical

03:20 processor. But sometimes there is no

03:23 thread ready to run on a given

03:24 processor. And not no important thread

03:27 and not no foreground app. What we mean

03:29 is that there's no runnable thread

03:31 available at all. Everything is waiting

03:33 for disk or waiting for a network packet

03:35 or waiting on a timer or waiting for a

03:37 lock or waiting for the user or it's

03:38 simply finished. And at that point,

03:40 theuler still needs to answer the

03:42 question, well, what thread runs now?

03:44 And the answer is the idle thread. So

03:46 each logical processor has an idle

03:48 thread. The system idle process is the

03:51 object that Windows uses to account for

03:53 these this group of idle threads. It's

03:55 not a normal application. You can't

03:57 close it to reclaim performance. You

03:59 can't uninstall your idleness. It's the

04:02 bottom of the scheduleuler's world, the

04:03 safe place the CPU lands when there is

04:06 nothing else useful to execute. This is

04:08 cleaner than making nothing a special

04:10 case because kernels hate special cases

04:12 because special cases grow teeth

04:14 eventually. It's much better to say that

04:15 every processor is always running some

04:18 thread and that sometimes that thread is

04:19 the idle thread. But the idle thread on

04:21 a modern PC does not sit there in a

04:23 tight loop saying, "Are we there yet?" a

04:24 billion times a second. That would be

04:26 insane. It would keep the processor

04:28 awake. it would burn power, generate

04:30 heat, and murder your battery for the

04:32 privilege of accomplishing absolutely

04:33 nothing. So instead, the idle path

04:36 becomes an opportunity to save power.

04:38 The simplest old school version of this

04:40 on the x86 is the old halt instruction.

04:43 Halt just tells the processor to stop

04:45 executing instructions until something

04:47 happens, typically an interrupt. That

04:49 alone is a giant improvement over a busy

04:51 loop because the core is no longer

04:53 fetching, decoding, and executing

04:55 useless instructions. But modern idle

04:57 goes much deeper. CPUs have performance

05:00 states and idle states. Performance

05:02 states, often called Pates, control

05:04 things like the frequency and the

05:06 voltage and what's going on with the

05:08 processor while it's active. Idle

05:10 states, or Cates, describe how deeply

05:12 parts of the processor can go to sleep

05:14 when there is no work to do. So, a

05:17 shallow idle state is quick to leave and

05:19 quick to enter, but saves less power. A

05:21 deeper idle state saves more power but

05:24 costs more time and energy to enter and

05:25 exit. So Windows has to make a judgment.

05:28 If the next timer is going to fire in

05:30 100 micros secondsonds, then diving into

05:32 a deep sleep state would be pointless.

05:34 And by the time you get settled in, it's

05:36 already time to wake up again. But if

05:37 the machine can stay quiet for 20

05:39 milliseconds, now the math changes. The

05:41 CPU can shut down more internal

05:43 machinery, reduce power, and come back

05:45 when the next interrupt rings its

05:46 doorbell. And that means the idle thread

05:48 is no longer just a trash can for spare

05:50 cycles. It's now part of the power

05:52 management strategy. And that strategy

05:54 only works if your software cooperates.

05:57 So if a program has nothing to do, it

05:59 should block. It should wait on an

06:01 event, a socket, a timer, a file

06:03 handler, or some other kind of

06:05 synchronization object. Because when it

06:07 does that, Windows removes the thread

06:09 from the ready Q. Theuler no longer

06:11 considers it runnable. And that opens

06:13 the door for the idle thread to run and

06:15 the processor can then potentially

06:16 sleep. But if a program busy waits, it

06:19 lies to theuler. It says, "I'm ready and

06:21 I have work to do." Even if all it's

06:23 doing is spinning in a loop, checking

06:25 whether something important changed, it

06:27 still looks and is runnable. So the CPU

06:29 keeps running it, maybe at low priority,

06:32 maybe plately yielding to real work, but

06:34 preventing idle nonetheless. And that

06:36 distinction matters more now than it did

06:38 in the old fixed speed world. A low

06:40 priority background task that burns CPU

06:43 may not make your foreground app slow,

06:45 but it can stop the processor from

06:46 entering deeper idle states. So the

06:49 machine feels fine, but the fan runs,

06:51 the laptop gets warm, the battery

06:53 disappears. You look at task manager and

06:55 nothing looks dramatic because the crime

06:57 is not performance. The crime is

06:59 preventing rest. And that's why idle on

07:02 a modern machine is not merely the

07:03 absence of work. It's a carefully

07:05 engineered state the system tries to

07:07 reach and preserve. It's also why CPU

07:10 usage is easier to misunderstand than

07:12 ever. When Task Manager says a system

07:14 idle process is at 95%, that usually

07:16 means the CPU is mostly unused, which is

07:19 good. It does not mean that the idle

07:20 processes is consuming 95% of your

07:23 system. It means that 95% of the sampled

07:25 processor time had no better work to do.

07:28 The idle process is not the pig of the

07:30 trough. It's just the leftover food,

07:33 which kind of makes it the pig of the

07:34 trough. So, forget that analogy. But

07:37 conversely, if the system idle process

07:39 is low, something is using the CPU. That

07:42 something might be an app or a service

07:43 or a driver, interrupt handling,

07:45 antivirus, indexing, compression, or a

07:48 browser tab that's decided to become a

07:50 space heater, or perhaps some background

07:52 service doing what background services

07:53 do best, which is making you wonder why

07:55 they exist. But even then, the aggregate

07:57 number can mislead you. Suppose you have

08:00 an eight logical processor machine, and

08:02 one old singlethreaded program pins one

08:04 logical processor at 100%. Overall CPU

08:07 usage may only show 12 or 13%. The

08:10 system as a whole is mostly idle, but

08:12 the program that you care about is

08:13 completely bottlenecked. From the

08:15 machine's point of view, there is plenty

08:17 of CPU left. From your point of view,

08:19 the app is stuck in molasses. But both

08:21 things are true. And that's why averages

08:23 are where the truth goes to wear a fake

08:25 mustache. And the reverse is also true.

08:27 A machine can show moderate CPU usage

08:30 and still feel terrible because the CPU

08:31 is not the bottleneck. It might be

08:33 waiting on disc. It might be paging

08:35 because memory is tight or it might be

08:37 stalled on network calls. It might be

08:39 thermally throttled. It might be

08:41 drowning in interrupts from a bad driver

08:43 or it might be stuck behind a lock held

08:44 by another thread that is itself waiting

08:46 for something else. Computers are very

08:49 good at arranging circular blame. The

08:51 system idle process helps you eliminate

08:53 at least one suspect. So if idle is

08:55 high, the CPU probably is not your main

08:57 problem. Not always, but usually. If

09:00 idle is low, then something is keeping

09:01 the processors busy and then you go

09:03 hunting. There's one more wrinkle, and

09:05 it's a big one. Timers. Modern operating

09:08 systems try hard to batch work. If 10

09:10 different programs each wake up once per

09:12 second at slightly different times, the

09:14 CPU may never get a decent nap. It's

09:17 wake, work, sleep, wake, work, sleep

09:19 over and over. So, Windows tries to

09:21 coales timers where it can, aligning

09:23 wakeups so that the machine handles a

09:25 burst of activity and then returns back

09:26 to idle. It's one of these clever

09:28 optimizations that users rarely ever

09:30 notice, but they will absolutely notice

09:32 it when it doesn't work. a badly behaved

09:34 app that wakes the CPU all the time and

09:36 can destroy battery life while barely

09:38 appearing in the performance charts.

09:40 It's like somebody walking into your

09:42 bedroom every 30 seconds to ask you if

09:43 you're asleep yet. So, the best idle

09:45 time is not just unused time, it's

09:47 uninterrupted unused time. And that's

09:50 also why operating systems have become

09:52 more aggressive about background work.

09:54 They defer it, they batch it, they run

09:56 it on a laptop when it's plugged in.

09:58 They avoid waking sleeping cores if one

10:00 active core can handle the work. They

10:02 may park cores entirely on hybrid

10:05 systems. They may prefer efficiency

10:06 cores for background tasks and reserve

10:08 performance cores for foreground

10:10 responsiveness. And the goal is not to

10:12 simply make the CPU graph look better.

10:14 The goal is to get useful work done

10:16 quickly and then get out of the way.

10:18 This is sometimes called the race to

10:19 idle. It sounds counterintuitive, but it

10:21 can be more efficient to run fast for a

10:23 short burst and then sleep deeply than

10:25 to run slowly for a long time while

10:28 never quite getting idle. Your CPU may

10:30 sprint to finish a task and then drop

10:32 into a low power state. And that spike

10:34 is not necessarily waste. It may be the

10:37 most efficient path back to doing

10:38 nothing. And doing nothing done properly

10:40 is one of the hardest jobs on the

10:42 machine. So the systemal process exists

10:44 for three main reasons. It gives theuler

10:47 a real thread to run when nothing else

10:49 is ready. Gives Windows and tools like

10:51 task manager a clean way to account for

10:53 unused processor time. And it provides

10:55 the entry point into the processor idle

10:57 behavior that lets modern systems save

10:59 power, reduce heat, and stay responsive.

11:02 That's the journey from the simple

11:04 embedded idle task to the modern Windows

11:06 idle process. That's the journey from

11:08 the simple embedded idle task to the

11:10 modern Windows idle process. The

11:12 embedded system just says run this

11:14 lowest priority loop so we can measure

11:15 what's left. The modern Windows version

11:17 says there's no work here. So, let's

11:19 account for that fact, predict how long

11:20 the silence might last, and then put as

11:23 much silicon to sleep as we safely can.

11:25 And that's why the old mental model is

11:27 useful but incomplete. On a fixed speed

11:30 system, idle time is wasted time. On a

11:33 modern system, idle time is an asset.

11:35 It's where battery life comes from. It's

11:37 where thermal headroom comes from. It's

11:39 what lets your CPU turbo when you

11:41 actually need it to because it wasn't

11:42 wasting heat 5 seconds earlier doing

11:44 nothing badly. The system idle process

11:46 is not your enemy. It's Windows saying

11:48 good news. The machine has spare

11:50 capacity. And on a modern computer,

11:52 spare capacity is not just unused

11:54 performance. It's potential silence,

11:56 potential battery life, potential

11:58 coolness, and potential speed later when

12:00 you need it. So the next time you see

12:02 the system idle at 98%, don't panic.

12:04 It's not a runaway process. It's not

12:06 malware. It's not Windows eating itself.

12:08 It's just a sound of your CPU waiting

12:10 politely for something worth doing. And

12:12 in a world where so much software seems

12:14 determined to burn every available cycle

12:15 just to animate the settings page, a

12:17 processor that knows how to do nothing

12:19 for a bit is a beautiful thing. If you

12:21 found today's episode interesting or

12:23 entertaining, remember that I'm mostly

12:24 in this for the subs and likes. So, I

12:26 would be honored if you would consider

12:27 leaving me one of each before you go

12:29 today. And if you're already subscribed,

12:31 thank you. In the meantime, and in

12:33 between time, I'll see you next time

12:34 right here in Dave's Garage.

12:37 >> Do it. Do it. Do it.

00:56 computational music theory.

01:05 from a professor of music cognition

01:28

01:29 All right.

01:32 I took the tea here today.

01:38 [DISCORDANT CHORD]

01:39 Right.

01:50 There's something about it.

01:52 That's like saying, I took the tea here, octopus.

01:54 Nothing wrong with octopus, but it just

01:56 doesn't fit the context of what happened before it.

02:00 Now, this double take that your brain does

02:02 can be measured using electrical potentials

02:04 on the surface of the scalp.

02:05 This is a picture of my mom getting

02:07 her brain potentials recorded.

02:08 And she's got 64 electrodes on her cap there.

02:12 And what those do is make recordings like this.

02:17 to expected and unexpected musical chords.

02:24 on the surface of the scalp.

02:29 of the unexpected chord, your brain is doing its double take,

02:32 or saying, oh, that was unexpected.

02:34 And 500 milliseconds, you get the brain saying, oh,

02:37 how do I integrate that into what happened before?

02:40 So this is telling us with millisecond accuracy

02:44 that we know about music.

02:46 There is something about our brains

02:47 that is very sensitive to what's grammatical in Western music.

02:51 So the question is, where does this knowledge come from?

02:53 How do we come to know what we know?

02:55 So to answer that question, we again

02:57 have to go all the way back to the ancient greeks.

02:59 Pythagoras found that if two strings are being played

03:02 together, where one string is twice the length of the other,

03:06 those two sound good together.

03:07 They sound consonant.

03:09 So this 2-to-1 frequency ratio is what supposedly brought us

03:13 closer to the Greek gods.

03:15 In fact, the word symphony originally

03:17 means vibrating in perfect harmony using

03:19 these mathematical integer ratios.

03:22 So this 2-to-1 frequency ratio is true of music all around

03:26 the world.

03:27 Now, different cultures divide that 2-to-1 frequency ratio

03:30 in different ways.

03:31 In our culture, the equal-tempered Western chromatic

03:33 scale divides them in 12 steps.

03:35 So this is how it sounds.

03:41

03:44 OK.

03:47 Why 2 to 1?

03:49 So the Bohlen-Pierce scale is based on a 3-to-1 frequency

03:52 ratio.

03:53 And within that, we've got 13 logarithmic divisions

03:56 of that scale.

03:57 So you still get some mathematical integer ratio.

04:00 So the Greek gods are not offended here.

04:02 But what this sounds like is completely

04:30 So I'm going to play you for about a minute a snippet

06:03 So what we're seeing here is the beginning of musical taste.

06:06 The more you listen to something,

06:08 But what I'm interested in is how learning occurs.

06:11 And it turns out that learning does not

06:13 occur with repetition but with variability.

06:15 In other words, the more different ways

06:59 One is Carol Krumhansl and her landmark book,

11:59 And by far, I think the most interesting for me part of this

00:19 PATRICK WINSTON: The Uniform Code of Military Justice specifies court martial for any officer who sends a soldier

00:27 into battle without a weapon. There ought to be a similar protection for students

00:32 because students shouldn't go out into life without the ability to communicate,

00:38 and that's because your success in life will be determined largely by your ability to speak,

00:43 your ability to write, and the quality of your ideas, in that order.

00:50 I know that I can be successful in this because the quality of communication,

00:57 your speaking, your writing, is largely determined by this formula. It's a matter of how much knowledge you have,

01:05 how much you practice with that knowledge, and your inherent talent, and notice that the T is very small.

01:12 What really matters is what you know. This point came to me suddenly a few decades ago when

01:19 I was skiing at Sun Valley. I had heard that it was Celebrity Weekend, and one

01:25 of the celebrities was Mary Lou Retton,

01:30 famous Olympic gymnast, perfect 10s in the vault. And I heard that she was a novice at skiing,

01:38 so when the opportune moment arrived, I looked over on the novice slope and saw this young woman who, when she became unbalanced,

01:46 went like that. And I said that's got to be her. That must be the gymnast.

01:53 But then, it occurred to me, I'm a much better skier than she is, and she's an Olympic athlete-- not only

01:58 an ordinary Olympic athlete, an outstanding one. And I was a better skier because I had the K, and I had the P,

02:08 and all she had was the T. So you can get a lot better than people who may have inherent talents if you have

02:15 the right amount of knowledge. So that's what my objective is today, and here's my promise.

02:20 Today, you will see some examples of what you can put in your armamentarium of speaking

02:28 techniques, and it will be the case that some one of those examples, some heuristic, some technique,

02:37 maybe only one, will make-- will be the one that gets you the job.

02:43 And so this is a very non-linear process. You never know when it's going to happen, but that is my promise.

02:48 By the end of the next 60 minutes, you'll have been exposed to a lot of ideas, some of which

02:55 you'll incorporate into your own repertoire, and they will ensure that you get the maximum opportunity

03:03 to have your ideas valued and accepted

03:09 by the people you speak with. Now, in order to do that, we have to have a rule of engagement, and that

03:17 is no laptops, no cell phones.

03:22 So if you could close those, I'll start up as soon as you're done. Some people ask why that is a rule of engagement,

03:31 and the answer is, we humans only have one language processor.

03:36 And if your language processor is enga-- could you shut the laptop, please? If your language processor is engaged browsing the web

03:44 or reading your email, you're distracted. And worse yet, you distract all of the people around you.

03:50 Studies have shown that. And worse yet, if I see a open laptop somewhere back

03:56 there or up here, it drives me nuts, and I do a worse job.

04:02 And so that ensures that all of your friends who are paying attention don't get the performance

04:08 that they came to have. So that's it for preamble.

04:13 Let's get started. First thing we talk about, of course, is how to start.

04:25 Some people think the right thing to do is to start a talk with a joke.

04:39 I don't recommend it, and the reason is that, in the beginning of a talk,

04:46 people are still putting their laptops away. They're becoming adjusted to your speaking parameters,

04:52 to your vocal parameters, and they're not ready for a joke.

04:58 So it doesn't work very well. They usually fall flat. What you want to do instead is start with empowerment promise.

05:06 You want to tell people what they're going to know at the end of the hour

05:13 that they didn't know at the beginning of the hour. It's an empowerment promise. It's the reason for being here.

05:19 What would be an example? Oh, I see.

05:24 At the end of this 60 minutes, you will know things about speaking you don't know now,

05:30 and something among those things you know will make a difference in your life. Yeah, that's an empowerment promise,

05:36 so that's the best way to start. So now that I've talked a little bit about how to start,

05:41 what I want to do is give you some samples of heuristics that are always on my mind when I give a talk,

05:48 and first of these heuristics is that it's a good idea to cycle on the subject.

05:56 Go around it. Go round it again. Go round it again. Some people say, tell him what you want to tell him.

06:05 Tell him again, and then tell him a third time, as if people weren't intelligent.

06:11 But the point is-- the reason is-- well, there are many reasons, one of which is, at any given moment, about 20% of you

06:19 will be fogged out no matter what the lecture is. So if you want to ensure that the probability that everybody

06:24 gets it is high, you need to say it three times. So cycling is one of the things that I always

06:31 think about when I give a talk. Another thing I think about is, in explaining my idea,

06:38 I want to build a fence around it so that it's not confused

06:45 with somebody else's idea. So if you were from Mars, and I was teaching you

06:50 about what an arch is, I might say to you, well, that's an arch. And that's not to be confused with some other things

06:57 that other people might think is-- this is not an arch.

07:02 That's not an arch. I'm building a fence around my idea so that it can be distinguished from somebody else's idea.

07:09 So in a more technical sense, I might say, well, my algorithm might similar-- might seem similar to Jones's algorithm,

07:15 except his is exponential, and mine's linear. That's putting a fence around your idea so that people can not be confused about how it

07:22 might relate to something else. The third thing on this list of samples

07:30 is the idea of verbal punctuation.

07:44 And the idea here is that, because people will occasionally fog out and need to get back on the bus,

07:52 you need to provide some landmark places where you're announcing that it's a good time to get back on.

08:00 So I might, in this talk, say something about this being my outline.

08:05 The first thing we're going to do is talk about how to start. Then we're going to deal with these four samples,

08:11 and among these four samples, I've talked about the first idea-- that's cycling.

08:16 The second idea, building-- and now, the third idea is verbal punctuation.

08:22 So I'm enumerating and providing numbers. I'm giving you a sense that there's a seam in the talk,

08:28 and you can get back on.

08:33 So now, we're on a roll, and since we're on a roll, can you guess what fourth idea might be here--

08:42 an idea that helps people get back on the bus?

08:48 AUDIENCE: Ask a question. PATRICK WINSTON: Yes? AUDIENCE: Ask a question. [INAUDIBLE]

08:53 PATRICK WINSTON: Ask a question, yes. Thank you. So ask a question.

09:05 And so I will ask a question-- how much dead air can there be? How long can I pause?

09:11 I counted seven seconds. It seemed like an eternity to me to wait and not say anything

09:16 for seven seconds, but that's the standard amount of time you can wait for an answer. And of course, the question has to be carefully chosen.

09:23 It can't be too obvious because then people will be embarrassed to say it, but the answers can't be too hard because then nobody will have anything to say.

09:32 So here are some sample heuristics you can put in your armamentarium and build up your repertoire of ideas about presentation.

09:43 And now, if this persuades you that there is something to know, that there is knowledge,

09:52 then I've already succeeded because what I want to convince you of, is if you watch the speakers you admire and feel

09:59 are effective, and ask yourselves why they're successful, then you can build up your own personal repertoire

10:06 and develop your own personal style. And that's my fundamental objective, and the rest of this talk is about some

10:12 of the things that are in my armamentarium that I think are effective. So next thing on our agenda, as we

10:20 start to discuss these other things, is a discussion of time and place. So what do you think is a good time to have a lecture?

10:27 11 AM? Yeah.

10:38 And the reason is most people at MIT are awake by then,

10:44 and hardly anyone has gone back to sleep. It's not right after a meal.

10:50 People aren't fatigued from this or that. It's a great time to have a lecture. So that brings me, next, to the question of what

10:56 about the place? And the most important thing about the place is that it be well lit.

11:09 This room is well lit. Problem with other kinds of rooms is that we humans,

11:16 whenever the lights go down, or whenever the room is dimly lighted, it signals

11:21 that we should go to sleep. So whenever I go somewhere to give a talk, even today, the first thing I do when

11:27 I speak to the audio-visual people is say, keep the lights full up.

11:34 Oh, they might reply, people will see the slides better if we turn the lights off, and then I reply,

11:42 it's extremely hard to see slides through closed eyelids.

11:50 What else can you say about the place? Well, the place should be cased, and I

11:58 mean that in a colloquial sense, of like if you're robbing a bank, you would go to the bank

12:05 some occasions before to see what it's like, so there are no surprises when you do your robbery.

12:13 So whenever I go somewhere to speak, the first thing I ask my host to do is to take me to the place

12:18 where I'll be speaking so that if there are any weirdnesses, I'll be able to deal with it.

12:26 Sometimes, it might require some intervention. Sometimes, it just might require me to understand

12:31 what the challenges are. So when I came here this morning,

12:36 I did what I typically do. I imagined that all the seats were filled with disinterested farm animals,

12:44 and that way, I knew that, no matter how bad it was, it wouldn't be as bad as that.

12:51 So finally, it should be reasonably-- it should be reasonably populated.

13:03 It should be the case that-- if there were 10 people in this hall,

13:09 everyone would be wondering, what's going on that's so much more interesting that nobody's here. So you want to get a right sized place that's--

13:17 doesn't have to be packed, but it has to be more than half full. So those are some thoughts about a time and place.

13:24 Next thing I want to talk about is a subject of boards and props and slides.

13:38 Well, these are the tools of the trade. I believe that this is the right tool for speaking

13:49 when your purpose is informing. The slides are good when your purpose is exposing,

13:56 but this is what I use when I'm informing, teaching, lecturing, and there's several reasons why I use it.

14:02 For one thing, when you use the board, you have a graphic quality.

14:10 It's the case that, when you have a board, then you can easily exploit the fact that you can use graphics

14:19 in your presentation. So that's the graphic quality that I like, and the next thing

14:25 I like is the speed property.

14:30 The speed with which you write on the blackboard is approximately the speed at which people can absorb ideas.

14:36 If you go flipping through a bunch of slides, nobody can go that fast.

14:44 Finally, one great property of a board is that it can be a target.

14:53 Many people who are novices at speaking

14:59 find themselves suddenly aware of their hands. It's as if their hands were private parts that shouldn't

15:06 be exposed in public, so right away, they go into the pockets, and this is considered insulting in some parts of the world.

15:14 Or alternatively, maybe the hands will go in back like this.

15:19 I was once in a convent in Serbia, and my host--

15:27 as soon as we entered, a nun came up to us and offered us a refreshment. And I was about to say, no, thank you,

15:33 and he said, eat that stuff or die. It's a question of local custom and politeness.

15:42 But then before anything happened there, the nun pulled my hands out like this

15:49 because it was extraordinarily insulting in that culture to have your hands behind your back.

15:54 So why is that? Well, it's usually supposed that that's that it has to do with whether you're concealing a weapon.

16:02 So if your hands are in your pockets or behind your back, then it looks like you might have a weapon,

16:09 and that's what I mean by the virtue-- one of these virtues of the board. Now, you have something to do with your hands.

16:15 You can point out the stuff. I was once watching Seymour Papert give a lecture,

16:22 and I thought it was terrific. So I went a second time-- first time to absorb the content, second time

16:28 to note style. And what I discovered is that Papert was constantly pointing at the board.

16:33 And then I thought about it a little while, and I noted that none of the stuff he was pointing to

16:38 had anything to do with what he was saying. Nevertheless, it was an effective technique.

16:46 So that's just a little bit about the virtue

16:52 of blackboards. Now, I want to talk about props. The custodians of knowledge about props

16:59 are the playwrights. Many decades ago, I saw a play by Henrik Ibsen.

17:05 It was Hedda Gabler. I remember vaguely that it was about a woman in an unhappy

17:11 marriage, and her husband was in competition for an academic job with somebody else.

17:17 And he was going to lose partly because he was boring, and partly because the competitor had just

17:23 written a magnificent book. By the way, this is back in the days before there were copying machines and computers.

17:30 Anyhow, as the play opens, there's a potbellied stove,

17:43 and in the beginning of the play, the potbelly stove, with its open door,

17:50 just has some slightly glowing embers. But the potbellied stove is always there,

17:57 and as tension mounts in the play, and you see this manuscript, this prop that Ibsen so artfully used, you just know

18:06 that something's going to happen, because as the play goes on, the fire gets bigger and hotter
