00:10 MICHAEL CUTHBELT: Hello everybody,

00:11 and welcome to our last video, at least for a while,

00:14 on music representation.

00:15 And I want to talk about a remarkable tool created

00:19 by a researcher at Stanford, Craig Stewart Sapp,

00:22 that he calls the Rosetta stone.

00:26 I'm going to be skipping a few slides from his presentation,

00:29 and I've added a few other things, but in this module,

00:33 I will also present his entirety of slides that he has given.

00:39 And my hat's off to Craig Sapp for all he's done

00:43 and his generosity.

00:46 So the Rosetta Stone was a stone discovered in, I think, 1799

00:52 and deciphered over the next--

00:56 I don't know-- 10 years or so.

00:58 That was a remarkable discovery, because up until that point,

01:04 Egyptian hieroglyphics such as those highlighted here

01:07 were not legible by anybody living at that point.

01:13 But the Rosetta Stone had two forms of Egyptian hieroglyphics

01:22 in the top two sections and also at the bottom,

01:25 the exact same text in Greek.

01:28 And so since people knew how to read ancient Greek,

01:31 they were able to go through each

01:33 of the signs of the ancient Greek

01:35 and figure out what the signs of the hieroglyphics

01:39 and the two forms of writing meant.

01:42 Craig Sapp's Rosetta Stone allows

01:45 us to look at how different digital representations of music

01:51 work by encoding the exact same melody in, I think,

01:56 almost two dozen different formats.

01:58 These are all the formats that have ever been used,

02:01 but it's a good chunk of them.

02:02 So here's the melody, and it has some interesting things.

02:07 Here it has different octaves.

02:09 It has key signature, time signature.

02:11 It has beaming information.

02:13 The only thing it really--

02:15 well, some of the things it doesn't

02:16 have are chords and triplets and things like that,

02:20 but once you see how this melody is encoded in a lot of formats,

02:24 you can figure out how all the other things might

02:27 be encoded in those formats.

02:30 So here's an example of a code that's not used as much today

02:34 but was once very important, playing an easy code.

02:38 And you can see that we have something like--

02:41 I can decipher, OK, maybe that's a G on clef on line two,

02:45 and then we have a flat on b 2/4.

02:50 And then we have an eighth note with a dot on C.

02:54 And then I guess the three means 32nd notes DC.

03:01 And there's a little bracket around it,

03:03 and that probably means they're beamed together.

03:05 Then we have two eighth notes on C beamed together.

03:09 We have slash means new measure and so on.

03:13 Throughout the whole thing, we can

03:15 see that, oh, maybe octave isn't encoded here or something

03:21 like that.

03:22 And we can figure out how those go.

03:25 Here is another format.

03:26 This is primarily used for folk songs called ABC.

03:30 And we can see that--

03:32 well, example.

03:34 Maybe that's the title of the piece.

03:36 2/4 key is F. L means the smallest possible.

03:42 Encoding is 16th note.

03:44 And then we see that C is worth three of those 16th.

03:47 D is worth, I guess, 1/2.

03:50 C is 1/2.

03:51 C is worth two of those.

03:53 That's the eighth note.

03:54 C is worth two of those.

03:55 We have a bar line and so on.

03:57 And we can see that the high C is encoded with C

04:00 with a apostrophe after it.

04:04 This is what's called DARMS code.

04:07 It was once highly used, but it hasn't really

04:10 been used very much recently.

04:12 And well, I don't know how to read DARMS code,

04:16 but I think that the numbers represent pitch.

04:20 Here we have an eighth with a dot.

04:22 And T means 32nd, I'm guessing, and so on.

04:27 We have some RSs, which might mean rest 16th note.

04:31 This is GUIDO Music Notation, which

04:34 uses backslashes to indicate certain kinds

04:37 of musical elements.

04:39 We can see clefs keys, meters are encoded in here.

04:43 Barlines are explicitly encoded.

04:45 And it looks like you put a slash before a duration.

04:53 And there's some notes that don't have durations,

04:55 but they seem to be the same duration as before and so on.

05:00 I think it looks like underscores our rest.

05:04 This is MuseData, which Michael Good

05:06 said was one of the inspirations behind MusicXML.

05:11 It's a little bit bigger format, takes more space.

05:14 It was one of what we used to use a lot,

05:18 these fixed position encodings, so

05:20 that if you're writing in a monospaced font,

05:23 every single place has a particular meaning.

05:27 So you can look at column eight or something like that

05:30 and see the duration.

05:31 And then, this was a major positive step because it encodes

05:37 duration in terms of the number of some things,

05:43 the number of 32nd notes and also separately the look

05:48 of the duration.

05:49 And so you can still see that in MusicXML

05:52 and formats that are still in use today.

05:54 I really like the use of these left and right square brackets

05:58 to indicate the start and end of beams.

06:00

06:03 Humdrum is a code that we have encountered a couple of times,

06:07 and here it is.

06:08 And maybe it's easier with humdrum

06:10 to rotate the musical examples so we can see how things go,

06:15 maybe, maybe not.

06:16 But we can see that there's Ls and Js that represent the starts

06:20 and ends of beams, and different octaves

06:23 are represented by doubling or tripling the letter.

06:29 LilyPond is actually a set of macros

06:32 for the scheme programming language, which

06:34 is a kind of variant on lisp.

06:37 And so you can actually write computer code in LilyPond.

06:42 And here we have the same representation.

06:45 You can see again backslashes, indicating starts

06:49 of larger musical elements, time signatures, barlines

06:54 that are explicitly encoded with what they look like, and so on.

07:00 Melisma was an interesting code format

07:04 that's a little bit similar to what we might have with MIDI.

07:07 And what we're doing here is we're encoding

07:10 only the numeric duration.

07:13 So we can say that, I guess, 125 is a 32nd note.

07:19 And we can figure out from there that 500

07:22 is an eighth note and so on.

07:24 And on the far right column, we have the pitch encoded.

07:28 So we're losing here beams and some other things.

07:33 We're actually even losing the clef and the time signature,

07:36 but we do have an info tag that tells us the key signature.

07:41 Allegro is a more compact version of the same format.

07:45 It looks like we have MIDI numbers, 72, 74, 72,

07:50 for C, D, C, and so on.

07:53 And I believe 64 is encoding the velocity.

07:58 That is how loud each note is.

08:01 And since we haven't encoded any dynamics here, they're all 64s.

08:05 And we have toward the end start and end offsets of each note.

08:10 I think if we can go through note 1,

08:12 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, nine would be a rest,

08:17 and at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, we have--

08:24 sorry.

08:25 We're not doing start and end.

08:26 We're doing start, offset, and duration.

08:28 And there we have a start offset note eight

08:32 of 2.5, duration of one.

08:34 And then the next element does not start at 3.5,

08:37 but it just starts at 3.75.

08:39 So we're not even encoding rests.

08:41 We're saying that they are gaps in the musical format.

08:48 Director musices is also a lisp based format, I believe.

08:52 That's why we have all these extra parentheses where we're

08:54 loading things into a stack, and we

08:57 can see that we're encoding the meter after the first note,

09:02 which is kind of interesting.

09:04 And 32nd notes are one over 32.

09:07 That's kind of nice.

09:09 The dotted eighth note is three 16th notes long.

09:13 So we see 3/16 can be an interesting format.

09:17 SCORE has come up at least once in class.

09:22 It is perhaps the best, most beautiful music editor ever.

09:29 This is how a user might input SCORE,

09:34 and it makes it a little bit easier to enter things.

09:36 You're putting slashes between notes and so on,

09:39 and then it generates an internal syntax

09:43 that specifies exactly where on the page every note is.

09:47 And so musical engravers really like

09:50 working with SCORE because you can precisely

09:53 move things around.

09:54 Probably a professional engraver would

09:56 have moved the C at the beginning of the second measure

10:00 a little bit to the right because it's a little bit close

10:02 to that bar line, and you might confuse the bar line for a stem.

10:07 So SCORE is sometimes still used,

10:10 even though it hasn't been updated in decades.

10:14 This is MusicXML.

10:16 As we've seen from Michael Good's presentation,

10:19 it is a much more verbose format.

10:23 Things are displayed-- you know-- it takes a lot more space

10:28 to do it.

10:29 But MusicXML was invented around the year 2000.

10:32 Some of these other formats were around since the '80s.

10:35 So there's a lot more space on the hard drive-- well,

10:37 there are hard drives now--

10:39 to be able to store all this information.

10:41 So here, Craig Sapp has simply highlighted the part 1 measure

10:48 in order to see how this would work in MusicXML.

10:52 MEI is another format.

10:54 You can't really see things here,

10:55 but it's very similar to MusicXML.

10:59 As we said, it's the format--

11:01 or as Michael Good said, is a format mostly used

11:04 by professional musicologists and almost nobody else

11:09 for encoding common Western music notation.

11:12 I don't see it as having advantages

11:15 over MusicXML, and in fact has many disadvantages

11:19 because it's not supported by many formats.

11:21 But MEI can also encode music such as Medieval music, which

11:27 uses different representation formats.

11:29 So it has a particular niche.

11:34 This is a standard MIDI file represented in binary.

11:37 And it's a little bit unfair to compare the two

11:41 because it's a binary format, so we can't really see anything.

11:45 But look at what's being highlighted.

11:47 Here we begin with 00 90, which is the indication for a note

11:53 off.

11:54 So we're ending the previous note.

11:56 If we go to the beginning of the next line, we can see 80,

11:59 which is the beginning of a note on, and then 4d, which--

12:04 let's see if I can still wear my hexadecimal.

12:07 So four times 16 is 64.

12:10 Add d to that, that is--

12:13 what is that?

12:16 I don't know, 14, 13.

12:18 And so you end up somewhere around 78 or so,

12:22 which is the representation of the note f.

12:25 And then the 40 after that is 64 in decimal.

12:32 And so that would be the velocity,

12:35 how hard we're hitting.

12:36 Since velocity hasn't been encoded in this

12:39 and there's a number between 0 and 127,

12:42 64 seems a pretty good number.

12:44 And then, we date that the note is turned off with the 90,

12:50 and we say it's turned off after a certain amount of time.

12:54 So how much time has passed.

12:56 And you'll see this 51 seems to be a representation

12:59 of the length of a 16th note.

13:04 If you really want to look at MIDI.

13:06 you want to use a translator.

13:08 There's one in music21.

13:10 There's one other places that will translate this format

13:13 into a series of events like no ons, no offs, pitch bends, time

13:18 deltas, which move us forward in time.

13:21 That will allow you to actually give this particular--

13:25 a fair shake.

13:28 You can see also this is NIFF format, which Craig Sapp has

13:35 translated some of the hexadecimals

13:40 into particular letters so that we can see what they are.

13:45 Somewhere in the middle of the page I see clef,

13:47 I see fing, fingering, I see a font change, glissando harp.

13:51 I'm not sure that this is--

13:53 oh, these are just all the things that could be in here.

13:56 So we haven't even gotten to encoding the piece yet,

14:01 but basically NIFF encodes where each shape is on the page.

14:06 It is a format used by music scanners.

14:10 It's not used very much anymore, but the idea

14:13 is that it's much more important to get an exact representation

14:16 of what the page looks like rather than

14:19 what it might encode.

14:21 The last format, which in this presentation

14:25 collects outputs first, isn't really a digital format at all,

14:29 but it is the Braille music code,

14:31 which is an encoding of music notation.

14:35 That was created by Louis Braille at about the same time

14:39 that he created the TeX Braille.

14:41 So he was really interested in music encoding also.

14:45 And we can see some parts of Braille that does encode a clef,

14:50 even though it's not really used in the reading,

14:53 because we're going to encode specific notes.

14:56 Why encode a clef?

14:59 Because blind and visually impaired

15:02 musicians often need to talk to musicians who have sight.

15:06 So it's easy to say, well, you know, it's in treble clef

15:08 and there's one flat key signature and so on.

15:11 And so there's a time signature and then--

15:14 that's not October 5.

15:16 It's octave five.

15:17 We set the octave, and we see that there's a C8th.

15:20 We encode an augmentation dot D 32nd, C 32nd, C 16th, F 16th,

15:28 and so on.

15:31 Interestingly, we can usually get both the note

15:34 and the duration into a six dot segment, which would represent

15:41 six bits or less than a byte.

15:43 So it's a very efficient encoding.

15:45 That makes reading music with your fingers very fast.

15:51 If you want to know more about the Rosetta

15:54 Stone and these various musical encodings,

15:56 I have also included Craig Sapp's watch all video.

15:59 Thanks for watching.

docs.text:
00:00 When most of us hear the word “freemason” we usually think of a band of brothers that

00:04 stretches across the world, a fraternity of moneyed men who engage in strange rituals

00:09 and greet each other with a secret handshake.

00:11 These people belonging to this mysterious nexus believe in a higher power and together

00:15 they share secrets and protect each other.

00:18 And when they meet at the lodge they do so with the doors closed to the world.

00:22 What happens at the lodge stays at the lodge.

00:25 The Master leads the ceremonies, and what he says will never become public knowledge.

00:29 The fact freemasonry is shrouded in so much secrecy does of course elicit us non-freemason

00:34 to be curious, so today we’ll try to separate the facts from the myth.

00:39 But let’s first go back to the beginning and see how it all got started.

00:43 What we know as freemasonry goes back to what were called the guilds of stonemasons and

00:48 cathedral builders back in Middle Ages Britain.

00:50 A guild was a kind of an association for certain kinds of artisans or merchants, so you could

00:55 call them clubs for skilled workers.

00:57 If you look at documents as far back as the 13th century you can find mentions of freemasonry,

01:02 although the language used is either Latin or Norman French.

01:05 So, it goes back a long way.

01:08 As you know, a mason is someone who works with stone, and the free part was supposed

01:13 to signify just that, that these skilled artisans were not feudally bound.

01:17 They were free.

01:18 A potential medieval Master Mason as a kid would be educated in languages and math, and

01:23 when in his teens he would learn how to work with stone.

01:26 Let’s remember that building things back then was very important, so learning how to

01:31 work with stone was seen as a huge deal.

01:33 As the kid grew into an adult he would become a journeyman, and once he became a master

01:37 mason he would gain a lot of respect.

01:40 So, now you can see why these guilds were respected.

01:43 In the 17th and 18th centuries these evolved into modern freemasonry, and people belonging

01:48 to this order believed in a higher power and brotherhood, with the masonic rituals based

01:52 on the myth of King Solomon’s Temple.

01:54 You can find manuscripts belonging to freemasonry that talk about the masons that built this

01:59 temple.

02:00 There were lots of manuscripts and these have been studied since.

02:02 We won’t go into what they all contain, but later they evolved into what are called

02:07 Freemasonry constitutions.

02:08 It’s said about 100 such manuscripts still exist, but very few of them contain details

02:14 of rituals and rites of passage.

02:16 All you really need to know is that there were lots of different groups of masons and

02:20 lots of texts talking about codes of conduct and sometimes rituals.

02:24 Masons basically joined ceremonies and members had certain rules to follow based on chivalry.

02:30 In 1717 the first Grand Lodge was established in England, and after that came more lodges.

02:35 You could call the Grand Lodge the governing body and lodges branches of that body.

02:40 What’s important to mention is that freemasonry was not especially a religious order, and

02:44 it actually at times banged heads with the Roman Catholic church.

02:47 As we said, Freemasons believed and still believe in a higher power, but you are not

02:51 supposed to discuss religion in regular Freemasonry.

02:55 Talking about politics is also verboten, although in short there was a split in Freemasonry

03:00 and some masons refused to follow the order that masons must believe in a deity.

03:04 That order came from the United Grand Lodge of England, and what happened was a masonry

03:08 schism, meaning split, and then we got both Continental and Anglo-American Freemasonry.

03:15 For instance, the latter group doesn’t allow political discussion but the former does.

03:19 The split was a big issue, and the two groups engaged in rivalry over the years.

03:23 This was significant, and it’s written that this rivalry in part contributed to the rift

03:27 that started the Mexican civil war.

03:29 So, there have been splits and disagreements among freemasons.

03:32 They are not all alike.

03:34 Some branches for instance allow women to join, and while freemasonry is global it’s

03:38 written that masons in Anglo-Saxon countries were predominantly white protestants.

03:43 There are also other branches that don’t belong to the official order of freemasonry,

03:47 so it’s actually quite complicated and the reported six million members don’t all follow

03:52 the same rules.

03:53 But what are the rules?

03:54 What do these people do?

03:55 What’s actually the point of becoming a freemason?

03:58 If African political leaders and wealthy American businessmen belong to masonic orders, surely

04:03 there is something to it?

04:05 In 2018 the BBC did an interview with a freemason, although this was a freemason belonging to

04:10 a women’s lodge.

04:11 Her husband was a mason, too.

04:12 She said there is nothing too strange about it, but she did have to pass three freemasonry

04:17 degrees to achieve her leading role at the lodge.

04:20 When you get this third degree you become a fully-fledged mason.

04:23 She didn’t give her name to the BBC, well, they didn’t print it we mean, and she would

04:28 not discuss what goes down at the ceremonies.

04:31 Those ceremonies are led by a master, but what he or she says cannot become public knowledge.

04:36 Not surprisingly, this kind of secrecy leads non-masons to thinking something really weird

04:40 must happen, but all she said was that it’s like being in a play and you just do your

04:45 bit.

04:46 She said there is no back-slapping and she doesn’t take part in any kind of nepotism,

04:49 meaning she’s not rubbing shoulders with people to get ahead in her line of work.

04:53 She said this to the BBC, “It's a bit like Facebook in that way.

04:57 You will come across people you've met in the past, certainly if you've lived in the

05:00 area for a number of years.

05:01 We come from all walks of life and professions but it becomes a network.”

05:05 She did say that the ceremonies are still based on the myth of King Solomon’s Temple,

05:09 but refused to say anything else.

05:11 This wasn’t good enough for us at the Infographics Show, and we wanted to know more.

05:16 We read that masons are supposed to follow a certain kind of etiquette, but the problem

05:19 is these codes of conduct are also kept secret.

05:22 We found out that masons are expected to learn about rituals, history, freemason symbols,

05:27 and people are supposed to understand how to act as a mason.

05:30 You have to give the Worshipful Master his due respect, and that means knowing where

05:34 to stand when he is around.

05:35 You can’t just turn up to a lodge with a bottle of beer in hand and start mingling.

05:39 There are strict rules to follow as to how you should comport yourself.

05:42 According to one website, it’s a bit like school.

05:45 You have to sit in the right place, wear the right clothes, stand when you speak, and it’s

05:49 considered bad manners to talk when others are talking.

05:52 When the master bangs that gavel, you must obey.

05:55 If you don’t, it’s said to be a massive discourtesy.

05:57 Don’t turn your back on this guy when he speaks, and some lodges will have a salute

06:01 you give to him.

06:02 It sounds strict, and it is.

06:04 You must also have good posture, or try to have, and don’t go around telling stories

06:08 about your blocked toilet bowl.

06:10 No “off-color” stories we are told, and it goes without saying that your phone should

06:14 not start beeping during the ceremony.

06:16 You will know all this of course because you have read the codes of conduct and from the

06:20 day you go to your first meeting you’ll be following these codes as you become an

06:24 Entered Apprentice, a Fellow Craft and in the end a Master Mason.

06:28 Part of these meetings will include giving degrees to members who have climbed a ranking,

06:32 this we know for sure.

06:33 It’s said that this graduation type ceremony is one of the biggest reasons they have ceremonies.

06:38 Yes, people listen to the master and they follow the rules and they say hello to their

06:42 mason buddies, but it seems many of the meetings are about giving degrees and telling people

06:46 how to act when this happens.

06:48 One person wrote that these ceremonies are basically an exercise in administration.

06:51 He wrote, “Deep and unfettered conversations on philosophy, science, arts, society, psychology,

06:58 governance, foundational texts are very rare these days, especially in the US and Canada.”

07:03 Another mason wrote that when he meets usually the start includes talking about the last

07:07 meeting and the minutes of that meeting.

07:09 They might then discuss older members and new members, or just talk about things that

07:13 need to be paid for, such as getting a new roof.

07:15 He wrote this: “Often there are various announcements of

07:18 upcoming events, discussion of community projects, or planning for a future activity.

07:23 Some meetings are reserved for ceremonies - such as admitting a new brother or advancing

07:26 one to a higher degree.

07:28 Others might honor members who have a substantial history of service in the Masons.

07:32 Still other meetings may have an educational presentation.

07:35 In my jurisdiction - Connecticut - the Grand Lodge requires every meeting to have at least

07:39 some component of Masonic Education.”

07:41 As we said, he wrote that during these ceremonies they must follow strict codes of conduct,

07:45 so it’s a rather serious affair.

07:47 He said at the end of this serious part, though, there are refreshments and people chat more

07:51 informally.

07:52 It all sounds a bit like a cross between a business meeting and a graduation, and perhaps

07:57 at times a TedX just with funny clothes and upright postures.

08:00 So, why is all this secret?

08:02 Another freemason said while when they make a member of the public a freemason during

08:06 a ritual it’s supposed to be secret, it’s hardly the biggest secret in the world.

08:10 He said yes, they don’t publish this ritual, but who publishes private business meetings.

08:14 Those rituals can change based on the lodge, but in the end the ceremony is about these

08:18 old codes of conduct and what it means to be a freemason.

08:22 It’s not as if babies are being sacrificed for the great higher power or members engage

08:26 is orgiastic behavior while howling like banshees under a blood moon.

08:30 You just need to know the secret codes to get in, just like entering a combination code

08:34 on a lock.

08:35 Every freemason we found online said the same thing.

08:37 It’s business, graduation, talking about members, and bringing in new members.

08:41 You’ve just got to follow the protocols.

08:43 Remember, stand up straight, listen to the master, and don’t let your Kanye West & Lil

08:47 Pump ringtone go off during the ceremony.

08:50 One journalist who interviewed a freemason in the UK said when he entered the lodge it

08:54 was full of freemasonry symbols.

08:55 He was told that during meetings people have to stand in the correct place.

08:59 It’s important where you stand in relation to the master.

09:01 He was told that new masons are given the rules, learn the codes, and are told how to

09:06 recognize another mason when not in a meeting.

09:08 This might not always be a secret handshake, but it is kept a secret.

09:12 If you are a mason and you talk about this to other non-masons you will likely be thrown

09:17 out of the order.

09:18 Another journalist who’d interviewed a freemason was told there are not just secret ways to

09:22 know who is a mason but each degree of freemasonry has its own password.

09:26 This was in his lodge at least.

09:28 When asked if anything weird went on, the mason said no, adding, “We had a man who

09:32 joined our lodge, he took the first degree and was disappointed that there was nothing

09:36 happening in the way of anything sinister and he left.”

09:39 He also said, “Here in Ireland we have a strict constitution which we follow closely.

09:43 I heard that there is a group of people in Ireland who are going into the rituals more

09:47 deeply, but I don't think there's anything untoward going on there.”

09:50 He said at his lodge it’s all about dressing up, doing some rituals, then having a good

09:54 old chat.

09:55 He said where he goes if you want to join you’ll have to be interviewed, have a background

09:59 check, and then it goes to the vote using black and white beans.

10:02 If they like you, you’re in.

10:03 Too many black beans, and you’re not welcome.

10:05 After hearing all this, would you like to be a freemason?

10:08 Are you already one of them and can you tell us more?

10:11 Tell us in the comments.

10:12 Also, be sure to check out our other video The Most Powerful Families Who Secretly Run

10:16 The World?

10:17 Thanks for watching, and as always, don’t forget to like, share and subscribe.

10:21 See you next time.

docs.text:
00:00 Have I ever told you about the time that

00:01 I made a core Windows routine about a

00:03 hundred times faster and Microsoft

00:05 somehow forgot to rename the campus

00:06 after me? Yeah, me neither. Because what

00:09 actually happened was I checked in the

00:10 code. Somebody in the code review said

00:12 something spiritually equivalent to

00:14 cool, nice one. And then everybody went

00:16 back to work, which is I later learned

00:18 exactly how it should be. But I was a

00:21 kid and when you're young, every clever

00:22 optimization feels like you've just

00:24 split the atom in your dorm room. Now,

00:26 the routine in question did something

00:27 almost offensively simple. It took an

00:29 iid, which is a comm interface

00:31 identifier, and converted it into the

00:33 familiar string form of a grid. You've

00:36 almost certainly seen these things

00:37 before. Curly braces, eight hex digits,

00:40 a hyphen, four hex digits, another

00:41 hyphen, and so on. If it looks like a

00:43 license plate designed by a mainframe,

00:45 the registry is full of them. And if you

00:47 use regedit, you'll see a lot of them

00:48 there. And your first instinct might be

00:50 to ask, Dave, why would anybody care?

00:53 How often do you really convert a grid

00:54 to a string? And that is exactly the

00:56 trap because in comm IIIDs are not

00:59 decorative. They are the fingerprints of

01:01 the entire object model. Comm is

01:03 basically a civilization built out of

01:05 tiny contracts and every one of those

01:07 contracts is identified by unique 128

01:10 bit number that says this interface is

01:12 this interface and not some interface

01:14 that merely looks pretty similar if you

01:15 squint. Query interface is built around

01:17 it. Marshalling depends on it. Proxy and

01:20 stub lookup depend on it. Registry

01:22 lookup depends on it. Debugging depends

01:24 on it. logging depends on it. So if COM

01:26 is a plumbing system, IIDs are stamped

01:29 part numbers on every valve, elbow, and

01:31 every adapter in the building. IIDs are

01:33 randomly generated and incorporate a

01:35 hash of your MAC address. And at 128

01:38 bits, they're functionally unique and

01:39 will never collide. Mathematically, it's

01:42 possible, but not likely to happen

01:44 before the proton decay of the universe.

01:46 And during my first months in the comm

01:48 team, I was trying to understand all of

01:49 this by doing what any sane new hire

01:51 would do back in those days when dropped

01:53 into a codebase of ancient machinery,

01:55 undocumented assumptions, and C++

01:57 written by people who clearly slept

01:59 under their desks a lot. So I single

02:01 stepped through it. I would sit there in

02:02 the debugger and ask innocent little

02:04 questions like, "What does co-initialize

02:06 ex?"

02:07 And then three hours later, I'd be 12

02:09 layers deep in apartment initialization,

02:11 TLS state, activation, plumbing, RPC

02:14 setup, and internal helper functions

02:15 with names that sounded like they've

02:17 been assigned by a committee after a

02:18 very long lunch. I even bought the book

02:21 inside Olay 2, which may be a very fine

02:23 book, but I'll admit something slightly

02:25 embarrassing. I was literally on the OA

02:27 comm team, and I don't think I truly

02:29 understood comm well until Don Box's

02:31 book came out a couple of years later.

02:33 And that's not a dig at anybody. Comm

02:35 was one of those technologies that

02:36 looked simple from orbit and then once

02:38 you got close, you realized the surface

02:40 was covered in trapped doors, rotating

02:42 knives, and small handwritten notes that

02:43 said things like, "We do this for 16-bit

02:45 compatibility." So, I learned the hard

02:47 way. I just followed the code. And the

02:50 more I followed it, the more I noticed

02:51 that everything eventually seemed to

02:52 turn into an IID, out of an IID, or into

02:55 a search for an IID. It's like being a

02:57 detective in a movie where every suspect

02:59 has the same last name for some reason.

03:01 Eventually, I found the function that

03:03 converted an iid to text. And as I

03:05 remember it, it was using the functional

03:07 equivalent of print f. Something like

03:09 take data 1, data 2, data 3, and the

03:11 eight bytes of data 4. Feed them through

03:13 a format string with percent 08x,

03:16 percent 04x, percent 02x, and so on. And

03:19 to be clear, that works. It's clean.

03:21 It's obvious. And it produces the right

03:23 answer. It's also a bit like using a

03:25 Swiss watch to hammer in a thumbtack.

03:27 Print f is magnificent because it's

03:29 general. It can format strings,

03:31 integers, floatingoint numbers, widths,

03:33 precision, padding, flags, signs,

03:36 alternate forms, left justification,

03:38 maybe localal sensitive details

03:40 depending on the implementation, and all

03:42 sorts of other things. It has to parse

03:44 the format string. It has to walk the

03:46 variable arguments, which means the

03:47 compiler can't type check it in the

03:49 normal way. It has to decide what

03:51 conversion you meant, how wide it should

03:52 be, how many characters to emit, and

03:54 where they should go. It's really a tiny

03:57 interpreter hiding in your C runtime.

03:59 And that's fantastic when you need a

04:01 tiny interpreter. But an iID string is

04:03 not a general formatting problem. It's a

04:05 16 byt to 32 hex digit problem with four

04:08 hyphens in fixed locations and maybe

04:10 braces depending on the convention.

04:12 There's no mystery. There's no

04:13 formatting language. There are no user

04:15 choices. There's not even any arithmetic

04:17 more complicated than take the high

04:18 nibble and end the low nibble. And you

04:20 already know that a bite is eight bits.

04:22 But some people have made it to

04:23 adulthood without actually noticing that

04:25 a single hex digit represents exactly

04:27 four bits. And that's why a bite is two

04:29 hex digits. One for the upper four bits

04:32 called a nibble and one for the lower

04:33 nibble. If you can learn to read

04:35 four-bit binary, you can actually

04:36 convert binary to 32-bit hex on the fly.

04:38 And it's a fun trick at certain cocktail

04:40 parties. Either way, the point is that

04:43 every bite becomes exactly two hex

04:45 characters. You take the top four bits

04:47 and you use them as an index into the

04:48 string zero through f. Write that

04:51 character. Then take the bottom four

04:52 bits and do the same thing. Do that 16

04:55 times and you have 32 hex digits. Put

04:57 the hyphens in at the correct places and

04:59 you've made a fully valid grid string.

05:01 And that's it. That's the whole magic

05:03 trick. But there's one little wrinkle

05:04 and it's the kind of wrinkle that

05:05 separates the I wrote some fast code

05:07 from the I wrote some fast code that

05:09 also works. A grid in memory is not

05:12 stored exactly the way it appears on the

05:13 screen. Unfortunately, at least not in

05:16 the little Indian machine like the x86

05:18 systems that we were mostly using. A

05:20 grid in memory is not stored exactly the

05:22 way it appears on the screen. at least

05:23 not on a little Indian machine like the

05:25 x86 systems that we were using. The grid

05:28 structure has a 32-bit data 1 field, two

05:31 16- bit fields called data 2 and data 3,

05:33 and then an 8bit data 4 array. When you

05:36 print data 1 as an integer, print f

05:38 naturally emits the number in canonical

05:40 human readable order. But if you simply

05:42 walk the bytes in memory from beginning

05:43 to end, data 1 would come out bite

05:45 reversed. Same with data 2 and data 3.

05:48 But data 4 is already bite by bite. So

05:51 the fast version can't just say dear

05:52 pointer please walk 16 bytes and tell me

05:54 what you see. That would produce a valid

05:57 looking lie which is the most dangerous

05:59 kind of lie in systems code. It has to

06:01 walk the bites in the right canonical

06:03 order on x86. That means rating the

06:06 bites in the order 3 2 1 0 for data 1

06:08 and then 54 for data 2 then 76 for data

06:12 3 and then 8 through 15 for data 4. And

06:15 once you have that order table the

06:17 conversion is brutally simple. Read a

06:19 bite, emit two hex characters, check

06:21 whether you've reached one of the hyphen

06:22 positions, and then keep going. Now,

06:25 somewhere out there, I can already hear

06:26 a viewer cracking their knuckles in the

06:28 comment section. Dave, this is premature

06:30 optimization. The root of all evil. Just

06:31 use the library. The compiler is smarter

06:33 than you. And besides, standard format

06:35 exists now. And congratulations. You've

06:37 made a good modern point from the

06:39 comfort of a machine that has more L1

06:41 cache than my dev box at the time had

06:43 for RAM. But this was not some random

06:45 dialog box code that ran once when the

06:47 user clicked about. This was comm. This

06:49 was core plumbing. This was code that

06:51 you might hit while initializing,

06:52 activating, registering, marshalling,

06:54 debugging, tracing, and generally trying

06:56 to make distributed objects behave like

06:58 local ones, which is already a polite

07:00 fiction requiring a lot of machinery.

07:02 Hot paths have a way of hiding inside

07:04 boring helper routines. And helper

07:06 routines are dangerous precisely because

07:08 everyone assumes they're too small to

07:09 matter. That's how performance dies. not

07:12 usually in one glorious bonfire, but by

07:14 a thousand tiny paper cuts, each one

07:16 defended by somebody saying, "Well,

07:17 surely this can't be the problem." And

07:19 so, one evening, I dialed in over Raz,

07:22 because this was the era when working

07:24 remotely meant that your modem made the

07:25 scream of an angry robot and then

07:27 connected you to the office at a speed

07:29 that today would make a smartwatch file

07:31 a workplace grievance. So, I was at home

07:33 connected over a phone line by modem,

07:35 rewriting a little iid string conversion

07:37 function because I was convinced that it

07:39 had been wasteful. And yes, a smarter

07:41 man might have instrumented it first. A

07:43 more disciplined engineer might have

07:44 written a benchmark, gathered traces,

07:46 measured call counts, and then presented

07:47 a tidy little table showing before and

07:49 after timings across representative

07:51 workloads. I did not do that. I just

07:54 looked at the print version, looked at

07:55 what the function was actually needing

07:57 to do, and thought, well, that can't

07:59 possibly be a fast way to do it. And

08:01 fortunately, in this case, youthful

08:02 arrogance and basic computer science

08:04 happened to be pointing in the same

08:05 direction. Now, the replacement code was

08:08 a basically a little nibble walker. It

08:10 treated the iid as bytes, but walked

08:12 them in the right order. For each bite,

08:14 it indexed into a static hex table

08:16 twice. Once for the upper nibble and

08:17 once for the lower nibble. It wrote the

08:19 characters directly into the output

08:20 buffer. And after the output index

08:22 reached the magic positions, it inserted

08:24 a hyphen. The hyphen part always

08:26 bothered me a little, though. The

08:28 canonical grid format has groups of

08:30 eight, four, four, four, and 12 hex

08:33 digits. So, the hyphens go after

08:34 character positions 8, 13, 18, and 23.

08:38 If you're counting the hyphens as

08:40 they're inserted. Well, my code did the

08:42 obvious thing that after writing each

08:44 pair of hex digits, it checks whether

08:45 the output index is one of those

08:47 positions. And if it is, it writes a

08:48 hyphen. And I never really love that. I

08:50 felt like there had to be a better way,

08:52 some elegant little branchless trick,

08:54 some mathematically satisfying answer

08:56 where the hyphens emerge naturally from

08:58 the topology of the grid like crystals

09:00 forming in a super saturated solution.

09:02 But at some point you have to remember

09:04 that you're not designing a cathedral.

09:05 You're converting an IID to a string. So

09:07 I shipped the obvious way. If you can

09:10 think of a faster way to do it, let me

09:11 know in the comments. Now thinking out

09:13 loud, if I were to do it today, I might

09:15 do it a little differently. I might

09:17 start with a template string full of

09:18 zeros and hyphens and then fill in only

09:20 the hex positions. Or I might use a

09:22 small table to output offsets. Or I

09:24 might unroll the whole thing because for

09:25 something this fixed, the most readable

09:27 code can sometimes be the one that

09:29 admits there is no real loop-shaped

09:31 problem here. But back then, the loop

09:33 was compact, correct, and much faster

09:35 than invoking the formatting machinery.

09:37 And when I say faster, I mean the

09:38 difference between hiring a moving

09:39 company and picking up the pencil by

09:41 yourself. Print f has to parse. My code

09:44 did not. Print f has to interpret a

09:46 miniature formatting language. And of

09:47 course, my code did not. Print f has to

09:50 handle all the cases, and my code had to

09:51 handle exactly one case. Print f

09:54 converts integers to text using general

09:56 purpose routines, but my code did two

09:58 table lookups per bite. And so Print F

10:00 is like a universal multi-tool, but my

10:02 version was more of a precision vera

10:04 screwdriver made for only one type of

10:06 screw. And that is the essence of good

10:08 optimization. Not making the general

10:10 case slightly more clever, but noticing

10:12 when the general case is using the wrong

10:14 tool entirely. Now, was it really 100

10:16 times faster? That's the number I

10:18 remember, but memory is sort of a

10:20 compression algorithm with a sense of

10:21 nostalgia. The exact factor is less

10:24 important than the shape of the result

10:25 because it wasn't 5% faster. It was not

10:28 the compiler did a little better with

10:29 the inlining case. It was a whole

10:31 different category of work. When you

10:33 replace a general formatter with fixed

10:35 stores and table lookups, you don't need

10:37 a PhD to predict the direction of

10:39 travel. But there's an important lesson

10:41 hiding in that because it's very easy to

10:42 take the wrong lesson from this story.

10:44 The lesson is not rewrite every print f

10:46 in your program by hand. Please don't.

10:48 That way lies madness, bugs, and a

10:50 future coworker quietly cursing your

10:52 name while trying to localize an error

10:53 message into finish. The lesson is that

10:56 generality has a cost and sometimes we

10:59 pay the cost in places where we don't

11:00 need the generality. Most of the time

11:03 that's fine. Most code is not hot. Most

11:05 code should be boring, obvious, and

11:07 maintained by somebody who has had a

11:08 reasonable amount of sleep. But when you

11:10 in a foundational layer and the

11:12 operation is fixed, tiny, and repeated

11:14 endlessly, it's worth asking whether the

11:17 fancy machinery is doing useful work or

11:18 merely wearing a little top hat while

00:01 In 2008, at approximately 11.30 pm, 75-year-old  Edward Benson was enjoying his retirement after

00:07 what had been a lifetime of blue-collar grind. He  was sitting at home, watching television when a

00:12 masked man stormed into his house. But Benson was smart.

00:15 He’d saved his wages all his life  and had a nest egg sitting inside

00:18 a vault. The only way to open it was through a  combination. That’s what the intruder wanted.

00:23 And he meant business. There was no way the old man was going to

00:26 give up the number. The home invader had expected  this to happen. He started swinging a machete at

00:31 him, hacking deep wounds into his body. The old man sustained serious injuries,

00:36 deep gashes to his arms, hands and head. Reluctantly, he backed down.

00:40 Pass me a towel, he said, so I can wipe  the blood out of my eyes. As he was wiping,

00:44 he told the invader he’d need his glasses  so he could see the numbers on the dial.

00:48 That’s when he ran for it. He locked himself in the

00:51 bathroom. But it was a futile attempt. The  intruder hacked at the door and kicked it in.

00:56 Benson had also managed to get a gun, but the  intruder was able to wrestle it out of his hands.

01:00 Blood now streaming down his face and  back, the old man twisted the dial and…

01:05 Click. $200,000,

01:08 money he could have left to his grandchildren. Except one of them had just gotten

01:12 his inheritance. 26-year-old James Alan

01:14 Benson of North Carolina had almost killed one of  the most important people in his life. A person

01:20 who had loved him since the day he was born. When Edward Benson was being stapled and stitched

01:24 back together at the hospital, he told the media  that James had once been his favorite. He was,

01:29 quote, “model” child. The “root of  all evil,” he said, meaning money,

01:34 had obviously got the better of him. Still, it was strange, because

01:37 they’d been getting along. They’d always been close.

01:39 But it was known that James had a new wife or  partner in China and he owed an attorney who’d

01:45 been trying to get her US citizenship.  He’d recently returned from a trip there

01:49 but had to go back to the US when  his money ran out and visa expired.

01:53 The FBI thinks he might have taken the  money and started a new life over there.

01:57 Someone in China, maybe even watching  this video, knows who he is. He’s now 43,

02:02 about 5 '8-9 (176+ cm) and 180 pounds (82kg)  with brown hair. He has connections to Cleveland,

02:08 New York, and North Carolina. If he’s in China,  he speaks the language and knows the culture,

02:12 so will come across as a long-term expat. And if that story’s theme was shame,

02:17 the topic of this next snippet of  extreme American violence is brutality…

02:21 Brutality and entitlement. 23.

02:25 On a warm July night, at a condo building  near the University of Illinois at Chicago,

02:29 two young men were knocking back beers. One was 21 year old Muaz ‘Moose’ Haffar,

02:34 a 5'5", (1.67 meters), competitive weightlifter.  The other was 27 year old Mantas Matulis,

02:43 who was carrying a stun gun. They had been drinking for a few

02:47 hours the building which was owned by Muaz’s  wealthy physician father. Syrian immigrants,

02:52 the family had made the most of  the American Dream. But that didn’t

02:55 interest Muaz. He just wanted to  drive around in the Mercedes his

03:00 dad had bought him and pick up girls. Feeling the effects of the beer, Haffar

03:06 and Matulis went out for a smoke. Shortly after,  two men walked past. One of them was 23-year-old

03:13 Tombol Malik, a political science student at the  University of Illinois. Malik was known to his

03:21 many friends as “sweet and easy-going”. He and his friend, Anthony Popelka,

03:31 had been at a party that night and  were heading back to their apartment.

03:36 Noticing that Matulis was bleeding,  Anthony Popelka asked if he needed any

03:41 help. For whatever reason, Matulis lashed  out, punching Popelka in the face. He then

03:47 attacked both Popelka and Malik with the stun gun. Feeling a sense of loyalty to his friend, Haffar

03:50 jumped in and started beating Malik with  a heavy bicycle lock. Within seconds,

03:55 it was wrapped around Malik’s head. As Popelka pleaded for the violence to stop,

03:59 Haffar kept beating Malik’s head in what would be  later described in court, as a “hammer motion.”

04:05 Two security guards would also testify that Malik  dropped to the ground unconscious, while Haffar

04:10 kept bludgeoning his face and head repeatedly. “Remember this face!” he screamed,

04:18 pacing around Malik’s limp and bloodied body. The autopsy showed Malik’s skull had been caved

04:22 in. There were 6 fractures and he’d been hit at  least 10 times while unable to defend himself.

04:28 It wasn’t a fight. It was a brutal, but cowardly, murder.

04:31 The evidence was undeniable. Haffar had repeatedly  pummeled an unconscious man’s head and both his

04:37 and the victim’s DNA were on the murder weapon.  In the US justice system, it was a slam dunk.

04:41 It would mean life in prison. Except… a bail of $900,000 was set, which Haffar’s

04:45 family paid with no problem. Being part-Syrian,  Haffar should have been a flight risk,

04:50 but the judge didn’t agree. Haffar was allowed  to remain free while holding onto his passport.

04:55 Inevitably, Haffar’s American dream came to  an abrupt end. He boarded a plane and flew to

05:00 Syria where he lived with his wealthy relatives. Matulis wasn’t so lucky. His parents couldn’t help

05:04 him out. At trial, it was heard he’d not only  used a stun gun, but while Malik lay prone on

05:09 the ground, Matulis ran up and took a “soccer  kick” to his head. It was a brutal attack for

05:14 which He would spend 5 years in prison  before being deported back to Lithuania.

05:18 Haffar remained in Syria where he lived a  good life and partied in nightclubs. His

05:24 father claimed his son was a victim. The  family refused to take any responsibility,

05:30 saying their son would never return to the US  because he, quote, “will not receive justice.”

05:35 Haffar remains a fugitive of American law. The US and Syria don’t have an extradition treaty,

05:40 but the US government has put pressure on  the Syrian authorities to send Haffar home.

05:44 It seems the Syrians are not playing ball. Haffar  later changed his name to Omar Al-Sawwaf and

05:52 gained full Syrian citizenship. According to Wikileaks data,

05:54 the US embassy in Syria wrote the Syrian  government a diplomatic complaint:

05:59 “The Embassy… does not understand the Syrian  government's refusal to turn over Haffar to

06:03 the proper U.S. authorities, since he is  an American citizen, properly charged in

06:08 a U.S. court with the crime of murder.” Initially, the Syrians were helpful.

06:13 US media reported that a Syrian police general  had told the State Department that his agents

06:18 had staked out a gym and a mosque and the Haffar  family home in Damascus. Haffar was arrested,

06:24 and the Syrian authorities had decided to  try him in Syria. But the Americans refused

06:28 to hand over evidence, believing Syrian  investigators would engineer an acquittal.

06:33 That could fall under double jeopardy laws  in the US. American authorities wouldn’t have

06:37 a right to charge him again for the same crime. Haffar’s father told the US media his son had been

06:43 tried in Syria and he’d been found not guilty.  The court determined he acted in self-defense.

06:49 It’s very possible there was more to the  story of how the men had first interacted,

06:53 but it didn’t take away from the brutality of the  crime. And US authorities were not certain any

06:58 such trial had taken place, stating that Haffar  was being protected by the Syrian government.

07:06 Unless Haffar leaves Syria where US authorities  can grab him, he’s gotten away with murder.

31:33 And that was it. He vanished. Everyone was in shock. Bishop seemed to

31:36 adore his wife and children. One of the family’s  best friends who played tennis with them said,

31:41 “None of us could understand why it  happened…I didn’t see any tension.”

31:45 The only thing investigators found  that might suggest a motive was he’d

31:49 been refused a promotion, and his wife  might have thought he didn’t try hard

31:53 enough. But according to his colleagues  and friends, it wasn’t a big deal. To them,

31:57 Bishop was a happy family man. The Washington  Post reported that there was “no evidence of

32:01 infidelity, or financial or job problems.” But he’d been seeing a psychiatrist because

32:06 he couldn’t sleep, and he was  prescribed sleeping pills.

32:09 It didn’t make any sense. It also didn’t help  that his professional life was steeped in secrecy.

32:14 For detectives, the murder was complete overkill,  suggesting a deep fury or mental breakdown,

32:19 but no one had seen anything close  to that in Bishop’s character.

32:22 The case went cold. The FBI wasn’t much  help, either, not even adding Bishop to

32:27 the Most Wanted List. It wasn’t until 2010

32:29 when local detectives got a break. They discovered something the FBI had apparently

32:34 not been able to find. Bishop had sent a letter  to a prison inmate 16 days after the murders. The

32:39 prisoner’s name was Albert Kenneth Bankston. He’d  been imprisoned at the United States Penitentiary

32:44 in Marion, Illinois, for a 1970 armed robbery of  the Citizens National Bank in Plain, Mississippi.

32:51 What was a top diplomat doing  writing to an armed robber?

32:54 And why had no one found that letter before? Bankston might be able to provide answers,

32:58 except he died from cancer in 1983. The letter from Bankston to

33:02 Bishop is in the WikiLeaks files today. At one point in the letter, Bankston wrote,

33:07 “Now in answer to your question. Yes, I am most  sure she is in North Carolina State Penitentiary.”

33:12 Was this in reference to a woman possibly seen  with Bishop in the days running up to the murders?

33:17 Was Bishop using Bankston to help him find  a killer for hire? Maybe in exchange for

33:21 a counterfeit passport which Bishop  would have likely been able to get.

33:25 We say that because Bankston  wrote, “I was only interested

33:28 in Mexico and/or Central America, as you know.” He also mentioned a man named David Paul Allen.

33:34 Robert Keefer, who was working as a  sheriff’s deputy in Montgomery County

33:37 (containing Bethesda) , investigated the  Bishop case for many years. He later said

33:41 he interviewed David Allen, telling the press: “Allen told us that Bishop had paid them some

33:46 money to kill the family... All this was  supposed to take place while he was over

33:49 in Europe on a business trip. It seemed to  me he paid them some cash and some jewelry.”

33:53 Keefer said the men turned Bishop down because  killing kids was against the criminal code.

33:58 But this is a theory. There’s  no evidence to back it up.

34:01 Keefer and his colleagues got to work trying  to find some evidence but then something

34:05 mysterious happened. The entire Bankston  file vanished. The detectives asked the FBI

34:10 about that and they were told it was because  one of their agents had taken over the case.

34:14 Yet, they tried to find this agent  and it was as if he was a ghost.

34:18 Keefer later told the media, “Nobody  could even tell us this guy existed.”

34:23 The only good thing was after 38 years,  the FBI put Bishop on the Most Wanted list,

34:28 which meant more resources going to the crime. And then the case became even stranger.

34:32 On March 19th, 2000, a woman named Lorene Klepacki  bought an old diary for $38 at a Flea Market at

34:39 North Carolina’s Greensboro Coliseum. On the  front, it was written, “Bradford Bishop Diary.”

34:44 The woman’s son looked that name up on the  internet, and soon, they were fascinated.

34:49 Diary: February 1967: “If you’re going to succeed in

34:52 the Foreign Service—make Ambassador before you’re  50—hold positions of responsibility—constant

34:57 dedication and considerable sacrifice  of time & thought are required.”

35:01 Same day: Toxic, degenerative psychoses… chronic,  low-level maniac, involutional megalomania.”

35:08 Dr. Frank Caprio, the psychiatrist who’d  treated Bishop, wouldn’t divulge details about

35:12 their relationship because of doctor-patient  privilege. But he did say Bishop was quote,

35:17 “heavily involved” with the CIA.  Bishop’s colleague at the State

35:20 Department said the same on the Today Show. Why this matters is Bishop could have lived a

35:25 double life. One of Bishop’s friends later  ventured that the murders may have been

35:29 revenge for Bishop’s work as “a spy.” His last diary entry in 1971 said:

35:35 “Your family grows more beautiful, and you  still stand on the threshold. Outwardly,

35:39 your accomplishments are great. …My, such  symbols, promotions, citations, languages,

35:44 degrees…You have soared to the heights  & plummeted, each time, to the depths.”

35:49 The detectives couldn’t be sure the diary was  Bishop’s but it certainly sounded like it.

35:53 But they also couldn’t be sure  someone hadn’t planted it. In the

35:56 world of intelligence, anything is possible. Because when Raymond M. Kight, Sheriff of

36:00 Montgomery County, got on the case, he started  pointing fingers at the CIA. In interviews,

36:05 he said he spent much of his professional life  investigating the crime and nothing made sense

36:10 to him. He told the LA Times, “My feeling is  that Bishop had CIA connections and training,

36:15 and that’s possibly how he was able to disappear.” He didn’t know what had happened. But he said he

36:20 wouldn’t rule out a connection to the CIA’s  MK-Ultra experiments. In those trials,

36:25 the agency used hallucinogenic drugs in attempts  to control minds and induce violent behavior.

36:30 He said, “I’m not so sure this didn’t  happen to Bishop.” How else, he said,

36:34 "do you go into your house and bludgeon  your wife, children, and mother?”

36:38 Still, this is just another theory. Bishop may have been seen over the

36:42 years in the US and also in Europe. He’ll be  89, and may still like the odd Scotch whisky.

36:47 He also loved dogs and spicy food. He has a cleft chin and a mole on

36:51 his left cheek and was 6’1” (1.85 meters)  and 180 pounds (81.6kg). It’s believed he

36:56 may have gone to Italy, Belgium, England, the  Netherlands, Germany, Spain, or Switzerland.

37:00 In 1979, a colleague who’d worked with him in  Africa said she was “absolutely certain” she’d

37:05 seen him in Stockholm, Sweden. She didn’t know he  was wanted for murder at the time. And in 1994,

37:11 a friend of the Bishop family said she  saw him on a train platform in Basel,

37:15 Switzerland. The woman said, “I realized it was  Bradford Bishop… The very next day, I called

37:20 the FBI… They never contacted me after that.” And if this story couldn’t get any more insane,

37:25 in 2022, a woman who didn’t know who her  biological father was got a DNA test. Her

37:31 father was Bradford Bishop. The FBI confirmed it. So, did Bishop have a secret life and plan to

37:36 murder his family, or was he involved in strange  and dangerous intelligence work, or both?

37:41 7. On August 1st, 1983,

37:44 a man named Sid Wells was at home in his apartment  near the University of Colorado at Boulder where

37:49 he studied journalism. Bright, intelligent,  he had big plans to become a journalist or

37:53 a fighter pilot for the United States Navy. And he was already famous. His girlfriend,

37:57 Shauna, was the daughter of  Hollywood legend, Robert Redford.

38:01 But Sid’s perfect life was about to shatter. Sid’s quiet new roommate, Thayne Smika, wasn’t

38:06 what he seemed. He hadn’t paid his rent and it  seems that was enough for him to shoot Sid in the

38:11 back of the head with a single 20-gauge shotgun. Shauna, and father Robert, were devastated.

38:16 Robert even stopped the production of his movie  “The Natural” so he could attend Sid’s funeral.

38:21 Police interviewed Smika who told them Sid had  been into cocaine, and he might have stolen some

38:26 from a dealer. Years passed, and Smika was always  a suspect, but in 2010, cold case investigations

38:32 led to an arrest warrant for 1st degree murder. And then, he was gone.

38:36 Police believe he might still be in California,  or maybe Mexico, living under a new identity.

38:41 Why he’d shoot someone over a little rental money  has always remained a mystery. But this man of

38:46 average height and average build with dark hair  and Spanish fluency is still on the run. He’ll

38:51 now be 67. There’s $10,000 in it for you if you  can provide information that leads to his arrest.

38:57 6. 15 year old Herbert

38:59 Pulgar had a tough start in life. He grew up in  the rough neighborhoods of Chicago. But somehow,

39:03 he managed to overcome a life of adversity. Then  when he was 15 years old he was pulled out of a

39:08 fire by Chicago’s firefighters and to say thank  you, he drew a design that won an art competition.

39:14 That design was turned into a sticker that  would go on all of Chicago’s city vehicles.

39:20 It was certain he would have died had those  men not have pulled him out of that fire. He

39:24 told the media the men were his heroes.  The sticker was the least he could do.

39:28 Two days after his son’s name was  splashed all over the newspapers,

39:31 his father made an appearance. But not for anything good. He was

39:35 in the newspaper for being armed and dangerous  and belonging to a street gang that sold cocaine.

39:39 Herbert Pulgar Senior, then 42, was on the run. But it gets worse.

39:45 The city of Chicago then tore every single  sticker Herbert Jr. had designed from city

39:49 vehicles, claiming that the hands  he’d drawn were making gang signs.

39:53 Herbert Jr.’s mom said the sticker controversy  sent her son on a “downward spiral” and like

39:58 father-like son, he went down a dark path When  he was 18, he was arrested for being a passenger

40:03 in a stolen van driven by a 13-year-old. As for his father, he’s still on the run,

40:08 possibly laying low in Venezuela. Now for a murder mystery.

40:12 5. “Bizarre”. That’s

40:15 what the Seattle Times called this story. 49-year-old sound engineer Tom Pfaeffle,

40:19 a man who’d once worked with Nirvana, The  Black Crowes and Heart, had just been killed.

40:24 He left a wife and 4 kids behind and a lot  of devastated friends in the music business.

40:29 In July, 2009, he’d been staying with his  wife at the Blue Spruce Motel in Twisp,

40:34 a scenic rural town in Okanogan County. They’d  been to a birthday party, but when they got back

40:39 to the motel, Tom accidentally opened the door to  another person’s room, believing it was his own.

40:44 The time was 10.40 pm… and the man in the room  went crazy. He opened fire, Tom and his wife

40:50 having to run and take cover behind a car. The shooter sprayed the motel with bullets,

40:54 hitting Tom and also hitting a man who  was reading a newspaper on his bed in an

40:58 adjacent unit. Tom later died at the hospital. The killer, a 57-year-old named Kino Gomez,

41:03 handed himself in and claimed he was defending  himself. Police said opening fire like that showed

41:08 a “total disregard for human safety.” One of his  colleagues later said Kino was “paranoid” which

41:13 was why he always carried a gun. Then he vanished.

41:16 He packed in his job as a road engineer and left  behind a note that suggested he was going into

41:21 the mountains to end his life. The note said the  justice system had already made up its mind of his

41:26 guilt, and he’d decided to, quote, “deprive  society of the circus it so bloody craves.”

41:32 Police found his abandoned car, but  not a body. It raised suspicions,

41:36 because Kino was an immigrant who’d been born in  the Philippines under the name Miguel Esquerra.

41:41 So, is he dead, or is he hiding  out with his relatives back home?

41:45 He’ll now be 73, 5'4” (1.63 meters),  and possibly 150 pounds (68kg).

41:50 4. There are three types of serious

41:52 criminals who fill much of the Interpol Red  Notice list. One of them is the standard murderer.

41:57 The others are guys who’ve assaulted women  or children. The last category are men who’ve

42:02 fully embraced their hatred toward Uncle Sam. Like Ahmad Abousamra, who grew up in the US

42:08 with Syrian parents. He did well for himself,  gaining a degree in computer science from the

42:12 University of Massachusetts Boston in 2006. But the force of the Jihad proved to be too

42:17 irresistible. As the war on terror  was in full-swing in the early 2000s,

42:21 Abousamra spent his time training at secret camps  in the Middle East. He occasionally came back to

42:26 the US where he was planning a major attack. The FBI got wind of this, and in 2009,

42:31 he was indicted on terrorism charges, but by  then he was already gone. He joined the Islamic

42:36 State in Syria and embraced his creative side  when he became chief editor for Dabiq magazine.

42:41 The magazine acted as a recruiting tool for men  who will bring about the “Day of Judgement.”

42:46 So, along with that and arranging assassinations  and bombings, Abousamra is a very wanted man.

42:52 There’s US$50,000 in it if you can get  him arrested, and suffice it to say,

42:56 he’s to be considered armed and dangerous. 3.

42:59 Al Gurhan Gurkan was one of Chicago’s finest. He was also very corrupt.

43:05 From 1999 to 2001, he had one of  his friends arrange a drug deal,

43:09 and when the drugs were being handed over, Gurkan  and another cop pretended to conduct a bust. After

43:14 the dealer ran away, they scooped up the drugs. The men took at least 9 pounds (4 kg) of cocaine,

43:19 2 pounds (0.9kg) of heroin, and 10  pounds of weed (4.5kg). Together,

43:22 it’s worth maybe $200,000–$350,000 wholesale,  or more like $600,000–$900,000 if they

43:28 could sell it in small amounts. It’s believed Gurkan might now be

43:32 in Turkey. He’s 56, average height and  average build with brown hair and eyes.

43:37 2. Police are sitting across from a

43:39 man accused of a serious crime. He tells them, “I  knew it was wrong… her desperation pulled me in.”

43:45 Her desperation. He was referring

43:47 to a middle-aged woman in Maryland’s  Montgomery County who he had lent $5,000.

43:51 Except she couldn’t pay it, so she offered  a solution: her teenage daughter would meet

43:56 him at the Silver Spring's Georgian  Colonies Club House for $100 a time.

44:01 After the first time, the girl, according to  police files, had asked her mom why she had to

44:06 go again. Mom of the year replied, “I've done bad  things to make you have a good life. Go with him.”

44:12 Both the mom and the man were caught. His  name is Bejarni Rivas, now in his late-50s,

44:17 who was hit with 13 charges. The mother  was hit with 11 and according to reports,

44:21 was possibly facing 100 years in prison. The media hasn’t published a follow-up story about

44:26 the mother’s sentence. But we know Rivas paid bail  and jumped across the border. He might now be in

44:31 Nicaragua. He was tried in absentia and convicted  on 9 counts, including human trafficking.

44:36 The Interpol website can’t decide how  tall he is or how much he weighs. But

44:40 he’s probably about average height and  weight with brown eyes and brown hair.

44:45 One thing that stands out is a small tattoo on  his hand between his thumb and index finger.

44:49 This last story is one that  has divided the public.

44:52 1. In some cases,

44:54 the absconded American offender is found  hanging out in another country but the

44:58 authorities there won’t send him back. Which is why officials in England won’t

45:02 send Irish-American Shawn Eugene Sullivan back to  the US to face the music. Sullivan is a chronic

45:08 predator who’d hurt three young women in the  90s in Eagan and Bloomington, Minnesota. Prior

45:12 to that, he’d received a suspended sentence for  a similar crime against two girls in Ireland.

45:17 In the US, Sullivan was charged with two  counts each of second- and third-degree

45:21 criminal sexual conduct, all felonies. But the  UK has said Minnesota’s restrictive treatment

45:26 program for sex offenders is “draconian”. Officials in England pointed to the special

45:31 Minnesota program. It started in  1988 and in 2015, had a total of

45:36 641 offenders on its books determined to  be psychopathic or sexually dangerous.

45:42 But some haven’t even been convicted of  a crime, and only one man up until 2015

45:47 had ever been released from the program.  He violated his parole, so was sent back.

45:52 Because of the program’s indefinite nature,  British authorities considered extradition

45:56 unethical. Critics of the decision have  pointed out that England and Wales also

46:00 operate indefinite detention systems, such  as Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP).

46:06 Patients sent to high-security psychiatric  hospitals can sometimes remain confined for

46:10 decades, even for life if they are well-known  serial killers like the Yorkshire Ripper.

46:15 Even so, Sullivan won’t be going  home. His accusers are furious,

46:19 calling the whole deal a “loophole in the  justice system that caters to the criminals.”

46:24 He’s now in his mid-50s and  possibly living in London.

46:27 These aren’t the only criminals to leave  intelligence agencies on edge. Some of

46:30 the cases the CIA has been linked to feel  like scenes pulled straight from a movie.

46:35 Find out more in “Most Wanted Criminals That  Terrify Even the CIA.” Or watch this instead.
