00:00 The stock market is at record highs... so  why is your money buying less every month?

00:04 This isn't a booming economy.  It's a hostage situation.

00:08 Most people think the stock market measures  the health of the U.S. economy. It doesn't,

00:12 not anymore. Today, it's a  liquidity sponge for global fear.

00:16 U.S. stocks aren't hitting record highs because  America is booming. They're hitting record highs

00:20 because everything else is collapsing.  Global money has fewer places to turn to,

00:25 so it floods into U.S. assets. Not because they're  perfect, but because they're the least bad option.

00:31 And keeping it there requires  one thing… your purchasing power.

00:34 To stop that money from leaving, the  government is devaluing your dollars

00:38 while keeping asset prices climbing. So if the economy is trapped,

00:41 how are all-time highs even possible? And  what are they doing behind the scenes to

00:45 your money that almost nobody notices? Take a look at the financial headlines and

00:49 the scream about American prosperity. It seems  like the country has never been better off.

00:53 The S&P is at an all-time high. Investment  records are being shattered as the biggest

00:57 stocks go up and up with every passing week. The  wealthiest companies in the world are only getting

01:02 wealthier. It all points to an economy  that is going from strength to strength.

01:06 So why are you paying much  more for almost everything?

01:09 The data proves that US households today are  having to spend more for their groceries,

01:13 their insurance premiums, and their utility bills. The costs of everything from fast food meals

01:18 to first-time homes are spiraling. People’s  wallets are being squeezed. Their financial

01:23 hopes and ambitions are suffocating. Meanwhile,  companies like Nvidia and Microsoft are hitting

01:27 record-high valuations. The system is broken.

01:31 It’s the paradox of America today. And  that shatters one of the most widespread

01:35 and dangerous misconceptions of modern times. People have been told that the stock market is

01:40 some sort of health indicator of the economy.  A good stock market means a good economy.

01:44 There used to be some truth to that. Unfortunately, times have changed.

01:49 And in 2026, the S&P 500 is no longer some  sort of gauge for the US economy. It’s not a

01:54 barometer of how well the average person is doing  or how financially stable the American population

01:59 is. Instead, the stock market of today is entirely  detached from the reality of the average American.

02:05 It has transformed into a massive vacuum, sucking  up capital from all over the world. The reason for

02:10 this can be summed up in a single word: Instability.

02:14 When markets and entire economies become unstable,  capital naturally flows towards the safest places.

02:19 Right now, the global economy is more fragile  than it's been in years. The world's biggest

02:23 investors aren't pouring money into American  companies because the U.S. economy is thriving.

02:28 There’s no alternative. To them, it's the safest

02:31 move available. Park capital in the world's  largest companies and most resilient markets,

02:36 not because they're risk-free, but because  every other option looks worse. This is the

02:41 reality of the modern-day “Fortress America”.  The US isn’t booming, it’s becoming a bunker

02:46 where global capital hides out during a crisis. And since so much money is streaming in, stock

02:51 prices and company valuations are skyrocketing. This creates a dangerous illusion.

02:56 Politicians and corporations can point to  the green arrows on the stock market charts

03:00 to argue that everything is going great.  Meanwhile, far and wide across the country,

03:04 millions of people are struggling to afford the  most basic of supplies and everyday essentials.

03:09 They’re being forced to spend more,  just to survive. Every dollar in

03:13 their pocket feels less valuable by the day. But if the US economy isn’t actually booming,

03:18 where is all this money coming  from to pump the stock market?

03:21 For years, China was seen as  the world's growth engine.

03:24 Global investors poured trillions into  the country. They bought real estate,

03:28 backed its tech giants, and fueled  the rise of its manufacturing sector.

03:31 Then, in 2023, it hit a wall. Geopolitical tensions. The

03:35 fallout from COVID. Regulatory crackdowns. A  nationwide property crisis. They all teamed up

03:40 to shatter investor confidence. When confidence disappears,

03:44 capital doesn't wait around. In August 2023 alone, investors pulled

03:48 a record $15 billion out of Chinese equities. And  there was only one place that money was going.

03:53 America. The largest national

03:55 economy in the world. The place with the deepest  bond market. The home of the global reserve

04:00 currency and the world’s mightiest military, with  unparalleled influence far beyond its borders.

04:06 All these factors all matter. It’s because of them that the US has

04:09 long been seen as a safe haven for investors.  The one sure place they can always retreat to

04:14 when other markets start to feel a little shaky. So, in 2023, tens of billions flooded into the US.

04:20 Some went into the likes of Treasury  bonds and money market funds.

04:23 But a huge amount of it headed  straight for American equities,

04:27 especially the so-called “Magnificent Seven”:  the 7 most influential and highly valued tech

04:32 companies whose market capitalizations (market  caps) rank among the largest in the market.

04:37 That select group includes Amazon, Apple,  Meta, Microsoft, and Tesla, all of which

04:42 saw enormous growth and record-setting inflows  at the exact same time as the Chinese exodus.

04:47 It’s a scenario we’ve seen play out before. The world panics. Foreign investors get

04:52 scared. Then colossal amounts  of cash go to hide in America.

04:56 This didn’t happen because the US economy  was doing so well at the time and investors

05:00 wanted their piece of the action. Ultra-wealthy  individuals and institutions weren’t buying up

05:05 US stocks because American consumers  were living their best-ever lives.

05:09 They did it because they saw that the whole global  economy was coming apart at the seams. They knew

05:14 that no matter how bad the situation got, the US  had advantages that no other nation could rival.

05:19 Its deep economy and powerful military gave  it incontestable geopolitical hegemony.

05:24 That, in turn, means that every  investment in a US-based business

05:28 enjoys a certain degree of protection. But as the world’s money rushed into

05:32 the US bunker, the country’s government  had a huge hidden problem waiting for it.

05:36 There’s a common misconception about debt. Most people think that it becomes more

05:41 dangerous, the bigger it gets. That’s not quite accurate.

05:45 In reality, debt is actually most dangerous  when its interest becomes unmanageable.

05:50 As long as you can afford to cover the cost  of the interest, the size of the debt doesn’t

05:54 necessarily matter all that much. This is why  people can technically max out their credit

05:58 cards and take out multiple loans without ruining  themselves, so long as they’re able to make the

06:03 minimum monthly payment. But when that payment  gets too high, that’s when things go south.

06:08 This applies at a national level, too. The United States government found out

06:11 the hard way in 2024. Up to that point,

06:14 the US national debt had steadily surged,  year on year, rising by trillions of

06:19 dollars. But politicians never seemed concerned. They continued to borrow massive amounts of money

06:24 to fund massive projects, stimulate the economy,  and counteract the effects of financial crises.

06:29 The overall debt level just kept on getting  bigger. Successive administrations kicked the

06:33 can further down the road and expected the next  set of leaders to deal with the consequences.

06:38 Those consequences hit home in a major way. As the Federal Reserve aggressively increased

06:43 interest rates in order to fight inflation,  annualized interest payments on America’s

06:47 national debt surpassed $1 trillion. From that  moment on, the US government had to spend more

06:52 just to pay the interest on its debt than it  spends on the entire national defense budget.

06:57 The world’s mightiest and best-funded  military force was suddenly more affordable

07:02 than an annual interest payment. It was the first time in history

07:05 that this had happened. And it sent alarm bells

07:07 ringing in Washington DC and far beyond. The US government was suddenly looking at

07:12 the frightening possibility of insolvency. It  had walked directly into a deadly debt trap.

07:17 Increasing interest rates had helped inflation.  But those same increases also affected the costs

07:22 of debt. This, in turn, put extra pressure on  the government’s finances, which were suddenly

07:27 between a rock and a hard place. There was no obvious way out.

07:30 Washington had to pay its interest to avoid  a systemic default. But it couldn’t afford

07:34 them by relying on regular tax revenues  alone. Raising revenues wouldn’t work,

07:38 as that could finish off the already struggling  economy. Cutting spending wouldn’t work, either,

07:43 as that could cause a complete societal collapse. In a trap like this,

07:46 the usual solutions simply don’t work. You have to find another option. A drastic measure

07:51 that allows you to work around the seemingly  impenetrable wall sitting right in front of you.

07:56 But how? How does a government pay a trillion  dollar credit card bill without crashing the

08:00 economy? Simple.

08:02 By changing the rules of the game. Let’s say you’re facing bills you can’t afford,

08:06 and you’re not able to improve your income in  any meaningful way to help you pay your debts.

08:10 What do you do? The obvious answer is

08:12 to seek some sort of financial assistance. Imagine you go into a bank and are offered

08:16 a long-term loan to help you keep up with your  existing debts. But it comes with an enormous

08:21 interest rate. Or, the bank says, you can take out  a short-term line of credit that will essentially

08:25 lower your monthly payments, temporarily. Faced with those two options, most people

08:30 would opt for the latter because it provides  the short-term relief they need. It buys

08:34 them time to hopefully figure things out. The US government did something similar.

08:38 But to understand this technique, you  have to understand how the government

08:41 traditionally borrows money. To do this, it relies on

08:44 Treasury securities, like bonds and bills. To be more precise, it typically issues a

08:48 mixture of long term bonds that can take up to 30  years to mature, as well as short term T-bills,

08:53 which mature in a matter of months or even weeks. A typical bond is like a fixed-rate mortgage,

08:58 locking in interest for an entire generation.  T-bills are more like credit cards;

09:02 you have to either pay them off or roll them  over on a constant basis, and their rates can

09:06 change very quickly from one month to the next. By 2023, the cost of issuing large amounts of long

09:11 term bond debt became increasingly unsustainable. Selling long-term bonds would've forced the

09:16 government to offer much higher interest rates.  Those same rates would've crushed mortgages,

09:21 business borrowing, and the broader economy. So they found another way.

09:24 By late 2023, roughly 80 to 85% of new government  borrowing had shifted to short-term T- bills

09:30 instead, avoiding a spike in long-term rates. It was like the government decided to max

09:35 out its credit cards, as opposed to  taking out a high-interest mortgage.

09:39 It worked… for a while. Washington managed to stave

09:42 off a serious crisis, keeping long term rates  lower than they would otherwise have been. This,

09:47 in turn, prevented mortgage rates from  reaching astronomical levels and avoided

09:50 a complete explosion of corporate debt. What’s more, the government’s debt

09:54 manipulation strategy also acted as a kind  of artificial pump for the stock market,

09:58 moving liquidity out of banks and into assets. But this was never going to be a long term fix.

10:03 It was a Band-Aid, covering a  wound but failing to heal it.

10:07 It saved the system from instant collapse,  but short term debt doesn’t just disappear. It

10:11 matures, very quickly, giving the government  trillions of dollars’ of debt to roll over

10:16 every few months at extortionately high rates. To counteract that, the Treasury needed a way

10:21 to print money without calling it money printing. When people think about the concept of countries

10:25 “printing money”, they imagine literal  printing machines and conveyor belts

10:29 churning out vast stacks of dollar bills. It rarely works like that these days.

10:33 If central banks physically printed trillions  of dollars out of thin air, everyone would

10:37 notice. The effects would be obvious, as  inflation soars and asset values explode.

10:42 Instead, the US government and Federal Reserve  often prefer to print money in a more subtle

10:46 way. They use a digital method called  shadow or stealth quantitative easing (QE).

10:52 This involves them electronically  creating new funds to buy assets,

10:56 like bonds and bills. They rely on tactics  that don’t attract as much attention as

11:01 more direct and blatant money printing. The methodology is sneakier, but the end

11:05 result is the same: the economy enjoys a  fresh burst of stimulation as liquidity

11:09 flows into the financial system. But ordinary  people feel their purchasing power decrease.

11:14 This is why the market is  sitting at record highs today.

11:17 It’s because the US dollar is being  intentionally and systematically

11:20 destroyed in order to essentially pay  off tens of trillions of dollars of debt.

11:25 It’s part of an intentional economic strategy  known as financial repression, designed to

11:30 funnel private savings into the public sector and  push more and more money towards government debt.

11:34 All without the government itself having  to either raise taxes or slash spending.

11:39 To start financial repression, a country  keeps interest rates artificially below

11:43 the inflation rate. When inflation surpasses  interest, the value of debt begins to decline.

11:48 For example, if inflation is at 5% but  interest rates on government bonds are at 4%,

11:54 then the actual value of the debt declines by a  whole percentage point each year. If you can keep

11:59 that going for several years, you’ll effectively  burn off quite a large chunk of debt without

12:03 physically having to pay it. But there’s always a catch.

12:07 And financial repression has a huge catch. It’s basically a hidden tax on the middle class.

12:12 This is what makes it far more insidious than  if the government were to simply announce that

12:16 it was hiking tax rates. Because financial  repression is so much harder to spot. It’s

12:21 not dramatic or in-your-face, but gradual  and surreptitious. This is what leads to

12:26 many people feeling confused whenever it’s used. They can see their investment accounts rising,

12:30 they can see the values of the market’s  biggest players rising, and they can

12:34 even see their salaries rising. On paper, you  might look a little richer. But in real life,

12:39 everything feels more expensive. Because a dollar is still a dollar…

12:43 it's just buying you less every year. The government prints money to keep

12:47 its zombie economy up and running, but all that  capital doesn’t actually flow evenly across the

12:51 entire economy. Instead, the vast majority  of it ends up in just 7 specific places.

12:56 Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Tesla,  Meta, and Alphabet, the company behind Google.

13:03 These brands don’t just dominate headlines and  market shares. They dominate the stock market,

13:07 too. When money loses its value and fear and  panic are setting in, big money doesn’t simply

13:12 spread out across the stock market. It goes for  the big names. The safe names. The fortresses.

13:18 The Magnificent Seven. That’s why those 7 companies

13:21 alone account for a staggering 33% of the entire  S&P 500’s total market cap. That is the highest

13:27 index concentration in modern history. And it’s important to understand

13:31 the big picture here. The S&P was originally formed as a

13:34 diverse representation of a broad cross-section  of America’s economy and industrial landscape.

13:40 Nowadays, however, when investors buy this index,  a large part of that investment floods into these

13:45 tech firms. When foreign capital enters America,  too, a lot of it goes straight to these companies.

13:50 Even retirement funds are increasingly being  soaked up by the likes of Microsoft and Meta.

13:54 It’s not because all the other  businesses in America are doing terribly.

13:58 It’s simply because there’s such a vast disparity  between the biggest names and everybody else.

14:03 The market has become incredibly top-heavy. When trillions of dollars need somewhere to go,

14:08 they don't flow into thousands of smaller  companies. They flow into the biggest

14:12 businesses with the ability to absorb them. But this creates a very dangerous situation.

14:16 It’s not healthy for a global financial system  to rest on the shoulders of just 7 tech firms

14:21 and the CEOs running them. It’s a dangerous  concentration of risk when a handful of

14:26 companies become a life raft for global capital. First, it assumes these firms can never truly

14:31 fail. That people will always scroll  Instagram, that Google will remain the

14:35 default search engine forever, and that  iPhones will never fall out of style.

14:39 Second, and more concerning, it concentrates  power while starving everything else.

14:43 Billions that could be flowing into  smaller companies, local businesses,

14:46 and the industries that actually keep society  running are instead pulled into just seven names.

14:51 So the overall index goes up, but in reality,  only these companies are reaping the rewards.

14:56 And this raises a key question: why  won’t the Federal Reserve simply

15:00 step in and fix this problem? Because it mathematically can’t.

15:04 This is the scariest part of all. The one data point that makes the whole

15:08 “economy is fine” story look convincing is the S&P  500. But that only holds true depending on how you

15:14 measure it. Measured in dollars, everything looks  fine. Stocks are up, charts are green, and the

15:19 index keeps breaking records without much effort. Measure it in gold and everything changes.

15:24 Because the dollar is no longer a reliable  yardstick, since the government has done so

15:28 much to diminish its value. Gold, however,  is the ultimate long-term store of value,

15:33 with literally decades of data to prove it. When you price the S&P in gold,

15:37 a harrowing truth emerges. It’s not going up.

15:40 In fact, it’s actually way  down compared to its 2021 peak.

15:44 Over 15% down, to be precise. That means those “record breaking

15:48 highs” that the headlines have been talking about  these past few years are actually based on lies.

15:53 They’re a currency-based illusion. The stock market isn’t actually gaining value

15:57 as quickly as it seems. Instead, the currency  that it’s priced in is losing its value. It’s

16:02 like being told that your house is getting  bigger, but in reality, the ruler you’re

16:06 using to measure it is simply getting shorter. The public has been told that the Federal Reserve

16:11 uses high interest rates to combat inflation  and keep prices as affordable as possible.

16:15 It’s supposed to be a tool for the public good. That claim no longer holds up.

16:19 Now, the Federal Reserve is actually trapped in a  state of “Fiscal Dominance”, forced to prioritize

16:24 government funding over controlling inflation. In other words, any notion of the Fed

16:29 being independent has gone up in smoke. It is forced to keep rates artificially low to

16:33 prevent the government slipping into insolvency.  It is compelled to keep printing money, via shady,

16:38 back-door practices, to prevent DC going bankrupt. It’s almost like a hostage situation.

16:43 The government is holding a gun to the  Fed’s head, forcing it to do what serves

16:47 DC best… even if that comes at great cost  to literally millions of American families.

16:52 There’s no other way out. If the Fed actually maintained

16:55 high enough rates to deal with inflation, the  government’s interest bill would explode, plunging

17:00 DC into an inescapable debt crisis. So, it has to  keep those rates down, keep the liquidity moving,

17:05 and devalue the dollar to protect the government. The trap has been well and truly sprung.

17:10 Permanent devaluation and continued  inflation are mathematically guaranteed.

17:15 So what are those at the  very top doing to survive?

17:18 It’s important to stay grounded in the  midst of this economic chaos. The world

17:22 isn’t ending. Society is not about to stop  functioning or completely collapse overnight.

17:26 But that doesn’t mean that  this situation isn’t serious.

17:29 People will continue to work,  companies will continue to function,

17:32 and trade will continue to flow. But the rules  that govern these systems have irrevocably,

17:37 irreversibly changed. The era of “easy money,”  predictable inflation rates, and unquestionable

17:42 American dominance is drawing to its end  and shifting into something very different.

17:46 Fortress America may have incredibly high  walls, but its foundations are showing their

17:51 cracks. They’re bending and breaking beneath  the crippling weight of ever-increasing debt.

17:55 The 1% know this. They’re being proactive,

17:59 moving their money where it needs to be. Seeing the value of the dollar decline and

18:03 realizing that this decline is only going  to get worse, they’re cashing in their

18:06 paper currency for anti-fragile assets. That primarily means gold, as well as

18:11 other hard assets that can’t be printed off by  Central Banks or devalued by Treasury decisions.

18:16 It’s one of the reasons why gold has also  reached historic highs in recent times.

18:20 Money is also flowing into critical infrastructure  and resources, too. Ultra-wealthy investors and

18:25 venture capitalists are buying up the likes  of farmland and other bedrocks of the future.

18:30 They’re tossing away increasingly worthless  pieces of paper in exchange for firm,

18:34 tangible assets that provide the  sort of stability the dollar can’t.

18:37 Because when trust in money starts to slip,  capital doesn’t disappear. It changes form.

18:42 And what it’s becoming tells you everything  you need to know about where this is heading.

18:46 The question isn’t whether the system is changing. It already is.

18:50 The question is who’s still  holding paper when it finishes.

18:54 It seems like the financial clock is already  ticking. But what happens when it hits zero?

01:02 Fopen is simple because the interface is

01:04 small. But it is magical because the

01:06 thing behind that interface might not be

01:08 a disk file at all. It might be your

01:10 keyboard. It might be your terminal. It

01:13 might be a pipe from another process. It

01:15 might be a serial port. It might be the

01:17 bit bucket at dev null or an infinite

01:19 stream of zero bytes from dev zero or

01:21 random data from the kernel or a pseudo

01:23 file in proc that does not exist on disk

01:25 in any normal sense but is actually

01:26 being synthesized by the operating

01:28 system while you read it. And with a

01:30 couple of related tricks, it might even

01:32 be the output of another program, a

01:34 network connection or a stream backed

01:35 entirely by memory. And the beautiful

01:38 part is that your code often does not

01:40 need to know. And that's the trick.

01:42 That's the whole Unix magic act in one

01:44 sentence. Take wildly different things,

01:46 make them look enough like streams of

01:48 bites, and suddenly tiny simple tools

01:50 can do absurdly powerful things. So,

01:53 let's go all the way back to the

01:54 beginning, or close enough to the

01:56 beginning that the beard gets darker and

01:58 the terminals get louder. Lately, I've

02:00 been spending about half my days working

02:02 under the original BSD Unix on my PDB11.

02:05 And everything that we're going to do

02:06 here actually works on any POSIX

02:08 compliant system, which means it'll even

02:10 work on a Windows box in most cases, at

02:12 least with the C runtime on your side.

02:14 And in old Unix, the process did not

02:17 begin life as an isolated little snow

02:18 globe. Instead, it was born with three

02:21 open IO channels already connected.

02:23 Standard input, standard output, and

02:25 standard air. In C, we know those as

02:27 standard in, standard out, and standard

02:29 air. But the names are actually the C

02:31 libraries view of the world. Underneath

02:33 them inside Unix are file descriptors,

02:35 and those are just small integers. For

02:38 example, standard input is descriptor

02:39 zero. Standard output is descriptor one,

02:42 and standard error is descriptor 2.

02:44 That's it. 0, 1, and two. The three most

02:47 famous integers in operating systems.

02:49 And they're not magic because of what

02:50 they are. They're magic because of who

02:52 sets them up. When you run a program

02:54 from the shell, the shell creates the

02:56 environment that the program will

02:58 inherit. If you type a command normally,

03:00 descriptor zero probably points to your

03:02 keyboard or your terminal input.

03:04 Descriptor 1 points at your terminal

03:06 output. And descriptor 2 also points at

03:08 your terminal output, but conceptually,

03:10 it's separate. And that separation turns

03:12 out to matter a great deal. If you run

03:15 program redirected to output.ext, the

03:18 shell arranges things so that on

03:19 descriptor one standard output, it no

03:22 longer points to the terminal. It points

03:24 at a file. The program usually has no

03:26 idea that this just happened. It just

03:28 writes to its standard output. Same as

03:30 always. The shell has swapped the

03:32 plumbing underneath it. So if you run

03:34 program redirected from input text, now

03:36 descriptor zero comes from a file

03:38 instead of your keyboard. And if you run

03:40 program with stream 2 redirected out to

03:42 heirs.ext now descriptor 2 standard air

03:45 goes to a separate file. This last one

03:48 is not some historical afterthought they

03:50 came up with later. It's one of the

03:51 reasons that Unix pipelines work as well

03:53 as they do. Standard output is for the

03:56 useful data that your program produces.

03:58 Standard error is for complaining. If

04:00 your program is generating a list of

04:01 file names and you pipe their list into

04:03 another program, you don't want random

04:05 diagnostic messages mixed into the data

04:07 stream like raisins and an otherwise

04:09 acceptable cookie. And this is the

04:10 genius reason why standard air exists at

04:13 all. It lets your program say, "Hey,

04:14 here's the data you asked for." And

04:16 separately say, "By the way, something

04:17 weird happened. One stream is cargo, the

04:20 other is radio chatter." This is where

04:22 C's file pointer enters the story. When

04:25 you write file pointer f equals f open

04:27 in a relay log with r as your flags,

04:29 what you get back is not the file. It's

04:32 not even strictly speaking the raw

04:33 operating system handle. On Unix, the

04:36 raw primitive is usually the file

04:37 descriptor, that small integer. What f

04:40 open returns is a pointer to a C library

04:42 object called a file. And that object is

04:44 doing more work than people realize.

04:47 Think of the file descriptor as a claim

04:48 ticket at the storage counter. The

04:50 colonel knows what the ticket means. It

04:52 knows whether it represents a real file,

04:54 a terminal, a pipe, or some device. A

04:56 file pointer, on the other hand, is like

04:58 hiring a little clerk to manage that

04:59 ticket for you. The clerk has a buffer.

05:02 The clerk remembers whether you're

05:03 reading or writing. The clerk knows

05:05 whether you hit an end of file or an

05:07 error. The clerk batches your request so

05:09 it doesn't have to run to the kernel

05:10 window for every single bite. That

05:12 buffer is crucial. Without buffering,

05:14 calling get C in a loop would be

05:16 catastrophically expensive because every

05:18 character might require a system call. A

05:20 system call is not just a function call.

05:22 It's a controlled transition from your

05:24 program down into the operating system

05:26 kernel. It's asking the grown-ups in the

05:28 restricted area to do something

05:29 privileged on your behalf. And that's

05:31 powerful, but it's not free. So,

05:33 standard IO cheats in the best way

05:35 possible. You ask for one character. The

05:37 C library quietly reads a larger block

05:39 from the kernel into a buffer. Then the

05:41 next 100 or thousand characters can come

05:43 straight out of memory. To your program,

05:45 it still looks like you're reading a

05:47 stream one bite or one line at a time.

05:49 underneath the library is batching the

05:51 work. That's also why print f sometimes

05:54 seems haunted. If standard out is

05:56 connected to a terminal, it is often

05:57 line buffered, meaning output appears

05:59 when you print the new line. If standard

06:01 out is redirected to a file or a pipe,

06:03 it may be fully buffered, meaning it

06:05 waits until the buffer fills up or you

06:07 flush it. Standard air, meanwhile, is

06:09 usually unbuffered or at least treated

06:10 much more urgently because error

06:12 messages are supposed to appear even

06:14 when things are going wrong. This

06:16 explains one of those little bugs that

06:17 every C programmer eventually meets in a

06:19 dark alley. You print a prompt like

06:21 enter your name and then you call

06:23 something to read the input and on your

06:25 machine it works fine. But in some other

06:27 environment the prompt doesn't show up

06:29 because there was no new line. The

06:30 output got buffered and nobody flushed

06:32 it. The fix isn't mystical. You just

06:34 call f flush on standard out. That's

06:36 like telling the little clerk, stop

06:38 holding on to that. Go deliver it right

06:40 now. And once you understand that file

06:42 pointer is a buffered object sitting on

06:43 top of a lower level OS handle, a bunch

06:46 of weird behavior suddenly starts making

06:48 some sense. If you mix print f with raw

06:50 write calls on the same descriptor, you

06:52 can get surprising results because the C

06:54 library and the kernel do not

06:56 necessarily agree about what data has

06:58 been physically moved yet. If you fork a

07:00 process after printing buffered output

07:02 before flushing it, both parent and

07:04 child may inherit the same pending

07:06 buffer and suddenly a line you thought

07:08 printed once comes out twice. The

07:10 computer's not confused. You are. And I

07:12 mean that in a supportive educational

07:14 sense. Now, let's talk about the little

07:16 mode strings because they look like

07:17 little magic spells. And quite frankly,

07:19 they are. R opens an existing file for

07:22 reading. W opens a file for writing,

07:24 creating it if necessary, and truncating

07:26 if it already exists. And truncating is

07:29 a plate word for everything that used to

07:30 be there is now entirely gone. So, I

07:32 hope you meant that. A opens for

07:34 appending, creating the file first if

07:36 necessary. Then you get the variants

07:38 like R+ and W plus and A+ which allow

07:42 both reading and writing each with its

07:44 own set of rules. On Windows, we also

07:46 care deeply about binary mode. So RB and

07:49 WB matter because text mode may

07:51 translate line endings. On Unix, binary

07:54 and text mode are essentially the same

07:55 thing because Unix looked at carriage

07:57 return line feed translation and decided

07:59 it had better things to do that

08:00 afternoon. But a pen mode deserves

08:02 special attention because it's much

08:04 cooler than it looks. Most programmers

08:06 think a pen mode just means the file

08:08 position starts at the end. That would

08:10 be useful but not magical. The real

08:12 value at least on pix systems is that

08:15 append mode is normally implemented with

08:16 a kernel flag called o append. And that

08:19 means every write goes to the end of the

08:21 file at the moment the write happens.

08:23 Not when you opened it, not when you

08:24 last saw it around when the kernel

08:26 performs the write. And that distinction

08:28 is everything. Imagine two programs both

08:30 writing to the same log file. Without a

08:32 pen mode, each one might do the obvious

08:34 thing. Seek to the end, write a line.

08:37 The problem is that both can seek to the

08:38 same end before either one writes. Then

08:41 one writes its line and the other writes

08:42 its line and either leaves with it or

08:44 over top of it. And now your log file

08:45 looks like it was assembled by raccoons.

08:48 The pen mode moves the go to the end

08:50 operation into the kernel's write path.

08:52 It means the write is attached to the

08:54 current end of the file as part of the

08:55 operation. for log files, audit trails,

08:58 server traces, and anything where

09:00 multiple writers might be adding

09:01 records. This is not just convenient.

09:04 It's the difference between a log and a

09:06 crime scene. There are some caveats

09:08 because there are always some caveats.

09:10 Standard IO buffering can still split

09:12 what you think of as one logical record

09:14 into more than one lower level, right?

09:16 Network file systems have historically

09:18 had their own special collection of

09:19 gremlins. And append mode does not make

09:22 your application protocol magically

09:23 atomic, but the basic idea is still

09:26 incredibly powerful. If you want to add

09:28 to the end of a file, ask the colonel to

09:30 enforce that rule instead of trying to

09:31 fake it in user mode. Let's say you open

09:34 a file with a plus, seek back to the

09:36 beginning, read a little bit, and then

09:37 write something. Most programmers expect

09:39 the write to happen wherever they last

09:41 sought to. But in append mode, that

09:43 write still goes to the end. The file

09:46 position matters for reading. The append

09:48 rule dominates writing. And that's

09:50 exactly the kind of behavior that seems

09:52 weird until you realize it's there to

09:53 prevent a race condition. Now, so far

09:56 we've been talking about regular files.

09:58 Nice normal files. Files with names and

10:00 sizes and blocks on disk and the kind

10:02 that your file explorer understands. But

10:04 if we stop there, we would miss the best

10:06 part. Because in Unix, a path name does

10:08 not have to refer to a regular disk

10:10 file. Open dev null for writing and

10:12 every bite that you write just vanishes.

10:15 It's not a metaphorical trash can. It's

10:16 a device exposed through the file system

10:18 namespace. Your program can f open

10:21 devnull with write and get a file

10:23 pointer and happily frrint f into

10:25 oblivion. Similarly, you can open dev

10:28 zero for reading and you get an endless

10:29 stream of zero bytes, not a giant file

10:32 full of zeros, a device that produces

10:34 zeros on demand forever. Open dev/

10:37 random and you can read random bytes

10:39 from the kernel again through a filelike

10:41 interface. Open dev tty and you can talk

10:43 to the controlling terminal even if

10:45 standard input and standard output have

10:47 been redirected. It's a pretty marvelous

10:49 hack to process pipe data but still ask

10:52 the user a question because your input

10:54 string might be coming from a file. Your

10:56 output might be going to some other

10:57 program but going to dev tty says no I

11:00 mean the actual human terminal attached

11:02 to this process. So it's not often you

11:04 need it but it's invaluable when you do.

11:07 And then there's proc, which is where

11:08 the file system starts to feel like a

11:09 magician is palming cards. On many Unix

11:12 like systems, files under proc are not

11:14 ordinary files sitting on a disk. They

11:17 are views into kernel state. When you

11:19 read them, the kernel synthesizes the

11:21 contents live. You can open something

11:23 that looks like a text file and read

11:25 information about the CPU, memory,

11:26 mounts, or processes. The file is the

11:29 interface. The bites are being invented

11:31 as you ask for them. Now, when I wrote

11:33 Task Manager on Windows, to get the

11:34 information about the running processes,

11:36 you'd call antiquery system information

11:38 twice. Once to figure out how big of a

11:40 buffer you needed, and then a second

11:42 time to deliver a snapshot of the

11:43 process data. Under Unix, you simply

11:45 open a file and read it. It's a vastly

11:48 different approach, superior in some

11:49 ways, inferior in others, but inarguably

11:51 more flexible. And that's the

11:53 philosophy. Don't make every program

11:55 understand every kind of object. Make

11:57 the objects look enough like files that

11:59 existing programs can inspect, redirect,

12:02 filter, log, and compose them. And that

12:04 brings us to one of the most practical

12:06 lessons in C API design. Whenever you

12:09 can write file functions that take a

12:11 file pointer instead of a file name. A

12:13 function that takes only a file name can

12:15 only be a file by name. But a function

12:17 that takes a file pointer can read from

12:19 a file, from standard in, from a pipe,

12:21 or from a device, or from a stream that

12:23 somebody else has already prepared. It's

12:25 much more flexible because it's less

12:27 presumptuous. It does not demand to own

12:29 the plumbing. A cool little example is a

12:32 function called something like copy

12:33 stream with a file in and a file out

12:35 inside. It just reads from one stream

12:37 and writes to the other. You can use it

12:39 to copy one disk file to another. You

12:41 can use it to copy one standard input to

12:43 one standard output. You can pipe

12:45 compressed data through it. You can feed

12:47 it dev zero. You can send its output to

12:49 dev null. It's all the same code,

12:51 different plumbing. It's not merely

12:52 convenience, it's leverage. Now, there

12:54 are some more advanced relatives of F

12:56 open that probably deserve their own

12:57 episodes because each one opens another

12:59 door. There's FD open, which lets you

13:02 take an existing Unix file descriptor

13:04 and wrap it in a file pointer. That

13:06 matters because not everything starts

13:07 life from a file name. Pipes, sockets,

13:10 duplicated descriptors, and inherited

13:12 handles may already exist. With FD open,

13:15 you can say, "I have this low-level

13:16 thing. Please give me back the nice

13:18 buffered standard IO interface on top of

13:20 it." Then there's file no, which goes

13:22 the other direction. given a file

13:24 pointer unless you ask for the

13:25 underlying file descriptor which you

13:26 might need for low-level operations like

13:29 select pull uh fsync fl stuff like that.

13:34 There's also f reopen which can redirect

13:36 an existing stream like standard out or

13:38 standard air from inside the program and

13:40 that's useful for old school logging

13:42 demon setup test harnesses and programs

13:44 that want to reroute their own output

13:45 without changing every printf. There's p

13:47 open for process open which gives you a

13:49 file pointer connected to another

13:51 process. You can run a command and read

13:53 its output as though it were a file.

13:55 That's both incredibly useful and mildly

13:57 dangerous, which is how you know it

13:59 comes from Unix. And then there are

14:01 memorybacked streams, custom streams,

14:03 socket wrap streams, and all kinds of

14:04 clever machinery that prove the same

14:06 point over and over again. File pointer

14:08 is not really about disk files. It's

14:10 about streams. But we don't need to

14:12 chase all those today because the core

14:13 idea is already powerful enough. The

14:16 reason fopen matters is not that it

14:18 opens files. Lots of things open files.

14:20 The reason fopen matters is that it sits

14:22 at the boundary between a very small

14:24 programming interface and a very large

14:26 operating system idea. You ask for a

14:28 stream. The operating system in the C

14:30 runtime conspire to provide you one.

14:32 Maybe the stream comes from flash

14:33 storage, maybe from a terminal, maybe

14:35 from a pipe, maybe from a paper tape

14:37 reader, maybe from a pseudo device,

14:39 maybe from a kernel generated illusion

14:41 wearing a file name as a disguise. Your

14:43 code gets to read bytes, write bytes,

14:45 flush buffers, detect end of file, and

14:47 handle errors using the same small

14:49 vocabulary. That's not accidental.

14:51 That's design. And it is a style of

14:53 design we should still admire. Modern

14:55 software often solves problems by adding

14:57 new layers, new protocols, new object

14:59 models, new services, new formats, new

15:01 dependencies, and so on until the simple

15:03 thing is buried under a parking garage

15:05 of architecture. Unix did something

15:07 different here. It made the interface

15:09 brutally simple, and it made the world

15:10 conform to it. Not perfectly, not

15:13 universally, not without some weird edge

15:14 cases, but well enough that half a

15:16 century later, a C programmer can still

15:18 write a tiny stream processing function

15:20 and automatically make it work with

15:22 files, terminals, pipes, devices, and

15:24 things that the original author never

15:26 imagined. And that's the real magic of

15:28 FOP. It's not a big function, not a

15:31 glamorous function. Does not have a

15:32 logo, a conference, or a certification

15:34 path, or a cloud pricing calculator.

15:36 It's just a little doorway. But on the

15:38 other side of that doorway is one of the

15:40 best ideas in computing. If you can make

15:42 things look like a stream of bytes, you

15:44 can compose them. And once you see that,

15:46 then f open data with R never looks

15:48 quite so boring. Again, if you found

15:50 today's episode interesting or

15:52 entertaining, remember I'm mostly in

15:53 this for the subs and likes. So, I would

15:55 be honored if you would consider leaving

15:56 me one of each before you go today. If

15:58 you have any comments or questions on

15:59 this episode, be sure to leave them in

16:01 the comments below. And if you use a

16:02 question mark, that means Glenn will

16:04 spot it and he will pull it out and we

16:05 will talk about it on Shop Talk on

16:07 Friday or at least the best of the

16:08 questions. We try to get to them all.

16:10 Uh, make sure you check episode out and

16:13 if you like it, subscribe over there.

16:14 It's on the Dave's Attic channel and

16:16 I'll put a link up here. In the

16:17 meantime, and in between time, hope to

16:19 see you next time right here in Dave's

16:21 Garage.

16:22 >> Do it, Lynn. Do it. Do it.

00:11 MICHAEL SCOTT ASATO CUTHBERT: So this

00:13 is an article I want to say just a few little things about it

00:17 that it's an article that was written for other academics

00:24 at the time.

00:25 So just so we know that it wasn't, at the time

00:28 it was published in 2004, really designed

00:31 that we were going to read it in class.

00:32 And we're going to have various academic articles in here.

00:37 So some people are old hats reading academic articles

00:41 in the Humanities or in Science, or in this case

00:44 at the intersection of Humanities and Science,

00:47 and other people have had less introduction to that.

00:51 So I just want to take a minute and say

00:54 how I approach reading a new article because we'll

00:57 have some of them up.

00:58 First, always take a second and think

01:01 about the title for a second and figure out, OK, is--

01:06 sometimes I even just write it down and put it

01:09 somewhere because when I'm not assigning articles,

01:13 there are things that you can put down at any point.

01:16 And so when I get to the point where I'm somewhere through it,

01:19 and I see they're not answering, they're not

01:21 talking about the title, they're not answering,

01:23 then I can throw it away.

01:24 You're not allowed to do that in this class,

01:27 but that's, you know, something to do.

01:29 Then I always start paying attention to the bold points

01:32 and try to see about that because I don't

01:35 read very fast and things.

01:37 So I'll want to jump ahead a bit.

01:39 But always read the introduction really carefully.

01:44 In some ways, if you have--

01:46 let's say, this would never happen to you,

01:49 but you're behind on a reading or something.

01:51 It's 10 minutes before class, and you're trying

01:53 to figure out what to do.

01:56 Don't read the whole thing fast.

01:58 Read the introduction really carefully, twice.

02:01 And that's because that's where almost everything should be

02:05 there if it's a good article.

02:08 Because you'll get to very specific things

02:11 as you get to your projects, we may get to the point

02:13 where you're assigning yourself articles,

02:15 or it's like, hey, look at these five articles

02:18 that I may have seen.

02:20 If at the end of the introduction,

02:22 again, you don't know anything what

02:24 it's going to be about, throw it out, move to the next article.

02:27 But a well-written article should give everything there.

02:31 I go to the pictures yet.

02:33 Next, I don't want to ever see that cliche a picture is

02:36 worth a thousand words in any of your things,

02:38 but it's kind of true.

02:39 So you can figure out, OK, what are we

02:41 going to be talking about?

02:43 From reading the introduction, I knew

02:44 we were going to be talking about music representation.

02:47 So I start asking, are these music representations

02:50 that are being talked about?

02:51 And then when I look at the text, I can do it.

02:53 I can see, OK, the next topic is issues of representation.

02:58 I've skimmed ahead, so I know there's

02:59 only two real topics in this, so this

03:02 should be the first half of it.

03:03 Oh, my gosh, that's why I remembered like, gosh, yeah, OK.

03:08 And just read the first sentence,

03:11 the first paragraph of that.

03:13 And go ahead and see if the ending tells you

03:20 what it's going to be about.

03:21 This is not like watching your favorite movie.

03:26 An academic article, you shouldn't

03:27 feel like you're spoiling the great reveal.

03:32 There's maybe five articles in my life

03:35 where I think if I read this way the first time I saw it,

03:40 I would have ruined the article.

03:42 All the rest, I just improved my--

03:44 so I can see that, OK, so we have

03:47 a problem of multiple requirements,

03:49 and we have some sort of a solution that doesn't work.

03:52 So then I can go back and read and try

03:54 to figure out what it is we're going to be talking about.

03:57 And we can see the final thing is

04:00 an introduction to the next section

04:03 and see that the second part is a case

04:05 study of one particular example of computational

04:10 and comparative and computational musicology.

04:14 And I can see OK, I probably should have

04:18 some fun looking at that later.

04:20 And then jump to the conclusion.

04:22 This article is great in that it does label its conclusion with--

04:28 where is it --the word conclusion.

04:30 Not every article does that.

04:32 But again, go ahead and read the last couple paragraphs

04:40 of the article, so you find where it ends.

04:43 Go back, and go ahead and figure out

04:46 what the article is going to be about.

04:49 When you're assigning articles to yourself--

04:52 and the articles just keep getting longer.

04:56 It's this weird thing that people

04:59 used to write things in typewriters, double

05:01 spaced in Courier 14 point.

05:04 Now we write single spaced in times New Roman 11 or 12

05:07 or something.

05:08 But people keep thinking that my article needs

05:12 to be 30 pages long, and that's actually

05:13 double the length of articles.

05:15 So they're starting to get too long.

05:17 I do encourage you to read like this.

05:20 And then only after you figure out

05:24 what the main conclusions of the article are--

05:31 this one is pretty obvious to those of us in this class

05:35 that you can use computational methods without giving up

05:39 humanistic values.

05:40 Only once we've done that, we go back.

05:43 Hopefully, you can skip notes the first time

05:46 you read, because if they've written well,

05:49 these should be additional parts or places that you

05:52 can look at later.

05:54 If it's a poorly written article,

05:55 then you have to read the notes to get to it.

05:59 And if it's a new subject, go ahead and look at the references

06:03 and see who appears a lot.

06:07 So you can see, OK, these are probably important people.

06:10 But OK, this guy Paul von Hippel, Huron, Huron, Huron,

06:15 Huron, Huron, Huron, I should probably,

06:17 if I want to go further, read something by Huron.

06:20 This is what I'm thinking.

06:22 Yeah, it's just more and more and more of them.

06:25 And then also, if there's anybody

06:28 that we recognize from the class.

06:31 You'll be looking at Eleanor Selfridge Field's writings

06:34 today.

06:34 She's awesome.

06:38 So with this in mind, these are some of the strategies

06:43 that I go through in looking at it.

06:45 And then the other great strategy is talk to people

06:49 and hopefully, they can give you their take on the article.

06:55 We can be richer for it.

docs.text: This video explains the differences between TCP and UDP protocols and their practical applications.

docs.title: Key Topics Covered
docs.text:
• TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) fundamentals
  • UDP (User Datagram Protocol) basics
  • Reliability vs. speed trade-offs
  • Use cases for each protocol type
  • Network performance considerations

docs.title: Analysis Points
docs.text:
• How TCP ensures data reliability through acknowledgments and retransmissions
  • UDP's lightweight approach for time-sensitive applications
  • Connection-oriented vs. connectionless communication
  • Error handling differences between protocols
  • Performance characteristics in various network conditions

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• TCP is preferred for reliable data transfer (web, email, file transfer)
  • UDP is better for real-time applications (gaming, streaming, VoIP)
  • Network conditions should guide protocol selection
  • Understanding both protocols is essential for network troubleshooting

00:07 and engineering have got to pay more attention

00:11 how to speak to the public.

00:13 I am convinced one approach is to embrace

00:16 the value of the visual-- that when we find better

00:20 vocabularies to express complicated ideas,

00:24 there will be less confusion across the globe about how

00:28 to make critical decisions that will affect

00:30 our health and our planet, to educate all our cultures on how

00:36 to distinguish between opinion and fact.

00:40 One approach is to engage the public in our conversations.

00:45 And we can do that creating honest, accessible, compelling,

00:50 even beautiful images of our research

00:53 so that our work will become less intimidating,

00:57 where your mother or father will not

00:59 be embarrassed to ask questions about the images they

01:03 see of your work.

01:04 That's part of the philosophy of this course,

01:07 in case you didn't notice.

01:08 But so much of what we do in our labs is difficult to explain.

01:13 So first, here's where I'd like to briefly touch

01:16 on the potential of visual metaphors.

01:19 For example, you've seen this music box

01:22 throughout this course.

01:24 I made the image for our book "No Small Matter"

01:27 to engage the reader to think about the language

01:29 of computation, a binary language, either on or off,

01:35 as this music box's clever system works.

01:38 It's either one or zero.

01:41 Take a good look and think about it.

01:44 Here's another one of these metaphors

01:46 along the same thinking of explaining binary language.

01:50 These are small drinking glasses viewed from above.

01:54 The ones filled with red (good shiraz, by the way!)

01:59 represent one in this binary system.

02:02 The empty glasses represent zero.

02:05 Again, for the book, "No Small Matter."

02:07 The first row across represents 12 in our everyday number

02:12 system.

02:13 If we add the second row, 22, the result in the third row

02:20 is 34.

02:22 12 plus 22 equals 34.

02:26 Here's another you've seen before.

02:28 We call it etching with light, suggesting

02:30 how some surfaces we work with in the laboratory can be etched

02:35 with various patterns.

02:37 And here, this cascade could suggest

02:40 how the flow of electrons change from one energy state

02:43 to another.

02:45 Here's one I think that works quite well.

02:47 These graduation chairs are lined up basically

02:51 to guide parents where to sit.

02:53 It's a metaphor for something called templated

02:56 or guided self assembly.

02:59 Just as when DNA replicates itself, each of its strands

03:03 guides the distribution of bases for the new strand.

03:08 Here's one that I did love making,

03:10 but maybe it doesn't quite work enough.

03:13 I wanted to show the counterintuiveness

03:16 of quantum mechanics.

03:18 Now, look at the shadow on the right.

03:21 It doesn't make sense, right?

03:23 In fact, that square shadow is impossible.

03:27 I made it with software.

03:29 And so it is with quantum mechanics-- so much

03:32 of the quantum phenomena simply just makes no sense at all.

03:36 Here's one from the Fermilab which

03:39 I thought was quite clever.

03:41 Take a guess at what this jelly bean jar is metaphorically

03:44 representing.

03:45 Take a moment.

03:47 And the fact that it's from Fermilab is a big hint.

03:50 So here's that information in a pie chart--

03:56 of course, more quantitative.

03:58 We are seeing the distribution of dark energy, dark matter,

04:03 and everything else in the universe.

04:05 I think we pay more attention to the jelly bean jar.

04:08 Do you?

04:09 What do you think?

04:11 Now, none of these visual metaphors

04:13 work completely on their own.

04:16 First, we need some sort of text to help

04:18 us look and think about it.

04:20 And most important, all metaphors

04:23 fall apart at some point.

04:26 And that conversation of where they fall apart

04:29 can be a powerful place to talk about the science.

04:34 I encourage you to start thinking

04:36 about creating metaphoric photographs that

04:39 teach the non-expert how to start

04:42 thinking about various scientific phenomena.

04:46 OK.

04:46 Let's switch gears and look at just a few

04:49 simpler ways to engage the public with our images.

04:53 How about using some of your new wonderful images

04:56 of your work for cards, or announcements, or posters?

05:01 Could be fun thinking about it.

05:04 The images you will begin making after this course

05:07 will be pretty compelling.

05:09 I'm sure of it.

05:11 Why not show them off outside the research community?

05:14 All I suggest is to think about ways

05:17 to incorporate some of your amazing new images

05:20 in ways to excite the public.

05:23 And who knows?

05:25 Someday, you might even get an exhibit

05:28 along the Champs-Elysees.

05:30 What do you think?

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 What’s the last thing that goes through your mind  when you’re shot in the head? Well… apart from the

00:04 bullet. We’re breaking down what happens in those  final moments - how the brain reacts, what you

00:09 might feel and why Hollywood gets it wrong.This is  what really happens when you’re shot in the head.

00:11 Ok, staring down the business end of a loaded  gun is hardly an everyday situation for many

00:12 of us. Even those who find themselves drawn  to more ‘armed and dangerous’ lines of work

00:12 are statistically unlikely to see a gun fight,  let alone be part of one. But the chances are,

00:12 if there’s a gun pointed at your head,  the person holding it might be reckless

00:12 – or desperate – enough to pull that trigger. Let’s say you’re standing just a few feet from

00:14 someone with a gun pointed squarely at your head.  Maybe it’s a mob hitman. Maybe a bitter ex. Or

00:20 maybe just a violent psychopath who left their  tinfoil hat at home. The reason doesn’t matter.

00:25 What does matter is that their aim  is solid. Their range is close. And

00:29 there's no chance they’re going to miss. The second that the trigger is squeezed,

00:33 before the bullet has even left the gun and  entered your soft squishy brain, there’s already a

00:38 whole lot going on. Inside the chamber of that gun  sits a cartridge – what most people wrongly call a

00:43 bullet. The bullet is the projectile at the tip  - the rest is the cartridge casing, packed with

00:48 propellant and sealed with a primer at the base. So, the gun is loaded and cocked. The firing pin

00:54 is held back under spring tension, resting  right behind the cartridge. And now - with

00:58 one final pull - it’s released. The firing pin  snaps forward, punching the primer at the base

01:03 of the cartridge. That tiny impact causes a spark,  igniting the chemical powder inside and creating

01:09 an instant explosion within the cartridge.  The propellant chemicals burn and generate

01:14 a lot of expanding gas, very quickly, causing a  massive build up of pressure. Being bottled up in

01:20 such a small place means there’s only really  one direction all that pressure can travel:

01:25 outwards. And bullet cartridges are  designed to channel the pressure

01:29 from that mini explosion – and all the kinetic  energy it causes – directly behind the bullet.

01:35 The bullet splits off from the end of the  cartridge, and is sent down the barrel at high

01:38 speeds. Most bullets are tapered into a point,  which both helps to reduce air resistance as they

01:43 come speeding out of a weapon. But that tapered  tip is also helpful for allowing the projectile to

01:48 penetrate wood, metal, or in this case, your head. Now, it’s important to bear in mind, everything

01:53 we’ve described so far has all occurred within  only a few seconds – it’s so fast that your

01:57 brain likely hasn’t even had a chance to  process half of what’s happened. And even

02:01 more unfortunately for you, that’s not the only  problem that your brain is going to have today.

02:05 Whenever we see gunshots on TV, in movies or even  inflict them on other players in video games,

02:11 deaths often seem to happen instantaneously.  Sometimes you might see a character struck by

02:16 a bullet and suffering a slow and painful  death and sometimes characters will shrug

02:20 off bullet wounds no problem. In real life, these  are all possible: instant death, a slow, agonising

02:26 fatal injury or surviving - although this is in  extremely rare cases. But it all comes down to a

02:32 myriad of factors, and while you might think that  a head shot is the fast track to our first instant

02:37 death option, you’d be surprised – and we’ve  found a real world example to prove that too.

02:43 First among these factors is all down to the  specifics; what type of firearm was used,

02:48 what size and calibre are the bullets it’s  firing. Then there’s the trajectory the bullet

02:52 was travelling and what angle it entered your  body. All of these might seem like small details,

02:57 but they can all mean the difference between life,  death and something arguably worse. That’s because

03:02 being shot, well, it’s all a matter of physics! Assuming we don’t know exactly what kind of load

03:07 out our shooter is packing, then let’s instead  focus on the next majorly important factor:

03:12 the bullet itself. When a bullet is fired and  hits a human body, all that energy behind it

03:17 is transferred onto you, the unlucky target.  Wherever it strikes the body is where the energy

03:22 is transferred to, and that tapered end means  it’s all focused onto a small point. This is what

03:27 causes direct damage to the body, as that pointed  end has enough momentum behind it not just to

03:33 break the skin, but to penetrate tissue and bone. Now, all that energy, concentrated into pushing

03:39 the point of that bullet through your head. Let’s  say you were directly facing the shooter when they

03:43 fired. That means the bullet is now spinning  through the air with enough kinetic energy to

03:47 break through the skin of your forehead and into  the epicranial aponeurosis – the dense fibrous

03:53 tissue that covers the upper part of your skull. By now, you might be thinking what kind of damage

03:57 you’d receive from a gunshot to the head? Or  rather, you would be, if you hadn’t just been

04:01 shot. Well, bullets can damage flesh and organs in  a few different ways - the first of which coming

04:06 as a result of a direct hit. This causes a bullet  to leave a permanent cavity in whatever is in its

04:11 path, which in this case happens to be you and  the contents of your head: namely your brain. So,

04:16 you’d likely be on the receiving end of what's  known as a TBI, or a traumatic brain injury.

04:22 In most urban areas across the U.S., gunshot  wounds are a leading cause of TBI’s. Roughly

04:27 12% of all TBIs are linked to firearms - whether  from violent assaults or accidental discharges.

04:32 And gunshot wounds to the head account for  about 35% of all TBI-related deaths. But,

04:38 if you’re thinking that means you have a 65%  per cent chance of survival, think again.

04:43 Gunshot wounds to the head are fatal around 90%of  the time, with most victims dying on the scene,

04:49 if not instantly. Though some victims can  survive the initial trauma – including one

04:53 we’ll talk about shortly – around half of these  survivors will die in the emergency room. So,

04:58 safe to say, your odds of sustaining a traumatic  brain injury? Pretty high. Odds of you surviving

05:02 it? Not so much. But what exactly causes  someone to die from a gunshot wound?

05:07 A wound where a bullet enters the body – or in  your case, the cranium – but does not travel far

05:13 enough to exit is referred to as a ‘penetrating  wound’. If a bullet is able to travel fast and far

05:18 enough through to exit the body, this is called  a ‘perforating wound’ - also known as a ‘through

05:23 and through’. In either instance, you’ve still  got a high velocity metal projectile penetrating

05:28 and travelling through your brain tissue. But  what an impact like this also causes is a wave

05:33 of pressure to be transmitted through that brain  tissue. The resultant damage from this pressure

05:38 wave – as well as the bleeding – can cause the  brain to swell, leading to a TBI and death.

05:44 There’s another type of injury that can also  occur when being shot, and that’s caused by

05:48 the shock waves of the bullet’s impact. Any  tissue surrounding the bullet as it travels

05:52 on its path can become caught up in a temporary  vacuum, created by the high speed and velocity of

05:57 the projectile. This vacuum can be forty times  the size of the actual bullet itself, warping

06:03 and stretching any tissue caught in its path. As the bullet burrows deep - or passes clean

06:08 through - it rips apart tissue, bursts blood  vessels, and unleashes a surge of pressure

06:13 inside your skull. But there’s also shockwaves  that are coming off the bullet. They ripple

06:18 outward from the bullet’s path like waves across  a pond, distorting and stretching brain matter in

06:23 every direction. And if that wasn’t bad enough,  some bullets can fragment on impact. This causes

06:29 small, sharp pieces of metal to become lodged  throughout any tissue the bullet passes through.

06:33 The severity of an injury and the extent of the  damage left by a gunshot wound to the head can

06:39 vary depending on the location. If the bullet  passes through the tip of your right frontal

06:43 lobe - just behind the forehead - and avoids the  base of the skull, you might actually be “lucky.”

06:49 That’s because this area doesn’t house as many  vital brain functions or major blood vessels as

06:54 deeper regions. But that still doesn’t guarantee  you’d survive the injury inflicted though.

06:59 If a bullet enters through the tip of your  left frontal lobe and travels downward toward

07:03 the temporal lobe and brainstem - then that’s a  different story. It would be travelling through

07:08 some of the most vital tissue inside your  head. That’s more likely to be lights out,

07:12 permanently. The same goes for if a bullet’s  trajectory went through any of the key blood

07:16 vessels in your brain. This could result in  a blood clot, which would rapidly expand,

07:21 compressing the vital tissues of your brain. If  that happens, you’re either dead on the scene,

07:26 or battling against more of that rapidly  increasing pressure inside your skull.

07:30 Whichever way you slice it, it’s not looking good.  If the bullet doesn’t directly penetrate your

07:35 vital brain tissue shortly after impact, then any  one of the resultant injuries will likely finish

07:40 you off… unless you happen to be extremely lucky. Remember how we mentioned some gunshot victims

07:46 survive their initial wound? Well, one of those  was 14-year-old Ahad Israfil, who was shot in the

07:51 head as the result of a freak accident. In 1987  while at work, Ahad’s employer allegedly knocked

07:57 a firearm onto the floor, which caused the weapon  to discharge. The bullet struck Ahad in the head,

08:03 destroying much of his brain tissue - in  particular his right cerebral hemisphere,

08:07 along with the right half of his skull.  He was immediately rushed to hospital,

08:11 where intensive care surgeons tried to save  his life. To their amazement, after five hours,

08:16 Ahad regained consciousness and tried to speak. The skin covering Ahad’s scalp actually survived

08:22 the injury, and plastic surgeons were able to  use a silicon implant to fill the resultant

08:27 hole in his skull - where the right half  of his brain had been. The skin was then

08:31 stretched over this implant to give Ahad more  of a natural appearance - the repairs to his

08:35 scalp meant he could even regrow his hair. But  if you’re thinking that Ahad lived a difficult

08:40 life missing half of his brain, think again. When a bullet damages someone’s right hemisphere,

08:45 this can leave the victim with motor and sensory  impairments on the left side of their body,

08:49 and vice versa. Functions like thought,  memory, speech and vision are controlled

08:53 by both sides of the brain working in tandem.  So, damaging one hemisphere can mean that

08:58 someone is still able to perform some of these  functions, more often in a limited capacity.

09:03 Incredibly though, Ahad Israfil not only regained  most of his mental faculties and is able to speak,

09:09 he even successfully obtained an honours  degree from his local university. He lived

09:14 a long life afterwards, eventually passing  away in an Ohio nursing home back in 2019,

09:18 over 30 years after surviving his traumatic  brain injury. His is a pretty remarkable

09:23 story and a great example of the human brain’s  capacity to recover even from severe injuries.

09:29 But if we were in your shoes, we wouldn’t exactly  put all our chips on miraculously getting better

09:34 after being shot in the head. You need a lot  of things on the bingo card in order to survive

09:39 a wound like that, but hey, maybe you get lucky. So long as the bullet entry point and exit wounds

09:44 aren’t too severe, and the bullet misses the  critical areas of the brain. It also needs to be

09:49 a low-caliber round, fired from a lower-velocity  weapon and the shooter can’t be too close.

09:54 You’d need immediate, high-quality medical  treatment, be in good health - not too old,

09:59 no major medical conditions - and your blood  pressure should be stable. And you don’t end up

10:03 with one of the several possible resultant  internal injuries from the gunshot… then

10:08 maybe survival would be on the cards for you. Think you'd survive a shot to the head? What

10:11 surprised you the most? Drop your thoughts below. No go check out What Happens When You Die?

10:13 or click on this video instead.
