00:00 [SQUEAKING]

00:02 [RUSTLING]

00:04 [CLICKING]

00:07

00:10 MICHAEL SCOTT ASATO CUTHBERT: Hello, computational

00:12 musicologist and music theorists.

00:14 While you're working on your own representation formats,

00:17 I want to introduce one representation format, indeed,

00:21 the most commonly used representation

00:24 format for common Western music notation scores.

00:27 And that is MusicXML created by Michael Good around the year

00:31 2000.

00:34 Looking over at the MusicXML website,

00:37 we can see their version of Hello World!

00:39 As you know, in programming traditions,

00:42 it's become traditional to print out

00:44 the word Hello, World to show how

00:48 a programming language works.

00:49 In music notation, it's become common, instead,

00:53 to show how note middle C would be represented,

00:58 whole note or something like that.

01:00 And here's the example of that middle C whole note in MusicXML

01:05 One of the things you can see in MusicXML,

01:08 just like any XML or HTML, we have

01:11 these things called tags which are enclosed in angle brackets.

01:15 Then we have a content for the tag,

01:18 and then the tag is closed with those same angle brackets

01:22 with a slash in front.

01:24 Tags can enclose other tags.

01:27 So the score part encloses a tag called part-name,

01:31 and then it's closed later.

01:33 And tags can also have attributes, id equals P1.

01:37 And we'll look at those in just a little bit.

01:41 Let's scroll down to the note.

01:43 So all of that is to set up what we might normally do for a note.

01:48 So a note is a tag called note.

01:51 Within it, there's a tag called pitch.

01:53 Within that, there's a tag called step.

01:56 And the step has a single letter.

01:59 This is very similar to music21.

02:02 In fact, I borrowed these concepts from here,

02:06 so that the accidental would be encoded elsewhere.

02:10 Then the octave is encoded as a single number,

02:13 then the pitch is closed.

02:15 After that, we have a duration tag.

02:18 And we'll get back to that in a second.

02:20 But it's duration 4.

02:22 And then there's something called

02:23 a type, which is different.

02:26 And it says whole, so it says that this note's type is

02:29 a whole note.

02:31 We have the duration and the type encoded separately,

02:36 because the type explains to notation software

02:40 how to represent this note, what it should look like.

02:44 And the duration, instead, tells it how long it is.

02:51 So you could, in theory, put a duration of any number

02:56 and a type of any number, and you

02:58 could make things that looked very

03:00 different from how they sounded or how they were represented.

03:03 In practice, most notation software

03:05 reads one or the other of these, so that's kind of too bad.

03:09 The duration 4 does not, like in music21 represent necessarily

03:14 four quarter notes.

03:16 What it does is it refers back to the last tag

03:20 within an attributes tag called divisions.

03:23 And this says how many parts should a quarter

03:28 note be divided up into.

03:30 So in this case, because the only note is a whole note,

03:34 we can just divide up the quarter note into one part,

03:37 not divide it at all, and then say

03:39 a whole note has four of these.

03:42 But if we were going to later have an eighth note,

03:46 then this would have to be at least 2,

03:48 because the quarter note can be divided into two parts.

03:51 If we might have 16th notes, it would need to be 4 because it

03:55 can be divided into four parts.

03:57 And if we were going to have 16th notes and triplets also,

04:02 then it would need to be 12 because you can divide it

04:06 into 12 different ways.

04:08 In practice, these divisions usually end up

04:12 being much higher numbers.

04:15 Some people use 16, 3, 8, 4, which is a power of 2.

04:19 I like using a high power of 2 multiplied by 3,

04:23 multiplied by 5, multiplied by 7,

04:25 so I can exactly represent triplets, quintuplets,

04:30 septuplets, things like that.

04:32 But you can change this division with each,

04:35 I think, at least each measure, so that you can make sure

04:38 that whatever you're going to be representing will be there.

04:42 We can also see that there's a key signature,

04:44 and that's marked in the number of fifths from C.

04:50 So remember your circle of fifths.

04:52 If you want a key signature of D major of two sharps,

04:56 that would be 2.

04:57 If you want B major, that should be 5.

05:01 If you want F major, well, we're going the other way,

05:04 so that's going to be negative 1, so we

05:06 can represent keys that way.

05:08 Time, you can probably figure out.

05:09 Beats and beat type are 4/4.

05:12 Could be called numerator and denominator.

05:14 But it is one of these things about MusicXML

05:18 that the format likes to show the musical meaning,

05:26 not just how it's going to be laid out.

05:28 We have the clef.

05:30 Instead of saying it's treble clef,

05:31 we say that it is a G clef on line 2.

05:36 And so here is some of the basics of MusicXML

05:41 You can go to musicxml.com and read more about this.

05:45 We're going to look at a few other components of MusicXML

05:49 before going on.

05:50 But you're not necessarily need to learn everything about it.

05:56 So if we're looking at how MusicXML works,

05:59 we're going to look at a slightly more complex example

06:02 than just a single quarter note.

06:04 We have a vocal part and then a piano part

06:08 represented on two staves.

06:11 Here, we're using a divisions that's

06:13 a higher number than 1, negative 3 for the key signature,

06:20 and then we can explicitly encode

06:22 that it's actually in minor So.

06:23 We're not in E-flat major.

06:24 We're in C minor, right?

06:26

06:29 There's transposition.

06:31 But we don't need to know that for this.

06:33 The pitch element, the note element, I'm sorry to say,

06:37 sorry, can also have ties on it and can have lyrics.

06:44 We can say that this is an end of a syllable that ends "meil."

06:48 And we end in extension.

06:50 This is another thing you can do in XML-based formats.

06:53 If you want to open a tag and immediately close it,

06:56 you can just put a slash at the end, instead.

06:58

07:01 We'll look at tied notes, even though it's just a little thing.

07:06 And that is that there are two different parts

07:10 in a tied note in MusicXML and for a number of things

07:14 in MusicXML.

07:15 There is the tie element which represents conceptually,

07:21 is this note tie.

07:22 And then there is the tied, with a D element.

07:26 And that says, how do we draw the tie on the page.

07:30 So you can draw a tie without having a note

07:33 that sounds tied or is conceived of as tied.

07:36 Or you can have sounds conceived of as tied but not drawn.

07:42 And this shows up in other places,

07:44 namely in accidentals because you can imagine a B-flat,

07:50 you conceive of it as a B-flat, but you also

07:53 put a flat sign in front of it.

07:54 The next B in that same measure, you conceive of it is B-flat,

07:59 but you don't put a flat sign in front of it.

08:01 So there's a distinction between how we represent a note on paper

08:07 and how we conceive of it.

08:09 And this is very important, also.

08:11 We can look over here at chords and see that a cord is simply--

08:17 here's a 3-note chord.

08:18 We start with a note.

08:19 It's a C in octave 4, And then we

08:24 have the next note has this empty chord

08:27 tag that says it's part of a chord of the previous note.

08:30 So in MusicXML, if you want to know

08:32 whether something is a chord, you

08:35 won't know it from the first node.

08:36 You'll only know it from the second note on.

08:38 Here's an example where we have E-flat

08:41 altered by negative 1 semitones, and then the next note G.

08:51 Here's a little example of multi-part music, and especially

08:56 this part where we have two different voices

09:01 in the same measure.

09:03 So we have two chords that can be represented as just

09:06 a single set of note elements.

09:10 And then we have a chord here and a chord here,

09:12 but in between, we have this separate voice

09:15 with separate stem directions and so on.

09:18 One of the things that MusicXML does,

09:21 is that when you get to a certain point,

09:23 you're reading through all of your durations.

09:25 They're all considered to be in a row.

09:27 You get to maybe the end of the measure,

09:29 and you can back up a certain number of divisions,

09:34 and then you can go forward again.

09:36 In this case, you would probably just back up 8.

09:40 But a lot of notation software seems

09:42 to only use backup to go to the beginning of the measure.

09:45 And then if you need to skip forward,

09:46 you use a forward again.

09:49 And it is also customary, though not strictly required,

09:53 I don't believe, but almost a lot of notation,

09:57 things that read MusicXML, we call them consumers of MusicXML.

10:01 A lot of them might have a problem

10:03 or might crash if you don't include what's customary, again,

10:07 then you end at the end of the measure

10:09 by going forward until the very end.

10:13 There's all kinds of other things on repeats,

10:16 on sound suggestions, and so on.

10:17 But one of the things you can see

10:19 is that, compared to some of the thoughts

10:21 we had on compact representations,

10:24 MusicXML is very verbose.

10:27 It takes up a lot of space on the screen.

10:30 It takes up a good amount of space on disk,

10:33 though not nearly as much as this video would ever take.

10:37 So there is a compressed format, and they call it MXL.

10:41 We call .XML or .musicxml, the file extension for standard

10:45 MusicXML format, and .MXL if it's just gzipped.

10:51 And right now, we're working on ways

10:53 so that a gzip archive can include the score, maybe

10:56 a compressed score, a transposed score, and also all

11:00 of the parts.

11:00 So new things are still coming out with MusicXML.

11:04 And we will turn to learning more about MusicXML

11:08 from the creator.

11:11

00:00 So, there they are, Aiden and Ellie, the only  survivors to have not succumbed to the apocalypse.

00:05 Still in their late teens, the two are  in their prime, at least when it comes to

00:09 making babies. The good news is they have the hots  for each other, but can they repopulate the Earth?

00:14 You all know that there’s a version of human  history that involves two folks getting it on

00:18 and kicking off mankind. Those two  star-struck lovers were Adam and Eve,

00:22 a couple that made the Garden of Eden their home.  We’re not exactly sure what kind of food they

00:26 had to sustain their lives in the garden, but  probably a bit more than the forbidden fruit.

00:31 As for Aiden and Ellie, there is  plenty of food on their lonely planet.

00:35 The old blue ball didn’t get whacked by an  asteroid or anything similarly cataclysmic.

00:39 It was forward-thinking artificial  intelligence that wiped everyone out,

00:42 but then it destroyed itself just before  it could finish off the last two humans.

00:46 The animals were still around. The AI was  programmed to ensure the sustainability of

00:50 the Earth at any cost, and then it figured out  that humans were going to destroy the planet,

00:54 so the only rational thing to do was to  destroy all humans. Yeah, whoever developed

00:58 that program sure upset a lot of folks. For the first couple of months,

01:02 Aiden and Ellie didn’t really think much  about starting mankind again. They spent

01:05 much of their time hanging out in rich people’s  houses and driving fast cars. Ellie almost drove

01:10 into a tree one day, and after that, the  couple decided not to take too many risks.

01:14 There was some serious business to take care of. Thankfully, they lived in Los Angeles, California,

01:19 which having a mild climate meant the couple  didn’t have anything to fear from a brutal

01:22 winter and the fact there was no electricity.  Let’s just say that while the apocalypse was a

01:28 bit of a downer, these two got very lucky  in terms of their chances of survival.

01:31 They also had the added bonus of not  being related. That’s a good thing

01:35 because studies have shown that when children  are born from folks who are related there’s a

01:39 higher rate of infant mortality. Even if the kids  survive, there’s a much higher chance that those

01:44 kids will be born with some kind of defect. Nonetheless, Ellie and Aiden’s offspring might

01:48 be born healthy, but what about the offspring’s  offspring? Now we run into difficulties.

01:53 In a study undertaken in Czechoslovakia  between the years 1933 and 1970,

01:58 scientists looked at the children of parents  who were first-degree relatives. First-degree

02:03 is someone in your direct family. Procreating with  these people isn’t generally a cool thing to do.

02:08 Even if first cousins get it on, the offspring  has double the chance of having a birth defect.

02:12 In that study, the kids who were born  to first-degree parents didn’t have

02:16 great outcomes. 40 percent of them had  very severe disabilities. 14 percent

02:20 of them died because of their disabilities. We have a very good real-life example of this,

02:25 featuring a man you might think was trying  to increase the population of his country.

02:29 That man was King Chulalongkorn of  Thailand, who ruled from 1868 to 1910.

02:35 This guy did a lot of good things  in terms of modernizing his country,

02:38 and he was also a formidable  baby-maker, just as his father had been.

02:42 That father was King Mongkut,  who had 82 children in total.

02:46 One of them was Chulalongkorn.  Following in his daddy’s footsteps,

02:50 Chulalongkorn had a lot of wives, consorts,  and concubines, adding up to 116 women in

02:55 total. To keep the bloodline pure, several of  his partners with whom he had children were

02:59 actually his half-sisters. Back in those days,  it still wasn’t clear how bad inbreeding was.

03:04 But the proof soon became evident  in the pudding, so to speak.

03:07 He had a kid with a half-sister named Daksinajar  Naradhirajbutri. It died just hours after it was

03:13 born. He had eight kids with half-sister Savang  Vadhana. One of them lived for just three days and

03:19 most of them didn’t make it to adulthood. Vadhana  herself lived until the ripe old age of 93.

03:24 She was the product of inbreeding. In fact, if you research what happened

03:28 to his 77 children, you see that many, and we  are talking many, didn’t live very long at all.

03:33 A lot of them died when they were barely  out of their fancy infant clothes.

03:36 Many others died in their twenties and thirties.

03:39 European royalty was also into keeping things in  the family to ensure the bloodline was pure and

03:44 also to make certain money and property stayed  with the family after someone passed away.

03:48 European inbreeding in royal families was very  evident in the Spanish Habsburg dynasty. Offspring

03:53 were often weak and sickly, and there was also  the now-famous deformity called the Hapsburg jaw.

03:58 The internet might have been down in Aiden and  Ellie’s brave new world, but they did have access

04:02 to books and libraries, and being the prudent  folks they were, they read up on inbreeding.

04:06 After going through a few books on the matter,  they were rightfully afraid their kids’ kids

04:10 would bite the dust just as soon as they let out  that first primal scream or perhaps spend their

04:15 short lives hobbling around while carrying  a jaw that would put Desperate Dan to shame.

04:19 The couple also read about the Colt family in  Australia and the marriage between June and Jim.

04:24 In short, June was the child of a brother and  sister. She married Jim Colt. They were in New

04:29 Zealand at the time. They had seven kids of  their own and moved to Australia. More kids

04:33 were born once those kids were old enough to  have children, but the Colts didn’t stray much

04:37 farther than their own home, if you get what  we mean. The children were born through incest.

04:42 A lot of the kids had defects, and some seemed  a little mentally deranged and did things like

04:46 hurt animals. Many were very sickly and prone to  disease. Incest wasn’t working out very well for

04:52 the family. When an investigator found them,  he said it was “like nothing I've ever seen.”

04:56 This story sent shivers down Aiden and Ellie’s  spines, with both of them just sitting for a

05:00 while in the library thinking about a team  of kids running around with fungal feet

05:04 trying to set cows on fire. But did it have to be that

05:07 way? That’s the big question today. Some, not many, of King Chulalongkorn’s

05:11 children that he had with his sisters went on to  have fairly normal lives, although admittedly it’s

05:16 hard to find kids who lived past the age of 40. Aiden and Ellie were now certain that a small

05:20 gene pool was going to lead to a future  offspring of physically and mentally

05:24 ill kids once their own children started  procreating. But what choice did they have?

05:29 They had one kid, a boy, and named him Carl.  Then they had another kid and they named him

05:34 Asher. Damn, they thought, two boys. Then Carl  accidentally killed Asher when they were fighting

05:39 over toys, after which Ellie and Aiden had a  third child and named him Sebastian. Another boy!

05:44 With not much to do, these two last adult  humans just kept pumping out kid after kid,

05:48 as many in fact as was possible given Ellie’s  natural aging process. The kids for the most

05:53 part grew up fine, but the kids’ kids  were a different matter altogether.

05:57 Let’s us explain something now, before we get  to the strange case of the extended family.

06:01 You’ve heard of that thing called DNA. Well, it  has packaged into it 23 pairs of chromosomes.

06:07 Within every chromosome, there are hundreds  of thousands of genes. It’s these things

06:11 that will determine human characteristics,  such as hair color, but some of them are

06:14 also bad to the bone, sometimes literally. Every gene has a couple of copies and they

06:19 are called alleles. When two people have a  child, they pass on one pair to the child.

06:24 There are dominant and recessive genes,  too. If one pair of genes is dominant,

06:28 you will have the trait of that  gene when it’s passed on to you.

06:31 With recessive genes, it is different, because  you need both pairs of genes to gain the trait.

06:36 For example, the gene for brown eyes is dominant,  so if you get that you will have brown eyes.

06:41 But for blues eyes, it is different, because that  gene is recessive. You’d need both recessive genes

06:46 to get blue eyes. In this case, both your  parents passed on blue-eyed pairs of genes,

06:51 but if one of your parents had the  brown-eyed gene, you’d get brown eyes.

06:54 Importantly, though, as you know, not all  children get the same DNA from their parents

06:59 unless they are twins. You get 50 percent of  your DNA from both parents, making 100 percent.

07:05 Now, imagine that DNA, say, from your mom was  half a pack of cards. When the next child is born,

07:10 the pack is shuffled, so that the next child  doesn’t get the same DNA with all the same genes.

07:14 But, if there were lots of children and  you kept shuffling the pack, at some point

07:18 some sets of genes will look similar to  another child’s. This is important to know

07:22 as we go along with the Ellie and Aiden story. The good news is that many defective traits

07:27 are carried in recessive genes. This is  great, because they aren’t very common,

07:31 and to get that harmful trait, you’ll have  to get a pair of them. This is exactly why

07:34 it is good to play the field with strangers. Ok, that’s a joke, but if your parents are related

07:38 there is a more chance they carry some defective  gene, and in that case, the child might get a pair

07:44 and one thing leads to another and a child is  born with a chin that looks like an old boot.

07:48 If there are generations all from the same gene  pool, at some point even with all the shuffling,

07:52 some bad genes might match up. The Hapsburg, Charles II of Spain,

07:56 was the man famous for his chin. It took  generations of inbreeding to make him like that.

08:01 In fact, he was born with scores of defects  and disabilities which made his life hell.

08:06 After many years of suffering, he died aged 38.  Just to give you an idea of what can go wrong,

08:11 here’s what his autopsy report said: “Heart was the size of a peppercorn;

08:14 his lungs corroded; his intestines rotten  and gangrenous; he had a single testicle,

08:19 black as coal, and his head was full of water.” When Ellie read that she fainted on the spot just

08:24 thinking about future generations of her family.  The first thing that came to mind was a grandkid

08:28 of hers looking like a character from a movie  she’d watched as a kid called “The Toxic Avenger.”

08:33 But then one day she was reading another book,  and something improved her grim mood. She read

08:38 the lines, “The evidence for the short-term  effects of low genetic diversity is very strong,

08:42 but all these things are probabilistic. There  are stories of incredible journeys back from

08:47 the brink - anything is possible.” You can get very lucky playing cards.

08:51 Ellie tried to translate that in laymen’s terms  and came to the conclusion that if she and Aiden

08:55 knocked out enough kids and those kids knocked  out enough kids then despite the fact there

09:00 will be lots of challenges (cow burning even)  some of the kids could possibly flourish and

09:04 the future of mankind could be in the bag. Ellie’s hair eventually turned a shade of

09:08 gray and at that time her beloved husband was a  formidable farmer. Things didn’t seem too bad,

09:13 but some of her grandkids had lives  that were, as one of her favorite

09:17 writers would have put it, “nasty and short”. She and Aiden had 10 sons, 18 daughters, in total.

09:23 They in turn had kids with each other,  because that’s just how things had to be.

09:26 Evolution actually wants us to be attracted to  people who are genetically different from us,

09:30 but the future of mankind demanded  they make do with each other.

09:33 Ellie was still worried, having read that there is  more chance of defects the more inbreeding takes

09:38 place, such as what happened to the Hapsburgs. If  only Ellie knew what genes all her grandkids had,

09:43 she could safely match them so children weren’t  born unhealthy, but that wasn’t possible.

09:48 She had a reason for some optimism though  when she read about the people of the

09:51 small island called Pingelap, who lived far  from the busy world in the western Pacific.

09:56 These people were almost wiped out in the  18th century when a typhoon struck the island,

10:01 but 20 of them survived. They flourished  after, even though a recessive gene

10:05 ensured that many years later a tenth of the  island was afflicted with color-blindness.

10:09 The thing was, this disorder, called complete  achromatopsia, was thought to have come

10:14 from one man. But it didn’t show up in the  population until the fourth generation. But still,

10:18 not everyone got it. This made Ellie happy. She sat there with the book in her hand and

10:23 with one of her granddaughters crying from a crib  nearby, she repeated those words in her mind,

10:27 “Anything is possible, anything is possible.” We are going to bounce back, she said under her

10:32 breath in a determined voice, even though  out of the corner of her eye she glimpsed

10:35 one of her less successful by-products giggling  while throwing an aerosol can into a small fire.

10:40 There was a long way to go yet, and what’s  called the “Founder effect” was in full

10:44 swing – meaning a profound lack of genetic  diversity as generations interbreed. Still,

10:49 while Ellie’s family admittedly all looked  very similar, she held out hope that in

10:53 generations to come there would be natural  mutations and some diversity would occur.

10:58 Since Aiden in those days seemed only  interested in tending to his vegetables

11:01 and cattle – he’d become so distant –  Ellie read more and more. In some ways,

11:05 they were a perfect couple, with she being the  academic one and he being so good with his hands.

11:10 One day Ellie told Aiden that there were instances  in history in which animals likely created entire

11:15 populations after starting as pairs. They were  eating when she looked at him and shouted “rats!”.

11:20 “What?” replied Aiden, feeling confused. She told  him a single pair of rats started a population

11:25 on some island and the rats thrived. He  then gave her a familiar look and said,

11:29 “Don’t tell me you read that on one of those  printouts from that old website, Quora.”

11:33 Ellie went quiet and returned to her  room, where she read the printout again.

11:36 It said, “Starlings in North America  originated from just 60 individuals;

11:41 there are a couple hundred million of them now,  most of which are nearly genetically identical.”

11:45 That seemed like good news, but she understood  that a “small population” was different

11:49 from the last two. She couldn’t find any examples  in her books when an animal species had gone down

11:54 to the last pair and then started up again. Ellie died first. She was 93. Aiden, 92,

12:00 held her hand as she drifted into the great  unknown. At her side were all her kids,

12:04 grandkids, and great-grandkids. One of them,  known as “Chinny” to the rest, made her moan

12:09 in distress just before passing away. The poor  kid had just put some broken glass in his mouth.

12:13 But she remembered some words written by a  scientist back in 2015. “If the whole world were

12:18 founded by two people, you would have to get lucky  in the genetic lottery many times.” Ellie and

12:22 Aiden might have been lucky, but as Ellie took her  dying breath she just couldn’t know. Surrounded

12:27 by all those faces, things didn’t look too bad. Nonetheless, she knew things could take a turn

12:32 for the worst, and she also knew that a  long time ago some researchers had said

12:35 you’d probably need 98 unrelated humans  to repopulate a planet, but there she was,

12:40 looking at people who had come from her and Aiden. So, could it happen, really, the repopulation of

12:45 the planet from these two? The answer is yes,  it could, maybe, but as those scientists said,

12:51 there would have to be a lot of luck. Perhaps if it did happen, thousands of years

12:55 later no one would believe the story of Ellie and  Aiden, the avid reader and the cabbage patch kid.

13:00 The reality is, scientists aren’t  sure how we evolved at the beginning,

13:03 but they certainly don’t think it all kicked  off with two randy people in the Garden of Eden.

13:07 They know there were different types of humans  (the homo genus) hanging about in Africa around

13:12 a couple of million years ago, such as Homo  habilis (handyman), Homo erectus (upright man),

13:18 and then it took quite a while for the  presence of Homo sapiens, uptight man.

13:22 Just kidding. It can be translated as wise man. Before homo sapiens, the oldest form of humans

13:27 mated with newer kinds of humans, such  as homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthals).

13:32 Neanderthals and modern humans also mated.  So, in short, it wasn’t as if there was only

13:36 a very small gene pool when things started. With that in mind, we can’t look at the case

13:41 of Ellie and Aiden and compare it with something  from the past. We can only hypothesize that if two

13:45 people were left alone on the planet they might  be able to fill it up again. It’s a long shot,

13:50 but Ellie and Aiden at least tried. After that, you really should watch

13:53 “Why It Would Suck To Live Through The End  Of The Universe.” Or, have a look at...

00:02 PROFESSOR: Trees are about the most basic data structure

00:05 that you're ever going to come across.

00:07 They pervade computer science and other subjects.

00:09 So let's talk about them.

00:11 And the simplest definition of a tree

00:13 is that a tree is a connected graph with no cycles.

00:16 In this setting we're talking about simple graphs, and trees

00:20 with undirected edges.

00:22 Well, in order to make sense of that,

00:24 we better have a definition of a cycle.

00:26 There's a picture of a typical tree,

00:28 but to be precise, what's a cycle in a simple graph?

00:32 Well, it's a closed walk of length greater than 2

00:35 that doesn't cross itself.

00:37 So the not crossing itself is the standard definition

00:40 of a cycle that we were using in a directed graph.

00:43 It simply means that it's a path, except that the beginning

00:47 and end vertex are the same.

00:48 So it looks like you start someplace at v,

00:52 and then you go around to a and to w,

00:54 and it's all distinct vertices as you go around in this path.

00:58 Except that the path ends where it

01:00 starts at v, which is what keeps it from being a path

01:02 and makes it a cycle.

01:04 Now, the length greater than 2 is

01:05 what is the difference between the definition of cycle

01:08 [? between ?] simple graphs and directed graphs.

01:12 And in a directed graph, it's perfectly possible

01:14 to have a self-loop of length, 1,

01:17 that is an interesting and important kind of cycle

01:19 to have.

01:19 But we forbid them in simple graphs,

01:22 because there's no way to avoid having a cycle of length 2,

01:26 because you always have the ability

01:28 to go back and forth across an edge-- that's not interesting.

01:31 And so we don't consider that to be a cycle.

01:34 A cycle, then, has to be of length greater than 2.

01:37 It also rules out the cycle of length 0,

01:40 which you get by taking a vertex all by itself.

01:43 OK, with that technical definition,

01:45 we now know what a cycle is in the simple graph,

01:47 and we understand the definition of tree.

01:50 Here are some more pictures of trees--

01:52 simple graphs with no cycles.

01:55 Now, they really come up all the time.

01:58 And why is that?

01:58 Well, there are family trees, which

02:00 you may be familiar with-- where you're

02:02 drawing a picture of the descendants of a given person,

02:06 and they keep branching out in a tree structure,

02:09 as traditionally displayed.

02:13 There are search trees, which come up all the time

02:15 in computer science, where you branch on the answer

02:18 to some question, which tells you which way to search next.

02:21 There are game trees, which we've already

02:22 discussed in this class, which are used

02:24 to define games and strategies.

02:26 There are parse trees, that come up in compiler technology,

02:31 and in language theory.

02:33 And there are spanning trees, which we're going

02:35 to be talking about some today.

02:38 Now, in addition to these places where trees come up,

02:42 there are a lot of different kinds of trees.

02:44 There's rooted trees, where there's some designated

02:46 vertex called the root, and you think

02:48 of getting to all the other vertices from the root.

02:54 There are ordered trees, where when you're at a given vertex,

02:57 there's a distinct order in which the exit

03:04 edges from a vertex-- there's a first one, and a second one,

03:07 and a third one, or a left one, and a next, left, most, and so

03:10 on, so that there is an order in which you

03:12 can choose to leave the vertex.

03:15 There are a binary trees, in which

03:17 each vertex has two ways out exactly-- or no ways out

03:22 if it's a so-called leaf.

03:24 And then there are a complete trees, whose definition

03:28 is not important to us, because we're not

03:30 going to consider any of these.

03:31 There's also, by the way, directed trees in which edges

03:35 have a direction, as in a [? di-graph ?] tree.

03:38 But we're not considering any of these.

03:40 We're going to focus on so-called pure trees, which

03:43 are unordered, unrooted, undirected,

03:46 and that's what we're talking about.

03:48 So let's examine some more properties

03:50 of trees and equivalent definitions of trees.

03:52 It will be important for theoretical reasons

03:55 and convenience to know lots of different characterizations

03:58 of trees.

03:58 So we're starting off with a definition which says,

04:01 it's a connected simple graph with no cycles,

04:05 but there's other ways to characterize it.

04:08 So an edge in a simple graph is called a cut edge,

04:11 if, when you remove it from the graph,

04:15 two vertices that used to be connected--

04:17 that is used to have a path between them--

04:19 cease to have a path between them.

04:21 So here's a simple graph illustration.

04:24 And that edge, e, is a cut edge, because if I delete it, then

04:29 there are now two components.

04:31 There used to be two vertices-- actually any

04:34 of the vertices here used to be connected

04:36 to any of the vertices there via that edge.

04:38 But once I've deleted that edge, all of those

04:41 vertices here and there that used to be connected no longer

04:44 are.

04:44 So that makes e a cut edge.

04:47 f is not a cut edge.

04:48 Because even if I delete f, there

04:51 is, in fact, still a path from every vertex

04:54 to every other vertex here, so that f is not

04:56 disconnecting anything.

04:57

05:00 And as I say, it's still connected after you delete it.

05:03 So now we get a simple way to characterize trees

05:06 in terms of cut edges-- because an edge is not a cut edge if

05:11 and only if it's on a cycle.

05:12 If you think about that, if it's on a cycle,

05:15 and you cut an edge out of a cycle,

05:18 then everything on the cycle is still

05:19 connected by going the other way around the cycle that

05:22 doesn't use that edge.

05:24 And if it's not on a cycle, then, in fact,

05:27 you can think through that deleting it

05:29 means that there's not going to be two paths between two

05:35 things at its endpoints.

05:37 And so it will separate them.

05:41 OK, so another way, then, to define

05:44 a tree is to say a tree is a connected graph where

05:47 every edge is a cut edge-- that is

05:50 as soon as you cut any edge out of a tree

05:52 it stops being connected.

05:55 That yields another way to say that something

05:58 is a tree-- a tree is a simple graph that is connected

06:02 and is edge-minimal, which, again,

06:04 means that if you remove any edge,

06:07 it stops having that property of being connected.

06:10 So its an edge-minimal connected graph.

06:12 That's kind of the reason why trees are so important,

06:14 because if you're trying to figure out a way

06:17 to get a whole bunch of things-- a whole bunch of vertices--

06:19 connected, a tree is going to have

06:22 the minimum number of edges that are sufficient to get them all

06:25 connected.

06:26 If you think about different nodes in a network that

06:30 need to communicate with each other,

06:32 and you want to know how many direct connections that there

06:34 have to be between these communication

06:37 centers in order for everybody to talk to everybody else,

06:40 the answer is-- it's got to be a tree on n vertices.

06:44 And a tree on n vertices is going

06:45 to have exactly n minus 1 edges.

06:48 So that gives you still another equivalent definition

06:51 of a tree.

06:52 A tree is a connected graph that has n vertices,

06:55 and n minus 1 edges.

06:57

06:59 A kind of dual way to think about it

07:01 is that a tree is an acyclic graph that

07:08 has as many edges as it possibly could

07:10 without having any cycles.

07:12 So typically, an acyclic graph might not be connected,

07:16 but as long as it's not connected,

07:17 you can keep adding edges that will connect things up

07:20 without creating cycles.

07:22 But the minute you get a tree, so

07:24 that everything is connected, you can't add another edge.

07:27 So an edge maximal acyclic graph is still another way

07:31 to characterize trees.

07:33 And maybe the most useful way is to say

07:36 that a graph, in which there is a unique path between any two

07:40 vertices, is a tree.

07:43 So of course, if there is a unique path-- in particular,

07:45 there's a path, so all the vertices have to be connected.

07:48 But what makes it a tree is that there aren't two different ways

07:51 to connect between two vertices, because as soon as there

07:54 were there would be a cycle.

07:56 And those are some of the basic ways that trees

08:00 can be formulated equivalently.

08:03 And in fact, there's lots more, but this is enough for today.

00:00 "You kids and your TikToks! When I was your age,

00:03 we were working in the mines!" Grandpa grumbles  between mouthfuls of mashed potatoes. "Okay,

00:09 boomer!" your 12-year-old cousin fires back,  eyes glued to his iPhone. "Skibidi toilet!"

00:14 And there you are, frantically scrolling  through job listings, trying to find

00:17 a side hustle to cover… well, living. But how did we get here? Why does it feel

00:23 like the generations are at war? It wasn’t  always like this. Sure, back in the 1800s,

00:27 they probably complained about how those darn  '1812-ers' were ruining the Revolutionary War

00:32 generation’s hard-fought legacy. But this  idea of labeling people by generations and

00:37 turning it into a culture clash? That’s  actually a 20th-century invention.

00:42 Generations used to be simple family  labels—until someone decided, "Hey,

00:46 let's study this… and fight about it!" And  now we have seven distinct generations,

00:51 each thinking they’re doing things right.  But why does it feel like a battleground for

00:55 who’s really to blame for the world’s problems? That’s exactly what we’re breaking down in this

01:00 episode of The Infographics Show- Every  Generation Explained. Find out exactly where

01:05 YOU fit in this generational showdown. The Greatest Generation - 1901 to 1927

01:11 This Generation was born at the start  of a new century filled with promise,

01:15 progress and excitement - but naturally, history  had different plans. The early years of this

01:20 generation would be filled with massive upheaval,  with many seeing World War I unfold and being

01:25 haunted by the specter of the Spanish Flu. But  amid this, they saw many leaps in culture - as

01:30 the roaring twenties took off and brought Jazz and  Swing music into the mainstream. But with every

01:35 up comes a down - and the Great Depression hit as  many of them were approaching adulthood, plunging

01:40 the entire world into economic uncertainty.  And then the rumblings of war started…

01:45 And that’s how this generation earned their name.

01:48 Most of this generation were of fighting  age when World War II broke out,

01:52 and they became associated with  the most iconic military triumph

01:55 the United States had ever seen. Although  there were many losses, they returned home

02:00 to celebrations and went on to great success  in business, culture - and of course,

02:10 you’re lucky enough to know one, ask them to  tell you a crazy story about the good old days.

02:14 With a legacy this large, it’s no surprise that  the next generation was sort of overshadowed.

02:20 Silent Generation - 1928 to 1945

02:24 The Silent Generation was also shaped by  these world events - but not in the same way,

02:28 as they grew up in a world in flux. The depression  shaped their childhood, leading to many growing

02:34 up in unsettled circumstances, and the war caused  wartime rationing. Many saw parents die in combat,

02:40 and grew up in a deeply patriotic  environment. Speaking out against

02:44 the government was frowned upon, and a strong  sense of collectivism was encouraged. And that’s

02:49 how this generation got its name - because  as soon as one war ended, another began.

02:54 This was the first generation  largely defined by the Cold War.

02:58 The threat of Communism was already alive and  well in America before this generation was born,

03:03 but once the Soviet Union got nukes, it was all  hands on deck. The name comes from the fact that

03:08 most of them were silent during the McCarthy  era, keeping their heads down and maintaining

03:12 a strong work ethic that had been instilled in  them in childhood. The term “Baby Boomers” comes

03:41 from the baby boom of the late 1940s and 1950s,  as all the World War II veterans returned home,

03:48 and the economy recovered from the depression and  wartime footing. The result? A higher standard of

03:53 living for Americans, a fast advance in commerce  and technology, and a whole lot of woo-hoo! And

03:59 soon, the babies started coming, resulting in a  massive generation of over 76 million Americans

04:05 alone - making them the largest generation. And  they grew up in a world that saw progress come

04:10 fast - this was the age of the Space Race,  of the Civil Rights Movement, of Woodstock,

04:15 and of the changes that led to what most  people view as a “typical American Childhood”.

04:20 But it was also an age of uncertainty and terror.

04:23 If the words “Duck and Cover” cause you to dive  under the nearest table, you might just be a Baby

04:28 Boomer! This was the era when nuclear annihilation  was the clearest and most present threat, as

04:33 events like the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the  world to the brink. Thus, Baby Boomers were raised

04:38 to be cautious and deeply patriotic. But this was  also the era of the Vietnam draft and the massive

04:43 anti-war movement that followed - something that  continues in how they impact politics to this

04:48 day. They’ve had four Presidents - Clinton, Bush  Jr., Obama, and Trump. They have a reputation for

04:55 leaning conservative, and their easier road  in the economy and employment rankles the

04:59 younger generations, but they’re as ideologically  diverse as the other generations - and as they

05:05 reach retirement age by the millions each year,  they show no signs of their influence waning.

05:10 With the Boomers casting such a long shadow,

05:12 is it any surprise that the next  generation is a little more…zen?

05:17 Generation X - 1965 to 1980

05:20 Known as the slacker generation by many of the  older generations, Generation X largely escaped

05:26 one major trial by fire - a major war that swept  them up. While the Baby Boomers largely fought in

05:32 Vietnam, this generation saw the latter days of  the Cold Wars as tension started to slowly ease.

05:38 The most significant war of this period, the  Gulf War, was a limited conflict that didn’t

05:42 involve a draft. And that led them to become  far more involved in domestic affairs - and far

05:47 more willing to question the powers that be. This  was the era where LGBT rights became a key issue,

05:53 and when the AIDS epidemic swept the  world. And while the world might not

05:56 have been in as much danger of immediate  annihilation, change was going to come fast.

06:01 And much of that cultural  shift would be on…the TV?

06:04 Today, Generation X is most associated not with  what they did - but with what they watched and

06:10 listened to. This is the era that MTV came on the  air, and the beginnings of the grunge movement

06:15 stepped onto the stage. It also saw a disturbing  rise in kidnappings and the rise of the Satanic

06:20 Panic, as fears shifted to the homefront and  parents became more protective of their kids -

06:25 spelling an end to the age of free-range childhood  and the beginning of helicopter parenting. Much

06:31 like the Silent Generation, this generation  is often seen as overshadowed by the ones

06:36 sandwiching it - and it has never had a President  even as its older members approach sixty.

06:41 Now it’s time to shift to the  kids - wait, they’re how old now?

06:45 Millennials - 1981 to 1996

06:49 Coming of age as the Cold War breathed its  last and a new era began, the Millennials

06:53 are associated with one thing more  than any other - technology. This

06:57 generation experienced a lot of whiplash  in their early years - growing up in the

07:01 era of Toys ‘R Us and wall phones as kids,  seeing the internet born as they grew up,

07:07 and entering a new digital landscape as they  hit high school or college. For the millennials,

07:12 especially those who saw the calendar roll  over to 2000 as they approached adulthood,

07:16 the world seemed full of promise and  excitement. Surely it was all uphill from here!

07:21 But just like the Greatest Generation, History  had its way of throwing a spanner in the works.

07:26 As soon as the new millenium rolled over,  chaos seemed to ensue. A near-tied Presidential

07:31 election with a controversial resolution led many  millennials to become disaffected with politics.

07:36 The 9/11 attacks in New York and Washington kicked  off a global war on terror - and while there was

07:42 no draft like in previous generations, it cast  a pall over young adulthood for many. Then, the

07:48 2008 financial crisis upended many millennials'  career plans. This has set them back in many ways,

07:54 with many living at home with their parents  long after previous generations and struggling

07:59 to find long-term employment. This has also  led this generation to become highly liberal,

08:04 with many of the generations young politicians  being iconoclasts like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

08:10 But while millennials are still often used as  shorthand for “Young people”, here’s a scary

08:14 statistic. The older millennials are now over 40 -  which means some of them are already grandparents.

08:20 Which means it’s time for someone  else to say “Okay, Millennial”.

08:24 Generation Z - 1997 to 2010

08:27 If the Millennials got a crash  course in technology as they grew up,

08:30 Gen Z are digital natives, with almost all  of them growing up with the internet being

08:34 a part of everyday life. They likely got cell  phones at a relatively young age, and those

08:39 quickly changed to smartphones - essentially  giving them a computer in their pocket at all

08:43 times. When the boomers talk about “Kids these  days will never understand - “ they mean this

08:48 generation - the majority of Gen Z has likely  never worked on a typewriter, used white-out,

08:54 or scanned a newspaper for movie listings. To  which they would answer…why would we need to?

09:00 But if you think that means they’re  checked out of reality…think again.

09:03 One thing that’s been clear about this  generation as they get older is that they

09:07 are highly engaged in politics and social  issues, with the internet being key in

09:11 increasing their awareness. They’ve played  a key role in the anti-war, gun control,

09:15 and anti-climate change movements - but often  prefer confrontational protest movements

09:20 to voting and organizing in the traditional  way. This has caused no shortage of headaches

09:25 for older generations, but progress  usually only goes one way, and it’s

09:29 still uncertain how they’re going to impact  politics around the world as they get older.

09:34 Which raises the question - what is  the next generation going to look like?

09:39 Gen Alpha - 2011 to ?

09:42 How do you judge a generation  that’s just barely started? Well,

09:46 if you ask most older people, they have no  problem! Much like Gen Z were digital natives,

09:51 Gen Alpha are smartphone natives - which means  they’ve never known a world without the constant

09:55 stream of information at their fingertips. This  has led to worries from teachers about them

10:00 having trouble with reading and attention span,  as they’re so used to getting their information

10:05 from short-form video like TikTok - and they’re  growing up just as AI becomes a massive concern.

10:12 But like with every generation,  there’s another side to that.

10:15 Even more so than Gen Z, Gen Alpha is highly  engaged in activism and passionate about justice.

10:21 They’re also the most tech-savvy generation ever,  not just playing it but creating it. More than

10:26 half of American kids under sixteen are members  of Roblox, a site that allows them to code games.

10:32 But they’re growing up in a world that’s more  unsettled than it has been since the cold war,

00:11 CARLA: Hi, everyone.

00:12 Good morning.

00:13 My name is Carla.

00:14 I'm going to be talking about a very fundamental concept

00:16 in aerodynamics.

00:17 But before I start, have you all gone in planes before?

00:21 Yeah?

00:22 OK.

00:22 Have you wondered, how does the pilot land the plane?

00:27 A little?

00:28 All right.

00:29 I'm going to explain two concepts that

00:31 will help you understand how you actually land the plane.

00:33 And these concepts are the concepts of lift and angle

00:37 of attack.

00:39 So I want you to picture a plane going through the skies.

00:45 And in real life, the planes don't fly perfectly horizontal.

00:49 They actually fly at an angle.

00:51 And we're going to draw a little plane going at an angle.

00:55 And this angle between the horizontal and the plane--

00:58 it's going to be known as alpha, the angle of attack.

00:04

00:04 When Watson receives a question, the first step

00:07 is question analysis.

00:09 One of the things Watson tries to figure out in this step

00:13 is what the question is looking for.

00:16 This is defined as trying to find the Lexical Answer

00:19 Type, or LAT, of the question.

00:23 The LAT is the word or noun in the question

00:26 that specifies the type of answer.

00:29 You should be able to replace the LAT with the answer

00:32 to complete the sentence.

00:34 For example, for the question, "Mozart's last

00:38 and perhaps most powerful symphony

00:40 shares its name with this planet," the LAT in this case

00:44 is "this planet."

00:47 If we replace this with the answer "Jupiter,"

00:50 it makes sense.

00:51 Mozart's last and perhaps most powerful symphony shares

00:55 its name with Jupiter.

00:58 For the question, "Smaller than only Greenland,

01:01 it's the world's second largest island," the LAT is "it's."

01:05 If we replace the LAT with the answer "New Guinea,"

01:09 it makes sense.

01:10 "Smaller than only Greenland, New Guinea

01:13 is the world's second largest island."

01:15 Unfortunately, the LAT is not "island,"

01:18 which would be more descriptive, since the sentence with "New

01:21 Guinea" in place of "island" does not make sense.

01:25 We can see in these two examples that sometimes the LAT is very

01:28 specific, like "this planet," and sometimes it's very vague,

01:33 like "it's."

01:36 If we know the LAT, we know what to look for.

01:40 However, in an analysis of 20,000 questions,

01:44 2,500 distinct LATs were found, and 12% of the questions

01:49 did not even have an explicit LAT.

01:51 They had LATs like "it's."

01:54 Furthermore, even the most frequent 200 explicit LATs

01:58 cover less than 50% of the questions.

02:02 So to enhance the question analysis step,

02:05 Watson also performs relation detection

02:08 to find relationships among words and decomposition

02:12 to split the question into different clues.

02:17 The second step in Watson is hypothesis generation.

02:21 The goal of this step is to use the question analysis of step

02:25 one to produce candidate answers by searching the databases.

02:30 In this step several hundred candidate answers

02:33 are generated.

02:35 For the question, "Mozart's last and perhaps most powerful

02:38 symphony shares its name with this planet,"

02:41 candidate answers could be Mercury, Earth, and Jupiter.

02:46 These are generated using various search techniques.

02:51 Then each candidate answer plugged back

02:54 into the question in place of the LAT

02:56 is considered a hypothesis.

02:59 For the question about Mozart's symphony,

03:02 hypothesis one would be the question

03:04 with "Mercury" in place of "this planet."

03:07 Hypothesis two would have "Jupiter"

03:09 in place of "this planet."

03:11 And hypothesis three would have "Earth"

03:13 in place of "this planet."

03:18 If the correct answer is not generated at this stage,

03:21 Watson has no hope of getting the question right.

03:25 Therefore, this step errors on the side

03:27 of generating a lot of hypotheses

03:30 and leaves it up to the next step

03:32 to find the correct answer.

03:34 In the next video, we'll discuss how steps three and four

03:38 score and rank the hypotheses.
