00:00 Last year, the amount of money spent on lobbying  hit a record $5.24 billion at the federal level

00:06 alone. And well, I don't know if you realized, but  there weren't even any major federal elections in

00:12 2025. When you factor in the upcoming midterms,  state and local level lobbying in addition to all

00:18 of the money spent outside of officially disclosed  channels, the volume of cash that is uh enabling

00:24 the lawmaking process is going to eclipse 11  figures within America alone this year. And by

00:30 all accounts, it's going to be a great investment.  A Cambridge University report found that out of

00:35 1,779 policy issues passed during their study,  the preferences of economic elites and special

00:42 business interests had a significant influence on  policy outcomes, which wasn't really the shocking

00:46 part. The shocking part was that the preferences  of average citizens had effectively no measurable

00:52 influence, even in large groups that were  extremely politically active. Oh, and this study

00:57 was done in 2014 when total political spending  was less than a quarter of what it is today.

01:03 Part of the reason why that spending has become so  ludicrous is not because the money is being used

01:08 to circumvent the will of the people. That battle  was won long ago. It's instead becoming a spending

01:13 battle between other lobbyists to see whose  special interest takes precedence over the lesser

01:18 donors. Now, I know the problem of political  lobbying is not exactly a surprise to anybody

01:23 anymore. Even here on this channel, whenever we  cover broken business models, from private equity,

01:28 private credit, corporate farming subsidies,  the gambling epidemic, data center subsidies,

01:32 corporate consolidation, healthcare, the  housing market, how you fund a retirement,

01:36 and all the way down to something as mundane as  how we collect economic data. Political lobbying

01:41 is at least part of the reason why things have  become so clearly messed up. But I promise you,

01:47 however bad you think it's gotten, it's worse.  We tend to think that money in politics begins

01:53 and ends with how much our elected officials  can pump into silly campaign ads and how many

01:56 lobbyists and industry group can pay to stock  the halls of the capital. But even if we were to

02:01 somehow reform this in its entirety tomorrow, we  only need to look to other countries to see it's

02:06 probably not going to fix all of our problems. Oh,  and of course, this is all assuming that everybody

02:13 was actually playing by those rules in the first  place. But when it comes to money and politics,

02:18 which groups give the most? In 2025, Open AAI and  Anthropic, valued at 830 billion and $380 billion,

02:27 respectively, escalated their federal lobbying  efforts. Hospitals, insurers, doctors, unions,

02:33 and pharmaceutical companies spent a record  $19 million lobbying Beacon Hill lawmakers

02:38 last year. National Association of Realtors at 54  million. The business roundt at 27. The American

02:44 political system is broken. It is corrupt.  It is significantly owned by the billionaire

02:52 class. Okay, so there's a lot of money going  into American politics. I know that alone isn't

02:59 surprising, but the headline spending numbers  adding up to a mere 10 billion in change are

03:04 really just the basic prices. The actual bill  is a lot bigger, and most of it never shows up

03:09 on the receipt of public disclosure. To see  this, we should start with the most obvious

03:13 sources of money in finance and then work  our way down to the most discreet. So yeah,

03:18 kicking off with direct campaign contributions.  Most people think that money in politics is only

03:24 writing big checks to politicians so they can fund  their increasingly expensive political campaigns.

03:29 Now elections have absolutely become more  expensive. Advertising directed by staffers is

03:34 almost unavoidable at this point, and presidential  candidates in particular are increasingly flying

03:39 private and running huge teams to manage longer  and more grandiose campaigns. But despite what

03:45 it may look like, there are actually pretty strict  limits on how much any individual person can give

03:50 to these candidates. Currently, the Federal  Election Commission cap on contributions to

03:54 any federal level elected official, including  the president, is $3,500 per election. So,

04:00 the primary and the general election, meaning  the absolute most a single person can give to

04:04 a candidate in one election cycle is $7,000.  The rules on this are strict and they are

04:10 actually enforced. Additionally, individual  contributors have to be real natural people. So,

04:16 if you are thinking you could just route your  contributions through a thousand shell companies,

04:20 congratulations. You are starting to think like a  political lobbyist. But in this particular case,

04:25 that is not allowed. Now, $7,000 from an  individual is a lot of money for most people,

04:31 but in the grand scheme of most election  campaigns, it is really just a drop in

04:35 the bucket and is unlikely to be enough on its  own to sway any policy at this level. You may

04:40 occasionally hear the phrase, "I can't believe how  little Congress people will sell themselves out

04:44 for when news breaks that a couple paid $10,000  to a campaign and it looks like they got tailored

04:50 legislative treatment." In reality, that is  normally just what is being disclosed through

04:54 official campaign contributions. And there is  normally a lot more money involved behind the

04:58 scenes. Direct contributions to a single campaign  are just the most obvious, most regulated, most

05:04 reported, and arguably least problematic way that  money gets into politics. Most people can outright

05:10 $3,500 checks every election cycle. But enough  people do make contributions that it is very

05:16 difficult for any single wealthy donor to stand  out based on their direct spending alone. Now, the

05:20 one exception to the FEC cap is that candidates  can put as much of their own money as they want

05:25 into their own campaign. And significantly wealthy  figures from both sides of the aisle like Michael

05:30 Bloomberg and Donald Trump have both campaigned  on their ability to do this. Bloomberg put roughly

05:35 $936 million of his own money into his  unsuccessful 2020 presidential campaign,

05:41 which lasted about a 100 days, making it by far  the most expensive per day campaign in American

05:47 history. Trump contributed over $56 million into  his own 2016 campaign and made it a big point that

05:53 this would separate him from other politicians who  need to keep their donors happy. Though, according

05:58 to public disclosures, he didn't contribute  any of his own money in 2020 or 2024. Now,

06:03 get used to hearing this, but even through direct  contributions, there are still some loopholes.

06:09 Individual contribution limits are $7,000, but  there is a very popular workaround called a

06:15 joint fundraising committee. Not to be confused  with my fellow broke dorm room friends back in

06:19 college who went by the same name. These allow  a single donor to write one enormous check that

06:24 could split across a candidate, a national party,  and multiple state parties all at once, filling

06:29 up the limits across all of these categories  in a single transaction. In the 2024 cycle,

06:34 a single donor could legally contribute over  $800,000 through one of these arrangements.

06:39 It's not great, but this alone is far from the  biggest reason why money in politics has gotten

06:44 so out of control. The $7,000 cap only applies to  direct contributions. And even with a multiple six

06:51 figure workaround, this money pales in comparison  to what is now being contributed very openly by

06:56 wealthy individuals through super PACs which have  no cap at all. Now, packs or political action

07:02 committees are organizations that can support  a specific interest, like a political campaign,

07:07 and were really just meant as a way for supporters  to organize and make their voices collectively

07:11 heard. Regular packs also have limits on how  much they are allowed to spend. Super PACs are

07:17 technically distinct from regular packs. Legally,  they aren't actually technically packs at all.

07:23 Instead, they are officially classified as  independent expenditure only committees, which

07:28 might sound like nerdy legal technicalities, but  it means that they can take in unlimited amounts

07:32 of money and spend unlimited amounts of money on  any issue they see fit, including the election of

07:38 individuals or the passing of specific laws. This  freedom to spend all they want comes on the one

07:44 specific condition that they do not directly  coordinate with the political campaign that

07:48 they are supporting. And even this lowest of bars  gets pretty openly ignored. These were the groups

07:53 that were enabled by the Citizens United ruling in  2010, which established that political spending is

07:58 protected free speech under the First Amendment.  The idea is that people with specific political

08:04 concerns should be allowed to use their free  speech to push a political agenda and spending is

08:09 part of that free speech. But to avoid it becoming  just an endound campaign finance limits, there

08:14 should be no direct coordination with the campaign  itself. This is broken pretty regularly and to

08:20 nobody's surprise, pretty flagrantly, too. Elon  Musk donated roughly $239 million to America Pack

08:27 in 2024 to support Donald Trump's presidential  campaign, making it one of the largest super PAC

08:33 operations in history. And the no cooperation rule  was uh well, the FC actually issued a ruling that

08:40 allowed super PACs to coordinate directly with  campaigns on door-to-door canvasing operations,

08:45 which America pack immediately took advantage of.  The campaign's own political director publicly

08:50 credited Musk's operation with conserving campaign  funds by outsourcing field operations to the super

08:55 PAC, which allowed Trump's campaign to redirect  money into ad spending. Now, spending money on

09:00 ads alone is obviously a big deal that can move  elections. Even here on YouTube, the amount of

09:06 money we make on the platform before major federal  elections increases significantly because of how

09:10 much is being spent on endless campaign ads. But  these messages don't actually require that much

09:16 coordination. The formula for political ads isn't  exactly that hard to reverse engineer. Say bad

09:23 things about the other guy and nice things  about your guy. which means in this space,

09:27 most super PACs find it a lot easier to keep  their legally mandated safe distance. But it's

09:32 also not the only place where they spend their  money. Data collection and processing is a huge

09:37 part of modern political campaigns. It's also  really expensive and a lot harder to hand over

09:42 without crossing the line of direct collaboration.  But even here, there are plenty of groups that

09:47 uh bend these rules. When JD Vance was first  running for senator in my home state of Ohio,

09:54 he was heavily supported by one of Peter Teal's  super PACs named Protect Ohio Values. It turns

09:59 out Teal has a thing for spending lots of money  to collect data on potential voters. Anyway,

10:05 the only problem was he couldn't just hand that  data over to Vance's campaign without it breaking

10:10 the arms distance rule of super PACs. So instead,  they just uploaded the data to an obscure blog for

10:15 his campaign team to stumble upon with the hope  that nobody else would find it. tucked away in an

10:20 obscure corner of the internet. This was of course  challenged for being a pretty blatant flouting of

10:25 the rules, but the case was ultimately dismissed.  Now, of course, hopefully it should go without

10:30 saying that this happens just as much on both  sides of the aisle. Democratic Alliance super PACs

10:35 spent comparable amounts in 2024. Future Forward,  a pro Harris super PAC, raised over $700 million,

10:42 and their coordination was probably a little  bit too close for the spirit of these rules as

10:46 well. In total, outside spending by super PACs and  other independent groups exceeded $4.5 billion in

10:52 the 2024 cycle, more than double what it was in  2016. Collectively, super PACs alongside direct

10:59 campaign finance is likely to exceed $10 billion  at the federal level this year. It's not great,

11:05 but at least we know it's actually happening  because, well, the money we can actually see

11:10 is far from the biggest problem. So, it's time  to learn how money works to find out just how

11:16 deep this goes, why even the most aggressive  campaign finance reform probably can't fix it,

11:20 and why nobody really seems to want to try. If you  have watched this channel for any amount of time,

11:26 you already know that most companies do not  actually care about your privacy. They sell

11:30 your data, they lose your data, and they treat it  like a line item on a balance sheet. Which is why

11:35 this video is sponsored by Cape. We have worked  with Cape before, and they have shipped a few

11:40 new features worth catching you up on. Cape is  a privacy focused mobile carrier that gives you

11:45 unlimited talk, text, and data, plus a stack of  security features no other carrier includes. They

11:51 recently rolled out an IMSI rotation, which swaps  the static subscriber ID your phone broadcast

11:58 every 24 hours, so carriers and advertisers cannot  track you in real time. They have also launched

12:03 secondary numbers, two extra real phone lines  built into your plan, so you can hand them out

12:08 for banking or shopping and keep your main line  private. And finally, disappearing call logs,

12:13 which autodeletes your call and text metadata  after 24 hours, so there is nothing to leak

12:18 or sell. Use code how many works 33 for 33% off  your first 6 months of Cape. Cape is available on

12:25 Apple, Google Play, and the Acrescent store. Link  in my description. Okay, so campaign donations and

12:32 super PACs are really just scratching the surface  of these issues. The problem is that when you

12:37 look deeper, it gets much worse. The first level  down is what is not at all sinisterly known as

12:43 dark money. Dark money is politically motivated  spending that gets redirected through various

12:48 organizations to push an agenda without any clear  disclosure and without any clear source. These

12:54 are typically structured as 501c4 nonprofits  which under IRS rules are allowed to engage

12:59 in political activity so long as it is not their  primary purpose. This means they can spend up to

13:04 49% of their budget on politics and never have  to disclose a single donor. The Brennan Center

13:10 estimates that over $1 billion in dark money was  spent in federal elections between 2010 and 2024.

13:16 And those are just the expenditures that could be  tracked. And well, by definition, the thing that

13:21 makes dark money dark is that most of it can't  be. A major example that we have covered just

13:26 recently is Build America AI which is a dark money  organization pushing the idea that America needs

13:31 to beat China and AI which very clearly feeds  into the business interests of hyperscalers and

13:36 AI labs that need red tape cut land allotted for  their data centers and maybe some bailout money

13:40 in case investor hype dies down. Now, obviously  this is not great, but at least in this case,

13:46 their completely transparent motives make them  pretty transparent, but the whole point of a dark

13:51 money group is that you cannot trace the money  back to the people who benefit from the policy

13:55 changes. And this has a few other advantages, too.  Under federal law, foreign nationals are banned

14:00 from donating to American political campaigns or  packs. But because 501c4 nonprofits don't have

14:06 to disclose their donors, there is effectively no  mechanism to enforce this for dark money groups.

14:12 A foreign government or foreign corporation can  donate to a 501c4 which then spends that money on

14:17 American ads with a political agenda and nobody  would ever know. The FEC has acknowledged this

14:23 loophole exists. Yet they have not closed it.  And then there are the corporate interests that

14:28 just throw away the middleman altogether. There  is really nothing stopping a major company from

14:33 just running its own ads pushing a very specific  political message. This is happening a lot at the

14:39 moment with companies claiming that their AI data  centers are going to be great for local economies

14:43 running ads in swing districts about job creation  and infrastructure investment that look a lot

14:48 like political endorsements but technically  aren't. So when work started to slow down,

14:54 we searched for new opportunities and we welcome  Meta which opened a data center in our town.

15:00 So long as they avoid FEC trigger words like vote  for or vote against and don't mention specific

15:05 legislation, it's really hard to regulate this as  political spending over a company just expressing

15:10 its own interests as protected speech. But it gets  worse. Everything we just covered, all of that is

15:17 really just the price of admission. The thing that  actually moves the needle once the politicians are

15:22 in Washington is lobbying. And lobbying is a very  different animal from campaign spending. Lobbyists

15:28 are in theory just concerned citizens with very  specific interests about very specific policies.

15:34 In reality, they are primarily highly paid field  experts from elite law firms funded by industry

15:39 groups to support a very specific agenda. Now, to  play devil's advocate a little bit here, a lot of

15:44 lawmakers are not experts in the things they are  creating laws on. So, being able to consult with

15:49 a diverse pool of industry specialists could  theoretically avoid designing laws that are

15:53 just dumb for their specific application. Laws  on technology probably shouldn't be exclusively

15:58 written by an 80-year-old senator who doesn't know  the difference between a coding language and their

16:02 high school transcripts. And that kind of makes  sense. But the problem is that almost all of the

16:08 work of actually drafting legislation gets passed  off to these lobbyists who get to word things

16:14 exactly how they want and ensure it won't get held  up in courts because they are the legal experts.

16:20 Congressional staffers have openly described how  lobbyists will hand them fully written legislative

16:24 text ready to be introduced. And because the  staffers are overworked and underresourced,

16:29 they will sometimes file it with barely any  changes. So really, in a lot of cases, the

16:34 lobbying firms are the lawmakers. The lawmakers  themselves are just the rubber stamp. Now, there

16:39 is the widely held assumption that this corporate  funded lobbying is working exclusively to cut red

16:44 tape and remove regulations. In reality, it  is often exactly the opposite. They want to

16:49 introduce regulation in exactly the right areas  to block potential new challengers from entering

16:54 their market. The pharmaceutical industry is  particularly good at this. They spent over $370

16:59 million on lobbying in 2024 alone, more than  any other industry that year, and a huge chunk

17:05 of that went towards ensuring that drug pricing  regulations are written in a way that protects

17:09 their existing patent portfolios while making  it harder for generic competitors to enter the

17:13 market. The old team at Micro did a great video  on this, explaining how internet providers lobbied

17:17 against municipalities looking to roll out their  own broadband and actually deliver a competitive

17:22 service. In both cases, getting the right kind  of laws passed was a lot more profitable than

17:27 having no regulations at all. There are now over  14,000 registered lobbyists in Washington alone,

17:33 which works out to roughly 26 lobbyists for every  single elected official in Congress. And if you

17:38 include the people doing lobbying adjacent work  who don't formally register, some estimates put

17:43 the real number closer to 100,000. And all of this  is just the federal level. State legislatores are

17:50 arguably worse because they get a fraction of the  media scrutiny. State level lobbying disclosure

17:55 requirements are weaker, staffs are smaller,  and individual lobbyists can have an outsized

17:59 influence on a state representative who might only  have one or two aids and no research budget to

18:04 independently verify what the lobbyist is telling  them. Of course, these people also coordinate the

18:09 efforts of everything we've already talked about.  They can suggest that a given company or industry

18:14 group would really like this type of legislation  and that conveniently they are looking to spend

18:19 a lot of money advertising this issue. A study  looking at 93 multinational corporations that

18:24 lobbyed for a single tax provision, the American  Jobs Creation Act of 2004, found that those firms

18:29 spent a combined $283 million on lobbying  and received $62.5 billion in tax savings,

18:36 working out to a return of $220 for every single  dollar spent. Those returns have to come from

18:42 somewhere, and that somewhere is the tax base, the  consumer or the competitor who got regulated out

18:47 of the market. Now, there is one other reason why  lobbying has become such an effective tool against

18:52 lawmakers. And this other reason also explains  one of the other logical questions you may have

18:57 had so far, which is why do lawmakers let this  happen? Yes, they want their re-election funding,

19:04 but there are alternative systems to get it. And  by just taking a step back if nobody else had

19:09 lobbyists to answer to or super PAC money funding  their campaigns, it means they wouldn't need it

19:14 either. They could change these laws because,  well, that's literally their job. And so far,

19:19 it looks like the only reason they don't want to  is because the other guy won't do it first. Beyond

19:24 the weird prisoners dilemma they have backed  themselves into here, it must be recognized

19:28 that for these lawmakers constantly begging for  campaign funding and playing nice with an army of

19:32 lobbyists telling them how to do their job has got  to be pretty demeaning. So even if they don't do

19:38 it for the good of their constituents, surely they  would be motivated to reform these laws just to

19:42 make their own job less humiliating, right? Well,  there is one good reason why they don't, and that

19:48 is the revolving door. Elected officials at the  federal level are paid well by the standards of

19:54 average Americans, but not by the standards of  the people they interact with on a daily basis.

19:59 A member of Congress earns $174,000 a year. The  median partner at a top lobbying firm in DC earns

20:05 well over a million. A huge unspoken way that  money gets into politics is the promise of a cushy

20:11 job for when they retire or get voted out. This  extends well beyond elected officials as well.

20:16 In our video on corporate consolidation, we found  that almost all of the previous FTC chairpersons

20:21 over the last two decades, with the exception of  Lena Khan, went on to get high-profile roles at

20:26 M&A law firms, specifically working on the kinds  of deals that the FTC should probably be blocking.

20:31 So yeah, the person whose job it is to block  anti-competitive mergers knows that in 2 years

20:36 they will probably be working for the firms doing  those mergers. That creates an incentive that no

20:41 amount of campaign finance reform can fix.  Now the number one most common career move

20:45 for elected officials after leaving politics is  to become a political lobbyist. In 2025 alone,

20:52 866 members of Congress and congressional staffers  made the move from Capitol Hill to K Street,

20:57 a 60% increase over the year before, and  a new record. In total, roughly half of

21:02 all former lawmakers end up working as political  lobbyists. Jack Abramoff, one of the few lobbyists

21:07 who has actually been convicted for pushing these  flexible laws too far, put it pretty bluntly when

21:12 he admitted that he would tell a congressional  staffer, "When you're done working on the Hill,

21:16 we'd very much like you to consider coming  to work for us." And that was most of his

21:20 job done. Every request from our office, every  request of our clients, everything that we want,

21:25 they're going to do. And not only that, they're  going to think of things we can't think of to do

21:30 it. Former representatives and staffers are the  perfect candidates to become lobbyists because

21:34 they know their way around the capital, but also  because they are a walking billboard showing

21:39 every current staffer that playing along with the  lobbyists is the path to a seven figure salary as

21:44 a lobbyist. Now, to be fair, there are cooling  off periods in place. Former members of Congress

21:50 are technically barred from lobbying for 1 to two  years after leaving office. But these rules are

21:54 trivally easy to get around. You can do strategic  consulting or government relations advisory work,

22:00 which is, and I cannot stress this enough, exactly  the same thing without technically registering as

22:05 a lobbyist until this period is up. And well, even  if you did somehow fully enforce the cooling off

22:10 period and close every loophole, it still wouldn't  fix the core problem because the incentive

22:15 is baked into the system the moment a staffer  realizes that the people they are writing laws for

22:20 are also the people who are going to sign their  next paycheck. But the revolving door at least

22:24 involves people who used to work in government.  The next channel of influence doesn't even require

22:29 that. Obviously, certain owners of major news  outlets have certain political leanings, and they

22:34 can put weight on candidates to support their  incentives or face unfavorable coverage. Now,

22:39 this one is really hard to quantify because media  influence doesn't show up in any spending report.

22:44 There is no FC filing for choose not to cover the  story or ran 17 segments on this topic instead

22:50 of that one. And no, this is not a segue to a  ground news ad, but the effects are very real.

22:55 The media landscape has become so partisan that  this is arguably even more important in primaries

23:00 than in general elections because the threat of  poor coverage from a politically aligned outlet

23:05 can end a primary campaign before it starts. If  you are running as a Republican and can't get onto

23:10 Fox News, you're kind of cooked. Hypothetically,  of course, social media platforms are now owned by

23:16 people with very specific political and business  interests. and the editorial decisions about what

23:20 gets amplified, what gets suppressed, and what  gets labeled as misinformation are being made by

23:25 the same people who are pushing for specific  policy outcomes. Even companies that are not

23:29 traditional media can also influence this by  suggesting they would feel more comfortable

23:33 advertising on networks that did or did not push a  certain political agenda. I can say from personal

23:38 experience that even down here at Little Works  Media Group, we have lost sponsors because we

23:42 pointed out things like the lunacy surrounding  current AI spending and the push for bailouts.

23:47 This is becoming a very real pressure even at  this level. And for better or worse, influencers

23:52 and independent creators are becoming a political  force. And then there's the one that nobody really

23:57 needs to talk about for very long because it is  exactly what it sounds like, straight up bribes.

24:03 Now, this kind of direct corruption isn't as  necessary as it used to be because of all of

24:08 the other legal channels we just went through,  but it does still happen and enforcement is,

24:12 to put it generously, relaxed. Senator Bob Mendez  was convicted on 16 federal charges in 2024 for

24:19 accepting gold bars, cash, and a Mercedes-Benz in  exchange for official acts, and his colleagues in

24:24 the Senate only moved to expel him after the  conviction, at which point he resigned before

24:28 a vote could take place. And Menendez isn't  alone. In 2024, Business Insider found that

24:34 over 100 members of Congress or their spouses made  stock trades and industries directly affected by

24:38 their committee work. A senator sitting on the  Armed Services Committee buying defense stocks

24:43 before a major procurement announcement is well  exactly what it looks like. And the stock act

24:48 that was supposed to prevent this is enforced  with fines of $200. $200 on a trade that could

24:54 net hundreds of thousands is not a deterrent. The  uncomfortable truth is that when you line up all

24:59 seven of these channels together, the direct  contributions, the super PACs, the dark money,

25:03 the corporate ads, the lobbyists, the revolving  door, the media influence, and yeah, the bribes,

25:08 what you are looking at is a system where the  legal options are so effective that the illegal

25:12 ones are almost redundant. Now, some people have  accused me of being a bit of a gloomy goose. So,

25:19 I want to talk about some actual genuine real  good news here. At a state level, there has been

25:24 some progress to circumvent the super PAC funding  enabled by the Citizens United ruling in several

25:29 states. And at least in state legislatores, it has  received unanimous support from both sides of the

25:33 aisle. This won't fix all of these problems, and  the legal techniques they are using won't work at

25:38 the federal level without a new Supreme Court  ruling, but this is still a step in the right

25:43 direction. Like always, the big Blizzard beat me  to covering this particular topic, so I will leave

25:47 a link to his video in the description alongside  some other articles. Unfortunately, the federal

25:52 level is going to need a little bit more work.  The obvious fix is to close the revolving door,

25:57 remove the financial incentive for lawmakers to  play along, and maybe hot tickler actually pay

26:02 elected officials enough that a lobbying salary  isn't a six-fold raise. Yes, that would cost more

26:07 money in government salaries, but it would be a  drop in the bucket compared to how much money is

26:11 lost through poor policy. Those 93 companies  that spent $283 million on lobbying and got

26:17 $62.5 billion back did not create that money out  of thin air. That money came from somewhere. And

26:23 that somewhere is the tax base, workers paychecks,  and consumers wallets. There have been efforts.

26:29 The For the People Act passed in the House in 2019  and again in 2021 with provisions to require dark

26:35 money disclosures and tighten revolving door  restrictions. It died in the Senate both times.

26:41 The Disclose Act, which would have required 501c4  groups to name donors who give them over $10,000,

26:46 has been introduced in every Congress since 2010.  It has never passed. But the only people who could

26:53 pass these reforms are the exact same people  who benefit from the current system. You are

26:57 essentially asking politicians to vote themselves  a stricter set of rules and a permanent ban on the

27:02 career they were planning to retire into. Now,  if you want to see all these systems actually

27:06 put together, go and watch this next video  to find out why we are already subsidizing

27:10 AI data centers. And don't forget to like and  subscribe to keep on learning how money works.

00:00

00:00 PROFESSOR: The well ordering principle

00:02 is one of those facts in mathematics

00:05 that's so obvious that you hardly notice it.

00:08 And the objective of this brief introduction

00:11 is to call your attention to it.

00:13 We've actually used it already.

00:15 And in subsequent segments of this presentation,

00:19 I'll show lots of applications of it.

00:23 So here's a statement of the well ordering principle.

00:25 Every nonempty set of nonnegative integers

00:28 has a least element.

00:30 Now this is probably familiar.

00:33 Maybe you haven't even thought about it.

00:35 But now that I mentioned it, I expect it's a familiar idea.

00:38 And it's pretty obvious too if you

00:40 think about it for a minute.

00:41 Here's a way to think about it.

00:44 Given an nonempty set of integers, you could ask,

00:47 is 0 the least element in it?

00:49 Well, if it is, then you're done.

00:51 Then you could say, is 1 the least element in it?

00:55 And if it is, you're done.

00:56 And if it isn't, you could say 2, is 2 the least element?

00:59 And so on.

01:00 Given that it's not empty, eventually you're

01:02 to hit the least element.

01:04 So, if it wasn't obvious before, there

01:07 is something of a hand-waving proof of it.

01:09 But I want to get you to think about this well

01:12 ordering principle a little bit because it's not-- there are

01:16 some technical parts of it that matter.

01:19 So for example, suppose I replace nonnegative integers

01:24 by nonnegative rationals.

01:26 And I asked does every nonempty set of nonnegative rationals

01:32 have a least element?

01:33 Well, there is a least nonnegative rational, namely 0.

01:37 But not every nonnegative set of rationals has a least element.

01:42 I'll let you think of an example.

01:46 Another variant is when, instead of talking

01:49 about the nonnegative integers, I just

01:51 talk about all the integers.

01:52 Is there a least integer?

01:54 Well, no, obviously because minus 1 is not the least.

01:57 And minus 2 is not the least.

01:59 And there isn't any least integer.

02:01

02:04 We take for granted the well ordering principle just

02:08 all the time.

02:09 If I ask you, what was the youngest age of an MIT graduate

02:13 well, you wouldn't for a moment wonder whether there

02:15 was a youngest age.

02:16 And if I asked you for the smallest number of neurons

02:19 in any animal, you wouldn't wonder

02:21 whether there was or wasn't a smallest number of neurons.

02:24 We may not know what it is.

02:25 But there's surely a smallest number of neurons

02:28 because neurons are nonnegative integers.

02:30 And finally, if I ask you what was the smallest number of US

02:33 coins that could make $1.17, again, we

02:37 don't have to worry about existence

02:38 because the well ordering principle knocks that

02:41 off immediately.

02:42

02:44 Now for the remainder of this talk,

02:46 I'm going to be talking about the nonnegative integers

02:48 always, unless I explicitly say otherwise.

02:50 So I'm just going to is the word number

02:52 to mean nonnegative integer.

02:54 There's a standard mathematical symbol

02:56 that we use to denote the nonnegative integers.

02:58 It's that letter N at the top of the slide

03:01 with a with a diagonal double bar.

03:05 These are sometimes called the natural numbers.

03:07 But I've never been able to understand or figure out

03:10 whether 0 is natural or not.

03:11 So we don't use that phrase.

03:13 Zero is included in N, the nonnegative integers.

03:17 And that's what we call them in this class.

03:21 Now, I want to point out that we've actually

03:23 used the well ordering principle already

03:25 without maybe not noticing it, even

03:28 in the proof that the square root of 2 was not rational.

03:32 That proof began by saying, suppose the square root of 2

03:35 was rational, that is, it was a quotient of integers m over n.

03:40 And the remark was that you can always express a fraction

03:44 like that in lowest terms.

03:46 More precisely, you can always find positive numbers m and n

03:51 without common factors, such that the square root of 2

03:55 equals m over n.

03:56 If there's any fraction equal to the square root of 2,

04:00 then there is a lowest terms fraction m

04:03 over n with no common factors.

04:07 So now we can use well ordering to come up

04:09 with a simple, and hopefully very clear and convincing,

04:14 argument for why every fraction can

04:17 be expressed in lowest terms.

04:19 In particular, let's look at numbers m and n

04:22 such that the square root of 2 is equal to m over n--

04:26 that fraction.

04:27 And let's just choose the smallest numerator that works.

04:30 Find the smallest numerator m, such that squared of 2

04:34 is equal to m over n.

04:36 Well, I claim that that fraction, which

04:40 uses the smallest possible numerator,

04:43 has got to be in lowest terms because suppose

04:46 that m and n had a common factor c that was greater

04:50 than 1-- a real common factor.

04:53 Then you could replace m over n by m over c,

04:57 the numerator is a smaller numerator that's

04:59 still an integer, and n over c.

05:00 The denominator is still an integer.

05:03 And we have a numerator that's smaller than m

05:05 contradicting the way that we chose m in the first place.

05:10

05:12 And this contradiction, of course,

05:14 implies that m and n have no common factors.

05:17 And therefore, as claimed, m over n is in lowest terms.

05:21 And of course, the way I formulated

05:23 this was for our application of the fraction that was

05:26 equal to the square root of 2.

05:27 But this proof actually shows that any rational number,

05:31 any fraction, can be expressed in lowest terms.

05:35

00:00 This week we'll be talking about probably one

00:06 of the most important aspects of photography, which is light.

00:10 As in photo-graphy [spoken phonetically],

00:12 writing or drawing with light.

00:15 It's a very content-rich conversation,

00:18 we're going to have, and could really, easily,

00:20 take up a full six-week course.

00:22 But for our purposes here, we're going

00:25 to give you something of an overview,

00:27 showing you various forms and characteristics

00:30 of some light sources.

00:32 We can't address every conceivable possibility.

00:35 But what we can do is tweak your curiosity, I hope,

00:39 so that you pay attention, very close attention, to what you're

00:43 seeing as you change your own light sources,

00:46 looking at the shadows for example.

00:49 How do they and they and the highlights

00:51 change as you move your light source?

00:54 And observe exactly what's going on when you make even

00:58 some very minimal changes.

00:59 Let's start with a very simple piece of equipment, a lightbox.

01:05 It's really easy to use when you're

01:07 working with transparent material,

01:09 just by placing your work directly

01:12 on top of the lightbox.

01:14 But you'll see also, later, it can

01:15 be also another general source of lighting.

01:19 So let's start with a picture of these two petri dishes

01:22 growing E. coli.

01:24 So that works.

01:26 In this image, we're seeing small pieces of colored plastic

01:30 shapes, about 3 millimeters across that are organizing,

01:34 or self-assembling at the interface

01:36 between two solutions.

01:38 They're becoming a flat assemblage at that interface.

01:42 And all I did was put the glass container

01:44 holding all the material on the lightbox.

01:48 And here, I'm making images of sugar crystals growing

01:52 on sticks.

01:53 You know, they serve you that sometimes

01:55 when you order a cup of coffee.

01:57 So here is one rendition on a lightbox of the sugar,

02:01 and what I decided to do for the next one

02:04 to simply invert the image, which we've seen before.

02:07 Here's a picture that I made a number of years ago,

02:10 which I still like.

02:11 It's a picture about light, a metaphor about light.

02:16 It was one of those lucky efforts

02:18 when I just set up a magnifier and the paper, [laughs]

02:21 and in about 30 seconds, I got the picture!

02:24 (Very unusual, by the way!) So the image

02:26 is intended to suggest a process of etching with light when

02:31 we talked about it in our book No Small Matter,

02:34 about nanoscience.

02:36 In this image of something I assume you recognize by now,

02:40 we see a different kind of lighting

02:42 that you've seen from previous images of the music box.

02:46 I shot from above with mostly daylight,

02:49 and then I turned on a little bit more

02:52 light from a Tungsten lamp above.

02:55 This is specific to this situation,

02:57 but you might find it helpful in yours.

03:01 Look what happens when you just simply click and turn

03:04 a light on.

03:05 From the light being off, to the light being on,

03:09 you'll see how the image drastically

03:11 changes by just adding an additional lamp

03:14 from above this fishing reel.

03:17 Yup [laugh], that's what it is, by the way,

03:19 it is a fishing reel placed in a translucent, green garbage can.

03:24 [laughs] I thought it was fun to see what kind of quality

03:27 I could get by shooting into a plastic, translucent garbage

03:31 can.

03:31 Very specific to say the least.

03:34 Again, just by adding one additional light -- this time,

03:38 inside the vacuum chamber I'm imaging ' we see what starts

03:43 as this kind of image, and becomes this image.

03:46 You'll see how it really changes with the simple addition

03:50 of just one light.

03:53 In this image of a triangular-shaped water drop --

03:57 it's actually an etched area on a surface onto which we placed

04:01 water ' you can see the reflection of the lamp

04:04 on the water drop.

04:06 We just directed a lamp onto the water.

04:10 That's considered direct lighting.

04:13 When I shine the lamp onto a card,

04:15 in this case, a gold card, the light then

04:18 bounced back onto the water drop and you'll

04:21 see a completely different quality of lighting.

04:24 This is called bounce lighting.

04:27 The bounce gives us diffuse lighting.

04:30 Let's compare the two.

04:31 Let's look at a quick test that I

04:35 made for us to see the difference between two

04:38 kinds of bounces.

04:40 In this case, the bounce lighting

04:42 will used as fill lighting.

04:44 We'll use a white card and then we'll fill with a mirror.

04:48 The main source of light is daylight from a window.

04:51 So, here's an image of the inside of the watch

04:53 that we've seen before, just with daylight

04:56 on an overcast day.

04:57 Here, I added a white card on the side of the watch

05:01 for a fill.

05:02 Here is a mirror reflecting the daylight, again, as a fill,

05:06 onto the watch.

05:09 Let's go back to the original 'just daylight'; then the card;

05:13 then the mirror; back to the watch alone;

05:18 then adding a card; then adding just the mirror.

05:23 Let's zoom in to see the subtle differences

05:26 in each of these cases.

05:28 Now depending on what your material is,

05:30 you might see much more dramatic changes.

05:33 But I encourage you to experiment with these ideas.

05:37 By the way, here's another image I

05:38 made, this time using both the card and the mirror as a fill.

05:43 Let's see them all together.

05:44

05:49 Light is all about shadows as well.

05:51 And it is quite remarkable how small changes can

05:54 change the shadow in images.

05:56 How a powerful direct light source

05:59 can produce a significant shadow, and that shadow does,

06:03 in this image, become a very strong compositional element.

06:09 Here's where I'm using the light on this wafer showing

06:13 the chip that sits next to it.

06:15 In this particular image, I was playing around;

06:18 I decided to just use a slant of light -- uh, maybe, uh,

06:23 Emily Dickenson would be happy with that.

06:26 On this image, I decided just to make

06:29 sure the light was covering the entire wafer.

06:32 I actually like the first one better,

06:34 but it's something to think about,

06:35 about using light in terms of making compositions.

06:40 In this image, I'm using a shadow

06:42 to better communicate what the grading on the surface

06:45 of this plastic is doing.

06:47 It's diffracting the light into different wavelengths.

06:50 I produced the shadow by placing a card

06:53 in front of the light source.

06:55 See how the image looks without the card.

07:00 Shadows alone can tell a story.

07:02 Here, we're trying to show something called the Marangoni

07:05 effect; you know, when you twirl a glass of wine we see some --

07:09 what some people call 'tears of wine'.

07:12 It's a complex phenomenon.

07:14 In this image, I tried for quite a

07:16 while to make an image depicting the Maragoni effect.

07:21 Not at all successful.

07:23 Finally, thinking that I should concentrate

07:26 on the glass, and the shadow that is being produced,

07:30 then I finally focused in on what is the Marangoni

07:35 effect on its own, as a shadow.

07:39 Now, for example, looking at this small assemblage, which

07:44 is about two centimeters across, I lit this with one light.

07:50 It's a monopoint, it's somewhat of a fiber optic source.

07:54 And you could see carefully, if you look at this image,

07:59 where does the light source come from,

08:02 and hopefully you will figure out that if the shadow is here,

08:07 then the light source has to be around here.

08:11 In this next one, I added a second light source

08:15 that not only lights the device as light to it,

08:19 but it also adds another shadow.

08:22 And in this next one, the second light source

08:26 has been altered in terms of its direction and the height

08:31 because the shadow that it casts is slightly longer and even

08:36 more so in this final image where

08:40 the light, the second light source,

08:42 is very low compared to where it was.

08:45 And you know that again because the shadow

08:48 is considerably longer.

08:50 Now, why bother looking at all this?

08:53 It really is, once again, learning

08:56 to see so that when you play with your own light sources

09:00 with your own devices, you're going

09:02 to pay not only great attention to lighting of your device,

09:08 but the shadows that the lighting will be producing.

09:12 It's important.

09:13 It might not seem that way at this point, but [laughs],

09:16 I promise you, it really is important.

09:19

00:00 Japan is the most earthquake  prepared country on Earth. So

00:03 why is it spending $67 billion on a backup plan? Because Tokyo isn't just Japan's capital. It's

00:09 one of the most important cities on Earth.  If it falls, the consequences won't stop at

00:13 Japan's shores. They would ripple through  the global economy, shatter supply chains,

00:17 and impact millions of lives around the world. That's why Japan is racing to build an entire

00:22 Shadow Capital... before the ticking  time bomb beneath Tokyo goes off.

00:26 But how long do we have? Japan already famously sits on

00:30 the Ring of Fire. But just off the coast is the  600 mile (966 km) long Nankai trough. The forces

00:36 there are so great that experts warn they result  in a megaquake about once every 100 to 150 years.

00:42 And they usually happen in pairs.

00:44 The last time two “megathrust” earthquakes  happened back to back was in 1944 and 1946.

00:51 We’re not quite near the 100 year mark yet…but  we’re not far from it. Japan's earthquake panel

00:56 warns there's a 60 to 90% chance the next massive  Nankai Trough earthquake will happen within the

01:02 next 30 years. So Japan’s government is preparing  for not only the worst; but the inevitable.

01:08 A megaquake coming for Tokyo.

01:10 The damage would be unthinkable. In April 2026,

01:14 authorities predicted that a megaquake  could trigger a tsunami more than 66

01:18 feet tall (20 meters). Tokyo and the  surrounding prefectures would be in

01:21 its path. It would result in 300,000 deaths…  at least. That’s with all of Japan’s current

01:27 earthquake preparation methods. The economic  devastation would hit at at least $1.5 trillion.

01:33 It would be a catastrophic disaster.

01:35 Why? Because financially, Japan has  put all its power in one, centralized,

01:40 earthquake-prone basket. 14 million people live  in Tokyo, and another 33.4 million people are

01:47 in the surrounding metropolitan area. It’s the  most populous metropolitan region in the world.

01:52 Japan is currently the fourth largest economy  in the world with a GDP of $4.2 trillion in

01:58 2025. It has some of the biggest names in  cars, electronics, tech, and robotics. And

02:04 the headquarters of more than half of all  its major corporations are located in Tokyo.

02:08 The concentration of economic power in  Tokyo is so big that it rakes in $1.1

02:13 trillion every single year. It’s equivalent to  the GDP of the Netherlands. Put it this way,

02:19 if the Tokyo metropolitan area were a country,  it would rank 18th in the world for GDP.

02:25 It’s an immense centre of financial power.

02:27 And it’s extremely vulnerable. And all this is located at the

02:31 intersection of 4 tectonic plates. Just  one 9.0 earthquake and Tokyo goes from

02:36 being one of the financial centers of the  world to finding itself in a perfect storm

02:40 of rubble, tsunami flooding, and even  potential volcanic ash and fallout.

02:45 Because after a previous disastrous Nankai rupture  in 1707, not was there a massive earthquake,

02:51 but Mount Fuji erupted. Massive tsunamis were  unleashed on Japanese coasts, and tens of

02:56 thousands of structures were destroyed.  The potential for damage is staggering.

03:01 It’s not just a Japanese problem.

03:03 It’s a tragedy for everyone. Because Japan controls a major share of a market

03:08 that the entire world relies on: semiconductors. Everything from your car and healthcare devices to

03:14 your computer, smartphone, TV, and satellite need  semiconductors. On a countrywide economic level,

03:20 a huge range of industries from manufacturing  and data centers to aerospace absolutely need

03:25 semiconductors to function. Enter Japan.

03:28 The country may not control the 50% of the  global semiconductor market it did in the 1980s,

03:34 but a huge amount of materials for the chips are  still made in the country. Japan has over half the

03:39 global market share for photoresists and silicon  wafers. It also has 88% of the global market share

03:45 for semiconductor coaters and developers. Since the majority of Japanese business

03:50 activity is concentrated in Tokyo,  a megaquake would be disastrous for

03:54 residents and paralyze the world economy. No one has estimated how bad the impact of

03:59 a semiconductor material disruption in Japan  would be to the rest of the world in terms

04:04 of absolute numbers. But the supply chain  would certainly be heavily impacted. With

04:08 Japan controlling such a massive share of the  global semiconductor market, replacing its lost

04:13 supply would be nearly impossible overnight.  Could the rest of the world even keep up?

04:18 The answer may lie in what happened before. In 2011, a devastating 9.0-magnitude earthquake

04:24 struck Japan's Tohoku region. Even though it's  a much less densely populated and financially

04:29 powerful area of Japan, it’s still home to some  Japanese tech manufacturing. One of the biggest

04:34 tech victims of the earthquake was NAND flash  memory, a vital component for iPads, iPhones,

04:40 SD cards, tablets, and much more. The  earthquake caused a power outage in a

04:45 Toshiba production facility; the company with  35% share in the global NAND flash market.

04:51 Despite being a short-term blackout, it  caused production of NAND flash memory to

04:55 fall by 20% for the next 2 months. Another tech product, DRAM chips,

05:00 was also impacted by the Tohoku earthquake.  Three wafer fabrication plants in Japan were

05:05 severely damaged or powered off by the earthquake.  Almost immediately, DRAM chip prices rose by 7%.

05:11 The impact of a Tokyo megaquake on the tech  industry, including global supply and prices,

05:16 would be a thousand times  worse than these examples.

05:19 Unfortunately, the financial  fallout wouldn’t end there.

05:22 Back in 1989, financial analyst Michael Lewis  warned that a Tokyo earthquake could trigger a

05:28 global stock market crash. All because of some  financial realities of the Japanese system few

05:33 people talk about or even realize. Only around 37% of Tokyo households

05:38 have earthquake insurance. This seems like  it would cover almost a large portion of any

05:42 quake damage. But it’s not even close.  That’s because commercial coverage only

05:46 extends to 20% of a property’s insured value. A National Report on the financial preparedness of

05:52 corporate Japan for natural disasters found that  these conditions create the largest “protection

05:57 gap”of any earthquake-prone region in the world. How do Japan’s $659 billion in

06:04 foreign securities tie into this? In 2022, Nigel Winspear, an international

06:08 expert in catastrophe modeling, decided to  test Japan’s effect on global stock markets.

06:13 Depressingly, his analysis  found that the risk Michael

06:16 Lewis identified in 1989 remains very real. Winspear’s report found that in the case of

06:22 a 7.9 magnitude earthquake in the Kanto region -  not even the highest possible magnitude scientists

06:28 predict - Japanese banks would need around  $690 billion to meet withdrawal demands. This

06:34 is partly due to the huge protection gap  Japanese property owners face. They would

06:39 immediately draw down their bank deposits to pay  for repairs and reconstruction. But for banks,

06:44 such a massive demand for deposits would  create an immediate liquidity crunch.

06:48 During one of the worst possible times. The stock market would be closed,

06:52 possibly for weeks. The domestic bond market  would freeze as banks turn from buying bonds

06:56 to selling off as many as they can. Japanese  banks would be left with only one option for

07:01 quick cash… selling off foreign securities. The $659 billion they hold are almost enough

07:07 to cover the potential $690 billion in withdrawal  demands. Meaning Japanese banks would have to sell

07:13 them all quickly. The U.S. and European markets  would be flooded with sell orders. Global prices

07:18 for U.S. and European stocks and bonds to plummet. That’s a major problem.

07:23 Japan is the largest creditor of the U.S.  government. It holds $1.2 trillion in U.S.

07:29 Treasury securities. Buyers would be shaken  seeing a meltdown like this. It would create even

07:34 more friction in financial markets. Raising the  very real possibility of a global market crash.

07:40 The most horrifying part? That’s not even the worst-case scenario.

07:44 This is the result of a potential 7.9  earthquake in the Kanto region. But

07:48 the Japanese government has said that the  potential of an earthquake between 8.0 and

07:52 9.0 in the next 30 years is 70-80%. Winspear’s report found that in this

07:58 worst-case scenario, the Kanto region would  experience $3 trillion in property damage and

08:04 $4.5 trillion in total economic losses instead. All this damage doesn’t even cover another,

08:09 even bigger issue. The political fallout.

08:12 Because in addition to being Japan’s  economic powerhouse, Tokyo is its one and

08:16 only seat of government and political power.  Cabinet meetings, parliamentary functions,

08:20 administrative services, would immediately be  suspended. It’s possible a significant amount

08:25 of administrative workers and politicians  would find either be injured, incapacitated,

08:30 or dead. How would the government be able to  continue functioning if the very foundations

08:34 of its seats of power fell to the ground? In June 2026, staring down the barrel of a

08:39 very likely megaquake, the Liberal Democratic  Party approved a bill to create the backup

08:45 of all backups… A second capital.

08:47 One that could step in to take over important  government functions, particularly in the

08:51 event of an all out national crisis like the  one major earthquake would cause. Ministries

08:56 and agencies could pick up where they left off  in a backup city. Though the current Japanese

09:01 administration hasn’t yet decided which city  that would be, there’s one likely candidate.

09:06 Osaka. The bill is part of a

09:08 wider agreement between the LDP and the JIP, the  Japan Innovation Party. The JIP is headquartered

09:13 in Osaka, so is pulling for its own city to take  the second capital title. But even though the

09:19 theoretical framework has been laid for a doomsday  protocol; that doesn’t mean it will be easy.

09:24 There have already been divisions. One of the biggest sticking points was

09:27 whether there should be referendums before  creating special administrative wards,

09:31 like Tokyo's, in a future second capital. Those  referendums had already failed twice in Osaka. A

09:38 compromise was eventually reached: only residents  of the city in question would be allowed to vote.

09:42 An even bigger question remains. Osaka may  be the favorite, but nobody knows which

09:47 city will actually be chosen. And that  uncertainty has reignited a decades-old

09:52 fight over Tokyo's dominance of Japan. In 1945, Tokyo accounted for 13% of Japan’s

09:58 population. By 2024, almost one in three  Japanese people lived in the Tokyo area.

10:03 As one Japanese newspaper, The Mainichi, puts  it, “Tokyo centralization has become a chronic

10:09 illness for Japan”. According to the  same editorial, policies implemented

10:13 by the Tokyo-based central government have  “stripped regions of their unique character”.

10:17 But the biggest problem may be Tokyo itself. A  country famous for technology still struggles with

10:23 outdated systems and slow digitalization. Without  strong incentives for companies to move elsewhere,

10:28 Tokyo keeps growing stronger, absorbing Japan’s  people, money, and opportunities while the

10:34 rest of the country falls further behind. So various cities and regions are seeing

10:38 this potential legislation as a chance to  acquire more political and financial power

10:42 for themselves… away from Tokyo. It will  likely set off an intense, and potentially

10:47 time-wasting competition between cities for  the honor of being Japan’s second capital.

10:52 But creating a second capital is complicated There’s more to it than just building backup

10:57 government offices. Japan’s entire financial  system and public infrastructure would have to

11:01 be redesigned to operate from 2 centers of power. One of the most important institutions taking the

11:06 plan seriously is the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the  country’s central bank and a pillar of Japan’s

11:13 economy. If even the BOJ has to prepare for a  second capital, it shows just how massive this

11:18 undertaking really is. Its current head office is  in Tokyo. But since the 2000s, the BOJ has been

11:24 creating emergency plans in the case of either a  total power failure at the head office, or worse.

11:29 It’s total destruction. Since the BOJ’s first ever branch was in Osaka,

11:34 it seemed like the natural city for the backup. If the BOJ Tokyo computer center goes offline

11:39 but the Tokyo office remains intact,  it continue running while processing

11:44 data through the Osaka backup center.  If Tokyo becomes completely unusable,

11:48 operations can be transferred entirely to Osaka. In other words, payments, settlements,

11:53 and other transfers that people in a post-natural  disaster crisis will be desperately in need of,

11:58 will continue without any problems.  To make sure that this plan will work,

12:01 the BOJ tests it every year, temporarily  shifting operations from Tokyo to Osaka.

12:06 The BOJ Osaka backup is like having a second,  identical Wall Street 300 miles (483 km) away.

12:12 To make sure the nation rebounds as quickly  as possible from a Tokyo earthquake,

12:16 new infrastructure projects are also being  planned accordingly. There’s a one trillion

12:20 yen - or $6,3 billion - Maglev project meant  to connect Tokyo to Nagoya and then Osaka.

12:26 The selling point of the new Maglev is speed.  It will run at around 310 mph (500 km/h). That’s

12:32 50% faster than the current shinkansen. The  Tokyo-Osaka trip would take just 67 minutes in

12:38 total. In comparison, the trip from Tokyo to Osaka  on the bullet train today takes about 2.5 hours.

12:43 But the construction of the line isn’t just  meant for speed; it’s also meant as a backup,

12:48 redundant transportation system for the current  bullet train between Tokyo and Osaka. Because

12:54 the shinkansen’s current route between the two  cities runs close to the Pacific Coast. It’s

12:59 considered highly vulnerable to a Nankai-caused  earthquake… and the tsunamis that might follow.

13:04 In contrast, 90% of the Maglev line runs through  tunnels in the mountains. This almost entirely

13:09 eliminates the Maglev’s vulnerability to  tsunamis. It also places the line further

13:14 away from the Nankai Trough. The design of the  Maglev train and rails also make derailment by

13:19 earthquake much less likely. The train levitates  above the track instead of sitting on rails. If

13:24 it’s pushed away from its track, it experiences  an even stronger magnetic force pushing it back.

13:30 So on paper, Japan seems prepared. The government, central bank,

13:33 and critical infrastructure are all building  backup systems to survive a Tokyo megaquake,

13:38 keeping the country running  even after an epic disaster.

13:41 But then you look closer. Because behind the impressive

13:45 preparations is a major weakness. Some of the most  important services Japan would depend on after a

13:50 disaster still have no concrete backup plan. Chief  among them, how the Prime Minister would actually

13:56 run the country from Osaka. Because the plan to  do so is vague, untested… and unlikely to work.

14:02 Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi agreed to the second  capital plan for Japan when she was desperately

14:08 seeking a coalition so her party, the LDP,  could remain in power. She needed the JIP on

14:14 her side. So, the plan to make a city - likely  Osaka - a backup capital for Japan was hatched.

14:19 But even though Takaichi approved the bill in  the summer of 2026, it has yet to pass the Upper

14:24 House. In fact, the deadline for deliberations  has already been extended. The bill itself is

14:30 also not a guarantee of much. Experts on Japanese  politics don’t think Takaichi is actually willing

14:35 to transfer real power from Tokyo to Osaka. International relations professor Stephen

14:40 Nagy says, “the JIP is… a regional party… it has  a vision of a more decentralised Japan that will

14:46 contribute to the economic growth of Osaka. There  is also the symbolism of moving some of the power

14:51 out of Tokyo. None of that appeals to the LDP.” Osaka is also generally more liberal,

14:57 which rubs the LDP the wrong way. As  Nagy continues to say, “the LDP has

15:01 no intention of diluting its own powers”. The legislation currently advancing through

15:06 Japan’s lawmaking bodies also sets limits  on the potential power of a second capital.

15:10 It ensures that the city chosen will work as a  functional backup; not a complete second capital.

15:16 While this may be the most practical and  affordable solution, it exposes the biggest

15:20 weakness of the plan. Osaka could keep the  government running during an emergency,

15:24 but it was never designed to become a permanent  center of power. Japan still has no real long-term

15:30 vision for governing from anywhere except Tokyo. Even the short-term plans have yet to be spelled

15:34 out and codified. There is no strategy drawn up  for how a prime minister would actually run the

15:39 government from anywhere other than Tokyo.  And the difficulties in doing so would be

15:44 immense for any government; but particularly for  Japan, due to some of its administrative quirks.

15:49 What happens to the people who keep  the country running? If politicians,

15:53 civil servants, and key administrators are  killed or injured, how would Japan replace

15:57 them? And how would thousands of personnel  be moved from Tokyo to Osaka on short notice?

16:02 In theory, the new Maglev could help. But  the revolutionary train system isn’t expected

16:06 to start operating until at least 2036… and  even that timeline is uncertain after years

16:12 of delays. So if the Tokyo megaquake happens  before then, Japan faces a terrifying question:

16:18 how do you relocate a government when the fastest  connection you were counting on doesn’t exist yet?

16:23 Assuming the earthquake  doesn’t strike before then.

16:26 That’s not even touching on the fact that  Japan’s government and corporations are

16:30 shockingly non-digital. A quick transfer  of government function and administration

16:34 seems very unlikely. Most people in Japan  still own and need a hanko stamp: a carved,

16:40 personalized stamp used for official documents  in place of a signature. So much of Japanese

16:45 government business is still conducted on paper. A 2023 report found that only 16.8% of Japanese

16:52 government records are digital. More than 4 in  5 official records are only preserved on paper.

16:58 This reality creates a nearly insurmountable  logistical hurdle for keeping the government

17:02 functioning in the event of a disaster that  would cause building collapse, flooding,

17:07 and fires. Digital files can be backed up  and uploaded to a cloud. Paper files would

17:12 be destroyed in the ensuing mess. That’s just the government.

17:16 The private sector is worse. A 2024 survey revealed that

17:20 17% of Japanese corporations only use  paper for internal documents. Meanwhile,

17:25 less than 10% of businesses are fully digital.  So over 90% rely on paper in some shape or form.

17:32 The potential devastation businesses might  experience after an earthquake is much worse.

17:36 Public discourse has also somewhat hindered the  advancement of a doomsday protocol for Tokyo.

17:41 Conservative newspapers have been critical  of the second capital plan altogether.

17:45 One publication, Yomiuri, wrote, “it does not  seem necessary to limit relocation sites for

17:51 ministries and agencies to a major city.  This is likely an issue to be considered

17:55 separately from the matter of the second capital.” They also dismissed the entire initial proposal

18:00 from the JIP as “difficult to understand.” The problem is that all this deliberation,

18:06 pushback, and uncertainty when it  comes to creating a second capital

18:09 is wasting precious time. Time Japan doesn’t have.

18:13 We are fast approaching the expected  date for the Nankai Trough to cause one

18:16 of its well-known megaquakes. And scientists  can’t predict exactly when it will happen.

18:22 Japan’s best hope at this point is that it  hits closer to the 150-year mark rather than

18:26 the 100-year mark. Because the latter situation  would put the next megaquake at 2044. The Japanese

18:33 government and financial institutions would  have just 18 years to complete one of the most

18:37 logistically challenging processes imaginable. Japan knows the clock is ticking. It

18:42 knows Tokyo is vulnerable. It knows a  disaster of historic scale is coming.

18:46 But knowing the problem and solving  it are two very different things.

18:50 Because when the Nankai Trough strikes,  Japan may discover that its greatest

18:53 weakness was never the earthquake itself. It was putting the fate of an entire nation,

18:58 and the global economy, into a single city. The Nankai Trough may be Japan’s next great

19:03 disaster… but it won’t be the first time the  country has faced a catastrophe of this scale.

19:08 Watch “How the Fukushima Disaster ACTUALLY  Happened” to see how a natural disaster turned

19:12 into one of the worst nuclear crises  in history. Or click on this video.
