• Title: Siren Head - EXPLAINED
  • Video ID: g2nXwiNl9tg
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 You decided to go hiking alone.

00:02 All those days indoors were starting to make you go a little stir-crazy, and even though

00:06 a thick blanket of fog was creeping in, you knew you just had to get out.

00:10 The local forest had a nice hiking trail – the kind of place where you could really get lost

00:14 in your thoughts.

00:15 But as you trudge through the foggy woods, bordered on all sides by thickets of towering

00:19 ever-greens, you hear a strange crackling noise.

00:23 Then harsh, modulated whispers, hissing out numbers and words with no logical configuration.

00:29 Must be an old radio, you think, and keep walking.

00:32 Just then you hear a quiet rustling in the trees behind you, and then footsteps, even

00:36 though you would have sworn you were alone.

00:38 Then it’s that crackling again, and those nonsense words and numbers.

00:43 “SIXTEEN.

00:44 THREE.

00:45 WOMAN.

00:46 FOURTEEN.

00:47 RIP.

00:48 DISGUSTING.”

00:49 It was like two voices at once, saying the same thing at exactly the same time.

00:53 You feel the hair on the back of your neck bristle, then you turn and see it.

00:57 Your jaw gapes in horror.

00:59 It’s huge – forty feet tall, rail-thin, with mummified skin clinging tight to its

01:04 bones.

01:05 You look up, hoping to see the creature’s face, but there is no face.

01:08 Just two metal sirens grafted to a long pole of flesh.

01:12 Before you can even scream, its long, spindly hands are already wrapping around your face.

01:17 You’ve just fallen victim to Sirenhead.

01:19 Like its numerous creepypasta predecessors, such as the Slender Man, Smile Dog, and The

01:25 Rake, Sirenhead is a kind of online cryptid that has entangled the internet in its web

01:29 of fear.

01:30 Despite only first appearing in August of 2018, this frightening, faceless monster has

01:34 become a hub of internet folklore and content creation.

01:37 It’s captured the imagination of thousands, appearing in countless pieces of fan art and

01:42 even popular indie games.

01:43 But what exactly is Sirenhead?

01:45 Where did it come from?

01:47 How did it get so popular and widespread in the first place?

01:49 And, like the best of urban legends, is there a hint of frightening truth behind the fiction?

01:54 Let’s start from the point of inception.

01:56 Sirenhead is the creation of Canadian illustrator and master of horror Trevor Henderson, better

02:01 known by his online handle of SlimySwampGhost.

02:04 Henderson is internet horror royalty, and is also no stranger to creating horrifying

02:09 online cryptids.

02:10 In fact, he’s already made a number of other iconic internet boogeymen.

02:14 These include Cartoon Cat, a terrifying, homicidal feline demon.

02:18 The Smile Room, a toothy nightmare hidden inside an abandoned bowling alley.

02:22 And the Fetid King , a mysterious and frightening entity able to manipulate technology, to name

02:27 just a handful.

02:29 But Sirenhead is, by far, Henderson’s most beloved creation.

02:32 He first appeared in a post on Henderson’s Tumblr blog back on August 19th, 2018, with

02:37 this image.

02:38 In the photo, taken at a distance, we see the imposing figure of Sirenhead looming over

02:42 an old, abandoned graveyard.

02:44 If this wasn’t creepy enough for you, the photo came with the following terrifying caption:

02:48 “She was on vacation with her husband and they were scoping out graveyards on the way,

02:52 as you do, when she saw it.

02:54 Rising out of the old cemetery, big as an old – macabre - telephone pole.

02:58 Was this some kind of bizarre art piece the authorities hadn’t gotten wise to yet?

03:02 Even as she stepped out of the car, the megaphones on its “head” screeched to life.

03:06 “NINE.

03:07 EIGHTEEN.

03:08 ONE.

03:09 CHILD.

03:10 SEVENTEEN.

03:11 REMOVE.

03:12 VILE.”.

03:13 A buzzing, doubled voice screamed random words at her.

03:14 At this point, it jerked into motion, striding down the hill towards her.”

03:17 The tags under the picture include the words “found footage”, perhaps even suggesting

03:21 some underlying truth to the events depicted here.

03:24 That’s enough to give anyone the willies.

03:26 After Sirenhead made his debut, thousands of people chimed in in response, stating just

03:30 how scary and captivating they found this strange new creature.

03:33 Little by little, Henderson began to drip-feed more information about this monstrous creature

03:37 to the public via his twitter account.

03:39 Each tweet painted a slightly more detailed picture of the horrifying threat we were dealing

03:44 with here.

03:45 In his first Twitter thread on the subject, Henderson stated that Sirenhead is the static

03:49 physical form of an unfathomable supernatural entity.

03:52 A being truly beyond any limits of human understanding.

03:56 For example, it doesn’t have eyes, but can still see.

03:59 Its teeth – hidden in gaping, fleshy mouths inside the sirens – are biological, but

04:03 the creature doesn’t eat.

04:04 It uses its similarities to a telephone pole to camouflage itself and hunt humans like

04:09 an ambush predator.

04:10 While its Siren-head can play siren noises, it typically communicates in odd snippets

04:15 of music or words.

04:16 It can also record and play back other sounds, similar to the sport-hunting alien from The

04:21 Predator, and is able to manipulate other noise-emitting devices.

04:23 In other words, while it might seem, at face value, like a brainless monster, Sirenhead

04:28 is an intelligent and powerful supernatural force.

04:31 While it spends large periods of time inactive, it can move scarily fast when it needs to

04:35 – say, for example, when it’s chasing you down through the woods.

04:38 It also tends to avoid major population centres, preferring to stalk areas where victims won’t

04:43 have anyone to save them.

04:45 But, as you’ll soon find out, that doesn’t mean you’re any safer tucked away at home

04:48 in the burbs…

04:49 In the second Tweet about Sirenhead, Henderson shared a frightening image of the creature

04:54 lurking in someone’s backyard.

04:55 The caption indicated that Sirenhead was responsible for the disappearance of a family of four

05:00 in their own home.

05:01 They were gone without a trace, with the neighbours just reporting the patio door being left open

05:05 in their absence.

05:06 The quiet suburbs are actually one of Sirenhead’s favourite hunting grounds, as shown by the

05:10 next frightening found photo shared.

05:12 When Sirenhead abducted people on the seemingly innocent streets outside their own homes,

05:17 there were always three commonalities: It was always people walking the side streets

05:21 on their way home, it was always dark by the time people started wondering where they were,

05:25 and it was always past the time when the street lights come on.

05:28 The fact that Sirenhead can also perfectly disguise itself as a normal street lamp just

05:33 adds another dimension of terror to the creature.

05:35 How can you ever feel safe walking past street lamps in the dark again?

05:39 Sirenhead can appear almost anywhere dark, secluded, and depopulated, so you can never

05:44 let your guard down when you’re in one of these areas.

05:46 He’s been spotted everywhere from Yellowstone National Park in 2016 to a darkened country

05:51 lake to the parking lot of an unassuming motel, always causing unexplained paranormal activity

05:56 and disappearances in his wake.

05:59 Worse still – for all members of the human race who like living safe, comfortable lives

06:03 – it’s been hinted that Sirenhead is part of a far grander and more dangerous picture,

06:07 almost like a “hype man” for some other unnamed but presumably far more powerful and

06:12 dangerous entity.

06:13 It has also been said that the proper collective noun for a group of Sirenheads is a “static”,

06:18 implying that Sirenhead may not even be a singular being, but just one member of a whole

06:23 species of dangerous cryptids.

06:25 Though Henderson himself has mentioned that he sees Sirenhead as more of a manifestation

06:30 than simple animal, and it doesn’t therefore abide by the same set of physical rules that

06:34 creatures from our plane of existence are forced to conform to.

06:37 Because of this, the true extent of Sirenhead’s power is unknowable, especially considering

06:42 that so many who encounter it don’t seem to live to tell the tale.

06:46 Though as with any good urban legend, Sirenhead’s legend didn’t end with its creator.

06:50 Sirenhead quickly became a worldwide sensation thanks to an unlikely force: Online indie

06:55 video games.

06:56 Two video game artefacts featuring Sirenhead were made initially, one being a mod for the

07:00 game Fallout 4 called “Whispering Hills”, and another five-minute Sirenhead game developed

07:05 by indie games studio Modus Interactive.

07:08 While neither of these games were an immediate smash hit back in 2018, they found a second

07:12 life a couple years later after being picked up by a number of prominent YouTubers..

07:16 From here, Sirenhead’s popularity exploded to unprecedented levels.

07:20 He quickly became the subject of countless creepypasta short horror stories the world

07:24 over, as well as hundreds or even thousands of pieces of fan art.

07:28 People were also making home-made Sirenhead dolls and action figures, Lego sculptures

07:33 and even Halloween costumes Outside the gaming community, Sirenhead was

07:36 becoming the internet equivalent of a household name.

07:39 The creature had gained its own subreddit, where fans feverishly discuss theories and

07:43 ideas and share fan-made content.

07:45 In early 2020, Sirenhead also gained a huge boost in popularity from TikTok, after user

07:50 Alex Howard posted a frightening CGI video of Sirenhead lumbering across a town in the

07:55 horizon while sirens blared menacingly.

07:58 This ten second clip not only scared the bejeezus out of the internet, but was also insanely

08:04 memeable.

08:05 Variations of the video were used in everything from making fun of the strange name of Elon

08:09 Musk’s new baby, to one particularly creative version where Sirenhead dances to South Korean

08:14 hit single “Gangnam Style.”

08:15 So, let’s pump the breaks for a second.

08:17 You’re probably wondering: If Sirenhead is just some character made by an online horror

08:21 artist, what’s all the fuss about?

08:22 It’s not like he’s real, right?

08:24 Well, the answer to that question might be a little more complicated than you’d imagine.

08:28 To fully understand, we need to take a look at one of the most iconic internet urban legends

08:32 of all time: The Slender Man.

08:34 This dapper, faceless, internet boogeyman was created by Eric Knudsen in 2009, but quickly

08:39 spun into a phenomenon with a life of its own, as you can find out in one of our other

08:43 videos, “How A Meme (Slenderman) Became Real.”

08:46 The Slender Man’s immense popularity quickly made him a fixture of the internet’s public

08:50 consciousness, much like Sirenhead, with fan art, costumes, spin-off games and fan films.

08:55 The dark ending of the Slender Man saga was a near-fatal stabbing supposedly inspired

09:00 by the character in 2014, and a pretty lame movie adaptation four years later.

09:05 Why is all this relevant to Sirenhead?

09:07 Because, if you read quite literally any article about him, you’re more than likely to see

09:11 the phrase “the next slender man” pop up.

09:14 And this comparison isn’t without merit – as both have starkly similar points of

09:18 origins and trajectories into popularity.

09:20 The lines between fiction and reality become blurred, and in a metaphorical sense, when

09:25 enough people believe in the urban legend, to them it might as well be real.

09:29 In a more spooky, mystical, supernatural sense, characters like Sirenhead and the Slender

09:33 Man are often associated with the concept of “Tulpas” or “Thought-Forms.”

09:37 This is the idea in paranormal circles – and proponents of Tibetan mysticism – that one

09:42 can quite literally believe a being into autonomous existence through the sheer force of their

09:47 psychic energy.

09:48 When you believe in the idea of Tulpas, the concept of the internet’s collective fear

09:52 bringing Sirenhead to life on some level is a real and tangible concern.

09:56 Sure, it may seem like a far-fetched concept, but is it any more far-fetched than the idea

10:01 of being stalked by a forty-foot extra-dimensional zombie with a siren for a head on the way

10:05 home from work?

10:06 At the end of the day, regardless of what you believe, it can’t be denied that something

10:10 special and terrifying has been brought into the world with Sirenhead.

10:13 Is Sirenhead real?

10:15 Well, ultimately, he’s as real as any urban legend – whether it’s the man with the

10:18 hook hand, the killer in the back seat, or the man making sinister calls from inside

10:22 the house.

10:23 And like any great urban legend, Sirenhead is sure to feel a whole lot more real next

10:28 time you’re walking home alone at night, you hear a faint crackle somewhere in the

10:32 distance, and you could swear you saw something move in the corner of your eye…

10:36 Check out “Russian Sleep Experiment – EXPLAINED” and “How A Meme (Slenderman) Became Real”

10:40 for more on the spookiest corners of the world wide web.

10:43 If, of course, you’re brave enough…

docs.text:
00:00 [SQUEAKING]

00:01 [RUSTLING]

00:03 [CLICKING]

00:06

00:11 MICHAEL SCOTT ASATO CUTHBERT: Hello, computational music

00:13 theorists.

00:14 Here's a short video on what some of the problems in MIR,

00:19 or Music Information Retrieval, are and how they can be

00:23 connected to music theory and musicology,

00:26 which is the main topic of this class, 21m.383.

00:31 These slides owe a lot to Avi Pfeffer, professor at Harvard,

00:36 who inspired them with his lectures.

00:40 The main question that we'll be working on

00:42 is, how do we move from sound that's made in the real world

00:49 to a score that's printed out or displayed on the screen?

00:53 What kinds of technologies are needed,

00:56 and what kinds of problems need to be solved in order to do this

00:59 really well?

01:00 Well, first, when we sing or play an instrument,

01:03 we're making actual sound waves in the real world,

01:06 so we need to solve the problem of how

01:08 to most accurately transform sound into a signal.

01:13 And this involves microphones and other devices,

01:16 and it's kind of a pure engineering problem

01:19 that we're not going to be focusing on in this class.

01:22 But it's very complex and very valuable,

01:25 and we offer some courses in the music department

01:27 that will help you do this better.

01:30 But once we've got the sound from the real world

01:34 into an electrical signal, we're working

01:38 in the time domain, as we call it,

01:41 and that is the amplitude of sound at a single moment--

01:46 forward, backwards, positive, or negative.

01:48 And we usually record in something close to CD quality

01:54 or 44,000 times per second.

01:56 We're measuring the amplitude as a 16-bit signed integer.

02:00 And so the sound, at this point, looks something like this

02:05 if this was, I don't know, an attack

02:08 of an instrument that's decaying,

02:09 maybe a piano or something of that sort.

02:14 The problem here is, how do we convert from the time domain

02:18 to frequency, to being able to say, OK, all these impulses add

02:24 up to a particular frequency?

02:27 How do we decode it from the signal

02:31 and understand that, hey, in this sound,

02:33 there's two principal frequencies that

02:36 are being heard?

02:38 And to do this, we use Fourier transforms,

02:41 and the fast Fourier transform algorithm

02:44 is something that is very good to know in order

02:48 to work in this field.

02:49 So now we have frequencies, and we

02:51 want to translate them to pitch and pitch connections.

02:57 And that's not just thinking about,

03:00 what is A, 440 hertz or something,

03:02 but which of those frequencies that pop up are

03:05 prolonged to make a particular pitch?

03:08 Because even while I'm speaking, there are particular frequencies

03:12 that are popping up, but they don't necessarily make pitches.

03:15 The attack on a flute isn't necessarily the pitch

03:21 that we want.

03:21 So which ones are connected for this?

03:24 And once we have these particular frequency pitch

03:26 connections, we want to move from there to pitch notes.

03:32 As we saw with the piano example,

03:35 there were two frequencies there.

03:36 Does that mean two pitches, or is

03:38 one of them a reverberation in the room?

03:41 Or if you're listening to another instrument,

03:44 maybe you hear seven pitches.

03:46 Six of them are higher and much quieter,

03:49 and you might think, oh, that's the overtone series

03:52 of that instrument.

03:53 And so going from pitch connections to pitch notes

03:56 involves an estimation of timbre.

03:59 What is the timbre of the instrument?

04:01 What is the overtone series that one expects

04:04 and who we remove them.

04:06 And from there, do we end up still with multiple pitches

04:08 in a chord?

04:11 Now that we know the musical pitches

04:15 that we're interested in, we want

04:16 to go from there to understanding

04:20 the duration of these pitches and the tempo of the piece.

04:24 And so there are particular algorithms

04:26 that we can use to estimate the duration.

04:29 I mean, one thing is you just look at milliseconds and things

04:32 and then say, OK, well, that's going

04:34 to be the most common note.

04:35 We'll call it a quarter note and so on.

04:38 And from there, we can estimate the tempo.

04:41 Or we can do it in the other way.

04:44 We can take all these pitches and try

04:47 to estimate a tempo based on, what are the recurring

04:51 onsets that seem to be beats?

04:54 And from there, go and figure out the duration-- quarter note,

04:58 half note, three beats long, something like that

05:01 for each of the notes.

05:03 So which direction do MIR people go?

05:08 It turns out that we usually create a sort of feedback loop.

05:12 So we try to do both at once, and estimations of tempo

05:16 lead to durations, which then can be rejected or accepted,

05:20 and estimations of the duration lead to estimations of tempo.

05:25 And so the technologies involved are

05:27 beat tracking and self-similarity detection

05:30 and others.

05:32 From the pitches, the duration, and the tempo,

05:36 we can create what we call the full notes or just the notes.

05:42 That is something from a pitch and a duration combined.

05:47 From all these full notes, we can

05:50 construct what we call a virtual score,

05:53 and that is the score as represented

05:56 purely as collections of notes and other events.

06:01 We might be estimating, at this point, crescendos

06:04 and decrescendos, and maybe we're

06:06 hearing certain notes are slurred,

06:07 and we're keeping these all as objects inside memory.

06:12 And so this involves the technology

06:14 of music representation, which we will be getting

06:17 to very soon in this class.

06:18 And so how might we represent a score, maybe as

06:22 a set of parts with measures and notes in between?

06:24

06:27 From the virtual score, we need to figure out, OK,

06:32 how is this going to look on the page or on the screen?

06:35 And so we perform layout estimation,

06:39 and we create a laid-out score where it's not just

06:42 notes inside of an array or a list or something

06:45 like that but actual positions on a page.

06:50 And this involves some technologies

06:52 that we'll be getting to in the class.

06:54 Here's an example of very poor layout estimation.

06:58

07:01 From the laid-out score, we choose

07:05 what the glyphs that would be appropriate are

07:07 and where are they going to be placed on the page?

07:11 A sample of some of the things that might

07:13 be involved in doing that.

07:17 And then once we have the laid-out score,

07:19 the glyph selection, and placement,

07:21 we move to pixel rendering, individual

07:25 dots no longer connected to any semantic meaning but just,

07:28 is this x, y coordinate going to be black, white, or something

07:33 in between or something else?

07:36 And from there, we have particular technologies

07:40 that we're going to need, such as screen

07:42 drawing, old-school cathode ray tubes, LED display, things

07:47 like that, or how to actually make a printer distribute ink

07:51 on a page.

07:51 And these, again, are engineering problems

07:53 that are beyond the scope of this class but still

07:56 very, very important.

07:58 So let's look, again, a summary of what we have here.

08:01 We move from the time domain to frequency,

08:04 frequency to pitch connections.

08:06 We estimate the duration and the tempo, creating full notes.

08:10 Create a virtual score or logical score.

08:13 Some people separate these two out.

08:15 Then we try to make the layout and to the output.

08:19 At each of these points in the process,

08:24 we can involve music theory or musicology,

08:28 and we can learn aspects about music theory or musicology

08:32 from the data that we're getting at this point.

08:35 So, for instance, the duration/tempo level,

08:39 we can start to ask, well, what are the most commonly

08:41 used rhythms in this piece?

08:43 And from there, hey, let's create a backing drum track

08:46 to accompany the soloist because we figured out

08:50 what kinds of durations, what kinds of rhythms

08:53 connect to this with a database, so on.

08:56 Or at the frequency to pitch connections level,

09:02 we can now understand, based on which

09:04 overtones were removed, what instruments were being used?

09:07 Are they playing in their natural ranges?

09:09 And from there, we might estimate

09:11 the year of this recording based on particular sounds

09:15 and sound artifacts or the year of the piece

09:18 based on instruments that are used and so on.

09:21 So these are places where music theory and musicology can

09:25 get data from this MIR process.

09:30 But there's another side that's been much less talked about

09:33 and it's a place of great potential

09:35 that I think people in this class

09:37 will be able to contribute to, and that

09:39 is going from music theory or musicology

09:42 back and using things that we know

09:46 about theory or history of music or music studies

09:49 to enhance the quality of the algorithms being

09:53 used in these places.

09:54 For instance, at the pitch connection level,

09:57 we can say, well, let's look at the metadata,

10:00 and it suggests that this is a piece by Mozart.

10:03 He died in 1791.

10:04 So let's look at those instruments.

10:06 Now, the frequency, overtone estimation was saying, OK,

10:12 the most likely instrument is electric guitar.

10:14 This is very likely wrong.

10:16 I mean, I don't know.

10:17 Maybe it's a modern arrangement, but it's pretty likely wrong.

10:21 Why don't you try this overtone profile of a fortepiano,

10:24 an early piano instead?

10:26 And wow, you find out, OK, that was the second-best score

10:30 but probably the best one when taking into account

10:33 the metadata on the piece.

10:34

10:37 Or we can use music theory and musicology

10:41 at the frequency-detection level.

10:43 So we might say, hey, all of the notes

10:44 you've been detecting around this note have been in E major.

10:47 And then you hear an A sharp, and that's a little fishy.

10:53 Oh, hey, there's a runner-up note

10:55 of A natural that was 95% as likely.

11:00 From a music-theory standpoint, I think that, more likely,

11:05 we've detected the wrong note.

11:07 So these are ways that music theory and musicology

11:10 can enhance this process.

11:13 Most exciting at all, though, is when parts of the process

11:18 feed into music theory and musicology algorithms

11:23 and are enhanced by it.

11:24 So we say, oh, hey, given these frequencies,

11:26 pitches, durations, we get the style of the piece,

11:30 and we suggest that it's from the swing era.

11:34 And then we can help later parts of the process by saying,

11:41 if the style of the piece is from the swing era,

11:43 when you do your virtual score, your logical score,

11:45 probably all those triplets, those "yum, ba bum, ba bum,

11:49 ba bum" should be written down and represented as eighth notes.

11:53 That's what, conceptually, they are.

11:55

11:57 But we can not just move forward.

12:00 We can, at the virtual score level,

12:02 maybe it's beginning to lay out the score,

12:05 and they're putting everything nicely into 3/4.

12:08 And the musicology or music-theory algorithm says,

12:12 well, these rhythms are highly unusual for 3/4 time.

12:17 Let's go back and rerun some of the previous steps with that

12:21 notion that that was highly improbable and try to make

12:25 the score again so we can move backwards in time,

12:28 redo a particular part of the process, rerun it,

12:32 and then maybe come up with a different result.

12:36 We'll put this in 6/8.

12:38 So here are some of the ways that music theory and musicology

12:41 can feed back into the MIR sound-to-score process.

12:47 Next time, sometime soon, I hope to say

12:50 how we can go the opposite direction, how

12:53 we can take a score and automatically perform it.

12:56 And even though we're going to be

12:58 going in the opposite direction, it

12:59 turns out that there's a totally different set of problems

13:02 that we have to solve.

13:04

02:45 location.

02:46 The main objective for U.S. forces was to take Kadena Air Base, which would then serve

02:51 as a launching point for Operation Downfall, the name given to the invasion of Japan.

02:55 Thousands of Allied ships, planes, and vehicles carried out attacks across the island, but

02:59 the Japanese were dug in and ready.

03:01 They launched kamikaze counter offensives and made sure to strike key targets to slow

03:05 the Allied advance.

03:07 It was a bloodbath for both sides.

03:09 The Battle of Okinawa resulted in the highest number of casualties of any battle in the

03:13 Pacific.

03:14 It’s estimated that somewhere around 160,000 military personnel died while fighting for

03:18 control of the island.

03:20 The United States lost close to 50,000 men while Japan lost somewhere between 80,000

03:24 to 115,000 people.

03:26 The saddest part is that the biggest loss of life was for the Okinawans themselves.

03:30 Nearly half of the 300,000 people who lived on the island before the attack died during

03:35 the battle.

03:36 Some were forced to enlist in the Japanese army, while others were innocent victims caught

03:40 in the firefights and bombings that took place across the island.

03:43 After months of fighting the United States secured victory on the island and gained control

03:47 of the airfield.

03:48 However, even once the majority of Japanese forces were defeated, the Americans still

03:53 had to contend with guerilla fighters and small Japanese units sprinkled around the

03:57 island.

03:58 They would hide in the forests and sabotage U.S. operations whenever an opportunity presented

04:02 itself.

04:03 Patrols often found themselves being ambushed out of nowhere as they let their guard down

04:06 thinking the enemy threat had been dealt with.

04:09 In fact, some Japanese soldiers never received word that the war had ended and continued

04:13 fighting for many years after Japan surrendered and World War II was officially over.

04:18 The loss of life and military assets during the Battle of Okinawa gave U.S. intelligence

04:22 pause.

04:23 If the Japanese were able to inflict such damage on a small piece of land hundreds of

04:27 miles away from their main island, what would it cost Allied forces if they were to invade

04:31 Japan itself?

04:32 The loss of life would be unimaginable, and it was hypothesized that it would take years

04:36 to finally subdue Japanese forces.

04:39 If there was another way to force Japan into surrendering, the U.S. needed to find it quickly.

04:43 As the Battle of Okinawa raged on in the Pacific, President Franklin D. Roosevelt died of an

04:48 intracerebral hemorrhage in the brain on April 12, 1945.

04:53 Harry Truman was sworn into office as the next President of the United States and immediately

04:57 started making difficult decisions about the war in the Pacific.

05:00 After word reached Truman that Okinawa had been secured at a great cost, he tasked his

05:05 advisors with finding a way to force Japan to surrender.

05:07 And he wanted it done with minimal U.S. casualties.

05:10 Unfortunately at the time, there was no good option.

05:13 It had become clear that Emporer Hirohito would not submit willingly.

05:16 In fact, everyone in Japan believed that they would win the war and were willing to lay

05:20 down their lives to make sure that happened.

05:22 Men, women, and children; military, civilian, and elderly; all Japanese citizens would rather

05:26 have died than surrender their country to a foreign power.

05:29 This meant that regardless of what Truman decided to do, lives would be lost.

05:33 The question was: just how many people needed to die in order for World War II to come to

05:38 a close?

05:39 Soon after the transition of power from Roosevelt to Truman, the new president was made aware

05:43 of a top-secret weapon that was being developed by scientists in Los Alamos, New Mexico.

05:47 It was known as the Manhattan Project—named after the location of the team’s first office

05:51 in New York City—and would result in the world’s first atomic bomb.

05:55 After the successful test of the first nuclear bomb ever created on July 16, 1945, at Alamogordo

06:01 Bombing Range, Truman believed that the atomic bomb could be his only way to force Japan

06:06 into surrendering.

06:07 Truman asked a committee of advisors led by the Secretary of War Henry Stimson to determine

06:12 if using the atomic bomb on Japan was the best course of action to end the bloody war.

06:17 After seeing the devastating effects of the nuclear explosion, the committee did not take

06:20 this task lightly.

06:22 They knew that if the U.S. detonated an atomic bomb on Japanese soil, the civilian casualties

06:26 would be immense.

06:28 But it was determined that an invasion of Japan would be even more costly for both sides.

06:32 Most of the committee concluded that the bomb should be used.

06:35 Stimson was a huge advocate that this was the right decision.

06:38 So, under the advisement of the committee, President Harry Truman issued the Potsdam

06:42 Declaration on July 26, 1945, which called for the unconditional surrender of Japan.

06:48 Truman warned that if the Japanese Emperor did not comply, there would be “prompt and

06:51 utter destruction.”

06:52 There was no way that Japanese leaders could have known what Truman was talking about as

06:56 they had never seen a nuclear explosion before or even knew that such a bomb existed.

07:01 This is one of the main problems with trying to justify that using the atomic bomb.

07:04 The Potsdam Declaration would have been outrageous to the Japanese Emperor and his advisors.

07:09 They knew that if the United States invaded their island, they could depend on the masses

07:12 to fight until the very last person fell.

07:15 The Japanese people would not give up their homeland to an invading enemy and the Japanese

07:18 leadership was pretty confident that they could cause enough casualties to the Allied

07:22 forces that, at the very worst, they would end up negotiating a truce.

07:25 This would allow Japan to make a few demands of their own such as maintaining control of

07:29 their country.

07:30 However, this was not an option for Allied forces.

07:33 They would not negotiate; it was either unconditional surrender by Japan or nothing.

07:37 When Truman did not receive a reply from Emperor Hirohito he gave the order to drop the bomb.

07:42 On August 6, 1945, a Boeing B-29 called Enola Gay took off from an airfield on Tinian Island.

07:48 In its cargo hold was “Little Boy,” the first atomic bomb ever to be used in war.

07:53 At 8:15 A.M.

07:54 the Enola Gay spotted Hiroshima.

07:56 The crew prepared to drop the bomb and get the hell out of dodge before it detonated.

08:00 The signal was given.

08:01 Red lights flashed as the bomb bay doors opened.

08:04 Little Boy was dropped 31,000 feet above the city of Hiroshima.

08:07 44 seconds later there was a bright flash as the atomic bomb detonated 1,500 feet before

08:12 hitting the ground.

08:13 Approximately 70,000 people were instantly incinerated by the blast.

08:17 The Japanese finally found out what Truman meant by “prompt and utter destruction.”

08:21 It’s unclear what exactly was being discussed by Japanese leadership immediately after the

08:25 bomb was dropped, but when no declaration of surrender came three days after Hiroshima

08:29 was bombed, the U.S. decided to try again.

08:32 On August 9, 1945, a different B-29 named Bockscar carried a second, larger, atomic

08:37 bomb named “Fat Man” towards Nagaski.

08:40 The bomb was dropped, and the instant it detonated, 40,000 more Japanese civilian and military

08:45 personnel were consumed in the fiery blast.

08:47 Both Hiroshima and Nagasaki had been wiped off the face of the planet by the atomic bombs.

08:52 Japan was now ready to surrender.

08:53 Talks between Japanese leadership and the United States began, and on September 2, 1945,

08:58 Japan officially signed documents of surrender on board the USS Missouri.

09:02 The question is: was the use of the atomic bomb justified by the United States?

09:06 Was there another way to convince Japan to surrender, or did tens of thousands of Japanese

09:11 civilians need to die?

09:12 We’ll present you with evidence for both sides of this argument, but you will ultimately

09:16 have to decide for yourself.

09:17 You may be surprised at which side you choose.

09:19 After the atomic bombs were dropped and the United States occupied Japan, some shocking

09:23 information was discovered about Japan’s plans for ending the war.

09:27 According to Japanese military officers and soldiers, they knew where the U.S. invasion

09:31 was going to land and had already begun preparing to inflict as much damage as possible to their

09:35 forces.

09:36 Their orders were to repel Allied forces for as long as possible and inflict casualties

09:40 by any means necessary.

09:42 Most of the Japanese military strategists knew that they would not be able to stop the

09:45 invasion.

09:46 But it was also known that the island's entire population would fight until they were all

09:50 killed.

09:51 Surrender was not an option for the Japanese people and they believed that was better to

09:55 die fighting than to lose their homeland to the invading force.

09:58 Knowing this, U.S. military leaders were convinced that they had made the right decision.

10:02 There were over 70 million people who lived on the island, and it was predicted that everyone

10:06 from children to grandmas would do their part to stop the invading Allied forces.

10:11 This included makeshift kamikaze runs by civilians using grenades or other explosives.

10:15 The carnage would have been unfathomable.

10:17 Therefore, by detonating the atomic bombs, the military concluded that tens of thousands

10:21 of U.S. soldiers' lives were saved along with millions of Japanese lives.

10:26 Another argument to justify the use of the atomic bomb is that war itself is inhumane.

10:31 The bombs dropped on Japan helped end World War II, and therefore, it was the right call.

10:35 To put it into perspective, in March of 1945, the United States dropped incendiary bombs

10:39 on Tokyo.

10:40 This caused massive fires to sweep across the city and consume everything in their path,

10:45 including civilians.

10:46 It is estimated that well over 100,000 people were killed in the Tokyo bombing.

10:50 So, was this any better than dropping an atomic bomb?

10:53 The long-term effects of both situations are different.

10:55 Over 1 million people lost their homes in the Tokyo bombing, but those who survived

10:59 did not need to worry about radiation poisoning and cancer like the survivors of the atomic

11:04 bomb blasts.

11:05 A home can be rebuilt, but death by radiation cannot be avoided.

11:08 It was also estimated by General MacArthur that even if the Japanese government was forced

11:12 to surrender after the invasion, there would still be countless guerrilla groups that would

11:16 hide in the forests and mountains on the island that would need to be dealt with.

11:19 They would continuously wreak havoc at U.S. installations and oppose the new government

11:24 that would be put in place.

11:25 MacArthur concluded it would take a million U.S. troops ten years to deal with the rogue

11:29 Japanese soldiers.

11:30 At that point, the war may have been over on paper, but the battle would still continue

11:34 for U.S. soldiers stationed in Japan.

11:36 It’s also important to note that many Japanese people still thought that they could win the

11:39 war even after the atomic bombs were dropped.

11:42 The Emperor himself needed to declare the war over, or the people of Japan would keep

11:46 on fighting.

11:47 The atomic bombs forced Japanese leadership to concede and to tell their citizens that

11:51 they had lost the war and it was now time for peace.

11:54 This led to several civilian and military groups taking up arms and revolting against

11:58 their own government as they believed there should be no surrender.

12:01 But these attempts to overthrow the government were put down by the Japanese military, and

12:05 the unconditional surrender commenced.

12:07 A less strong argument for using the atomic bomb, yet one that Harry Truman used after

12:11 he left office, was that Japan started it.

12:14 This may sound childish but many Americans wanted revenge for what the Japanese did at

12:18 Pearl Harbor.

12:19 In 1958, the City Council of Hiroshima passed a resolution condemning Truman for ordering

12:23 the atomic bomb to be dropped on their city.

12:25 Truman responded that he did not blame the council for condemning what he did, but he

12:29 claimed the United States had “been shot in the back,” referencing the attack at

12:32 Pearl Harbor.

12:33 He concluded his letter back to the council that the atomic bombs saved hundreds of thousands

12:37 of Americans and Japanese lives.

12:39 Therefore, it was justified.

12:40 Some historians think that the American people would have forced Truman to use the atomic

12:44 bomb even if he had decided not to initially.

12:47 As more and more American soldiers died in the war and information about the successful

12:51 test of a nuclear bomb in New Mexico got out, the public would have pressured Truman to

12:55 use the new weapon of mass destruction, or they would be happy to elect someone to office

12:59 who would.

13:00 It’s hotly debated whether demonstrating the capability of the atomic bomb by dropping

13:03 it on an uninhabited piece of land for the Japanese to see would have been enough to

13:08 cause them to surrender.

13:09 Many scientists in Truman's initial committee of advisors believed that this show of force

13:13 would indeed have been enough.

13:15 However, the military personnel felt differently.

13:17 The Japanese people were so invested in the war that merely demonstrating the atomic bomb's

13:22 potential may have been seen as an empty threat.

13:24 Therefore, it was concluded that the bomb must be dropped on a city that had military

13:29 significance.

13:30 The decision of which cities to bomb did not fall to Truman but to military leaders.

13:34 Both Hiroshima and Nagasaki were chosen because they had military manufacturing facilities.

13:38 However, this does beg the question: why couldn’t the bomb just have been dropped on a military

13:42 facility away from any major cities?

13:44 There were plenty of Japanese bases that were isolated from civilian populations, so why

13:49 couldn’t one of these have been the target?

13:50 This question has also been debated over the decades without any clear answer as to why

13:54 hitting a military base couldn’t have been tried first.

13:57 This brings us to an unsettling idea.

13:59 Maybe dropping the atomic bombs on two Japanese cities was not justified.

14:03 The main reason why many believe that dropping the atomic bombs was unethical is that the

14:07 U.S. military intentionally targeted civilian populations.

14:11 Many believe that the United States used terrorist-like tactics to force the Japanese government to

14:16 surrender.

14:17 Even current military ethics courses in the United States make justifying the dropping

14:20 of the atomic bombs difficult.

14:22 When tough decisions need to be made during war and collateral damage is inevitable, the

14:26 proportionality of benefit to cost needs to be weighed.

14:29 It’s agreed upon by many military officials and historians today that the destruction

14:33 of military targets at Hiroshima and Nagasaki was nowhere near proportionate to the loss

14:38 of civilian life.

14:39 This makes dropping the bombs on these cities an unjustifiable choice.

14:42 For people who think dropping the atomic bomb was necessary but that a military target should

14:46 have been chosen, it’s often cited that the bomb should have been dropped in the southern

14:50 part of Kyushu.

14:51 It was here where Japanese troops were massing to mount a defense against the U.S. invasion.

14:55 Not only would this have been of strategic significance, but it would have minimized

14:59 the civilian casualties by targeting an area that was mostly filled with military personnel.

15:03 And although some believe that dropping a demonstration bomb wouldn’t have resulted

15:07 in Japan surrendering, not everyone sees it this way.

15:10 If the United States had detonated a bomb where high-ranking Japanese officers could

15:14 see it, it’s very plausible they would recommend to the Emperor that peace talks should begin

15:18 immediately.

15:19 Also, if the demonstration didn’t work, the next option still wouldn’t have to be

15:22 blowing up a city full of civilians, as they could have tried dropping the bomb on a military

15:26 base first.

15:27 But the fact that the very first target was a densely populated city where 70,000 people

15:32 were obliterated by a single bomb seems like an extreme first choice when there were other,

15:36 more justifiable options.

15:38 Many historians also believe that if a demonstration atomic bomb was used, the Emperor of Japan

15:42 would be willing to enter negotiations.

15:45 Although it’s probable the U.S. would have refused this option as they wanted Japan's

15:48 unconditional surrender.

15:50 But it has been argued that if the United States had been willing to negotiate, Japan

15:53 would have come to the table after an atomic bomb demonstration.

15:56 In fact, even without a demonstration, it’s thought that most high-ranking officials in

16:00 the military and government already knew the war was lost.

16:03 So, it’s not out of the realm of possibility that if the United States had been willing

16:07 to let Emperor Hirohito stay in power, Japan would have surrendered.

16:11 This would have all been possible without the mass murder of over 100,000 civilians

16:14 by atomic bombs.

16:16 But there was another factor that would have almost certainly led to the surrender of Japan.

16:20 It had nothing to do with nuclear explosions or the United States.

16:23 Instead, at the same time the U.S. was dropping its second atom bomb, the Soviet Union declared

16:28 war on Japan.

16:29 There was no way that Japan could have defeated both the U.S. and Allied forces in the Pacific

16:34 as well as the Soviet Union advancing from the west.

16:37 Japan knew this, and it’s very plausible that if the United States had waited for the

16:41 Soviet Union to declare war on Japan, they would never have had to drop the atomic bombs

16:45 in the first place.

16:46 Japan’s plan at the time was to cause enough American losses that they would be forced

16:50 to negotiate a settlement.

16:52 The average Japanese citizen and soldier might have believed that Japan could still win the

16:56 war, but the leadership was not under the same delusion.

16:59 They were just weighing their options and trying to figure out the best outcome.

17:02 However, once the Soviet Union declared war on Japan, it was only a matter of time before

17:06 they became overwhelmed on multiple fronts.

17:08 As soon as the Soviet Union joined the battle, they steamrolled their way through Japanese

17:12 lines in Manchuria and pushed deeper and deeper into Japanese controlled territories.

17:16 Once this happened Japan likely would have sought out a deal with the United States even

17:19 if they hadn’t dropped the atomic bombs.

17:21 The reason for this is because Japan already knew that if the Soviets invaded, it would

17:25 have been a very different type of occupation than if the United States was in charge.

17:29 Japan likely already had information about the way that occupied territories in Europe

17:33 were being treated by the Allies versus the Soviets.

17:36 The Soviets did not have the best reputation.

17:38 They tended to incorporate territories into the Soviet Union and brutally strip them of

17:42 their national identity.

17:44 Knowing this, Japan may have seen occupation by the United States as a better option if

17:48 they were to surrender.

17:49 And since the Soviets were closing in quickly, Japan may have reached out to the U.S. and

17:53 surrendered even if the atomic bombs hadn’t been dropped.

17:55 And if this is the case, then the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were not

17:59 justified at all.

18:00 There is no doubt that at the time, the majority of the American public believed using the

18:04 atomic bomb was completely justified.

18:07 In fact, a Gallup poll that was conducted almost immediately after the bombs were dropped

18:10 in 1945 found that 85% of Americans approved of the decision.

18:15 This is a huge amount of support, which may be why Truman felt pressure to give the order.

18:19 It is important to remember that although Truman authorized the use of atomic weapons,

18:23 a committee of military personnel made the decision of where to strike.

18:26 In a Pew survey conducted in the last several years, the sentiment of the American people

18:30 has changed drastically about the use of atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

18:35 Now only around 50% of U.S. citizens believe it was justified.

18:38 There are probably several reasons for this.

18:40 For one, many of the people who were alive during World War II and were impacted by Pearl

18:45 Harbor are no longer with us.

18:47 People who are further removed from such a tragic event tend to have less emotional investment

18:51 and, therefore, may think more critically about a decision that cost the lives of over

18:55 100,000 civilians.

18:56 We also now know much more about the long-term effects that nuclear weapons can have on people

19:01 and the terrible diseases that can result from radiation poisoning.

19:04 Many individuals don’t think anything justifies killing so many civilians, even during a World

19:09 War.

19:10 This is especially true since there were other options besides dropping the atomic bombs

19:13 on heavily populated cities.

19:15 There are arguments to be made for both sides of the atomic bomb debate, but there are a

19:19 few undeniable facts.

19:20 The United States targeted cities with civilians when they had the option of demonstrating

19:24 the power of the atomic bomb on uninhabited land or against strictly military personnel.

19:29 The Japanese were also probably willing to sit down for peace talks even without the

19:33 bombs being dropped, especially after the Soviet Union declared war on them.

19:37 All that being said, the atomic bombs definitely played a major role in forcing Japan to surrender

19:42 and ending World War II.

19:43 If the United States had invaded the main island of Japan, many more people would have

19:47 died than perished as a result of the atomic bombs.

19:50 This does not necessarily justify the use of atomic weapons on Hiroshima and Nagaski,

19:54 but it does make you think if it was the best option in a really bad situation.

19:59 Now watch “What Was It Like to Be a Kamikaze Pilot?”

20:01 Or check out “What If There Was A Nuclear War Between the US and Russia?”

docs.text:
00:00 Some call it the elixir of the gods, others call it hooch.

00:03 A fancy cocktail might taste good but it comes at a price: your health.

00:07 Let’s find out what the actual benefits are to giving up alcohol.

00:11 Seconds after you stop drinking, your liver slowly filters out the toxins and sugars found

00:15 in the alcohol.

00:16 The molecule ethanol is what makes you feel drunk.

00:18 It does this by binding to receptors in your brain.

00:21 Most notably ethanol binds to glutamate neurotransmitters, which in turn causes the brain to respond

00:26 slower to stimuli.

00:27 Along with glutamate neurotransmitters there are several other receptors that ethanol binds

00:31 with that slows brain function.

00:33 The result of these inhibited receptors is what we call drunkenness.

00:37 The reversal of this process can take a while, and the hangover that ensues after a heavy

00:40 night of drinking is a mix of your body trying to get rid of the ethanol and other harmful

00:44 molecules, along with dehydration.

00:47 Unfortunately, if enough ethanol builds up in your system, it can kill you.

00:51 After about an hour, your body has filtered your blood several times and metabolized the

00:54 drinks you’ve had.

00:55 The time it takes your body to break down the alcohol directly correlates to the amount

00:59 consumed.

01:00 About an hour after you stop drinking your body starts to feel tired due to the high

01:03 amount of energy it uses to remove the alcohol from your blood.

01:06 And since it takes about six hours for your body to completely break down all the ethanol

01:10 in your system and bring the sugar, water, and other nutrient levels back to normal,

01:15 the lingering effects of drunkenness will persist.

01:18 After you’ve had your last sip of alcohol your body needs more rest than usual to recover

01:22 from your attempts to poison it.

01:24 Unfortunately, until you get past this stage, it is difficult to have a good night’s sleep.

01:27 In fact, recent research suggests that alcohol actually increases alpha wave patterns in

01:31 the brain, which are only supposed to be present while you’re awake.

01:34 This implies that alcohol tricks the brain into thinking the body is awake when it is

01:38 really trying to sleep.

01:39 But there is good news, if you manage to not drink for 6 to 12 hours your body physically

01:44 starts to change for the better.

01:46 For one thing, alcohol has been shown to weaken your immune system.

01:49 This may leave you susceptible to viruses and bacteria that are present at bars and

01:53 parties.

01:54 About 24 hours after you stop drinking, however, your immune system returns to normal.

01:57 This is the first of many changes that will occur from sobriety.

02:00 If you are a heavy drinker or alcoholic another much more noticeable change to your body will

02:04 occur around 24 hours after you stop drinking.

02:07 This is when withdrawal really starts to kick in.

02:10 Your body may still crave the chemical changes that occur when you drink, and therefore,

02:14 you would start to develop symptoms such as the shakes, cold sweats, increased pulse,

02:18 nausea, and anxiety.

02:20 These will eventually pass but the amount of time these withdrawals last is based on

02:23 each person and how much alcohol they usually consume on a daily basis.

02:27 Congratulations!

02:28 If you make it 3 to 5 days without drinking the real benefits of sobriety start to kick

02:32 in.

02:33 You may find that your blood pressure begins to drop and you will overall feel less stressed.

02:38 Doctors often recommend that people with high blood pressure reduce the amount of alcohol

02:41 they consume, so even if this is not your goal, less than a week after you stop drinking

02:45 your body will be grateful for the much needed break.

02:48 You might also notice your appetite begins to decrease about a week after you stop consuming

02:52 alcohol.

02:53 This is one of the reasons that people tend to lose weight when they quit drinking.

02:56 The other reason is that on average each drink you’re consuming contains a couple of hundred

03:00 calories.

03:01 And since the sugars in alcohol don't break down in your body very well, much of it gets

03:05 stored as fat.

03:06 If you can give up drinking for an entire week you may also find your skin looks and

03:10 feels better.

03:11 This is because your body is now more hydrated.

03:13 Not only does alcohol make you pee more often, but it also decreases your antidiuretic hormone

03:18 levels, which play a role in allowing your body to reabsorb water.

03:22 Somewhere around the seven-day mark after you stop drinking these hormone levels are

03:25 back to normal and your body is retaining more water.

03:28 This is good not only for your skin but for your body overall.

03:32 Again it is important to remember that the time between when you stop drinking and start

03:36 seeing these benefits will vary depending on the person and how much alcohol they previously

03:40 consumed.

03:41 A couple of weeks without alcohol you may find your cognitive abilities start to improve.

03:45 This is because the brain, like many parts of your body, is resilient.

03:48 The damage done to your neural pathway by the ethanol can be reversed.

03:52 You will never regain memories from when you blacked out while drinking or recover thoughts

03:57 that were obliterated from overconsumption of alcohol, but many of your neural connections

04:01 will heal themselves over the coming weeks and months.

04:04 You will see even bigger benefits if you quit for more than 1 or 2 weeks.

04:07 WIthout the pressure of filtering alcohol, your kidneys will begin to repair themselves.

04:11 Like the liver, the kidneys filter out toxins.

04:13 They are not quite as affected by alcohol as the liver is, but overconsumption can definitely

04:17 cause damage over time.

04:19 After a couple of weeks of no drinking, the kidneys will heal enough to maintain proper

04:22 fluid levels, waste excretion, and hormone balances.

04:26 If enough damage is caused to the kidneys from excessive drinking you will feel much

04:29 better once they are healed.

04:31 The organ that takes the brunt of the damage when you drink is the liver.

04:35 It is a vital structure and without it, you can’t survive.

04:38 So, about three weeks to a month after you completely stop drinking, your liver will

04:41 begin to thank you.

04:42 It is around then that the tissue will start to regenerate fully and the liver will repair

04:47 itself.

04:48 Without having to worry about alcohol, your liver can focus on breaking down other toxins

04:51 that are produced by the body, which overall will make you feel healthier.

04:54 The regeneration of damaged tissue takes time, but it happens much quicker when you stop

04:58 drinking.

04:59 A month or two after your last sip of alcohol your liver will be working at full power again.

05:04 Just reducing the amount of alcohol you consume on a weekly basis can be beneficial for your

05:08 liver.

05:09 But if you really want to thank this vital organ for all it’s done to keep you alive,

05:13 there is nothing better than giving it a rest from breaking down alcohol.

05:16 And if liver regeneration wasn’t a big enough benefit, there is another major change that

05:20 will occur to your body after not drinking for around a month or two.

05:23 I’m sure you’ve heard that a glass of wine a day can improve the health of your

05:26 heart.

05:27 Well, too much drinking can also damage your heart and increase your chances of having

05:31 a heart attack or a stroke.

05:33 Around two months after you stop drinking your heart will have repaired most of the

05:36 damage caused by overconsumption of alcohol.

05:38 However, the best thing you can do to increase heart strength is to exercise.

05:42 By reducing or completely stopping your alcohol consumption and exercising more, your heart

05:47 can become stronger and healthier.

05:49 Even though this next change doesn’t directly impact your body, something amazing happens

05:53 when you’ve stopped drinking for a few months.

05:55 Your bank account suddenly start looking healthier too!

05:58 Having more money could lead to less stress in your life, which would definitely be beneficial

06:02 for your health.

06:03 Research has shown that people who drink socially end up spending between $500 to $1,200 on

06:07 alcohol annually.

06:08 But if you live in a more expensive city and enjoy going out for drinks frequently, these

06:12 numbers can be much higher.

06:13 People who stopped drinking have noticed that the money they saved was enough for a downpayment

06:17 on a car or to take the vacation they’ve always wanted to go on.

06:21 These are clearly positive impacts on your life that may result in less stress and increased

06:25 happiness.

06:26 Interestingly, stress has very similar effects on the body as alcohol does.

06:29 It can increase blood pressure, cause heart problems, negatively affect your skin, and

06:33 cause depression.

06:35 Months after you stop drinking your body may feel a hundred times better due to a combination

06:39 of less stress and allowing your organs to repair themselves.

06:42 One of the most surprising changes to your body after you stop drinking happens without

06:46 you even feeling anything.

06:48 The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has found that alcohol can be a carcinogen.

06:52 This means that there is a chance the substance can cause cancer.

06:55 The research suggests that people who consume large amounts of alcohol are at higher risk

06:59 for certain types of cancer, which makes sense when you think about it.

07:03 Since your body technically sees alcohol as a toxin, and your liver is responsible for

07:07 removing that toxin, it is no surprise that people who are heavy drinkers have a high

07:10 risk of developing liver cancer.

07:13 Some research also suggests that alcohol can cause an increased risk of cancer in the esophagus

07:17 as well.

07:18 More research needs to be done, but there does seem to be a correlation between heavy

07:21 alcohol consumption and increased risk of cancer.

07:24 This means that once you stop drinking, you are actually lowering the chances of your

07:27 body developing cancer.

07:29 And this benefit doesn’t just persist for a few years, but for the rest of your life.

07:33 Just to be clear, most doctors and scientists agree that occasionally drinking alcohol poses

07:37 very minimal health risks.

07:38 In fact, consuming alcohol in moderation may have some health benefits.

07:42 However, health problems arise when overconsumption occurs.

07:45 But to be fair, this is true with almost anything you put into your body.

07:49 When you stop drinking your body goes through several changes over time.

07:52 But even if you only reduce the amount you drink, similar beneficial effects can occur.

07:57 If you are planning to do something like sober January, or want to cut off alcohol for a

08:01 bit to see how it goes, just know that you will definitely feel better after the initial

08:05 shock to your system.

08:06 However, the health effects that come from long-term sobriety probably won’t occur

08:10 just in a single month.

08:12 If you want to drink from time to time that’s okay.

08:14 You can still receive some of the benefits mentioned in this video just by limiting your

08:17 alcohol consumption to one drink or less a day.

08:20 By reducing alcohol intake your body can recover and you can live a long and happy life while

08:24 also having a glass of hooch every now and then.

08:27 Now watch “Most Expensive Drink in the World.”

08:29 Or check out “I Went To A Bar Alone And This Is What Happened - SOCIAL EXPERIMENT.”
