00:00 The inside job that helped Hitler rise to power.  A huge coverup of the most horrifying moment of

00:05 the Vietnam War. And a secret CIA weapon that  could kill you without ever leaving a trace.

00:11 They sound crazy, but these are just some  of the most insane conspiracy theories

00:14 that turned out to be completely true! And  we’re going to let you in on all the secrets.

00:19 My Lai Massacre Cover Up. Sadly, there is no shortage

00:22 of atrocities committed during the Vietnam  War, but there is one so awful and so damning

00:27 to the United States that the truth about it was  intentionally hidden from the public. The My Lai

00:32 Massacre took place in the small Vietnam hamlet  of My Lai, on March 16th, 1968. That morning,

00:38 US soldiers entered the village on a search and  destroy mission. While the region where My Lai

00:43 was situated was controlled by Viet Cong guerilla  fighters, the American troops found no sign of

00:48 enemy combatants in the area, only civilians. That didn’t stop the United States own soldiers

00:53 from setting huts on fire, murdering between 347  to 504 innocent Vietnamese people – including

01:00 as many as fifty children under the age of four  – and committing acts of assault so deplorable

01:05 against the women of My Lai that we can’t actually  describe them here on YouTube. Even worse, the

01:10 barbaric actions of these troops were initially  praised by the US as fabricated reports claimed

01:15 that over a hundred and twenty of these needlessly  murdered civilians had actually been Viet Cong.The

01:20 truth about the My Lai Massacre wouldn’t emerge  until a year later, and became emblematic of the

01:25 US’ war efforts in Vietnam. The conflict had  already been widely criticised and protested,

01:31 and now it looked like America had lost any  sense of morality when it came to the actions

01:35 of its troops in Southeast Asia. Military secrecy  around the killings ultimately made it all the

01:40 more shocking when the revelations were made  public when former soldiers spoke out about

01:45 it. These weren’t just crimes against humanity  perpetrated against innocent women and children

01:50 by American troops, but acts that the US Army  leadership had conspired to sweep under the rug.

01:56 Among the slew of court martials that followed,  Lieutenant William Calley was accused of directing

02:00 the My Lai Massacre, and as a result was convicted  of premeditated murder and sentenced to life

02:06 behind bars. Sickeningly, he only served  three and a half years of house arrest,

02:10 before having his sentence commuted… at  the behest of then-President Richard Nixon.

02:15 But if you think that’s crazy, it’s nothing  compared to the true conspiratorial weirdness

02:19 that came out in the Church Committee Findings. Named for the US Senator at the helm, Frank Church

02:24 was the chair of the Senate Select Committee to  Study Governmental Operations with Respect to

02:29 Intelligence Activities. This was a 1975 Senate  investigation into alleged illegal activity

02:35 carried out by the US’ own intelligence agencies,  including the Federal Bureau of Investigation,

02:40 the Central Intelligence Agency,  and the National Security Agency.

02:44 Church Committee findings included multiple  attempted assassinations of other countries’

02:49 political figureheads, including President Fidel  Castro of Cuba, as well as the presidents of the

02:54 Dominican Republic and the Democratic Republic  of the Congo. There was COINTELPRO, a covert

02:59 operation conducted by the FBI to infiltrate  specific domestic organizations like civil

03:05 rights activists, feminists, environmentalists,  people protesting the Vietnam War, and communists.

03:11 It considered these groups ‘subversive’,  and sought to discredit them.

03:15 The Church Committee also brought to light Project  Mockingbird, an effort by the CIA to leverage

03:20 its relationships with journalists to control the  flow of information in the news. Project MINARET,

03:25 wherein the NSA was working with telecommunication  companies to monitor individuals on a watch

03:30 list – a list that included Senator Church  and other members of the Church Committee.

03:34 And, were it not for the work of the Church  Committee, the world might never have learned

03:38 about the horrendous CIA experiments that took  place as part of Projects MKULTRA and MKNAOMI.

03:44 But these weren’t even the strangest  findings of the committee… stay tuned

03:48 to hear about the CIA’s secret weapon. The findings made by the Church Committee,

03:52 as horrifying as they were, led to important  reforms when it came to how US intelligence

03:56 agencies operate. Congressional committees were  to oversee the future activities of the FBI,

04:01 CIA and NSA, and famously President Gerald Ford  issued Executive Order 11905, which banned the

04:08 carrying out of political assassinations. Let’s head back to Europe, though,

04:12 and peer into the dark plot that helped install  one of history’s greatest monsters: This is

04:17 the Reichstag Fire and the Nazi Power Grab. There’s no denying that the Nazi Party went

04:22 about assuming power over Germany in the most  brutal way possible during the early thirties.

04:27 On February 27, 1933, the Reichstag, which  was used as the home of Germany’s Parliament,

04:32 was burned to the ground. The attacks were  initially blamed on communists, with Dutchman

04:37 Marinus van der Lubbe playing the role of pasty. Thanks to van der Lubbe being a communist, Adolf

04:42 Hitler – already Chancellor at this time – used  the fire as justification for forcibly expelling

04:47 any left leaning or communist politicians out  of Parliament, and had them imprisoned so they

04:53 couldn’t oppose the Nazi Party in the elections  that took place a month later in March 1933.

04:58 Hitler successfully turned Germany against  communists by declaring that they were

05:02 threatening to take over, thus allowing the Nazis  to win more seats in the elections and helping

05:07 them to assume power over the country. It's hardly a stretch to conclude that

05:10 the Nazis were responsible, especially  given how partial they were for burning

05:14 books and attacking other institutions  that challenged their fascist ideology.

05:19 Operation Gladio…

05:20 Would you believe us if we told you that,  following the end of the Second World War,

05:24 armed resistance operatives were carrying out  clandestine missions in European countries?

05:28 No it wasn’t remnants of the Nazi party  or the USSR… it was the United States.

05:33 Codenamed Operation Gladio, these covert  missions were a direct collaboration between

05:38 the personnel of what would become the Central  Intelligence Agency, NATO, and the Western Union.

05:43 Operation Gladio consisted mainly of ‘stay behind’  operations - This involved countries embedding

05:48 sleeper agents in their own territories,  who would lie in wait to be deployed in the

05:53 event of an enemy invasion from nations like the  Soviet Union, which was steadily amassing power.

05:59 These stay-behind operatives would  establish resistance movements

06:02 within their home countries, then, should a  Soviet onslaught roll in, they’d stay put,

06:07 and work as spies from behind enemy lines. So, what did Operation Gladio actually entail?

06:12 Operatives were used to carry out political  assassinations, psychological warfare,

06:17 and false flag operations, essentially,  a smorgasbord of nefarious deeds,

06:21 against left wing parties in Western Europe. This  often meant aligning with anti-communist militias

06:27 and right wing terrorists as Gladio’s network of  secret operatives captured, tortured, and killed

06:32 anyone suspected of having communist leanings. To this day though, the US Department of State

06:36 denies the truth that their own operatives were  backing terrorist groups, and that Gladio was

06:41 only a way to aid Western European countries  from resisting a potential Soviet invasion.

06:46 But the CIA messing with Europe is one  thing - what about the FBI killing dozens

06:51 of Americans back in the good old US of A? During the Prohibition Era, the FBI was involved

06:57 in trying to develop ways to prevent bootleggers  from brewing illegal alcohol. In order to do that,

07:02 they increased the amount of methanol, a poisonous  substance found in the same industrial alcohol

07:07 that bootleggers would use to make liquor. While  intended to discourage people from drinking,

07:12 this increase led to thousands of deaths. For over a decade, the United States banned

07:17 both the sale and production of drinking  alcohol, and federal law enforcement devoted

07:22 significant resources to tackling the illegal  attempts people made to circumvent these laws.

07:27 Speakeasies and smuggling networks were primary  targets for law enforcement, as was bootlegging,

07:32 which had itself become a lucrative business  for organized crime syndicates. But the moment

07:37 one operation was busted, another  quickly appeared to take its place.

07:41 To limit the publicly available supply of alcohol,  law enforcement and federal regulators devised a

07:46 new strategy. As bootleg alcohol was typically  produced by distilling industrial alcohols,

07:51 US officials figured that, if it became  legally mandated that toxic additives had

07:56 to be included in these products, then they  could cut off the supply before consumption.

08:01 So, the US Treasury Department  ordered companies to add quinine,

08:04 methyl alcohol and additional toxic chemicals  to industrial alcohol as a deterrent.

08:09 A deterrent that didn’t work. On Christmas Eve of 1926, 60 people

08:14 were admitted to the Bellevue Hospital in New York  as a result of poisoned alcohol - 31 of which died

08:20 in the next few days. Many had inadvertently  consumed methanol, industrial strength alcohol

08:25 that was legal under federal law, but extremely  poisonous. And that’s just a snapshot of the

08:30 staggering number of deaths that occurred as a  result of alcohol poisoned by these chemicals.

08:35 While it’s often misinterpreted that the  FBI deliberately poisoned drinking alcohol,

08:39 it can’t be understated the unethical lengths  that the United States’ federal government went

08:43 to in order to curb public consumption  of alcohol and illegal bootlegging.

08:48 They might not have been dropping  mercury into bottles of whiskey,

08:51 but the US government did increase the level of  toxic chemicals present in industrial alcohols,

08:57 knowing full well that these were being used  distilled in order to be sold and drunk.

09:01 Speaking of incredibly dangerous things to put  into your body… Ever heard of Project MKNAOMI?

09:06 The now infamous Project MKULTRA is often  cited when talking about crazy conspiracies,

09:11 but its successor often flies under the  radar. Project MKNAOMI was a joint operation

09:17 between the CIA and the US Department of  Defense that ran for almost two decades,

09:22 between the fifties and the late sixties.

09:24 The goal of Project MKNAOMI was to conduct  research into chemical and biological warfare,

09:29 specifically determining what substances  and chemicals could be used to either kill

09:34 or incapacitate a target… and then developing  devices that could diffuse these materials.

09:39 While MKULTRA had a strong emphasis on mind  control experiments, MKNAOMI focused on ways

09:45 to weaponize bacteria and viruses, knockout  gases, lethal poisons, and delivery systems

09:51 that could be used to administer them. The CIA’s Technical Services Division was

09:55 tasked with developing a whole arsenal  of lethal or incapacitating materials,

09:59 with the US Army’s Special Operations Command  assigned to assist with the testing. Afterall,

10:04 what are friends for? Perhaps most notably,  MKNAOMI led to the creation of a number of

10:09 guns that were modified to fire darts coated in  deadly biological agents. These were strong enough

10:15 to incapacitate guard dogs, allowing covert agents  to infiltrate an area; then, a remedial chemical

10:21 agent could be used to reawaken the dogs upon the  agents’ exit, covering their tracks as they left.

10:27 While officially declassified information  about Project MKNAOMI is hard to come by,

10:31 a CIA memo that proposed using biological  weapons to target crops was uncovered in

10:36 1967 by the Church Committee - and we’ve  got more about what else that committee

10:41 revealed to the world coming up shortly. After this memo was discovered, President

10:45 Richard Nixon was forced to ban the military  use of biological weapons in November 1969,

10:51 and Project MKNAOMI was dissolved. However,  despite the president’s orders, in 1970, one rogue

10:57 CIA scientist stole approximately eleven grams  of a deadly shellfish toxin with help from SOC

11:04 personnel at Fort Detrick, Maryland. This  dangerous toxin was then stashed in a CIA

11:09 owned lab, going undetected for over five years. But it’s not just the US that gets involved

11:15 in sinister secret plots. Sometimes, it’s US  allies. Such was the case in The Lavon Affair.

11:21 While arguably not as infamous as the likes  of Gladio, or other US led covert operations,

11:26 the Lavon Affair was no less deplorable. Planned  by the Israeli Military Intelligence in 1954,

11:32 under the innocuous codename of Operation  Susannah, this was a false flag operation.

11:38 During the summer of 1954, a group of Egyptian  Jewish people were recruited by Israel’s military

11:44 intelligence to attack multiple civilian targets  in Egypt. These included Egyptian, American and

11:49 British owned businesses, cinemas, libraries and  US educational centers throughout the country.

11:55 These recruits were instructed to plant bombs  in these establishments, and upon detonation,

12:00 the attacks were to be pinned on communists, the  Muslim Brotherhood – a Sunni Islamist organization

12:05 in Egypt – or unspecified local nationalists. The operation began when the sleeper cell,

12:10 consisting of eight Egyptian Jews, bombed the  post office in Alexandria. Within weeks, six other

12:16 buildings were also targeted, with the Egyptian  government eventually being tipped off – allegedly

12:21 by the person overseeing the operation – about  where the next bombing was planned to take place.

12:26 With that information, they were able to swoop in  and arrest the bomber, then capturing the entire

12:31 covert Israeli cell of eleven suspects. While the  bombings didn’t result in any civilian deaths,

12:36 four of the operatives died, two of them after  being captured and another two being sentenced

12:40 to execution by the Egyptian government.  Two more were acquitted at their trial,

12:45 and the remaining five received varying prison  sentences that ranged from seven years to life.

12:50 But the lingering question in all this is why?  Well, the intent of this failed false flag was

12:55 to pin the blame on organizations that opposed  Egypt’s leader, Gamal Abdel Nasser. It was hoped

13:00 that the subsequent chaos would convince Western  governments that Nasser’s regime over Egypt was

13:05 unstable, and therefore prompting these nations  to withdraw any financial or military support.

13:10 After the operation failed, Israeli defence  minister Pinhas Lavon was implicated in

13:14 orchestrating the bombing attacks and was  consequently forced to resign, leading to the

13:19 incident being referred to as the Lavon Affair.  Israel continued to publicly deny that they’d

13:24 had any involvement in the Lavon Affair until  as recently as 2005; the surviving Egyptian

13:29 agents who had been involved in the attacks were  awarded certificates of appreciation by the then

13:33 President of Israel, Moshe Katsav - the covert  agent equivalent of a participation medal.

13:39 But that isn’t the last piece of military  subterfuge we’ve got on the docket today.

13:43 Far from it, in fact. So let’s dive into  the infamous Gulf War Syndrome cover up.

13:47 Following the end of the Gulf War – which took  place between 1990 and 1991 – a concerning number

13:53 of veterans who had fought in the conflict  reported developing unusual symptoms after

13:57 returning home. Reports came in from Gulf  War veterans in the United States, Canada,

14:01 Austria and Denmark. But for those returning  home to the UK and suffering from this strange

14:06 Gulf War Syndrome, the health issues they  reported would be suspiciously silenced…

14:11 In every reported case, soldiers who  had been previously fit and healthy

14:15 seemed to suddenly develop a litany of  unusual illnesses and symptoms. These

14:19 ranged from experiencing chronic fatigue,  hypertension, muscle pain, cognitive issues,

14:24 a lack of coordination, outbreaks of  rashes and other skin conditions, diarrhea,

14:29 as well as symptoms related to  Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

14:32 What made this so unusual though, compared to the  illnesses suffered by veterans of previous wars,

14:37 was that there seemed to be a much higher rate  of symptoms and at much greater intensity among

14:42 those who’d fought in the Gulf War. The primary  cause that’s been attributed to this is exposure

14:47 to sub-lethal amounts of chemical warfare  agents, particularly nerve gas, as well

14:52 as the inhalation of smoke from oil well fires,  and exposure to pesticides and depleted uranium.

14:58 In the United Kingdom, several assessments  of the affected veterans were carried out to

15:01 determine if there was any link between those  experiencing these symptoms. But Kings College

15:06 London was unable to determine any common  causality among sufferers. Meanwhile, other

15:11 countries like the United States were quicker to  recognize the existence of this Gulf War Syndrome.

15:15 The UK’s Ministry of Defence vehemently denied  that such a condition existed, despite the

15:20 overwhelming evidence among veterans from the  Gulf War. They would eventually relent in 2005,

15:25 and subsequent research was conducted in 2009  that further confirmed Gulf War veterans were

15:30 more likely to report symptoms compared to other  veterans. They were also twice as likely to have

15:35 suffered from PTSD and reported a poorer  quality of life following their service.

15:40 However, as recently as 2010, an overwhelming  majority of the UK’s Gulf War veterans hadn’t

15:45 received any form of compensation from their  government and claims for war pensions have been

15:50 denied to those who served in the Gulf War and  reported to be suffering with Gulf War Syndrome.

15:55 Sometimes, governments conspire to shaft large  groups of people. Sometimes, it’s just one very

16:00 unfortunate dude. Welcome to The Dreyfus Affair The Dreyfus Affair took place in France between

16:05 the late nineteenth and early twentieth  centuries. It surrounded one Alfred Dreyfus,

16:10 an artillery captain within the French army.  In 1894, after a seemingly damning letter of

16:15 evidence was discovered, Dreyfus was accused of  selling French military secrets to Germany and was

16:20 convicted of treason… Wrongly convicted. Working in the German Embassy in Paris,

16:25 a French spy named Major Hubert-Joseph Henry  uncovered a partially ripped up letter in a

16:30 waste basket. The handwriting that had been used  to pen the letter resembled that of Dreyfus,

16:35 leading to what would become a controversial  arrest and accusation levied against the man. The

16:40 public were quick to believe the charges slammed  against Dreyfus owed purely to the fact that he

16:44 was Jewish. Antisemitic groups in France at the  time amplified the notion of his guilt, especially

16:50 the newspaper La Libre Parole, which claimed that  Dreyfus exemplified the disloyalty of French Jews.

16:56 Dreyfus was court-martialed and sentenced to life  in prison on Devil’s Island, located off the coast

17:01 of French Guiana. In a harrowing public ceremony  following his conviction, he had the French army’s

17:06 insignia torn off his uniform and his sword  broken before being paraded in front of a crowd

17:12 who hurled antisemitic insults at him and even  called for Dreyfus to be executed for treason.

17:18 However, in 1896, evidence would come to light  that implicated a different French officer, named

17:23 Ferdinand Walsin-Esterhazy, as the true traitor.  This started swaying public support for Dreyfus,

17:29 but after Esterhazy’s subsequent court martial, he  was quickly found not guilty and fled the country.

17:34 Dreyfus was court-martialed a second  time in 1899, and found guilty again,

17:39 yet France was still deeply divided over the case.  Days later, Dreyfus received a full pardon from

17:44 the French president, and then in 1906 he would  be fully exonerated and reinstated into the army.

17:50 Antisemitism is undeniably a horrible  blight on the planet. Just like nuclear

17:54 war. And what do we have to thank for  that? The Manhattan Project, of course!

17:58 In a post Oppenheimer world, almost  everyone’s heard of the Manhattan Project,

18:02 the infamous World War Two collaborative  research and development program between

18:06 the United States, United Kingdom and Canada  that produced the very first nuclear weapons,

18:11 irreversibly altering the course of history. Between 1942 and 1946, the project resulted in two

18:17 distinct types of bombs; the Thin Man, a fission  based nuclear weapon, and the Little Boy, the

18:22 more complex, implosion type nuclear weapon, both  designed by nuclear physicist and the destroyer

18:28 of worlds himself, J. Robert Oppenheimer. But at the time, public knowledge about the

18:32 Manhattan Project was severely limited. The goal  of security officials linked to the Manhattan

18:37 Project was to keep word about the development of  atomic bombs from reaching Nazi Germany and their

18:42 Axis power allies, in particular Japan, who would  suffer the first ever nuclear attacks in history

18:48 as a direct result of the Manhattan Project. Details of the program were also kept a secret

18:52 from the Soviet Union; despite the USSR being  aligned with the USA, UK and other Allied Forces,

18:58 the United States regarded them as a potential  future enemy. However, some Soviet spies were

19:03 successful in infiltrating the Manhattan  Project headquarters in Los Alamos, and

19:07 disseminated information about the program back  to Russia, which helped speed up the development

19:12 of the Soviets’ very own nuclear bombs. There were also a surprising amount of

19:16 leaks during the 1940s from American journalists,  some of them small and inconsequential, but others

19:21 far more damning. Around the time of the Second  World War, the United States operated a program of

19:26 voluntary press censorship that allowed its Office  of Censorship to… sternly rebuke journalists that

19:32 reported on a list of prohibited topics. Essentially, any censorship that took place

19:36 usually went into effect after important  information had already been published.

19:41 One of the worst violations in relation  to the Manhattan Project occurred in 1944,

19:46 when a reporter for the Cleveland Press, the  unfortunately named John Raper, discovered that

19:51 a military operation was occurring in Los Alamos  while he had been on vacation in New Mexico. Raper

19:57 had no idea that atomic bombs were being developed  there, but he erroneously reported the location

20:02 and approximate size of a classified military  science facility, n provided local witness

20:07 accounts of explosives being tested on the site,  and worst of all, he named Oppenheimer as the

20:12 scientific director of the Manhattan Project. At the behest of Major General Leslie Groves,

20:17 the US Army’s director of the Manhattan Project,  the Office of Censorship was able to prevent

20:22 any follow up articles being published. This  included one being planned by Time magazine,

20:26 to ensure further information about the project  couldn’t be spread any further. Groves also

20:31 considered drafting John Raper in retaliation for  his article, only relenting when he learned that

20:36 the journalist was in his sixties, and hardly at  a prime age to be forced into military service.

20:41 Next up is a scientific study  that breached moral and ethical

20:44 boundaries on a truly unprecedented scale. The Tuskegee Syphilis Experiment was a study

20:49 that ran from 1932 until 1972. Funded by the  United States government and carried out by the US

20:56 Public Health Service and the Centers for Disease  Control and Prevention, the goal of the research

21:01 project was to examine the effects and symptoms  of syphilis when left untreated. And at the time,

21:06 there was no known cure for the disease. In order to make their observations, the

21:10 Public Health Service enrolled around six hundred  impoverished African American sharecroppers - 399

21:16 with syphilis and 201 without - many of whom had  never even visited a doctor before. They were

21:23 enticed by an offer of free medical care, however  the people behind the study intentionally refused

21:28 to explain exactly what they were examining in the  men that would unwittingly become test subjects.

21:34 Those participating in the Tuskegee  Experiment were falsely told they were

21:37 being treated for ‘bad blood’, a colloquial,  non-specific term used in the area to

21:43 describe a number of different ailments. The participants were given placebos such

21:47 as aspirin and mineral supplements, and told  that this would treat their condition. However,

21:51 some fifteen years into the study, in 1947,  a treatment for syphilis was discovered in

21:57 the form of penicillin. The Public Health  Service neglected to tell these men the

22:01 truth at any point, nor did they offer the  widely available antibiotic which had since

22:05 become the standard treatment for syphilis. In fact, the researchers offered no medical

22:10 care to these men as their condition progressed,  even as some of them started to go blind, suffered

22:15 other severe health problems or even went insane  due to syphilis. Over the course of the study,

22:20 28 participants passed away due to syphilis, and  a further one hundred died from complications

22:26 linked to the disease. Forty of the participants’  spouses were also diagnosed with it, and it had

22:31 been passed on to almost twenty children. A year after the story broke and sparked

22:35 public outrage, Congress held multiple hearings  looking into the Tuskegee Experiment. In 1974,

00:00 Hey, I'm Dave. Welcome to my shop.

00:02 Today's episode starts with what looks

00:04 like a very simple question. How hard

00:06 could it possibly be to add a third

00:08 brake light to an old car? And the

00:10 answer, as usual, is hard enough to

00:13 actually be pretty interesting. Because

00:14 this isn't just a story about sticking a

00:16 red LED strip on a bumper and calling it

00:18 a day. This is a story about taking a

00:21 1970 Lincoln Continental Mark III, a car

00:24 with only about 12,000 mi on it from

00:26 new, a car that still looks like it

00:28 slipped through a wormhole from Nixon's

00:30 first term, and adding an otherwise

00:31 invisible modern safety system without

00:33 drilling any holes in it, without

00:35 hanging some ugly plastic wart in the

00:36 rear window without making it look like

00:38 somebody attacked the classic luxury car

00:40 with the RGB lighting aisle from a micro

00:42 center. So, why should somebody watch an

00:44 entire episode about an LED taillight if

00:46 they're never actually going to build

00:47 one? Because the tail light is just the

00:49 visible part. The interesting part is

00:51 the translation layer hidden beneath it.

00:53 It's a tiny case study in embedded

00:55 systems, signal isolation, automotive

00:57 power, human factors, legacy

00:59 integration, state machines, timing

01:01 tolerances, safety priorities, and

01:03 difference between it works in my bench

01:04 and it works in the car. It's also a

01:07 story about translation because on one

01:09 side you've got a 55-year-old electrical

01:11 system built from switches, bulbs,

01:13 flashers, copper wire, and the kind of

01:15 cultural optimism that says a seatback

01:17 ending halfway up your spine is probably

01:19 all the neck protection a tough guy like

01:21 me really needs. And then on the other

01:23 side, you've got a modern ESP32

01:25 microcontroller running at hundreds of

01:26 millions of cycles per second, driving

01:28 individually addressable LEDs, parsing

01:30 timing windows measured in milliseconds,

01:32 and making decisions about whether the

01:34 car is breaking, turning left, turning

01:36 right, backing up, or doing some

01:37 combination of those things all at the

01:39 same time. And in between those worlds

01:41 is the really interesting part. A little

01:43 circuit board whose entire job is to

01:45 listen to classic cars speak in 12vt

01:48 grunts and translate that into clean

01:50 digital facts. And the reason all this

01:52 matters is pretty simple. Old cars are

01:54 beautiful, but they were not designed

01:56 for a world where the person behind you

01:57 might be checking a text message,

01:59 adjusting Apple CarPlay, eating fries,

02:02 and driving an 8,000lb SUV with the

02:04 kinetic energy of a small moon. And the

02:06 Mark III has another problem, which is

02:07 that it does not exactly have modern

02:09 head and neck support. So getting

02:10 rear-ended in this car is not something

02:12 I'm eager to experience as an

02:13 educational exercise. In fact, it's

02:16 something I'll go to some lengths to

02:17 actively avoid. Modern cars have a

02:19 center high-mounted stop lamp or CHMSL

02:22 because people notice it. It sits

02:24 higher. It's closer to the driver's line

02:26 of sight. And it gives the person behind

02:28 you another chance to realize that the 2

02:30 and 1/2 ton landot ahead of them is

02:32 actually stopping. But the Mark III

02:34 predates that requirement by a long way.

02:35 And I don't want to bolt anything

02:37 obvious onto the car. When the lights

02:39 are off, I want the car to look entirely

02:41 original. Not mostly original. Not

02:43 original except for the obvious LED bar,

02:45 but original. And fortunately, the car

02:47 gave me one tiny gift. Under the bottom

02:49 edge of the trunk, just above the

02:51 bumper, there's a gap of about/ an inch.

02:53 It's not perfectly straight, cuz of

02:55 course it isn't, but it runs across the

02:57 rear of the car in almost exactly the

02:59 place that you'd want to hide a light.

03:01 That became the slot, the little shadow

03:02 line where 6 ft or so of addressable

03:04 LEDs could disappear until called into

03:06 service. And this is where a simple

03:08 lighting project turns into a systems

03:10 project. If you're doing this on a

03:12 modern car, you might be tempted to go

03:14 looking for a CAN bus message because

03:16 there might be a nice little packet

03:17 somewhere that says the brake pedal is

03:19 down, the left signal is active, the

03:20 right signal is active, reverse is

03:22 selected, and maybe even what radio

03:24 station the driver is listening to. But

03:26 this car is from 1970. There is no CAN

03:29 bus. There's no body control module.

03:32 There's no friendly digital truth just

03:34 waiting to be queried. They're just

03:35 wires. And unfortunately, the wires do

03:38 not say what you wish they said. At the

03:40 rear of the Lincoln, I can see the left

03:42 lamp, and I can see the right lamp, and

03:44 I can see the backup lamps, but there's

03:45 no separate signal that says the brakes

03:47 are active. There is no separate signal

03:49 that says the left turn signal is

03:51 active. The same rear lamp can mean

03:53 different things depending on time and

03:55 context, and that is the whole trick.

03:57 Imagine the left rear lamp turns on.

03:59 What does that mean? It might mean the

04:01 driver is now signaling left. But it

04:03 might also mean that the driver has

04:05 pressed the brake pedal and that both

04:06 rear lamps are on. It might mean we were

04:08 in the middle of a more complicated

04:09 state where the brakes are being held

04:11 down and one side is blinking because

04:14 turn. And that last case is the one that

04:16 turns the whole thing from a wiring job

04:18 into a state machine. We're

04:19 old-fashioned here in America and we

04:21 like things certain ways. We likes our

04:23 front signal lights amber and our rear

04:24 signal lights red and never the twain

04:26 shall meet. And while we're progressive

04:28 enough to finally allow amber rear

04:29 signals these days, if you're into that,

04:31 in 1970 there was just no chance.

04:33 Society just wasn't ready yet. And so in

04:35 those days, our rear signals were always

04:37 as red as the flags of our thermonuclear

04:39 adversaries. Which is all to say that on

04:42 an old American car like this, the brake

04:44 lights and the turn signals share bulbs.

04:48 illuminate. But if you were stopped at

04:50 an intersection with the brake pedal

04:51 down and then you signal right, the left

04:53 lamp stays on solid while the right lamp

04:55 blinks. Electrically, that is not

04:57 braking plus a right signal as a nice

04:59 clean pair of digital facts. Because

05:01 electrically the one side's steady and

05:03 the other side is alternating. The car

05:05 knows what it means because the car

05:06 created the actual condition. But my

05:09 circuit only gets to observe the

05:10 aftermath. That means it has to infer

05:12 the driver's intent. And inference is

05:14 where things get interesting. The

05:16 simplest version would say that if both

05:18 lamps are on, we're breaking. If only

05:20 the left lamp is blinking, we're

05:21 signaling left. If only the right lamp

05:23 is blinking, we're signaling the right.

05:24 And if neither is on, we're just driving

05:26 along, probably looking terrific. But

05:28 that's not enough because the real world

05:30 refuses to stay in the simple state

05:31 diagram that you would draw on the

05:33 whiteboard. For this, the

05:34 microcontroller has to know not only

05:36 what lamps are doing right now, but how

05:38 they got there. It has to remember

05:40 whether braking was already active. So,

05:42 it has to watch for edges, those moments

05:43 when the lamp changes from off to on. It

05:46 has to measure the timing between the

05:47 left and right sides. And if both sides

05:49 come on close enough together, say

05:51 within some small timing window, that is

05:53 probably the brake pedal being pressed,

05:54 even if there's two switches. But if one

05:57 side starts blinking by itself, that's

05:58 probably a turn signal. And once the

06:01 braking state has been detected, braking

06:03 remains active until both lamps are no

06:05 longer active. This is one of those

06:07 problems that looks trivial until you

06:09 actually try to code it correctly. The

06:11 brake animation itself is designed to be

06:13 conspicuous without being too

06:14 ridiculous. It starts illuminated

06:16 immediately because the whole point is

06:18 to say stop right now, not after a cute

06:20 startup animation. Then it blooms

06:22 outward from that initial center,

06:24 expanding until the entire strip becomes

06:26 red. During the first few moments, it

06:28 also pulses between medium and full

06:30 brightness, but it never actually goes

06:31 dark. That distinction matters because a

06:33 brake light that disappears during its

06:35 own attention getting animation is

06:36 defeating the purpose. The goal is not

06:39 to create a little time square under the

06:40 trunk. The goal is to be noticed by the

06:42 person behind me before physics holds a

06:44 vote on how the rest of my day is going

06:46 to go. I'm going to be very careful here

06:48 and say that I'm not claiming the system

06:50 is street legal. I looked at the

06:52 relevant lighting rules, particularly

06:53 FMVSS number 108 because that is the

06:56 federal standard that deals with vehicle

06:57 lamps and associated equipment. But

06:59 unless you have the right equipment, the

07:01 phototric testing, the mounting

07:02 validation, and all the rest of the

07:04 whole certification process, you should

07:07 not pretend that your garage project is

07:08 suddenly a certified automotive lighting

07:10 component. So for our purposes, this is

07:12 a show use only project and any legal

07:15 interpretation you make for your own car

07:17 is between you, your local laws, and the

07:19 officer who may not share your

07:20 enthusiasm for addressable LEDs. That

07:23 said, I still wanted to design it as

07:24 responsibly as I could. Red means

07:26 braking, amber means turn signal, white

07:29 means reverse, and the emergency mode,

07:31 which I added simply because it looks

07:32 extremely cool in the garage, is not

07:34 connected to the vehicle in any way that

07:36 allows it to activate accidentally. cuz

07:39 out of an abundance of caution, that

07:40 input is tied to ground. So, it can't

07:42 suddenly decide to do a red and blue

07:43 police style animation while I'm out on

07:45 public roads. But if you are a police

07:47 officer with an undercover 1970 Mark

07:49 III, then first of all, congratulations

07:51 on having tremendous taste. Say hi to

07:53 Canon for me. But for the rest of us,

07:55 this mode is for demonstration only.

07:57 Now, let's talk about the hardware

07:58 because this is where the project

07:59 becomes less like car customization and

08:01 more like building a small embassy

08:03 between two hostile electrical nations.

08:05 A car's electrical system is not a

08:07 polite 12vt clean. It's a nominal 12vt

08:10 system, which means it might be 12 volts

08:12 or maybe even 11 with the engine off,

08:14 closer to 14 or 15 when the alternator

08:16 is charging, lower during cranking, and

08:18 full of spikes, dips, inductive

08:20 nonsense, and the general electric mood

08:22 swings of an old vehicle. The ESP32,

08:25 meanwhile, expects civilized low voltage

08:27 power. It does not want to be introduced

08:30 directly to the Lincoln's lighting

08:31 harness any more than you want to drink

08:32 from a rusty fire hose just cuz you're

08:34 very thirsty. So, the board needed three

08:36 big functional blocks. It needed a power

08:39 supply to turn the vehicle's messy 12 to

08:41 15V world into a regulated 5V for the

08:44 microcontroller. It needed input

08:46 protection and isolation so the car's

08:48 lighting signals could be sensed safely.

08:50 And it needed the ESP32 itself, which

08:52 would run the logic and drive the LED

08:54 strip. My first approach, a similar

08:56 project for my 1970 GMC truck, actually

08:59 used relays. And relays are wonderfully

09:02 intuitive. The vehicle's 12volt signal

09:04 energizes the coil, the relay closes,

09:06 and a separate isolated 5V signal goes

09:09 to a GPIO pin. There's something

09:11 reassuringly mechanical about it. You

09:12 can hear it click. You can understand it

09:14 in one glance, and it works. But it's

09:16 not the best way to do it. There is a

09:18 better way. And for this PCB, I used

09:20 optoouplers. An optooupler is one of

09:23 those components that feels like a magic

09:24 trick until you realize how simple it

09:26 really is. Inside the little chip is an

09:28 LED and a light sensitive transistor or

09:30 detector. When the vehicle side sends

09:33 current through the internal LED side,

09:34 it shines across a tiny gap inside the

09:37 package. The detector on the other side

09:39 sees the light and switches the

09:40 microcontroller side signal. And so the

09:43 two sides are electrically isolated.

09:45 There is no copper path between the car

09:47 circuit and the ESP32's GPIO pin. The

09:50 information crosses the gap as light.

09:52 That is elegant. It is also exactly the

09:54 sort of thing you want when you're

09:56 connecting a delicate microcontroller to

09:58 a noisy automotive circuit. We don't

10:00 need to share the car's electrical

10:01 chaos. We only need to know whether a

10:03 lamp circuit is active or not. The PCB

10:05 itself was laid out in easy EDA, which

10:07 is made by JLCPCB, and that was all new

10:10 to me, but surprisingly approachable.

10:12 And one of the nice things about the

10:13 modern hobby electronics world now is

10:15 how absurdly powerful the tooling has

10:17 become. You can lay out the schematic,

10:19 assign real parts, route the board,

10:21 inspect it in 3D, and in some cases,

10:23 have the whole thing manufactured and

10:24 assembled for you. That still feels a

10:26 little like science fiction to somebody

10:28 who remembers etching their own PCBs.

10:30 For this project, I ordered bare PCBs

10:32 and then soldered the parts myself, cuz

10:34 I was only making one or two. The

10:36 connectors all live along one edge of

10:37 the board because in a car installation,

10:39 connector sanity matters. First, there's

10:42 an LED strip connector with ground,

10:44 data, and power. And then come the

10:46 vehicle inputs, backup lights, auxiliary

10:48 input, left tail light, right tail

10:50 light, chassis ground, and vehicle

10:52 12volt power. The power stage is a buck

10:54 converter, a switching regulator that

10:56 efficiently steps the car's voltage down

10:57 to 5 volts. A linear regulator would

11:00 burn the extra voltage away as heat,

11:01 which is fine for tiny currents, but bad

11:03 for anything bigger. A buck converter

11:05 works more like a little electronic

11:07 flywheel, rapidly switching energy into

11:09 an inductor and then smoothing it out

11:11 with capacitors so the output stays

11:12 regulated even as the input wanders

11:14 around. And then because no project is

11:17 complete without discovering something

11:18 awkward while explaining it, I realized

11:20 an important detail while planning this

11:22 episode. The board's 5V supply is

11:25 carefully regulated and the ESP32 is

11:27 being treated properly. But the LED

11:29 strip I used in this version is a 12volt

11:31 strip which means I just fed it directly

11:33 vehicle power. It works perfectly on the

11:35 bench and in the install. But from a

11:37 design purity standpoint, it's not ideal

11:40 cuz as we noted, the vehicle supply can

11:42 be noisy and the voltages can vary

11:43 substantially. The better design would

11:45 either regulate the 12volt LED supply as

11:48 well or use a 5V LED strip powered from

11:50 the clean 5V regulator on the PCB.

11:53 That's probably the easiest. It should

11:55 be able to handle the current of the

11:57 entire strip. Or at least that's the

11:58 plan. That's one of the fun things about

12:00 not knowing very much about electronics.

12:05 decades ago. The relay version works,

12:09 better. And when it comes to any kind of

12:10 engineering, better has a flavor that

12:12 never really gets old. Now, a quick word

12:15 on the LEDs themselves. Because

12:17 addressable strips are one of the most

12:18 enjoyable things to play with in modern

12:20 electronics. A typical RGB LED strip of

12:23 this type lets you control each LED

12:25 individually. You don't simply turn the

12:27 whole strip red. You say LED number zero

12:29 is red at this brightness. LED number

12:31 one is red at this brightness. And LED

12:33 number 27 is amber. Each LED receives

12:36 data, keeps the part meant for itself,

12:38 and passes the rest down the line. That

12:56 in the whole chain, the refresh rate is

12:59 noticeable flicker. In software terms,

13:06 instead of pixels on a monitor, the

13:08 pixels are stretched across the rear of

13:09 a Lincoln. And like any display, what

14:08 want the LED animation running at its

14:10 own schedule and slowly drifting out of

14:12 phase like a badly dubbed movie. So when

14:14 the left lamp transitions from off to

14:16 on, the left signal animation resets and

14:18 starts again. Every flash from the car

14:20 becomes a timing sync mark. The LED

14:23 strip takes its cue from the original

14:25 lamp. That gives the result that the

14:27 amber animation always appears perfectly

14:29 synchronized with the vehicle's own

14:30 signal cuz it's not trying to replace

14:32 the car's lighting logic. It's following

14:34 it and it's enhancing what was already

14:35 there. And that distinction is

14:37 important. The system is deliberately

14:39 parasitic in the benign sense. It

14:41 observes the car. It does not take over

14:43 the car. It does not interrupt the

14:45 factory brake signals at all. It does

14:47 not sit between the driver and the

14:48 original lamps. So, if my board were to

14:50 fail, the factory light should continue

14:52 doing what they always did. And that's

14:54 the right philosophy when adding

14:56 electronics to a classic vehicle,

14:57 especially one that you want to keep

14:58 original. The modification should be

15:00 reversible and it should at least fail

15:02 in the least dramatic way possible.

15:05 There's also a neat little philosophical

15:06 point here about old systems and new

15:08 systems. The Lincoln's wiring harness

15:10 does not know what a state machine is.

15:12 It was not designed to express six

15:14 different semantic states through a nice

15:15 API. It just energizes wires. But when

15:18 you observe those wires over time, then

15:20 information appears. A single sample is

15:23 ambiguous, but a sequence over time has

15:25 meaning. And that's not just automotive

15:27 electronics. That's computing in

15:28 general. A bit is just a bit until you

15:30 know where it came from, when it

15:32 changed, and what state the system was

15:33 in before it changed. Context turns

15:36 voltage into information. And the best

15:38 example is breaking. Suppose the ESP32

15:41 sees the left lamp on and the right lamp

15:42 on. If those two events occur within a

15:44 small window of one another, it knows

15:46 that's breaking. But suppose the left

15:48 lap has been on for a while and the

15:50 right lamp is now blinking. That's

15:52 probably breaking while signaling right.

15:54 The same two inputs sampled at different

15:56 moments mean different things. And this

15:58 is why naive input pooling would give

16:00 naive answers. The timing window exists

16:02 because the ESP32 is much faster than

16:05 the system. is watching. The

16:07 microcontroller can observe the world

16:08 with absurd precision compared with the

16:10 mechanical and electrical realities of a

16:12 1970s car. If you ask it where the two

16:14 lamps turned on at exactly the same

16:16 time, the answer will almost always be

16:18 no. Because exactly to a 240 MHz

16:21 microcontroller is not the same as

16:22 exactly to a couple of brake light

16:24 switches, a turn signal switch, and

16:25 50-year-old wiring. The code has to be a

16:28 little forgiving. Within a few

16:30 milliseconds, we consider them

16:31 simultaneous enough. That's a

16:33 surprisingly common engineering pattern.

16:35 The smarter part of the system has to

16:36 learn not to be too smart. Precision

16:38 without tolerance becomes brittleleness.

16:40 Once braking starts, the system remains

16:42 in braking mode until both rear lamps

16:45 are off at the same time. That prevents

16:48 just because one side is blinking due to

16:52 behaves like a driver expects. If I'm

17:00 keep saying this car is stock while also

17:02 allowing the amber turn animation to

17:04 communicate direction where appropriate.

17:07 clarity is the real design work because

17:09 you can make animations that are

17:10 visually impressive but semantically

17:12 confusing. You can make something that

17:14 looks amazing in a garage and terrible

17:16 in traffic. You can make a brake light

17:18 that's so clever it becomes ambiguous

17:19 and ambiguous lighting on the back of a

17:21 car is a bad idea. So the animations

17:23 need to be restrained. Red is brake,

17:25 amber is turn, white is reverse. Motion

17:27 supports meaning. It does not replace

17:29 meaning. The emergency mode is the one

17:31 exception and that's why it is isolated.

17:33 It uses red and blue for demonstration

17:36 purposes and it strobes and it takes

17:37 advantage of full color capability of

17:39 the strip. It's fantastic for showing

17:41 what the hardware can do. It's also

17:43 exactly the kind of thing you don't want

17:44 to accidentally trigger in public. Now,

17:46 mechanically, the install is almost as

17:48 important as a circuit. A classic car

17:50 like this deserves a light touch. The

17:52 strip needs to be hidden, aligned,

17:53 protected, and serviceable. It has to

17:55 survive vibration, temperature changes,

17:57 moisture, and the general indignities of

17:59 being mounted near the rear bumper of an

18:01 actual car. Bench projects live in ideal

18:03 conditions, but car projects live in the

18:05 weather, next to exhaust, next to

18:07 vibrating sheet metal, and downstream

18:09 from every puddle that you drive

18:10 through. I don't drive through puddles,

18:12 but mounting it is not just about making

18:14 it pretty. It's also about strain

18:16 relief, routing wires safely, avoiding

18:18 sharp edges, and making sure that

18:19 nothing can chafe through over time.

18:22 Automotive wiring failures aren't often

18:23 dramatic failures. They're slow

18:25 mechanical failures because a wire rubs

18:27 against the bracket or a connector hangs

18:28 where water collects. A solder joint is

18:31 asked to be a structural member. And

18:33 then one day, the thing that worked

18:34 perfectly in the garage becomes an

18:35 intermittent gremlin. And intermittent

18:37 gremlins are where hobby projects go to

18:38 become folklore. The other important

18:40 installation detail is that this system

18:42 is not trying to visually modernize the

18:44 car when it is off. That was the whole

18:46 premise. I don't want somebody walking

18:47 up to the Lincoln at a show and

18:49 immediately seeing a strip of LEDs. I

18:51 just want them to see the car. So, the

18:53 lighting only reveals itself when it has

18:55 something to say. And that is, I think,

18:57 the difference between a tasteful

18:58 modification and a gadget bolted to an

19:00 unwilling host. The best modifications

19:02 understand the object that they're

19:04 modifying. A 1970 Continental Mark III

19:06 is not a tuner car. It's not a cyberpunk

19:09 prop. It's a rolling personal luxury

19:11 coupe from an era when a hood could have

19:12 its own weather system. The lighting

19:14 should respect that. Hidden when silent,

19:16 unmistakable when active. And that is

19:19 why the final effect works so well. When

19:21 the brakes are applied, the red bloom

19:22 across the back of the car feels modern,

19:24 but not out of place entirely. It looks

19:26 like something the car might have had if

19:28 the technology had existed, and if the

19:29 safety rules of the time had demanded

19:31 it, then that's kind of the sweet spot.

19:33 There's also something satisfying about

19:35 solving this with a real PCB instead of

19:36 a dangling science experiment.

19:38 Breadboards are great for proving a

19:40 concept, but they are terrible for

19:42 permanence installations. Proto boards

19:44 are better and I've used them

19:45 successfully, including in the GMC. But

19:47 a custom PCB changes the character of

19:49 the project. The connections are

19:51 deliberate. The layout is repeatable.

19:52 The board has a purpose. It stops being

19:54 some wires in a microcontroller and

19:56 becomes a little embedded system. That

19:58 little embedded system has a job.

20:00 Observe, infer, decide, and display in a

20:02 loop. That pattern shows up everywhere

20:04 in computing. Sensors produce noisy,

20:06 incomplete signals. Software

20:08 reconstructs state. Outputs communicate

20:10 intent. Whether you're building a cloud

20:12 monitoring pipeline, a robot controller,

20:14 or a brake light for a classic Lincoln,

20:16 the basic loop is the same. The hard

20:18 part is not reading the inputs. The hard

20:20 part is understanding what the inputs

20:22 mean. That's the real lesson. Good

20:24 projects are not just a pile of clever

20:26 parts. They are constraints resolved

20:28 elegantly. The main constraint here was

20:30 make a modern visible third brake light,

20:32 but don't change the look of the car.

20:34 Don't depend on a CAN bus that doesn't

20:40 electrical noise. Don't confuse turn

20:42 signals with brake lights. Don't let a

20:43 demo mode become a roadside conversation

20:45 with the cops. And don't make it ugly.

20:51 regulated power supply, an ESP32, and a

20:54 state machine that understands that two

20:56 complicated story if you listen to them

21:16 happening in between them. The car

docs.text:
00:00 AI is coming for your job. Right now.

00:03 Entire industries are being decimated by the  AI machine. Jobs being wiped as human workers

00:08 are replaced by automated algorithms  that can do the same tasks faster,

00:13 more efficiently… and more importantly, cheaper. We’ve already seen it in finance. In healthcare.

00:18 In customer service, logistics, and manufacturing.  One by one, AI is taking over the work that

00:24 millions of people thought was untouchable. But  one profession seemed immune to the takeover…

00:29 Law. Or at least, that’s what lawyers thought…

00:32 Since the 1960s, legal firms have relied on the  billable hour. Companies charged their clients not

00:37 on a case-by-case basis, but an hour-by-hour  basis. Clients not only paid for the firm’s

00:43 expertise, but for the time invested. Poring over  contracts, drafting documents, digging through

00:48 specific files or legal precedents all take time. Each hour was recorded, multiplied by a fixed

00:54 rate, and billed to the client, who then happily  paid, believing that every second of the firm’s

01:00 time was indispensable. It’s why the legal  industry became so valuable. It’s why the

01:04 biggest firms were able to rake in ridiculous  amounts of revenue, year on year. The public

01:09 bought into the illusion that the finest legal  minds were working tirelessly on their cases.

01:14 Behind the scenes, it was a different story. The illusion was smoke and mirrors.

01:18 Those at the top often relegated many of their  most time-consuming tasks to junior associates;

01:23 These entry-level employees still received  sizable salaries, but they brought in more

01:28 money to the firm overall through numerous  billable hours they put in each week.

01:32 The legal field functioned like a pyramid. At the top were the most elite,

01:37 experienced partners and firm owners. They were the faces of their firms and

01:41 spent much of their time liaising with clients  and cultivating relationships. At the bottom of

01:45 the pyramid, propping up everything else, were  the juniors. The people doing the hard work,

01:50 grinding through tedious tasks. Day in and day out.

01:54 Firms saw a simple path to  success: hire more juniors.

01:58 More bodies meant more billable hours charged  to clients. That meant that more money flowing

02:02 into the firm, and the pockets of its partners. It was a successful and lucrative system. One that

02:08 lasted decades, even as the legal world evolved.  Lawyers got access to technology that could speed

02:13 certain processes, but large parts of their work  were still entirely reliant on someone looking

02:18 over documents and textbooks. Then came AI.

02:21 And the whole pyramid began to crumble. Across the legal sphere, partners are

02:26 making the kinds of decisions that wouldn’t  have seemed logical just a few years ago.

02:30 Graduates are finding it harder to get work as  firms abandon the age-old “just keep hiring”

02:34 approach that served them so well before. Clifford Chance, one of the world’s largest

02:39 law firms, has made dozens of roles redundant.  PwC, another giant, has openly stated that the

02:46 rise of AI will lead to fewer workers being hired. Whole categories of legal work are now being taken

02:51 over, automated, and optimized by AI. An industry  built on the bedrock of “every hour is immensely

02:57 valuable” is now having to wake up to a new  reality. One in which every hour of work can be

03:02 condensed to a couple of clicks and an algorithm. Partners have seen what AI can do. And it’s left

03:07 them with a dilemma: do they keep hiring new  junior recruits, or do they embrace AI and let

03:13 technology take over the grunt work? The answer is obvious.

03:16 A first-year associate at a major  law firm today will command an

03:20 approximate base salary of around $235,000. That’s not including things like bonuses,

03:26 healthcare, and other costs related  to office space, equipment. Some firms

03:30 cover some of the costs related to junior  employees’ post-graduate education, too.

03:35 For years, the price tag didn’t actually matter  as far as the firm’s bottom line was concerned.

03:40 Even if it spent a quarter of a million  dollars on a junior associate’s salary,

03:44 that same employee would bring in several  times that amount in billable hours.

03:48 They were self-contained and highly profitable  factories, churning through reams of work and

03:53 producing far more money than they cost to run. Now firms can upgrade to a factory that is a

03:58 thousand times faster, able to operate around  the clock… and more importantly, cheaper to run.

04:03 A junior associate costs $235,000. A  ChatGPT Plus subscription costs $20.

04:10 That difference is too vast for anyone to ignore. Why would any firm worth its salt bother itself

04:15 with sourcing talent, hiring junior associates,  paying for their education, training them up,

04:20 allocating office space to them, and  paying them six figure salaries when

04:24 they could just get AI to do it all for  them for a tiny fraction of the cost?

04:28 Even with laser focus and a decent work rate,  people can only process so much information at a

04:33 time. The average worker will need to spend around  2 minutes on every page. That’s several hours of

04:39 work for a 100 page document. AI, meanwhile, is  capable of reviewing a thousand contracts in just

04:45 a few hours. It’s a 75% reduction in time.  It can operate infinitely faster than entire

04:50 teams of legal experts. Without the mistakes  that overworked lawyers might make. It only

04:55 takes one momentary lapse from a junior to miss  something important or make a mistake that ends

05:00 up costing the firm time and money. AI doesn’t have that problem.

05:04 But it doesn’t mean that lawyers don’t matter. The ones at the top are still needed. Their

05:09 unique abilities and experience are  still as valuable as ever. But the

05:13 work of the underlings – the repetitive  labor that forms the foundations on which

05:17 everything else sits – is no longer required. It’s easy to see, then, why so many firms see

05:23 no other option but to invest in AI and ease  off on the number of entry-level positions.

05:28 This isn’t something that law firms  and partners “opt into” or decide on.

05:32 It’s something that is being forced upon them.  They either go with the flow and adapt to the new

05:37 legal order if they want to survive. The billable hour is changing.

05:41 They can’t keep charging clients  hundreds of dollars an hour for

05:44 tasks that a computer can complete in  seconds for fractions of a single cent.

05:48 Clients recognize the new reality, too. There are already reports of them refusing

05:53 to pay for the likes of foundational  legal research and document reviews.

05:57 As one business litigation firm  owner from California states:

06:00 “The fact is that lawyers charge clients for  a lot of tasks that can be better and more

06:05 efficiently handled through automation and AI.  As clients realize this, they will refuse to pay

06:10 lawyers… to perform tasks that a computer  could easily handle for almost nothing.”

06:14 Legal firms have lost a  significant source of revenue.

06:17 But they have discovered a tool that  can save them a lot of time and money.

06:21 The entire playbook of the legal field  is being rewritten before our eyes.

06:25 The people at the top are sacrificing  those at the bottom to not only keep their

06:29 jobs positions, but to become even more powerful. The people at the peak of the pyramid are somehow

06:34 set to become even richer out of all of  this. That’s despite the fact that their

06:38 firms can no longer charge clients  for countless hours of paperwork.

06:42 They don’t need to deal with the overheads, the  costs, or the burdens involved with hiring and

06:46 managing associate workers. These apex  predator legal professionals can now

06:51 reach unprecedented peaks of productivity. A single elite-level partner can now carry

06:56 out an entire firm’s worth of work quicker and  easier than they ever imagined. They can hoard

07:01 every single piece of profit they generate in  the process, since none of it needs to “trickle

07:05 down” to those lower down the ladder. But while the predators prosper,

07:10 everyone else suffers. The people in the middle and down at

07:13 the lower ends of the legal firms are about to see  their paths of progression extinguished overnight.

07:18 The lawyers who just want to build their careers  and take on the tedious but necessary aspects of

07:23 legal work are being forced out of the industry. There’s no safety net to catch them.

07:28 In order to cover up the sheer brutality of this  maneuver, the legal industry has created a sort

07:33 of smokescreen. A new career path has been  hastily pieced together: the Legal Engineer.

07:38 It sounds intriguing at first. Prestigious, even.

07:42 A post that combines legal work with technological  excellence. A legal profession for the AI era.

07:48 People are already attempting to build hype and  excitement around this new job. They’re selling

07:52 students on the idea of some sort of “hybrid”  career where they can explore new technologies

07:57 while pursuing their passions for justice. The numbers behind the “Legal Engineer”

08:01 role seem equally optimistic. Data shows that AI adoption among

08:06 legal firms jumped from 19% to 79% between  2023 and 2024 alone. The job market for legal

08:14 engineers exploded in a similarly broad style. Dig deeper and evidence also suggests that the

08:20 majority of so-called “engineers” are placed  into sales and customer success departments of

08:25 legal technology vendors. These aren’t lawyers.

08:28 They barely even qualify for the  category of “legal professionals.”

08:32 They’re salesmen in suits; the law  industry equivalent of someone who

08:35 used to be or wanted to become a doctor but  instead ended up as a pharmaceutical rep.

08:40 These roles are focused entirely around  software implementation. They exist to

08:44 accelerate the automation of the legal industry. The entire career is a modern-day Trojan Horse.

08:50 People who would have dedicated their lives  to courtroom cases and the justice system are

08:54 being funneled into positions that undermine  their ambitions. They’re being tricked into

08:59 playing leading roles in the destruction of  the very industry that means so much to them.

09:04 And those at the top know  exactly what they’re doing.

09:06 They realize that the days of junior associates  climbing up the corporate ladder are done.

09:11 But they can’t just announce that. They  can’t say they’re freezing all hires and

09:15 abandoning young talents entirely. So, they make up a new role,

09:20 claim it’s the perfect path for aspiring  legal professionals to follow, and outsource

09:24 the dirty work to the next generation. They  snatch up the best and brightest graduates

09:29 and shepherd them into vendor-side roles,  promising that it’ll all work out in the end.

09:33 But it won’t. These young professionals

09:35 are being given made-up titles like “Solutions  Consultant” and “Legal Technologist. Then they’re

09:40 being tasked with selling AI solutions to the  firms that might have hired and trained them.

09:45 They’re being brainwashed into dismantling the  very ladder that they were supposed to climb.

09:49 It’s a dark and seedy scheme. The worst part of all is that

09:53 even these “Engineers” aren’t immune to  the inevitable collapse. Their “Trojan

09:58 Horse” will go up in flames just like every other  entry-level role once AI has been integrated into

10:03 the majority of firms. Then, the services  of legal engineers are no longer needed.

10:08 And that may happen sooner than people realize. AI isn’t just spreading like wildfire across the

10:13 legal landscape; it’s also getting smarter by  the day, especially when it comes to reading

10:17 and analyzing language. While it’s a complex  form of it, law, at its core, is language.

10:23 It’s all about words, rules, patterns, and terms. The exact things that AI is able to learn quickly.

10:29 For centuries, the complexity of legal texts  meant that they could only be successfully

10:33 parsed by people who dedicated themselves  to the field. The people who spent years

10:37 learning legal language and studying the  intricacies of contracts and agreements.

10:42 AI models don’t need to do that. To them, a 100-page legal draft is

10:46 simply a collection of data points that can be  extrapolated, analyzed, and understood in the

10:51 time it takes a person to blink their eyes. They didn’t even need years of training and

10:56 development to reach this point. By 2023,  months after ChatGPT’s public release,

11:01 GPT-4 passed the Uniform Bar Exam. And it passed with flying colors.

11:06 It exceeded the average score  of real legal graduates.

11:10 By 2025, AI had gone further. OpenAI’s  o3 model earned A+ to B grades on 8

11:16 finals from the University of Maryland. It took time for the legal profession and

11:20 the wider world to actually realize, but the truth  is that from the moment AI came into existence,

11:25 the future of the sector was already determined.  Junior associates were doomed and t high-profile

11:31 partners would abandon their entry-level employees  in favor of cheap generative subscriptions.

11:36 But the problem with their approach is  that it’s only focused on the short term.

11:39 Because if firms stop hiring junior associates,  how will the next generation of senior partners

11:44 ever rise up? If young pros aren’t spending their  formative years training under senior mentors,

11:49 then who is going to be handling boardroom  negotiations in 10, 20, or 30 years from now?

11:55 The top partners today don’t  have an answer for that.

11:57 Even worse, they don’t care about finding one. Because they’re still making money. More money

12:03 than ever. And since many of them will retire  before the big problems actually appear,

12:07 why would they? Why would they mind that an  estimated 44% of all legal tasks can now be

12:14 fully automated by commercially  available AI-powered software?

12:17 They wouldn’t. But they should.

12:19 Everyone should. Because when 44% of

12:22 all legal tasks are being done by AI, that  means 44% of a trillion dollar marketplace

12:28 is gone. Around half a trillion dollars’ worth  of annual corporate expenditure will leave law

12:33 firms and flow into the software industry. The numbers only get uglier from there.

12:38 When a law firm transitions from human-oriented  workflows that can be billed at several

12:42 hundred dollars per hour to instant, automated  pipelines, the cost to execute many tasks falls

12:48 dramatically. Once the AI takeover is complete,  firms will receive less money for almost half

12:53 of all legal tasks. It’s unsustainable.

12:56 Not for those at the very top, of course. They’ll  continue to take charge in cases of courtroom

13:01 litigation and corporate contract signings. But for absolutely everyone else below

13:06 them the future is grim. For thousands of  middle and entry-level legal professionals,

13:11 the system is broken. It’s being dismantled  by those that were supposed to protect it.

13:16 And nothing can stop this process now. So, will AI replace lawyers?

13:21 Not entirely. The profession will always

13:23 call for a certain level of human judgment. People  will continue to represent their clients, whether

13:28 it be in courtrooms or boardroom negotiations. But AI will and is already changing the industry

13:33 forever, not just in terms of “improving  efficiency” and “optimizing workflows,”

13:37 but in wiping out entire careers. And they’ll never be seen again.

13:42 Whether we like it or not, the AI revolution  is here. But what other careers are in

13:46 the firing line? Watch “Top 20 Jobs AI Will  Replace” to find out. Or click on this video.

05:27 architecture known as the unius and

05:29 later cubus which allowed a wide range

05:31 of peripheral devices to connect

05:33 seamlessly vastly expanding the

05:34 computer's versatility in its

05:36 applications now the unius was a

05:38 revolutionary Innovation because it

05:49 drives and other peripherals could
