docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Somewhere in secure vaults, encrypted  messages intercepted over the last decade

00:04 are being stored and cataloged. And the timer to unlock them

00:07 is heading toward zero. Most people assume their

00:10 encrypted data is safe forever. It isn't.  Intelligence agencies are harvesting it,

00:15 so they can decrypt it later. They’re just  waiting for a faster computer to read them.

00:20 If they're right, the fallout  won't stop at private messages.

00:23 The scenarios security experts worry about include  failing infrastructure, frozen financial markets,

00:29 and a world where passwords suddenly mean nothing. The most valuable data breach in history

00:33 hasn't happened… yet.

00:35 The threat of quantum computing  is a real threat to society.

00:39 These computers use the laws of quantum  mechanics to solve problems that would

00:42 take today's machines millions of years. And  theoretically they're exceptionally good at it.

00:47 In 2024, the Global Risk Institute surveyed  industry experts. They estimated a 19% to

00:52 34% chance that, by 2034, a quantum computer  powerful enough to break modern encryption

00:58 will exist. The day it does, the systems  protecting everything from bank transfers

01:03 to government networks become vulnerable. This is how it plays out when the clock hits zero.

01:08 At T-minus 0, the first thing to fail is identity. Every secure website, banking app,

01:14 software update, and VPN relies on digital  certificates. They’re essentially online ID

01:19 cards that prove something is who it claims to be. Right now, those certificates are protected by

01:24 encryption so strong that even the world's  fastest supercomputers would need longer

01:28 than the age of the universe to crack them. But a quantum computer would change that.

01:33 Suddenly, websites can be impersonated. A fake  software update could be sent to millions of

01:38 computers, and servers, and every one of them  would accept it as real. Messages seem to come

01:43 from trusted sources when they’re really spam. It’s all because trust on the internet is built in

01:48 layers. Breaking a single trusted authority  can affect a number of systems below it.

01:53 At T-plus 2 hours, the damage  reaches the physical world.

01:57 Much of the power grid still runs on decades-old  control systems built for an era when fake

02:02 commands weren't a realistic threat. Now those commands can be imitated.

02:06 Safety relays begin tripping, shutting down  substations and transmission lines in response

02:11 to instructions it believes are legitimate. Surges  begin to blow up substations. Grid operators are

02:17 plunged into a no-win situation.They’re forced to  choose between trusting systems they can no longer

02:22 verify or run everything by hand. That’s when the blackouts hit.

02:27 Cities go dark. Hospitals and  other critical infrastructure

02:30 are forced to rely on backup generators.  No software patch is bringing this back.

02:35 Recovery happens one section at a time. When the clock hits T-plus 12 hours,

02:41 money stops moving. The global financial system depends

02:44 on secure digital messages to verify transfers  between banks. Every day, the SWIFT system routes

02:50 around $5 trillion in transfers. That daily flow  is larger than the entire yearly output of Japan.

02:57 Now it has collapsed. Banks can’t be certain that

03:00 transfers are real. Trading floors freeze.  The paperwork that lets goods cross borders

03:05 stops clearing, and supply chains seize up.  No firm will take on risk it can’t verify.

03:10 In early 2026, researchers at Citi modeled  what would happen if just one of America's

03:15 5 largest banks lost access to the system  that moves money between institutions. A

03:21 single day attack could cost $2 trillion to  $3.3 trillion. That is a 10% to 17% drop in

03:28 US output. A loss that size does not clear in a  day. The country goes into a 6-month recession.

03:35 That’s just one bank. In a single day.

03:38 When T-plus 48 hours arrives,  the second shock comes with it.

03:42 For years, governments and intelligence agencies

03:44 have been gathering encrypted data that  remained locked behind security walls.

03:48 Those walls are gone. Archived emails, messages, documents,

03:52 and communications that were once deemed secure  suddenly become accessible. At the same time,

03:57 systems across factories, logistics, and  communications networks continue receiving

04:02 malicious updates. The internet has gone  into survival mode. Nothing can be trusted.

04:07 To most people, none of this looks like  cryptography. A card gets declined for

04:11 no obvious reason. Hospitals go back to  paperwork. Your banking app still works.

04:16 It just can't tell the difference between  your bank and someone pretending to be it.

04:20 That little padlock on the address bar was  doing far more than most people realized.

04:25 It was holding the internet together. This disaster doesn't begin the

04:28 day the quantum computer arrives. It happened years before that,

04:32 while nobody was paying attention.

04:34 In 2021, the NSA openly admitted that  adversaries were already harvesting

04:38 encrypted data. They were just waiting for the  key to open it. But they aren’t alone. Other

04:43 global intelligence agencies are doing the  same thing. No one wants to be left behind.

04:48 Every day, vast amounts of the world's data flow  through undersea cables stretching across oceans.

04:53 It’s a bottleneck of information and that  makes them the ideal place to capture it.

04:58 At this point, most people have the  same reaction: "Can't we just update the

05:02 encryption when quantum computers arrive?" That works for future data. But for the

05:07 information that’s already out there? It’s too late.

05:10 Anything intercepted today can be stored for years  and decrypted later. Once someone has a copy, you

05:16 don't get to take it back. That's what makes this  threat different from a normal cybersecurity flaw.

05:21 When a vulnerability is discovered, you patch it  and move on. But now, the data can be stolen first

05:26 and decrypted later. Which means the clock isn't  ticking from the day the quantum computer arrives.

05:32 It's ticking from the day  the information was sent.

05:35 The real prize isn’t the conversations in  your group chats. It’s state secrets, weapons

05:40 designs and financial arrangements. The things  that can become leverage in a few years time.

05:45 It’s a long term heist. Something that doesn’t  need to succeed immediately. Everything encrypted

05:50 today can be copied in bulk and stored. That changes everything.

05:54 Storage is getting cheaper. Keeping large  tranches of stolen data is no longer an issue.

05:59 For a state-level actor, keeping vast archives of  intercepted traffic costs almost nothing compared

06:04 to the value of what might be unlocked. So the strategy is simple.

06:08 Take everything now and  decide later what it’s worth.

06:11 No one outside those systems knows what  has already been collected. And there’s

06:15 no obvious way to tell. Because nothing  looks broken as the data is still there.

06:20 It just has an invisible copy somewhere else.

06:23 To find out why all this data

06:25 might be at risk, you have to understand  the lock that is supposed to protect it.

06:29 That lock depends on one  bizarre property of numbers.

06:33 Take two huge numbers and multiply  them together. A computer can do it

06:38 in a fraction of a second. But  when you start with the answer,

06:40 figuring out which two numbers created  it can take around 300 trillion years.

06:46 That’s what the security  of the internet relies on.

06:48 It's the reason why you can enter a credit card  number on a website and trust that nobody can

06:54 steal it. The same principle protects  your bank login, your private messages,

06:58 and the chip inside your passport. For decades,  it’s worked, because nothing could reverse that

07:03 answer fast enough to matter. But a quantum computer can.

07:06 There is a method, specifically designed for these  machines, called Shor's algorithm. It does the one

07:12 thing ordinary computers never could. It  finds hidden patterns inside those giant

07:16 numbers and uses them to reverse the process. The problem was something called qubits,

07:22 the quantum equivalent of the bits inside  a normal computer. Unlike ordinary bits,

07:26 qubits are incredibly fragile, and you  need huge numbers of them working together

07:31 to unlock a quantum computer's full power. Early estimates suggested you would need tens of

07:35 millions of qubits to threaten modern encryption.  Nobody had built more than a few hundred.

07:41 Then the estimates started to fall. In May 2025, a Google researcher showed

07:45 that the job might be done with fewer than 1  million qubits. That’s 20 times fewer than his

07:51 own estimate just 6 years earlier. Just one  year later, the figure dropped below 100,000.

07:57 None of this means the supercomputer exists  today. The best quantum chips on earth still run

08:02 somewhere between 100 and 1,000 usable qubits,  and they’re still fragile and error-prone.

08:07 IBM`s largest quantum computer holds just over  1,100 of them, still nowhere enough to break

08:13 encryption on the scale required. Building one  big and stable enough to break real encryption

08:18 could easily take another decade. But it’s getting closer.

08:22 Every piece of encrypted data sitting in those  vaults becomes exposed the moment the machine

08:27 arrives. Now, something drastic is happening. A race to rebuild the locks of the entire internet

08:32 before the ultimate codebreaker is finished.

08:35 Trying to crack encrypted data isn’t a new thing. It had been going on for years, long before most

08:41 people had heard the word quantum. But  while hackers tried to break the code,

08:45 a small group tried to replace it. For almost a decade, most of that work

08:48 ran out of a government lab in Maryland, an  agency called National Institute of Standards

08:53 and Technology, or NIST. The decisions made  there impact nearly every device you own.

08:58 NIST sets the standards that keep the modern  world running. When it approves a technology,

09:03 the world pays attention and adopts them. So when quantum computers threatened to

09:08 crack the locks protecting the internet,  there was one question: what replaces them?

09:13 The decision made by NIST analysts and researchers  would shape the security of billions of people.Get

09:18 it wrong, and everything from your bank  account to the power grid would be at risk.

09:22 In August 2024, after 8 years  of testing, they delivered.

09:26 NIST published the first encryption standards  built to survive a quantum computer:

09:30 one system to establish a secure connection,  another to prove that connection is authentic.

09:36 Their names aren’t exactly glamorous, ML-KEM and  ML-DSA, but what they represent is historic. For

09:44 the first time, the internet had locks designed  for a world where quantum computers exist.

09:49 The old encryption was a puzzle you cracked  by working backwards. The new kind is built

09:53 like a multi-dimensional geometric grid that’s  deliberately obscured by mathematical noise.

09:58 If you already hold the key, the path is  obvious. If you don’t, there is no shortcut.

10:03 The team then built a backup grounded in  a fundamentally different problem. This

10:07 ensures that even if the first is ever cracked,  the world wouldn’t have to start from scratch.

10:12 The biggest names in tech have already begun  swapping out their locks. Google switched the

10:16 new encryption inside Chrome. Apple rebuilt the  system behind iMessage around it. Cloudflare,

10:22 Amazon, and Signal have all made the move, in  most cases without their users noticing a thing.

10:27 Now governments are paying attention. A 2022 US law ordered every federal

10:32 agency to hunt down its old encryption and start  replacing it, with a hard deadline of 2035. The

10:38 finance world got the same message, with its  main security group telling banks to begin

10:42 the switch now rather than wait. But this comes with a warning.

10:46 A few years ago, one of the most promising  new methods, an algorithm called SIKE,

10:50 seemed to be rock solid. Then two researchers  broke it wide open. Not with a quantum computer,

10:56 but with an ordinary computer. It only took an hour.

11:00 The lesson was that no lock  stays unbreakable forever.

11:03 That's why the most advanced systems are  being redesigned around a different idea:

11:07 agility. When the next breakthrough arrives, they  want to swap out their encryption as easily as

11:12 changing a tire. It turns what could have been a  global emergency into a routine software update.

11:18 But inventing a better lock  was never the hard part.

11:21 The hard part is replacing the old one. Because the internet isn't a single machine.

11:25 It's billions of devices, millions  of servers, decades of software,

11:29 and infrastructure that was never designed  for a change this large. Every phone,

11:35 browser, bank, satellite, power plant, and  government system has to make the transition.

11:41 That’s where this starts to fall apart.

11:43 Changing the lock on one website is  simple. Changing it on everything,

11:44 all at once, is the largest forced  upgrade in the history of computing.

11:48 The US government alone expects to spend  $7.1 billion just to upgrade its civilian

11:53 systems. That number doesn’t include the  military and the intelligence agencies.

11:58 Spread the same job across every bank,  hospital, and power company on the planet,

12:02 and serious estimates climb past $1 trillion. The entire Y2K cleanup of the late 1990s,

12:09 by comparison, cost somewhere between $300  and $600 billion. This is bigger than that.

12:15 But money is the least of the problems.  The deeper issues are physical. The new

12:19 quantum-proof locks are larger and heavier than  the ones they replace. They use more memory,

12:24 more bandwidth, and more power. On a laptop  or a data-center server, nobody will notice.

12:29 The problem is everything else. A smart meter bolted to the side of a house.

12:33 A pacemaker in someone`s chest. A sensor on a  pipeline expected to run for 15 years on a single

12:39 battery. These were designed around the small,  light locks of today, with nothing to spare. Some

12:45 of them simply can’t carry the heavier locks. So the upgrades arrive unevenly.

12:50 The cloud can absorb most of the change  almost overnight. The edges of the network

12:54 can't. Billions of smaller devices humming  in the background are left behind. Many built

12:58 into infrastructure that's nearly impossible to  access without ripping it apart. So for years,

13:04 every system caught in the transition has to carry  both locks at once: the old one and the new one.

13:10 Many devices won't be upgraded at all. They'll keep running long after everyone

13:14 knows they're vulnerable. They’re just too  expensive to replace, too important to shut down.

13:19 It’s the start of a slow, spreading digital dark  age. Huge stretches of the world keep running

13:24 on locks everyone already knows are broken. And this is where the people in charge should be

13:28 panicking. While Western governments and companies  spend years replacing vulnerable systems,

13:33 one device at a time, their rivals are pursuing  a very different strategy. Instead of upgrading

13:38 the old network, they're building a new one. One  designed for a post-quantum world from the start.

13:44 And they're building it in space.

13:46 China has spent years working  on something the West mostly

13:50 ignored. Not better code, but physics itself. The approach is called quantum key distribution,

13:55 and it turns the whole problem on its head.  For decades, encryption has relied on a simple

14:00 assumption: that certain mathematical  puzzles are too difficult to solve.

14:04 But difficult isn't the same as impossible. A powerful enough computer could always change

14:09 the equation. Quantum key distribution  takes a different approach. Instead of

14:13 trusting a math problem, it trusts the laws  of physics. The encryption key is carried by

14:18 individual particles of light. And according  to quantum mechanics, the act of measuring

14:23 one of those particles inevitably disturbs it.  The moment anyone tries to intercept the key,

14:28 they leave evidence behind. A fingerprint. Eavesdropping gives itself away.

14:33 In March 2025, Chinese scientists used a satellite  called Jinan-1 to share one of these keys between

14:39 a station near Beijing and another near Cape Town,  South Africa, about 8,000 miles (12,875 km) apart.

14:45 On the ground, China has also built roughly  1,200 miles of dedicated quantum network

14:51 connecting secure sites between Beijing and  Shanghai. More satellites are already planned,

14:56 extending the system even further. So why doesn`t everyone simply switch

15:00 to physics and forget the software fix? Because this isn't a software upgrade.

15:04 A software upgrade is easy. Push an  update, and billions of devices can

15:08 switch to a new encryption standard overnight. Quantum key distribution doesn't work like that.

15:13 Its security comes from the physical world,  from photons traveling through specially

15:17 designed networks. It needs special hardware:  dedicated fiber lines or a direct link to a

15:23 satellite. You have to build it. That’s the difference.

15:26 A handful of nations will be able to protect  their most sensitive communications with the

15:31 laws of physics. Everyone else will remain  on the open internet, patching software,

15:35 upgrading systems, and hoping it works. Security becomes something you can

15:39 either afford or you can`t. And all of it traces back to a

15:43 single mistake made decades ago.

15:45 For half a century, digital security has depended  on a simple fact about computation. Some problems

15:51 are easy to do, but extremely difficult  to undo. We built the entire online world

15:56 on the faith that some doors were, for  all practical purposes, locked forever.

16:01 The mistake was believing  that would always be true.

16:04 Those problems were never genuinely impossible.  They were only impossible for the kind of computer

16:09 we knew how to build. A quantum computer is not  just a faster version of the machine on your

16:13 desk. It runs on entirely different rules, and on  these specific problems, those rules let it walk

16:19 straight through doors we thought were sealed. We mistook the limits of our own technology for

16:24 a law of nature. It was like building a city  on a fault line nobody knew existed. For years,

16:29 the ground felt perfectly solid. Until it moved.

16:33 And that's why no software update can fully  solve this problem. The new locks will help,

16:37 they might even protect us for decades. But  trust online was never permanent. The digital

16:42 world is changing… and when the foundations  change, you don't just replace the locks.

16:46 You rebuild the structure sitting on top of them. Because every password, every digital signature

16:51 depends on the same question: How do you prove  who you are when the old proofs no longer hold?

16:57 You don't.

16:58 The new digital world is already taking  shape and its first casualty is the

17:01 thing you use a dozen times a day: The password. It won’t be gone overnight, but it's something you

17:07 can no longer rely on by itself. What replaces it,  is something physical. A key you tap or plug in.

17:13 A fingerprint or a face. A hardware key you plug  in or tap against your phone. You can already see

17:19 the shift in passkeys, now rolling out across  Google, Apple, and other major platforms. The

17:24 proof of who you are is moving out of the cloud,  and back into the physical world you can touch. It

17:29 changes what attacks can reach in the first place. These systems are now reaching nationwide levels.

17:34 Countries are adopting old-fashioned analog  backups; deliberately simple machines that

17:39 can’t be hacked from thousands of miles away. Estonia, which runs nearly its entire government

17:44 online, already keeps full copies of its state  records on secure servers abroad and offline,

17:50 in what it calls a data embassy. Now,  other governments are copying the idea.

17:55 For the rest of us, the change will feel  small at first. An extra tap to log in. A

17:59 device you suddenly have to keep track of. It’s  an extra step in exchange for better security.

18:04 But it’s the end of something bigger. The internet we grew up with was built on a very

18:09 simple and generous assumption. That encrypted  meant private, and that anyone, anywhere, could

18:14 be trusted just enough to do business with. That  open, borderless, instant network doesn’t survive

18:20 beyond this. What takes its place is more guarded,  more broken up, more rooted in the physical world.

18:25 It trades convenience for survival. There’s no other choice.

18:29 The secrets locked away today will  keep being leaked, unlocked long after

18:33 we have forgotten about them. Some will be  worthless by then. Some will be essential.

18:38 There is a thin thread of hope in all of  this. We might be able to make a change

18:42 to the digital locks before the ultimate  quantum computer arrives. But the age of

18:46 taking digital trust for granted is over. Security shouldn’t be taken for granted.

18:49 From here on, privacy and proof aren’t the  default. They’re things we will need to build, on

18:54 purpose, into everything we make. The age when we  could assume the locks would simply hold is over.

18:57 The belief that the locks would  simply hold… no longer exists.

19:00 Despite all our best efforts, the online  world has always been vulnerable. But what

19:04 happens when those weaknesses are exploited  at a scale we’ve never seen before? Find out

docs.text:
00:00 The 9/11 terror attacks scarred a  nation - and even decades later,

00:04 some things still don’t add  up. Like who knew about it?

00:07 Was there insider trading? And the  case of a strange disappearance...

00:11 Find out the answer to these mysteries and more

00:13 on this episode of The Infographics Show -  “Things About 9/11 That Don’t Make Sense”.

00:18 September 11th, 2001.

00:20 The world was shocked as coordinated  terror attacks hit the United States.

00:23 Members of Osama Bin Laden’s Al Qaeda terrorist  cult hijacked planes, using them as weapons

00:29 to hit high-profile targets.Two jets slammed  into the World Trade Center in New York City,

00:34 killing over 2,000 people and reducing the iconic  towers to rubble. A third plane hit the Pentagon,

00:39 killing hundreds. And a fourth - headed  for the Capitol Building - was brought

00:43 down in a Pennsylvania field by the  heroic actions of its passengers.

00:47 It was the deadliest terror attack in history.

00:49 Everyone knows someone who questions the official  story of 9/11. They usually have an elaborate rant

00:55 about how jet fuel can’t melt steel beams. And  when you question them on what actually happened,

01:00 they’ll tell you “The lizard people just  want us to think the towers blew up.” Those

01:05 conspiracies have been explored and debunked  many times over. But over twenty years later,

01:09 there’s still some things that just don’t  make sense about the horrifying day.

01:14 #9.

01:15 For one thing, the entire circumstances of the  attack seem surreal to those who grew up in its

01:20 aftermath. Unlike most terror attacks since, the  attack was extremely low-tech. The terrorists,

01:25 organized in groups of four or five,  boarded planes holding only box cutters.

01:30 They took the plane hostage, forced the  pilot to give up control or killed them,

01:34 and piloted the plane into its intended  target. It seems like a well-planned - if

01:39 simple - operation. But there’s one  thing that still raises some eyebrows.

01:43 Why did Mohammed Atta travel to Portland,  Maine the night before the attack?

01:48 On September 10th, 2001, Mohamed Atta picked  up his fellow hijacker Abdul-Azzia Al-Omari

01:54 at a hotel in Boston. From there, they drove a  rented car north to Portland - almost two hours

02:00 away. Surveillance footage captured the pair  checking into a Portland hotel that evening.

02:04 They were also seen making ATM withdrawals,  browsing the aisles of a local Wal-Mart,

02:08 and in the parking lot of a nearby Pizza Hut. Some believe Atta was conducting surveillance

02:13 detection, making sure no one was tailing him.  Others think it was a strategic move - security

02:17 at Portland’s airport may have been lighter than  Boston’s. Another theory was he was planning

02:22 for last-minute delays or meeting with an  unknown accomplice. Whatever the reason,

02:27 on the morning of September 11th, Atta boarded a  flight back to Boston. Once he landed, he received

02:32 a call from Marwan Al-Shehi, another 9/11 hijacker  - believed to be the green light for the attacks.

02:37 Atta would go on to hijack American Airlines  Flight 11, crashing it into the North Tower.

02:42 Despite years of investigation, Atta’s trip to  Portland remains one of the most mysterious pieces

02:47 of the 9/11 puzzle.

02:50 One of the scariest things about 9/11 was the  uncertainty in the immediate aftermath. Thousands

02:55 of people died - but very few bodies were found.  Almost all the casualties in New York and on the

03:00 planes were essentially vaporized, with their  families desperately seeking any evidence of

03:04 their loved ones’ so they could have some degree  of closure. Many disappeared without a trace.

03:10 One was Sneha Anne Phillip, an  Indian-American physician who

03:13 was last seen on September 10th  near her home in Lower Manhattan,

03:17 shopping at a department store. She  likely made her purchases and went home.

03:20 And then, no trace of her was ever seen again.

03:23 Unlike most of the 9/11 victims, there are no  reports of her being on-site, and no eye-witnesses

03:29 ever reported seeing her. Her family has reason  to believe she was there - she was a physician,

03:34 and may have gone to the World Trade Center to  offer medical assistance. But few of the doctors

03:38 who were on-site went into the towers themselves.  Instead, they were helping people who were injured

03:43 after escaping. And while people did die on  the ground due to falling debris and fires,

03:48 those were the bodies most likely to be recovered  intact. Multiple investigations by the NYPD and a

03:53 private investigation commissioned by  Phillip’s husband turned up nothing.

03:57 Which has led many people to  wonder - is everything as it seems?

04:01 Phillip had a troubled past before the events  of 9/11, being fired from her job at Cabrini

04:06 Medical Center due to tardiness and alcoholism.  She complained to police that an intern groped

04:11 her during a staff night out. The case would  later be dropped and Phillip was charged with

04:15 filing a false police report. It seemed like  her life was spiraling before the terror attack.

04:20 Could she have faked her  death or died in another way,

04:23 and it was completely ignored in  the chaos of the terror attack?

04:26 Her family has been suing to have her  officially confirmed as a victim of the

04:30 9/11 attacks, allowing her to be  honored officially. And in 2008,

04:34 an appeals court gave them their wish and  she was added to the Ground Zero Memorial.

04:39 That’s the legal outcome - but any hard  evidence remains painfully hard to come by.

04:43 And in the immediate aftermath, confusion reigned.

04:47 #7.

04:48 Osama Bin Laden and his Al Qaeda terror network  quickly claimed responsibility for the attacks,

04:53 and he became the world’s public enemy #1. But  he came from a very big family - the son of a

04:59 billionaire Saudi oil baron who had multiple  wives and 50 children. And he was considered

05:04 the black sheep - most of his family were  jet-setting businesspeople, with devoutly

05:08 Muslim beliefs. They had no affiliation to terror  groups and viewed Osama as a disgrace. In 2001,

05:14 the Bin Laden family was spread around  the world… including in the United States.

05:18 It was one of the strangest affairs that  took place in the days after the attacks.

05:22 Flights were grounded for two days, and strictly  regulated after that. And it would be several

05:28 weeks before one of the most controversial  flights to happen in that time was revealed.

05:32 On September 13th, twelve members of the  Bin Laden family who were in the U.S. were

05:37 put on a plane and evacuated back to  Saudi Arabia. When this was revealed,

05:41 it caused some outrage - why were the  relatives of our enemy being evacuated?

05:46 And many asked - why were they such a priority?

05:49 This was conspiracy fodder of the highest degree,  with some arguing it showed that the government

05:54 was in on the attacks or at least collaborating  with the Bin Laden family. But less conspiratorial

05:59 individuals said that most of the Bin Ladens  in the country were high school and college

06:03 students. And besides, money talks - reportedly  the evacuations were kick-started when one of

06:08 Bin Laden’s brothers sought help from the Saudi  Embassy. Saudi Arabia had good relations with

06:13 the Bush administration, thanks to their many oil  deals and geopolitical significance. The likely

06:18 scenario is that they were evacuated for their  protection due to fears of reprisals, but it

06:24 still raised some eyebrows - and the government  has been tight-lipped about it ever since.

06:28 But one figure might be at the center of it all.

06:31 #6.

06:32 The biggest question regarding 9/11 has  always been “who knew”? The most common

06:37 suspect has been George W. Bush. Many people  insist that the US President must have known

06:41 in advance and allowed the attacks to  happen so he would have an excuse for

06:45 war. There’s no evidence for that - but  his close ties to the Saudi government

06:49 continue to draw scrutiny. Almost all  the hijackers were from Saudi Arabia,

06:54 and so was one of the most mysterious figures  related to the attacks, Omar Al-Bayouni.

06:59 Did this Saudi intelligence  agent know what was coming?

07:02 Although of Egyptian descent, Al-Bayouni’s  family had settled in Saudi Arabia,

07:06 where he became a well-connected  figure with reported ties to the

07:09 Saudi government. He also reportedly had  close ties to known terrorist associates,

07:14 including helping two of the eventual  hijackers find housing in San Diego.

07:18 And by the time the attacks hit, he was gone.

07:21 He was in the UK pursuing a PhD when  the towers fell, and ten days later,

07:25 he was arrested in a joint US-British operation.  The evidence of his links to terrorist associates

07:30 was strong, including many phone calls to a  key Bin Laden associate, Ziyad Khaleel and

07:36 Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs cleric Fahad  al-Thumairy. Al-Thumairy denied knowing Bayoumi,

07:42 despite telephone records showing at least 60  calls between them. But the British weren’t

07:47 able to produce any hard evidence of his knowledge  or involvement, and they ultimately released him.

07:52 He would soon return to Saudi  Arabia…and disappear off the map

07:56 completely. His association with the  attack has never been fully proven,

07:59 but an FBI report indicates that they  believe there’s a better-than-even chance

08:04 he was a conspirator. But if anyone wants  answers, they’ll have to find him first.

08:09 But there’s one site on Ground Zero that  causes more controversy than any other.

08:13 #5.

08:14 In late 2000, two of the 9/11 hijackers -  Khalid Almihdhar and Nawaf Alhazmi - rented

08:20 a room in San Diego from a man who  was an undercover FBI informant.

08:25 The informant - whose identity has never  been released to the public - was a tested

08:29 asset for the Bureau. He prayed with the  two men and helped them adjust to life

08:33 in the U.S. - he even assisted one of them in  opening a bank account. But he never provided

08:38 their names to his FBI handler. And perhaps more  importantly, the handler never asked. At the time,

08:44 Almihdhar and Alhazmi were already persons  of interest to the CIA, having attended an

08:48 al-Qaeda summit in Malaysia just months earlier. The pair moved into the informant’s house in

08:53 September 2000. Almihdhar moved out six weeks  later, and Alhazmi left by the end of the

08:58 year. During that time, both men attended flight  school in preparation for the devastating attack.

09:03 It wasn’t until after the 9/11 attacks  that the informant recognized the names

09:07 being reported in the media. He called his  handler and revealed that the hijackers

09:11 had been his roommates. There’s no evidence he  intentionally concealed their identities - but

09:15 it still remains a glaring example of  miscommunication between intelligence agencies.

09:20 A CIA alert naming the two men as potential  terrorists had been issued on August 23,

09:26 2001. But by then, the opportunity was gone. As  one counterintelligence expert later queried, why

09:32 didn’t the agent ask more questions? Or at least  explore the possibility of recruiting new assets?

09:38 And it wasn’t the only  mystery that lingered on 9/11.

09:41 #4.

09:42 He’s called the “last person  killed in New York on 9/11”,

09:46 but he wasn’t a worker in the towers or a  first-responder. His name was Henryk Siwiak,

09:51 and he was a Polish immigrant minding his  own business in the Brooklyn neighborhood of

09:55 Bedford-Stuyvesant. A former Polish government  worker, he was visiting his sister in New York

10:00 and decided to get a job to send money back to  his family. While he didn’t speak much English,

10:04 he was a hard worker and managed to  get a job as a construction worker.

10:07 But on that fateful day, he  would meet a shocking end.

10:10 After his job site shut down for  the day after the terror attacks,

10:14 he walked across the Brooklyn Bridge and went to  interview for a job cleaning a local supermarket.

10:18 Through a series of miscommunications,  he was given the wrong directions for the

10:22 store address, and went to what was a fairly  dangerous, crime-ridden neighborhood. There,

10:27 eyewitnesses reported hearing an argument,  followed by some gunshots. Siwiak was found

10:32 on the pavement, bleeding out from  a fatal gunshot wound to the chest.

10:36 And over 20 years later, his  murder has never been solved.

10:40 Not surprisingly, this was mostly attributed  to one thing - the police were completely

10:44 occupied by the massive terror attack  in Manhattan. It left zero resources for

10:48 investigating a routine homicide. This has  led Siwiak’s case to gain extra notoriety,

10:53 but even in the best of times, a murder  where the murder weapon is never found

10:56 is extremely hard to solve. But there  were other odd factors to the killing,

11:01 such as the fact that no money was taken from  Siwiak. Did his killer think the mild-mannered

11:05 foreign man may have been involved with the  attack? The cold case is only getting colder.

11:10 And it’s far from the only false accusation  of involvement that has cropped up.

11:14 #3.

11:15 While some conspiracy theories relating to 9/11  are more outlandish - with people claiming the

11:20 towers were destroyed by explosives planted by the  government - most of them simply focus on who to

11:26 blame. In the immediate aftermath of the attacks,  a lot of suspects, including the U.S. government,

11:31 had fingers pointed at them. But in later years,  conspiracies focused on another target - Israel,

11:37 who were among the greatest enemies of Osama  Bin Laden. And people who insist they must

11:42 have been involved even point to some specific  targets - the so-called “Dancing Israelis”.

11:47 So what has made this theory stick around so long?

11:50 First off, there’s no evidence that anyone  else was involved in 9/11 besides Osama Bin

11:56 Laden and his network of terrorists - he  proudly took credit for the attacks. But

12:00 some people insist that a group of Israelis was  arrested near the towers a short time after 9/11,

12:06 reportedly laughing and celebrating the attacks.

12:09 There’s no evidence of how they were acting -  but a deep dive into government files did reveal

12:14 six Israeli nationals were arrested in lower  Manhattan, and later deported back to Israel.

12:19 It’s believed that the six men were  likely Israeli intelligence agents,

12:22 here collecting information on the attacks.  Israel viewed Al Qaeda as a serious security

12:27 threat at the time. Many countries likely  have spies in the country at all times,

12:31 and it only becomes a serious issue when they’re  trying to access secret or high-risk information.

12:36 But in the immediate aftermath of  9/11, security stepped up big time

12:40 and deported a lot of people who may  have been slipping under the radar.

12:44 And so they went back - leaving a trail  of decades-long conspiracies behind them.

12:49 But if there’s one question that’s been lingering  all these years, it’s this - did anyone know?

12:54 #2.

12:54 Some of the more outlandish conspiracy theories  claim that the attacks were masterminded in the

12:58 United States, but most simply allege that it  was allowed to proceed without being reported.

13:03 Some claim the government wanted to have an  excuse to start a war in the Middle East,

13:07 while others claim a massive insurance scam on the  World Trade Center. But no evidence has emerged of

13:12 advanced knowledge by the top power brokers at the  time - but it did emerge in a very unlikely place.

13:18 A high-school classroom.

13:20 It was September 6th, 2001, and English  teacher Antoinette DiLorenzo was greeting

13:25 a new year of students. Her class was  heavily composed of Pakistani immigrants,

13:29 and one of the boys made a disturbing comment  to his Bensonhurst classmates. He claimed that

13:34 the World Trade Center wouldn’t be standing  next week. She chalked it up to a bad-taste

13:39 teenage joke - but then watched in horror as  the prophecy came true. She quickly called

13:43 the authorities, and the FBI and NYPD  tracked the boy down to interrogate him.

13:48 So did this boy have advanced knowledge  of the world’s deadliest terror attack?

13:52 All these years later, we don’t have a clear  answer. The boy claimed he was only joking,

13:57 and his family backed him up - but the coincidence  was such that many people were dubious. The police

14:02 ultimately decided that it was just a case of  the world’s worst-timed joke and no charges

14:07 were ever filed. The most convincing  evidence was that none of the hijackers

14:11 involved in the attack were of Pakistani  background. Fifteen were from Saudi Arabia,

14:16 two were from the United Arab Emirates,  one from Lebanon, and one from Egypt.

14:21 That makes the connections needed for this random  boy to overhear talk about it much less likely.

14:26 But maybe the most bizarre story to  come out of 9/11 indicates that a

14:30 lot of people may have known - and  they made a lot of money off it.

14:35 #1.

14:36 Was there insider trading on 9/11?

14:38 It’s one of the biggest scourges of the insurance  world - people who have advance knowledge of an

14:43 event profiting off it by making trades on the  stock market. It’s what sent Martha Stewart to

14:48 prison, and many Senators faced allegations  of it during the Covid-19 pandemic. The most

14:53 common source of it is when people who work in a  specific company know that the company is about

14:57 to be sold or make a big announcement. They buy  or sell more shares while the price is right.

15:03 But would anyone sink so low as to profit  off a terror attack - and tell no one?

15:08 It was only a week after the attack  when The Times, a London-based paper,

15:12 announced that it was investigating whether  unusual trades happened as a result of advance

15:17 knowledge of the attacks. A massive number of  shares of insurance companies and airlines were

15:22 sold off before the attack, in countries  in Europe as well as Japan and the US.

15:27 This was especially high in the cases of United  Airlines and American Airlines - the two airlines

15:33 whose planes were used in the hijacking. In fact,  it was the highest amount of these stocks ever

15:37 traded on the Chicago Exchange - and the  investors who sold made millions off it.

15:42 The possibility of insider trading  was raised with the 9/11 commission,

15:46 and the fact-finders eventually found  explanations for the unusual trading.

15:50 Both the trading of United and American  shares, which happened on different days,

15:54 were linked to trading strategies  circulated by investment newsletters.

15:58 There was a thorough investigation by the SEC into  the American-based trades, and by intelligence

16:04 agencies into the foreign trades - but no evidence  of advance knowledge of the attack was found.

16:09 But that didn’t stop the digging.

16:11 As the post-9/11 era wore on, damaged hard  drives were discovered in the ruins of the

16:16 World Trade Center - which were transferred  to an elite data recovery company, Convar,

16:20 for retrieval. The German-based  company conducted an investigation

16:24 for US authorities into possible evidence  of criminal insider trading, and was able

16:29 to restore several hundred hard drives over  the next year. However, the 9/11 committee in

16:33 2003 stated that they had not received any  valuable information from the hard drives.

16:38 With no hard evidence of insider trading, much  of the discussion of the topic has turned on

16:43 speculation. As late as 2010, an independent  report claimed that there were at least thirteen

16:49 informed trades that would only make sense if  the investors knew something big was coming.

16:54 The international team of experts pointed to  an unusual increase in trading activity in the

16:58 days before the attacks. But with no hard  evidence, no one has ever been charged for

17:03 insider trading - and it’s likely they never  will. If someone did know and used it to make

17:08 money rather than dropping a dime, it would be the  biggest scandal in the financial sector’s history.

17:14 What do you think is the most overlooked  detail about 9/11? Share your thoughts below.

17:18 Want to know what happened in 9/11  on that fateful day? Check out “What

17:22 Happened Immediately After 9/11” for  all the grim details. And the good news

17:26 is…we got him. Watch “How SEAL Team Took  Down Osama Bin Laden (Minute by Minute)”

17:31 for the tale of the tape of how  the Al Qaeda leader met his end.

docs.text:
00:00 Welcome to this video on anarchist philosophy. Today we explore the key concepts that define anarchist thought.

00:15 Anarchism is not chaos, but rather a philosophy that seeks to eliminate hierarchical authority and promote voluntary cooperation.

00:30 The core principles include mutual aid, direct action, and solidarity among individuals and communities.

00:45 We believe that people can organize themselves without the need for centralized control or coercion.

01:00 This approach has been applied in various contexts, from community organizing to alternative economic systems.

00:00 There's a phrase that can cost a company

00:02 a fortune. And the worst part is that it

00:04 usually sounds like good teamwork. Oh, I

00:06 assumed you knew. And that's it. There's

00:08 no siren, no flashing beacon. Nobody

00:10 slams a big red button on a console.

00:12 Just a little social shortcut passed

00:14 quietly from one person to another until

00:16 it eventually shows up in the real world

00:18 wearing coveralls and carrying a wrench.

00:20 Today I want to talk to you about

00:21 neurodiversity in the workplace, but not

00:23 as a slogan or as a bumper sticker and

00:25 not as a poster in the lunchroom and not

00:27 as one more mandatory training module

00:29 that everybody clicks through while

00:30 waiting for their coffee. I want to talk

00:32 about in the context of industrial work

00:33 where assumptions are not merely

00:35 inconvenient but can become physical.

00:37 They can become pressure, heat, stored

00:39 energy, ignition sources, fatigue

00:41 cracks, vapor clouds, and sometimes an

00:43 incident investigation with diagrams and

00:45 arrows showing how we got from what

00:46 everybody thought to what nobody

00:48 verified. And I want to do that for an

00:50 audience that already understands the

00:52 stakes. TC Energy operates one of the

00:54 largest natural gas pipeline networks in

00:56 North America with tens of thousands of

00:58 kilometers of pipe, compressor stations,

01:00 meter stations, control rooms, field

01:02 crews, engineers, operators, land

01:04 representatives, integrity specialists,

01:07 project teams, and contractors all

01:09 joined together into one living

01:10 industrial system that moves energy

01:11 across Canada and beyond. DC Energy

01:14 describes its natural gas network as

01:16 93,600 km of pipeline supplying more

01:19 than 30% of the natural gas consumed

01:21 across North America daily. That scale

01:24 is impressive, but scale has a

01:25 personality all of its own. A small

01:27 assumption inside a small system is a

01:29 nuisance, but a small assumption inside

01:31 a continental energy system is a seed.

01:33 You may not see anything grow from it

01:35 today. You may not see anything

01:37 tomorrow. But if the conditions are

01:38 right, if the shift handover is vague

01:40 enough, if the alarm is familiar enough,

01:42 if the required documents are thick

01:44 enough or if the procedure has a

01:45 sentence that everybody interprets

01:47 slightly differently, then eventually

01:49 that seed can find water and sprout. And

01:51 that's where somebody like me can be

01:53 useful. I'm autistic and it's not

01:55 something I lean into as an identity.

01:57 It's just who I am. And while I always

01:59 knew I was pretty different, I had no

02:00 real idea why. I was diagnosed late

02:03 after decades of thinking that I was

02:04 merely odd in some very specific ways. I

02:07 knew that I was literal. I knew that I

02:09 could be intense and that it could be

02:10 like flipping a switch. I knew I had a

02:12 low tolerance for ambiguity when a

02:14 precise answer ought to exist. I needed

02:16 to know what was inside of everything.

02:18 And I knew that social situations

02:20 sometimes felt like a game where

02:21 everybody else had been given the rules

02:22 and I was expect to infer them from

02:24 facial expressions, pauses, and how

02:26 quickly people reach for their jackets.

02:28 But I didn't know it was autism. When I

02:30 was first diagnosed, it caused me to

02:32 replay much of my life from a new angle.

02:34 Suddenly, old memories that had been

02:36 filed under just Dave being Dave

02:37 acquired a different label. Like the

02:39 first time I met Bill Gates in his

02:41 backyard while I was still an intern at

02:42 Microsoft. My manager was introducing me

02:45 and effectively bragging on me that I

02:46 had completed an impressive set of

02:48 projects in just 4 months. The problem

02:50 was that it had actually taken 3 months.

02:52 So I interrupted him with the

02:53 correction. 3 months. To me, that was

02:56 the accurate value. To everybody else, I

02:58 had just soiled a social moment for no

03:00 useful reason. But that same instinct

03:02 that made me correct in a relevant

03:03 detail in a backyard conversation is

03:05 also the same instinct that in a

03:07 different life might have made me

03:08 interrupt a control room discussion to

03:10 ask, wait, do we actually know what the

03:12 valve's current position is, or are we

03:13 inferring it from the command that we

03:15 just sent to the valve? And there's the

03:17 knife edge of neurodiversity at work.

03:19 That same trait that could be socially

03:21 awkward can be operationally priceless.

03:23 Because in industrial systems, there is

03:25 a dangerous difference between what was

03:27 commanded, what was indicated, what was

03:29 assumed, and what is actually physically

03:31 true. If you work around pipelines,

03:33 compression, measurement, pressure

03:34 control, excavation, isolation,

03:37 electrical systems, or hot work, you

03:39 already live in that difference. You

03:40 know that a valve showing closed on a

03:42 screen is not identical to a valve being

03:44 closed out in the field. You know that a

03:46 lock on a hasp is not identical to

03:48 isolation unless the energy state has

03:50 actually been verified. You know that

03:52 the line was slept is not identical to

03:53 we have confirmed that the atmosphere is

03:55 safe. You know that the contractor

03:57 understands is not identical to the

03:59 contractor can repeat back the hazard

04:01 and the control. You know that well we

04:03 always do it this way is not a control

04:05 measure. That's a cultural fossil. And

04:07 today I want to make the case that

04:08 neurodeiverse employees including people

04:10 with autism, ADHD, dyslexia and other

04:13 forms of non-standard cognition can be a

04:15 powerful defense against those fossils

04:17 hardening into failure. But first we

04:19 need an example. I wanted to find a good

04:21 example of an industrial accident to use

04:23 here, but finding one where nobody died

04:25 was challenging. And yet, we need one

04:27 serious enough that nobody can dismiss

04:29 it as just office politics wearing a

04:30 hard hat. So, back in July of 1983, when

04:33 I was in 10th grade, and Air Canada was

04:35 bringing the new Boeing 767 into

04:37 service, and it came with it a quiet but

04:40 important transition. Fuel calculations

04:42 were now being done in metric. The

04:44 aircraft did not have a fully working

04:45 fuel level system. So the crew and

04:47 ground staff relied on manual

04:48 measurements and calculations to

04:50 determine how much fuel was actually

04:52 aboard. And somewhere in that chain, a

04:54 value was treated as pounds per liter

04:56 when the aircraft actually needed kilog

04:58 per liter. That sounds like a routine

05:00 math error, but it wasn't merely

05:02 arithmetic. It was a system caught

05:03 between two measurement cultures,

05:05 imperial habit and metric requirement.

05:07 and a new aircraft, degraded

05:09 instrumentation, unclear ownership, and

05:11 just enough routine confidence that

05:12 nobody stopped the process and asked the

05:14 brutally simple question, uh, what units

05:17 are we actually using here? The result

05:19 was that a state-of-the-art widebody

05:21 airliner departed with far less fuel

05:23 than required and at 41,000 ft somewhere

05:25 over Manitoba, both engines flamed out.

05:28 Imagine that cockpit for a moment. No

05:30 thrust, no mechanical engine driven

05:32 power, no comforting turbine sound, just

05:35 a Boeing 767 that has suddenly become

05:37 the world's largest sail plane. Captain

05:39 Bob Pearson and first officer Maurice

05:41 Quintel managed the glide, founded old

05:44 air base at Gimley, Manitoba, and put

05:46 the aircraft down on what had become a

05:47 drag strip, avoiding people on the

05:49 ground picnicking and saving everybody

05:50 on board. It was a brilliant piece of

05:52 airmanship, but the heroics at the end

05:55 should not distract us from the lesson

05:56 at the beginning. The aircraft did not

05:58 run out of fuel because Canada went

06:00 metric. It ran out of fuel because the

06:02 organization became bilingual in

06:04 measurement before it became fluent in

06:05 verification. And that is precisely why

06:08 this story matters in an industrial

06:09 workplace. A number without units is not

06:12 just a number. It's worse. It's a trap

06:14 wearing a name tag. Pressure, flow,

06:16 torque, wall thickness, distance, gas

06:18 concentrations, temperature, and fuel

06:20 load all become dangerous when the unit

06:22 or assumption behind them is merely

06:24 implied. And this is where neurodeiverse

06:26 thinking can be a real operational

06:28 asset. Some autistic minds are unusually

06:30 bothered by ambiguity. Not because we're

06:32 trying to be difficult, but because

06:34 undefined values do not feel complete.

06:37 We may be the person who asks the

06:38 painfully obvious questions like, "Is

06:40 that PSI or kilopascals?" or "Is that

06:42 valve closed by command or verified

06:44 closed in the field?" "Is that isolation

06:46 assumed or proven?" It can sound really

06:48 pedantic right up until the moment when

06:50 the entire safety case depends on the

06:52 answer. Now, I'm not trying to make the

06:54 case that somebody with autism is

06:55 automatically smarter or more detail-

06:57 oriented, more diligent, or more safety

06:59 conscious. That would be nonsense and

07:01 more than a little insulting to

07:02 everybody else. But our brains seem to

07:04 naturally abhore ambiguity. It's a

07:07 genetic predisposition that gets

07:08 reinforced by a lifetime of being

07:10 confused and burned by ambiguity in

07:12 other aspects of our life, particularly

07:13 in the social realm. So, for me,

07:16 proceeding while relying on untested

07:17 assumptions is like stepping across one

07:19 of those glass floored skywalks. You can

07:21 do it easily enough and intellectually

07:23 you believe it's perfectly safe, but

07:25 there's still a primitive part of the

07:26 nervous system saying something is very

07:28 very wrong. Sometimes I've been overcome

07:30 by that feeling without even knowing

07:32 why. It's like a feeling of panic you

07:34 sometimes get on the way to the airport

07:36 where you suddenly wonder if you really

07:37 have your passport, your keys, and your

07:38 wallet. Sometimes I'll get that feeling

07:41 in the middle of a code check-in, for

07:42 example, and makes me stop to analyze

07:44 why. Usually, there's a reason that I

07:46 feel that way. I just don't know it yet.

07:49 Not every autistic person is a safety

07:51 savant and not every neurotypical person

07:52 is careless. But many autistic people do

07:55 share this particular discomfort with

07:56 ambiguity. We often want terms defined,

07:59 states confirmed, assumptions named,

08:01 sequences written, exceptions handled,

08:03 and handoffs made explicit. We often

08:05 struggle with the soft social bandwidth

08:07 that tells everyone else when the room

08:08 is done with a topic. We may keep asking

08:11 after the comfortable answer has arrived

08:13 because the comfortable answer is not

08:14 the same as a complete one. And we've

08:16 all been in meetings with that one

08:18 person. The person who asked the

08:19 question at the end of the meeting just

08:21 as everybody else has mentally already

08:22 stood up needlessly extending what was

08:24 already a long session often merely to

08:26 justify their own presence at the

08:27 meeting. And I'm begging you, don't

08:29 confuse this with that because sometimes

08:31 it's a nerdiverse person trying to get

08:33 clarification on something the rest of

08:34 you assume that everybody knows but

08:36 which may not actually be known by

08:38 everybody in the same way. That can be

08:40 annoying in a meeting. It can also be

08:42 the only thing between an assumption and

08:44 an incident. Imagine for a moment that

08:46 the person holding the clipboard and the

08:47 tarmac for that Air Canada 767 had been

08:50 just a little bit autistic. Not a

08:52 genius, not a savant, not Rayman in a

08:54 reflective vest, but simply the kind of

08:56 person who gets physically uncomfortable

08:57 when a number arrives without a unit

08:59 attached to it. So the fuel figure is

09:01 written down, the density is written

09:03 down, the required uplift is written

09:04 down, everybody is busy, the process is

09:07 familiar enough to feel safe, and the

09:09 social momentum is all pushing towards

09:11 sign it and get moving along. But this

09:13 person pauses, taps the page, and asks

09:15 the question that sounds almost too

09:17 basic to be worth asking. Is this pounds

09:19 per liter or kilograms per liter? And

09:21 that's the whole point. In many

09:23 organizations, that question would feel

09:25 annoying because everybody is supposed

09:26 to know what the number means. It might

09:28 even qualify as a stupid question. But

09:30 supposed to know is not a unit of

09:32 measure. It's not a control. It's just

09:34 an assumption wearing a hard hat. A

09:36 neurodeiverse mind may be less willing

09:38 to accept the implied context and more

09:40 likely to insist the hidden parts be

09:42 made visible. Show me the unit. Show me

09:44 the conversion. Show me the independent

09:46 check. That little pause, that moment of

09:48 socially inconvenient precision might

09:50 have stopped the entire chain before it

09:51 ever left the ground. And that's the

09:53 value I want leaders to understand. The

09:56 employee who asked the obvious question

09:58 is not always slowing the work down.

10:00 Sometimes they're preventing the work

10:01 from speeding confidently in the wrong

10:03 direction. The cost of that question

10:05 might be 30 seconds on the tarmac. The

10:07 cost of not asking it was a powerless

10:09 Boeing 767 gliding over Manitoba. And

10:12 there's a subtle but critical

10:13 distinction here. The first instinct

10:15 after a near miss of some kind is often

10:17 to go hunting for the person closest to

10:18 the mistake. Who signed it? Who missed

10:20 it? Who should have known? But that line

10:22 of questioning can turn a technical

10:23 failure into more of a courtroom drama.

10:25 And once people feel cross-examined, the

10:27 truth starts wearing body armor. The

10:29 more useful question is colder, cleaner,

10:31 and far more powerful. What do we

10:33 actually know that does not depend on

10:35 this assumption being true? That's the

10:37 question that cuts through the fog. Not

10:39 do we trust the gauge, but what second

10:41 source agrees with it? Not did the

10:43 procedure say it was isolated, but how

10:45 did we physically prove that the energy

10:46 was gone? Not was everybody told, but

10:49 can the person actually doing the work

10:50 explain the hazard back to us? In high

10:53 consequence systems, confidence is not

10:55 evidence. Independent verification is

10:57 evidence. That distinction matters,

10:59 especially in high hazard work. Blame

11:01 makes people defensive. Precision makes

11:03 system safer. A neurodeiverse employee

11:05 who is trained and well supported can

11:07 become very good at precision without

11:09 automatically turning it into blame. At

11:11 the end of the day, they tend to be more

11:12 driven to understand the how and the why

11:14 than the who. Anyway, now if you're in

11:17 industry and you have your own

11:18 procedures, your own standards, your own

11:19 management systems, your own control

11:21 room practices, your own integrity

11:23 programs, your own emergency response

11:24 structures, and your own safety culture.

11:27 I'm not here to pretend I know anything

11:28 about your internal systems. I don't.

11:31 But physics does not care whose logo is

11:33 on the truck. Gas pressure does not care

11:35 how senior someone is. A flange does not

11:37 care whether the meeting was respectful.

11:39 Stored energy does not care whether the

11:41 assumption felt obvious to everyone

11:43 else. And a right of way does not care

11:45 whether the person with the excavator

11:46 probably understood the locating marks.

11:49 Industrial reality is beautifully

11:50 democratic that way because it ignores

11:52 everybody's opinion equally. And that's

11:54 why ambiguity is so expensive. It lets

11:57 people preserve social comfort in the

11:59 moment by moving uncertainty into the

12:01 field. Accepting ambiguity is a social

12:03 convention we follow to speed things

12:05 along, but it always transfers the risk

12:07 downstream. Think about a shift

12:09 handover. On paper, it's simple. One

12:11 crew transfers the state of the

12:13 operation to another. In reality, it's

12:15 one human brain trying to serialize a

12:17 messy physical system into a language

12:18 while another human brain reconstructs

12:20 it under time pressure. Any missing

12:22 context becomes a little trap door. But

12:24 with time constraints, we use shorthand

12:26 and assumptions. We had some trouble

12:28 with the transmitter earlier, but it's

12:29 fine now. Well, what does fine mean?

12:31 Stable, calibrated, bypassed, in alarm,

12:34 but acknowledged, replaced, verified

12:35 against a local gauge, temporarily

12:37 ignored because maintenance is coming on

12:39 Monday anyway. Or how about we isolated

12:41 that section? Well, what does isolated

12:43 mean? Valve closed, locked, tagged,

12:45 depressurized, verified, zero energy, or

12:47 just merely removed from normal

12:49 operation? Or the contractor knows about

12:51 the crossing but knows what exactly?

12:53 knows there is a pipeline, knows the

12:55 depth, knows the tolerance zone, knows

12:57 the hand dig requirement, knows who to

12:59 call if conditions differ, knows that

13:01 frozen ground, bad light, or snow cover

13:03 can make yesterday's certainty into

13:05 today's gas. Neurotypical teams often

13:07 rely on context and convention to

13:09 compress those details. You develop

13:11 something of a shortorthhand. Most of

13:12 the time, that compression works and

13:14 saves valuable time. Language would be

13:16 intolerable otherwise. But in hazardous

13:19 work, compression must be done

13:20 carefully. It's the difference between a

13:22 good fitting and one that was almost

13:23 tight. Autistic cognition often resists

13:26 that compression. We may ask for the

13:28 uncompressed version. And yes, sometimes

13:30 we ask at the most inconvenient possible

13:32 times. But if your system has no room

13:34 for that question, the system is brutal.

13:36 In that case, don't hate the player. Fix

13:38 the game. I learned this the hard way in

13:40 my own career, though mostly with

13:41 software and people rather than pipes

13:43 and pressure. When I was a precocious

13:45 pre-teen of about 12, I used to ride my

13:46 bike down to Radio Shack and spend as

13:48 much time as they would allow me on

13:49 their computer. One day the store

13:51 manager needed it back for store

13:53 business and I said, "Well, I'm going to

13:54 save my work." He asked if I was telling

13:56 him or asking him, and I replied

13:58 honestly and without a hint of teenage

13:59 rebellion. I'm telling you. I did not

14:02 understand that the social convention

14:03 required deference in that situation. I

14:05 was merely reporting an operational

14:07 requirement. The work had to be saved

14:09 before the machine could be used. Now,

14:11 translate that trait into fieldwork. A

14:13 socially smooth employee might hear, "We

14:15 need to move this along." And infer that

14:16 further questions are unwelcome. A

14:18 literal employee might hear the same

14:20 thing and say, "I understand the

14:21 scheduled pressure, but we still have

14:23 not verified isolation." Depending on

14:25 the culture, that person is either a

14:27 pain to work with or a lifesaver. The

14:29 reality is that they might be both at

14:30 the same time. And the best

14:32 organizations learn to distinguish

14:33 friction from resistance. Friction slows

14:36 motion. Resistance prevents movement in

14:38 the wrong direction. They feel similar

14:39 in the moment, but they are not the same

14:41 thing. This is where the costs and

14:43 benefits of neurodiversity become

14:45 tangled. An autistic employee may be

14:47 unusually reliable with routines,

14:49 details, pattern recognition, and

14:50 rule-based work. They may remember the

14:53 abnormal reading from 6 weeks ago that

14:55 everybody else has already forgot. They

14:57 may notice that the procedure says

14:58 verify in one section and confirm in

15:00 another and then seek out to find out

15:02 what the actual difference is. They may

15:04 be the one person in the room who cannot

15:05 let go of the mismatch between the plan

15:07 and the site conditions. That's the

15:09 benefit. The cost is that they also may

15:11 get stuck on a detail that is truly not

15:13 important. They may have trouble

15:14 prioritizing if everything else feels

15:16 like a rule. They may struggle with

15:18 noisy environments, last minute changes,

15:20 vague feedback, political conversations,

15:22 or the emotional temperature of a room.

15:24 They may sound angry when they're

15:26 actually just anxious or concerned. They

15:28 may look bored when they're overloaded.

15:30 They may fail to perform the expected

15:31 facial expressions when someone gives

15:33 them good news. I've done all of that. I

15:35 once had a classic car restored, a 1969

15:38 Pontiac Laurentian that my father bought

15:39 new and later gave to me in ' 84. The

15:42 restoration shop did beautiful work.

15:44 When I finally inspected it, I was

15:45 deeply moved, but I did not perform the

15:47 expected emotional reaction. No tears,

15:49 no dramatic television reveal, no

15:51 collapsing into the arms of the crafts

15:52 people. I inspected it carefully,

15:54 thanked them, paid the bill, and went

15:56 home. Years later, I realized they may

15:58 have expected a much bigger response.

16:00 So, I wrote to the owner to explain that

16:01 I had been genuinely impressed, but I'd

16:03 probably failed to show it properly. He

16:05 replied that he had thought about my

16:07 reaction many times over the years, and

16:09 that was a hard lesson. Internal

16:10 appreciation does not automatically

16:12 become external communication at work.

16:15 That can look like disengagement. It can

16:17 look like disrespect. It can look like

16:18 the person does not care and sometimes

16:20 they care so much that they've gone

16:22 quiet because their system is

16:23 overloaded. That is why managers matter.

16:25 A neurodeiverse employee in a bad

16:27 environment can become isolated,

16:29 defensive, underused or treated as a

16:31 problem to be managed. The same employee

16:33 in a good environment can become a kind

16:34 of humanindependent check not because

16:36 they are better but because they are

16:37 different in a useful direction. If the

16:40 unspoken rule is don't make the meeting

16:41 awkward, then the autistic employee has

16:43 two choices. They can make the meeting

16:45 awkward and pay for it, or they can

16:47 learn to mask until the very difference

16:48 that you hire them for becomes hidden.

16:50 Masking is the process of acting more

16:52 neurotypical than you naturally are. And

16:54 I've done it for decades, and I'm doing

16:55 it right now. It can help you fit in,

16:57 but it also burns energy that could have

16:59 gone into the work. That is the bargain

17:01 many of us make. We spend our best

17:03 thinking trying to look normal. Then

17:04 everybody wonders why they're not

17:05 getting our best thinking. The workplace

17:07 fix is not complicated, but it does

17:09 require discipline. Send the agenda

17:11 before the meeting. Write down

17:12 decisions. Define terms. Attach units to

17:15 numbers. Make ownership explicit. Give

17:17 people a way to raise a concern before

17:19 the job starts, not after the incident

17:20 review. Don't rely on hallway context

17:23 for safety critical information. Don't

17:25 make charisma in a crowded room the only

17:27 path to influence. And when somebody

17:29 asks the uncomfortable question, train

17:31 leaders to respond with curiosity before

17:33 status defense. Good question. Let's

17:35 verify those four words can change a

17:37 culture because the issue is not whether

17:39 everybody is smart enough. They probably

17:41 are. The issue is that smart people

17:42 still operate inside social systems.

17:45 They notice rank. They notice

17:46 irritation. They intuitively know when a

17:48 manager wants the answer to be yes. They

17:50 know when the project is behind

17:52 schedule. They know when the room has

17:53 emotionally moved on. And once enough

17:55 people sense that the room wants the

17:57 answer to be yes, the safest technical

17:58 answer can start to feel like the

18:00 riskiest social one. And that's what I

18:02 mean by social convention as a hazard.

18:04 Nobody writes a procedure manual that

18:06 says, "If the senior person appears

18:07 impatient, skip the awkward question,

18:09 but organizations sometimes operate as

18:11 if they had." Nobody writes, "Treat

18:13 silence as confirmation, but meetings do

18:15 it every day." Nobody writes, "Assuming

18:17 the person doing the work understood the

18:18 hazard because everybody nodded, but

18:21 handovers do it all the time." And

18:23 nobody writes, "The person who keeps

18:24 asking about edge cases is not a team

18:26 player." But some cultures teach exactly

18:28 that without ever saying those words. A

18:30 high reliability organization must do

18:32 the opposite. It must make the awkward

18:34 question normal and okay. It has to make

18:36 verification more socially acceptable

18:38 than assumption. It has to make I don't

18:40 understand safe to say because the

18:42 person who does not understand may be

18:43 the only person in the room who is not

18:46 silently sharing the wrong assumption.

18:48 That is where neurodiverse people can

18:50 help. We may not always pick up on the

18:51 invisible paragraph everybody else is

18:53 reading. We may not know that the

18:54 meeting is supposed to be over. We may

18:56 not understand why a vague answer

18:58 satisfied the room. We may be less

19:00 impressed by hierarchy when the facts

19:01 are unresolved. That can be dangerous if

19:03 it becomes disrespect, but it can also

19:05 be essential. In a high consequence

19:07 organization, truth has to outrank

19:09 status. The junior person has to be able

19:12 to stop the job. The contractor has to

19:14 be able to say the conditions differ.

19:16 The operator has to be able to challenge

19:18 the engineer. And the engineer has to be

19:20 able to challenge the schedule. The

19:22 schedule does not get a vote if the

19:23 hazard is real. And for those of us that

19:25 are neurodiverse, there is

19:27 responsibility on our side, too. We do

19:28 not get a free pass to be dicks simply

19:30 because we're accurate. We do not get to

19:32 treat every uncertainty as a five alarm

19:34 emergency. We do not get to assume that

19:36 because we see one detail, everybody

19:37 else is negligent for not seeing it

19:39 first. Sometimes the emotionally

19:41 intelligent person in the room is

19:42 tracking a bigger issue that we missed.

19:44 Sometimes the supervisor is balancing

19:46 constraints that we don't understand.

19:48 Sometimes the detail is real, but the

19:50 way we deliver it determines whether

19:51 anybody else can use it. So if you are

19:53 nerverse and you can see the assumption,

19:55 name it clearly. Don't point out just

19:57 the flaw, help define the fix. If you're

19:59 worried, explain the mechanism. If you

20:01 need time to process, say so. If you're

20:04 asking because you don't understand,

20:05 make that clear. And if you believe

20:07 something is unsafe, be direct, but

20:08 anchor your concern in evidence. This is

20:11 how difference becomes useful. The best

20:13 teams need both forms of intelligence.

20:15 They need the person who spots the

20:17 assumption and the person who can get

20:18 the room to hear it. They need the field

20:20 expert who knows what actually happens

20:21 at minus30 in Alberta and then the

20:23 engineer who knows what the calculation

20:25 assumed at room temperature. They need

20:27 the control room operator who sees the

20:28 trend and the technician who knows the

20:30 transmitter has been flaky since the

20:31 last storm. They need a safety

20:33 professional who understands the

20:35 procedure and the crew lead who knows

20:36 where the procedure meets. Mud, fatigue,

20:38 noise, and time pressure. Neurodiversity

20:40 is not a replacement for experience.

20:42 It's a multiplier when combined with

20:44 experience. And that is the real

20:45 business case for neurodiversity at TC

20:48 Energy or any other high consequence

20:49 organization. Not charity, not optics,

20:52 not compliance. It's another way to see

20:54 the system, another way to challenge

20:56 drift. Another way to detect the gap

20:57 between what the organization believes

20:59 and what the field is actually doing.

21:01 And that takes us back to the Gimly

21:02 glider. Somewhere in that chain, a

21:04 number lost its unit. And because the

21:06 number looked familiar, the assumption

21:08 survived long enough to become physical.

21:09 It became altitude. It became silence in

21:12 the engines. It became a powerless

21:13 Boeing 67 gliding over Manitoba. That is

21:16 the lesson. Assumptions do not remain

21:18 abstract. In industrial work, they

21:20 eventually become something you can

21:22 touch, smell, hear, or measure.

21:24 Pressure, flow, heat, gas, motion,

21:26 stored energy, a missing unit. A valve

21:28 believed closed. A drawing believed

21:30 current. A contractor believed informed.

21:32 A condition believed unchanged. So the

21:34 next time somebody asks the awkward

21:35 question, maybe don't rush past it.

21:37 Maybe they are being difficult. Maybe

21:39 they missed a social cue. Maybe they are

21:41 overfocused on a detail. Or maybe they

21:43 just notice that the number has no unit.

21:45 And in a business where reality always

21:47 gets the final word, that might be

21:48 exactly the person you need in the room.

21:51 Thank you. If you found this discussion

21:52 to be informative or entertaining,

21:54 remember I'm mostly in this for the subs

21:55 and likes, but I have written two books

21:57 on autism, Secrets of the Autistic

21:58 Millionaire and the non-visible part of

22:01 the autism spectrum, both of which are

22:03 available on Amazon, and I'll put links

22:04 in the video description. The first book

22:06 covers more of the employment aspect,

22:08 and the second book is more about how to

22:10 manage it for yourself. Vex.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: The Challenger Space Shuttle Disaster - Explained (Minute by Minute)
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: The Challenger Space Shuttle Disaster - Explained (Minute by Minute)
  • Video ID: kZmpYh5Wxto
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 73 seconds after launch.

00:02 The Challenger space shuttle rises higher and  higher toward space. Its iconic white solid rocket

00:07 boosters roar as flames spew out the back of them.  The flight crew has continued to communicate with

00:12 launch control since lift-off. No one knows that  anything is wrong and that in the next second,

00:16 tragedy will strike. A fire rages along the  side of the right booster as fuel escapes

00:21 due to a compromised seal. In moments, the  supporting struts connecting the rockets to

00:26 the orange external fuel tank will experience a  catastrophic failure. The booster will slam into

00:31 the tank. The rocket fuel will ignite,  and there will be a massive explosion.

00:35 April 4, 1983: T minus 2 years and 9  months until the Challenger disaster.

00:41 “All systems go. Prepare for liftoff,” mission  control says over the intercom to the Challenger

00:46 flight crew. This will be the space shuttle's  maiden voyage. The boosters ignite, and the184

00:51 foot, 4.5-million-pound space shuttle thrusts  toward space. The first mission was a success,

00:57 and the Challenger space shuttle will end up  flying 6 more missions that year. The shuttle

01:01 is reliable, but every time it launches into  space and lands after re-entry, a toll is taken

01:06 on the spacecraft. Constant repairs need to be  made while old components are swapped out for

01:11 new ones. Engineers who work on the shuttle day  in and day out warn NASA that the stresses that

01:16 constant missions to space place on the space  shuttle may lead to tragedy in the future.

01:21 July 19, 1985 T minus 6 months  until the Challenger disaster.

01:26 “We are pleased to inform you that you have  been selected to become the first teacher

01:30 to go to space.” Christa McAuliffe can’t believe  the words she has just read. Several months ago,

01:36 she submitted her application to the  NASA Teacher in Space Project along with

01:41 11,000 other educators. Never in her wildest  dreams did she believe she would be chosen.

01:45 However, this letter confirms that she will, in  fact, be going to space and that she will be lucky

01:50 enough to share this incredible experience with  students across the country when she gets back.

01:55 McAuliffe teaches at Concord High  School in New Hampshire. When she

01:58 tells her colleagues the news, they  are elated. Her family, friends,

02:02 and students are all extremely happy for her.  As a part of the Teacher in Space Project,

02:06 she will conduct two lessons from orbit and embark  on a lecture series across the United States to

02:11 share her experience with students. This will  be done to highlight the importance of teachers

02:16 in the country and hopefully inspire students  to pursue careers in technology and science.

02:20 Over the next several months, McAuliffe  joins her fellow crewmates at Johnson

02:24 Space Center in Houston, Texas, where they  train and prepare for their coming mission.

02:28 Francis R. Scobee will be the commander  of the spacecraft. In April of 1984,

02:33 he piloted Challenger mission STS-41-C which  deployed a new satellite and repaired a damaged

02:39 satellite before returning to Earth. Since then,  he has been an instructor pilot for the Shuttle's

02:43 747 carrier aircraft. This will be his first  space command, and he couldn’t be more excited.

02:49 Piloting the mission will be Michael J. Smith.  He has flown 28 different types of civilian and

02:54 military aircraft and logged 4,867 hours  of flight time. Judith A. Resnik will be

03:00 one of the mission specialists on board.  Resnik had been part of Astronaut Group 8,
