03:04 which was the first to include women on the  team. She has developed a variety of software

03:09 and procedures that are utilized throughout  NASA. She has been to space before aboard

03:13 the STS-41-D mission in August 1984. This was the  very first mission of the space shuttle Discovery.

03:19 Two other mission specialists are a  part of the Challenger crew as well.

03:22 Ronald E. McNair flew aboard Challenger in  February 1984 during mission STS-41-B. It

03:29 was on this mission that he became the second  African American man to fly in space. Ellison

03:33 S. Onizuka was the first Asian American  and the first person of Japanese origin

03:38 to reach space during his time aboard the  space shuttle Discovery during STS-51-C.

03:43 The final crew member aboard the upcoming  Challenger launch designated STS-51-L is

03:48 Gregory B. Jarvis. He’s the payload specialist.  This will be his first time in space, although

03:53 he had been slated to fly aboard a different  shuttle in April of 1985, but his spot was given

03:59 to U.S. senator Jake Garn instead. Then a similar  situation happened again in early January 1986

04:05 when U.S. representative Bill Nelson took his  place aboard another space shuttle. Now Jarvis

04:10 finally has the opportunity to reach space where  he can put his astronaut training to good use.

04:15 But like every other member of the crew, he will  never actually make it beyond Earth’s atmosphere.

04:20 January 22, 1986: T minus 6 days  until the Challenger disaster.

04:25 The Challenger crew eagerly awaits confirmation  of whether their mission is a go or not. A

04:30 high-ranking NASA officer enters the room with  a frown on his face. “Sorry about this crew,

04:35 but we’re going to have to delay your mission  until 61-C gets back. Their assignment ran into

04:39 delays, and their shuttle isn’t due to land  until tomorrow.” The Challenger crew looks

04:43 at one another in dismay. They are eager to  get going. Every mission to space is special,

04:48 and even for veteran astronauts,  it’s what they dream about doing

04:51 every night. It’s as if the stars are  beckoning them to reach for the unknown.

04:55 January 27, 1986: T minus 1 day  until the Challenger disaster.

05:01 Challenger mission STS-51-L is planned to have  an early morning lift-off the following day.

05:06 The astronauts toss and turn in their beds in  anticipation. A chill sweeps across Florida

05:11 as if foreshadowing the ominous events that  will happen in the coming hours. The launch

05:15 pad becomes covered in thick ice; the metals  that make up the space shuttle and boosters

05:20 contract slightly with the cold. As engineers  check the spacecraft over and over again to

05:24 make sure it’s in an acceptable condition for  launch, a disturbing realization surfaces.

05:29 “Sir, I want to reiterate that I am concerned  about the reliability of the seals in the

05:33 rockets,” an engineer explains to  his superior. For over two years,

05:37 the engineers and technicians that work  in the shuttle program have warned that

05:40 the space shuttles are being overused.  The crafts are sturdy and well made,

05:44 but every machine has its breaking point,  and it feels as if, after dozens of flights,

05:49 it’s only a matter of time before something  tragic happens. The NASA official acknowledges

05:53 the engineer's concern but does nothing  more. The launch will commence as scheduled,

05:58 regardless of the warnings voiced by the men  and women working directly with the spacecraft.

06:02 January 28, 1986: 9:00 a.m.: T minus 2 hours  and 38 minutes until the Challenger disaster.

06:09 The sun is rising higher and higher over the  Atlantic Ocean. A crowd gathers around Cape

06:14 Canaveral to watch the launch at Kennedy Space  Center scheduled for later that morning. There

06:18 are members of the press, local residents, and  people who have traveled from around the world

06:22 to watch the launch. Many are there to witness  the historic event of the first teacher to go

06:27 to space. Excitement and anticipation fill  the air. This will be the 25th space shuttle

06:32 launch and the 10th Challenger mission.  All other flights have been successful,

06:36 so there is no reason to suspect  today should be any different.

06:39 The astronauts don their suits and proceed  to their launch vehicle. They are greeted by

06:44 cheers as they step off their transport and  proceed towards the elevator that will carry

06:48 them to the cockpit of the Challenger.  Mission control in Houston prepares to

06:51 track and monitor the space shuttle's progress.  Telemetry coming in from hundreds of sensors is

06:56 recorded and double-checked to make sure that  Challenger is ready. The astronauts strap in,

07:01 and the shuttle door is sealed behind them.  The cockpit is quiet except for the sounds

07:05 of switches being engaged while Socbee and  Smith check the systems on board. There is

07:09 a sense of anxiousness, excitement, and pride  as the seven-person crew prepares for launch.

07:14 McAuliffe looks out the window directly  ahead of her at the blue sky. Just beyond

07:18 the atmosphere lies the edge of space. A bird  flies pasts; McAuliffe smiles. Soon she will

07:24 be doing something that only a handful  of people in all of history have done.

07:27 She checks her safety harness and leans  back in her seat, releasing a long sigh.

07:32 Besides the crew, the shuttle also  carries a Tracking and Data Relay

07:36 Satellite designated TDRS-B. Also in the  cargo bay is the Spartan Halley spacecraft,

07:41 which is designed to be released from Challenger  to study Halley’s Comet for two days while the

07:46 celestial object approaches the sun. The small  satellite will then be picked up by the Challenger

07:50 crew and brought back to Earth so scientists can  analyze the data it has collected. Tragically,

07:55 no one and nothing aboard Challenger will  survive to perform this series of tests.

07:59 January 28, 1986: 11:38: T  minus 10 seconds until launch.

08:06 Due to weather conditions, the launch  has been delayed yet again. However,

08:09 the atmosphere is beginning to  cooperate. The sky clears up,

08:12 and the wind clams. Commander Scobee and Pilot  Smith check their sensors and instruments one

08:17 last time as they prepare for the rockets to fire.  Mission control reaches the end of its countdown.

08:22 10. 9. 8. 7. 6. We have main engine  start. 4. 3. 2. 1 and liftoff.

08:32 Moments before the engines ignite and the space  shuttle rises, the solid rocket ignition command

08:38 is sent. The boosters roar to life. The space  shuttle and earth around the launchpad begin

08:42 to shake. The sound travels across the water and  reaches the bystanders watching the space shuttle

08:47 launch from miles away. Astronaut Judy Resnik is  heard over the intercom. “All right!” she yells.

08:52 Challenger Space Shuttle achieves liftoff.

08:55 After the rockets ignite eight 25-inch-long,  7-inch-wide exploding bolts fire. The Challenger

09:01 space shuttle is free to rise into the  sky. The deafening boom of the engines,

09:06 massive amounts of smoke, and intense heat roll  across the launch pad. A quarter of a second

09:11 after launch, sensors record the first vertical  motion of Challenger as it begins its ascent.

09:16 Unknown to anyone on board or at mission control,

09:18 an abnormal black smoke is seeping out of the  right solid rocket booster near the location of

09:24 one of the O-ring joints. This is the first sign  that something is about to go terribly wrong.

09:29 1 second after liftoff.

09:30 “Here we go!” Pilot Michael Smith  says over the intercom. As the space

09:35 shuttle proceeds toward the heavens, the  black smoke coming from the right rocket

09:38 seems to be slowing down.

3 seconds after liftoff.

09:41 Launch commentator Hugh Hariss has just finished  the countdown and pauses for a moment to watch.

09:46 He announces on NASA-SELECT television,  “Liftoff of the 25th space shuttle mission,

09:51 and it has cleared the tower." The  abnormal black smoke coming from

09:54 the bottom of the solid rocket booster  appears to have disappeared completely.

09:58 5 seconds after liftoff.

10:00 All systems go. There are no anomalies  detected by anyone at this point in the

10:04 launch. The three liquid-fueled main engines  on the back of the space shuttle are throttled

10:08 up from 90% to 104% thrust. Everything is  going according to plan. At mission control,

10:14 data processing systems engineer A.F. Algate  confirms liftoff. There is a cheer in the room

10:20 then everyone immediately goes back to monitoring  their stations. Suddenly, there is a data blackout

10:25 from the space shuttle. No one panics. This is to  be expected as the flames and structures around

10:30 the launch complex interfere with the radio  signals being sent to the antenna complex.

10:34 But there is one piece of data that is slightly  unnerving. “I’m reading the internal pressure

10:39 on the right-side booster to be 11.8 pounds  per square inch higher than normal,” one of

10:44 the technicians in mission control says. The  rocket is still within acceptable parameters,

10:48 but this initial data point will be used later on

10:51 to identify when the Challenger space  shuttle began to run into trouble.

10:54 8 seconds after liftoff.

10:56 Once Challenger is in the open air, Pilot  Smith begins a roll maneuver that puts the

11:01 crew in a heads down position so the top  of the space shuttle is pointing towards

11:04 the Earth and the bright orange external  fuel tank is towards the sky. "Houston,

11:08 Challenger. Roll program," Commander  Scobee says over the intercom.

11:12 "Roger roll, Challenger," Astronaut Dick  Covey says from mission control. "Good roll,

11:16 flight," Flight dynamics officer Brian  Perry confirms from the control room.

11:20 19 seconds after liftoff.

11:22 The Challenge space shuttle begins  to shake. There is a sudden violent

11:26 thrust to the side. The crew grits their  teeth as Michael Smith pulls on the flight

11:30 stick slightly. With the help of the NAV  system, the space shuttle realigns itself,

11:34 and Challenger is back on course. "Looks like  we've got a lot of wind here today,” says Smith

11:38 over the intercom. Commander Scobee confirms  the assessment. They begin throttling down the

11:42 three main engines of the space shuttle to 94%  thrust as planned at this point in the flight.

11:47 21 seconds after liftoff.

11:49 Challenger’s roll maneuver is completed,  and all systems confirm it is on the proper

11:54 trajectory to reach orbit. Commander  Scobee looks out the cockpit window,

11:57 hoping to get a glimpse of the land  below. "It's a little hard to see

12:00 out my window here,” he says. The  engines continue to throttle down.

12:04 28 seconds after liftoff.

12:06 "There's 10,000 feet, and Mach point  five,” Smith says over the intercom.

12:10 Challenger is now traveling at half the speed  of sound and is 10,000 feet above the surface

12:15 of the planet. It’s at this point that the  space shuttle begins reaching the region of

12:19 maximum aerodynamic pressure. Mission control  confirms that engines are throttling down to

12:24 94% and remind the flight crew that they will be  throttling down to 65% thrust in a few seconds.

12:29 35 seconds after liftoff.

12:31 Smith begins to throttle down the engines some  more. All data indicates that the shuttle’s

12:36 computer systems are making the proper adjustments  to deal with the wind shear. 5 seconds later,

12:40 Smith confirms that they have reached  Mach 1. Scobee adds that they are passing

12:45 19,000 feet in altitude.

45 seconds after liftoff.

12:48 There is a bright flash slightly behind the  space shuttle’s right wing. Moments later,

12:52 there is a second bright flash.

12:54 48 seconds after liftoff.

12:56 A third flash appears downstream  of Challenger's right wing.

12:59 The crew can’t see these ominous explosions,  but a 70-millimeter tracking camera captures

13:04 them as it zooms in on the shuttle for  a close-up view. Everyone who is viewing

13:08 the footage is baffled at what they are  witnessing. Suddenly an orange ball of

13:12 flames erupts from under the right wing. This  fireball is coming from the right booster.

13:16 The Challenger crew and mission control  have no idea that anything is wrong as

13:21 the space shuttle’s telemetry  all reads nominal. The fireball

13:24 from under the wing merges with the  flames of the solid rocket boosters.

13:27 58 seconds after liftoff.

13:29 Challenger accelerates past 1,539 miles per  hour or 2,477 kilometers per hour. It has an

13:37 altitude of 26,127 feet or 7,963.5 meters.  Scobee gives the command to throttle the

13:45 engines back as planned. Smith confirms the  command. Mission control confirms that the

13:50 three engines of the space shuttle  have throttled down to 65% thrust.

13:54 While this is happening, the tracking  camera on the ground observes the first

13:58 evidence that there is now something seriously  wrong with the right solid rocket booster. An

14:03 abnormal plume of smoke has begun pouring  out of the rocket. The Challenger crew has

14:07 no sensors in the cockpit that display the  performance of the solid rocket boosters and,

14:11 therefore, are unaware that  they are in serious danger.

14:14 A second later, Challenger passes through the  region of maximum aerodynamic pressure, which

14:19 pushes against the space shuttle and its boosters  with 720 pounds of pressure per square foot or

14:25 7,750 pounds per square meter. The plume of smoke  coming from the side of the booster intensifies.

14:31 Inside the booster itself, an O-ring has  disintegrated, the very same component

14:37 that engineers at NASA were warning would fail  if the space shuttle launches were not dialed

14:42 back. The O-ring on the booster was meant  to seal the joints between separate parts

14:45 of the rocket and prevent the leaking  of fluids and gasses from one chamber

14:49 to another. With the O-ring destroyed, fuel  is making its way through the booster and

14:54 igniting due to the intense heat of the flames.  A continuous inferno is expelled from the right

14:59 booster along the side furthest away from the  space shuttle. The windows in the cockpit give

15:03 Scobee and Smith limited visibility, and they  are not able to see the fire from the shuttle.

15:08 60 seconds after liftoff.

15:10 "Feel that mother go!" Smith says over the  intercom. Another member of the crew is heard

15:15 yelling with joy in the background. At that  moment, mission control receives data that

15:19 indicates the internal pressure in the right  side solid rocket booster has begun to drop.

15:24 It’s not known at the time, but this severe drop  in pressure is the result of the hole created by

15:28 the ignited fuel spewing out the side of  the rocket where the O-ring has failed.

15:33 The flames pouring out of the side of  the rocket begin to lick the fitting

15:36 attachments that couple the back end of the  booster to the external fuel tank on the

15:40 underside of the space shuttle. This starts  to degrade the integrity of the couplings.

15:44 62 seconds after liftoff.

15:46 Challenger shudders once again from high  wind speeds. The shuttle rolls slightly

15:51 to compensate as it passes 35,000 feet and  approaches Mach 1.5. The wind is worse than

15:57 predicted and stronger than any of the  previous 24 shuttle missions. However,

16:01 it’s still within acceptable limits, even if  it puts slightly more stress on the shuttle.

16:05 64 seconds after liftoff.

16:08 The flame in the right side booster changes shape  suddenly as the heat from the fire melts through

16:13 metal plating, and liquid hydrogen begins  to fuel the fire. The glow on the outside of

16:18 the booster intensifies. As the force of the  raging fire builds up, it begins to move the

16:22 engine nozzle in large arcs. This momentum  begins to shift the space shuttles course,

16:27 which the computer then adjusts for. The  right booster’s thrust levels are thrown

16:31 off due to the leaking fuel and fire burning  on the side. However, the NAV system manages

16:36 to compensate. Tremors vibrate through the  cockpit as the hydrogen fuel is ignited but

16:41 gets lost in the turbulence experienced due  to the massive acceleration and wind sheers.

16:46 66 seconds after liftoff.

16:48 "Throttle up, three at 104,” mission control says  over the com. Houston and the Challenger flight

16:53 crew are still unaware of the fire coming  out of the middle of the right booster,

16:57 and other than a drop in pressure, there is no  indication that there is a serious problem. The

17:01 fire outside of the shuttle spread further. The  flames creep toward the belly of the shuttle,

17:05 where the external liquid hydrogen tank  is located. The pressure inside the fuel

17:09 tank suddenly begins to drop, indicating that an  alarming amount of liquid hydrogen is leaking out.

17:15 The fuel tank gauge plummets inside the cockpit,

17:18 but Smith and Scobee don’t notice it as they  are focused on throttling up the engines and

17:22 preparing to disengage the boosters. Even if  either crewmember was looking at the fuel gauge,

17:27 the rapid dropping of pressure happened so  quickly that there was nothing they could have

17:31 done. The fuel tank can only be disengaged  when all other engines are turned off,

17:35 and the shuttle is in a benign aerodynamic  environment higher up in the atmosphere. If

17:40 they had disengaged the fuel tank to get away  from the leak at this stage, the Challenger

17:44 would have been forced into the fuel tank and  the still-burning solid rocket booster exhaust.

17:49 68 seconds after liftoff.

17:51 The fire spewing from the side of the  rocket connects to the exhaust plume.

17:55 The liquid oxygen propellant being fed into  the main engines of the space shuttle falls

17:59 drastically. Smith continues to throttle  up the engines to reach 104% thrust.

18:04 72 seconds after liftoff.

18:06 The back end of the right booster is ripped  away from the external fuel tank. The strut

18:11 that had been securing it has been compromised  and failed. The back end of the right booster is

18:16 now moving up and down relative to the space  shuttle and fuel tank. Another explosion,

18:20 likely from the stress and leaking  fuel, occurs higher up on the booster

18:24 near Challenger’s cabin. The flame near  the top of the booster grows rapidly,

18:28 creating an enormous fireball. The nozzles of  the engines on the back of the space shuttle

18:32 begin moving at a rate of 5 feet per second in  order to compensate for the unhinged booster.

18:37 The top of the right booster is  still connected to the fuel tank,

18:40 but the loose back end causes a burst  of lateral acceleration that jerks

18:44 the shuttle. The main engine pressure  decreases. Engine nozzle motion rates

18:48 are off the chart. Things are very, very bad.  Challenger sends its final navigation update.

18:54 73 seconds after liftoff.

18:56 “Uh oh…” Smith says. These will be the last words  uttered over the comms by any of the Challenger

19:02 crew. It’s not clear what Smith is referring  to, but it’s likely that several sensors begin

19:06 showing clear signs that something is wrong. The  fuel tank and loose booster begin breaking apart.

19:11 The shuttle jerks the opposite way it had moments  before. The right booster is now producing 100,000

19:17 pounds of thrust less than the left booster.  The unbalanced acceleration begins forcing

19:22 the right booster up into the liquid  oxygen section of the external fuel tank.

19:26 Liquid hydrogen and oxygen begin leaking out of  the external tank. A cloud of fuel accumulates

19:31 outside. The right-side booster pushes  further into the fuel tank and increases

19:36 the amount of liquid oxygen being expelled.  Milliseconds later, the inevitable happens.

19:40 There is a bright flash of light located between  the Challenger shuttle and the external fuel tank.

19:46 The leaking fuel has been ignited. The fireball  engulfs the space shuttle. There is a crackling

19:51 sound over the intercom as ground transmitters  search for a signal that is no longer there.

19:55 Another explosion occurs near the front of the  external fuel tank. This ignites the remainder of

20:00 the fuel inside the front section of the tank,  causing it to detonate. Challenger’s engines

20:05 redline and the computer initiates an emergency  shutdown. Main engine 3 goes first, followed by

20:11 number 1. The last telemetry signal from the space  shuttle is sent while it is being torn apart.

20:16 74 seconds after liftoff.

20:18 The radio signal from Challenger goes silent.

20:21 Another explosion occurs near the space shuttle's  nose. The cockpit with all seven members of the

20:26 crew is engulfed in flames as the rocket fuel  in the forward reaction control system ignites.

20:31 The debris of the destroyed shuttle continues  traveling upward at Mach 1.92, or approximately

20:36 twice the speed of sound. It reaches an altitude  of 46,000 feet or 14,021 meters. Challenger’s tail

20:43 emerges from the fireball around the same moment  that a wing can be seen. The fuselage and payload

20:48 bay are torn apart by the rush of air forced in  from the tail being ripped off, overpressurizing

20:53 the payload bay and breaking it apart from the  inside out. Wires and electrical cables flail

20:58 behind the fuselage like tentacles. The satellites  in the cargo bay are ejected into the air.

21:03 The crew cabin arcs out of the flames  and smoke. It seems to be intact,

21:07 although there is a gaping hole where it  used to be connected to the rest of the

21:11 shuttle. Some of the crew may still be alive and  awake, but when the Challenger is ripped apart,

21:15 all of the air is sucked out of the cockpit,  and a dramatic pressure drops results in

21:19 everyone passing out. For this mission, the  astronauts did not wear pressurized suits

21:24 during liftoff. As they slump in their seats  unconscious, oxygen deprivation settles in.

21:29 Any crewmember who is still alive will  suffocate within the next few minutes.

21:33 The two solid rocket boosters continue  to fly upwards at different angles,

21:37 now free from the struts that connected  them to the external fuel tank.

21:40 1 second after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

21:43 Mission control does not yet know that the  Challenger space shuttle has exploded. "One

21:48 minute 15 seconds. Velocity 2,900 feet per second.  Altitude nine nautical miles. Downrange distance

21:54 seven nautical miles," says Stephen Nesbitt,  the public affairs officer at mission control.

21:59 2 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:02 A parachute emerges from the carnage, giving  people hope. But as the tracking camera focuses,

22:07 it turns out to be the nose cap of the  right solid rocket booster. Smoke and

22:11 flaming debris arc outward from the blast.  The rocket boosters continue to fly upward,

22:15 leaving a corkscrew trail of smoke behind them.

22:18 15 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:21 "Flight, GC, we've had negative contact,  loss of downlink," says ground control

22:26 engineer N.R. Talbott. It’s at this  point that mission control is aware

22:29 something tragic has happened and  is trying to figure out exactly

22:32 what happened. They are informed that the  Challenger space shuttle has been lost.

22:36 36 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:39 A self-destruct signal is sent to the  rogue solid rocket boosters triggering

22:43 an emergency detonation. Both rockets explode  in a plume of black smoke. Debris falls back

22:48 towards the Earth. Without the weight  of the space shuttle and fuel tank,

22:51 there was no telling how far the rockets  would have gone before burning the last

22:55 of their fuel. They needed to be detonated  to eliminate the risk of them crashing back

22:59 to Earth in a populated area rather than in  the desolate waters of the Atlantic Ocean.

23:04 1 minute and 31 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

23:07 Multiple sources have now confirmed

23:10 that Challenger STS-51-L has been  lost. Rescue efforts are launched.

23:14 2 minutes and 11 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

23:18 The TV tracking camera spots the first pieces  of the space shuttle crashing into the ocean.

23:22 33 seconds later, the crew cabin slams into  the waves of the Atlantic at approximately 200

23:28 miles per hour or 322 kilometers per hour. At a  breaking force 200 times that of normal gravity,

23:34 the crew cabin disintegrates on impact and  sinks 100 feet to the bottom of the ocean.

23:39 For the next few minutes, debris continues to  splash down into the ocean east of Patrick Air

23:44 Force Base. A cloud of brown smoke lingers  over the surface of the water as a result

23:48 of the hydrazine rocket fuel that covered the  wreckage as it entered the ocean. Mission control

23:53 pinpoints the crash site as being approximately  28.64 degrees North and 80.28 degrees West.

23:59 5 minutes after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

24:02 The broadcast on NASA television has been  eerily quiet as everyone tries to take in

24:07 what just happened. The camera view switches  from the ocean back to the grandstand at

24:11 the press site. Observers stand with their  backs to the camera, looking up at the sky,

24:14 where a white cloud of smoke still lingers.  White wisps of haze extend from the explosion

24:19 site like weeping willow vines indicating  where burning debris fell from the sky.

24:23 8 minutes and 5 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

24:27 "This is mission control, Houston. We are  coordinating with recovery forces in the field.

24:31 Range safety equipment, recovery vehicles intended  for the recovery of the SRBs in the general area,"

24:36 says Stephen Nesbitt in a somber voice. The  only thing left to do is go through the data,

24:41 recover as much of the space shuttle as  possible, and determine what caused the

24:45 horrific accident that led to the loss of 7  people aboard the Challenger space shuttle.

24:49 March 7, 1986, 1 month and 10 days after  the Challenger space shuttle disaster.

24:54 The USS Preserver bobs up and down in  the dark waters of the Atlantic Ocean.

24:59 A dive team has just been deployed to  scout the hypothesized location of the

25:03 Challenger cabin. The divers locate  the wreckage that was the front of

25:06 the space shuttle and confirm that the  bodies of the crew are still inside.

25:09 The aftermath of the Challenger  space shuttle disaster.

25:12 All space shuttles are immediately grounded, and  any upcoming launches are canceled pending a full

25:18 investigation of what happened to the Challenger.  NASA and a group of men appointed by President

25:22 Ronald Regan, known as the Rogers Commission,  begin looking into the chain of events that led to

25:27 the loss of the space shuttle and its crew. It’s  concluded that the space shuttles are being pushed

25:31 too hard, and the concerns of engineers working on  the crafts are being ignored or overlooked. What

25:37 it came down to was that NASA has been trying  to accomplish too much with too little funding.

25:42 The investigation also determines that  the two rubber O-rings, which led to

25:46 the fuel leak in the right booster and eventual  catastrophic explosion of the external fuel tank,

25:50 were compromised by the severe cold from  the night before the launch. Unfortunately,

25:55 even if the crew had been aware of a problem  at liftoff, there would have been no way for

25:59 them to avoid the disastrous consequences.  The space shuttle wouldn’t have been able

26:03 to survive a high-speed separation even if it was  attempted before the external fuel tank exploded.

26:08 On June 6, the report is given to the President,  who determines Marshall Space Flight Center in

26:13 Huntsville, Alabama, Morton Thiokol Inc.,  and NASA as a whole are responsible for the

26:18 Challenger disaster. Marshall Space Flight  Center constructed the shuttle boosters,

26:22 engines, and tank, while Morton Thiokol  manufactured and built the booster motors.

26:27 It’s also uncovered during the investigation from  several engineers who testify that they expressed

26:32 concerns specifically about the O-rings and their  seals to their supervisors for at least two years

26:37 prior to the loss of the Challenger. The Rogers  Commission recommends that communication between

26:42 engineers and NASA management be tightened,  quality control procedures be improved,

26:46 and several more checkpoints be added  to the shuttle safety advisory panel.

26:50 On September 29, 1988, the space shuttle Discovery  launches with five veteran astronauts on board.

26:56 This is the first mission since the Challenger  disaster. The space shuttle program lasts for

27:01 23 more years. On July 8, 2011, Atlantis launches  from Cape Canaveral. It will be the 135th space

27:08 shuttle mission. Atlantis lands on Jul 21, 2011,  marking the official end of the space shuttle era.

27:14 Two space shuttles were lost during the 30  years that they were in use. On February 1,

27:19 2003, Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated as  it reentered the atmosphere, and on January 28,

27:25 1986, Challenger exploded due to a faulty  O-ring. Both crafts held a crew of 7, all of

27:30 which were lost and all of which were heroes. Now watch “Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima and

27:35 Nagasaki (Minute by Minute)” Or check out “What  If USA Launched a Nuclear Bomb (Minute by Minute)”

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: How SEAL Team Took Down Osama bin Laden (Minute by Minute)
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: How SEAL Team Took Down Osama bin Laden (Minute by Minute)
  • Video ID: knjliFs3gR8
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 For almost ten years, the United States had been tirelessly searching for one man - Osama

00:04 Bin Laden, the terrorist mastermind behind the September 11th attacks that killed almost

00:08 three thousand Americans and triggered a war that was still raging today - May 2nd, 2011.

00:15 While the United States had toppled the Taliban, the government that was sheltering Bin Laden

00:18 at the time of the attacks, they had never been able to capture or kill the man.

00:22 That was about to change.

00:23 The CIA had been searching for Bin Laden’s secret base for years with no luck.

00:27 He had managed to escape from Afghanistan, which was under US occupation, and travel

00:32 to the neighboring country of Pakistan.

00:34 But in the mountainous, rural regions of Pakistan, with little government oversight, it was easy

00:38 for him to stay under the radar.

00:39 The government had been looking for leads for years, but finally got their break in

00:43 2010, when their leads led them to a compound in Abbottabad.

00:47 They began taking surveillance footage of the compound, and determining the best way

00:50 to breach it.

00:51 What followed was one of the trickiest intelligence-gathering operations in US history.

00:55 The compound was heavily guarded and in enemy territory.

00:59 The US had to rely heavily on local help to gather intelligence, and over a period of

01:03 months they spied on the three-story building.

01:06 They learned every detail about the building, but a lot was still missing.

01:09 For one thing, the infamous terror leader was incredibly secretive - so secretive, that

01:13 they were never able to capture an image of him coming in or out of the building.

01:17 So everything was still circumstantial, but after an extended period of time, they were

01:21 able to conclude that this was were Osama Bin Laden.

01:24 Now it was time to take action.

01:25 It was April 29th when President Obama was briefed on the details of the operation.

01:31 Many within his security team were skeptical about the operation - after all, if it went

01:35 wrong, top US troops would either be killed or remain trapped behind enemy lines.

01:39 Not only would this be a disastrous loss of life, but it would potentially expose many

01:43 of the US’ biggest secrets if they were interrogated and forced to reveal classified

01:47 information.

01:48 And with the doubts that Bin Laden truly in the compound, many didn’t feel it was worth

01:52 the risk.

01:53 Ultimately, the President disagreed - and he gave the okay to the operation that would

01:57 become Operation Neptune Spear.

01:59 And the people carrying it out would be the best of the best.

02:02 Meet Seal Team 6.

02:04 An elite squadron of the highly-trained Navy Seals, they answer directly to the Joint Special

02:08 Operations Command and carry out some of the most highly classified operations the US government

02:13 is involved with.

02:14 These include hostage rescue, special espionage missions, counterterrorism, targeting of enemy

02:19 infrastructure, and direct action against the deadliest of US enemies - like Osama Bin

02:23 Laden.

02:24 They would be briefed on the mission, which would be classified as capture-or-kill.

02:28 Officially, the US has the policy of never killing an enemy who has already surrendered

02:32 - but no one involved in the mission had any delusion that Osama Bin Laden would ever surrender.

02:37 And to pull this all off they had to implement some risky strategies.

02:41 The planning had been going on for the better part of a year, since the intelligence reports

02:45 started coming in, and many strategies had been considered.

02:48 The easiest would have been a joint operation with Pakistani military forces - but the Pakistani

02:53 government wasn’t exactly friendly and the US was worried that Bin Laden could be tipped

02:57 off in advance.

02:58 The US also considered striking at the compound with stealth bombers, which could atomize

03:02 Bin Laden - but there would be no way of following up to ensure he was already dead, and the

03:06 tricky terror leader had managed to escape US operations before.

03:09 So instead, the government decided to go old-school.

03:13 Seal Team 6 would be flown in using modified Black Hawk helicopters that were designed

03:17 to be quiet and would be able to fly in under enemy radar.

03:20 The Pakistani military had been heavily trained and supplied by US advisors, so their capabilities

03:25 were known - and the US was confident they could get around them.

03:28 The goal was to get to the compound without being detected or challenged by the Pakistani

03:32 forces - and once the target was down, they would be able to beat a hasty retreat.

03:37 May 1st, 1:22 PM.

03:39 Defense Secretary Leon Panetta received the word from the President, and directed Admiral

03:44 William McRaven to move ahead with the operation.

03:47 Within the next two hours, President Obama and his national security team would move

03:50 to the Situation Room to watch the whole thing unfold over night-vision images transmitted

03:55 to them from a drone.

03:56 The roughly 24 Navy SEALS sent on the mission would temporarily be transferred to the control

04:01 of the CIA, so it would technically not be a military mission and would not be classified

04:06 as an act of war.

04:07 These were going to be some of the most critical minutes in the US’ modern history - and

04:11 for the men on the ground, every single minute would count.

04:14 While the roughly two dozen SEALs were the ones who would breach the compound, there

04:17 were 79 commandos and a dog involved in the raid.

04:20 The dog, a Belgian Malinois named Cairo, was there to alert the SEALs to any sudden activity

04:25 - including the Pakistani military approaching the compound, or anyone trying to escape.

04:29 The core team was backed up by a dog handler, interpreters, pilots, intelligence agents,

04:34 and tech experts who would make it all possible.

04:36 But the success or failure of the mission would hinge on the men entering the compound.

04:40 And one wrong move could spell doom.

04:43 3:30 AM - give or take.

04:45 Two helicopters descend on the Abbottabad compound.

04:47 While the other helicopters stand by in case they’re needed, these two will carry out

04:51 the primary mission.

04:52 Flying low to the ground, the stealthy Black Hawk helicopters hover over the compound grounds.

04:56 While the first deploys ropes to lower its team to the ground, the other heads to the

05:00 far northeast corner to covertly drop off its interpreter, dog, handler, and four SEALs.

05:05 If everything went smoothly, they would soon be at the compound.

05:08 But everything didn’t go smoothly.

05:10 While the helicopters weren’t detected and they didn’t come under hostile fire, mother

05:13 nature had something to say.

05:15 The first helicopter flew into what’s known as a vortex ring state - an air phenomenon

05:19 caused by higher-than-expected temperatures creating an air vortex.

05:22 The rotor’s air pressure didn’t diffuse properly, the helicopter was knocked off balance,

05:26 and it grazed the back of the compound wall.

05:29 The tail rotor was seriously damaged, and the helicopter started rolling over.

05:33 The quick-thinking pilot drove the helicopter into the ground nose-first, preventing a total

05:37 collapse, and the SEALs and crew were able to escape unscathed after a rough landing.

05:42 Now the only question was - had this blown their secret mission?

05:46 The answer seemed to be no, as there was no sign of aggression from the compound.

05:49 The SEALs had successfully weathered a crash landing without being detected, the helicopter

05:54 was secure against the compound walls, and the other helicopter had landed safely outside

05:58 the compound.

05:59 The rest of the team was scaling the walls, and the whole team was reunited.

06:02 The next step was breaching the compound - and that’s where the SEALs’ explosives team

06:06 came in.

06:07 They needed to get in quickly and hit the people inside with shock and awe.

06:10 Outside, preparation was key - but once they were inside, every second would count.

06:14 Ten years of searching had come down to this.

06:17 3:33 AM - To get through the security, the SEALs used portable explosives to blow open

06:22 the doors of the compound’s guest house, one by one.

06:25 They breached the compound and began storming up the stairs.

06:28 The first room they encountered on the first floor contained two adult males - but none

06:32 of them was Osama bin Laden.

06:33 They were detained, but they weren’t the target.

06:35 More disturbing - every floor seemed to contain small groups of children.

06:39 This wasn’t just a terrorist compound - it was a home where the terrorists kept their

06:42 families, regardless of all the danger they were putting them in.

06:45 And with every floor the SEALs ascended, the danger would escalate.

06:49 3:35 - What happened next?

06:51 Reports of that may vary.

06:52 As they reached the second floor, they encountered more resistance.

06:55 This is where Bin Laden’s courier, Abu Ahmed al-Kuwaiti, was found - and SEAL Mark Owen

07:00 would controversially write a book on the firefight.

07:03 He claimed that al-Kuwaiti was armed and fired on the SEALs.

07:06 While one SEAL was lightly injured, they returned fire and killed the evil courier.

07:09 However, intelligence sources later said that the SEALs were able to get the drop on the

07:13 man after cutting power to the compound and eliminated him without him fighting back.

07:17 What was clear was that they still hadn’t encountered the man himself.

07:21 3:37 - It was time to ascend once again, and the resistance became fiercer the further

07:26 the SEALs headed into the house.

07:27 They had encountered the courier, as well as his brother and wife, and all enemies had

07:31 either been killed or captured.

07:33 As they ascended the staircase, they encountered another enemy - and this one provided a glimmer

07:37 of hope.

07:38 After the Al Qaeda soldier was killed, the SEALs identified him as a son of Osama Bin

07:42 Laden - one of the terror leader’s many progenies who followed in his footsteps.

07:46 And if he was there, the odds were good his father wasn’t far away.

07:50 3:39 - There was only one floor left to be breached, the third - and the SEALs were steeling

07:55 themselves for yet another disappointment.

07:57 This was clearly a high-level Al Qaeda compound, but Bin Laden had been notorious for staying

08:01 one step ahead of his pursuers, and he could be far away by now.

08:04 But as they breached the third floor, it became clear this time was different.

08:08 In the third floor’s main room was Osama Bin Laden - seemingly unarmed and wearing

08:12 the loose-fitting tunic he was usually seen wearing in his many propaganda videos.

08:16 The SEALs got their first glimpse of him as he stuck his head out of the bedroom…

08:20 And they didn’t miss their opportunity.

08:22 They immediately fired, wounding him.

08:24 However, he was able to retreat back into the bedroom, and the SEALs pursued.

08:28 The room was revealed to contain many of Bin Laden’s female relatives, including several

08:32 of his wives.

08:33 One approached the SEALs, as if she was charging - and the SEALs quickly shot her to wound,

08:37 grabbing her and advancing further towards the terror leader.

08:40 Osama Bin Laden had nowhere left to run, and America’s most skilled soldiers were right

08:44 outside his door.

08:45 What happened next?

08:47 Reports vary.

08:48 Matt Bissonnette, one of the SEALs on site, claims that Bin Laden had been mortally wounded

08:51 by the initial shots as they approached.

08:54 His wives were trying to protect him, and the SEALs were forced to act as any one of

08:57 them could have an explosive device.

08:59 But when they pushed past them, they found Bin Laden on the ground, mortally wounded.

09:03 As he moved, they fired multiple shots and neutralized the terror leader for good.

09:07 But another SEAL had a very different story.

09:09 Robert J. O’Neill would become one of the first SEALs to identify himself as one of

09:13 the men on the mission, and had a much more dramatic recollection of the events.

09:17 In his retelling, Osama bin Laden might have been wounded, but he was far from neutralized.

09:22 In fact, he was strong enough to grab one of the women in the room and hide behind her,

09:26 using her as a human shield.

09:27 As bin Laden pushed the hapless woman towards the SEALs, O’Neill quickly fired two shots

09:32 directly into bin Laden’s forehead and killed him.

09:34 Which report was accurate?

09:35 The Navy after-action report favors Bissonnette’s retelling.

09:39 And just like that, one of the most notorious enemies of the United States was no more.

09:44 The SEAL team radioed back “For God and country - Geronimo, Geronimo, Geronimo”

09:48 - officially confirming that the enemy had been killed in action.

09:51 The entire affair had taken less than fifteen minutes from landing to the elimination of

09:55 Osama bin Laden, one of the most efficient operations in US military history - and it

09:59 had been completed without a single death or serious injury to the entire Navy SEAL

10:03 team.

10:04 Watching from the situation room, President Obama uttered the words the entire White House

10:08 team had been waiting to hear - “We got him.”

10:10 But the mission wasn’t over just yet.

10:13 3:55 - The SEAL team members quickly sprung into action, securing bin Laden’s body and

10:17 moving it downstairs.

10:18 They would be exiting shortly, but there was still some extensive cleanup work to do.

10:22 The compound might be a source of vital intelligence, and they thoroughly searched the room and

10:26 surrounding area.

10:27 They found two weapons in the room - an assault rifle and a pistol - but the efficient team

10:31 had managed to neutralize bin Laden before he could reach them.

10:34 They weren’t loaded - indicating that the Al Qaeda leader was not expecting a firefight.

10:38 But what to do about the other residents?

10:40 Almost everyone who had engaged the US troops with weapons had been killed, but the compound

10:44 was full of civilians.

10:45 The US had no desire to take all the women and children found there into custody, so

10:49 they non-violently restrained them and left them outside the compound to be found by Pakistani

10:54 forces.

10:55 Most didn’t put up any resistance - besides the injured wife of Bin Laden, Amal Ahmed

10:59 Abdul Fatah.

11:00 She berated the SEALs in Arabic for the entire duration of the clean-up mission, and it seemed

11:05 the Yemeni woman was a true believer in her late husband’s mission.

11:08 She, like most of the people found there, would eventually be deported from Pakistan

11:11 back to their home countries in the Middle East.

11:13 And now, it was time to make a clean getaway.

11:16 4:05 - Bin Laden’s body and every important piece of intelligence or evidence had been

11:21 secured.

11:22 Taking what they needed, the first helicopter was loaded and primed for takeoff.

11:25 Much like the landing, this was a low take-off to avoid detection.

11:28 For those back in the United States, the SEALs were heroes - but this was an unauthorized

11:32 mission, and it was unlikely the Pakistani forces would be grateful if they were caught

11:36 there.

11:37 But much like the first time, SEAL Team Six pulled off a perfect getaway and exited the

11:40 compound.

11:41 But there was one more matter to attend to.

11:43 4:08 - The damaged Black Hawk helicopter that crashed in the compound would not be leaving

11:48 through the sky and Pakistani forces would be there shortly.

11:51 The chopper contained vital information about US military capabilities - because it wasn’t

11:55 just a standard helicopter and had been outfitted with stealth features.

11:59 So before they departed, the troops used the same portable explosives like the ones they

12:03 had used to breach the compound - and gave their fallen chopper an explosive send-off.

12:07 This only took minutes, and soon one of the backup helicopters brought on the mission

12:10 arrived, scooped up the remaining Navy SEALs, and flew them off to join the first helicopter.

12:15 The mission was over - and now it was time for a long ride.

12:18 5:53 - The ride back was over an hour and a half - more than three times the length

12:23 of the mission that killed Osama bin Laden.

12:25 But now that it was over, they had to get back to safe territory - back in US-occupied

12:29 Afghanistan, where the Americans had been fighting since the days after the September

12:33 11th terror attacks.

12:34 While it was unlikely the Pakistanis would fire on a US chopper if it was detected, a

12:39 stealthy escape would go much smoother, so the US troops had used some disinformation

12:43 efforts.

12:44 As the various explosions led to crowds before takeoff, an Urdu-speaking American military

12:48 officer claimed it had been a Pakistani operation being carried at the compound and to keep

12:53 their distance.

12:54 It worked, and the American landed safely at Bagram Airfield - carrying the body of

12:58 Osama Bin Laden.

12:59 Now it was time to deal with the aftermath.

13:02 7:01 - Back at the White House, the celebration was tempered by one question - was it really

13:07 him?

13:08 Bin Laden was infamous for using body doubles, and there had been multiple times where it

13:11 was thought he had been killed only for it to turn out to be a feint.

13:14 So everyone waited anxiously for the results of preliminary examinations of the corpse

13:18 - and over an hour after the SEALs arrived in Afghanistan, a new report came in indicating

13:22 that the notorious rogue was actually dead.

13:25 This time, the United States had gotten their man.

13:28 And the American public was about to find out.

13:30 It was the evening of May 1st when word started going around that the President was going

13:34 to be making a speech on TV that night.

13:36 Usually, when Barack Obama made a planned speech, it was early in the evening during

13:40 prime time - often to the annoyance of everyone who was trying to watch their favorite TV

13:44 show.

13:45 But this unplanned speech on short notice was different - and political watchers kept

13:48 waiting until the President ascended the podium at less than half an hour to midnight.

13:53 And as soon as he opened his mouth, people knew this was big.

13:56 11:35 - “Tonight, I can report to the American people and to the world that the United States

14:01 has conducted an operation that killed Osama bin Laden, the leader of Al Qaeda and a terrorist

14:06 who’s responsible for the murder of thousands of innocent men, women, and children.”

14:10 As the President paid tribute to the many who had died in bin Laden’s terror attacks,

14:14 a spontaneous celebration erupted around the country.

14:16 It was just short of ten years since the September 11th terror attacks, and many Americans lived

14:21 in fear of the next attack.

14:23 As word got around, large groups of fans attending sports games screamed in joy.

14:27 Democrats exulted in the biggest foreign policy win of the Obama Presidency - and Republicans

14:32 celebrated the end of an enemy while wondering if they should even bother running against

14:36 him next year!

14:37 And there was only one thing left to do.

14:40 12:59 - It was a little over an hour after President Obama’s speech, and the troops

14:44 had one major piece of business left to attend to - what to do with Osama bin Laden’s body?

14:49 The terror leader had been fully tested and examined, and they were sure he was their

14:53 guy.

14:54 He had been checked for any vital intel, and the body had no more secrets to give up.

14:57 The only thing left to do was dispose of the body, but there was one problem with that.

15:01 No one wanted him!

15:03 Bin Laden was wanted in just about every country on the planet, and even the countries where

15:07 he had sought refuge - Pakistan and Afghanistan - considered him an outlaw.

15:11 No country would want to give him a grave, because it would be a massive target for radical

15:15 activity.

15:16 No one wants to have an Al Qaeda pilgrimage in your country every year.

15:19 So why not just cremate his body and be done with it?

15:22 Cremation is against Islamic tradition, and as hated as the terror leader was, the government

15:26 still wanted to respect his faith.

15:28 No need to anger his followers any more than they already were - given that their leader

15:32 had just been eliminated.

15:33 Fortunately, there was an alternative.

15:35 Bin Laden’s body was loaded on the aircraft carrier Carl Vinson, and the US government

15:39 called the government of Saudi Arabia for approval to dispose of the body.

15:43 He was a Saudi citizen, after all, and the Saudis were important allies of the US government

15:47 at the time.

15:48 And the Saudi response was - we don’t care what you do with him, just don’t make it

15:52 our problem!

15:53 The plan to bury Osama bin Laden at sea was approved, and the body was treated with Muslim

15:57 religious rites.

15:58 There was even a brief reading of Arabic religious statements, at which point the body was draped

16:02 in a white shroud, place in a bag loaded with hundreds of pounds of iron chains, and placed

16:06 on a wooden board.

16:08 As the board was tilted forward, Bin Laden’s body slipped into the sea - ensuring the terror

16:12 leader would never have a grave that could be visited by loyalists, or targeted by enemies.

16:17 And now that the entire operation was over, there was only the cleanup to attend to.

16:21 It was roughly 3 AM local time in Pakistan when their Army chief received a phone call

16:25 informing the country of the operation that took place in their borders.

16:29 The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff filled him in on the details - and likely

16:32 smoothed over some angry words.

16:34 While there was some brief dispute of whether any Pakistani forces had been involved, the

16:38 government denied this and reports stated that the Pakistani planes which scrambled

16:42 to the location had only arrived after all the US forces had departed.

16:46 This is not where the aftermath ended through.

16:48 The raid that killed Osama bin Laden had played out over less than an hour, but the follow-up

16:52 would span years.

16:54 Controversies centered around the legality of the raid on foreign soil - although the

16:57 laws passed after 9/11 gave the US wide latitude to eliminate threats abroad.

17:02 Pakistan wasn’t pleased with the US operating on their soil, and the US wanted to know more

17:06 about bin Laden’s network of support in Pakistan.

17:09 Neither got too many answers.

17:10 Conspiracy theories persisted about bin Laden being alive - although the US government releasing

17:15 some photos of the terror leader’s corpse largely put those to rest.

17:19 And there was one more inevitable act.

17:21 Once the operation was partially declassified, various members of the team started putting

17:25 out memoirs.

17:26 Some varied in details - and most made the person writing the book out to be the hero.

17:30 So naturally, it wasn’t long before Hollywood came calling.

17:33 Only a year and a half after the death of Osama bin Laden, the movie “Zero Dark Thirty”

17:38 was released and its pick for the hero was…a fictional intelligence analyst played by Jessica

17:43 Chastain.

17:44 Because it wouldn’t be a key moment in American history without Hollywood putting its own

17:47 spin on it.

17:48 Want to know more about this famous manhunt?

17:51 Check out “Weird Things Navy SEALs Discovered in Osama Bin Laden’s Compound”, or watch

22:03 can measure the black and the level of

22:28 towards gray. It doesn't have to be all

22:36 example of white thinking. Is all white

22:38 thinking terrible? Absolutely. And we

22:40 call that mania. So shift away from

22:43 black or white to gray. That is the most

22:45 fundamental weeding you can add.

69:04 Thursday, well, why did Sweden come out there?

69:07 And what does that make sense?

69:09 You could put limits or caps on it,

69:11 and say, these are only low dollar accounts.

69:13 You can only have X 100 euro, or X 100 krona,

69:18 or Y number of dollars.

69:19 And it's really just small transactional accounts,

69:22 equivalent to $20 bills, not $100 or 500 euro notes.

69:27 So you can put limits or caps, or no interest rates,

69:30 and so forth.

69:32 Do you make it widely accessible, and so forth?

69:35 So there's all these design considerations,

69:38 which I'm guessing Rob, you've talked

69:41 to a bunch of central banks.

69:42 Where do they come out on these issues, as you see it, in 2018?

69:46 ROBLEH ALI: You've got a lot of different opinions on it.

69:48 I think the limits and caps thing is a hard thing

69:50 to practically implement.

69:51 That was always the sort of skepticism

69:56 around that-- it's like if you have these accounts,

69:58 and you say, well, we're going to only have one per person,

70:00 we're going to cap it at a certain amount of money.

70:02 What practically happens in a wrong--

70:05 is the government really going to say, well, no,

70:07 you can't put any more--

70:08 Like there'll be a lot of political pressure

70:11 in any crisis, so I think caps are really seen as viable.

70:17 And then, I think the interest bearing thing is interesting.

70:19 I mean, the only reason cash doesn't

70:21 bear interest is because it's technologically difficult

70:23 to make a paper bear interest.

70:25 So I think with digital currency,

70:30 they might as well give yourself the option.

70:31 Say, yeah, well, we can set the interest rate

70:33 to zero if you want to, but why limit yourself to say,

70:37 well, we won't charge interest?

70:38 Because it's again-- it's like that's

70:40 a limitation that comes from the technology

70:41 of physical banknotes, and there's no real need

70:44 to import it into the digital world, when you could achieve

70:48 the same effect by just setting the rate at zero

70:50 if you want to.

70:52 GARY GENSLER: And one of the reasons that some countries are

70:55 exploring this option, is they think

70:57 it'll be easier to do monetary policy,

70:59 because you're going to have negative interest rates.

71:01 Physical cash makes it hard for-- oh, nobody

71:05 like that, huh?

71:06 No, the two Elenes, you don't like negative interest rates?

71:11 But for a while, we effectively had negative interest rates.

71:17 Certainly for corporate deposits.

71:20 But if everything was digital, and there was no physical cash,

71:25 central banks say we could actually

71:27 go and have no lower bound, no zero bound to interest rates.

71:33 ROBLEH ALI: I guess you, in a way,

71:34 you don't necessarily need that.

71:36 Because if you can just create more money

71:38 and pump it into the economy, it has the same effect, right?

71:41 GARY GENSLER: Right, so what Rob is saying

71:43 is you could affect that by supply of money,

71:46 rather than the pricing of money.

71:48 And so there's both.

71:51 One of the most interesting to me is the second bullet point--

71:54 is a token or account based.

71:56 And the two merge together, in a sense.

71:59 This piece of paper is a token.

72:03 Nobody's keeping an account that when I hand this to Rob-- here,

72:06 you can take it, Rob.

72:09 That's your fee, remember.

72:12 So that's a token based bit of money, that's

72:15 what is called token based.

72:17 Token based money is more anonymous,

72:19 and you can keep it more anonymous.

72:21 Account base is when you're actually

72:23 keeping the ownership somewhere on a registry.

72:26 Even though that $20 bill is registered somewhere,

72:29 it has a serial number, it's a token based bit of money.

72:33

72:35 The Swedes, interestingly, say they'd have to change the law--

72:41 their own central bank laws-- for one of these two.

72:44 And now I can't remember.

72:45 But they have-- if it's token base,

72:49 it would come under their e-money laws,

72:51 and I think they don't need to change the law to do that.

72:54 But in Sweden, they would have to change their central bank

72:58 laws to do e-deposits, because they would literally

73:01 be opening up their central bank to something other

73:05 than commercial banks.

73:06 That's it-- they have to go to their legislative body

73:10 and parliament to actually do an account based, and not

73:13 a token based, if I recall.

73:16 So there's some also legal reasons

73:18 why you might need to do one or the other,

73:20 but one would have more anonymity than the other.

73:22 ROBLEH ALI: I think it's worth noting,

73:24 on these token versus account models,

73:27 it's not well-defined what people mean when they say taken

73:29 and accounts.

73:30 So different central banks will say this,

73:32 and mean different things.

73:34 And also people who work on Bitcoin will think about--

73:37 so when I see tokens, I think about particular structure

73:40 and transactions, which Bitcoin has.

73:42 And when I think about accounts, I

73:44 think of structure of transactions that Ethereum has.

73:47 And that's how I distinguish between those two things.

73:49 But I think having spoken to different central bankers,

73:52 they think about it differently, because e-money is like--

73:56 you could think about it as--

73:57 I mean to me, that's an account based system.

74:00 But some bankers think about it--

74:02 some central bankers think about that as token based.

74:05 So it's worth noting that the definitions are

74:08 very fluid in this area.

74:11 GARY GENSLER: So we're going to save this for Thursday.

74:15 I'm not going to go through this--

74:16 it was in one of the readings.

74:18 Garratt, who testified in Congress,

74:21 was so popular with this, then the Bank

74:23 of International Settlement picked up this thing

74:25 called the money flower.

74:27 But I'm going to save this, I want to kick this to Thursday.

74:30 But it's basically the four things--

74:32 widely accessible, is it digital, is its central bank,

74:35 is it token based?

74:37 And depending upon where these intersect,

74:40 you can take any form of money.

74:42 You could say, well, it's not central bank issued,

74:44 its token based, private digital tokens,

74:48 is down on the right hand corner is one little piece of it.

74:52 It's just a way to take these four important features.

74:57 And we already have central bank digital money,

75:01 which is in the middle of all this, it's called reserves.

75:04 But we're going to hold this for Thursday--

75:08 but this crazy little money flower,

75:11 central bankers who are in this world,

75:14 they've been using this, because this Professor Garratt came up

75:18 with it.

75:19 I mean, I've seen this in other papers.

75:21 ROBLEH ALI: It's very important.

75:22 GARY GENSLER: They love it, you know.

75:23 I don't know.

75:24 Money and flowers together, there you go.

75:27 But Rob, I don't know if you want

75:29 to come up and help close it, but these

75:31 are the ones we're going to talk about on Thursday.

75:33 And since Rob won't be here on Thursday,

75:35 I'm kind of curious if he has a point of view on any of these--

75:38 and you can see them here, as well.

75:40 ROBLEH ALI: The UK one is actually being stopped.

75:42 So I read something recently that the UK government--

75:46 I assume at the prompting of the Bank of England,

75:48 although their fingerprints are not directly on it,

75:50 I can imagine that they were behind it.

75:55 I think Uruguay is an interesting one.

75:58 I recently went to a presentation

76:00 by Uruguay central bank, and what's interesting about

76:03 that project is that it was actually live and out there

76:07 in the hands of people, paying for things in shops.

76:11 And I think that's what distinguishes it

76:12 from a lot of the other projects.

76:16 So for example, the ones that Gary's talked

76:18 about earlier in, say, Singapore and Canada,

76:21 are really just in-house creative concepts,

76:24 whereas the Uruguay project was something

76:26 that actually has worked, and they've taken an early form.

76:31 The Swedish one, again, is fairly early stage.

76:35 The e-krona is not out there yet,

76:37 they're just starting to explore it.

76:39 The Tunisia one was interesting--

76:41 I've spoken to one of the guys working on that.

76:43 And again, that's interesting because it's a live project.

76:46 It's continuing-- unlike the Uruguayan project,

76:48 it's a continuing project.

76:51 So it'll be interesting to see how it plays out there.

76:53 And I think the reason being is a lot of the thing that

76:56 puts off central banks from actually doing it,

76:58 is they don't know what effect it would have on the banking

77:00 system, or whatever.

77:01 And I think you will start to see--

77:03 when you start to see people actually trying

77:05 it, and deploying a central bank digital currency

77:07 in the real economy, then you will

77:10 have a real pilot, or a real world example,

77:13 that you can then research and say,

77:15 well, actually the effect was this.

77:16 Because at the moment, a lot of the debate around central bank

77:19 digital currency, what would be the effect

77:21 be on the banking system?

77:22 This is conjecture, you can build a model.

77:24 But it's very difficult.

77:25 But I think once you start to see countries actually

77:28 issue them, then you get the evidence in.

77:30 And then I think you'll see a cascade effect.

77:33 It will be very quickly, then, the technology is proven out,

77:35 and then more and more countries will issue them.

77:37 And also because of the funding effect,

77:39 Gary talked earlier about the cash--

77:44 like US dollars, physical cash, is effectively $1.6 trillion

77:48 of interest-free borrowing by the US government.

77:51 And if, say, the US government issued digital dollars,

77:54 then arguably you could retire half the national debt

77:58 and replace it with money.

77:59 So there are these big fiscal implications.

78:02 And the Body of the Commonwealth paper,

78:04 which my colleagues at [INAUDIBLE] wrote, I think,

78:06 two years ago, sort of addresses that fiscal element.

78:10 And I think that will be a big attraction to politicians

78:12 looking to spend money.

78:14 GARY GENSLER: And before we close, Simon,

78:16 because you're rarely with us, but from your perspective,

78:20 either from your chief economist days at the IMF,

78:23 or just because you--

78:25 Simon hosts the Tuesday night blockchain seminar dinners,

78:30 by the way, too, for three years.

78:31 So Simon is way ahead--

78:34 one might say he was kind of a blockchain Bitcoin

78:36 maximalist three years ago.

78:38 I think you've moved more to the middle--

78:41 you can self-declare where you are.

78:43 And Simon, Johnson, and Nehan, Narula,

78:45 and Michael, Casey, and I, are going

78:47 to be standing up a blockchain lab course in the spring.

78:52 So Simon?

78:54 Your question is, what do you think about all this,

78:56 and maybe for both of you in the last minute,

78:58 when are we going to see a true central bank test this out?

79:02 I mean, there's nine of them on this page that

79:03 are kind of feeling it out.

79:07 SIMON JOHNSON: I don't think there's any technical problem

79:09 here at all.

79:10 I think Rob has clearly put this out on a long time ago.

79:12 I think the issue comes down to what Rob said,

79:14 what does it do to credit?

79:16 Who really wants to find out the hard way?

79:18 And what does it do-- what happens

79:20 in a crisis when everyone-- you know,

79:21 let's say you're not paying interest

79:23 on a digital central bank currency,

79:25 and you can get interest on your bank account,

79:27 but there's a crisis.

79:28 And you say, well, I don't want to have this--

79:30 be holding the liability of a private bank anymore,

79:32 I want to be holding the liability of the central bank.

79:35 Doesn't everyone run to the central bank?

79:36 And what does that do to credit?

79:38 And how you're going to figure this out,

79:40 without actually running something like on [INAUDIBLE]..

79:42 GARY GENSLER: And two predictions--

79:43 how many years before our country actually--

79:46 because 180 countries, nine of them

79:49 are already bubbling around.

79:51 Two of these-- Ecuador stopped, Uruguay maybe stopped,

79:56 and the UK Royal Mint might have been

79:58 stopped by its own government.

79:59 But when do you think we're going

80:02 to see a country actually have a direct digital account

80:08 to their reserves?

80:09 For the retail public?

80:10 ROBLEH ALI: It could be a couple of years.

80:12 I mean, Tunisia is the closest to--

80:13 up on that list--

80:15 but a couple of years.

80:16 For the first one, yeah.

80:18 I mean, we're early [INAUDIBLE] years,

80:20 within two years, at least, possibly.

80:22 GARY GENSLER: So back together on Thursday.

80:27 We're going to dig back into these nine,

80:28 and talk a little bit more about the money

80:30 flower and the readings, which I think, as I always do,

80:34 I list them.

80:34

80:37 Some of those are more fun, and they're shorter readings,

80:41 as well.

80:42 So I will see you all on Thursday at 2:30 to 4:00,

80:48 and I thank you once again.

80:51 [APPLAUSE]

80:53
