docs.text:
00:00 You just spent $1,500 on a brand  new laptop… and it’s already ruined.

00:04 Before you even break the seal on the box, tech  companies have made a dirty deal to cripple your

00:09 computer’s performance. They took massive payouts  to install bloated software onto your system.

00:13 And this program will act like  a parasitic performance tax,

00:16 draining your processing speed, and  exposing your laptop to hackers.

00:20 You thought you bought a quality machine pc,

00:22 but hardware giants sold your  system’s brain to a predator.

00:25 It’s a common sight for anyone  booting up a computer for the

00:27 first time. A pre-installed trial  for McAfee Antivirus. You didn’t

00:31 choose it, and you didn’t install it.  It was already there. Waiting for you.

00:35 The moment you log in, the clock starts ticking.

00:37 And so does the psychological warfare.

00:39 Banners constantly warn you that your  trial is about to run out. Another will

00:43 scream that your laptop is exposed. All  the while, a red icon parks itself in the

00:47 corner of the screen and never leaves. Every  single panic inducing message is a ruthless

00:52 sales pitch your computer manufacture  was paid to force onto your desktop.

00:56 It’s all designed to force your hand.

00:58 McAfee even has a name for you. You’re part  of their “conversion pool”. A section of the

01:03 market of potential customers who don’t  physically search out the antivirus tool.

01:07 Those annoying pop-ups are  part of the business plan.

01:10 But it gets more insidious than that.

01:12 A McAfee browser extension hitches a ride to  track the links you click on. It’s watching

01:16 what you browse and the sites you visit. And when  that free trial runs out, the scanning stops. But

01:22 McAfee doesn’t leave. It stays on your desktop  and the notifications get even more blatant.

01:26 McAfee officially calls  this “longstanding exclusive

01:29 partnerships” with the leading PC brands. Dell and HP sit at the top of that partner list,

01:34 alongside Lenovo, Asus, Acer and Samsung.  McAfee’s agreement locks these brands in. A

01:40 rival antivirus firm with a better product can’t  buy that slot, simply because McAfee outbid them.

01:45 McAfee effectively cornered the antivirus market.

01:48 Around 285 million PCs were shipped in 2025. When  Microsoft pulled support for Windows, the upgrade

01:54 triggered a 8.1% spike in global computer sales.  Lenovo, HP, and Dell control over half the market.

02:01 That means millions of unsuspecting consumers are  already counting down to a forced subscription.

02:06 No one in the store mentioned it. The tech  industry will say you’re not forced to keep it.

02:11 But removing it needs a completely separate  download. And there’s a reason for that.

02:15 Money.

02:16 Industry sources estimate that McAfee pays  around $5 to $15 for access to machines.

02:21 On a single laptop, that’s pocket  change. But across the entire market,

02:25 it’s a huge amount of money. Manufacturers

02:28 can clear $140 million dollars just for  allowing McAfee access to the desktop.

02:32 PC makers survive on thin margins.  The top 5 companies are locked in a

02:37 price war battle for customers and  need to adjust prices to attract

02:40 them. Then there’s assembly and shipping  costs that eat away at balance sheets.

02:44 But McAfee’s preload money is pure  profit. It lands before the laptop

02:48 is even sold. But it doesn’t  stop there. Browser toolbars,

02:52 tracking cookies, and useless media players  are included in the agreement. Together,

02:56 this mountain of bloatware can knock as much as  $60 off the sticker price of the finished laptop.

03:01 But none of that appears on the spec sheet.

03:03 The laptop just looked cheaper because  software companies bought space inside

03:07 it. And the retailers saw an opportunity. In  2008, Best Buy started charging customers a

03:12 $30 fee in 2008 to strip the  preloaded software off a new PC.

03:16 So the shelf price came down  because the junk went on.

03:20 Then you could pay somebody to take it back off.

03:22 For McAfee, it’s a no brainer. Attracting  a customer normally costs money via

03:26 marketing. But by cutting a deal, the  customer is delivered to them directly.

03:30 But McAfee doesn’t want you using a trial.

03:33 They want your credit card.

03:34 Internally, the company pushes something  called Activation to Pay on all customers.

03:39 It’s essentially turning free trials  into paid subscriptions. And they work

03:42 hard at it. McAfee explicitly told  Wall Street that it would get better

03:46 at tricking people into paying  for software they never wanted.

03:49 It seems to be working.

03:51 By the end of 2021, the antivirus was running  on over 600 million devices. The same year,

03:56 a massive 72.8% of McAfee’s revenue came  from customers falling into this trap.

04:02 Sure, McAfee isn’t the only preinstalled  software that’s on laptops and PCs.

04:06 But the difference is the absolute  havoc it wreaks once it’s on there.

04:10 To prove how bad it was, an independent  testing lab in Austria put 16 antivirus

04:15 products against each other. They ran the  experiment on a Windows laptop with 8GB of

04:19 RAM. The lab called that setup high-end, so  a cheaper laptop would perform even worse.

04:25 The researchers timed every action  an everyday user does on a laptop,

04:28 from opening files to browsing the internet.  Then they collected the data and distilled

04:33 it into a single number called the Impact  Score. The lower the score, the less drag.

04:38 The lightweight antivirus  software, ESET scored 1.4.

04:42 McAfee got 11.5.

04:44 So the software no one asked for  creates a drag 8 times heavier

04:48 than the lightest option. McAfee  won’t necessarily crash a system,

04:52 but it definitely causes a slower  machine than one without the bloatware.

04:56 When the lab carried out a deeper dive,  McAfee received mediocre scores in the

05:00 task a computer performs almost  constantly: opening applications,

05:04 like a Word file or a PDF. The rival products  got top marks, but McAfee failed to qualify.

05:10 But the lab withheld one critical result:  system boot times. Certain cybersecurity

05:15 programs load after the desktop opens.  Everything looks fine initially,

05:19 then it starts to slow down. This  window is when the system is at its

05:24 most vulnerable. The software could achieve  a better score just by turning up late.

05:28 As frustrating as a slow computer is,  it’s not really dangerous. But when

05:32 that pre-installed security system suffers  a catastrophic failure, the fallout is huge.

05:37 In April 2010, McAfee shipped a routine update  that told the software a critical Windows

05:41 operating file was a virus. The software  reacted, locking the vital code away.

05:47 It was an unmitigated disaster.

05:49 Every computer running McAfee automatically  downloaded the update at the exact same second.

05:53 Within hours, Windows computers fell into endless  reboot loops. Then the blue screens of death

05:58 spread through corporate networks, workstations  died mid-task, and whole offices went dark.

06:03 McAfee pulled the file that same day,  shipped a patch version, and released an

06:07 emergency repair tool. The company pleaded  with customers to stop downloading updates

06:11 entirely. A cybersecurity giant was telling  its customer base the safest move was to not

06:16 use it. Microsoft had to step in and issue  manual instructions on how to reboot the

06:21 computers. A single bad line in a definition  file bricked PCs across the world in a day.

06:27 McAfee had the power to do this because  of its location in your computer.

06:30 Antivirus programs operate in the system's  kernel. That’s the core of the operating

06:35 system. The place with permission to touch  anything on the system. To stop a virus,

06:39 McAfee positions itself in front of every  file you open. It’s the only way it can

06:43 stop a threat. Handing over that access  is like handing somebody the master key

06:47 to every room in your house. It’s useful…  right up until somebody steals the key.

06:52 And that power makes it an attractive target.

06:55 Security researchers at Google’s Project Zero  proved that a single broken file inside the

06:59 kernel could take over your computer.  Sometimes nobody even had to open it.

07:03 On July 19th, 2024, the world saw this firsthand.  A bad update from CrowdStrike crashed 8.5 million

07:11 Windows computers in hours. The man who ran  CrowdStrike during the global blackout was George

07:15 Kurtz. He was McAfee’s worldwide chief technology  officer during their 2010 crash. He left a year

07:21 later to build a rival company after watching  someone wait 15 minutes for McAfee to load.

07:26 Microsoft has had enough.

07:27 The company launched a new  security platform in July

07:30 2025 that allows antiviruses to run in user mode,

07:34 where the ordinary apps live. Now the industry  is getting on board. It seems like they’ve

07:38 realized the current design is fundamentally  dangerous and the companies selling it know.

07:43 So that means people should be rushing to  delete McAfee from their computers, right?

07:47 Except it’s not that easy.

07:49 The standard Windows uninstaller can’t fully  remove McAfee from the system. Services and

07:53 drivers are usually behind. To completely scrub  it, users have to go to McAfee’s website and

07:59 download the Consumer Product Removal  tool. It needs a 12 megabyte download,

08:03 full administrator rights, and then  a system reboot. Even after that,

08:08 hundreds of registry keys stay behind.  Empty folders sit where the program used

08:12 to be. Background pieces keep running until  later security tools flag the mess as junk.

08:17 The reason for all this is  buried in the company accounts.

08:20 The subscription money doesn’t go toward  product development. In McAfee’s last full

08:24 year as a public company, they brought  in $1.92 billion. They burned through

08:29 $375 million for sales and marketing. And $184  million was spent on research and development.

08:36 The company spent more than twice as much finding  customers as it spent building the product.

08:41 That’s because McAfee is drowning in debt.  When Intel bought the company for about

08:45 $7.7 billion in 2010, the biggest  deal it had ever made. But by 2016,

08:50 its value had dropped to $4.2 billion. Poor  public perception and predatory products were

08:55 damaging the shareprice. Intel had seen enough  and sold 51% to the private equity firm TPG.

09:02 So roughly 45% of the price had evaporated.  Nothing about the software on your laptop

09:07 changed in those years. Only the  owners did. TPG slashed costs,

09:11 axing staff and closing offices.  Then it did what private equity does.

09:15 It borrowed against the  company it had just bought.

09:18 A new credit line pushed total debt obligations to  $4.8 billion. That money went to the owners. None

09:24 of it went into creating a desirable product.  McAfee went public again in October 2020,

09:29 at $20 a share, and most of the debt came with  it. It sold its enterprise division in 2021 for

09:36 $4 billion to pay off loans and  give shareholders a healthy payday.

09:40 That same year, a new group of private  equity firms took over. The deal came

09:44 to over $14 billion including debt, and  well over 70% of that was borrowed money.

09:50 Subscription costs are just covering the interest,

09:52 and whatever’s left belongs to the owners. A company in that position can’t develop a

09:56 better product. Every dollar that isn’t servicing  debt has to go into finding the next subscriber.

10:02 That’s why McAfee antivirus still drags the way  it does. Nobody at the top is paid to fix it,

10:07 and plenty of people are paid to keep selling it.

10:09 By the end of 2021, McAfee had 20.1  million subscribers. But to Wall Street,

10:14 they weren’t customers, they were assets.  Each one is a payment method on file,

10:19 renewing on schedule, at a  price that continues to rise.

10:22 And this desperate chase for  revenue has landed them in trouble.

10:25 In 2006, McAfee paid the SEC a $50 million  penalty over claims they artificially inflated

10:31 their revenue by $622 million. To pull off a fraud  of this size, they used a method called “Channel

10:38 Stuffing”. The company used secret cash payments,  heavy discounts, and under the table rebates to

10:43 force products onto distributors. Then they  logged then booked those shipments as revenue.

10:48 It settled without admitting or denying any of it.

10:51 Now, the same playbook is being  used. McAfee is manipulating the

10:54 revenue numbers to satisfy Wall Street and  will deal with the legal fallout later.

10:59 The cashflow has to arrive, regardless  of anyone actually wanting the software.

11:03 Which is why the renewal screen on  your desktop stops being a formality.

11:07 In May 2026, India’s Central Consumer  Protection Authority, or CCPA, targeted

11:12 McAfee. Not because of their prices or faulty  software, but because of 2 buttons on a desktop.

11:18 At the end of a subscription, a customer was  forced to weigh up 2 options. The first said

11:23 “Renew Now”, on a bright red background. The  second said “Accept Risk”, in muted grey.

11:29 There was no cancel button.  No skip. And no decide later.

11:33 To stop paying, you’d have to click a button  saying you accepted the risk. The CCPA said

11:38 McAfee couldn’t be sure a customer would be hacked  for not agreeing to their terms and conditions.

11:43 The wording was a deliberate scare tactic  designed to panic the user into subscribing.

11:48 The CCPA also found the colors  played a psychological role.

11:51 The “Accept Risk” was made to look like  the wrong answer. India had experience

11:55 with these shady tactics, having already  banned 13 similar designs in 2023 alone.

12:00 But there were over 355,000 renewals because of  the screen while it was live. McAfee scrambled

12:07 to change the button in December 2025,  and “Accept Risk” became “Skip” or “No,

12:12 thanks” after receiving complaints. It was a  preemptive move to avoid a regulatory fine.

12:17 It didn’t work.

12:18 McAfee was hit with a penalty, but  the fine amounted to just over $1,000,

12:23 which barely registers next to  the money generated from the

12:25 pop-up. McAfee subscriptions auto-renew  unless you hunt down the off switch.

12:30 And the renewal price isn’t  the price you signed up for.

12:33 A standard subscription starts at a  reasonable $39.99. But by the time

12:37 the auto subscription kicks in, it rises  to $110. That’s a jump of roughly 175%.

12:44 And with many customers card details  on file, the new charge is applied

12:48 before the current term even runs out.  Renewal rates sit between 80% and 90%.

12:53 That single number is what McAfee’s  multi-billion valuation is built on.

12:57 Certain security guarantees are  turned off when the subscription

13:00 is cancelled.But finding that cancel  button is intentionally difficult.

13:04 It’s buried in menus and hidden behind  a password most people haven’t touched.

13:08 It’s how McAfee makes money.

13:10 It’s also how they ended up in court. In 2014, McAfee faced a federal lawsuit

13:15 in California for their covert billing  practices. Loyal customers were being

13:19 penalized with hefty price hikes, compared to  new customers, for the exact same software.

13:24 McAfee settled, paying $80 million and admitted  no wrongdoing. Anybody who filed a claim got

13:30 $11.50 back on a subscription that costs $110. But

13:34 nothing changed. McAfee kept running  the exact same play. That lawsuit was

13:38 swiftly followed by Britain’s competition  regulator knocking on the door in 2018.

13:42 Despite all this scrutiny,  the button is still there.

13:45 Now, McAfee is facing pressure  from regulators… and competitors.

13:49 Windows 11 is sold with Microsoft  Defender switched on by default,

13:52 at no extra cost. macOS runs its own  XProtect underneath. The product McAfee

13:58 built its name selling now comes as  standard on most operating systems.

14:01 For a subscription business,  that’s a serious problem.

14:04 So McAfee decided to pivot. They now  sell identity monitoring, VPNs, and

14:08 deepfake detection. And those are genuine, modern  problems. Scams keep getting better, fake video

14:14 keeps getting cheaper to produce, and there’s  serious money to be made in solving both. But

14:19 all 3 of those products run on trust, and trust  is the one thing McAfee burned to the ground.

14:24 They built their empire by invading your  machine before you even opened the box.

14:28 They boosted their revenue by making  it almost impossible to cancel. And

14:32 they were fined for making customers believe  they were at imminent risk of being hacked.

14:36 Now that exact same company wants  you to trust them with your identity.

14:39 It’s a risky business model, but McAfee  always seems to find a way. Because

14:43 they don't need to write good software  anymore. They just need software that

14:47 arrives uninvited, refuses to leave  and charges you for the privilege.

14:51 That’s why the company is still worth $14 billion.

14:54 And it’s why your laptop was never really  yours. Somebody got paid to make sure of that.

14:59 McAfee aggressively pushes their product,

15:01 but is it actually protecting you from  real threats? How bad can hacking actually

15:05 get? Watch “10 Most Dangerous Hackers of  All Time” to find out. Or click on this.

docs.text:
00:00 Your body is being hijacked!

00:02 You are no longer in control.

00:04 Microscopic entities are flooding through your systems and using your own cells against

00:08 you!

00:09 What is happening?

00:10 How do you stop these foreign invaders?

00:11 Well it depends.

00:12 Let’s take a step back and ask: what is attacking you?

00:15 Is the pathogen a virus or bacteria?

00:18 This single question could be the difference between life and death.

00:21 There are ways to kill bacteria that will not kill a virus and vice versa.

00:24 So, let’s take a look at what the similarities and differences are between a virus and a

00:29 bacteria.

00:30 Knowing the difference could save your life.

00:31 Both bacteria and viruses are microscopic, meaning they are too small to see with the

00:35 naked eye.

00:36 They can enter your body through any opening, but most often they enter through the nose

00:40 and mouth.

00:41 Are bacteria and viruses living things?

00:44 This is the first distinction between the two pathogens that we will make.

00:48 Bacteria is most certainly alive.

00:50 In order to be classified as a living thing something must have five traits.

00:54 The traits are: it’s made of cells, it grows and reproduces, it responds to stimuli in

00:59 the environment, it can pass on genetic information, and it must maintain homeostasis or an internal

01:04 balance.

01:05 If just one of these characteristics is missing, it is not considered a living thing.

01:10 Bacteria meet all the requirements.

01:11 They are made of a single cell that divides to reproduce and maintains homeostasis as

01:16 their environment changes.

01:17 Bacteria are likely the most diverse kingdom of living things on the planet.

01:21 There are billions of different species of bacteria.

01:23 Not only that, there are trillions of bacteria in your body right now!

01:28 Bacteria in your body outnumber your own cells by about ten to one!

01:32 Think about how crazy that is.

01:34 Just in sheer numbers there are more bacteria in you than your own cells.

01:38 Biology is fascinating!

01:40 This brings up a really good point though.

01:42 If there are so many bacteria in you why aren’t you dead, or at least sick all of the time?

01:47 Aren’t bacteria harmful to your body?

01:49 For anyone who has had food poisoning caused by bacteria you wished you were dead at the

01:53 time.

01:54 Recently scientists have discovered that bacteria play an important role in making up your body's

01:58 microbiome.

01:59 Bacteria are actually beneficial in many ways.

02:01 They can help you digest foods and keep your skin healthy.

02:04 We have come to realize that bacteria actually make your life better.

02:08 Without a healthy microbiome of bacteria in your body you wouldn’t be able to eat certain

02:11 foods and you’d become sick more often.

02:14 We now know bacteria are living things.

02:16 They are single celled and have all of the characteristics of life.

02:19 They are diverse and found everywhere around the world.

02:22 Bacteria can be harmful, but they are also beneficial to your body.

02:25 So are viruses the same way?

02:27 The short answer is no.

02:29 Viruses and bacteria have more differences than similarities.

02:32 Let’s start with what seems like a basic question.

02:35 Are viruses alive?

02:37 Well… it’s complicated.

02:39 Depending on who you ask in the scientific community you will get a different answer.

02:43 Viruses are in a grey area between living and nonliving things.

02:47 For example, they cannot reproduce without hijacking the cells of a host.

02:51 This means that they don’t really have the characteristic of reproduction.

02:54 All other living things can reproduce without taking over another organism's cells and using

02:59 it for their own purposes.

03:00 Living things either find a mate and reproduce, like humans, or split in two using a form

03:06 of asexual reproduction like bacteria.

03:08 Viruses can’t do either of these things.

03:11 Another characteristic of a living thing is that they respond to their environment.

03:15 Viruses again are in a weird grey area where they don’t so much respond to their environment,

03:20 as change it.

03:21 Viruses change the genetic code of cells to suit their needs.

03:24 They can cause cells to make copies of themselves, along with protein shells that carry them

03:28 to new cells to infect.

03:30 Viruses are tricky both in the way they use our cells against us and identifying if they

03:34 are a living thing or not.

03:37 Bacteria on the other hand will respond to their environment.

03:38 They will make more copies of themselves when there is an abundance of resources or swap

03:43 their genetic code with other bacteria around them if a beneficial trait arises that helps

03:47 the species survive.

03:49 Evolution by natural selection also is an important concept when discussing living things.

03:54 All living things evolved from a species in the past.

03:57 You, me, bacteria, we all evolved from an organism that started life on this planet

04:02 billions of years ago.

04:03 Granted, you and bacteria went through many different changes and evolutionary steps,

04:08 but humans and bacteria both evolved from earlier species.

04:12 This is just how life works on our planet.

04:14 Viruses again blur the line here.

04:16 Viruses most definitely do change over time.

04:19 This is why you have to get a different flu shot every year.

04:21 Although viruses are missing several characteristics of a living thing they do seem to evolve.

04:26 And they seem to evolve fast.

04:29 Species evolve when a mutation in the DNA occurs that gives an organism a new trait.

04:33 Mutations are random mistakes in the DNA, so some are good, some are bad, and some don’t

04:39 have any effect on an organism's survival at all.

04:42 But with viruses it would seem mutations happen so often, and so rapidly, that a new form

04:46 of a virus can evolve almost overnight.

04:48 Are bacteria living things?

04:50 Yes they are.

04:51 Are viruses living things?

04:53 Ehh, they straddle the line between living and nonliving.

04:57 Us humans like to make things clear cut and binary.

04:59 Either yes or no.

05:01 Unfortunately, viruses don’t fit into one category or another, which can scare and frustrate

05:05 us.

05:06 We talked about the benefits of bacteria.

05:08 But you may be wondering, do viruses give us any benefits?

05:11 Or are they just little hijacking machines that make us sick?

05:14 Well, one benefit of viruses is that weak or less harmful ones can help boost your immune

05:18 system.

05:19 If you get the common cold, and it makes you a little sick, your body may develop resistance

05:23 to a more malicious virus with a similar genetic makeup.

05:27 In this case your body would be better able to fight off the new virus thanks to the weaker

05:30 virus you got earlier in your life.

05:33 But let's talk about one of the coolest benefits a virus can have for you.

05:37 Let’s talk about bacteriophages.

05:39 A bacteriophage is a virus that kills bacteria.

05:42 It targets a specific type of bacteria, infiltrates it, takes over, and destroys it.

05:47 It’s pretty awesome when you think about it.

05:48 Like little microscopic warfare happening inside your body.

05:51 Imagine you have a harmful bacteria multiplying away inside of you.

05:55 It’s making you sick and causing a lot of distress.

05:58 Then a virus that has been lying dormant in the mucus lining of your gastrointestinal

06:02 tract awakes from its slumber.

06:04 The viruses start attacking the harmful bacteria by injecting them with their genetic code

06:08 and taking over.

06:09 Eventually the bacteriophages kill all the harmful bacteria and are either evacuated

06:13 from your system or lie dormant again waiting for their next victim.

06:17 That is pretty cool stuff if you ask us.

06:20 Bacteriophages are viruses that only kill bacteria, so they pose no threat to your cells.

06:25 As of yet we know of no bacteria that kills viruses, but there are countless different

06:30 viruses that can kill bacteria.

06:32 There is one last aspect of viruses that makes them unique and different from bacteria.

06:37 We promised that biology is fascinating and if we haven’t already delivered we are about

06:42 to.

06:43 When viruses infect us and hijack our cells they can embed small chunks of their DNA into

06:47 our DNA.

06:48 Although this is rare it has been happening for millions of years.

06:51 So, over time the viral DNA that has snuck into human DNA has accumulated.

06:55 Your DNA right now is actually comprised of around ten percent virus DNA.

07:00 Think about that.

07:01 One tenth of the genetic code that makes you you, is actually virus DNA!

07:05 Like mutations, the chunks of viral DNA in our genome were inserted randomly.

07:09 Some of it is harmful, such as viral DNA that can cause cancer.

07:13 Other pieces of viral DNA have been beneficial to us humans over our evolutionary history.

07:18 There is evidence that some of the virus DNA in our genome helped in the development of

07:22 the human placenta.

07:23 Also, if you enjoy eating cereal, bread, or any other food high in starch, you can thank

07:28 viruses for providing humans with the gene that allows us to digest the complex sugar.

07:33 Viral DNA is responsible for creating starch digesting enzymes in our pancreas cells.

07:38 Without virus DNA in our genome we would all be on a starch free diet right now.

07:42 Bacteria are beneficial to humans in a lot of ways.

07:45 Most especially in shaping our microbiome and digestion of foods.

07:49 However, only viruses can claim the honor of changing our DNA and influencing the course

07:53 of human evolution.

07:55 Have we mentioned how cool biology is yet?

07:57 Now let’s talk about the differences in preventing or killing viruses and bacteria.

08:01 The first and most important distinction to make when treating a pathogen is to identify

08:05 if it is a virus or a bacteria.

08:08 This is important because only certain medicines work for certain types of pathogens.

08:12 Antibiotics are used to kill bacteria.

08:15 Antibiotics will only kill bacteria.

08:17 Hence the name anti meaning against and biotic meaning living.

08:20 So antibiotics are only used to kill living things, in this case bacteria.

08:25 Since viruses are complicated and don’t reproduce using cellular division, antibiotics

08:30 have no effect on them.

08:31 It is important that you can distinguish between viruses and bacteria to make informed decisions

08:36 about medication being recommended for an illness.

08:38 We know bacteria are living things.

08:40 All living things are subject to the pressures of natural selection.

08:44 When the environment of a bacteria changes, let’s say an antibiotic is introduced, the

08:48 bacteria will be killed by it.

08:50 That is unless a random mutation allows one bacteria to become resistant, and therefore,

08:54 able to fight off the antibiotic.

08:56 If this happens that species of bacteria will keep on multiplying and could lead to severe

09:00 illness or death.

09:02 Antibiotic resistance is a process that is driven by natural selection.

09:05 The bacteria can literally evolve in your body to become resistant to antibiotics.

09:09 This is why it is so important to take the correct dosage, for the correct amount of

09:13 time, when prescribed antibiotics by your doctor.

09:16 Even if you stop showing symptoms you must complete your antibiotic regimen, because

09:20 if you don’t, the bacteria you were trying to kill are more likely to develop resistance

09:24 to that antibiotic.

09:25 We see this in certain parts of the world with Tuberculosis.

09:28 Like we’ve said, living things tend to evolve over time, otherwise that species would go

09:32 extinct.

09:33 Bacteria are no exception.

09:35 So if antibiotics only kill bacteria how do we kill viruses?

09:39 There are two types of medicines that doctors use.

09:42 The first is antiviral medication.

09:44 The drugs must be administered within a certain time frame, and are only effective while the

09:48 medicine is in the patients system.

09:50 When you travel to areas of the world with yellow fever, you can take an antiviral yellow

09:53 fever drug.

09:54 You have to take the pills as prescribed by the doctor, before and during your trip, in

09:59 order for the drug to be effective.

10:01 The antiviral uses chemicals that kill the virus, but only if those chemicals are in

10:05 your system when the virus infiltrates your body.

10:08 Vaccines can be used to prevent or kill both a virus or bacteria.

10:11 Every vaccine is different and made to kill one type of pathogen.

10:15 Vaccines typically use a weakened or dead form of the pathogen to activate the immune

10:19 system.

10:20 When the weakened or dead pathogen enters your body your immune system identifies it

10:23 and makes antibodies that mark it for destruction.

10:26 After your immune system comes in contact with the vaccine it will remember what the

10:30 virus or bacteria looked like, so if you ever are infected with the actual pathogen your

10:35 body already has immunity to.

10:37 Then your immune system will do what it does best and destroy the pathogen before it can

10:41 make you sick.

10:42 Vaccines work the same way against bacteria and viruses.

10:45 We have learned a lot over the years about viruses and bacteria.

10:48 We know they have some similarities, but are different in many ways.

10:52 It is thanks to scientists and doctors that we know so much, and can protect ourselves

10:56 from harmful pathogens like bacteria and viruses.

10:59 It is also thanks to scientists and doctors that we understand the importance bacteria

11:03 and viruses can play in human evolution and health.

11:06 What it comes down to is that biology is cool and scientists are awesome.

11:11 That is why when scientists and doctors recommend certain precautions to prevent a disease,

11:15 we should all listen.

11:16 If you are team virus then check out our video Why Spanish Flu Killed Over 50 Million People

11:21 - Deadliest Plague in Modern History.

11:23 If you are team bacteria check out Why Would a Scientist Inject Himself with 3.5 Million

11:29 Year Old Bacteria?

11:30 Just make sure you wash your hands with soap and hot water for 20 seconds after finishing

11:34 the videos.

docs.text:
00:00 It's Friday night, the end of a long  week, and you decide to have a drink…

00:04 maybe two or three. We've all been there.  But have you ever wondered what's really

00:09 happening to your body when you start  drinking alcohol? Today on the channel,

00:13 we’re exploring what happens to your body –  minute by minute – when you drink alcohol.

00:17 We’ll examine each of these concepts (backed  by science, of course) through the lens of our

00:21 character, Sarah. We’ll follow her on her night  out—and beyond—breaking down the changes in her

00:26 body from the very first sip of her cocktail.  Ready to see what happens? Let’s head to the bar.

00:32 It's 10:06 p.m., and Sarah takes her first sip of  a skinny margarita—her go-to drink after a long

00:37 work week. That tangy, sweet flavor aside, what's  going on inside? The alcohol, called ethanol,

00:43 is a small molecule absorbed rapidly. Within  minutes, it's traveling through her bloodstream.

00:48 The vibrant bar atmosphere surrounds Sarah.  The clinking of glasses, casual chatter,

00:53 and upbeat music fill the air. This sensory  overload usually feels a bit much for her,

00:58 but as the alcohol starts to take effect,  it blends into a pleasantly muted buzz.

01:03 A wave of warmth spreads through Sarah's body.  Alcohol acts as a vasodilator, expanding her blood

01:08 vessels and leading to a feeling of warmth.  However, this also means that her body loses

01:13 heat more quickly, explaining why some people  feel cold later in the night after drinking.

01:18 It’s 10:21 pm. What’s going on inside  Sarah’s body? Let's zoom in! We see the

01:24 alcohol molecules from Sarah's margarita begin  their journey. A small portion, about 20%, is

01:30 absorbed directly through the lining of her mouth,  entering her bloodstream almost immediately.

01:34 The rest of the margarita travels down her  esophagus and into her stomach. Here, another

01:39 small portion, about 20%, of the alcohol enters  the bloodstream through the stomach lining. Once

01:44 in the bloodstream, alcohol takes a whirlwind tour  of the body, impacting various organs, especially

01:50 the brain. This initial absorption can explain  why people feel the effects of alcohol so quickly.

01:55 The remaining alcohol continues to Sarah's  small intestine. The walls of the small

01:59 intestine are lined with tiny,  finger-like projections called

02:03 villi. These villi provide a huge surface  area to absorb nutrients… and alcohol.

02:08 The alcohol rapidly passes  through the villi and into

02:11 the network of blood vessels surrounding  the small intestine. Now it enters the

02:14 portal vein, which acts like a highway  transporting it directly to the liver.

02:19 The liver is bathed in a surge of alcohol-rich  blood. Keep in mind that while the liver is the

02:24 powerhouse of detoxification and will work  hard to break down the ethanol molecules,

02:29 its capacity is limited. It can only  process so much in any given time period.

02:34 When the liver can't keep up, the excess  alcohol continues to circulate throughout

02:37 Sarah's body via her bloodstream. This  is how alcohol ultimately reaches her

02:42 brain and other organs, causing the changes  we'll witness as Sarah's evening continues.

02:47 It's 10:39 pm, and with the first drink down,

02:50 Sarah is feeling a slight buzz.  Typically a pretty anxious person,

02:53 Sarah finds herself a bit less stressed.  Alcohol reduces activity in the amygdala,

02:58 the part of the brain associated with fear and  anxiety. But while this might feel good at the

03:03 moment, chronic reliance on alcohol for stress  relief can actually worsen anxiety over time.

03:08 Sarah leans back into her chair and takes a deep  breath. A sense of ease washes over her. The

03:14 worries that were nagging in her mind seemed  to fade into the background. This isn't just

03:19 her imagination; there's a biochemical reason  behind the shift. Alcohol acts as a depressant,

03:24 slowing down the activity of the  central nervous system. This means

03:28 that messages between Sarah's brain  cells are traveling a little slower

03:31 than usual. It's kind of like putting the  brakes on her usual whirlwind of thoughts.

03:36 As her thoughts quiet down, so does the  activity in her sympathetic nervous system,

03:40 which is responsible for our "fight-or-flight"  response. Her heart rate slows slightly,

03:45 her breathing becomes easier, and  any muscle tension she is holding .

03:50 A subtle change has come over Sarah’s  face. Her cheeks are slightly flushed,

03:53 and her eyes have a slight sparkle. This is  due to the blood vessel dilation we mentioned

03:58 earlier. As Sarah catches a glimpse of  herself in the mirror behind the bar,

04:01 she feels a little more attractive. This boost  in self-perception is a common effect of alcohol,

04:06 as it lowers inhibitions and can  temporarily increase self-confidence.

04:10 Alcohol affects the neurotransmitters in her  brain. It boosts the release of dopamine – the

04:15 "feel-good" chemical – making her feel  happier and more relaxed. Simultaneously,

04:20 alcohol suppresses glutamate, the brain's  primary excitatory neurotransmitter.

04:24 This slowdown is starting to slightly  impact her judgment and coordination.

04:29 Sarah’s usual social inhibitions start to fade,  and she starts talking to the guy next to her

04:34 at the bar. Conversation feels easy. Alcohol,  often known as a “social lubricant,” dampens

04:39 the activity in the prefrontal cortex of the  brain – the region responsible for judgment,

04:43 planning, and impulse control. This  makes it easier for Sarah to strike up

04:47 conversations with strangers and feel more  at ease in the social setting of the bar.

04:51 But it’s a delicate balance. While the  relaxation might feel nice at this point,

04:56 if Sarah continues drinking,  this effect will intensify,

04:59 potentially leading to poor judgment and impaired  decision-making further into her evening.

05:04 It's 10:55 pm, and with a second drink in  hand and almost finished, the alcohol level

05:10 in Sarah's blood is rising pretty rapidly. The  liver, our body's chemical processing plant,

05:15 is working hard to metabolize the alcohol. But  the liver can only handle about one standard

05:19 drink per hour. When it gets overwhelmed, excess  alcohol continues to circulate in the bloodstream.

05:25 Sarah swirls the remaining liquid in her  glass. The ice cubes clink hollowly with each

05:29 circle. She catches the bartender’s eye  and orders a third cocktail. The bar,

05:34 dim and tucked away, is starting  to blur a little around the edges.

05:37 It’s 11:16 pm, and Sarah has decided to buy a  round of shots for a group of strangers. While the

05:43 gesture feels generous at the moment, her impaired  judgment is making her less aware of the potential

05:48 financial strain of this decision. It also  increases the pace of her alcohol consumption.

05:53 Sarah is much more talkative than usual  and feels more and more confident. This is

05:58 because alcohol is further depressing the areas  in the brain associated with social anxiety and

06:03 judgment. However, her motor skills are also  starting to become increasingly impaired.

06:08 As the drinks keep coming, Sarah feels  more shifts. She senses a giddy lightness

06:13 she hasn't experienced in ages. Her  words, normally measured and precise,

06:17 tumble out in a stream, no  longer carefully filtered.

06:21 Sarah regales the bartender – a quiet, middle-aged  man named Pete – with stories about her demanding

06:27 boss, her disastrous dating life, and the  time she accidentally glued her fingers

06:32 together during a home improvement project.  It all comes spilling out, punctuated by

06:36 bouts of laughter that are just a touch too  loud for the subdued atmosphere of the bar.

06:41 The buzz that had been a pleasant hum  before is now a full-blown symphony

06:45 in Sarah’s head. Her movements  are becoming less deliberate,

06:48 her glass sloshing a bit as she sets it down,  a napkin fluttering to the floor unnoticed.

06:54 It’s 11:57 pm. When getting up to use the  restroom, Sarah accidentally bumps into a table,

06:59 almost knocking over someone else's drink.  She laughs it off and attributes it to

07:03 the dim lighting, but in reality, alcohol is  subtly affecting her coordination and balance.

07:08 Sarah’s blood alcohol concentration continues  to rise, affecting her vision, speech,

07:13 and balance. She’s continuing to experience  blurred vision and slurred speech. All of

07:17 this is due to the way alcohol continues to  disrupt communication between her brain cells.

07:22 The lights above the bar seem to pulse in rhythm  with her heartbeat. As she sips her next cocktail,

07:27 the world tilts just a touch. It seems funny  now that there is this lack of coordination,

07:32 as if someone else is in charge of her body.

07:34 Pete, the bartender, asks Sarah a question, which  she barely hears. She tries to respond, but her

07:39 words seem to trip over one another, a jumbled  mess that leaves a frustrated laugh in her throat.

07:44 At 12:32 am, with multiple cocktails and a shot in  her system, Sarah is definitely feeling drunk. Her

07:50 phone slips out of her hand as she tries to take  a selfie. It takes her several tries before she

07:55 manages to catch it. Her slower reflexes make  normally simple tasks slightly more difficult.

08:00 Sarah's appetite is starting to kick in. While  alcohol can temporarily increase appetite,

08:05 in the long run, it can disrupt hormones  that regulate hunger and fullness,

08:09 potentially leading to unhealthy eating habits.  Leptin suppresses appetite, while glucagon-like

08:14 peptide-1 (GLP-1) regulates food intake… and both  of these are inhibited when drinking alcohol.

08:21 She clumsily calls Pete over and orders  the enchiladas, but he informs her that

08:25 the kitchen is closed. She starts to  search on her phone for restaurants still

08:29 serving food and asks some of the other  patrons at the bar for recommendations. Then,

08:33 she stumbles next door to a slightly livelier  bar, where she orders another cocktail.

08:38 It’s 1:12 am, and Sarah has tried to maintain  her confident buzz and relaxed demeanor,

08:43 but she’s not feeling so hot. After drinking  far too much than her liver can handle,

08:47 she’s reeling from the effects. The upbeat music  she usually enjoys now feels too loud and chaotic.

08:53 She also misinterprets a friendly smile from  another bar patron as a flirtatious gesture.

08:58 Alcohol has altered her perception of  sound and social cues. When she tries

09:02 to flirt back and the stranger walks away,  Sarah feels a sweeping sense of rejection.

09:07 Coupled with an exaggerated emotional  state is a physical feeling of nausea,

09:11 and Sarah runs to the bathroom to vomit.  Throwing up is the body’s defense mechanism

09:16 for a variety of reasons. First, when the body  recognizes alcohol as a toxin and wants to get

09:21 rid of it as quickly as possible, vomiting  is one way to expel the excess alcohol.

09:26 Additionally, when your liver breaks down alcohol,  it produces a toxic byproduct called acetaldehyde.

09:31 If you drink too much, your liver can't process  the acetaldehyde fast enough, leading to a

09:32 buildup that makes you feel sick. Vomiting helps  your body get rid of some of the acetaldehyde.

09:32 Finally, alcohol directly irritates your  stomach lining. This irritation can lead

09:36 to nausea and vomiting, especially if you  drink a lot in a short period, like Sarah.

09:41 After a fellow patron helps hold Sarah’s  hair back as she throws up in the bathroom,

09:46 Sarah knows it’s time to go.  She gets a cab and heads home,

09:49 falling asleep in her clothes and  makeup on top of her comforter.

09:53 It’s 7:02 am, and Sarah wakes up with a  pounding headache and a hazy memory of

09:58 last night. That headache? It's partly  due to dehydration caused by alcohol,

10:03 which also greatly disrupted her sleep. After a  night of strange dreams and sweating profusely,

10:08 her body is still working to clear  the remaining alcohol from her system.

10:11 Alcohol's sleep disruption is a double-edged  sword. While drinking may help you fall asleep

10:16 initially, the quality of sleep is severely  compromised. REM sleep – crucial for memory

10:21 and emotional processing – is suppressed,  leaving you feeling groggy and unrested.

10:26 Sunlight pierces through a sliver  in Sarah’s blackout curtains,

10:29 a searing lance of pain across  her throbbing skull. She groans,

10:33 her head feeling as though it were filled  with angry wasps. Each movement sends fresh

10:37 waves of nausea through her body. Her stomach  churns, and her mouth is a desert landscape.

10:43 Dehydration is a major hangover culprit.  Alcohol acts as a diuretic, suppressing a

10:48 hormone called vasopressin, which regulates fluid  levels. Not only does this increase urination,

10:53 but paired with nausea and potential  vomiting, it can leave you dehydrated.

10:58 Fragments of the previous night  flickered back in painful flashes:

11:01 the laughter that turned too loud, the  spilled drinks, Pete's worried frown.

11:06 A wave of shame washes over Sarah. How  much had she drunk? What had she said?

11:11 Alcohol-induced memory blackouts are frighteningly  common. As blood alcohol concentration rises,

11:17 the hippocampus, the brain's memory  center, is impaired. Long-term memory

11:21 formation can be blocked, leaving you with  frustrating gaps in your recollection.

11:25 Sarah presses a shaking hand to  her temple. She would need to piece

11:29 together the night and retrace her steps—a  daunting task considering the state of her

11:33 brain. There was the lingering sense of having  done something reckless. She vaguely remembers

11:38 falling onto a table, and was that a  stranger holding her hair back while

11:42 she vomited in the bathroom? Everything  is just a little too foggy for her liking.

11:47 It’s 8:14 am, and after tossing and turning in bed  for a while, Sarah stumbles towards the kitchen,

11:52 each step a measured battle against the persistent  nausea. Her goal sits on the countertop – a tall,

11:58 frosted glass left out since the night before. She  fills it to the brim with icy water. Rehydration

12:04 is crucial to hangover recovery. Alcohol's  diuretic effect leaves you severely depleted,

12:09 throwing your electrolyte balance  off-kilter. Replenishing these

12:12 lost fluids can help ease symptoms  like headaches, fatigue, and nausea.

12:16 Alcohol also depletes vital nutrients, including  potassium, magnesium, and zinc. While water is

12:22 crucial, supplementing with electrolyte-rich  drinks or foods like bananas, sports drinks, or

12:27 broth can aid in restoring balance. Unfortunately,  there's no magical cure for a hangover. The body

12:34 simply needs time to metabolize the alcohol and  repair the damage. While rehydration and rest

12:39 are essential, the lingering effects  may well persist throughout the day.

12:43 So, does everyone’s body respond to alcohol  similarly? Or are there certain risk factors

12:48 Sarah has? While it's easy to assume that everyone  experiences a night of drinking the same way,

12:53 that's not true. While the immediate effects  of Sarah's drinks felt unpleasant enough,

12:58 there are hidden factors that might  make her especially vulnerable to

13:01 the longer-term effects of alcohol.  Let's examine some of those risks.

13:05 First, there’s the fact that Sarah’s a  female. Biology plays a big role here.

13:09 Women generally metabolize alcohol  slower than men, leading to a higher

13:13 concentration in their blood. They also tend  to have a higher percentage of body fat,

13:17 which means less water to dilute the alcohol,  making its impact stronger. These factors could

13:23 contribute to both negative short-term  and long-term consequences for Sarah.

13:27 What about weight? It’s true that a person  with a smaller body will feel the effects of

13:31 alcohol more strongly than someone with  a larger body, even if they consume the

13:35 same amount. This is because the alcohol is less  diluted in the bloodstream of someone smaller.

13:41 Next, there’s the factor of food intake  before and during drinking. In Sarah’s case,

13:45 she worked until 7:00 pm, then  went home, showered, got ready,

13:48 and went out… but skipped dinner, thinking she’d  get a bite sometime during the night. Not having

13:54 eaten beforehand was detrimental to her, and by  the time her appetite intensified later in the

13:59 night, the local kitchens were closed.  Drinking on an empty stomach accelerated

14:03 the absorption of alcohol into her bloodstream,  intensifying its impact on her brain and body.

14:08 There are also risk factors associated with  medications and other substances. It's vital

14:13 not to mix alcohol with anything else without  consulting a medical professional. Even common

14:18 over-the-counter medications or certain herbal  supplements can have dangerous interactions when

14:23 combined with alcohol, exacerbating the effects  of both. Sarah is on anti-anxiety medication,

14:29 which puts her at greater risk of feeling  the intense effects of excess alcohol.

14:33 It's crucial to remember that these  individual risk factors can compound

14:37 over time. The more frequently Sarah  drinks, and the more heavily she drinks,

14:41 the higher the risk of alcohol impacting her  health in the long run in a wide variety of ways.

14:47 While today’s hangover feels awful,  it's a short-term consequence of

14:50 Sarah's alcohol consumption. What's  more concerning is that repeated,

14:54 excessive alcohol use can put a strain on her  body, silently increasing her risk for serious,

14:59 chronic health problems over time.  Let's look at some of those risks.

15:03 First, there’s liver damage. Our liver takes  the brunt of processing the alcohol we drink.

15:08 It's resilient, but long-term, heavy drinking  can lead to a buildup of fat in the liver,

15:12 inflammation (hepatitis), and, eventually,  irreversible scarring known as cirrhosis. A

15:18 damaged liver can struggle to function properly,  which has widespread effects on the entire body,

15:23 from swelling known as edema to loss of menstrual  cycle to, possibly and eventually, cancer.

15:29 In fact, alcohol is a known carcinogen,  contributing to the development of several

15:34 types of cancer. The risk is associated with all  kinds of cancers, including those of the mouth,

15:39 throat, esophagus, liver, colon, and  breast. The more you drink and the

15:43 longer the duration of heavy drinking,  the higher your overall risk becomes.

15:48 Then, there’s potential heart disease. Chronic  alcohol consumption weakens the heart muscle and

15:52 disrupts its rhythm, increasing blood  pressure and making it harder to pump

15:57 blood efficiently. Over time, this raises the  risk of heart attack and stroke. Even light

16:01 to moderate drinking has been linked to a  slight increase in cardiovascular risks.

16:05 How about mental health? Alcohol and mental  health have a complex, two-way relationship.

16:11 For some people, drinking can become a way to numb  negative emotions or cope with stress. However,

16:17 chronic alcohol use can actually worsen  existing conditions like anxiety and

16:21 depression, even increasing the risk of  developing new mental health disorders.

16:26 These conditions can all develop insidiously.  Sarah might not immediately feel the impact

16:31 of chronic alcohol use, but if she has  regular occurrences of heavy drinking,

16:35 the damage might be silently accumulating  inside her body. Understanding these

16:39 risks highlights the importance of  responsible alcohol consumption.

16:43 Sometimes, the line between social drinking  and something more problematic can blur.

16:48 For some people, alcohol use can become  difficult to manage, leading to a condition

16:52 called Alcohol Use Disorder, or AUD. It's a  chronic, relapsing medical condition where

16:58 someone can't control their alcohol intake,  even when it causes significant harm.

17:04 Understanding the signs of AUD is  crucial. Let's break down some key

17:07 symptoms. Note that AUD comes in  varying degrees – mild, moderate,

17:11 or severe. These signs might be subtle at first  or only become noticeable during difficult times.

17:17 The first thing to look for is cravings – a strong  desire or compulsion to drink alcohol. Sarah might

17:23 find herself thinking about alcohol frequently,  and those thoughts may become hard to ignore.

17:28 Then, there’s the loss of control.  Having trouble limiting the amount

17:31 of alcohol consumed or the duration of  drinking episodes. For someone with AUD,

17:36 the intention of "just one drink"  might often spiral into several more.

17:40 Additionally, there’s the dependence factor.  This includes things like building a tolerance,

17:45 which means needing more alcohol to feel  the same effect, or experiencing withdrawal

17:50 symptoms like shakiness, nausea,  or insomnia when stopping drinking.

17:54 It's important to understand that AUD is  not a sign of weakness or a moral failing.

17:59 It's a complex disease influenced by a mix of  genetic predispositions, environmental factors,

18:05 and individual psychology. The earlier  someone with AUD seeks professional help,

18:10 the better their chances of successful recovery.

18:12 Now check out “What Happens To Your Body When You

18:15 Stop Drinking Alcohol.” Or  watch this video instead!

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: What Made The Black Death (The Plague) so Deadly?
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: What Made The Black Death (The Plague) so Deadly?
  • Video ID: m5q-PIN3KSE
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 In October of 1347, 12 ships dropped anchor at a Sicilian port.

00:05 Those who eagerly approached were met with a grisly sight.

00:08 Almost all aboard were either dead or barely alive, their skin erupting with blackened

00:14 boils that dripped blood and pus.

00:16 In horror, the Sicilian authorities demanded the ships set sail, but though they left,

00:22 the damage had already been done.

00:23 The Black Death was now in Europe and millions would die in what is considered one of the

00:28 greatest disasters in history.

00:30 Let’s explore how the bubonic plague wiped out at least a third of Europe’s population,

00:35 if not more, in this episode of the Infographics Show, What Made the Black Death so Deadly?

00:41 Europe was hit hard by the plague, but it was not hit first.

00:44 It was also not unaware of a disease that was already bringing widespread death and

00:48 destruction elsewhere.

00:50 Before the infested ships arrived in Sicily rumors of a frightful sickness devastating

00:55 the populations of first China and then India, Egypt, Persia, and Syria had spread near and

01:00 far.

01:01 While no one knew what caused it or why, it seemed to follow trade routes spanning the

01:06 Near and Far East.

01:08 Further, when it appeared, it was by all accounts unstoppable.

01:12 Those struck by the Black Death would begin to swell at the lymph nodes located in their

01:16 groin area or under arm regions.

01:18 The growths would soon develop into large blackish blue egg-sized lumps, or for the

01:23 even less fortunate, expand to the size of apples.

01:26 These would then fester and ooze various bodily fluids.

01:29 Beyond this, those with the disease could develop any combination of a series of additional

01:34 symptoms.

01:35 These included fever, pain, chills, sweating, upset stomach, and diarrhea.

01:40 Almost always, this was followed by death.

01:43 According to those who observed its effects first-hand, all it appeared to take was brief

01:47 physical contact with the clothing of someone who was sick to pass the disease on to another.

01:52 Though, some doctors claimed that it was the spirit leaving the body of the deceased that

01:56 infected others as it passed by.

01:59 Obviously, at this point in history the real methods of disease transmission were not yet

02:03 well understood.

02:04 Without understanding it, most were helpless to defend against it.

02:07 Few areas other than some islands cut off from the rest of Europe by the sea made it

02:12 through the pandemic plague-free.

02:14 The rest of the population was not so lucky.

02:16 The bacterium infiltrated virtually every European city’s defenses and many who appeared

02:21 perfectly healthy one day could be dead a few days later.

02:25 It was uncommon though possible for someone to survive a week or two before he or she

02:30 died.

02:31 Compounding problems further, those with the disease would typically be asymptomatic for

02:35 the first few days and so no one would be aware that they had caught it.

02:38 This meant that successfully isolating them from the rest of society at this point was

02:42 all but impossible.

02:44 Those who tried the next best thing to protect themselves by fleeing for the country were

02:48 not safe there either.

02:49 The plague decimated livestock as well and countless pigs, cows, chickens, goats, and

02:54 sheep who also died a brutal death.

02:57 This was such a problem that it led to a shortage of wool throughout the continent.

03:01 While many European areas had a death figure of around 30%, 90% of the Italian city of

03:07 Florence perished.

03:08 Sometimes, bodies of the deceased remained where they had died as there were not enough

03:12 people still living to bury them.

03:14 Thousands of French villages in addition to areas in other locations were left without

03:18 a single remaining soul.

03:20 The Black Death had mercilessly transformed them into ghost towns.

03:24 In some instances, nature eventually took over, and areas that people once called home

03:29 were re-claimed by surrounding forest.

03:31 It took aerial photography following the end of World War I to rediscover these locations

03:36 as places where men, women, and children once lived.

03:39 Most estimates place Europe’s death total between 50 and 70 million, or around thirty-some

03:44 percent, though the CDC claims it killed as much as 60% of the population, which is considerably

03:50 more.

03:51 World-wide estimates typically range from 155 to 200 million.

03:55 The world at the time was a mere 500 million people, so nearly half of all of its’ inhabitants,

04:01 or again according to some sources even more, were killed.

04:04 So how was it that the Black Death was able to spread so quickly and wipe out so many,

04:09 people and animals alike?

04:11 Well for one, as previously mentioned, there was little in the way of scientific knowledge

04:15 in the 1300s.

04:16 Not only did people not understand the plague’s causes or modes of transmission, but there

04:21 were also countless failures in how those in the medical field attempted to treat it.

04:26 It is true that Yersina pestis, the bacterium behind the Black Death, or bubonic plague,

04:30 is highly contagious.

04:32 It can also be spread in many ways, though obviously contaminated spirits aren’t one

04:37 of them.

04:38 Many believe that in its later stages it had the ability to morph into an airborne strain

04:42 that could be passed on to a new host via a simple sneeze or cough.

04:45 However, all strains, airborne or those in the more initial stages that are not, are

04:50 believed to have been transferred through flea or lice bites.

04:53 And many animals in addition to countryside livestock serve as hosts for the bacterium

04:58 and blood sucking pests.

04:59 Examples are things like squirrels, rabbits, chipmunks, and mice.

05:03 However, many in the scientific field have argued that by far the worst contributor to

05:07 the spread of the Black Death was the urban rat and its flea.

05:11 Part of the reason for this belief is that rats have been observed to develop symptoms

05:15 quite similar to those in people, and in cases of the modern-day plague many people with

05:19 the sickness had accompanying bites from fleas.

05:22 Recent outbreaks often follow what’s known as ‘rat falls’ as well, or when the rodents

05:27 die off in record amounts for whatever reason.

05:29 Thus, the most prevalent theory is that the Black Death all began when rats with the plague

05:34 died and their fleas then looked for more blood in another readily available source,

05:38 which would at times be human.

05:41 Upon being bitten by the contaminated flea this person would then be exposed to the deadly

05:45 bacteria.

05:46 Seemingly in support of this theory, ships during the mid-1300s were commonly infested

05:50 with the furry rodents who thrived in their dark.

05:53 moist environment.

05:54 And following the death ships’ arrival in Sicily the plague continued to spread further

05:58 following a trade route pattern, as it had previously in Asia, to other port locations

06:03 throughout Europe and as far down as North Africa.

06:06 However, more recently there have been some proposed tweaks to this rat-based theory.

06:11 As we just mentioned, the Black Death, after all, is not the only outbreak of the plague

06:15 in the world’s history.

06:16 There have been outbreaks before as well as after, and those that took place more recently

06:21 followed a different pattern entirely.

06:23 Europe’s black death spread much faster, and as far as historical records are concerned

06:27 there was no mention of a mass rat die-off in the days or months preceding it.

06:32 Now, some scientists suggest that it was human fleas and lice that were the true culprits

06:37 behind Europe’s version of the disease.

06:39 In this case fleas would bite infected people and then move on to others, one by one, who

06:43 happened to be in the nearby vicinity.

06:45 They describe the underlying mathematical model that a rat-flea spread follows is quite

06:49 different from a human-flea or lice one.

06:52 And, when information was plugged into simulations the human-flea model more closely matched

06:56 data from seven of nine plague-hit European cities.

07:00 Those with this newest evidence admit that the causes of the plague are surrounded by

07:04 ongoing controversy.

07:05 However, whether the fleas were of the human or rat variety, it is blood sucking pests

07:10 of one kind or another that likely passed it on successfully and so very quickly.

07:15 It also turns out that the Black Death may not have been causing mass devastation all

07:20 by itself.

07:21 When victims bodies were exhumed from mass graves in England anthrax spores were also

07:25 discovered along with them.

07:26 If anthrax was occurring at the same time as the plague this would definitely have made

07:31 things much worse.

07:33 Anthrax cannot only be passed by coming into contact with sweat, saliva, or tears but also

07:38 by mere skin contact.

07:40 In other words, at the time of the Black Death pandemic, people could have come down with

07:44 a life-threatening disease of one kind or another in pretty much every conceivable way.

07:49 It is possible anthrax and other diseases made people extra susceptible to the plague

07:53 due to already compromised immunity.

07:55 Also, it is possible that the body count of those claimed by the Black Death included

08:00 victims that actually died from anthrax or other diseases.

08:03 Beyond its quick transfer from host to host and the contributions of additional disease,

08:09 the way the Black Death was treated failed to help and may have actually helped kill

08:13 victims or spread it further unintentionally.

08:16 For example, at least initially, medical practitioners would do such things as perform bloodletting

08:20 on patients with the plague.

08:22 This is where they cut into veins or arteries in the necks or arms of those who were sick,

08:27 so that their blood flowed freely.

08:29 This procedure was nothing new and, in fact, dated back as far as to the times of ancient

08:34 Egypt and Greece.

08:35 Historical figures believed that to be healthy the body needed the right balance of blood,

08:39 phlegm, and bile.

08:41 Bloodletting was believed to correct a possible imbalance of too much blood which is what

08:45 caused the person to get sick.

08:48 Unfortunately, the procedure appeared to be as ineffective for the victims of the plague

08:51 as it was for Charles II or George Washington centuries later.

08:55 While Washington awoke with a sore throat and King Charles suffered a seizure, following

09:00 bloodletting treatment both died shortly thereafter.

09:03 Boil-lancing was another technique used as a form of treatment which was just how it

09:08 sounds.

09:09 Someone would essentially lance, or stick a pointy object, into the boils to drain them

09:13 of their gooey contents.

09:14 If this wasn’t done, they would only continue to grow larger and, in time.

09:18 poison their host due to the mass build-up of dead blood and pus.

09:22 Then again, popping them could also cause death due to toxic shock.

09:26 Beyond the patient likely dying, the boils contained highly contagious matter and possibly

09:30 spread the disease yet further.

09:32 Other methods such as the burning of various herbs or immersing the sick in vinegar or

09:36 rosewater were also, unsurprisingly, ineffective.

09:39 In time, after failure upon failure and in an attempt at self-preservation, many doctors

09:45 simply stopped accepting patients.

09:47 Even priests began refusing to perform last rites out of danger for their own safety.

09:52 Where man failed nature did little to help either.

09:55 Not only did people have little idea of how to handle the plague, but they were genetically

09:59 prone to succumbing to it.

10:01 Studies of the remains of the European population at the time determined that only 0.2% had

10:07 a gene that offered them any form of immunity.

10:10 The other 99.8% had none.

10:12 Since so many of those who were susceptible to the plague died from it, they did not pass

10:16 their genes on further to the following generations.

10:19 Many of those who did have the gene lived on to procreate.

10:22 This is why Caucasian Americans now have a 15% chance of having some resistance to the

10:27 disease.

10:28 This is pretty good news considering the modern form of the plague is still around today.

10:33 One encounter via the 12 so-called death ships would go on to wipe out men, women, and children

10:39 to such an extent that it would change the tide of history.

10:42 What do you think, was it passed on by human or rat fleas?

10:46 Let us know in the comments!

10:47 Also, be sure to check out our other video called Could the Black Death (The Plague)

10:51 Happen Again?!

10:52 Thanks for watching, and, as always, don’t forget to like, share, and

10:56 subscribe.

10:57 See you next time!

docs.text:
00:00 This is eve online, a massive  multiplayer online spaceship

00:03 game which is probably best know for two things.

00:07 Making headlines about it’s massive in game  conflicts involving tens of thousands of players

00:12 and it’s incredibly realistic in game financial  system which can make loosing a virtual spaceship

00:16 just as consequential as loosing a  phone or a car in the real world.

00:21 Countless magazines, and even much more successful  YouTube channels have talked about these two

00:25 factors individually, but where I think they get  really interesting is when they merge together.

00:31 For a game about spaceships set 21,000 years in  the future, EVE is surprisingly realistic, and

00:38 that realism extends to these massive  wars in the sense that they are expensive.

00:43 The in game currency called ISK has an approximate  exchange rate of about $6 per billion in game isk.

00:49 Although it must be mentioned that trading this  in game currency directly back or forth for real

00:53 life money is actually against the rules of the  game for now at least and will get you banned.

00:59 Even still, this shows that in game assets have a  very tangible real world value on the grey market,

01:05 so when you see headlines about trillions  of ISK been lost in these epic battles

01:10 it gives you an idea of just how expensive  it can be to wage entire wars in EVE Online.

01:15 But this all begs a bigger question…

01:17 Who or what funds these wars?

01:20 With a price tag of hundreds of thousands of  real world dollars and nothing but virtual

01:23 space pride in return, it doesn’t  sound like a very good deal… Right?

01:28 Well, it’s time to learn how space  money works, if you enjoy this video

01:32 please consider liking and subscribing for  new video’s like this one made every week.

01:37 Ok so there are three really interesting  and unique ways these major wars have been

01:41 funded over the past 2 decades that this game has  existed. But let’s start with the most basic one.

01:46 The game is home to a selection of  megacorporations that are run entirely

01:50 by players, similar in many ways to… guilds in  world of warcraft, only on a much larger scale.

01:56 Now the largest of these corporations effectively  run like nation states, they have defined borders,

02:01 a standing military, taxation, industry  and of course command structures.

02:07 These large institutions will inevitably but  heads with other similar entities over resources,

02:12 territory, or you know just for fun. At  the end of the day it is a video game

02:16 so the reasons to go to war can simply be to  entertain the members of these corporations.

02:21 Now what will normally happen is that the  individual participants in these wars will need

02:25 to provide their own combat ships, funded out  of the money they make in game themselves.

02:30 But if these ships are lost in battle the  mega corporations will pay to replace them.

02:34 They do this because ultimately they  will need manpower to win these wars.

02:38 Ensuring that people aren’t too afraid  of losing their ships will mean that

02:41 their players will keep on logging in and  yoloing into these devastating space battles.

02:46 Now these Ship Replacement Programs, or  SRP will most often be funded by the taxes

02:50 collected from these corporations  during times of relative peace.

02:54 The industrialist get given a safe and secure  piece of territory to conduct their business

02:58 and in turn they need to pay a portion of  their profits to a central authority which

03:03 will then fund a military program to maintain or  potentially even expand this protected territory.

03:09 Effectively it’s exactly the same as what happens  with every government ever in the real world.

03:14 Now this is fine in theory, but often times  these industrial entities don’t have the

03:19 capacity to wage war themselves. In these  circumstances they can call on mercenary

03:24 entities that do nothing but wage war  on other people’s behalf for a fee.

03:29 Again not overly dissimilar to what  happens from time to time in the real

03:32 world with military contract corporations like  academi performing a very similar function.

03:37 Now so far we have been looking at relatively  minor wars, the ones that might be a big deal

03:42 to the players of the game and s___posters  on R/EVE (Pronounced AR Slash EVE) but are

03:46 not exactly that remarkable to an  uninvolved onlooker like you or I.

03:50 But this all changed around 5 years ago.

03:53 You see EVE’s economy is so realistic and

03:56 so diverse that at one point there  were virtual casino’s in the game…

04:00 these were founded, funded and operated entirely  by regular players using the in game currency.

04:06 Of course, these casino’s generated massive  profits just like most of them do in the real

04:11 world. Now these in game profits were great  and all but there wasn’t much that they could

04:16 do with them on an individual level. That  kind of money could buy every spaceship

04:20 in the game many times over so they needed  something grander to put their money towards.

04:24 The logical answer was to sell the  in game money for real world money

04:28 whether it was allowed or not. Sure they  risked getting banned from a video game

04:33 but the collective total of ISK that these  casino’s generated was worth millions of dollars,

04:38 so that was a risk a lot of these  casino owners were willing to take.

04:44 This was especially convenient given  that the thousands of transactions the

04:47 casino’s handled daily were the perfect  cover from in game money laundering.

04:52 It was almost impossible to distinguish  between transactions that were legitimate

04:56 and those that weren’t. Again very  similar to casino’s in the real world

05:00 which are continually in the news for  being centre’s for money laundering.

05:03 However the more “honourable” casino owners,  decided to use their space dollars to buy

05:09 something not available on  the public market… Influence.

05:13 2016 kicked off the so called  Casino Wars, as the “I Want ISK”

05:17 Online Casino funded a coalition of player  corporations to wage war on the single most

05:21 powerful player corporation in the game which had  wronged the casino in a previous business deal.

05:27 In reality all of these other player  run organisations were looking for

05:31 any excuse to go to war in an attempt to bring  the “imperium” as it is known in check. They

05:37 simply lacked the financial backing to  undertake such a significant challenge.

05:41 But with the casino’s writing the cheques (as a  way to prove a point as to what happens when you

05:45 dishonour a business deal) one of the most  devastating wars in the game’s history was

05:49 enabled which in turn gave us the PC gamer  articles about spectacular space battles.

05:54 And yes, the finances behind it might  be a little bit less spectacular,

05:58 but that does not mean they  are any less interesting.

06:02 Now shortly following this war the developers

06:04 of EVE online decided to put an  end to these player run Casino’s.

06:07 Now they said they had their own reasons but  most players speculate it was a combination

06:12 of wanting to cut down on the trade of  in game money for real money, and also

06:16 as a response to player backlash over these  entities having too much power over the game.

06:21 What this meant was that in 2020 there  was a new funding model required.

06:26 The old belligerents from the casino  war were ready to go at it again,

06:30 only this time a few things were different.

06:33 For starters the casino’s were no more,  which meant that no side would have

06:37 limitless funding given to them. What’s more  is that 2020 was a year of working from home

06:42 with no options for entertainment besides sitting  in front of a computer playing video games.

06:47 This was all shaping up to create potentially  the largest conflict in the game’s history,

06:51 a conflict that would also be the most costly.

06:54 The most crucial battles during  this conflict were inevitably going

06:57 to be decided by who could bring more of the  largest ships in the game to bear, the titans.

07:02 These ships are extremely powerful, and were  at least up until recently extremely rare,

07:08 but changes in the game in recent years  had meant that the industrial powerhouses

07:12 could produce these once legendary  ship’s as if they were ford model t’s.

07:16 This didn’t mean they were  any less expensive however,

07:19 it just meant the powers that be had to bring  more of them to keep up with their opposition.

07:23 The side that had previously been funded  by the casino’s were happy to just fund

07:27 this war in the traditional way, using  the tax money they had collected over

07:30 the years of peace and prosperity  to foot the bill for these battles.

07:33 But the imperium had a better idea, they had  seen how finance had decided their fate in 2016,

07:40 and were keen to ensure they were  economically dominant going into

07:43 the war of 2020. So they once again  looked to reality for inspiration.

07:49 War bonds are often issued by governments  during periods of all out conflict.

07:53 This is because modern wars are  expensive, and raising taxes

07:57 is often impossible if the entire economy  has been dedicated towards the war effort.

08:02 So government bonds are issued so that people  can invest in their own nation’s victory.

08:08 The imperium did exactly this,  they sold off a series of bonds,

08:12 that would pay interest to their own members.

08:14 This was obviously great for the  imperium itself because it got the

08:18 much needed injection of capital it  needed to go off and fight the war,

08:21 but it was also great for the  members of the group as well.

08:24 Scams, and financial fraud are commonplace in eve

08:27 and there is no regulation around taking  someone’s stuff and never giving it back.

08:32 In fact these types of swindles are probably  the thing that eve is third best known for.

08:36 But while having a totally  unregulated financial system is

08:39 great for cool stories it’s  terrible for investing,

08:42 because well anything you invest can and likely  will just be stolen off you, so why bother.

08:48 These war bonds presented an  opportunity for players to

08:50 invest in an asset that didn’t have  quiet the same risk of being stolen.

08:55 For clarity, the imperium would be fully  within their right’s to turn around and

08:59 tell these investors to get stuffed, but the  hit to their entities reputation would likely

09:04 not be worth it, especially if they ever wanted  to sell war bonds again to fund future wars.

09:10 Now that doesn’t mean that these in game financial  instruments are totally without risk, if the

09:15 imperium get’s destroyed in this ongoing war,  well then, these bonds aren’t going to get paid.

09:20 In the real world analysts  call this sovereign risk,

09:24 and it’s no less important here as it  is in the land of internet spaceships.

09:28 But for now at least this war is still ongoing  and is likely to provide gaming magazines and

09:33 aspiring youtube channels alike many more  things to talk about, like the fact that

09:38 this games financial market predicted the short  squeeze on Gamestop, so make sure to like and

09:42 subscribe if you want to see us make a video on  that, and in the meantime go and watch our video

09:47 to find out if the world bank is really an evil  empire. Thanks for learning, How Money Works.
