00:00 Welcome to this video on anarchist philosophy. Today we explore the key concepts that define anarchist thought.

00:15 Anarchism is not chaos, but rather a philosophy that seeks to eliminate hierarchical authority and promote voluntary cooperation.

00:30 The core principles include mutual aid, direct action, and solidarity among individuals and communities.

00:45 We believe that people can organize themselves without the need for centralized control or coercion.

01:00 This approach has been applied in various contexts, from community organizing to alternative economic systems.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Why You Wouldn't Survive 1 Day in CECOT... World's Largest Mega Prison in El Salvador
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: Why You Wouldn't Survive 1 Day in CECOT... World's Largest Mega Prison in El Salvador
  • Video ID: mNlKWWgmpus
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 It’s 2023, you’re a hardened member of Mara  Salvatrucha - better known as the infamous

00:06 MS-13 - and the government of El Salvador has  just sentenced you to a fate worse than death.

00:12 You’re forced like cattle into the back  of a heavily armored vehicle; tight-packed

00:16 flesh covered in gang tattoos holds you in place.  There’s barely space in this scorching vehicle for

00:21 you and the others to breathe. The guards stripped  you and gave you an uncomfortable cavity search,

00:27 leaving you violated and humiliated in  nothing but a pair of white shorts. An

00:31 unsympathetic police barber shaved you bald,  row by row of hair, just like all the others.

00:37 If you raise your head in transit,

00:39 a guard barks at you in Spanish to  get your head down, you worthless dog!

00:43 He wields his nightstick. You get the  impression that there’s nothing he’d

00:46 like more than cracking open the back of your  skull, flecking the naked skin of your fellow

00:51 prisoners with your blood. Just to send a  single message: Where you’re going, you’re

00:56 not considered human anymore. You’re an animal,  and when animals misbehave, they get put down.

01:01 You bow your head again. A wise choice - There’ll  be plenty of beatings later, so why start early?

01:07 But before you disappear back into the  sea of anonymous prisoners, you see it:

01:11 A glowing fortress, wreathed in barbed wire  and illuminated by piercing floodlights. It

01:16 makes Alcatraz look like Disneyland. It makes  Rikers look like a resort in Cancun. Hell,

01:21 after a few years here, Guantanamo  Bay would look like a health retreat.

01:25 This is the Centro de Confinamiento del  Terrorismo, or the Terrorism Confinement

01:30 Center. We’ll call it CECOT. You won’t find  another prison like this anywhere in the world.

01:35 But you’re not being sent here alone. There  are trails of buses in front of and behind you,

01:41 like some almost endless centipede of human  misery. You’re just one tiny percentage

01:45 point in a statistic - A tidal wave of 2000  prisoners, all being transferred at once,

01:51 as part of El Salvador’s sweeping efforts to  bring the country’s gang activity to its knees.

01:56 At its worst in 2011, El Salvador was  considered the murder capital of the

02:00 world. Peaking at 71 murders per hundred thousand.  In 2015, that number had risen to over 100 deaths

02:06 per hundred thousand. One day even saw 62  people murdered in 24 hours. Gang violence

02:12 had completely overtaken the Central American  country. Year after year, brutal gang warfare

02:17 saw the army roaming the streets just to keep  the country from falling into total collapse.

02:22 The government needed to take drastic measures.

02:24 You’re about to enter one  of those drastic measures.

02:27 Opened in 2022, very few people have  had the chance to see inside CECOT,

02:31 aside from the flood of prisoners being sent  there - including you. The media are not

02:35 allowed in. Lawyers are not allowed in. Human  rights groups are not allowed in. It’s closed

02:41 down almost entirely to the outside world. All  that civilians know about the facility has been

02:46 gleaned from satellite imagery, footage that the  El Salvador government has filmed and released.

02:51 The buses grind to a halt in a large grid outside  the prison. Some deep animal part of you feels

02:57 like you’re outside a slaughterhouse, and your  skin begins prickling with panic. You were a

03:02 bad dude on the outside - a robber, a killer, an  unquestioning enforcer of one of El Salvador’s

03:08 most feared gangs. Here, you’re a frightened  little child again, wishing for your mommy.

03:14 But you don’t get your mommy. You get manhandled  out of the bus by a huge man in riot gear,

03:19 clapping you in long cuffs that bind your  hands behind your back and connect to your

03:23 legs. The same thing is happening to hundreds,  then thousands, of other men around you. You

03:28 feel a nightstick press against the back of  your neck and instinctively bend over before

03:33 they can even start applying pressure.  Good boy. That’ll serve you well here.

03:37 The guards bark orders and corral you inside  like sheep. Of course, you obey. You and all

03:42 the others are practically naked, and even if  you managed to overpower one of the riot squad

03:47 guards specifically trained to beat you into  a fine puree, an expert sniper in one of the

03:52 nearby guard towers would put a round through  your head before you even had time to fart.

03:57 Right now, there are estimated to be  around 16,000 men in CECOT. That would

04:01 max out most prisons around the world.  The second largest prison in the world,

04:05 Silivri Penitentiaries Campus in  Turkey, manages to host a population

04:09 of around 22,000 inmates. CECOT is built  to double that, with a capacity of 40,000.

04:16 Even getting to the prison is a challenge.  President Nayib Bukele wanted to build it

04:20 far away from civilization. There are  no towns or cities nearby. No public

04:25 buildings or schools. The prison itself has  its own water supply and electric generators,

04:30 meaning it has even less need to connect  with anyone or anything external. That’s

04:35 why you spent so many hours roasting with your  fellow convicts in the back of that prison bus.

04:40 As you’re dragged into the main hall and  forced to boy down in lines for inspection,

04:45 you find yourself wondering how  one prison complex could hold so

04:48 many people. And the answer to that  is simple: It’s unimaginably huge.

04:54 There are eight prison blocks covering around 57  acres total but the plot of land for the prison

04:59 is an enormous 410 acres total. There are 19  guard towers perched high above the complex,

05:05 surveying everything. There are four layers  of walls surrounding the prison blocks,

05:10 each one is nearly ten feet tall and two feet  thick, with coils of barbed wire draped over

05:15 the top. And of course, you can’t forget  about the 15,000-volt electric fence too.

05:21 Surveillance cameras are in operation  24/7 and cover practically every square

05:25 inch of the facility. Nothing happens  off-camera. Should a riot break out,

05:29 they have a fully stocked armory with racks  and racks of firearms as well as heavy riot

05:34 gear for their guards. Even the US army  would have a hard time storming CECOT.

05:39 And you’re just a common thug  for hire. You’ve got no hope,

05:42 buddy. So, what have you got to  look forward to now you’re here?

05:45 When you first arrive, prisoner or not, you’re  subject to an intense screening process. Even

05:50 if you’re not an inmate, the guards at  CECOT have large X-ray machines that scan

05:54 you from head to toe to look for contraband.  You’ll also be asked to disclose any tattoos,

05:59 and if you don’t, they have the right to strip  you to check for themselves. The gangs in El

06:03 Salvador have a culture of tattooing their  members to cement their allegiance for life.

06:07 If you’ve got gang ties, you’re not getting  in unless it’s in handcuffs and white shorts.

06:12 Once you’ve been scanned,  searched again, beaten down,

06:15 and noted in the prison inventory, it’s time  for your first night at CECOT to begin. Part

06:19 of you just feels relieved that you’ll  finally be able to sleep after what’s

06:23 felt like the longest day of your life - But  we’ve got some bad news for you there, too.

06:27 The guards organize you into groups by cell  block and chase you, your hands on your head,

06:32 your back bowed over. If you lag behind,  you might take a nightstick to the spine

06:36 or the ankle, or feel the electric  burn of a stun gun on your bare skin.

06:41 They run you like the bulls of Pamplona  until you reach your cell, at which point,

06:45 a swift kick to the ass sends you tumbling in,  the reinforced metal door slamming behind you

06:50 once all of the others assigned to  this cell have been trapped there,

06:53 too. This is when you start to notice a number  of horrifying things about your new home.

06:59 For starters, the lights are always on. They  don’t switch them off at night, they don’t even

07:03 dim them, they are on 24/7 at full blast. Bright  harsh artificial light floods every communal cell.

07:10 There are 80 beds to a cell. We say beds, they  have no mattresses or bedding on them. Instead,

07:15 they’re harsh bunk bed frames, stacked four  high, with nothing to lie on but flat metal.

07:21 In the corners of the cells, right by the bars,  are two toilets. Next to them are two wash basins,

07:26 but the flow of water in these  is controlled by a guard outside

07:29 the cell. So that’s 80 prisoners in a cell  sharing just two toilets. Except it isn’t.

07:35 It seems that El Salvador is actually  cramming more than 80 in each cell.

07:39 We hope you don’t mind having plenty of roommates.

07:41 When a BBC reporter asked the director of the  prison exactly what the capacity of CECOT was,

07:46 the man smiled and said “Where you  can fit 10 people, you can fit 20.”

07:50 Can you imagine a worse night’s  sleep? Being in a brightly lit cell,

07:54 with over 100 other people, all the most  hardened gangsters in Central America,

07:59 lying on a metal sheet, with two shared toilets  stinking out the cell. Human rights groups have

08:05 estimated that prisoners in CECOT have just  0.6 square meters of personal space each.

08:11 That number falls far below the 4 square  meters mandated in the European Union.

08:16 There are solitary confinement cells too,  and to many, they might be preferable,

08:21 but they’ve got their trade-offs  too. Instead of a metal bed frame,

08:24 you have a slab of concrete to lie on. You get  one toilet. One wash basin. And while the communal

08:29 cells are always bathed in artificial light, you  have the opposite problem. No light at all, either

08:35 artificial or natural, meaning you just have to  sit in darkness all day stewing in your thoughts.

08:41 And at CECOT, one thing is for sure:  You’re not having pleasant thoughts.

08:45 Before we tell you about the horrors that  await you when you wake up in the morning,

08:49 we’ve got an important question to  answer: Why does El Salvador need

08:53 such a massive prison? Who are the men  arriving here and when will they leave?

08:58 We mentioned earlier a particular day in  El Salvador when 62 people were killed.

09:03 This was the 26th of March 2022. It was the  bloodiest day in the country’s history and

09:08 the final straw for the Salvadoran people.  President Bukele announced a radical new

09:12 approach to combating gang warfare.  Have been nominated largely for his

09:16 tough stance on gangs back in 2019, it was time  for him to put his money where his mouth was.

09:22 His plan was a sweeping raft of changes  that removed almost all of the barriers

09:26 preventing the police from arresting gang  members. Known as the régimen de excepción,

09:31 it was a national state of emergency.

09:33 The changes affected almost every stage  of the legal system. Criminals no longer

09:37 had access to legal counsel and  they could be held five times

09:41 longer without charge. Options like  bail and house arrest were removed,

09:46 and police could now monitor civilian  communications without the need for a warrant.

09:50 Sentences were also massively increased.  Previously, a convicted gang lord would

09:55 get 6-9 years in prison. That shot up to 40-45.

09:59 Lower gang members saw their potential sentences  rise from 3-5 years up to 20-30. Even if you

10:05 were caught sharing gang-related information  you could end up behind bars for 15 years.

10:11 One of the ways that gangs all around the  world have avoided long prison sentences

10:15 has been by using children and teenagers for  the risky leg work. A young teenager can be

10:20 easily manipulated. What’s more, they  will get a lenient sentence and be out

10:24 sooner so they’re an expendable workforce  for the gang leaders to use as shields.

10:28 Not anymore. El Salvador lowered the age of  criminal responsibility from 16 to 12. That’s

10:35 right, actual 12-year-olds could get locked  up for decades for their roles in gangs.

10:40 Soldiers and heavily armed police swarmed the  streets, looking for any trace of evidence that

10:45 somebody was gang-affiliated. They would  raid houses indiscriminately and set up

10:50 security checkpoints on almost every major  road. Anyone passing through the checkpoint

10:54 would not only need to provide a photo ID  and proof of address but also demonstrate a

10:59 valid reason for travel. Their cars would be  searched from top to bottom. If the people

11:03 manning the checkpoints even suspected  the person could have ties to gangs,

11:07 they would ask the person to strip them and  then search their body for any gang tattoos.

11:12 This policy was massively supported up  and down the country. 78% of Salvadorans

11:18 ‘strongly support’ the crackdown. A staggering  91% of them are in favor. That’s just 9% of the

11:25 country that is neutral or anti-crackdown. The  measures were only supposed to last for 30 days,

11:30 but here we are well over two years later  and they’re still in place. That’s because

11:35 consistently every month parties across the  government of El Salvador vote to extend them.

11:40 So far, over 79,000 people have been arrested  for gang affiliation. In a country of just

11:46 6.5 million people, that’s over 1% of  their population being detained in just

11:51 two years. It’s a monumental shift and one  that has brought its own set of challenges.

11:56 The Salvadoran prison system was not  designed to house this many criminals,

12:00 nowhere close. Prisons all around the country  quickly filled to capacity. When the question

12:05 of funding came up Nayib Bukele drew a hard line  that only won him more favor. He would not take

12:11 funding away from schools, hospitals, or good  public services to feed these prisoners. Instead,

12:17 their meals went down from three to two per  day, consisting of just beans and tortillas.

12:22 But a longer-term solution was needed,  one that Bukele was already prepared for.

12:26 CECOT. A brand new 40,000-capacity prison  miles away from civilization. A proverbial

12:32 hole in the ground where they could throw  the country’s gangs and let them fester.

12:37 You know, the same hole in the ground  where you’re currently festering.

12:40 Let’s head back there and see how  your evening is going, shall we?

12:43 You don’t know what time you wake up. The  harsh lights overhead didn’t let you sleep

12:47 in the first place. The constant talking,  shouting, and fighting through the night

12:51 kept you from drifting off for more than  a few minutes at a time. At one point,

12:55 one of the tougher guys shoved you out of  the bed he wanted and you fell 8 feet onto

13:00 the concrete floor. It’s down here you  decided to spend the rest of the night,

13:04 rather than risk getting shivved for  something only marginally more comfortable.

13:08 You’re desperate to go to the bathroom, but  there’s not much you can do. One toilet in

13:12 your cell has been blocked for two  weeks now, the other got blocked

13:16 over the weekend. They’ll probably call in a  plumber… Sometime over the next year or two.

13:20 A guy shoves you in the back and you crack  your head against a bunk frame. It’s an

13:24 early lunch today. Plastic trays loaded  with cost-saving beans and tortillas,

13:29 with sickly boiled eggs on the side,  are passed through the bars one by one.

13:33 You join near the back of the line and  have to eat your cold food on the floor.

13:37 They never give out cutlery, the forks  and knives could be used as weapons,

13:41 so you have no choice but to eat with your hands  like some depressed chimp at the local zoo. A lot

13:43 of the guys in the cells have pretty poor hand  hygiene, especially with the toilet situation,

13:48 so stomach viruses are common - Which has, in  turn, made the toilet situation even worse.

13:53 You’ve avoided getting sick so far  but it’s only a matter of time.

13:57 Before you’ve even had a  chance to eat your nasty egg,

14:00 everyone is up and moving again. It’s  time for your 30 minutes. Lucky you.

14:05 Every day, you get to spend half an hour  outside. It’s easily the best part of the day,

14:09 as long as the handcuffs aren’t  done up too tight. As expected,

14:12 the guard takes a dislike to you and  pinches the shackles extra tight today;

14:17 you feel it chafe the skin of your  wrists with every movement you take.

14:20 You and your 100 cell mates shuffle meekly out  into the sweltering sun for your ‘exercise’. Some

14:26 guys try to do push-ups, some half run around  as best they can with their ankles chained,

14:31 and most just sit against the  fence breathing in the fresh air.

14:35 It’s over before you know it.

14:37 Bundled back inside by guards, the  excitement of your day is over before

14:41 it’s even 11 AM. Not that you know that.  Time’s long gone. Every day blends into

14:46 the next and the next. And most of them  are spent how you are spending your time

14:50 now. Sitting around on either a hard  bunk or hard concrete, doing nothing.

14:55 Every five days, you get your head shaved. The  four days in between usually have nothing to do,

15:00 the boredom slowly turning your brain as  soft and cold as those revolting eggs.

15:05 The fights are the only interesting part  of the day. The guards usually just let

15:08 the prisoners settle their own differences,  not worth wading into a cell with 100 angry

15:12 prisoners just to stop one criminal from getting  his face smashed in. Worst comes to worst,

15:17 they’ll flood the cell with tear gas  and send the riot squad in to drag

15:21 out the corpse. Everything else was  considered a waste of prison resources.

15:24 You think about your family. You never got to  say goodbye to any of them, it all happened

15:29 so quickly. One minute you were sitting on  your couch, the next the military police

15:32 were kicking down your door and hauling you  away. Does your mother know where her son is?

15:37 Does your daughter understand that her dad  loves her? Will she think you just abandoned

15:41 her? Will your younger brother see sense  and choose a different life? Or is he in

15:45 the next cell block over from you right  now going through the exact same thing?

15:49 While CECOT is immensely popular in El Salvador  and has indisputably helped the country get on

15:55 top of gang violence, you cannot ignore the  glaring human rights violations. So far,

16:00 not one person who has been sent to CECOT has been  released. Inmates arriving here face the very real

16:05 possibility that they will live out the rest of  their days stuck here without ever even getting

16:10 a hypothetical release date to hope for. Human  rights campaigners have accused it of being

16:14 the death penalty on a mass scale, minus the  injections, nooses, or lethal electric shocks.

16:20 With so many thousands of prisoners being  apprehended without access to proper legal

16:25 counsel, there inevitably will be a significant  proportion of innocent men behind bars. That

16:30 happens even in the best justice systems in the  world, but in one where the convicts’ rights have

16:35 been eroded to the point of almost non-existence,  it’s likely happening alarmingly often.

16:40 The lack of access to the prison is also  a massive red flag. Journalists, lawyers,

16:45 and NGOs are all either denied access or  taken around in very focused controlled

16:50 circumstances where the guards do their  best to show off the prison to the world.

16:54 The prisoners themselves have no  access to the outside world. They

16:57 are not allowed to make phone calls  or send letters like in other prisons

17:01 across the globe. They live totally  cut off from the rest of humanity.

17:05 There is a reason for this. In  countries overrun with gang warfare,

17:09 prisons can end up being pretty ineffective.  Gang leaders locked away can often still call

17:13 the shots from behind bars thanks to burner  phones that get smuggled in by visitors,

17:18 new inmates, or corrupt guards. The black market  in prison can become a hotbed of crime as drugs,

17:24 weapons, and other contraband are exchanged  freely amongst inmates. To a large extent,

17:29 gangs can continue to operate in  and through the prison system.

17:33 Not in CECOT. As extreme as the  measures are, they have snuffed

17:36 out communication among gang leaders. Lock  them away and they are dead to the world,

17:41 leaving a power vacuum in their wake. Inside  the prisons without a thriving black market,

17:46 they can’t disrupt and control things in the  way they once did. They’ve lost their power.

17:51 Some of that comes down to the way guards  are treated too. Bukele himself admits that

17:55 El Salvador had made mistakes in how they  treated their guards previously. Prisons

18:00 run by gangs saw many inmates living in  more luxury than the guards themselves,

18:04 as they’d enjoy a free flow of  drugs, prostitutes, and alcohol,

18:08 while the guards were working long shifts  in terrible conditions. Bribery was rampant.

18:13 But now, Bukele has made sure to treat  the guards much better. CECOT has great

18:18 recreational facilities for its staff.  They have gyms, lounges, and much better

18:22 working conditions. There are 1,000 guards, 600  soldiers, and 250 police officers working on

18:29 site. That works out at 40 inmates per guard,  a high ratio, but when you consider how many of

18:34 those inmates are packed into just one cell, you  can see how much more power the guards now have.

18:40 They monitor everything, they control  everything. The inmates have no power anymore.

18:46 Now check out “50 Things Nobody Tells You  About Being in Prison.” Or watch this instead!

00:00 Over the last year, the car market has kind of  been going through something. Toyota, Volkswagen,

00:06 GM, Ford, Nissan, Volvo, and almost every other  bigname car manufacturer has seen widespread

00:11 disruptions alongside massive profit drops.  And they were the lucky ones. Honda recently

00:17 posted its first annual loss in just under 70  years of operations. And not to be outdone,

00:22 Stalantis recorded the largest loss from an  automaker outside of a major global recession.

00:27 Embodying his company values, the Stalantis CEO  broke down a turnaround planned that involved

00:32 going allin on V8, which was announced exactly  two days before the start of the war in Iran. Now,

00:39 I know you guys don't want to hear me say tariff  disruption, consumer debt, and the K-shaped

00:44 economy for another 15 minutes this week. And  the well uh good news is that there is a little

00:49 bit more going on here. Even at the top end of  the market, Porsche saw its profits drop by 99%,

00:55 encouraging them to sell off the ultra premium  Bugatti brand Land Rover and the artist formerly

01:00 known as Jaguar also saw profit fall by 99%.  And even the king of the K, Ferrari themselves,

01:06 have seen their shares decline by around 30% since  the last time we covered the car market on this

01:11 channel just 6 months ago. Of course, this stock  trend was not helped by the Ferrari Magic Mouse,

01:17 but that's actually worth addressing later on.  For now, I know you might all be getting some

01:21 sort of schadenfreude, seeing these companies  start to struggle after taking advantage of

01:25 accommodating economic conditions to screw  consumers for the past 5 years. But like always,

01:30 it's important to understand what is actually  happening behind the scenes in these companies

01:34 to see how it is going to impact you. An auto  company with facilities here in Indiana tonight

01:40 is reporting losses of $2.7 billion. Profits  at German car maker Porsche plunged by nearly

01:47 96% in the first nine months of this year.  US auto giant Ford says it's taking a $19.5

01:54 billion right down as it kills off several all  electric models. BYD says it sold 2.3 million

02:00 battery powered cars globally in 2025. Car  payments are becoming harder to afford for

02:06 many families as rising costs for essential  items continue to strain household budgets.

02:11 There is a reason why I spend so much time on this  channel talking about cars, despite personally

02:16 driving a 15-year-old CRV, and that's because for  the past 100 years, the car market, alongside the

02:21 construction industry, has been the canary in the  coal mine for the wider economy. A healthy car

02:26 market normally employs a lot of people in good  paying union jobs. It helps a country maintain

02:31 its industrial base. And on the opposite side of  the same coin, if people are buying lots of cars,

02:36 it's a clear indication that they can at the very  least qualify for a loan to make seven years of

02:40 irresponsible monthly repayments. Car makers can  help to both build a healthy economy and indicate

02:46 its health at the same time. But they can also do  the opposite. So to put everything into context,

02:52 car sales in 2025 were actually at their highest  level since the pandemic here in America.

02:57 Worldwide, the number of new cars sold fully  recovered and actually exceeded pre-pandemic level

03:02 sales, which should be cause for celebration,  right? What's more is that because the average

03:08 new car has become so much more expensive,  even after adjusting for inflation, the amount

03:12 of actual revenue car companies are making has  never been higher, even though unit volumes are

03:17 still down from their all-time peak. But then  the question is why are all of these companies

03:22 doing so badly at the same time that the market  itself is theoretically doing better than ever?

03:28 Growing sales naturally shouldn't go handinhand  with collapsing profit, right? Or perhaps an even

03:33 better question is if this is what is happening  to these companies during a good sales year,

03:39 what's going to happen to them when sales  actually slow down again like what is kind

03:43 of already happening right now? Well, there are  really four big problems beyond the immediately

03:47 obvious that are hurting car makers today. And the  first is what I like to call the great flip-flop.

03:53 A name that I really hope catches on. If you go  back through almost every one of those headlines

03:57 talking about massive profit haircuts, you'll  find the car makers themselves all citing the

04:02 same thing, electric vehicles. Now, there are two  very big reasons why they are trying so hard to

04:07 point this out, and we will get to that soon. But  beyond some accounting trickery, this is still an

04:12 industry-wide problem. Honda's first loss since  1957 came with the company pointing straight at

04:18 the billions it had poured into getting ready  to build electric cars it now isn't going to

04:22 sell. Stalantis turned a $5.5 billion profit  into a $26 billion loss. And around 25 billion

04:28 of that was write downs as it quietly backed out  of its EV plans. Ford booked nearly $20 billion

04:34 in adjustments and admitted its electric division  alone lost almost 5 billion in a single year. Even

04:40 the ones that stayed in the black still took a  hit. GM turned a $2.7 billion profit for the year,

04:46 but quietly scrapped its plans to go all electric  by 2035 and wrote down around $ 8.7 billion of EV

04:52 investment. For the last decade, a lot of these  major car manufacturers thought they were playing

04:56 a game of catch-up to the EV leaders in the space,  pushed by significant investor pressure from

05:01 shareholders that wanted Tesla level valuation.  But a lot of them are now realizing that the

05:06 demand they were all chasing is a lot softer  than they were expecting. The early adopters

05:10 that wanted an EV have already purchased one.  And as the market is flooded with more options,

05:15 it isn't necessarily driving people to make  the switch. It's just dividing the original

05:20 pool of customers between more brands. According  to research from Cox Automotive, even existing EV

05:25 owners are considering a switch back to internal  combustion engine or hybrid vehicles. Across the

05:30 entire industry, outside of the purely electric  automakers, most companies have been quietly

05:35 rolling back their bold projections that  they would be a purely EV automaker within

05:39 a decade. In America, in particular, this has been  accelerated by a cut down in EV credits and, well,

05:45 up until recently, some pretty cheap gas that  made it a lot easier to keep the Canyon Narrow

05:49 on the road. So, the industry as a whole has seen  where this is going and they are all announcing

05:54 major resets on their EV strategy. Now, to be  completely fair and put this back into context,

05:59 part of that rethinking process is rethinking all  of the book value they assigned to the tooling and

06:06 research that went into developing EV platforms  and building the plants to produce them. A plant

06:10 that was supposed to stamp out a million electric  F-150s a year is just worth a lot more than one

06:16 that is only producing 10,000 in reality. A lot  of the companies that have announced those 99%

06:21 profit drops are really just taking this year to  readjust their balance sheet and record a loss

06:25 because they know everybody else in the industry  is doing the same thing so they won't look quite

06:30 as bad. They are kind of like the zebra crossing  the river. They know they need to do it and

06:35 they know there are angry shareholders in the  water. But if they all do it at the same time,

06:39 it's much less likely that they will  be singled out. Now, on the other hand,

06:43 I know this makes it all sound like nothing but  an accounting illusion. But behind all of this,

06:47 there is still a serious problem. These write  downs still represent real money that companies

06:52 piled into a technology and capital infrastructure  that they thought would be the future and generate

06:56 them substantial returns, but turned out just  to be underutilized and rapidly depreciating,

07:01 which is probably an important lesson to keep in  mind for no other reason in particular. Anyway,

07:07 on top of this, the ongoing cost of running  research, development, and production lines for

00:00 What if NASA's next mission to the  Moon isn't exploration… it's control?

00:04 For decades, we were told the Moon belonged  to everyone. Since Neil Armstrong planted the

00:09 Stars and Stripes, the Moon has remained one  of humanity's few truly neutral frontiers.

00:13 A place where any nation capable of reaching  it could conduct research and exploration.

00:18 But is that era about to end? Could the future of the Moon look

00:22 less like one giant leap for mankind… and  more like a massive American stronghold?

00:27 Is NASA really preparing to build a  massive autonomous lunar fortress,

00:31 powered by cutting-edge drone technology, to  secure one of the Moon's most valuable locations?

00:36 Because if that's true, the new race to the  moon won't be about getting there first.

00:41 It'll be about deciding who gets to stay. Right now, Shackleton Crater is one of the

00:45 most important locations on the ,oon. Located at  the lunar south pole, it's one of the moon's most

00:50 unusual geographical features. The crater's  rim rises high enough that some of its peaks,

00:55 known as the Peaks of Eternal Light, receive  sunlight for nearly 90% of the lunar day.

01:00 But inside the crater, conditions  couldn't be more different.

01:03 Constantly shrouded in darkness, it creates a  cold trap that flash-freezes everything inside

01:08 it. The crater has been examined by unmanned  spacecraft, and its findings indicated that

01:12 water ice is likely present. It’s one of the  most inhospitable spots on our only satellite.

01:18 And one of the most valuable.

01:20 NASA recently revealed a 3-stage timeline that  will take the United States back to the moon

01:25 for the first time since 1972. The agency is  pouring more than $20 billion into the effort,

01:30 with the goal of putting astronauts back on  the lunar surface within the next few years.

01:34 But this isn't just about planting another flag.

01:37 It’s about dominance.

01:39 America wants to establish a foothold on the  moon. And that’s where phase three comes in.

01:44 Known as "Sustained Human Presence," the program  would create a lunar base capable of hosting

01:48 not just astronauts, but eventually long-term  residents. For the first time, humanity would

01:53 have a permanent station on another world. It  will be built in the Shackleton crater and result

01:58 in a massive perimeter around the crater that  covers over 31,000 square miles (80,209 sq km).

02:03 Astronauts won’t just be exploring the moon.

02:06 They’ll be claiming it.

02:08 The plan is for the base to be protected by  some of the most advanced drone technology ever

02:12 developed. Drones will map and track the lunar  surface as well as moving around independently.

02:17 But these aren’t only the cameras, they’re  the security. These drones will arrive on the

02:22 surface of the moon long before any humans  set foot there. They’ll eventually be used

02:26 to create an autonomous surveillance network as  the Shackleton Crater falls under U.S. control.

02:31 But NASA isn’t kickstarting the race to the moon.

02:33 It's been going for a long time already.

02:36 While the public only learned about these  ambitious plans in May 2026, NASA had already

02:40 been laying the groundwork for years. Phase 1  will take place between 2026 and 2029, and is

02:46 planned to involve 25 launches - 21 of which  will land on the moon. Most previous missions

02:52 to the moon using unmanned spacecraft have been  done to send a single surveillance spacecraft.

02:57 This time it’s different.

02:59 The goal is to deliver up to four tons of  infrastructure to begin the process of building

03:03 the moon base in stages and transform  one of the Moon's harshest environments

03:07 into somewhere hospitable. At the heart of  NASA's plan is the Mark 1 Endurance Lander,

03:13 built by Jeff Bezos' space company, Blue Origin. For years, Bezos watched from the sidelines as

03:18 Elon Musk's SpaceX dominated the modern space  race. Now, he's been handed one of the most

03:23 important missions in its history. And he'll have to deliver.

03:27 The first phase, known as Moon Base I, will see  the Endurance lander begin its initial missions

03:32 to the Moon. These early flights are designed to  test its capabilities by targeting the Shackleton

03:37 Connecting Ridge and ensuring its landing and  propulsion technologies can operate safely.

03:42 Once these missions are complete, the lander will  begin unloading its first payloads of technology.

03:47 This includes high-resolution cameras and  a laser-reflecting device designed to help

03:52 future spacecraft pinpoint and navigate  lunar locations with far greater precision.

03:57 Because many more will be coming.

03:59 Griffin Mission One, a lunar lander developed  by robotics company Astrobotic Technology will

04:04 play a key role in Moon Base II. While Blue  Origin will handle the human landing systems,

04:10 Griffin Mission One will focus on building the  heavy surface infrastructure. One of its key

04:14 developments is the FLEX Lunar Innovation  Platform. It’s a multi-purpose lunar rover

04:19 designed to operate across the surface  as the base begins to take shape.

04:23 This rover will carry the payloads delivered  from Earth, taking them exactly where they’re

04:28 needed as construction of the lunar base begins. For Moon Base III, Blue Origin and Astrobotic

04:33 will be joined by additional partners as the  mission moves into its most advanced stage yet.

04:38 This phase will see the deployment of the Nova-C  Trinity Lander built by Intuitive Machines.This

04:44 mission will be bringing in specialized  analytical technology that will explore to

04:48 study magnetic anomalies on the Moon and  investigate the mysterious lunar swirls

04:53 that continue to puzzle scientists today. For the first time, this stage of the program

04:57 also expands beyond the United States,  bringing in international cooperation from

05:01 partners including South Korea’s space  program and the European Space Agency.

05:06 But cooperation is just the  first step toward control.

05:09 As NASA begins to deliver the infrastructure  to pave the way for human habitation,

05:13 it’s also preparing for the biggest perimeter  in human history. While the first stages of the

05:17 Moon Base are advancing, Nasa’s Jet Propulsion  Laboratory is getting ready for a 2028 mission

05:23 that will determine whether the entire  mission is a success… or a failure.

05:27 The Moonfall Drones are autonomous “hopping”  devices inspired by the success of NASA’s

05:32 Ingenuity Mars Helicopter. They’ll be  carried aboard the Elytra spacecraft,

05:36 which will transport a quartet of 550-pound  (250 kg) drones toward the lunar surface.

05:42 But instead of landing with them, the main  spacecraft will release them in transit.

05:46 This will allow the drones to deploy  independently once they reach the Moon.

05:50 And from that moment on, there’s no  control ship… and no second chance.

05:55 They’re on their own. Once they reach the lunar surface,

05:57 they will use up to 10 high-definition  cameras to create a map of hard-to-reach

06:02 terrain within the crater. The drones will  reportedly feature technology that allows

06:06 information to be independently gathered. This  is important because it will allow NASA to create

06:12 a real-time survey grid over the lunar South  Pole, long before a crew sets foot on the moon.

06:17 Because what comes next is humans stepping into

06:19 one of the most unforgiving  places in our neighborhood.

06:22 There have been plans for moon bases for decades  now, although most of them fell more into the

06:27 realm of science fiction rather than reality. The  talk about how to power such a huge undertaking

06:32 often leaned towards solar power. It would be  sustainable, easy to maintain, and reliable.

06:37 There’s just one problem.

06:39 It wouldn’t work.

06:40 The lunar cycle only provides  solar power for 50% of the month,

06:44 which plunges the moon into  darkness for a 14-day night.

06:47 It’s not possible to create a level of storage  that would carry you through half the month.

06:51 Battery backups would be incredibly expensive,  hard to transport, and subject to failure.

06:56 And that would mean death. The Shackleton Crater is one of the coldest places

07:00 on the Moon, where the long lunar night can drop  temperatures to around -400°F (-240°C) for over

07:06 336 hours. That’s similar to conditions on Pluto,  the frozen dwarf planet at the edge of our solar

07:13 system. The goal is to create a climate-controlled  moon base that can sustain human life long-term.

07:18 Human excursions outside would be limited  and performed in climate-controlled suits.

07:23 But to do that, a new form  of power will be needed.

07:26 The crown jewel of NASA’s Moon base plan is  its Fission Surface Power project. Developed

07:31 in partnership with the Department of Energy, it  would use a self-sustaining nuclear power system

07:36 capable of keeping the base running  regardless of lunar night, solar storms,

07:40 or supply delays. The long-term goal  is to be used as part of a Mars colony,

07:44 but it will make its debut on the moon.  Fission has a lot of advantages. It’s

07:48 small and lightweight, and can be  duplicated for future outposts.

07:53 If it works, the power problems will be solved.

07:55 This fission power system - still in  active development and scheduled for later

07:59 deployment - is expected to generate up to 40  kilowatts of energy for the base. That’s roughly

08:04 equivalent to the electricity needed to power  around 30 households on Earth for an entire year.

08:09 But those households aren’t operating on the Moon. They don’t have the same stakes attached to them.

08:14 On the moon, a power failure will be measured  in hours before everyone on the base freezes

08:19 to death. There is no room for error here, and  the technology is experimental. There will be

08:24 an inherent level of risk for anyone who joins  this moon base project. But according to NASA,

08:28 it’s a risk worth taking. Because there’s a secret  in the darkest recesses of the Shackleton Crater.

08:34 One that might be worth dying for.

08:36 During the early days of the space  race, it was exactly that… a race.

08:40 The world was in the throes of the Cold War,  with 2 superpowers jockeying for advantage.

08:45 No one was sure what would happen if  the Soviets got to the moon first.

08:48 Would they declare it sovereign territory  and threaten military assaults if anyone

08:52 else tried to land there? In the end, the  US’ victory allowed for a future where

08:55 the final frontier would be neutral  territory that anyone could explore.

09:00 Now, people are trying to keep it that way. The Artemis Accords were introduced in 2020

09:04 as a set of non-binding agreements shaping the  future of space exploration under NASA’s Artemis

09:10 program. Today, 67 countries have signed on,  including the United States, much of Europe,

09:15 and rising space powers like India, Japan,  South Korea, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE.

09:20 But two major players are noticeably absent. Russia, and China, both long-standing space

09:25 rivals of the United States. And China,  in particular, has made no secret of

09:29 its ambition to build a lunar base of its own. So is the US about to violate its own principles?

09:35 One of the foundations of the Artemis Accords  is that all activities in space should be for

09:39 peaceful purposes. Nations should commit to  transparency and a mutually beneficial sharing

09:44 of scientific information. This would seem to  prevent national appropriation of the moon.

09:49 But the US has a loophole for that. Section 11 of the Artemis Accords

09:52 requires signatories to avoid any activity that  could cause harmful interference with another

09:58 nation’s operations in space. On paper, that makes  large scale development on the Moon difficult.

10:04 But further down, there’s a key caveat. The wording says “...the nature and existence

10:09 of safety zones is expected to change over time  reflecting the status of the relevant operation”.

10:15 That gives the governments some leeway in  creating so-called safety zones on the moon.

10:19 It just so happens that the US’ idea of what  constitutes a safety zone is very large.

10:24 Critics of the current program point to the  1967 Outer Space Treaty, which was signed before

10:29 the US had won the space race. It essentially  limited the moon and all other celestial bodies

10:35 to peaceful uses. This was signed by the USSR, at  a time when the United States had the high ground,

10:40 and has been abided by ever since. China was added  to the treaty in 1983. Of course, the fact that

10:46 only the US has ever landed people on the moon  has largely rendered it moot. But that might be

10:51 changing. Critics of the US’ current plan say it  stands the risk of creating a space arms race.

10:57 But it might be on the verge of already happening.

10:59 Because there’s something on the moon that  might be the key to the entire solar system.

11:04 People are watching the current US mission  with interest, because on the surface,

11:08 it has chosen one of the most difficult  spots on the moon to stake its set up base.

11:12 Anything exposed to the depths of  the crater will be flash-frozen.

11:15 That’s exactly why it has to be here.

11:18 Space might look peaceful at first glance, but  it’s constantly in motion. The cosmos is always

11:23 carrying particles from other celestial bodies,  with water ice being one of the most common.

11:28 It can drift in small amounts, or it can be  carried frozen solid on comets. What form it takes

11:33 will depend on where it lands. Any that lands in  the Shackleton Crater will remain frozen solid,

11:39 maybe for eons. It’s estimated that there  might be over 100 million metric tons of

11:43 water ice locked down there in the crater. That’s  more than 40,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools.

11:48 In the space race, that might be an ace card.

11:51 One of the biggest challenges of creating a  moon base will be keeping everyone who lives

11:55 there alive. Food will likely be a combination  of pre-packaged astronaut meals, delivered to the

12:00 base, and produce grown on the moon after  gardens are started in the early stages.

12:04 But water will be harder to come by. The  human body can go longer without food than

12:08 it can without water. Just a few days without  the latter can mean death. If the US can find

12:14 a reliable source of water on the moon, it  can make life on its moon base sustainable.

12:18 The US might have just unlocked the  key to long-time life on the moon.

12:22 But that’s just a jumping-off point.  NASA and many of its partners have

12:26 their sights set on Mars next,  and for that, you’ll need energy.

12:30 The Shackleton Crater is surrounded by the Peaks  of Eternal Light, the high ground of the crater’s

12:35 rim. They’re exposed to the sun for 90% of the  lunar year. By setting up solar panels there,

12:40 the base would be equipped with a strong  backup of energy that could be useful for

12:44 keeping the base running… or powering  any vessel that lands on the satellite.

12:48 But NASA isn’t the only space agency with its  eye on this incredibly valuable real estate.

12:53 The United States’ moonshot has a very  ambitious end goal. The goal is to first

12:57 deliver the infrastructure through unmanned  missions, then begin landing astronauts in 2028.

13:03 After that, a second phase follows:  27 launches, 24 lunar landings,

13:08 and more than 132,000 pounds (59,874 kg) of  additional payload delivered to the surface.

13:13 From 2029 to 2032, the focus shifts again:  building the infrastructure needed for sustained

13:19 human life on the Moon. During this time, early  colonists would work alongside autonomous systems

13:24 to expand and maintain the base, along  with its growing research networks.

13:28 It’s a wildly ambitious plan. One  many experts say is overly rushed.

13:33 But the United States is trying to beat the clock.

13:35 That’s because they have a rival. The  International Lunar Research Station,

13:39 or ILRS, is a joint China-Russia-led project  aimed at creating a lunar base of its own.

13:45 It will be operated by the 2 great powers with  a tense relationship with the United States,

13:50 alongside Pakistan, Egypt, Venezuela, South  Africa, and Serbia. They've been planning it for a

13:55 long time. China has been doing unmanned missions  on the moon since 2007. Russia’s Roscosmos agency

14:01 has been launching its own probes on the  moon, albeit with a more erratic record.

14:05 But now they want to beat the US to the moon.

14:09 The ILRS timeline looks a lot like the American  one at first, with the process starting in 2026.

14:14 That’s when joint operations will start, as cargo  deliveries begin to the surface of the moon.

14:19 Once that is pulled off, the next phase  will begin establishing facilities

14:23 both in-orbit and on the surface,  as the base starts taking form.

14:27 This will take place from 2031 to 2035, putting  it behind the US’ schedule. But no one is sure if

14:33 the US timeline can be pulled off. This base  is expected to be utilized from 2036 onward.

14:38 It’s the location that worries the U.S.

14:41 China and Russia have been fairly cagey  about the location planned for the base or

14:45 how large it will be. But the location is  planned for the lunar south pole as well.

14:49 It’s not clear if the target  is the Shackleton Crater,

14:51 but the location’s water-rich environment  makes it a highly inviting target.

14:55 That means the US isn’t just in a  moonshot to duplicate its past success.

14:59 It’s in a race to maintain  its domination of space.

15:02 Not since Sputnik has the United  States been behind in the Space Race,

15:06 and it’s never had to answer one big question.

15:08 What happens if someone else gets  there first and claims their territory?

15:12 With resources on the moon looking inviting  and Mars looming as the next great frontier,

15:17 a space war may become inevitable. That’s why the  United States is looking at the moon in a way no

15:22 one can ignore. A nuclear-powered fortress right  on top of the most resource-rich spot on the moon,

15:28 patrolled by the most advanced drones in the  world, would certainly send that message.

15:33 Now it just has to deliver.

15:35 When NASA had to beat the Soviets to the moon, it  relied on the best scientists who were willing to

15:39 work for the government. But now, it has access to  a whole new pool of talent from the tech sector,

15:44 motivated to deliver on this  impossible-seeming timeline.

15:47 They know that if they pull this off, the rewards  are massive both personally and professionally.

15:52 But they also know that if they fail, there’s  much more at stake than their stock holdings.

15:56 If the US loses the new space race,  there might be no catching up this time.

16:00 Because this one isn’t just for bragging rights.

16:03 It’s for the keys to the cosmos.

16:06 The technology for spaceflight may  be about to take a quantum leap.

16:09 Watch “20% Speed of Light!!  NEW Light Engine Is INSANE!”

16:14 to find out what might be powering the future  of space travel, or watch this video instead.

01:01 As this talk suggests, it's going

03:25 frames.

03:26 All of these are open models except for DALL-E 3

03:29 that I've shown in the previous slide.

03:34 As a cautionary note, I'm going to be interchangeably using

03:40 diffusion and flow in this talk, which also means

03:43 that the points and the discussions

03:46 that we'll do in this talk, they will apply to both diffusion

03:52 and flow models.

03:54 Flow model-- I like to explain them

03:58 is a generalization of diffusion models.

04:03 But they are not exactly the same.

04:05 But for the purposes of this talk,

04:08 I'll interchangeably use them.

04:12 Now let me try to give you some context as to how

04:15 diffusion models work.

04:17 I like to think of diffusion models as the following.

04:20 What happens when we start from a random noise drawn

04:25 from a Gaussian?

04:26 And we then try to slowly denoise it over a period of time

04:32 unless we get something realistic.

04:34 It can be an image.

04:35 It can be a video.

04:36 Or it can be even a piece of audio as well.

04:40 But the crucial point is we are starting

04:46 from a pure random noise, and then we

04:48 are iterating over a period of time, denoising it,

04:52 so that it becomes a clean and realistic representation of what

04:56 we want, so it can be considered as some of an iterative

05:01 denoising process.

05:03 And we can also condition this denoising process.

05:06 When we try to condition with text descriptions,

05:09 we can do tasks like text-to-image

05:13 like we are seeing here.

05:14

05:18 Now the thing is, diffusion models

05:20 can have different variants, like when we are operating

05:26 directly on the pixel space, that family of model

05:32 is typically referred to as pixel space diffusion model.

05:36 But pixel space diffusion is pretty

05:38 intensive from both memory and compute standpoints, which

05:43 is exactly why operating on the latent space

05:47 is almost the de facto for diffusion models.

05:51 And in this diagram, we can get a sense of how

05:54 latent space diffusion works.

05:56 Now we need to have some of an encoder and a decoder

06:01 in order to be able to encode the pixel representation

06:05 of an image into its latent representation.

06:08 And then when we are converting that latent space

06:12 into the pixel space, we need to have some decoder.

06:15 Or typically, for the case of latent space diffusion models,

06:19 we usually use a VAE, which has an encoder variant as well

06:25 as a decoder variant.

06:27 So yeah, just note that this talk is mostly

06:32 going to be about latent space diffusion models.

06:35 But the approaches are fairly general enough.

06:38 They will also apply equally.

06:40 They should apply equally to pixel space diffusion models

06:44 as well.

06:46 Now, let's try to also see how different components

06:51 within a diffusion model are connected with one another

06:56 because unlike language models or visual language models,

06:59 diffusion, any modern state of that diffusion model

07:03 is not a single model.

07:05 That's a very important distinction to be aware of.

07:08 Now let's say we want to take this text prompt,

07:13 and we want to generate a video out of it.

07:15 Now let's see what are the typical components that

07:19 are involved and how they are connected.

07:23 Now, to be able to have salient representations

07:26 of the textual description, we need

07:28 to have text encoder, which is fairly intuitive.

07:32 And then once we have the text embeddings out,

07:35 we start the-- this is the inference workflow, by the way.

07:40 Now, with the text embeddings out,

07:42 we start off with a pure random noise as I was mentioning.

07:48 These are our noisy latents as we are operating on the latent

07:52 space, and we also need to have access

07:55 to a component we term as scheduler,

07:58 which is a nonparametric component, which

08:00 takes care of-- which basically makes

08:03 the model aware of the position it is in the entire denoising

08:08 trajectory.

08:10 And this is the beast that we will try to optimize.

08:15 But more on that later.

08:17 It can be a typical unit-like architecture

08:20 or a transformer-like architecture.

08:23 And broadly, this is referred to as the diffusion network, which

08:28 is conditioned on the time step, like the position

08:31 in the denoising iterations that it is in,

08:34 the text embeddings in this case,

08:36 and also the noisy latents.

08:38 And then we invoke it over a period of time, hence the loop.

08:43 Now, once we get our refined legends out the diffusion

08:46 network, it's passed off to a decoder,

08:50 and we finally get our frames.

08:52 In case of an image, it will just be a single frame or just

08:55 the single final image.

08:58 Now, now that we have some very basic understanding

09:03 of the different components that are involved

09:06 in a standard text-to-image or text-to-video diffusion model,

09:10 and how those components are connected with one another,

09:13 how they draw the chronology in the whole inference workflow.

09:17 I'll try to now motivate why we might

09:21 have to optimize them to be able to make anything

09:25 useful out of them.

09:28 Now let's try to look at the memory

09:30 footprint of the individual model-level components

09:33 in a fairly state of the art and recent model called Flux.

09:38 It uses two text encoders, which is also

09:42 kind of common in the literature of text-to-image diffusion

09:45 models.

09:48 For Flux, it uses two text encoders.

09:51 It has got a T5-XXL, and it has got a clip large.

09:55 If you are interested in knowing why we need different text

10:01 encoders and why that might be beneficial,

10:03 we can talk about it later.

10:05 But in the interest of time, I'll just keep going.

10:07 But that's an interesting question to ask.

10:11 And then you have got the transformer, which

10:13 is like the diffusion network.

10:15 And as we can see, it has got the highest footprint.

10:18 And you have got the decoder, which

10:21 will be responsible for taking the defined latents out

10:24 of the transformer and then decoding it back

10:26 to the pixel space.

10:28

10:31 And as I was mentioning, the transformer

10:33 or the diffusion network here is the most compute intensive unit.

10:39 And it's compute bound, unlike language models.

10:42 Hence, consequently, the optimization literature

10:48 from the language modeling world might not

10:51 carry over to the diffusion world very gracefully.

10:57 Now, even when using the brain float16, which

11:00 is very common in the diffusion world,

11:03 it takes about 34 gigs to generate a 1024

11:08 by 1024 resolution image, which is standard,

11:18 So I hope you we can see how these numbers are

11:23 kind of staggeringly high because if we have

11:27 to wait for about 7 seconds to generate one single image,

11:31 it's not good.

11:34 And then videos can be even worse, like a fight.

11:42 720p video can take about 30 minutes to generate fairly

11:48 state-of-the-art open video generation model.

11:53 Now these numbers are heavy.

11:55 These numbers should concern us in case

11:59 we are interested in operationalizing some

12:01 of these models because long-running tasks

12:04 are bad for user-facing applications.

12:07 It hinders interactions because if the interactivity aspect

12:12 of creative applications is hindered,

12:17 it's not good for your users, and it's also power inefficient.

12:21 And it also slows down the overall rate

12:25 at which you would want to iterate and make

12:27 some improvements to these models.

12:29 So it's kind of a bad experience for both the developers

12:33 as well as the users of these models.

12:37 Now, as I was hinting at the iterative transformer.

12:43 It's at the root of all evil here,

12:46 basically, because it's both compute bound

12:49 and same time very memory hungry now and a natural question

12:55 because the transformer takes the most

12:58 amount of time in the whole generation workflow.

13:01 A natural question here to ask would be

13:04 do we just optimize for speed?

13:07 But what happens when you also try

13:10 to motivate the entire optimization

13:14 landscape with an application, the application

13:17 in which this diffusion network is going to get used?

13:21 If we consider things from that perspective.

13:26 There will be other factors that will influence

13:28 the whole process, like the use case in which this network is

13:32 used, the level of user interaction,

13:46 So I think I was able to motivate

13:50 why you would want to work with an optimized version

13:56 of the diffusion network, and also why speed might not just

14:01 be the only factor that we want to care about in this case.

14:07 Hence, I am going to talk a little more about how

14:12 optimization becomes a factor that transcends well

14:16 beyond just speed.

14:17

14:20 Effectively and essentially, I like

14:22 to think of the whole optimization

14:25 landscape as a few guiding principles, when should,

14:31 when should the optimization take place?

14:34 And in this case, the motivation basically comes from the app

14:38 where should we perform optimization.

14:42 And in this case, it's roughly going

14:43 to be the diffusion network, the transformer model.

14:47 That's the most compute-intensive element

14:50 in our workflow.

14:51 And do we know what we want to optimize?

14:54 Do we want to optimize throughput?

14:56 Do we want to optimize memory?

14:58 Or do we want to optimize both?

15:02 And how should we optimize?

15:03 This is where this talk is going to be focusing on.

15:08 So yeah, if we are going to be discussing

15:10 a couple of different recipes and approaches

15:13 as to how we can optimize the transformer network

15:17 and also how we can go beyond that.

15:22 Now I think there needs to be more motivation and more

15:28 awareness to be put when it comes to the kind of hardware

15:33 that we have access to especially when we are deploying

15:37 these models.

15:38 Now in this picture, we can see how the throughput immediately

15:43 improves when we try to use shapes that are particularly

15:48 optimized for a given hardware.

15:50 Now, on the extreme right-hand side,

15:52 the bar shows, it's basically configured

15:58 with the most optimized shapes for a given hardware,

16:01 and it gives us the most amount of throughput.

16:04 And the number of total model parameters is not changing.

16:08 That's not changing.

16:20 of the transformer blocks and so on.

16:22 And it shows how just changing that

16:24 and how optimizing that with respect to the given hardware

16:28 can immediately render some positive gains

16:32 in terms of throughput.

16:34 So that's what I was mentioning.

16:38 Nontrivial gains can come from kernels

16:41 that are hyper specialized for a given hardware,

16:44 and also model architectures where the shapes of the model

16:49 are kind of optimized and have been made efficient with respect

16:55 to the hardware.

16:56 It's going to be operationalized.

17:00 Now there's also this aspect of efficiency

17:05 that's going to keep coming up because we

17:07 want to make our model as efficient as possible.

17:11 But efficiency is also often a term that has so many misnomers.

17:16 The popular belief is smaller models are almost always faster

17:20 and more efficient.

17:21 The reality is no, not always.

17:24 And I have this very popular figure from this paper called

17:29 "the efficiency misnomer" as the title of my slide goes.

17:33 It basically shows how models with higher number of parameters

17:38 may not have the highest number of flops,

17:42 and also it may not have a lower throughput.

17:48 Now, in this case, it's basically reversed.

17:51 That is, the models with a lower number of parameters

17:55 has more flops and has a lower amount

17:58 of throughput than their apparently heavier counterparts.

18:04 So that kind of drives this point home.

18:07 That efficiency may not always be related to models

18:11 being smaller.

18:13 There are more angles to take a look at it.

18:16

18:19 Now the big elephant is also transformer.

18:22 I'm going to keep coming back to this transformer thing.

18:26 But also, when it comes to high resolution generation of images

18:31 and videos, the effects of the compute-bounded regime

18:39 of our transformer can become really, really evident.

18:43 First, the inputs are of high dimensional.

18:46 For example, for 4K image generation,

18:51 even if we were to operate with a compression factor of 8x,

18:55 we have got this huge dimensionality problem.

18:58 We have got batch size.

18:59 Then we have nominating channels, which

19:02 can be 64, 128, and so on.

19:05 And then you have got your latent width and latent--

19:09 you have got your latent height and latent width,

19:11 which is also like 512 and 512.

19:14 Now doing attention at this high-dimensional space can

19:19 immediately restrict--

19:21 can immediately impose memory implications as well as

19:27 speed implications.

19:28 Two very popular ways to deal with this high-dimensionality

19:32 problem, in order to achieve some efficiency gains,

19:36 is we increase the compression factor, like from 8x,

19:41 we compress even higher, maybe 16x or 24x,

19:45 and we try to recover the lost information through other means.

19:52 There are several works that have explored this,

19:55 but I just wanted to give you a high-level overview

19:58 of the typical things that are done

20:00 when we have this problem of high-dimensional representation

20:04 spaces.

20:05 Now when we-- just to elaborate a bit further on this point,

20:11 when we try to compress higher and higher,

20:14 we also end up losing a lot of information redundancy, which

20:18 might be actually necessary study in order

20:21 to model the expressivity into the overall workflow.

20:25 And if we do miss out on that, our quality can take a huge hit.

20:31 Now, that's also why it's essential to try

20:35 to recover the information loss incurred

20:38 during this heavy compression, so some kinds of other means.

20:44 And as a motivating example, I want

20:46 to show you this picture from this very popular

20:52 high resolution image synthesis model called SANA,

20:55 which also happens to operate on a highly compressed latent

20:59 space.

21:00 And as we can see, using extreme compression

21:05 can have significant gains on the speed.

21:11 So in this case, we can see a 25x reduction in the generation

21:15 latency when operating with 4K images.

21:19

21:24 Now, the good thing about trying to do

21:31 this more from a first principles approach

21:34 is these approaches should be complemented

21:38 with the kinds of techniques that we

21:39 have for latency optimization, for example,

21:42 maybe an optimized kernel or maybe

21:45 using things like FlashAttention.

21:47

21:50 So at this point in time, I would

21:52 expect us to have a good understanding of how

21:58 we can optimize the model architecture

22:00 and also have a model architecture

22:05 that respects the hardware that it will get deployed to.

22:10 Now, ultimately, since we are also

22:12 focusing on the applications in which these models are going

22:17 to be used, I think it also makes sense

22:20 to try to think about how we can also optimize

22:23 a little bit for the use case.

22:25 So let's see how.

22:28 So we know that my model is topping

22:33 all the standard generation benchmarks.

22:35 That's all well and good.

22:38 But the use cases in which the model

22:40 is going to get deployed to, they might be different.

22:44 For example, maybe the model would

22:46 be needed for photorealism.

22:48 So in that case, the users would demand for specific attributes

22:53 to be better than others.

22:55 And then maybe the model will be used in the context

22:59 of interactive generation.

23:00 In those cases, we would rather have real-time interaction

23:05 and lowest possible latency.

23:07 And maybe quality doesn't matter that much.

23:11 So in these cases, we will have to finetune whatever model

23:17 that we have for specific needs.

23:19 And that entire process should be driven by the use cases.

23:25 Now one such way to do that, one such way to inject

23:30 some form of use case awareness would

23:32 be to do preference alignment, where the model is finetuned

23:35 to output what's preferred.

23:38 In this case, you have got a text prompt, a cyberpunk

23:41 cat with a neon sign that says Sana,

23:44 and you have got two images, two candidates.

23:48 Now, the model will be trained on this triplet,

23:51 and it will be basically trained to output what

23:55 the users typically prefer.

23:57

23:59 We might also want to extend the way users prompt these models.

24:06 So far, we have been seeing text-to-image models, which

24:10 is basically users provide natural text description of what

24:16 they want to see in the final outputs.

24:18 Maybe that's not sufficient.

24:19 Maybe I also want the output image

24:23 to follow a particular pose.

24:26 Maybe I want to condition the model with more structural forms

24:30 of inputs such as pose, segmentation, map,

24:33 Canny map for example.

24:35 And in this case, I'm basically prompting the model

24:38 with a certain pose as well as a textual description.

24:43 And as you can see, it works, basically.

24:46 So maybe the textual prompt was not enough.

24:49 And hence there was a need to allow

24:52 the users to have more control over what they can

24:55 provide to the model as inputs.

25:00 If training is not possible because training

25:02 is an expensive gig, even with parameter efficient finetuning,

25:05 the results might be far from expected.

25:09 In those cases, we can also incorporate things

25:11 like inference time scaling, where we might want

25:16 to search for better noise.

25:18 As we saw a couple slides back, when performing inference

25:23 with diffusion models, we try to start from a random noise,

25:27 and then we try to denoise it.

25:29 We could search for better noise,

25:31 like the initial noise could be better because not

25:35 all noises are equal.

25:37 They are not going to lead to same quality outputs.

25:42 So we might want to search for better noise,

25:46 or maybe we want to search for a better prompt.

25:49 And it's also possible to search for both, actually.

25:54 Now this gives us a depiction of what I wanted to convey.

26:00 So you basically generate an image from a language prompt.

26:05 And then you compute some metric.

26:08 In this case, it's the ClipScore.

26:11 And then if the metric is OK, then all good.

26:16 Our job is done.

26:18 If the metric is not OK, maybe we

26:20 ask some language model to come up with a better prompt.

26:24 And then we enter into this interactive scaling framework.

26:34 Now Clip Score here I used clip score as a motivating example.

26:39 But this metric should be use case-specific.

26:44 So this is the last section of my talk, where

26:47 I want to give you a flavor of some

26:49 of the more advanced optimization techniques

26:52 that we can incorporate.

26:55 So knowledge distillation is already very popular.

26:58 We have had many papers in the community

27:01 that talk about this technique.
