00:00 Chaos has erupted in Iraq as a gang of bloodthirsty ISIS commandos attack the US Embassy.

00:05 Wielding assault rifles, improvised explosives, and lethal machetes, they lead a cunning assault

00:11 that takes the guards by surprise and puts the diplomats and embassy staff inside at

00:15 risk of a terrible fate.

00:17 But just when things start looking hopeless, salvation arrives: An elite thirty-man platoon

00:22 swoops in, routing the attackers and putting them down with some well-placed shots from

00:27 their assault rifles, while another among their numbers lays down a hail of suppressing

00:31 fire with his M240 bravo.

00:34 The day is saved by this crack team of US military operatives, but all this raises one

00:39 question: Was that the Marines or the Army?

00:41 You might have heard the terms ‘Army’ and ‘Marines’ used interchangeably in

00:44 movies or on TV, but the Marines and Army are two entirely different entities.

00:49 Heck, they’re not even in the same military branch!

00:52 Whether you call them Jarheads, Devil Dogs, or Leathernecks, there’s a lot more to the

00:56 USMC than you probably know.

00:58 So let’s give our boys in scarlet and gold a Semper Fi, an OORAH, and plenty of yummy

01:04 crayons, as we find out exactly what makes the United States Marines different from the

01:07 regular army.

01:09 There are way more differences than you think!

01:11 With over a million members serving in active duty, the US has one of the largest militaries

01:16 on the planet, divided into six distinct branches.

01:19 There’s the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, the Coast Guard, the Space Force (yes, really),

01:24 and, of course, the United States Marine Corps, or USMC.

01:28 Most of the time, it’s pretty easy to deduce the general function of each military branch

01:33 from its name alone; the Air Force, for example, specializes in aerial warfare.

01:37 Then there’s the Navy, which wouldn’t be out of place patrolling the seas in large,

01:41 heavily armed ships.

01:42 The Marines don’t feel quite so obvious - From name alone, you might correctly assume

01:47 they conduct missions at sea.

01:49 But hold on, isn’t that what the Navy’s for?

01:52 Yes, but that’s because the Navy and the US Marines often work hand in hand, with the

01:57 Marine’s primary job being conducting amphibious operations- something no other branch of the

02:01 US military can do.

02:03 The missions the US Marines are sent on typically involve landing on a hostile piece of beachfront

02:08 property, and kicking the current proprietors out- permanently.

02:12 But you’ll also find Marines hundreds of miles inland- doing the same job you’d expect

02:16 the Army to do.

02:17 Sounds confusing right?

02:19 Don’t worry, when you break it down it makes much more sense.

02:22 The Army’s purpose is acting in defense of the United States, typically by completing

02:26 missions that take place primarily on land against hostile forces that have acted against

02:31 the national security interests of the US.

02:33 So, the Marines are, in essence, the Army for the Navy.

02:38 Or, if you prefer to think of it like this, you can imagine them as a smaller and more

02:42 pinpointed hybrid of both these branches - with the training and equipment to conduct missions

02:47 on land and at sea.

02:49 While Marines need to be prepared for any type of mission, wet or dry, the Army is only

02:53 tasked with duties that take place on solid ground, although it’s not uncommon for the

02:58 different specialized branches of the US military to work together collaboratively.

03:02 Joint operations like these are vital for securing objectives that call for the skills

03:06 of multiple different branches of the military.

03:09 In the case of the Marines, being a force that can operate from both land and sea, its

03:13 members can assist other military units in missions that require getting personnel from

03:18 sea to land where they may not have been previously trained to do so.

03:22 But the Marines’ other specialty is their role as a quick reaction force, United States

03:27 Marines are often referred to as ‘the tip of the spear.’

03:30 They consist of combat-ready specialized units that are trained to respond to urgent situations

03:35 and conflict operations wherever and whenever necessary.

03:39 Marine Expeditionary Units must remain prepared for combat at all times and are among the

03:44 first to respond to dangerous situations.

03:46 However, Marines aren’t meant to conduct heavy combat operations on their own- they

03:51 don’t even have tanks anymore.

03:53 This is where the Army comes in, with the Marines acting as a fast, agile, and flexible

03:57 quick-reaction force, and the Army bringing the big guns right behind them.

04:01 Although the two forces undergo different types of training, there is often room for

04:05 overlap between the Army and the Marines, and their capabilities can even complement

04:09 each other.

04:10 That being said, even though all Marines are trained to engage in amphibious warfare, very

04:15 few in the US Army are.

04:17 Most Army units are assigned a specific terrain or type of warfare to specialize in.

04:22 These can include airborne or mountainous infantry or even the famed US Army Rangers.

04:27 This is by far one of the hardest specialties to achieve, but doing so will result in a

04:31 soldier serving in the United States Ranger Regiment - an elite special operations unit

04:37 famous for conducting missions deep within enemy territory, amongst severe adverse conditions.

04:42 Meanwhile, all Marines are considered amphibious troops- but lack the type of training that

04:47 a US Army mountain division might have, for instance.

04:49 When it comes to who out of the Army or Marines is better equipped, it’s definitely the

04:54 former.

04:55 The US Army has consistently been the first of the two to receive rollouts of newer weapons.

04:59 Take the M4A1 carbine, for example.

05:02 This assault rifle is a shorter version of the M16, capable of both semi-automatic and

05:06 automatic fire.

05:08 While it’s now used by both forces, the Army was the one equipped with it first, long

05:12 before the Marines eventually adopted the weapon.

05:14 This also applies to newer weapon add-ons and attachments such as optical sights, lasers,

05:20 and hand grips.

05:21 We’ve seen this recently with the M4, as the Picatinny rails on the weapon’s receiver

05:25 and handguards make it compatible with various attachments.

05:28 This includes the M203 under-barrel grenade launcher, which is widely used by the US Marines.

05:34 Meanwhile, the Army is adopting the M320 as its primary grenade launcher, which can be

05:39 fired as a stand-alone firearm or mounted to other weapons like an M4.

05:44 The point is, the Marines do get their hands on all the fancy new firearms and attachments

05:48 eventually, it just tends to be much later than the Army.

05:51 A further difference between the Marines and the US Army is their flags and iconography.

05:56 The US has several separate flags that are each designed for specific branches of the

06:00 military.

06:01 The flag of the US Army was originally designed with the seal of the US War Office, as well

06:05 as the words ‘United States Army,’ their star emblem insignia, and the year 1775 emblazoned

06:12 over a white background.

06:13 1775 is the year in which the US Army was officially established, making it the oldest

06:18 branch of the United States’ vast military.

06:21 The official motto of the US Army is ‘This We’ll Defend’ and has been ever since

06:26 they played a pivotal role in gaining independence for the US during the Revolutionary War.

06:31 The branch has an impressive service record, being involved in nearly every major armed

06:35 conflict that the US has been a part of, either domestically or overseas.

06:40 This includes both World Wars, as well as the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

06:44 Meanwhile, the flag representing the Marine Corps has changed numerous times over the

06:48 years, largely due to it being a part of the US Navy for so long before becoming its own

06:53 distinct entity.

06:54 In fact, the modern-day incarnation of the Marines’ flag did not see use until as recently

06:59 as the twentieth century.

07:01 Their official insignia is the Eagle, Globe, and Anchor, which are all present on the current

07:06 iteration of the Marine Corps flag.

07:08 First adopted in 1955, this flag features a globe intersected by an anchor, with an

07:13 eagle standing on top of the globe with its wings spread and a ribbon in its beak.

07:17 The flag also bears the Latin phrase ‘Semper Fidelis,’ the official motto of the United

07:22 States Marines, which has become something of a legendary phrase amongst its members.

07:27 Translating to ‘Always Faithful,’ and frequently shortened to “Semper Fi,” it

07:32 can often be heard being yelled, cheered, or used as a greeting among current and former

07:36 Marines, intended to remind them of their close commitment to their comrades and nation

07:41 both.

07:42 But enough sweating the small stuff.

07:43 Let’s talk about size, duties, and operational structure.

07:47 The US Army is split into three distinct units: the Army, the Army Reserve, and the National

07:52 Guard.

07:53 As well as engaging in warfare on battlefields outside of the US, the Army also has a responsibility

07:58 to protect America domestically, meaning in times of national crisis or even invasion,

08:03 you’d be more likely to see the US Army on United States soil, while the Marines handle

08:08 things in foreign territory.

08:10 Compared to the Army, there are also a comparatively small number of Marine Corps personnel in

08:14 service.

08:15 As of 2020, there were over 180,000 Marines actively serving, with a further 32,000 in

08:21 reserves, compared to the over 450,000 active duty soldiers in the US Army, 325,000 in reserves,

08:28 and almost 177,000 active personnel in the National Guard.

08:32 These reserve forces operate in extremely similar manners across the Army and the Marine

08:36 Corps; in the case of the Army Reserves, they provide additional troops and support to the

08:41 regular Army, with many reservists serving in their spare time.

08:45 For the Marines, their reserves are expected to be ready to leave civilian life and join

08:49 their fellow Marines in combat assignments or assist in national emergencies should the

08:53 need arise.

08:55 Given that they are a smaller force that operates with fewer service members than the Army,

08:58 it’s no surprise that the Marine’s main recruiting slogan is ‘the Few and the Proud,’

09:03 emphasizing that they only accept the highest caliber of troops.

09:07 Engaging in operations on both land and sea, Marines can be found stationed at military

09:11 bases on land and aboard warships.

09:14 Marines are often tasked with protecting US naval bases, as well as the Navy’s warships

09:19 and other areas of national interest that are located near coastlines.

09:23 Members of the US Marine Corps also have a particular responsibility that the Army does

09:27 not have: They’re charged with protecting United States embassies on foreign soil.

09:32 Being the only part of the US military with this duty, the Marine Corps has its own specific

09:36 sub-group that deals with providing the heightened levels of security required for guarding American

09:42 embassies: the Marine Corps Embassy Security Group.

09:45 Another key factor that differentiates the Marine Corps and the US Army is their training

09:50 programs.

09:51 Basic training for new recruits in the US Army is roughly ten weeks long and is normally

09:55 followed up by Advanced Individualized Training, where soldiers are given additional training

10:00 to prepare them for their future specialties we mentioned earlier, whether that be a specialty

10:05 in certain environments and terrains, or specific tactics.

10:08 According to some – although certain members of the US military will disagree on this - Marine

10:13 boot camp is generally considered to be more mentally and physically challenging compared

10:17 to the Army’s basic training program or that of other US military services.

10:22 Lasting around twelve to thirteen weeks, approximately 40,000 Marine hopefuls undergo this training

10:27 every year.

10:28 Beforehand, they have to be screened, have their overall health assessed, and must pass

10:32 a fitness test in order to begin their training.

10:35 Any recruits that fail this physical examination will go on to receive individual, personalized

10:40 attention and additional training until they can pass and enter the Marine Corps.

10:45 While these processes are similar in timeframe, each training course differs based on the

10:49 routes each prospective candidate decides to specialize in.

10:52 In either case, both the Marines and the Army expect all those who enlist to complete their

10:57 basic recruitment training before they are permitted to advance into specialization training.

11:02 Where successful Army recruits go on to Advanced Individualized Training schools after their

11:06 basic training, Marine hopefuls are enrolled in Military Occupational Specialty schools.

11:11 Both the Marines and Army also receive higher education training.

11:15 Annapolis, Maryland, is the home of the US Naval Academy.

11:18 This is a university dedicated to training both male and female officers, referred to

11:23 as midshipmen, over the span of four years.

11:25 Full tuition costs are sometimes even covered if a candidate enters active duty with the

11:30 Marines directly after they graduate.

11:32 Both the Navy and Marines receive graduates from the Naval Academy, given that the Marines

11:37 operate under the Navy.

11:39 Meanwhile, over in Quantico, Virginia, you’ll find the United States Marine Corps Officer

11:44 Candidates School.

11:45 This one is slightly different, instead of offering a four-year degree course, it provides

11:49 potential candidates with either two six-week courses or the same thing condensed into one

11:54 ten-week version.

11:55 These are usually attended by those enrolled in commissioning programs aimed at college

11:59 students and graduates who have previously completed degrees prior to enlisting with

12:04 the Marines.

12:05 Any midshipmen who complete the program are entitled to receive a commission as a second

12:09 lieutenant; this will often see them placed in command of a platoon consisting of 16 to

12:14 44 soldiers, including two or more rifle squads.

12:17 Meanwhile, the Army has the United States Military Academy located in West Point, New

12:22 York.

12:23 Much like the US Naval Academy, it provides Army recruits with a separate four-year course,

12:28 one designed to prepare these students for active service following their graduation.

12:31 Also, much like the aforementioned Naval Academy, West Point will grant free tuition to anyone

12:37 who enters active military duty upon the completion of their degree.

12:40 The Army’s equivalent of the Marine’s officer training program is their own Officer

12:45 Candidate School in Fort Benning, Georgia.

12:47 This school also offers courses specifically for college graduates, and after they have

12:52 completed a vigorous twelve week course, these graduates will also be awarded the rank of

12:55 Second Lieutenant, only within the United States Army instead.

12:59 So, while their training might be different, and the courses for enlistees will also differ,

13:04 the ways in which the Marines and Army recruit and teach their prospective soldiers follow

13:08 a similar pattern.

13:10 After all, if it ain't broke, don't fix it.

13:12 Speaking of similarities between the two, the US Army and Marine Corps also share many

13:16 organizational elements when it comes to basic unit structure.

13:20 A platoon normally consists of three to four small squads of between 25 and 50 troops and

13:25 is usually commanded by a lieutenant.

13:27 The Army and Marines both organize their soldiers into large companies, which are typically

13:32 made up of three to four platoons.

13:34 These are then further split up into squads, and then fire teams.

13:38 Although these can vary depending on mission requirements, a typical fire team will consist

13:42 of only four members, sometimes even fewer.

13:45 Among these are an automatic rifleman, a grenadier, another rifleman, and a designated fire team

13:51 leader.

13:52 The role of the leader is to ensure that the other members of the fire team are operating

13:55 as a cohesive unit, with the rifleman acting as the primary asset for both the US Marines

14:00 and the Army.

14:01 A typical Marine Corps rifle platoon contains three rifle squads.

14:05 Each squad is led by a sergeant who has three fire teams under their command.

14:09 Then, every one of these smaller fire teams is led by a corporal, who oversees the automatic

14:14 rifleman, assistant automatic rifleman, and rifleman.

14:17 In some cases, a fire team leader will be equipped with an M16 assault rifle that has

14:21 an M203 grenade launcher attachment, allowing him to act as a quasi-grenadier.

14:25 A platoon of the US Army, however, will normally contain squads with fewer troops despite their

14:32 greater overall number of active duty personnel.

14:35 Sergeants or staff sergeants are normally the ones assigned to lead rifle squads, as

14:38 well as fire teams consisting of about four soldiers.

14:42 Army fire teams have a team leader present, and their composition can vary but typically

14:46 includes an automatic rifleman, a grenadier, and another rifleman.

14:50 One of the riflemen in each Army squad is also sometimes designated as the marksman,

14:56 specially trained to engage targets with precision fire.

14:59 In each of the Army’s platoons, given that their fire teams are much smaller, there are

15:02 usually enough troops to form an additional fire team: the infantry weapons squad.

15:07 This squad contains fire teams that are proficient in the use of the M240B machine gun and the

15:13 Javelin missile system.

15:14 The organization of these two military branches’ troops is not perfectly identical, however,

15:19 as an Army platoon will typically have a radiotelephone operator and a medic on duty.

15:24 By contrast, Marine platoons have a radio transmitter operator and a corpsman, although

15:29 these troops essentially fulfill the same functions.

15:32 The Marine Corps and US Army’s platoons also operate under the orders of commanders

15:36 who are in charge of entire companies and battalions.

15:40 These commanding officers also have heavy weapon elements at their disposal, such as

15:44 a Mortar Section.

15:45 Naturally, neither the soldiers of the US Army nor the Marines are made to occupy the

15:49 same rank or position for the entire duration of their active service.

15:53 The specialization options that are offered to both can extend well into their military

15:58 careers, should troops seek to progress and further develop their skills.

16:02 For example, one of the more challenging options that US Army soldiers can pursue is airborne

16:07 qualification, which requires a soldier to undergo a three-week course in parachuting.

16:12 This also applies to soldiers who wish to join the aforementioned Rangers, although

16:16 success isn’t guaranteed here.

16:17 This elite unit of the Army, and mainstay of plenty of action movies and Call of Duty

16:23 games, is so prestigious that they require members to graduate from a specific Ranger

16:27 School or be selected by the Ranger Assessment and Selection Program.

16:31 Or, should a soldier also be trained as a sniper, by being selected for and graduating

16:36 from a specialized sniper school.

16:38 There are also additional specialization options for US Marines who are looking to advance

16:43 in their military career.

16:45 Marines can compete to become scout snipers, who, as you can imagine, provide accurate

16:49 long-range fire support for infantrymen on the ground.

16:52 Then, there’s the Reconnaissance Marines and Force Recon Marines.

16:56 These sub-divisions are designed to track down enemy forces and then relay their locations,

17:01 troop numbers, and activities back to commanding officers.

17:04 Although the two branches have their differences, in ideal military operations, they can work

17:08 in unison to ensure that the US Military achieves even its most challenging objectives.

17:13 And to avoid that wrath being directed towards you, make sure you don’t ask a former Marine

17:19 what unit he served in during his time in the Army!

17:22 Now check out “US Special Forces vs Wagner Group - Battle of Kasham.”

17:26 Or watch “What Actually Went Wrong In Afghanistan”

  • Video ID: vUYR5zv6gqU

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 If you've got a big chunk of your savings  sitting in a bank account... you're losing money.

00:03 Your balance might look the same, but your buying  power isn’t. You worked hard, played by the rules,

00:09 kept your money safe and waited for a rainy  day. But here's what almost nobody told you...

00:14 The moment your cash earns less than  inflation, your savings start to disappear.

00:18 The banks know this. And they say nothing. So how did the safest place for your money

00:23 become one of the easiest ways to lose wealth? In 2022, the average American savings account

00:28 paid just 0.06% interest, while inflation across  the country soared to just over 9%. That means

00:35 if you had $10,000 sitting in the bank, a  year later it could only buy what roughly

00:40 $9,100 bought 12 months earlier. That’s  $900 gone without you spending a dime.

00:47 This was the year people began paying attention.

00:50 But it wasn’t a one off.

00:51 For almost 15 years, the Federal Reserve  kept benchmark interest rates near zero,

00:56 and banks followed. If you did everything  financial advisors recommended,

01:00 built an emergency fund, avoided debt,  and kept 6 months of expenses in cash,

01:04 you got rewarded with a national average  savings rate hovering around 0.1%.

01:10 Put another way, you could leave $100,000  in a savings account for a full year and

01:14 earn enough interest to pay for a nice  dinner, assuming nobody orders wine.

01:19 Rates did eventually move. When the Fed  spent 2022 and 2023 hiking aggressively

01:24 to fight the inflation monster spawned by  the pandemic, banks followed. For a while,

01:29 savings yields climbed to levels  nobody had seen in over a decade.

01:33 But better is relative. Today, the  national average sits at 0.61%,

01:38 nearly 10 times the 2022 low, and  still nowhere near enough to keep

01:43 up with anything but the mildest inflation.  The rate moved, but the numbers don’t track.

01:48 You wouldn’t call this a full-blown economic  crisis since things like this don’t tend to

01:52 make the headlines. This is more of a slow bleed,  something too gradual to set off any one alarm.

01:57 Economists have a name for  what was happening: the money

02:00 illusion. It’s the habit of judging your  financial life by the number printed on

02:04 your bank statements instead of what  you can actually buy in real terms.

02:08 It’s when a 3% raise feels like,

02:10 well, a well-earned raise, even though  prices have climbed 4% in the same time.

02:15 The brain keeps score in nominal dollars, while  reality keeps score with what those dollars are

02:19 actually worth. The two scoreboards only  agree when inflation happens to be zero,

02:24 which it is… zero percent of the time.

02:27 The losses don’t feel like losses.

02:29 When you find a flaw in your home security that  could get your house robbed or your car stolen,

02:33 you fix it. But when that same  risk is stretched across decades,

02:36 it feels so detached that most people  stop worrying about it altogether.

02:40 That’s the savings crisis in a nutshell.

02:43 2022 accelerated a process that had  been happening for years. Only now,

02:47 several years later, are people beginning to  feel what had been happening to them all along.

02:52 In April of 2020, Americans did something  they’d never achieved in any measurable

02:56 sense before. They saved 33.7% of every  dollar that came into the household.

03:02 That was more than three times the historical  average. Higher than during the 2008 financial

03:07 crisis, higher than the stagflation of  the 1970s, and the highest monthly saving

03:11 rate since the Bureau of Economic  Analysis began tracking it in 1959.

03:16 It sounds like Americans suddenly became  incredible savers. They didn't. To understand why,

03:21 it's worth knowing how a saving  rate actually gets calculated.

03:24 The Bureau of Economic Analysis measures it as  income minus taxes and spending. In April 2020,

03:31 the month everything hit the  fan during the global pandemic,

03:34 income actually spiked with the largest jump on  record. It was almost entirely because CARES Act

03:40 stimulus checks and expanded unemployment  benefits landed in accounts all at once.

03:44 In that same month, spending collapsed since  entire national economies were suddenly welded

03:50 shut. All the restaurants got closed, the flights  were grounded, and retail was shuttered. There

03:55 was, quite literally, nowhere to put the money. So 33% got saved and now we know why.

04:01 Government checks arrived, and with the  future suddenly uncertain, people did what

04:04 they always do in a crisis: they prioritized  liquidity. Because in a genuine emergency,

04:09 a dollar you can access in 10 minutes  is worth more than one locked away in an

04:13 index fund you'd have to sell at a loss. And by conventional financial advice,

04:18 that’s completely rational. Build an  emergency fund. Keep cash on hand. The

04:22 problem isn't saving the money, it's what  happens to it after the cushion is built.

04:26 Behavioral finance has a name for this instinct:  the flight to safety. When uncertainty rises,

04:31 people move toward the assets that  feel safest and are easiest to access,

04:36 even if they aren't the ones most likely to  hold their purchasing power. Traditionally,

04:40 that means things like gold or government bonds. But the asset doesn’t have to be financial.

04:45 In March of 2020, this reflex sent  Americans sprinting toward an asset

04:49 with genuinely bizarre investment fundamentals…

04:52 Toilet paper.

04:53 Store shelves emptied within days because  everyone assumed everyone else was about

04:57 to panic. The only rational move then was to  out-panic them first. People who’d never in their

05:02 lives given a moment’s thought to bath tissue  liquidity were suddenly hoarding 48 packs like

05:07 they’d just gotten inside information on a market  squeeze. Nobody needed a 12 month supply of TP,

05:13 but they did need to not be the one household  that ran out while everyone else had some.

05:18 That’s flight to safety in its purest form.

05:20 Cash works on similar logic. Nobody needs $30,000 sitting in

05:24 a 0.06% savings account, collecting less over  a year than the extra charge on a few vending

05:30 machine purchases. But they do need enough cash to  survive when life stops going according to plan.

05:36 The irony is that the same dollars  people viewed as their safety net

05:39 in April 2020 became the asset hit hardest  by inflation. Every other major asset had a

05:44 way to adjust. Stocks could reprice overnight.  Real estate could reset within a season. Wages,

05:50 slowly and unevenly, could rise as workers moved  into a labor market suddenly desperate for them.

05:56 Cash had no mechanism at all. It just absorbed  whatever inflation showed up that year.

06:01 The idea makes sense on paper. But paper

06:03 doesn’t show you what happens  to your money year after year.

06:06 Imagine you drill a hole in a bucket small  enough that anything inside wouldn’t gush

06:10 out. You pour water in from the top at a rate  just slightly slower than it’s leaking out,

06:16 and then you walk away. When you come back  in an hour, you won’t be surprised to find

06:20 that the bucket holds less water than when  you left. You don’t need a physics degree to

06:24 figure it out. Every person watching that  bucket knows what the outcome will be.

06:28 Hand those same people a savings account instead,

06:30 and somehow the identical outcome  gets treated as a mystery.

06:34 The Federal Reserve sets a number called  the federal funds rate. That’s the price

06:38 of borrowing money overnight.  That number determines what

06:40 your bank is willing to pay you for  the privilege of holding your cash.

06:44 From March 2020 to March of 2022, the  Fed held that rate at essentially zero.

06:49 During the same 24 month span, prices didn’t sit  still. Inflation was positive every single month,

06:55 and by the back half of that window, it  was accelerating hard on its way to that

07:00 9.1% peak. Do the subtraction of what your  savings account paid you, minus what prices

07:06 did to your money for any month of that window  and the answer never once comes out positive.

07:11 This is the bucket.

07:13 The Fed is the tap, and it was  set deliberately to trickle.

07:17 Inflation is the hole in the bottom, and  for 2 straight years, the hole was open

07:21 wider than the tap was flowing. This wasn’t  any secret. It was in all the Fed statements,

07:26 covered by every financial outlet. But  nobody looked or cared, because the bucket

07:30 just weighs slightly less at the end of the day.  It doesn’t announce it’s actively losing water.

07:35 The whole process is known as a negative  real interest rate. It’s when the return you

07:40 were promised is smaller than the amount those  dollars lose in purchasing power over the same

07:44 stretch. So while the market looks healthy, your  statement balances are going up penny by penny,

07:50 and nobody is selling anything at  a loss, the drip is still there.

07:54 When it doesn’t stop for years on end,

07:56 it starts to feel less like a fluke of  bad timing and more a deliberate policy.

08:00 When the Fed expands the money supply,  it’s doing exactly what a concert venue

08:04 does when it prints an extra 35,000  tickets for a 10,000 seat room.

08:09 In the process, each ticket that existed  before that got a little less valuable.

08:13 Nobody had to touch the one you already  owned to make that happen. There just had

08:17 to be more of them in circulation. That’s what happened with the U.S.

08:21 money supply. From 2020 to 2024,  it grew from about $15.4 trillion

08:26 to nearly $20.8 trillion, an increase of 35.1%. The problem is, the economy didn’t produce 35.1%

08:35 more goods, services, or places to spend that  money. But the number of dollars chasing those

08:40 things still increased all the same. Why?

08:43 Because a government that just spent  trillions of dollars it didn’t collect

08:47 in taxes still has to pay for that  spending somehow. Printing extra

08:51 money is a much less painful option than  the alternative, which is raising taxes.

08:56 When COVID hit, Washington needed money  immediately. Stimulus checks, expanded

09:00 unemployment, forgivable loans to keep small  businesses afloat. And it needed it right away.

09:06 Governments that need cash they haven’t  collected yet all tend to do it the

09:10 same way. They just borrow it, selling  bonds to whoever’s willing to buy them.

09:14 When there aren’t enough outside buyers willing  to absorb all the debt the U.S. is issuing at the

09:19 price it wants, the Federal Reserve steps  in. It buys a large portion of it itself,

09:24 using dollars that didn’t exist until  the moment that transaction happened.

09:28 It’s known as quantitative easing.

09:31 Functionally, it’s the government handing  out extra money and the Fed writing the

09:35 check to cover them. Naturally,  the check clears because the Fed

09:38 is the one institution in the country that's  allowed to write a check that never bounces.

09:42 This was all by design.

09:44 The emergency plan.

09:45 If you flood the system with cheap enough  money in a way that keeps the credit flowing,

09:49 you can keep businesses from collapsing  and save the economy. In the short term,

09:53 it worked. The post-COVID recession that  could’ve rivaled 2008 lasted only about 2 months.

09:59 But every extra dollar that got printed  was enacted at the expense of the money

10:03 already sitting in people’s pockets.  Nobody noticed, but the bill for the

10:07 emergency rescue came hiding in plain  sight after years of the same old same old:

10:12 The highest inflation in 4 decades.

10:14 By 2023, the Fed’s rate hikes had pushed savings  yields to levels nobody working today had ever

10:20 seen, with some banks paying close to 5% just to  hold your cash. For a brief, beautiful moment,

10:25 saving money actually beat inflation. It  felt like the leaky bucket had been repaired.

10:30 Then two doors started closing on savers at once. Neither had anything to do with the other.

10:36 The first was when banks started walking that  ceiling back down and the Fed cut its benchmark

10:40 rate 3 times at the end of 2025. They did  this on the theory that inflation had been

10:45 beaten and it was safe to loosen up again.  Savings yields followed the same rope back

10:50 down they’d climbed a year earlier, because  that’s the one lever savers never control.

10:55 The second door was closed on  the other side of the planet.

10:57 In February 2026, the U.S. and Israel struck  Iran. The fallout choked off the Strait of Hormuz,

11:03 the passage roughly a fifth of the world's oil  physically has to travel through to reach a buyer.

11:08 Oil markets don't care whose war it is or  why it started. They reprice immediately,

11:14 everywhere. Gas at the pump followed  within days, and the average household

11:17 ended up bleeding out several hundred  extra dollars over the following months.

11:21 By the middle of 2026, savers found themselves  standing between these two closing doors at

11:26 the same time. The yield on their account was  heading down because policymakers had decided,

11:31 based on old data, that the danger had passed.  The price of literally everything trucked,

11:36 flown, or shipped was heading up  because of a war nobody saw coming.

11:40 Inflation, which had cooled all the way  toward the Fed’s target the year before,

11:44 spiked back up to 4.2% in May  2026, its worst reading since

11:48 2023. It eased slightly to 3.5% in June  as fighting settled into an uneasy pause.

11:54 The crazy part is that most Americans are  learning the hard way that these things

11:54 are completely out of their control.  None of them voted to start a war with

11:55 Iran that made gas cost more. None of them  voted to slash what their savings pay out.

11:55 Their balance absorbs both consequences anyway,  automatically, through no fault of their own.

11:55 None of this is hard to fix.

11:57 According to Bankrate’s most recent survey on  the subject, the average American has kept the

12:01 same savings account for 17 years, and the same  checking account for 19. Few of these people

12:06 did any real calculations to land on their bank  of choice. They just picked one close to them,

12:11 one they’d heard of, maybe ones  their parents used and that’s it.

12:15 When Bankrate asked people directly  whether they’d be willing to switch

12:18 to a better-paying account if  it cost them absolutely nothing,

12:21 two-thirds of savers still said no. When it comes  to hard-earned savings, people, for some reason,

12:27 are not in the business of weighing the effort  of switching accounts against the reward.

12:31 Scripps News recently profiled a woman who’d  been quietly setting money aside for her child.

12:35 Ordinarily, responsible saving would be the order  of the day. Years passed without her touching the

12:40 account, precisely the type of behavior  a savings account is supposed to reward.

12:45 Instead, her bank flagged the account as  dormant, closed it, and forwarded the balance

12:50 to her state’s unclaimed property office. It’s a  legal process called escheatment that every state

12:55 in the country runs in some form. When she went  looking for the money, the state’s own database

13:00 didn’t show it either. It simply fell into the gap  between one system’s recordkeeping and another’s.

13:05 Banks are required to try to reach an  account holder before handing over the

13:09 balance to the state. They usually send  a letter to whatever address is on file,

13:13 or try the phone number a few  times. If those don’t work,

13:17 the account gets treated as abandoned whether or  not the person who owns it is alive and employed.

13:22 State treasuries are currently holding  an estimated $70 billion in unclaimed

13:26 property from dormant savings  accounts, uncashed paychecks,

13:30 forgotten security deposits,  and old investment holdings.

13:33 Roughly 1 in every 7 Americans has money  sitting in that pile right now without

13:37 knowing it. California alone is sitting  on more than $15 billion of it. In the

13:42 most recent fiscal year on record, states  managed to return only about $4.5 billion

13:46 of the total back to its rightful owners,  a fraction of what's actually being held.

13:50 Most bank accounts get flagged as  dormant after just 3 to 4 years

13:54 of zero customer-initiated activity. Even crazier,

13:58 the interest posting to the account  automatically doesn't count as activity.

14:02 In other words, the bank crediting you  a few cents a month isn't enough to keep

14:05 the account alive in the eyes of the law. It  has to be you, logging in, making a deposit,

14:10 doing something the system can attribute  to a living, paying-attention human.

14:15 Cash losing value to inflation is a slow leak  nobody notices because the number on the screen

14:20 keeps getting bigger. An account escheated to  the state disappears in a completely different

14:25 way. The balance disappears, replaced by a  record sitting in a government database you

14:29 probably never knew you needed to search. The threats are different, but the mistake

14:34 is the same: assuming money left alone  is automatically protected. It isn’t.

14:38 Money that nobody actively manages is under  threat from inflation shrinking its value or

14:43 inactivity rules that take it away entirely. The most dangerous thing you can do with your

14:48 money isn’t spending it. It’s  not paying attention to it.

14:51 No matter how much you save or earn, it’s  clear the system is against you. Find out

14:56 why in ‘The game is rigged. You will  NEVER be rich.’ Or click on this video.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: FBI vs CIA - How Do They Compare?
Video Information
docs.text:

  • Video ID: vebNxWGotC8

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 You may not know the ins and outs of these two American agencies, but there is little

00:03 doubt you haven’t spent a significant amount of time enthralled by their actions, whether

00:07 that is through the news media, documentary film, or regular old Hollywood films.

00:11 Both are, to some extent, shrouded in mystery; both can be blamed for duplicity at times,

00:16 bearing the scars of numerous scandals, and they are still currently the target of conspiracy

00:20 theorists.

00:21 Whatever your view, this duo are both catalysts of excitement, intrigue and apprehension.

00:26 While we can’t promise you the often secret workings of the agencies, we can provide you

00:30 with a few minutes of fascinating facts, in this episode of the Infographics Show, FBI

00:34 vs CIA.

00:35 Don’t forget to subscribe and click the bell button so that you can be part of our

00:39 Notification Squad.

00:40 We will start with an abridged history of both agencies.

00:42 The FBI, or the Federal Bureau of Investigation, was the brainchild of Attorney General Charles

00:46 Bonaparte.

00:47 In 1908, he and President Theodore Roosevelt agreed that the justice department needed

00:51 a corps of special agents.

00:53 At the time, it had no name, and it’s said that the two men were not sure how to recruit

00:57 agents.

00:58 According to the FBI website, Bonaparte jokingly told the president they should have men shoot

01:01 at each other and whoever survives gets the job.

01:04 The Bureau of Investigation (BOI) was created soon after, and 34 people were hired at first

01:08 to work as special agents across all of America’s state borders.

01:11 In 1935, it officially became known as the FBI, and prohibition became its raison d’etre.

01:18 As you well know, this meant investigating mobsters we still see on the big screen today,

01:22 and from 1924-1972, the controversial crime-busting icon known as J. Edgar Hoover was the director.

01:29 Mobsters weren’t Hoover’s only concern, and much of the FBI’s resources were spent

01:32 on investigating political radicals during the Great Depression, which later included

01:36 diminishing the impact of Americans with communist sympathies.

01:40 The FBI’s historical cases are of course too many in number to list, but some famous

01:44 investigations include the stick-up robbing sweethearts Bonnie and Clyde, the white collar

01:48 crimes of the company Enron, the JFK Assassination, the murder of three civil rights workers in

01:53 Mississippi, Watergate, and of course 9/11.

01:56 The FBI currently has its headquarters in Washington, D.C, and there are 56 field offices

02:01 in major US cities, as well as more than 350 smaller offices around the country.

02:05 It also has about 60 offices in other countries.

02:07 It employs about 35,000 people in all, which as well as special agents, include scientists,

02:13 intelligence analysts, language specialists, and those with a considerable IT acumen.

02:17 Contrary to popular belief, the FBI does not just shoo the police aside during big investigations,

02:22 because it has no right to.

02:24 State and local officers work with the FBI.

02:27 The Central Intelligence Agency, or CIA, was an intelligence agency focused on national

02:31 security and not domestic crimes, though the twain can sometimes overlap.

02:35 The CIA’s main concerns are terrorism, weapons of mass destruction, knowing what dangers

02:40 or political upheavals are happening around the world – this could be called spying

02:43 – and more recently cyber-intelligence.

02:45 It was created on July 26, 1947 when Harry S. Truman signed off on the National Security

02:51 Act.

02:52 One of the main impetuses to create such an agency was the attack on Pearl Harbor.

02:55 It has been involved in numerous conflicts, again too many to recount, but those include

02:59 the 1953 Iranian coup d'état, attempting to enact a military coup in Indonesia, trying

03:04 to quash all kinds of pro-Communist movements around the world, the Vietnam War, and controversially

03:09 arming rebel forces when the USA believed it suited them.

03:12 The CIA is an intelligence agency, but one that uses its brains and brawn to manipulate

03:17 countries, governments, factions outside of governments, in the interest of American national

03:21 security.

03:22 The number of people working for the CIA is not something the agency discloses, but its

03:26 employees cover many areas of expertise.

03:28 It’s a very secret organization, but it does release millions of pages of its findings,

03:32 much of that being historical, what we might call after the fact.

03:36 Unlike the FBI, the CIA website states that it never monitors US citizens, although it

03:40 also states it will if “there is a reason to believe that an individual is involved

03:45 in espionage or international terrorist activities.”

03:48 Many of its workers are in Washington DC, at its headquarters in Langley, Virginia,

03:52 but agents are also stationed, often working undercover, all around the world.

03:56 Do these two agencies work together?

03:57 Well, this is also a matter of controversy and people have written books that delineate

04:01 a war between the agencies.

04:03 The CIA’s website states that the relationship is strong, as threats to national security

04:07 come in all sorts of guises and so information can be shared.

04:10 That information might relate to drug trafficking, money laundering, organized crime, and terrorism.

04:15 Nonetheless, after 9/11, a congressional report stated that because intelligence was not shared

04:20 responsibly, a possible counter-action did not happen.

04:23 The New York Times wrote, “They failed to counter the threat from Al Qaeda even though

04:27 they had known for years that its leader, Osama bin Laden, was determined to attack

04:30 the United States.”

04:31 So, yes and no, they work together, but it seems the relationship may be somewhat difficult

04:36 at times.

04:37 The CIA is focused on collecting intelligence and cannot make arrests, on the other hand,

04:41 the FBI could technically investigate a CIA agent and make an arrest if that agent violated

04:47 federal law.

04:48 So, what do you have to do to get on one of these teams?

04:50 To join the FBI, you must be between the age of 23 and 37.

04:54 You need a four year degree, 3 years’ work experience, and have a driver’s license.

04:57 You might also have a qualification in one of the following categories: Language, Law,

05:01 Accounting, Computer Science/Information Technology, or it just says “Diversified”.

05:06 Your skills will then be prioritized, and this could come under lots of things from

05:10 accounting to law enforcement to military expertise to finance.

05:14 Few applicants are actually selected, and even after all that, you will have to pass

05:17 a series of difficult tests.

05:19 You’ll have to be fairly fit and be able to sprint 300 meters, do a load of push-ups

05:23 and run for 1.5 miles.

05:25 After that you’ve got medical checks, background checks and polygraphs to pass.

05:29 Get through that, and you could become anything from a regular FBI officer to a sniper or

05:33 a behavioral analyst.

05:34 You will also need to spend 20 weeks training at the FBI Academy in Quantico, Virginia.

05:39 In interviews, former agents have said getting into the FBI is a long, arduous process.

05:43 Not surprisingly, the CIA is pretty strict too on who it accepts, and to reiterate, not

05:48 all workers are covert spies.

05:50 You could be doing anything from specializing in math or economics.

05:53 Most of its clandestine service employees are aged between 26 and 35.

05:57 Like the FBI, background and medical checks, and polygraphs will be part of the interview

06:01 process.

06:02 Again you’ll need a university degree, know your international affairs, and if you have

06:06 travelled the world and know a few languages, the CIA states that is a bonus.

06:09 The CIA says on its website that some of the skills needed are to be able to analyze data,

06:13 have strong negotiation skills, discretion, diplomacy, have criminal investigative experience,

06:18 and if your degree is in criminology, homeland security, or emergency management, that helps,

06:22 too.

06:23 You’ll have to undertake a 56-day Criminal Investigation Training Program and train for

06:27 a further 18 months at its headquarters.

06:29 If you want to get a taste of what it’s like working at the CIA, you can work as an

06:32 intern at any time of the year.

06:34 This, no doubt, should you prove yourself useful, will get your proverbial “foot in

06:38 the door”.

06:39 It generally lasts 90 days, and you won’t need to take the polygraph.

06:42 Which would be the best place to work?

06:43 That depends on a lot of things.

06:45 One important matter when working for the CIA is secrecy if you are an agent.

06:49 As its website points out in bold as IMPORTANT: “Friends, family, individuals, or organizations

06:54 may be interested to learn that you are an applicant for or an employee of the CIA.”

06:59 It goes on to say that it is in your best interests not to tell anyone.

07:02 It’s very probable this was in bold because it alludes to what kind of life you are getting

07:06 into.

07:07 On the upside, for some people the life of a covert operator might be very exciting.

07:11 You may know things that go against your conscience, you may see things that you never wanted to

07:15 see.

07:16 It just depends how deep you go.

07:17 In one interview, a former CIA agent responded when asked if all the stress was worth it:

07:21 “I ask myself the same question every goddamn day.

07:24 Was any of it worth it?”

07:25 The FBI won’t involve the stress of remaining a kind of mystery to one’s own friends and

07:29 loved ones.

07:30 You’ll probably have much more chance of being killed on the job, as the FBI’s Hall

07:34 of Honor can show you.

07:35 You are dealing with criminals and that means sometimes seeing the aftermath of their destruction.

07:39 In one interview, a former agent said that was not the worst part, but the fact that

07:42 you spend much of your life away from your family.

07:45 You can at least tell them about what you do though.

07:47 The former agent told Business Insider, “There's only a very small amount of information that

07:51 an FBI agent would not be able to share with someone…

07:54 we can usually talk about what we are working on or have worked on in the past.”

07:58 As for wages, there are many scales when working for the FBI.

08:00 A new agent according to one salary website receives about $47,000, but a senior agent

08:06 might earn more than $130,000 a year.

08:09 A CIA website puts wages for special investigators anywhere from $74,000-$137,000.

08:13 Again, it really depends on what capacity you work for these agencies.

08:18 Be sure to check out and subscribe to our new Youtube channel called Fuzzy and Nutz!

08:21 You’ll learn something new, while trying to figure out why Nutz is always trying to

08:24 kill her good buddy Fuzzy!

08:25 The first episode is called, “What happens if you drink liquid nitrogen.”

08:28 Give it a watch and let us know what you think.

08:30 See ya next time!

00:00 What did the Subway employee who thought  filming himself wiping sandwiches on a

00:04 toilet seat was going to make him  famous, and the American teacher

00:07 who started a classroom Fight Club for her  Middle School students to settle disputes

00:12 have in common? Both were stupid enough to  post these videos online and lost their jobs

00:17 from it. And they are FAR from the only ones. In today’s episode of The Infographics Show,

00:22 we’re looking at the dumb youtube  videos that got people fired.

00:27 20. In 2018,

00:29 a young man walked into Starbucks in Philadelphia  and ordered an iced coffee and as per usual,

00:35 the employee asked him his name, which was Sam. The thing is, Sam had a stutter, so it came out

00:41 more like S-s-s-am. After having a  good laugh at this guy’s expense,

00:44 the barista wrote down his name with the extra  S’s. Just like every other interaction today,

00:50 someone filmed it all and uploaded it. Starbucks apologized and fired the barista,

00:55 and as an act of corporate kindness, the  company offered to give Sam a $5 gift voucher,

01:00 just 95 cents short of the price of a  cappuccino- way to go the extra mile, Starbucks.

01:05 We’ve got quite a few crimes lined up for you  today, but let’s start with this, one of the

01:09 stupidest things we’ve heard in quite some time. 19.

01:13 In 2016, two paramedics working  in Florida’s Okaloosa County were

01:17 found to have been in a “selfie war” with  each other. That sounds pretty harmless,

01:22 but not when they started put unconscious  people in their selfie photos and videos.

01:27 The paramedics, a 24-year-old woman, and a  33-year-old man, did all of this in the backs of

01:32 their ambulances. They’d switch on the camera and  act around with people who were sometimes injured,

01:38 and even dying. 41 patients starred in the  selfies, aged anywhere between 24 and 86,

01:45 which didn’t impress those people’s family  members when the truth finally came out.

01:49 Of course, they were both fired. Let’s lighten things up for this next one.

01:53 18. In 2009, five

01:55 YouTube videos might have put you off ordering  Domino’s pizza for life. The clips consisted

02:00 of a man doing things like sticking cheese up  his nose and wiping salami around his butt.

02:06 The man, along with his female colleague who  was the camera person and creative director,

02:10 went viral and ended up being watched by  millions of people. Then internet sleuths

02:16 got on the case and figured out the location of  the restaurant was in Conover, North Carolina.

02:21 As Domino’s scrambled to rescue  its, cough, impeccable reputation,

02:25 the two employees were fired. He got six months  in jail and she got a 45-day suspended sentence,

02:31 and 200 hours of community service. The man later said the videos were posted

02:35 without his consent, which didn’t help Domino’s at  all because people were now wondering what happens

02:41 to pizzas when someone doesn’t make a viral video. All in all, they deserved to be fired,

02:46 but we think these next victims of a viral  video were treated a little too harshly.

02:51 17. We found a few incidents of American

02:54 nurses making videos at work and posting them on  social media, but our favorite is the one from New

02:59 Orleans when seven nurses put on what we think  was a stunning dance performance to rapper NLE

03:05 Choppa’s hit song, “Slut me out.” YouTube wouldn’t  like it if we repeated the words in this song, so

03:11 let’s just say you would serenade Grandma with it. The dance routine included various acts, including

03:17 one nurse spreading her legs in a wheelchair and  another using hospital equipment to mimic her

03:22 giving oral sex. There was a lot of twerking and  what the media called “obscene gestures” although

03:28 uniforms remained on at all times and no patients  appeared throughout the entire performance.

03:33 We’ll feature more nurses later in the video,  but the next one will involve patients.

03:39 16. Imagine being fired for saving someone’s life!

03:43 That’s exactly what happened to lifeguard Tommy  Lopez who was videoed rescuing a drowning man.

03:48 Tommy was working at Hallandale Beach in Florida  in 2012 when he saw a swimmer in distress. He

03:54 quickly did his best Baywatch routine and ran  into the ocean, helping the drowning swimmer,

04:00 who was later taken away in an ambulance.  Tommy literally saved this guy’s life.

04:05 He was fired because the company he worked  for said he’d moved out of his section of

04:10 the beach. They eventually offered him his job  back, but he turned it down. On top of that,

04:15 they later gave this guy the key to the city! Now for one of a handful of incidents involving

04:20 a wayward teacher. 15.

04:23 In today’s classrooms, cell phones are  just as useful as pens and that means

04:27 a lot of teachers are losing their jobs,  sometimes fairly, and sometimes unfairly.

04:33 A female teacher was fired because her  Facebook page showed her holding a…severed

04:37 child’s head…Just kidding. She was holding  a bottle of beer, enough to get her fired.

04:42 Another US teacher was made unemployed  after saying on social media that

04:46 her 10th-grade students were “rude,  disengaged, lazy whiners.” Come on,

04:51 when aren’t 10th-grade students like that? And in 2024, a teacher in Detroit was fired

04:57 because she refused to take down videos  of her rapping. One of the parents at the

05:01 school didn’t think her raps were appropriate.  We’ve seen her videos and let’s just say they’re

05:06 not exactly in the same league as “Slut me out.” But sometimes the victims of a firing have kind of

05:12 asked for it, such as this next person. 14.

05:16 Have you ever received a package and inside  the thing you’ve bought is smashed to pieces?

05:22 Sure you have, and it might be because of  a delivery driver who’s having a bad day,

05:27 such as the FedEx guy in 2021 who was launching  parcels onto porches like they were javelins.

05:33 The owner of the house invested in a smart  doorbell and caught the driver in the act.

05:38 The house owner wrote next to the video he  posted online, “Every package I’ve received

05:43 since I’ve moved into my new home has been dented  or broken. I bought a camera… now I know why.”

05:49 The video got over 500,000 views and  the delivery guy has since been told

05:54 his parcel-throwing days are over. Maybe  he should try out for the Olympics instead.

06:00 13. There are a lot of videos out there

06:02 that show people driving public transport who  probably shouldn’t be driving public transport,

06:08 such as the New York bus driver in 2018 who  was videoed watching clips on YouTube as he

06:13 sped down the street, intermittently looking up to  check he wasn’t about to kill all his passengers.

06:19 When your passengers think it's safer  to ride in a New York subway car rather

06:23 than a bus, you know you're doing a bad job. Let’s now look at something quite disturbing.

06:29 12. In 2016, a nursing

06:31 assistant in Kenosha, Wisconsin, was fired after  it was revealed she’d been uploading very private

06:36 videos from the place where he worked. One of the videos featured a 93-year-old

06:40 Alzheimer’s patient in a state of undress.  Another showed the nurse helping an elderly

06:45 patient empty his bowels. The 21-year-old  assistant was later called “immoral” for

06:50 what the court commissioner said was “one of the  most disgusting cases I’ve heard in a long time.”

06:55 We found a lot of videos online of people doing  very bad things in nursing homes, but let’s now

07:01 return to something a little more humorous. 11.

07:04 It happened in a Subway outlet in 2021 and  involved what the media called a Subway

07:10 sandwich artist… Yep artist. That’s what  Subway calls a low-paid worker who throws

07:14 bits of vegetables and meat into a sloppy bun. Anyway, this artist filmed himself arranging

07:20 food on one of the restaurant’s toilet seats  while trashing his job and saying bad things

07:25 about Subway. He also walked over various food  items he’d placed on the floor. He was obviously

07:30 stressed by his art, but as far as we know,  he didn’t go as far as cutting off his ear.

07:35 It turned out this 21-year-old man had worked all  over the place and had posted videos to various

07:41 social media platforms, not all of them with him  doing nasty things to the food. When asked why

07:46 he did it, he channeled his inner creativity and  said he was struggling to find a purpose in life.

07:52 Well, at least he has internet fame  to fall back on…as does this next man.

07:57 10. The story is about a snowplow

08:00 driver in Massachusetts who calls himself “Dogg.”  He was fired in 2013 by the city of Lowell after

08:07 taking videos of himself driving down the street  in his plow. That doesn’t sound so bad. Well, Dogg

08:14 wasn’t just clearing the roads- he was burying  vehicles and blocking driveways with an avalanche

08:20 of snow. And he enjoyed every single moment. He tried to plead his innocence, saying he

08:25 was just doing his job. The residents of Lowell  weren’t impressed, and neither were city chiefs,

08:31 and Dogg was sacked. But that didn’t stop  Dogg uploading one more video- an apology.

08:38 Let’s move away from the USA for this next one. 9.

08:42 In 2013, a bunch of hardworking miners in  Australia lightened up their day by performing

08:47 an underground version of the Harlem Shake. We  think they did a pretty good job, but their bosses

08:52 at the mine in Western Australia weren’t impressed  and made 15 men unemployed in what might have been

08:59 the biggest mass firing in viral video history. It seems a bit cruel to fire men for merely

09:04 dancing. A spokesperson for the mine  explained why, telling the media,

09:08 “Underground mining has strict safety standards  as there are accidents and fatalities.”

09:13 C’mon, give the guys a break. They didn’t  even take off their safety helmets.

09:17 Maybe this next guy also  deserved a bit of a break.

09:20 8. In 2015, a former

09:22 Chief Financial Officer at a medical device  company in Arizona was on food stamps because

09:27 of a video he’d posted of himself back in 2012. Adam Smith filmed himself criticizing Chick-fil-A

09:33 at a drive-thru where he ordered a glass  of free water and subsequently exploded

09:38 into a tirade about how much he despised the  company, unleashing on the drive-thru server.

09:44 It wasn’t that food that Smith was angry  at, he was addressing accusations from

09:48 staff about homophobia that appeared in  the news. Sure, he shouldn’t have taken

09:52 it out on a low-paid worker, but it seems  he certainly paid back his debt to society.

09:57 Smith was unhireable. He went from earning  $200,000 a year and having over $1 million

10:03 in stock options to claiming social security  benefits. Every interview he went to someone

10:08 would realize, “Ah, that’s the Chick-Fil-A guy.” We imagine this next person will also find it

10:14 difficult to get another job. 7.

10:17 In 2024, a teacher in the Raytown School District  of Kansas lost her job just 12 hours after a video

10:23 showed her performing a WWE-style smackdown on one  of her students. She apparently hit the student,

10:29 got her in a chokehold and slammed her to  the floor. Another student said the battle

10:33 royale started after a bunch of girls  refused to leave the bathroom and the

10:37 victim hit the teacher’s phone out of her hands. The school later released a standard statement

10:42 saying MMA-style disciplining of students was  “not in alignment with our values and practice.”

10:47 Now let’s go way back in time  to the Olden Days of MySpace.

10:52 6. We’ve already seen

10:54 how you get sacked from McDonald’s but what  about Burger King? In 2008, Timothy Tackett,

10:59 also known as Mr. Unstable, had a long day at  work. There’s no better way to relax than a warm

11:05 bubble bath. The only problem was that Timmy  did it in one of the sinks in the restaurant.

11:11 Tackett pleaded his case, saying he scrubbed  the sink before getting in. But Burger King

11:15 weren’t happy - that kind of behavior belongs  at the Golden Arches - and Timothy was sacked,

11:20 along with the duty manager. As for this next one, well,

11:24 worse things have happened. 5.

11:26 Paris is known as the city of love but not in  Disney’s eyes. In 2022, a man was down on one knee

11:33 outside Sleeping Beauty’s castle at Disneyland  Paris and was about to propose to his girlfriend.

11:39 Everything was going to plan until a  Disney employee wearing Mickey Mouse

11:43 ears ran in between the couple, snatched the  ring, and ordered them to move away. This

11:48 was obviously your employee-of-the-year kind  of guy, but the whole thing was videoed and

11:52 soon the jobsworth was at the sharp end of that  thing we’ve come to love called public outrage.

11:59 The video of this romance wrecker went  viral and the heartbroken couple were

12:03 offered a free vacation- which they refused. Disney said the employee had been dealt with-

12:08 which sounds terrifying. We don’t know  if Mickey and the boys took care of him

12:12 or he was sacked, but either way his  mouse ears-wearing days were over.

12:18 4. Then there

12:19 was the mass firing of a bunch of lifeguards at  a city swimming pool in El Monte, California.

12:24 They filmed themselves doing the Gangnam  Style dance back when that kind of thing could

12:28 make you internet famous. Of course, anyone who  actually likes that song should never be allowed

12:33 to work in public again, and that’s exactly  what the pool bosses said, relieving these

12:38 men of their jobs. Well, they might not have  said it like we did, but the guys got fired.

12:44 In total, 14 of them lost their jobs. The pool  bosses described the hip-thrusting and gyrating

12:49 as inappropriate and disgusting. Hey, we don’t like the song,

12:53 but “disgusting” is taking things a bit far. But, after a public outcry, they were invited

12:58 back to work. They refused the offer, and now 2.4  million people have suffered from psychological

13:04 abuse after watching that video on YouTube. Ok, top three and the next one is one of the

13:09 funniest stories we have for you today. 3.

13:13 This entry takes place in a Walmart store in  Canada’s Alberta province in 2018. The star of the

13:18 story wasn’t fired, he was about to quit, but we  can guarantee his days with Walmart were numbered.

13:25 He decided to speak his mind through the intercom  to a store full of shoppers. The 17-year-old

13:30 began his rant with, “Attention all shoppers,  associates and management, I would like to say

13:35 to all of you today that nobody should work here.” That was a great opening, which he followed with,

13:41 “I’m sick of all the bogus writeups, and my job.” After calling out his assistant manager,

13:45 he left the store a hero and never looked back,  later posting the video on Facebook with the

13:51 title, “How I quit my job today.” Now for some more naughty nurses.

13:55 2. In 2017, a patient

13:58 was lying unconscious in an operating room at  the Clínica Santa Cruz Hospital in Colombia.

14:03 As you’d expect, the atmosphere is  one of profound seriousness…Er, no,

14:08 not at all. It’s like a carnival in there. One of  the nurses whips out her phone and we see five of

14:13 her colleagues dancing around the unconscious  naked body of a man who's been prepped for

14:17 an operation. Music plays, the nurses laugh and  twerk… the only thing that’s missing is balloons.

14:23 You’d think the hospital would be proud  to have such happy workers, but no,

14:28 they fired all the five women accepting they  were all “good workers” but “must accept the

14:32 consequences” for breaking surgery protocol. Right, what about this teacher who ran a Fight

14:38 Club? 1.

14:39 Call us old-fashioned, but we think the first  rule of Fight Club should be: don’t do it with

14:45 12-year olds. A female teacher at the Mesquite  Middle School in Texas obviously doesn’t agree.

14:50 In 2023, she was said to have “encouraged” her  students to settle disputes the old way. But it’s

14:57 not as brutal as it sounds- before each scrap,  she outlined what was acceptable and unacceptable.

15:03 After all, her students weren’t animals. As the boys and girls, some evidently better at

15:07 fighting than others, fought it out with the desks  pushed back, the teacher watched on, telling the

15:12 students there was a 30-second fight limit. The  media said some of the fights ended with students

15:17 having to clean the blood from their faces. You’d think this was a one-off, but another

15:22 teacher in a Florida middle school also ran a  Fight Club in her classes. This teacher also had

15:27 a 30-second limit, with the added rules of no hair  pulling, no screaming, no yelling, and no phones.

15:34 There were phones. That’s how she got caught. Now you need to watch this X-rated hit, “Most

15:39 Evil Kids in the History of Mankind.” Or, have  a look at “Kids Who Remember Their Past Lives.”

00:00 The following content is provided under a Creative Commons license. Your support will help MIT OpenCourseWare

00:06 continue to offer high-quality educational resources for free. To make a donation or view additional materials

00:13 from hundreds of MIT courses, visit MIT OpenCourseWare at ocw.mit.edu.

00:21 JAKE XIA: This is the second time we are having this class. We had it last year in a smaller version.

00:27 That was for six units of a credit, and we had it once a week. And mostly practitioners from the industry,

00:36 from Morgan Stanley, talking about examples how math is applied in modern finance.

00:48 And so we got some good response last year. So, with the support of the math department,

00:53 we decided to expand this class to be 12 units of credit

00:58 and have twice a week. So, we have every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon from 2:30 to 4:00, as you know, in this classroom.

01:05 So last year, Dr. Vasily Strela and I-- by the way,

01:13 I'm Jake Xia and that's Dr. Vasily, and we were the main instructors last year.

01:18 Now we doubled it up to four main instructors. That's Dr. Peter Kempthorne and Dr. Choongbum Lee.

01:26 The reason we doubled up the main instructors is we have newly added math lectures, mostly focusing

01:35 from linear algebra, probability to statistics, and some stochastic calculus to give you the foundation

01:42 to understand the math will be used in those examples in the lecture taught by the practitioners

01:52 from the industry. And the purpose of this course is really to give you a sampling menu to see how mathematics is applied

02:02 in modern finance and help you to decide if this is a field that you would be-- RECORDED VOICE: Thank you, for using WebEx.

02:08 Please visit our website at www.webex.com.

02:14 JAKE XIA: OK, you heard that. And so hopefully, this will give you enough information

02:21 to decide this is a field you would like to pursue in your future career. In fact, last year when we finished the class,

02:29 we had a few students coming to work in the industry. Some work at Morgan Stanley, some work at elsewhere.

02:35 So that's really the goal. And at the same time, obviously, you

02:43 will further solidify your math knowledge and learn new content.

02:51 And we put the prerequisite about the math part a bit later.

02:56 So I will use today's first lecture's time to give you an introduction, really,

03:02 to prepare you some basic background knowledge about the financial markets.

03:08 Some terminologies will be used, which you may not have heard before.

03:13 So before I get into the introduction, I always like to know who are actually in the classroom,

03:19 so let me ask you a few questions. You just need to raise your hands so I know roughly what kind of background and where you are.

03:28 So how many undergraduate students are here?

03:33 So I would say 80% percent.

03:38 How many graduate students are here, just to verify? Yep, that's about right, 20%.

03:44 And how many students are in finance and business major?

03:51 Just one. And how many of you are a math major?

03:56 Most of you. How many of you are engineering majors?

04:02 A few. How many of you actually are from other universities?

04:08 Great, because last year we had quite a few, so I want to specifically tell you that you're very welcome to attend the classes here.

04:17 So it's open door. And last year I remember we had a couple of students

04:22 from Harvard. That's where I actually work right now.

04:29 I forgot to mention that, but I'm affiliated with both the math department and the Sloan school

04:35 here. So anyway, thanks for that. We will be doing a bit more polling along the way,

04:41 mainly to get feedback of how you feel about the class. Last year we had it online, so if you

04:48 feel the class is going too fast, or the math part is going too slow, or the finance part is a bit confusing,

04:55 the easiest way is really just to send us emails, which you will find from the class website.

05:02 So anyway, today-- VASILY STRELA: And all of us got MIT emails. JAKE XIA: Yes. We all have MIT emails, which are listed on the website.

05:10 VASILY STRELA: [INAUDIBLE]. JAKE XIA: And obviously, we have offices here.

05:17 You can easily stop by Peter and Choongbum's offices. And Vasily and I probably will be less often on campus,

05:26 but we'll be here quite often and definitely love to be more. So anyway, I will start today's lecture with a story,

05:35 and a quiz at the end. Don't worry, it's not a real quiz. Just going to ask you some questions

05:40 you can raise your hand and give your answer. But let me start with my story.

05:46 This is actually my personal story. I want to tell you why I tell the story later.

05:52 But the story actually was in the mid '90s. I just left Salomon Brothers -- that was my first financial

06:01 industry job -- to go to Morgan Stanley in New York to join

06:06 the options trading desk. So the first day, I sat down, I opened the trading book,

06:15 I found something was missing. So, I turned around, I asked my desk quant.

06:22 I said, where is the vega report? So, let me show you.

06:27 So that's the story.

06:33 So I'm obviously not going to tell you the story of Pi

06:39 or "Life of Pi." That's not a financial story. The rest of the story, alpha, beta, delta, gamma,

06:45 theta, which you will learn from Peter and Choongbum and Vasily's classes.

06:50 So I'm going to talk about vega. So by the way, before I tell you the story, what's unique about vega on this list?

06:57 AUDIENCE: It's not a Greek letter. JAKE XIA: It's not a Greek letter. That's right. So I turned around and asked my desk quant, I said,

07:04 where's the vega report? But how many of you actually know what a vega is?

07:09 OK, lot of people know. So anyway, I'm not going to-- just for the people who haven't heard about it before, it's

07:16 a measurement about a book or portfolio or position's sensitivity to volatility.

07:22 So, what is volatility? Which again, you will learn more in rigorous terms

07:29 how it's defined in mathematics. But the meaning of it is really a measurement or indication

07:36 of how volatile, or what's the standard deviation of a price can change over time.

07:43 That's all you need to know right now. I'm not going to ask you questions later. So my desk quant look at me, said--

07:52 this is supposed to be options trading desk, so he look at me puzzled.

07:58 So instead of answering my question, he handed over me a training manual for new employees and new analysts.

08:06 So I opened the training manual and looked it through. I actually found my answer.

08:12 So actually, at Morgan Stanley this is not called vega, it's called kappa.

08:17 So now, I remember to call it kappa. Kappa is actually a Greek letter. So further, I look on the same page

08:25 there was actually a footnote, which I copied down. So the footnote about why it's called kappa at Morgan Stanley.

08:39 Kappa is also called vega by some uneducated traders at the Salomon Brothers.

08:45 That's where I came from. I just joined. They have mistaken vega as a Greek letter

08:50 after gambling at Vegas. So anyway, so that was my first day.

08:58 So obviously, I learned how to call kappa very quickly, because I came from Salomon Brothers.

09:05 And I called it kappa in the last 17 years, but you will hear people calling it vega.

09:12 Obviously, I have probably more people calling it the vega. But anyway, so that's my first day at Morgan Stanley.

09:19 But why did I tell you the story? What point I try to make?

09:24 So this story is actually-- when you think about it, mathematical or quantitative finance is a rather new field.

09:33 A lot of these terms were newly introduced. And the pricing model of options, as you know,

09:42 was introduced in the Black-Scholes in the '70s, or some of the ground work may be done a bit earlier.

09:49 But it's not like finance was a quantitative profession

09:55 to start with. So what we witness in the last 30 years was really a transformation of the trading profession coming

10:04 from mostly under-educated traders. Some of them typically joined the firms in the mail room

10:13 and became trader later on. That's typical career path. And to nowadays, if you walk on the trading floor,

10:20 you talk to the traders, most of them have advanced degrees and quite a few of them have very high training

10:29 in mathematics and computer science. So what has changed over the last 20 or 30 years?

10:36 I myself, personally, was probably one of the data point experiencing this change.

10:44 And I certainly didn't expect I would be doing this when I was at MIT, but I

10:51 did that in the last 20 years. So the point I'm trying to tell you

10:59 is, before you dive into any details of mathematics

11:04 or any concept in finance in this class, just bear in mind,

11:11 this is a field developed in the last mostly 30 years, or even

11:16 shorter. And what you really need to ask questions is-- it's not really is it right or wrong in mathematics,

11:26 is it right or wrong in physics? So, how the concepts are established

11:31 and defined and verified. Because this is a field-- the transformation

11:37 about the participants, products, models, methodology,

11:42 everything are changing very rapidly. Even nowadays, they're still changing. So with that, I will give you some background

11:51 on how the financial markets actually started,

11:57 and that's really the history part of this industry.

12:03 So, when we talk about markets, we know in early days people need to exchange goods.

12:10 You have something I don't have, I have something you don't have, so there's exchanges.
